Myosin heads bind to actin, pivot and release, pulling the thin filament. Calcium exposes the binding sites on actin so myosin can bind; ATP is used to break the cross-bridge, re-cock the myosin head and provide energy for the cycle. Relaxation occurs when calcium is removed and binding sites are covered again. (5 marks)
  7. Describe the roles of insulin and glucagon in the control of blood glucose concentration, and explain how they illustrate homeostasis. Answer: Insulin is secreted when blood glucose rises and lowers blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake by cells and glycogenesis and by other effects; glucagon is secreted when blood glucose falls and raises blood glucose by promoting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. They work in opposition to keep blood glucose within limits. This illustrates homeostasis and negative feedback because each hormone opposes the deviation of blood glucose from the set point. (5 marks)
  8. Define homeostasis and explain the principle of negative feedback, using one example. Answer: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment within limits. Negative feedback is the control principle in which a change from the set point is detected and the response reduces the change, returning the variable toward normal. Example: in temperature control, if body temperature rises, sweating and vasodilation increase heat loss, returning temperature toward the set point; if it falls, shivering and vasoconstriction reduce heat loss or increase heat production. (5 marks)
  9. Describe the roles of FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone in the human female, and the role of testosterone in the male. Answer: FSH and LH are pituitary hormones involved in controlling the reproductive system and sex hormone release; in females, oestrogen and progesterone are involved in the female reproductive cycle, including control of the cycle and maintenance of pregnancy; in males, FSH and LH are involved in spermatogenesis and testosterone is involved in male development and spermatogenesis. (5 marks)
  10. Describe ADH and explain its role in homeostasis. Answer: ADH, anti-diuretic hormone, is released when the body needs to conserve water; it acts on the kidneys to increase water reabsorption, reducing water loss in urine and helping maintain water balance. This is a homeostatic function because it keeps the internal water balance within limits. (4 marks)
  11. Describe plant coordination with hormones and explain what is meant by a tropic response. Answer: Plants coordinate responses with hormones such as auxins, which control growth. A tropic response is a directional growth response to a stimulus; phototropism is growth toward light, and gravitropism is growth in relation to gravity. Auxins redistribute in the plant and cause differential growth, so the organ bends. (5 marks)
  12. Explain the role of restriction enzymes and sticky ends in gene technology. Answer: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific recognition sequences. Some cuts produce sticky ends, short single-stranded overhangs. If two pieces of DNA are cut with the same restriction enzyme, their sticky ends are complementary and can base-pair, allowing them to be joined by DNA ligase and made into a recombinant molecule. (4 marks)
  13. Describe the polymerase chain reaction and explain why it is useful. Answer: PCR amplifies a specific DNA sequence in vitro through repeated cycles in which the DNA is heated to separate the strands, primers anneal at cooler temperatures, and a heat-stable polymerase extends the primers to make new copies, so the target sequence doubles each cycle. It is useful because it allows a small DNA sample to be amplified enough to study or use in diagnosis or forensics. (5 marks)
  14. Describe gel electrophoresis and explain how a gene probe can be used with it. Answer: Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size in an electric field; DNA moves toward the positive electrode, and smaller fragments move faster, giving a banding pattern. A gene probe is a labelled single-stranded DNA or RNA sequence complementary to a target sequence; it hybridises to the target fragment so the specific band can be detected. Electrophoresis separates by size; the probe identifies a specific sequence by base-pairing. (5 marks)
  15. Describe the use of a vector and a selectable marker in genetic modification, and explain insertional inactivation. Answer: A vector such as a plasmid carries foreign DNA into a host cell; the DNA is inserted into the vector, the vector is introduced into the host by transformation, and a selectable marker such as an antibiotic resistance gene lets only transformed cells survive. If the foreign DNA is inserted into the marker gene, the marker may be inactivated, so recombinant cells can be distinguished from non-recombinant ones by their phenotype. (5 marks)
  16. Give the main applications of genetically modified organisms and one concern about them. Answer: Applications include producing human proteins in microorganisms, improving crops for pest resistance, herbicide tolerance or nutrition, and producing organisms for research or medicine. A concern could be gene flow to wild relatives, effects on non-target organisms, development of resistance, or ethical issues such as ownership of genes, labelling and consumer choice, and the distribution of benefits and risks. The concern depends on the specific use. (5 marks)
  17. Describe gene therapy and distinguish somatic from germ-line gene therapy, including one ethical issue with germ-line therapy. Answer: Gene therapy uses gene technology to treat a condition by introducing, removing or altering genetic material in cells. Somatic gene therapy affects body cells and is not inherited; germ-line gene therapy would alter heritable DNA and would be passed to offspring. A germ-line ethical issue is that changes to the germ line are heritable, so they affect future generations, raising questions about consent, unforeseen consequences and how far it is right to alter the inheritable genome. (5 marks)
  18. Explain how gene technology is useful both as a research tool and as a practical technology. Answer: As a research tool, gene technology lets us copy genes, probe genomes, sequence DNA, and modify genes to study gene function and disease. As a practical technology, it lets us produce therapeutic proteins, improve crops, and develop diagnostics and therapies. The same techniques are used for both understanding biology and for applications. (5 marks)
  19. Describe the main stages in producing a genetically modified bacterium that makes a human protein. Answer: The human gene is cut out using a restriction enzyme, or otherwise obtained; a plasmid vector is cut with the same enzyme so the ends match; the gene is inserted into the plasmid and the recombinant plasmid is sealed with DNA ligase; the plasmid is introduced into bacterial cells by transformation; transformed cells are selected using a marker; and the bacteria are grown to produce the human protein, which is then harvested. (5 marks)

Revise this topic by matching each numbered specification point to one mechanism, one example and one reason. Practise the receptor examples, the synapse and neuromuscular junction with the calcium step, the sliding filament contraction with ATP and calcium, the insulin-glucagon system with homeostasis, and the gene technology techniques matched to their purposes. Check that you can say where each thing happens and why, not just what it is. Then move on to the next topic and the related practicals, because the practicals are the way the specification ties the ideas to hands-on work.

title: Exam technique: Algebra — Equations
content:
### What earns the marks
To earn full marks on this topic, students need to demonstrate the ability to calculate, show that, explain, describe, justify, and state their answers clearly. For 2.5 Equations, students should be able to calculate solutions to linear and quadratic equations, show that their solutions are correct, and explain their methods. When solving simultaneous equations, students should be able to justify their choice of method and state their answers clearly. Working should be shown for all calculations, especially when using the quadratic formula or completing the square.
### Traps
Common mistakes include forgetting to multiply through by the LCD when working with fractions, adding instead of subtracting when eliminating variables in simultaneous equations, and not verifying answers by substituting them back into the original equation. Another trap is not defining the unknown clearly in word problems, leading to incorrect equations.
### Memory hooks
To make this topic easier to remember, students can use the mnemonic 'LCD' to recall the steps for solving linear equations with fractions. They can also use the pattern of 'add, subtract, multiply, divide' to remember the order of operations when solving simultaneous equations. A shortcut for completing the square is to remember that the constant term is always -(b/2)^2 + c. Students can also sanity-check their answers by graphing the related functions or using a calculator to verify their solutions.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 10-15% of the total exam time. Students should budget around 20-30 minutes to answer questions on this topic, depending on the difficulty and complexity of the questions. It is essential to read the questions carefully and allocate time accordingly to ensure that all parts of the question are answered.

title: Functions — Study Notes
content:
Functions

A function maps each input in the domain to exactly one output in the range.

Composite Functions

fg(x) means f(g(x)) — apply g first, then f. Order matters.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 1, g(x) = x². Then fg(x) = 2x² + 1 but gf(x) = (2x + 1)².

Inverse Functions

f⁻¹ reverses f: f⁻¹f(x) = x. To find it, swap x and y in y = f(x) and rearrange.

Example: f(x) = 3x − 2 gives f⁻¹(x) = (x + 2)/3.

An inverse exists only if f is one-one. If not, restrict the domain (e.g. f(x) = x² for x ≥ 0 has f⁻¹(x) = √x). Graphically, y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x, and the range of f becomes the domain of f⁻¹.

Transformations

NotationEffect on y = f(x)
f(x) + atranslation up by a
f(x + a)translation left by a
a f(x)vertical stretch, factor a
f(ax)horizontal stretch, factor 1/a
−f(x)reflection in the x-axis
f(−x)reflection in the y-axis

Exam tips: state the domain of any inverse; when combining transformations, translations inside the bracket act in the opposite direction to the sign.

title: Astronomy and Cosmology — Study Notes
content:
Astronomy and Cosmology

Luminosity and Intensity

Luminosity L is total power radiated (W). Intensity at distance d: I = L/(4πd²) — the key to distances.

Standard candles (Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) have known L, so measuring I gives d.

Example: the Sun: I = 1370 W m⁻² at d = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m gives L ≈ 3.9 × 10²⁶ W.

Stellar radii (25.2)

A star radiates as a black body of surface temperature T, so L = 4πR²σT⁴. Rearranged, R = √(L / 4πσT⁴). Luminosity therefore depends on both radius and temperature.

Example: with L = 3.9 × 10²⁶ W and T = 5800 K, R = √(3.9 × 10²⁶ / (4π × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 5800⁴)) ≈ 7.0 × 10⁸ m.

Doubling the temperature at fixed radius multiplies L by 2⁴ = 16. A cool red giant can be far more luminous than the Sun because its radius is very large.

Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann

  • Wien: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K — hotter stars are bluer
  • Stefan: L = σAT⁴, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸

Hubble's Law

Galaxies recede with v = Hd, H₀ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Redshift z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c for small z.

Example: a galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at v = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 100 × 3.09 × 10²² ≈ 6800 km s⁻¹.

The Big Bang

Evidence: Hubble expansion, cosmic microwave background (2.7 K), hydrogen/helium abundance. Age estimate: t ≈ 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years. The fate question: critical density, Ω.

Exam tips: convert Mpc to metres (×3.09 × 10²²) before Hubble arithmetic; distinguish redshift of light from distance ladder methods.

Standard candles and the cosmic distance ladder

A standard candle is an object whose luminosity is known, such as a Type Ia supernova or a Cepheid variable star. Comparing its known luminosity with its observed brightness gives its distance, using the inverse-square law. Stellar radii can be found in the same way: the luminosity L = 4πR2σT4 links radius, surface temperature and output power.

Exam tip: state which assumption you are making, such as that the star radiates as a black body, before you calculate the radius.

Worked example: distance from parallax

A star has a parallax angle of 0.25 arcseconds when observed from opposite sides of the Earth's orbit. The distance in parsecs is d = 1/p = 1/0.25 = 4.0 pc. One parsec is about 3.26 light-years, so the star is roughly 13 light-years away. Parallax is the most direct distance method, and it works only for nearby stars.

Inverse-square law for brightness

The apparent brightness of a star falls as the inverse square of its distance. A star that is four times as far away appears 4² = 16 times fainter, for the same luminosity. This is why luminosity, which is intrinsic, must be distinguished from apparent brightness, which depends on distance.

Hubble's law and the expanding universe

  • Hubble's law states that v = H₀d, where v is the recession speed and d is the distance.
  • With H₀ ≈ 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, a galaxy 100 Mpc away recedes at about 7000 km s⁻¹.
  • Redshift shows that most galaxies are moving away from us, which is evidence that the universe is expanding.

Exam point: the Big Bang model gives an age for the universe of about 13.8 billion years, consistent with the cosmic microwave background, which is the faint, nearly uniform radiation left from the early universe.

title:
Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI12 Unit 1, Topic 2 Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression. It covers membrane structure and properties, osmosis and the different kinds of membrane transport, the structure of proteins and how they are built from amino acids, the structure of DNA and RNA and how DNA replicates, the genetic code and how genes work, transcription and translation, mutations and their effects, patterns of inheritance including sex linkage, cystic fibrosis as an example of a gene mutation in humans, and genetic screening and its ethical and social issues. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Cell membranes and the fluid mosaic model

The cell surface membrane (plasma membrane) is a phospholipid bilayer; each phospholipid has a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails, and the heads face out and in while the tails face each other, making a barrier to charged and water-soluble substances. The fluid mosaic model is the accepted interpretation: the membrane is fluid — the phospholipids and proteins can move laterally in the layer — and mosaic because it contains a variety of proteins embedded in or attached to the bilayer, including channel proteins and carrier proteins for transport, receptor proteins for signalling, and proteins for cell recognition. The model is an interpretation of data — it was built from evidence such as electron micrographs and the ability of membranes to fuse and to self-seal — and it explains the structure and properties of cell membranes and how they control what enters and leaves the cell. Cholesterol in the membrane reduces fluidity at high temperatures and prevents the membrane from becoming too rigid at low temperatures.

2. Core Practical 3 — investigating membrane properties

Investigate membrane properties including the effect of alcohol and of temperature on membrane permeability. A typical method uses beetroot cylinders, which contain the red pigment betalain in their vacuoles; as the membrane is damaged, pigment leaks out and the colour of the surrounding solution deepens. Cut cylinders to the same length, wash off surface pigment in distilled water, then place them in water at a range of temperatures or in different concentrations of alcohol for a fixed time, remove the tissue and measure the concentration of pigment in the solution with a colorimeter. As temperature rises or alcohol concentration rises, the membrane proteins denature and the lipid bilayer is disrupted, so permeability increases and more pigment leaks out; a control at room temperature or in distilled water shows the baseline. Record the colorimeter reading for each tube, plot a graph of permeability against temperature or against alcohol concentration, and explain the trend in terms of the effect on membrane proteins and lipids.

3. Osmosis and how water moves across membranes

Osmosis is the net movement of free water molecules through a partially permeable membrane, down a water potential gradient — from higher water potential to lower water potential. Water potential is the tendency of water to move; adding a solute lowers it, so a concentrated solution has a more negative water potential than a dilute one, and pure water has the highest (zero) water potential. If a cell is placed in a solution of higher water potential than its contents, water enters by osmosis and the cell swells; if it is an animal cell it may burst (haemolysis); if it is a plant cell the cell wall prevents bursting and the cell becomes turgid, which supports the plant. In a solution of lower water potential, water leaves and the cell shrinks — animal cells crenate and plant cells become plasmolysed, with the membrane pulling away from the wall. A recommended additional practical is to investigate tissue water potentials using plant tissue (for example potato or onion epidermis) and graded concentrations of a solute: place tissue in solutions of different molarity, note the change in length or mass, and find the concentration at which there is no change — that concentration has the same water potential as the tissue.

4. Passive transport, active transport, endocytosis and exocytosis

Passive transport needs no energy input because substances move down their concentration gradient. Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration; small, non-polar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse directly through the phospholipid bilayer, while ions and large polar molecules cannot. Facilitated diffusion is the movement of specific particles down their concentration gradient through channel proteins or carrier proteins — channel proteins form water-filled pores for ions, and carrier proteins change shape to carry molecules across. Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient (from low to high concentration) and needs energy directly from ATP; carrier proteins use ATP to pump substances across, as in the sodium–potassium pump. Endocytosis is the bulk movement of material into the cell inside a vesicle formed from the plasma membrane; phagocytosis takes in solid material and pinocytosis takes in fluid. Exocytosis is the reverse — material is moved out of the cell in a vesicle that fuses with the plasma membrane, as in the secretion of proteins and neurotransmitters. Carrier and channel proteins are involved in facilitated diffusion and active transport; the key difference is that active transport needs ATP and moves substances against their gradient.

5. Protein structure: from amino acid to three-dimensional shape

Amino acids are the monomers of proteins; the basic structure of an amino acid is an amino group, a carboxyl group and a variable R group all attached to a central carbon, with a hydrogen on the remaining bond. There are around 20 amino acids found in proteins, differing only in their R group, and the sequence of amino acids in a protein is its primary structure. Amino acids join by condensation reactions to form peptide bonds, making dipeptides and then polypeptides; a polypeptide chain is a protein's primary structure and it determines everything about the protein. The secondary structure is the local folding of the chain into alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between the peptide bonds. The tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of the whole polypeptide, held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions; it gives the protein its specific shape and therefore its function. Globular proteins are roughly spherical and usually soluble and active — haemoglobin is the classic example, with four polypeptide chains and a haem group each carrying one oxygen molecule, and it shows quaternary structure (several polypeptides together) plus the importance of the three-dimensional shape for its oxygen-carrying function. Fibrous proteins are long, insoluble and structural — collagen is the example, made of three polypeptide chains wound into a rope-like triple helix, giving strength for tendons, ligaments and skin. The shape of a protein determines its function, so a change to the primary structure can alter the folding and disable the protein.

6. DNA structure and replication

A DNA molecule is made of two nucleotide strands twisted into a double helix. Each nucleotide is made of a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group and a base — either adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) or thymine (T). The two strands run antiparallel and are linked by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases — A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds) and C pairs with G (three hydrogen bonds). RNA is similar but has ribose instead of deoxyribose, uracil instead of thymine, and is usually single-stranded. The two strands are complementary, so knowing one strand tells you the other, and the two strands separate at replication. DNA replication is semi-conservative: the double helix unzips, each strand acts as a template, and free nucleotides pair with their complementary bases; DNA polymerase joins the nucleotides into a new strand. The result is two identical DNA molecules, each with one old strand and one new strand. Meselson and Stahl's experiment supported this: they grew bacteria in a medium with a heavy isotope of nitrogen (15N), then moved them to a 14N medium and examined the DNA by centrifugation; the first generation was a single hybrid band (not one heavy and one light, which would be conservative replication), and later generations showed a mixture of hybrid and light bands — exactly what semi-conservative replication predicts and ruling out the conservative and dispersive alternatives.

7. The genetic code and how it works

The genetic code is the set of rules translating the base sequence of mRNA into the amino acid sequence of a protein. It is a triplet code — three bases (a base triplet on DNA, a codon on mRNA) code for one amino acid; it is non-overlapping — each base is read once in order; and it is degenerate — more than one codon can code for the same amino acid, which is why many mutations change a base but not the amino acid. Part of the code is a stop codon that signals the end of translation; there is no amino acid for it. A gene is a sequence of bases on a DNA molecule that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. In transcription, the gene is copied into a complementary mRNA molecule by the enzyme RNA polymerase, using the DNA template (antisense) strand; the mRNA is complementary to the template strand and the same as the coding (sense) strand except with uracil in place of thymine. mRNA leaves the nucleus and attaches to ribosomes in the cytoplasm; transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules carry amino acids to the ribosome, each with a three-base anticodon that pairs with the mRNA codon, so the ribosome joins the amino acids into a polypeptide chain in the order of the codons until a stop codon is reached.

8. Mutations: the changes and their effects

A mutation is a change in the DNA base sequence. A substitution replaces one base with another — it may do nothing, change one amino acid, or, rarely, create a stop codon that shortens the protein. An insertion adds one or more bases and a deletion removes one or more; because the code is read in triplets, an insertion or deletion not in a multiple of three causes a frameshift, changing every amino acid after the mutation and usually destroying the protein's function. Mutations are the only source of new alleles, and most have no observable effect — they may be in non-coding DNA, or a degenerate codon and amino acid may stay the same, or the changed protein still folds and works. Some mutations give rise to cancer (if they affect control of the cell cycle) or to genetic disorders. Ionising radiation such as X-rays and ultraviolet light, and some chemicals such as those in tobacco smoke, can increase the rate of mutation by damaging DNA.

9. Patterns of inheritance: monohybrid crosses, pedigree diagrams and sex linkage

A gene can have different alleles; the genotype is the alleles an organism has, the phenotype is the observable feature. Dominant alleles show in the phenotype even when heterozygous; recessive alleles only show when homozygous. A monohybrid cross is the inheritance of one gene with two alleles; the typical ratios are a 3:1 phenotype ratio in the F2 of a monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes, but only if the alleles are completely dominant and the gene is autosomal. Sex linkage is the inheritance of a gene on the X chromosome — because males have only one X, a recessive allele on it shows in their phenotype even though they are effectively hemizygous; red-green colour blindness and haemophilia are human X-linked conditions that are more common in males. Pedigree diagrams record which family members show a trait and are used to work out whether a trait is dominant or recessive and whether it is autosomal or sex-linked. Codominance is when both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote, as in the ABO blood group system where IA and IB are codominant and i is recessive, giving the four blood groups A, B, AB and O.

10. Cystic fibrosis: a mutation that affects three systems

Cystic fibrosis is caused by a mutation in a gene that codes for a chloride ion channel protein; in the most common form a deletion of three bases removes a single amino acid from the protein, so the channel does not work properly. As a result, chloride ions and water cannot move properly across cell membranes, and the mucus and other secretions become abnormally thick. In the gaseous exchange system the thick mucus blocks the airways and makes it hard to breathe and to clear infections; in the digestive system the pancreatic duct is blocked so digestive enzymes from the pancreas cannot reach the gut, so food is not digested and absorbed properly, and the person may be malnourished; in the reproductive system the vas deferens is often absent or blocked in males, causing infertility. Treatments include physiotherapy and antibiotics for the lungs, and enzyme supplements with meals for digestion, and newer treatments aim to correct the underlying defect.

11. Genetic screening: what it can do and the issues it raises

Genetic screening can identify carriers of recessive alleles (people who have one normal allele and one faulty allele and are unaffected but could pass the allele on), and prenatal testing can check a fetus: amniocentesis takes a sample of amniotic fluid at around 15–17 weeks, and chorionic villus sampling takes a sample of placental tissue at 8–12 weeks. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis is used with IVF to test embryos before implantation and select unaffected ones. Each raises ethical and social questions — the safety and reliability of the test, the risks of miscarriage with invasive prenatal testing, the right to know or not to know, who decides which conditions to test for, the possible choice to terminate a pregnancy, anxiety and guilt, and the risk that screening could be used to select non-medical traits. Students should be able to identify and discuss these from religious, moral and social viewpoints and to evaluate the implications of prenatal genetic screening.

12. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working through each section and checking that you can draw a cell membrane from the fluid mosaic model and label the phospholipid bilayer, the proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins; state the difference between diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport, and give an example of each; outline the steps of DNA extraction (a simple practical with strawberries or onions is useful to remember); and carry out a genetic cross with a Punnett square and interpret the ratios. Revise by drawing protein structure from amino acid to tertiary, then drawing the DNA double helix and explaining semi-conservative replication and the Meselson–Stahl evidence. After this topic, revise Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development, because the same DNA and protein-synthesis processes control cell differentiation and the cell cycle.

Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration; small, non-polar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse directly through the phospholipid bilayer, while ions and large polar molecules cannot. Facilitated diffusion is the movement of specific particles down their concentration gradient through channel proteins or carrier proteins — channel proteins form water-filled pores for ions, and carrier proteins change shape to carry molecules across. Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient (from low to high concentration) and needs energy directly from ATP; carrier proteins use ATP to pump substances across, as in the sodium–potassium pump. Endocytosis is the bulk movement of material into the cell inside a vesicle formed from the plasma membrane; phagocytosis takes in solid material and pinocytosis takes in fluid. Exocytosis is the reverse — material is moved out of the cell in a vesicle that fuses with the plasma membrane, as in the secretion of proteins and neurotransmitters. Carrier and channel proteins are involved in facilitated diffusion and active transport; the key difference is that active transport needs ATP and moves substances against their gradient.

5. Protein structure: from amino acid to three-dimensional shape

Amino acids are the monomers of proteins; the basic structure of an amino acid is an amino group, a carboxyl group and a variable R group all attached to a central carbon, with a hydrogen on the remaining bond. There are around 20 amino acids found in proteins, differing only in their R group, and the sequence of amino acids in a protein is its primary structure. Amino acids join by condensation reactions to form peptide bonds, making dipeptides and then polypeptides; a polypeptide chain is a protein''s primary structure and it determines everything about the protein. The secondary structure is the local folding of the chain into alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between the peptide bonds. The tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of the whole polypeptide, held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions; it gives the protein its specific shape and therefore its function. Globular proteins are roughly spherical and usually soluble and active — haemoglobin is the classic example, with four polypeptide chains and a haem group each carrying one oxygen molecule, and it shows quaternary structure (several polypeptides together) plus the importance of the three-dimensional shape for its oxygen-carrying function. Fibrous proteins are long, insoluble and structural — collagen is the example, made of three polypeptide chains wound into a rope-like triple helix, giving strength for tendons, ligaments and skin. The shape of a protein determines its function, so a change to the primary structure can alter the folding and disable the protein.

6. DNA structure and replication

A DNA molecule is made of two nucleotide strands twisted into a double helix. Each nucleotide is made of a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group and a base — either adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) or thymine (T). The two strands run antiparallel and are linked by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases — A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds) and C pairs with G (three hydrogen bonds). RNA is similar but has ribose instead of deoxyribose, uracil instead of thymine, and is usually single-stranded. The two strands are complementary, so knowing one strand tells you the other, and the two strands separate at replication. DNA replication is semi-conservative: the double helix unzips, each strand acts as a template, and free nucleotides pair with their complementary bases; DNA polymerase joins the nucleotides into a new strand. The result is two identical DNA molecules, each with one old strand and one new strand. Meselson and Stahl''s experiment supported this: they grew bacteria in a medium with a heavy isotope of nitrogen (15N), then moved them to a 14N medium and examined the DNA by centrifugation; the first generation was a single hybrid band (not one heavy and one light, which would be conservative replication), and later generations showed a mixture of hybrid and light bands — exactly what semi-conservative replication predicts and ruling out the conservative and dispersive alternatives.

7. The genetic code and how it works

The genetic code is the set of rules translating the base sequence of mRNA into the amino acid sequence of a protein. It is a triplet code — three bases (a base triplet on DNA, a codon on mRNA) code for one amino acid; it is non-overlapping — each base is read once in order; and it is degenerate — more than one codon can code for the same amino acid, which is why many mutations change a base but not the amino acid. Part of the code is a stop codon that signals the end of translation; there is no amino acid for it. A gene is a sequence of bases on a DNA molecule that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. In transcription, the gene is copied into a complementary mRNA molecule by the enzyme RNA polymerase, using the DNA template (antisense) strand; the mRNA is complementary to the template strand and the same as the coding (sense) strand except with uracil in place of thymine. mRNA leaves the nucleus and attaches to ribosomes in the cytoplasm; transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules carry amino acids to the ribosome, each with a three-base anticodon that pairs with the mRNA codon, so the ribosome joins the amino acids into a polypeptide chain in the order of the codons until a stop codon is reached.

8. Mutations: the changes and their effects

A mutation is a change in the DNA base sequence. A substitution replaces one base with another — it may do nothing, change one amino acid, or, rarely, create a stop codon that shortens the protein. An insertion adds one or more bases and a deletion removes one or more; because the code is read in triplets, an insertion or deletion not in a multiple of three causes a frameshift, changing every amino acid after the mutation and usually destroying the protein''s function. Mutations are the only source of new alleles, and most have no observable effect — they may be in non-coding DNA, or a degenerate codon and amino acid may stay the same, or the changed protein still folds and works. Some mutations give rise to cancer (if they affect control of the cell cycle) or to genetic disorders. Ionising radiation such as X-rays and ultraviolet light, and some chemicals such as those in tobacco smoke, can increase the rate of mutation by damaging DNA.

9. Patterns of inheritance: monohybrid crosses, pedigree diagrams and sex linkage

A gene can have different alleles; the genotype is the alleles an organism has, the phenotype is the observable feature. Dominant alleles show in the phenotype even when heterozygous; recessive alleles only show when homozygous. A monohybrid cross is the inheritance of one gene with two alleles; the typical ratios are a 3:1 phenotype ratio in the F2 of a monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes, but only if the alleles are completely dominant and the gene is autosomal. Sex linkage is the inheritance of a gene on the X chromosome — because males have only one X, a recessive allele on it shows in their phenotype even though they are effectively hemizygous; red-green colour blindness and haemophilia are human X-linked conditions that are more common in males. Pedigree diagrams record which family members show a trait and are used to work out whether a trait is dominant or recessive and whether it is autosomal or sex-linked. Codominance is when both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote, as in the ABO blood group system where IA and IB are codominant and i is recessive, giving the four blood groups A, B, AB and O.

10. Cystic fibrosis: a mutation that affects three systems

Cystic fibrosis is caused by a mutation in a gene that codes for a chloride ion channel protein; in the most common form a deletion of three bases removes a single amino acid from the protein, so the channel does not work properly. As a result, chloride ions and water cannot move properly across cell membranes, and the mucus and other secretions become abnormally thick. In the gaseous exchange system the thick mucus blocks the airways and makes it hard to breathe and to clear infections; in the digestive system the pancreatic duct is blocked so digestive enzymes from the pancreas cannot reach the gut, so food is not digested and absorbed properly, and the person may be malnourished; in the reproductive system the vas deferens is often absent or blocked in males, causing infertility. Treatments include physiotherapy and antibiotics for the lungs, and enzyme supplements with meals for digestion, and newer treatments aim to correct the underlying defect.

11. Genetic screening: what it can do and the issues it raises

Genetic screening can identify carriers of recessive alleles (people who have one normal allele and one faulty allele and are unaffected but could pass the allele on), and prenatal testing can check a fetus: amniocentesis takes a sample of amniotic fluid at around 15–17 weeks, and chorionic villus sampling takes a sample of placental tissue at 8–12 weeks. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis is used with IVF to test embryos before implantation and select unaffected ones. Each raises ethical and social questions — the safety and reliability of the test, the risks of miscarriage with invasive prenatal testing, the right to know or not to know, who decides which conditions to test for, the possible choice to terminate a pregnancy, anxiety and guilt, and the risk that screening could be used to select non-medical traits. Students should be able to identify and discuss these from religious, moral and social viewpoints and to evaluate the implications of prenatal genetic screening.

12. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working through each section and checking that you can draw a cell membrane from the fluid mosaic model and label the phospholipid bilayer, the proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins; state the difference between diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport, and give an example of each; outline the steps of DNA extraction (a simple practical with strawberries or onions is useful to remember); and carry out a genetic cross with a Punnett square and interpret the ratios. Revise by drawing protein structure from amino acid to tertiary, then drawing the DNA double helix and explaining semi-conservative replication and the Meselson–Stahl evidence. After this topic, revise Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development, because the same DNA and protein-synthesis processes control cell differentiation and the cell cycle.

title: Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development Revision Notes
content:
Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development

Biology AS Edexcel IAL Topic 3 covers the ultrastructure of eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells, microscopy, cell division by mitosis and meiosis, fertilisation, stem cells, and genetic control through gene expression, epigenetics and inheritance.

  • Cells are the basic units of all living organisms sharing common features, organised hierarchically from cells to tissues, organs, and organ systems.
  • Eukaryote ultrastructure includes nucleus, nucleolus, ribosomes, rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, centrioles, lysosomes, and Golgi apparatus, with rER and Golgi cooperating in protein transport and extracellular enzyme formation.
  • Prokaryote ultrastructure features a cell wall, capsule, plasmid, flagellum, pili, ribosomes, and circular DNA.
  • Microscopy relies on magnification and resolution, using light and electron microscopes, with specimen staining essential for contrast, alongside Core Practical 5 for light microscopy, graticule measurements, and cell drawing.
  • Genetics involves gene loci, linkage, and meiosis ensuring genetic variation through independent assortment in metaphase I and crossing over in prophase I.
  • Mammalian gametes feature adaptations like the acrosome in sperm and zona pellucida in eggs, leading to fertilisation via the acrosome and cortical reactions and nuclear fusion, paralleled in flowering plants by pollen tube growth and double fertilisation.
  • The cell cycle and mitosis produce genetically identical daughter cells for growth and asexual reproduction, assessed quantitatively via mitotic indices and Core Practical 6 root tip squashes.
  • Stem cells can be totipotent or pluripotent, found in morula and blastocysts, enabling specialisation through differential gene expression, alternative splicing post-transcription, and epigenetic DNA methylation and histone modification.
  • Phenotypes reflect interactions between genotype, environment, multiple alleles, polygenic inheritance displaying continuous variation, and heritable epigenetic changes.

Worked example

Calculate the actual length of an organelle measuring 45 mm in an electron micrograph with a magnification of ×30,000. Using the formula actual size = image size ÷ magnification, convert 45 mm to micrometres by multiplying by 1000 to get 45,000 um. Then calculate 45,000 um ÷ 30,000 = 1.5 um.

Key points to remember

Students frequently lose marks by confusing the roles of the rough endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi apparatus; rER folds and transports newly synthesized proteins, whereas the Golgi apparatus modifies, packages them into vesicles, and produces extracellular enzymes. In microscopy calculations, always ensure image size and scale bar units match before dividing by magnification. Remember that crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis, not mitosis, and independent assortment happens in metaphase I. For epigenetics, be precise: DNA methylation involves methyl groups added to cytosine bases inhibiting transcription, while histone modification affects chromatin condensation, and both can be passed on following cell division.

title: Exam technique: Algorithms & Programming
content:
### What earns the marks
To earn full marks on this topic, students need to demonstrate their ability to design and problem-solve using algorithms, as stated in statement 7. For calculate questions, show working and justify answers. For explain and describe questions, provide clear and concise pseudocode or flowcharts. For justify and state questions, provide a reason or explanation for the answer. 
### Traps
Common mistakes include not using ENDIF/NEXT/ENDWHILE terminators in pseudocode, not recording condition results in trace tables, and not testing boundary values. Correction: always use terminators, record condition results, and test boundary values. 
### Memory hooks
To remember the difference between validation and verification, use the mnemonic 'valid' for checking data format and 'verify' for checking data accuracy. To remember the linear search algorithm, think of 'looking for a book on a shelf'. To sanity-check an answer, test it with a simple example. 
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 20-30% of the paper, and students should budget around 30-40 minutes to answer the questions. Make sure to read the questions carefully and manage time effectively to earn the maximum marks.

title: Exam technique: Mensuration
content:
### What earns the marks
For circles, sectors and arcs, the fraction of 360 stated earns the method mark: write 60/360 before multiplying. For cylinders, cones and spheres, the formula quoted earns a mark on its own, so write Volume = (1/3) pi r squared h even when confident. For compound shapes, split earns marks: compute each part separately, then add or subtract with a clear statement.
### Traps
Error: 2 pi r used for area. Correction: circumference versus area check first. Error: omitting 1/3 for cones and pyramids. Correction: quote the formula every time. Error: using diameter as radius in a semicircle cut-out. Correction: halve the diameter before any pi work. Error: forgetting the square root in a Pythagoras step. Correction: label squared lines as squared.
### Worked example
A cylinder has radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. Its volume is πr²h = π × 9 × 10 = 90π ≈ 282.7 cm³. A sector of angle 60° in a circle of radius 6 cm has arc length (60/360) × 2π × 6 = 2π cm.
### Check yourself
A trapezium has parallel sides 5 cm and 9 cm and a perpendicular height of 4 cm. Find its area. Use ½(a + b)h = ½ × (5 + 9) × 4 = 28 cm². State the units and show the substitution before the final value.

title: Probability — Study Notes
content:
Probability

Basic Rules

For an event A with P(A) = p: 0 ≤ p ≤ 1, and P(A′) = 1 − P(A). For mutually exclusive events, probabilities add: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). For events that can occur together, subtract the overlap:

  • P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)

Venn Diagrams

Draw the universe first, then the events. Fill from the intersection outwards: if P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.25, then only-A = 0.35, only-B = 0.25, neither = 0.15. Every region must sum to 1.

Tree Diagrams

Branch probabilities multiply along a path; outcomes at the end of complete paths add. Draw one branch set per stage of the experiment. For two draws without replacement from a bag of 5 red and 3 blue: P(RR) = (5/8)(4/7) = 20/56.

Conditional Probability

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) — the probability of A given that B has occurred. The condition shrinks the sample space.

Example: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Then P(A | B) = 0.2/0.4 = 0.5, so A and B are independent since P(A | B) = P(A).

Independence

A and B are independent exactly when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B). Do not confuse independent (no influence on probabilities) with mutually exclusive (cannot co-occur). Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are never independent.

Exam tips: convert every "given that" into a conditional. With trees, label the second-stage branches with conditional probabilities; they are usually different from the first stage when drawing without replacement.

Exam method: combined events

The addition rule gives P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). For mutually exclusive events the intersection is empty, so P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). Draw a Venn diagram to place each probability in its region before calculating.

Independent events satisfy P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B). Test independence by checking this equation rather than assuming it, because the question may give the joint probability and ask you to decide.

The conditional probability P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Events are independent exactly when P(A | B) = P(A).

Tree diagrams suit sequential events without replacement. Multiply along each branch and add the branches that give the outcome required.

Exam cue: State whether events are independent or mutually exclusive, because the two are different and the formula depends on it.

title: Operating Systems — Study Notes
content:
Operating Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): OS roles, memory/process management, hardware–software layer, interrupts, buffers, utility software.

1. What an OS does

Manages memory, processes/files, I/O via drivers, security (users, permissions), and provides the UI (CLI/GUI) between user, applications and hardware.

2. Memory and process management

  • Paging/segmentation move programs in/out; virtual memory extends RAM to disk when RAM is full.
  • Multitasking: scheduler gives each process time slices; context switching saves/restores state.

3. Interrupts and buffers

Interrupts signal events (I/O complete, timer); CPU saves context, services via ISR, resumes. Buffers hold data in transit (printing) so slow devices don't block the CPU; spooling queues jobs.

4. Utility software

Disk formatter, defragmenter (reduces head movement on HDDs; unnecessary for SSD), backup scheduler, compression, antivirus, file compression.

5. UI and drivers

CLI: precise, scriptable, low overhead. GUI: icons/windows, discoverable, more resources. Device drivers translate OS calls to hardware specifics — each device needs its own.

Exam tips: "manage" verbs earn marks: manages memory, manages processes, manages peripherals; explain virtual memory by RAM-full scenario, not definition alone.

title: Energy, Work & Power — Study Notes
content:
Energy, Work & Power

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): stores and transfers, KE/PE, work, energy sources, power, efficiency.

1. Energy stores & transfers

Stores: kinetic, gravitational, elastic, chemical, nuclear, thermal. Transfer mechanisms: mechanically, electrically, heating, waves. Energy is conserved overall; transfers via work done.

2. Formulas

  • KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh.
  • Work W = Fd (force along displacement, joules).
  • Power P = W/t = E/t; P = Fv for constant speed.

Example: 0.5 kg at 4 m/s: KE = 4 J. Lift 2 kg by 3 m: PE = 60 J (g = 10).

3. Energy sources

Renewable: solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biofuel, tidal — replenished. Non-renewable: fossil fuels, nuclear — finite. Discuss reliability, cost, pollution for "evaluate" questions.

4. Efficiency

Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input (×100%). Sankey diagrams show losses.

Example: motor: 150 J useful from 600 J → 25%.

5. Energy-chain problems

Equating KE loss to PE gain: v = √(2gh) for frictionless drop; braking distance grows with v².

Exam tips: define work as "force × distance moved in the direction of the force"; use g = 10 unless told otherwise; efficiency is a ratio — no units.

title: Numerical Measures of Central Tendency — Study Notes
content:
Central Tendency: Mean, Median and Mode

The Mean

For data x₁, ..., xₙ the mean is

  • x̄ = Σx/n

For a frequency table with midpoints x and frequencies f: x̄ = Σfx/Σf. The mean uses every value, so a single extreme value drags it — that is its main weakness.

The Median

The median is the middle value: position (n + 1)/2 for ordered raw data. With n even, average the two middle values. The median ignores the size of extreme values, so it describes skewed data more honestly. For grouped data, estimate the median by linear interpolation within the median class.

The Mode

The most frequent value. A dataset may have no mode or several. For grouped data the modal class is the one with the highest frequency density (frequency ÷ class width), not the highest frequency.

Effects of Data Changes

Adding a constant a to every value adds a to the mean and median (the mode too) but leaves the spread untouched. Multiplying every value by b multiplies mean and median by b.

Coding

Subtract a constant and divide by a convenient width: y = (x − a)/b. Then x̄ = b·ȳ + a. Coding simplifies arithmetic and always preserves the relationship — the coded mean decodes exactly.

Example: data 2, 4, 4, 10: mean = 5, median = 4, mode = 4. Change 10 to 100: mean = 27.5, median and mode unchanged — the mean chased the outlier.

Exam tips: always state which average you used and why. When asked to compare two distributions, pair a central measure with a spread measure; a mean without a spread is only half an answer.

Exam method: mean, median and mode

For ungrouped data, the mean is the sum of the values divided by the number of values. The median is the middle value of the ordered list, at position (n + 1)/2, and the mode is the value that occurs most often. Always order the data before finding the median.

For grouped data, the mean is Σfx/Σf using the class midpoints. The modal class is the class with the highest frequency, and the median class is the one containing the (n + 1)/2 th value.

Each average suits different data. The mean uses every value, so an outlier pulls it away from the centre, while the median is unaffected by extreme values. Say which average is more representative when the question asks you to comment.

Changing one value changes the mean but may not change the median, which is useful to check a calculation.

Exam cue: When the question gives a mean and asks for a missing value, form the equation Σx = n × mean and solve for the unknown.

title: Continuous Random Variables — Study Notes
content:
Continuous Random Variables

Probability Density Functions

A continuous variable X is described by a density f(x) with f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫f(x)dx = 1 over all x. Probabilities are areas:

  • P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx

Single points have zero probability, so strict or loose inequalities make no difference: P(X < 2) = P(X ≤ 2).

Finding Unknown Constants

Piecewise densities carry an unknown k: impose that the total area is 1 (and continuity at joins where required). One equation, one unknown.

Example: f(x) = kx on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area: k·(2²/2) = 2k = 1, so k = ½.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = ∫x·f(x) dx
  • E(X²) = ∫x²·f(x) dx
  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))²

The mean is the balancing point of the area under the density. For symmetric densities the mean sits at the symmetry point — worth spotting before integrating.

The Median and Mode

The median m solves ∫₋∞ᵐ f(x) dx = 0.5 (left half of the area). The mode is the x maximising f(x). For uniform densities the median is the midpoint.

Uniform Distribution

If f(x) = 1/(b − a) on [a, b], every point is equally likely. Then E(X) = (a + b)/2 and Var(X) = (b − a)²/12 — memorise both; they are quick exam marks.

Exam tips: always verify ∫f = 1 before computing anything else. Sketch the density — area intuitions catch algebra slips. Median questions are integration-to-0.5 questions; set them up before calculating.

Exam method: density functions

A probability density function f must satisfy f(x) ≥ 0 for all x and the total area under it must equal 1, so the integral of f over its whole domain is 1. Use this to find an unknown constant before asking for any probability.

For a continuous variable, P(a ≤ X ≤ b) is the integral of f(x) from a to b. The endpoints carry no probability, so strict and non-strict inequalities give the same answer. Outside the given domain f(x) = 0.

The cumulative distribution function F(x) = P(X ≤ x) is the integral of f from the lower end of the domain up to x. The median m satisfies F(m) = 0.5, and the mode is where f is largest.

Expected value E(X) is the integral of x f(x) over the domain, and the variance is E(X²) minus the square of E(X). Write each integral with its limits before evaluating.

Exam cue: Sketch the density over its domain first. A linear density is a triangle or trapezium, and the area of the shape gives the total probability quickly.

title:
Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment — Edexcel International A2 Level Biology

This revision note covers the biology topics that sit behind the energy use of cells and animals and behind the maintenance of the internal environment. It is built around the specification statements rather than around a loose theme, so each numbered section reflects one or more things the specification expects a candidate to be able to do. The note is deliberately at exam depth: it explains the reasoning, gives the worked examples and comparisons that examiners look for, and lists the common mistakes that lose marks in this topic. Use it to check what you actually know and to practise the kinds of answer the specification rewards.

1. Why respiration matters and what the topic is for

Respiration is the set of reactions that release energy from nutrient molecules and couple that energy to the work cells do. The main nutrient in most questions is glucose, and the main energy currency that respiration produces is ATP. The practical point is that cells do not get energy directly from glucose; they get it from ATP, and respiration is the process that links the fuel to the currency. Understanding respiration therefore means understanding where the energy comes from, how the cell captures it, and how that energy is used in muscles and in the rest of the body.

The topic also connects to the internal environment, because muscles and tissues can only work properly if the internal conditions stay within limits, and because the energy demand of the body changes when muscles work. The link between respiration, muscles and the internal environment is that exercise changes the demand for ATP, which changes the demand for oxygen and fuel and the production of waste, and the internal environment has to respond. If you see the topic as one connected question about supply, demand and control, the parts will fit together rather than staying as separate facts.

2. Aerobic respiration as a sequence of stages, not a single reaction

Aerobic respiration is not one enzyme-controlled reaction but a sequence of stages: the stages are glycolysis, the link reaction, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm and breaks glucose into pyruvate, producing a small amount of ATP and reduced NAD. The link reaction and the Krebs cycle happen in the mitochondrial matrix and produce reduced coenzymes and carbon dioxide. Oxidative phosphorylation happens in the inner mitochondrial membrane and uses the reduced coenzymes to make the bulk of the ATP and to reduce oxygen to water.

The important idea is that respiration is staged: each stage does a specific job and the stages are connected. Glycolysis starts the breakdown of glucose. The link reaction converts pyruvate and removes carbon dioxide. The Krebs cycle oxidises the acetyl group and harvests hydrogen. Oxidative phosphorylation harvests the energy from the hydrogen and passes it to ATP. A good answer says that respiration is staged, gives the four stages in order, and says where each occurs. It does not say that respiration is a single reaction that turns glucose into ATP in one step, because that is not what happens and it loses marks.

A good answer also says that oxygen is the final electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation and that this is why the process is aerobic: without oxygen the chain stops and ATP production from oxidative phosphorylation stops. The link between oxygen and ATP is one of the reasons aerobic respiration yields more ATP than anaerobic alternatives, because the full oxidation is completed and the hydrogen carriers can be re-oxidised at the end of the chain. If you can say that, you have the aerobic idea in a form that scores marks.

3. Glycolysis: the investment and payoff phases and the net yield

Glycolysis is the first stage of respiration and it happens in the cytoplasm. It phosphorylates glucose, splits the phosphorylated intermediate, and then oxidises triose phosphate, producing pyruvate, a small net yield of ATP and reduced NAD. The investment phase uses ATP to phosphorylate glucose and its intermediates; the payoff phase produces the ATP and reduced NAD that make glycolysis worth doing.

The classic net yield for the overall equation taught in this specification is often stated as producing a small amount of ATP per glucose, with the rest coming later from the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. The important point is not to memorise only the number but to understand that glycolysis produces pyruvate, ATP and reduced NAD, and that the ATP comes from substrate-level phosphorylation, while the reduced NAD is a carrier of hydrogen that will feed into oxidative phosphorylation if oxygen is available. A good answer says that glycolysis phosphorylates glucose, splits it, oxidises triose phosphate, produces pyruvate and a small amount of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and produces reduced NAD. It does not say that glycolysis makes the most ATP, because it does not; that comes later.

The intermediate phosphorylation is the reason glycolysis is not just a simple split. Glucose has to be primed with phosphate so that it can be split and so that the triose phosphate can be oxidised. The ATP investment at the start pays off later, which is why the net yield is what it is. If you can say that, you have the logic of glycolysis rather than just a list of steps.

4. The link reaction and the Krebs cycle: decarboxylation and hydrogen harvesting

The link reaction converts pyruvate into acetyl coenzyme A, releasing carbon dioxide and reducing NAD. The Krebs cycle then oxidises the acetyl group, releasing more carbon dioxide, producing ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and generating reduced NAD and reduced FAD. The carbon dioxide released in these stages is the CO2 that the cell, and the organism, must dispose of, and the hydrogen carried by the reduced coenzymes is what feeds oxidative phosphorylation.

The link reaction is the bridge between glycolysis and the Krebs cycle. Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion, is oxidised and decarboxylated to form the acetyl group, which is attached to coenzyme A. The Krebs cycle then uses the acetyl group to regenerate oxaloacetate and to produce the reduced coenzymes and substrate-level phosphorylation that are the point of the cycle. A good answer says that the link reaction converts pyruvate to acetyl coenzyme A with release of CO2 and reduced NAD, and that the Krebs cycle oxidises the acetyl group with release of CO2, production of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and production of reduced NAD and reduced FAD. It does not say that the Krebs cycle happens in the cytosol, because it happens in the mitochondrial matrix. It also does not say that the Krebs cycle is the stage that uses oxygen, because oxygen is used in oxidative phosphorylation, not in the cycle itself.

The main conceptual point of the Krebs cycle is that it is a cycle that oxidises a two-carbon acetyl group and harvests hydrogen, releasing carbon dioxide along the way. The ATP made by substrate-level phosphorylation in the cycle is small compared with the ATP from oxidative phosphorylation, but the cycle’s real job is to supply the reduced coenzymes. If you can say that, you have the role of the Krebs cycle rather than just a sequence of intermediates.

5. Oxidative phosphorylation and the role of the inner membrane and oxygen

Oxidative phosphorylation is the stage that makes the most ATP and the stage where oxygen is used. It happens on the inner mitochondrial membrane, where the reduced coenzymes deliver hydrogen and the energy from the electrons is used to pump protons, creating a proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis as protons flow back through ATP synthase. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor at the end of the chain, and water is formed.

The key point is that ATP is made by chemiosmosis, not by a single enzyme directly handing a phosphate to ADP. Energy from the electron transport chain is used to pump protons from the matrix to the intermembrane space, and the resulting proton gradient is what drives ATP synthesis when protons flow back through ATP synthase. Oxygen accepts the electrons at the end of the chain and combines with protons to form water, so without oxygen the chain stops and the gradient cannot be maintained. A good answer says that oxidative phosphorylation happens on the inner mitochondrial membrane, that the energy from the electrons pumps protons, that the proton gradient drives ATP synthesis through ATP synthase, and that oxygen is the final electron acceptor forming water. It does not say that ATP is made directly by the electron transport chain itself; it is made by ATP synthase using the proton gradient.

The distinction between the electron transport chain and ATP synthase is important because it is one of the places where a lack of precision loses marks. The chain creates the gradient; ATP synthase uses it. If you keep that distinction clear, you can explain why a poison that blocks the chain, or a lack of oxygen, stops ATP production. The model is also the reason that the inner membrane is folded into cristae: it increases the surface area for the proteins of the chain and for ATP synthase. If you can say that, you have connected the structure to the function.

6. ATP as the energy currency and why respiration is staged

ATP is the immediate energy currency that respiration supplies to the cell. The energy for most cellular processes does not come directly from glucose or food; it comes from the hydrolysis of ATP. Respiration exists so that the energy in food can be used to regenerate ATP, and then the ATP can be used for endergonic processes, active transport, movement and biosynthesis. The role of ATP is to act as a small, reusable and immediately available packet of energy that can be used where and when it is needed.

The reason respiration is staged rather than a single big burn is that staged release is more controllable and more efficient in the biological sense. The energy is not released all at once as heat, but in a way that the cell can use to phosphorylate ADP; the carrier molecules handle the hydrogen and the energy between stages; and the stages can be regulated according to the cell’s needs. A good answer says that respiration is staged so that the energy is released in manageable amounts that the cell can use to make ATP, and that ATP is the energy currency used by the cell. It does not say that the stages are only for historical reasons or that the cell could simply burn glucose in one step for the same practical result, because the control and capture are the point.

The link between ATP and work is that ATP hydrolysis is endergonic to reverse but exergonic in the cell’s direction, so it provides energy for processes that would not otherwise occur. The cell uses ATP to drive active transport, to drive movement including muscle contraction, and to drive biosynthesis, and respiration is what keeps the ATP supply up. If you can say that, you have the currency idea in a form that scores marks.

7. Contraction as sliding filaments, not shortening of the filaments themselves

Muscle contraction works by the sliding filament model, not by the filaments shortening. The actin and myosin filaments slide past one another, so the sarcomere shortens even though the filaments themselves do not get shorter. The thick filaments are myosin, the thin filaments are actin, and the contraction happens when myosin heads bind to actin, pivot, release and re-bind further along, pulling the thin filament past the thick one.

The important point is that contraction is sliding, and that the length of the filaments does not change. A good answer says that during contraction the filaments slide past each other so the sarcomere shortens, that the filaments themselves do not shorten, and that myosin heads bind to actin and pivot to pull the thin filament past the thick one. It does not say that the filaments shorten; it says that they slide. That is one of the most common mistakes in this topic, because it is easy to think that contraction means the filaments get shorter when it actually means they get closer together and the overlap increases.

The energy for the sliding is provided by ATP. ATP is used both to power the power stroke and to detach the myosin head so the cycle can repeat. The calcium ions that are released into the sarcoplasm when the muscle is stimulated allow the myosin head to bind to actin in the first place. The full story is therefore ATP plus calcium plus the filament arrangement, but the most important exam point is the sliding filament idea itself. If you can say that, you have the contraction idea in a form that scores marks.

8. The role of ATP and calcium in the contraction cycle

The contraction cycle uses ATP and calcium. Calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum when the muscle is stimulated, and the calcium allows the myosin head to bind to actin by exposing the binding sites. ATP then is used to break the myosin-actin link and re-cock the myosin head, and another ATP is hydrolysed to position the head for the next stroke. When calcium is removed and the binding sites are covered again, the muscle relaxes.

A good answer says that calcium exposes the actin binding sites so myosin can bind, that ATP is used to break the cross-bridge and re-cock the head, and that the cycle is powered by ATP hydrolysis. It also says that relaxation happens when calcium is removed and the binding sites are covered. It does not say that relaxation uses no ATP, because it does not; the detachment and repositioning of myosin need ATP, and that is one reason rigor mortis happens, because ATP is no longer available and the myosin stays bound. If you can say that, you have the energy story of contraction in a form that scores marks.

The calcium role is essential, not optional. Without calcium, the myosin heads cannot bind to actin and the muscle cannot contract, even if ATP is present. ATP alone is not enough; you need calcium to start the cycle and ATP to keep it going. If you can keep that distinction clear, you can answer the question correctly and avoid the common mistake of saying that ATP alone is what starts contraction.

9. ATP supply during exercise and the limits of aerobic capacity

During exercise the demand for ATP rises, and the rate of respiration must rise to match it. Aerobic respiration can supply ATP for sustained moderate exercise, but when the rate of demand exceeds the rate at which oxygen can be supplied, the muscle shifts toward anaerobic pathways and the balance of products changes. The point is that exercise is a test of the energy supply system and of the system that supports it, including breathing and circulation.

Aerobic respiration is efficient and sustainable, but it depends on oxygen delivery. If oxygen delivery cannot keep up, the cell relies more on pathways that do not need as much oxygen, and this changes the products. A good answer says that aerobic respiration supplies ATP efficiently but needs oxygen, that during strenuous exercise the demand may outstrip oxygen supply, and that this forces a shift in the balance of ATP production. It does not say that the muscle simply switches off aerobic respiration and does nothing else; it says that the balance shifts. The energy story is continuous, not a simple on-off switch.

The practical point is that sustained exercise depends on the ability to deliver oxygen and remove waste, which is why breathing and heart rate rise. The biology here ties respiration, muscle and the internal environment together, because the muscle cannot work unless the supply system keeps up and the internal conditions stay tolerable. If you can see that, you can answer the questions that link the parts, which are often where the higher marks are.

10. The response to exercise: heart rate, breathing rate and breathing volume

During exercise, heart rate, breathing rate and the volume of air breathed per breath all increase. The heart pumps faster and harder to deliver more oxygenated blood to the muscles and to remove more carbon dioxide and heat. Breathing increases in frequency and depth to bring in more oxygen and to remove more carbon dioxide. The point is that the body responds to the higher demand on several fronts at once.

The increase in breathing is not just faster breathing; it is also deeper breathing, so the volume of air exchanged per minute rises more than the rate alone would suggest. The increase in heart rate rises the rate of blood delivery, and a stronger heartbeat can also increase the stroke volume, so the cardiac output rises. A good answer says that during exercise breathing rate and depth increase, that heart rate increases, and that these changes raise the supply of oxygen and the removal of carbon dioxide and heat. It does not say that only breathing rate changes, because depth matters too. It does not say that the heart only beats faster, because the strength of the beat can change as well.

A common mistake is to describe the response to exercise only in terms of breathing, or only in terms of heart rate, when the question asks for both. A good answer gives both and links them, because they are part of the same supply system. The internal environment is what both systems are serving: without the increased supply, the muscles cannot work and the internal conditions would drift out of limits. If you can say that, you have the response in a form that scores marks.

11. Thermoregulation, vasodilation and vasoconstriction, and the control of heat loss

Thermoregulation is the control of body temperature, which is part of homeostasis. The body controls heat loss and heat production to keep temperature within limits. When the body needs to lose heat, blood vessels near the skin surface dilate, allowing more blood flow near the surface so heat is lost to the environment; this is vasodilation. When the body needs to conserve heat, those vessels constrict, reducing blood flow near the surface and reducing heat loss; this is vasoconstriction.

A good answer says that vasodilation increases blood flow near the skin surface and increases heat loss, and that vasoconstriction reduces blood flow near the surface and reduces heat loss. It does not say that vasodilation happens only when it is hot and vasoconstriction only when it is cold, as absolute rules, though that is the typical pattern, because the system is about control, not just a fixed setting. The deeper point is that the skin blood flow is one of the ways the body moves heat around and loses it, and that the control is part of homeostasis.

Other responses to overheating may include sweating, which cools by evaporation, and behavioural changes. Responses to cold include shivering and reducing heat loss by vasoconstriction. The important idea is that the body has both heat-loss and heat-production responses, and that homeothermy is maintained by balancing them. A good answer says that the body controls temperature by adjusting heat loss and heat production, names vasodilation and vasoconstriction as examples of changing heat loss, and mentions that the responses are part of homeostasis. If you can say that, you have the thermoregulation idea in a form that scores marks.

12. The concept of the internal environment and why homeostasis matters

The internal environment is the fluid environment around the cells, and homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite changes outside and inside. The idea is important because cells can only work properly within a limited range of conditions, so the internal environment has to be kept within those limits: water balance, temperature, pH and the concentrations of substances have to be controlled, and respiration and exercise put demands on all of them.

Homeostasis is not a single process but a collection of control systems. Negative feedback is the main control principle, in which a change from the set point is detected and the system acts to bring it back. A good answer says that homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment, that cells can only function within narrow limits, and that negative feedback is the main control mechanism. It does not say that the internal environment never changes, because it does change; it says that it is kept within limits. That is the difference between a mark-scoring answer and one that treats homeostasis as meaning no change at all.

The link to respiration and muscles is that exercise stresses the internal environment: it produces heat, carbon dioxide and water, changes pH in the tissues and the blood, and demands more fuel and oxygen. Homeostasis has to cope with all of that, and that is why the topic brings together respiration, muscles and internal environment control. If you can say that, you have the unifying idea that makes the topic more than three separate lists.

13. Negative feedback and the way control systems work

Negative feedback is the main control principle in homeostasis. A change away from the set point is detected by a receptor, the information is passed to a control centre, and effectors act to reduce the change and bring the variable back toward the set point. The effect opposes the change, which is why it is called negative feedback. This is the principle behind temperature control, blood glucose control and the control of many other variables.

A good answer describes the components of a negative feedback system: receptor, coordination or control centre and effector, and says that the response reduces the original change. It does not describe positive feedback as the main homeostatic mechanism, because positive feedback amplifies the change and is used in a small number of cases such as childbirth, not as the general principle. The general principle is negative feedback, and the exam questions on this topic usually test that principle. If you can say that, you have the control idea in a form that scores marks.

The point of negative feedback is that it reduces the error from the set point. It does not have to eliminate the change entirely; real systems have a normal range. A good answer therefore does not say that homeostasis keeps every variable exactly constant at all times; it says that it keeps the variable within a normal range by opposing deviations. If you can say that, you have the principle and its limitations both correct.

14. Water and solute balance, and why the internal environment has to manage them

The internal environment has to manage water and solute balance because cells depend on the water potential of their surroundings. If the internal environment is too concentrated, water leaves cells by osmosis; if it is too dilute, water enters cells. Either can disrupt cell function. The control of water and solute balance is therefore part of homeostasis, and it connects to respiration and muscles because the body gains and loses water through breathing, sweating and urine, and because the balance matters for the tissues that are doing the work.

A good answer says that water and solute balance are part of homeostasis, that cells depend on the water potential of the internal environment, and that changes in water potential can move water by osmosis and affect cell function. It does not say that water balance is only about drinking, because the body also loses water in breathing, sweating and urine, and gains it in food and drink. The point is that the balance is dynamic and has to be controlled. If you can say that, you have the water-balance idea in a form that scores marks.

The link to respiration is that breathing loses water vapour, so respiration and breathing are part of the water balance as well as part of the gas exchange. The link to exercise is that sweating loses both water and heat, so the same response that cools can also disturb water balance.
