It is built around the specification statements rather than around a loose theme, so each numbered section reflects one or more things the specification expects a candidate to be able to do. The note is deliberately at exam depth: it explains the reasoning, gives the worked examples and comparisons that examiners look for, and lists the common mistakes that lose marks in this topic. Use it to check what you actually know and to practise the kinds of answer the specification rewards.

1. Why respiration matters and what the topic is for

Respiration is the set of reactions that release energy from nutrient molecules and couple that energy to the work cells do. The main nutrient in most questions is glucose, and the main energy currency that respiration produces is ATP. The practical point is that cells do not get energy directly from glucose; they get it from ATP, and respiration is the process that links the fuel to the currency. Understanding respiration therefore means understanding where the energy comes from, how the cell captures it, and how that energy is used in muscles and in the rest of the body.

The topic also connects to the internal environment, because muscles and tissues can only work properly if the internal conditions stay within limits, and because the energy demand of the body changes when muscles work. The link between respiration, muscles and the internal environment is that exercise changes the demand for ATP, which changes the demand for oxygen and fuel and the production of waste, and the internal environment has to respond. If you see the topic as one connected question about supply, demand and control, the parts will fit together rather than staying as separate facts.

2. Aerobic respiration as a sequence of stages, not a single reaction

Aerobic respiration is not one enzyme-controlled reaction but a sequence of stages: the stages are glycolysis, the link reaction, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm and breaks glucose into pyruvate, producing a small amount of ATP and reduced NAD. The link reaction and the Krebs cycle happen in the mitochondrial matrix and produce reduced coenzymes and carbon dioxide. Oxidative phosphorylation happens in the inner mitochondrial membrane and uses the reduced coenzymes to make the bulk of the ATP and to reduce oxygen to water.

The important idea is that respiration is staged: each stage does a specific job and the stages are connected. Glycolysis starts the breakdown of glucose. The link reaction converts pyruvate and removes carbon dioxide. The Krebs cycle oxidises the acetyl group and harvests hydrogen. Oxidative phosphorylation harvests the energy from the hydrogen and passes it to ATP. A good answer says that respiration is staged, gives the four stages in order, and says where each occurs. It does not say that respiration is a single reaction that turns glucose into ATP in one step, because that is not what happens and it loses marks.

A good answer also says that oxygen is the final electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation and that this is why the process is aerobic: without oxygen the chain stops and ATP production from oxidative phosphorylation stops. The link between oxygen and ATP is one of the reasons aerobic respiration yields more ATP than anaerobic alternatives, because the full oxidation is completed and the hydrogen carriers can be re-oxidised at the end of the chain. If you can say that, you have the aerobic idea in a form that scores marks.

3. Glycolysis: the investment and payoff phases and the net yield

Glycolysis is the first stage of respiration and it happens in the cytoplasm. It phosphorylates glucose, splits the phosphorylated intermediate, and then oxidises triose phosphate, producing pyruvate, a small net yield of ATP and reduced NAD. The investment phase uses ATP to phosphorylate glucose and its intermediates; the payoff phase produces the ATP and reduced NAD that make glycolysis worth doing.

The classic net yield for the overall equation taught in this specification is often stated as producing a small amount of ATP per glucose, with the rest coming later from the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. The important point is not to memorise only the number but to understand that glycolysis produces pyruvate, ATP and reduced NAD, and that the ATP comes from substrate-level phosphorylation, while the reduced NAD is a carrier of hydrogen that will feed into oxidative phosphorylation if oxygen is available. A good answer says that glycolysis phosphorylates glucose, splits it, oxidises triose phosphate, produces pyruvate and a small amount of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and produces reduced NAD. It does not say that glycolysis makes the most ATP, because it does not; that comes later.

The intermediate phosphorylation is the reason glycolysis is not just a simple split. Glucose has to be primed with phosphate so that it can be split and so that the triose phosphate can be oxidised. The ATP investment at the start pays off later, which is why the net yield is what it is. If you can say that, you have the logic of glycolysis rather than just a list of steps.

4. The link reaction and the Krebs cycle: decarboxylation and hydrogen harvesting

The link reaction converts pyruvate into acetyl coenzyme A, releasing carbon dioxide and reducing NAD. The Krebs cycle then oxidises the acetyl group, releasing more carbon dioxide, producing ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and generating reduced NAD and reduced FAD. The carbon dioxide released in these stages is the CO2 that the cell, and the organism, must dispose of, and the hydrogen carried by the reduced coenzymes is what feeds oxidative phosphorylation.

The link reaction is the bridge between glycolysis and the Krebs cycle. Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion, is oxidised and decarboxylated to form the acetyl group, which is attached to coenzyme A. The Krebs cycle then uses the acetyl group to regenerate oxaloacetate and to produce the reduced coenzymes and substrate-level phosphorylation that are the point of the cycle. A good answer says that the link reaction converts pyruvate to acetyl coenzyme A with release of CO2 and reduced NAD, and that the Krebs cycle oxidises the acetyl group with release of CO2, production of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and production of reduced NAD and reduced FAD. It does not say that the Krebs cycle happens in the cytosol, because it happens in the mitochondrial matrix. It also does not say that the Krebs cycle is the stage that uses oxygen, because oxygen is used in oxidative phosphorylation, not in the cycle itself.

The main conceptual point of the Krebs cycle is that it is a cycle that oxidises a two-carbon acetyl group and harvests hydrogen, releasing carbon dioxide along the way. The ATP made by substrate-level phosphorylation in the cycle is small compared with the ATP from oxidative phosphorylation, but the cycle’s real job is to supply the reduced coenzymes. If you can say that, you have the role of the Krebs cycle rather than just a sequence of intermediates.

5. Oxidative phosphorylation and the role of the inner membrane and oxygen

Oxidative phosphorylation is the stage that makes the most ATP and the stage where oxygen is used. It happens on the inner mitochondrial membrane, where the reduced coenzymes deliver hydrogen and the energy from the electrons is used to pump protons, creating a proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis as protons flow back through ATP synthase. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor at the end of the chain, and water is formed.

The key point is that ATP is made by chemiosmosis, not by a single enzyme directly handing a phosphate to ADP. Energy from the electron transport chain is used to pump protons from the matrix to the intermembrane space, and the resulting proton gradient is what drives ATP synthesis when protons flow back through ATP synthase. Oxygen accepts the electrons at the end of the chain and combines with protons to form water, so without oxygen the chain stops and the gradient cannot be maintained. A good answer says that oxidative phosphorylation happens on the inner mitochondrial membrane, that the energy from the electrons pumps protons, that the proton gradient drives ATP synthesis through ATP synthase, and that oxygen is the final electron acceptor forming water. It does not say that ATP is made directly by the electron transport chain itself; it is made by ATP synthase using the proton gradient.

The distinction between the electron transport chain and ATP synthase is important because it is one of the places where a lack of precision loses marks. The chain creates the gradient; ATP synthase uses it. If you keep that distinction clear, you can explain why a poison that blocks the chain, or a lack of oxygen, stops ATP production. The model is also the reason that the inner membrane is folded into cristae: it increases the surface area for the proteins of the chain and for ATP synthase. If you can say that, you have connected the structure to the function.

6. ATP as the energy currency and why respiration is staged

ATP is the immediate energy currency that respiration supplies to the cell. The energy for most cellular processes does not come directly from glucose or food; it comes from the hydrolysis of ATP. Respiration exists so that the energy in food can be used to regenerate ATP, and then the ATP can be used for endergonic processes, active transport, movement and biosynthesis. The role of ATP is to act as a small, reusable and immediately available packet of energy that can be used where and when it is needed.

The reason respiration is staged rather than a single big burn is that staged release is more controllable and more efficient in the biological sense. The energy is not released all at once as heat, but in a way that the cell can use to phosphorylate ADP; the carrier molecules handle the hydrogen and the energy between stages; and the stages can be regulated according to the cell’s needs. A good answer says that respiration is staged so that the energy is released in manageable amounts that the cell can use to make ATP, and that ATP is the energy currency used by the cell. It does not say that the stages are only for historical reasons or that the cell could simply burn glucose in one step for the same practical result, because the control and capture are the point.

The link between ATP and work is that ATP hydrolysis is endergonic to reverse but exergonic in the cell’s direction, so it provides energy for processes that would not otherwise occur. The cell uses ATP to drive active transport, to drive movement including muscle contraction, and to drive biosynthesis, and respiration is what keeps the ATP supply up. If you can say that, you have the currency idea in a form that scores marks.

7. Contraction as sliding filaments, not shortening of the filaments themselves

Muscle contraction works by the sliding filament model, not by the filaments shortening. The actin and myosin filaments slide past one another, so the sarcomere shortens even though the filaments themselves do not get shorter. The thick filaments are myosin, the thin filaments are actin, and the contraction happens when myosin heads bind to actin, pivot, release and re-bind further along, pulling the thin filament past the thick one.

The important point is that contraction is sliding, and that the length of the filaments does not change. A good answer says that during contraction the filaments slide past each other so the sarcomere shortens, that the filaments themselves do not shorten, and that myosin heads bind to actin and pivot to pull the thin filament past the thick one. It does not say that the filaments shorten; it says that they slide. That is one of the most common mistakes in this topic, because it is easy to think that contraction means the filaments get shorter when it actually means they get closer together and the overlap increases.

The energy for the sliding is provided by ATP. ATP is used both to power the power stroke and to detach the myosin head so the cycle can repeat. The calcium ions that are released into the sarcoplasm when the muscle is stimulated allow the myosin head to bind to actin in the first place. The full story is therefore ATP plus calcium plus the filament arrangement, but the most important exam point is the sliding filament idea itself. If you can say that, you have the contraction idea in a form that scores marks.

8. The role of ATP and calcium in the contraction cycle

The contraction cycle uses ATP and calcium. Calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum when the muscle is stimulated, and the calcium allows the myosin head to bind to actin by exposing the binding sites. ATP then is used to break the myosin-actin link and re-cock the myosin head, and another ATP is hydrolysed to position the head for the next stroke. When calcium is removed and the binding sites are covered again, the muscle relaxes.

A good answer says that calcium exposes the actin binding sites so myosin can bind, that ATP is used to break the cross-bridge and re-cock the head, and that the cycle is powered by ATP hydrolysis. It also says that relaxation happens when calcium is removed and the binding sites are covered. It does not say that relaxation uses no ATP, because it does not; the detachment and repositioning of myosin need ATP, and that is one reason rigor mortis happens, because ATP is no longer available and the myosin stays bound. If you can say that, you have the energy story of contraction in a form that scores marks.

The calcium role is essential, not optional. Without calcium, the myosin heads cannot bind to actin and the muscle cannot contract, even if ATP is present. ATP alone is not enough; you need calcium to start the cycle and ATP to keep it going. If you can keep that distinction clear, you can answer the question correctly and avoid the common mistake of saying that ATP alone is what starts contraction.

9. ATP supply during exercise and the limits of aerobic capacity

During exercise the demand for ATP rises, and the rate of respiration must rise to match it. Aerobic respiration can supply ATP for sustained moderate exercise, but when the rate of demand exceeds the rate at which oxygen can be supplied, the muscle shifts toward anaerobic pathways and the balance of products changes. The point is that exercise is a test of the energy supply system and of the system that supports it, including breathing and circulation.

Aerobic respiration is efficient and sustainable, but it depends on oxygen delivery. If oxygen delivery cannot keep up, the cell relies more on pathways that do not need as much oxygen, and this changes the products. A good answer says that aerobic respiration supplies ATP efficiently but needs oxygen, that during strenuous exercise the demand may outstrip oxygen supply, and that this forces a shift in the balance of ATP production. It does not say that the muscle simply switches off aerobic respiration and does nothing else; it says that the balance shifts. The energy story is continuous, not a simple on-off switch.

The practical point is that sustained exercise depends on the ability to deliver oxygen and remove waste, which is why breathing and heart rate rise. The biology here ties respiration, muscle and the internal environment together, because the muscle cannot work unless the supply system keeps up and the internal conditions stay tolerable. If you can see that, you can answer the questions that link the parts, which are often where the higher marks are.

10. The response to exercise: heart rate, breathing rate and breathing volume

During exercise, heart rate, breathing rate and the volume of air breathed per breath all increase. The heart pumps faster and harder to deliver more oxygenated blood to the muscles and to remove more carbon dioxide and heat. Breathing increases in frequency and depth to bring in more oxygen and to remove more carbon dioxide. The point is that the body responds to the higher demand on several fronts at once.

The increase in breathing is not just faster breathing; it is also deeper breathing, so the volume of air exchanged per minute rises more than the rate alone would suggest. The increase in heart rate rises the rate of blood delivery, and a stronger heartbeat can also increase the stroke volume, so the cardiac output rises. A good answer says that during exercise breathing rate and depth increase, that heart rate increases, and that these changes raise the supply of oxygen and the removal of carbon dioxide and heat. It does not say that only breathing rate changes, because depth matters too. It does not say that the heart only beats faster, because the strength of the beat can change as well.

A common mistake is to describe the response to exercise only in terms of breathing, or only in terms of heart rate, when the question asks for both. A good answer gives both and links them, because they are part of the same supply system. The internal environment is what both systems are serving: without the increased supply, the muscles cannot work and the internal conditions would drift out of limits. If you can say that, you have the response in a form that scores marks.

11. Thermoregulation, vasodilation and vasoconstriction, and the control of heat loss

Thermoregulation is the control of body temperature, which is part of homeostasis. The body controls heat loss and heat production to keep temperature within limits. When the body needs to lose heat, blood vessels near the skin surface dilate, allowing more blood flow near the surface so heat is lost to the environment; this is vasodilation. When the body needs to conserve heat, those vessels constrict, reducing blood flow near the surface and reducing heat loss; this is vasoconstriction.

A good answer says that vasodilation increases blood flow near the skin surface and increases heat loss, and that vasoconstriction reduces blood flow near the surface and reduces heat loss. It does not say that vasodilation happens only when it is hot and vasoconstriction only when it is cold, as absolute rules, though that is the typical pattern, because the system is about control, not just a fixed setting. The deeper point is that the skin blood flow is one of the ways the body moves heat around and loses it, and that the control is part of homeostasis.

Other responses to overheating may include sweating, which cools by evaporation, and behavioural changes. Responses to cold include shivering and reducing heat loss by vasoconstriction. The important idea is that the body has both heat-loss and heat-production responses, and that homeothermy is maintained by balancing them. A good answer says that the body controls temperature by adjusting heat loss and heat production, names vasodilation and vasoconstriction as examples of changing heat loss, and mentions that the responses are part of homeostasis. If you can say that, you have the thermoregulation idea in a form that scores marks.

12. The concept of the internal environment and why homeostasis matters

The internal environment is the fluid environment around the cells, and homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite changes outside and inside. The idea is important because cells can only work properly within a limited range of conditions, so the internal environment has to be kept within those limits: water balance, temperature, pH and the concentrations of substances have to be controlled, and respiration and exercise put demands on all of them.

Homeostasis is not a single process but a collection of control systems. Negative feedback is the main control principle, in which a change from the set point is detected and the system acts to bring it back. A good answer says that homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment, that cells can only function within narrow limits, and that negative feedback is the main control mechanism. It does not say that the internal environment never changes, because it does change; it says that it is kept within limits. That is the difference between a mark-scoring answer and one that treats homeostasis as meaning no change at all.

The link to respiration and muscles is that exercise stresses the internal environment: it produces heat, carbon dioxide and water, changes pH in the tissues and the blood, and demands more fuel and oxygen. Homeostasis has to cope with all of that, and that is why the topic brings together respiration, muscles and internal environment control. If you can say that, you have the unifying idea that makes the topic more than three separate lists.

13. Negative feedback and the way control systems work

Negative feedback is the main control principle in homeostasis. A change away from the set point is detected by a receptor, the information is passed to a control centre, and effectors act to reduce the change and bring the variable back toward the set point. The effect opposes the change, which is why it is called negative feedback. This is the principle behind temperature control, blood glucose control and the control of many other variables.

A good answer describes the components of a negative feedback system: receptor, coordination or control centre and effector, and says that the response reduces the original change. It does not describe positive feedback as the main homeostatic mechanism, because positive feedback amplifies the change and is used in a small number of cases such as childbirth, not as the general principle. The general principle is negative feedback, and the exam questions on this topic usually test that principle. If you can say that, you have the control idea in a form that scores marks.

The point of negative feedback is that it reduces the error from the set point. It does not have to eliminate the change entirely; real systems have a normal range. A good answer therefore does not say that homeostasis keeps every variable exactly constant at all times; it says that it keeps the variable within a normal range by opposing deviations. If you can say that, you have the principle and its limitations both correct.

14. Water and solute balance, and why the internal environment has to manage them

The internal environment has to manage water and solute balance because cells depend on the water potential of their surroundings. If the internal environment is too concentrated, water leaves cells by osmosis; if it is too dilute, water enters cells. Either can disrupt cell function. The control of water and solute balance is therefore part of homeostasis, and it connects to respiration and muscles because the body gains and loses water through breathing, sweating and urine, and because the balance matters for the tissues that are doing the work.

A good answer says that water and solute balance are part of homeostasis, that cells depend on the water potential of the internal environment, and that changes in water potential can move water by osmosis and affect cell function. It does not say that water balance is only about drinking, because the body also loses water in breathing, sweating and urine, and gains it in food and drink. The point is that the balance is dynamic and has to be controlled. If you can say that, you have the water-balance idea in a form that scores marks.

The link to respiration is that breathing loses water vapour, so respiration and breathing are part of the water balance as well as part of the gas exchange. The link to exercise is that sweating loses both water and heat, so the same response that cools can also disturb water balance. If you can see those links, you can answer questions that cross the parts, which are common at this level.

15. The role of the kidneys in the internal environment, briefly and at the right level

The kidneys are central to the internal environment because they control the composition of the urine and so the balance of water, ions and waste products in the blood. They remove waste from the blood and adjust the water and solute content of the body. In this topic the kidneys matter because they are one of the systems that keeps the internal environment within limits, and because the products of respiration have to be dealt with by the body as a whole.

A good answer describes the kidneys as organs that remove waste from the blood and help control water and solute balance, and links them to homeostasis and to the disposal of waste from respiration. It does not overreach by describing every nephron detail if the question does not ask for it; the key point is the role in the internal environment. The kidneys are part of the disposal and balance system that allows respiration and exercise to happen without wrecking the internal conditions. If you can say that, you have the right level.

The important idea is that the body is an integrated system: respiration makes ATP and produces waste, muscles use ATP and produce heat and waste, and the internal environment systems, including the kidneys, breathing and thermoregulation, keep the whole thing within limits. If you can see the integration, you can answer the questions that ask for the links, which are often the best-marked ones.

16. CPIR and the iodide concentration problem; the direction of control

The basics of thermoregulation include the idea that blood vessel diameter in the skin changes to control heat loss, and that the control is part of homeostasis. The anatomy point that is often tested is which vessels are involved and how they control the flow near the surface. In the skin, arteriole vasodilation and vasoconstriction change the flow to superficial vessels, and the presence of a rich superficial vessel bed lets the skin lose more heat when it is hot and conserve more when it is cold.

A good answer says that vasodilation near the skin surface increases heat loss and vasoconstriction near the skin surface reduces it, and that this is part of the way the body controls temperature. It does not say that the skin is the only place where this happens, or that the control is the only thermoregulatory response, because sweating, shivering and behaviour also matter. The point is to include the skin response correctly as part of the system, not to pretend it is the whole system. If you can say that, you have the idea in a form that scores marks.

The direction of control matters: more flow near the surface when hot, less when cold. A common mistake is to invert the relationship, so the answer says vasodilation happens in the cold, which is wrong. If you keep the direction straight, you can avoid that mistake. The reason the direction matters is that the surface vessels are the main route for losing heat to the environment, so opening them loses heat and closing them conserves it. If you can say that, you have both the direction and the reason.

17. Heat gain, heat loss, and the difference between conserving and producing heat

The body has two broad ways of dealing with cold: conserve the heat it has and make more heat. Vasoconstriction conserves heat by reducing loss from the skin surface. Shivering produces heat by making muscles contract repeatedly, which costs ATP and releases heat. Behavioural changes such as curling up, putting on clothing or moving to a warmer place also help. A good answer says that the body can conserve heat by vasoconstriction and produce heat by shivering and by other means, and that both are part of thermoregulation and homeostasis.

The distinction between conserving and producing heat is useful, because it helps explain why the responses are not all the same kind of thing. Vasoconstriction reduces loss; shivering increases production. A good answer makes that distinction, because it shows that the body has more than one tool for the job and that the tools work differently. If you can say that, you have a better answer than one that just lists “shivering, vasoconstriction” without saying what each does.

The energy angle is important too, because shivering uses ATP and therefore links back to respiration. Shivering keeps you warm by burning fuel, so it is not free; it increases the demand for ATP and therefore for oxygen and fuel. That is the kind of connection that examiners like, because it ties the topic together. If you can say that shivering increases respiratory demand, you have the link between thermoregulation and respiration.

18. The internal environment under exercise stress: what is pushed and what copes

Exercise pushes several variables at once, which is why the topic groups respiration, muscles and the internal environment. Muscles use ATP faster, so respiration must deliver more ATP, which raises the demand for oxygen and fuel and increases the production of carbon dioxide and heat. The heart and lungs respond to meet the oxygen demand and to remove the carbon dioxide. Thermoregulation responds to the heat. Water and solute balance are affected by sweating and by the increased rate of exchange. The overall point is that exercise is a stress test for homeostasis.

A good answer says that exercise raises ATP demand, that respiration and the supply systems respond, that more carbon dioxide and heat are produced, and that the internal environment systems, including breathing, circulation and thermoregulation, have to cope with the change. It does not just list the responses; it says that the internal environment has to keep working despite the stress. That is the unifying idea, and it is why the topic is taught as a unit rather than as three unrelated parts. If you can say that, you have the big picture in a form that scores marks.

A common mistake is to describe the responses as if they were isolated, with no mention of what they are responding to. A good answer links the response to the demand: the heart rate rises because the muscles need more oxygen; the breathing rises because the body needs to supply oxygen and remove carbon dioxide; the cooling responses rise because exercise generates heat. If you can make those links, you are answering at the higher level. The detail is only as good as the reasoning behind it.

19. How to read a respiration question and what examiners want

When a question asks about respiration, the examiner usually wants the pathway and the logic behind it, not just the final number. Say what the stages are, where they are, what they produce and why the process is staged and aerobic. If the question asks about the role of oxygen, say that oxygen is the final electron acceptor and that this is what allows oxidative phosphorylation to continue. If the question asks about ATP yield, say that most ATP comes from oxidative phosphorylation and that glycolysis and the Krebs cycle contribute smaller amounts by substrate-level phosphorylation. If you can do that, you can read the question the way the specification intends.

For muscles, the examiner usually wants the sliding filament idea, the role of ATP and calcium, and the reason the filaments do not shorten. If the question asks about contraction, say that the filaments slide past each other so the sarcomere shortens, that myosin heads bind to actin and pivot, that ATP powers the cycle and is needed for detachment, and that calcium exposes the binding sites. If you can do that, you can answer the muscle questions correctly and avoid the common mistake of saying that the filaments shorten.

For the internal environment, the examiner usually wants homeostasis, negative feedback, the key variables that are controlled, and the way the body responds to exercise or to temperature change. If the question asks about the response to exercise, include both heart rate and breathing rate and volume, and explain what each is doing. If the question asks about thermoregulation, include vasodilation and vasoconstriction and the direction of control. If you can do that, you can answer the internal environment questions at the right level.

20. How the parts connect: respiration powers muscles, muscles stress the internal environment, the internal environment has to cope

The topic is really about a chain: respiration makes ATP, muscles use ATP to do work, and the work changes the internal environment so the control systems have to respond. Respiration supplies ATP from glucose; the ATP is used for muscle contraction and for other cell work; muscle work produces heat and carbon dioxide and stresses the water and solute balance; the body responds by increasing supply and by controlling the internal conditions. The chain is why the topic is grouped together: the parts belong to the same system, even though they are listed under different headings.

A good answer can trace the chain: glucose to respiration to ATP to muscle contraction, muscle contraction to heat and CO2 production, heat to thermoregulation and CO2 to breathing and circulation. It can say that the internal environment system has to keep the body within limits while the muscles demand more and the metabolism produces more waste. It does not treat respiration, muscles and internal environment as three unrelated topics; it treats them as parts of one metabolic and homeostatic picture. That is what the topic is for, and it is what the better questions are testing. If you can see the chain, you can answer the questions that span the parts, which are often where the higher marks are.

21. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use this note by working through each section and checking that you can describe the stages of aerobic respiration and where they occur; explain the reason respiration is staged and aerobic; describe glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle; describe oxidative phosphorylation and the role of the inner membrane and oxygen; explain the role of ATP as the energy currency; describe the sliding filament model of contraction and say that the filaments do not shorten; describe the role of ATP and calcium in the contraction cycle; explain ATP supply during exercise and the limits of aerobic capacity; describe the response to exercise in breathing rate, breathing depth and heart rate; describe thermoregulation including vasodilation, vasoconstriction, shivering and other heat-loss and heat-production responses; explain homeostasis and negative feedback; and explain water and solute balance and the role of the kidneys in the internal environment. After this topic, revise the related systems, because the associations matter and the best questions ask for the links.

The note is long because the topic is broad and the specification asks for the biology behind the everyday events of exercise, temperature control and energy supply. A revision note has to cover the respiration pathway, the contraction mechanism, the exercise responses and the homeostasis principles in enough detail to be useful, and it has to link them, because the exam questions do. Study it section by section, check yourself against the specification statements, and practise the kinds of answer that explain rather than list. Then move on to the next topic and the related practicals, because the practicals are the way the specification ties the ideas to hands-on work.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying that respiration is one reaction that turns glucose straight into ATP, instead of a sequence of stages.
  • Saying the filaments shorten during contraction, instead of sliding past each other.
  • Saying that ATP alone starts contraction, instead of calcium exposing the binding sites first.
  • Saying the Krebs cycle happens in the cytoplasm, or that it is where oxygen is used.
  • Saying ATP is made directly by the electron transport chain, instead of by ATP synthase using the proton gradient.
  • Forgetting that oxygen is the final electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation.
  • Saying that breathing rate alone is the response to exercise, forgetting breathing depth and heart rate.
  • Inverting vasodilation and vasoconstriction, so vasodilation is linked to cold and vasoconstriction to heat.
  • Treating homeostasis as meaning the internal environment never changes, instead of staying within limits by negative feedback.
  • Forgetting that sweating and breathing both affect water balance, not just drinking and urine.
  • Saying positive feedback is the main homeostatic mechanism, when negative feedback is.
  • Saying that glycolysis produces most of the ATP from respiration; it does not.
  • Describing thermoregulation responses without saying whether they conserve or produce heat.
  • Missing the link that exercise stresses the internal environment so the control systems have to cope.

Exam-style questions

  1. Describe aerobic respiration and state the role of oxygen in the process. Answer: Aerobic respiration is a sequence of stages: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, and oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Glycolysis produces pyruvate, ATP and reduced NAD; the link reaction and Krebs cycle produce reduced NAD and reduced FAD and release CO2; oxidative phosphorylation uses the reduced coenzymes to make ATP and oxygen is the final electron acceptor, forming water. Oxygen is needed so the electron transport chain can continue and the bulk of ATP can be made. (6 marks)
  2. Explain why respiration is an energy-releasing process but still needs to be staged rather than happening in one reaction. Answer: Respiration releases energy from glucose but a single reaction releasing all the energy at once would mostly waste it as heat; the stages release energy in manageable amounts that the cell can use to phosphorylate ADP to ATP, the energy currency for cell work. Stage-by-stage release also allows regulation of the rate to match the cell’s needs. (4 marks)
  3. Describe the sliding filament model of muscle contraction and state the role of ATP in it. Answer: During contraction the actin and myosin filaments slide past each other rather than shortening themselves, so the sarcomere shortens. Myosin heads bind to actin, pivot and pull the thin filament toward the centre, then detach and re-cock. ATP is required for the myosin head to detach from actin and be re-cocked for the next cycle, so the contraction is powered by ATP hydrolysis. (5 marks)
  4. Explain the roles of calcium and ATP in the control of muscle contraction and relaxation. Answer: When a muscle is stimulated, calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and exposes the binding sites on actin so myosin heads can bind; ATP is used to power the cross-bridge cycle and to detach the myosin heads. Relaxation occurs when calcium is removed and the binding sites are covered again; ATP is still required for detachment, which is why a muscle without ATP stays contracted, as in rigor mortis. (5 marks)
  5. Describe the response of the body during exercise in terms of heart rate and breathing rate, and explain why each increases. Answer: During exercise heart rate increases to deliver more oxygenated blood to the muscles and to remove more carbon dioxide and heat, and breathing rate increases along with breathing depth to bring in more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide. Both responses increase because the muscles’ ATP demand rises and the supply and waste-removal systems must keep up with the increased metabolism. (5 marks)
  6. Describe how the skin blood vessels help control body temperature and state the direction of the response in each case. Answer: Blood vessels near the skin surface dilate in heat, increasing blood flow near the surface and increasing heat loss to the environment; they constrict in cold, reducing blood flow near the surface and reducing heat loss. This is part of thermoregulation and homeostasis, along with other responses such as sweating or shivering and behavioural changes. (4 marks)
  7. Define homeostasis and explain the principle of negative feedback with one example. Answer: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment within limits. Negative feedback is the control principle in which a change from the set point is detected and the response reduces the change, returning the variable toward the set point; for example in temperature control, if body temperature rises, effectors such as sweating and vasodilation increase heat loss, reducing the temperature back toward normal. (5 marks)
  8. Explain why water and solute balance are part of homeostasis and what happens if the internal environment becomes too concentrated or too dilute. Answer: Cells depend on the water potential of the internal environment; if it becomes too concentrated, water moves out of cells by osmosis, and if it becomes too dilute, water moves into cells. Either change can disrupt cell function, so the concentrations of water and solutes must be controlled. The body loses water in breathing, sweating and urine, so water balance is dynamic and must be regulated. (5 marks)
  9. Explain the link between respiration and muscle activity during exercise and why sustained vigorous exercise can exceed the body’s aerobic capacity for a time. Answer: Muscle activity uses ATP, so respiration must increase to supply ATP; aerobic respiration is efficient and sustainable if oxygen supply is sufficient, but during vigorous exercise oxygen delivery may not keep up with demand, so the muscle relies relatively more on pathways that do not need oxygen and produces different products, which is why breathing and heart rate rise and why the body shifts its metabolism. (5 marks)
  10. State what the kidneys do to help maintain the internal environment. Answer: The kidneys remove waste from the blood and help control water and solute balance by adjusting the composition of the urine, so they are important for maintaining the composition of the internal environment and for disposing of the waste products of metabolism including the CO2-related and other wastes that result from respiration. (4 marks)
  11. Describe one example of negative feedback in the human body and identify the receptor, control centre and effector in that example. Answer: In temperature control, temperature receptors detect a rise in core or skin temperature, the hypothalamus acts as the control centre, and effectors such as sweat glands and skin blood vessels respond by increasing heat loss, returning temperature toward the set point. If temperature falls, effectors such as shivering and vasoconstriction reduce heat loss or increase heat production. (5 marks)

Revise this topic by matching each numbered specification point to one mechanism, one location and one reason. Practise the respiration stages and their products, the sliding filament idea with ATP and calcium, the exercise responses and the thermoregulation responses, and the homeostasis and negative feedback principle with examples. Check that you can say where each process happens and why, not just what happens. Then move on to the next topic and the related practicals, because the practicals are the way the specification ties the ideas to hands-on work.
content:
Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment — Edexcel International A2 Level Biology

This revision note covers the biology topics that sit behind the energy use of cells and animals and behind the maintenance of the internal environment. It is built around the specification statements rather than around a loose theme, so each numbered section reflects one or more things the specification expects a candidate to be able to do. The note is deliberately at exam depth: it explains the reasoning, gives the worked examples and comparisons that examiners look for, and lists the common mistakes that lose marks in this topic. Use it to check what you actually know and to practise the kinds of answer the specification rewards.

1. Why respiration matters and what the topic is for

Respiration is the set of reactions that release energy from nutrient molecules and couple that energy to the work cells do. The main nutrient in most questions is glucose, and the main energy currency that respiration produces is ATP. The practical point is that cells do not get energy directly from glucose; they get it from ATP, and respiration is the process that links the fuel to the currency. Understanding respiration therefore means understanding where the energy comes from, how the cell captures it, and how that energy is used in muscles and in the rest of the body.

The topic also connects to the internal environment, because muscles and tissues can only work properly if the internal conditions stay within limits, and because the energy demand of the body changes when muscles work. The link between respiration, muscles and the internal environment is that exercise changes the demand for ATP, which changes the demand for oxygen and fuel and the production of waste, and the internal environment has to respond. If you see the topic as one connected question about supply, demand and control, the parts will fit together rather than staying as separate facts.

2. Aerobic respiration as a sequence of stages, not a single reaction

Aerobic respiration is not one enzyme-controlled reaction but a sequence of stages: the stages are glycolysis, the link reaction, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm and breaks glucose into pyruvate, producing a small amount of ATP and reduced NAD. The link reaction and the Krebs cycle happen in the mitochondrial matrix and produce reduced coenzymes and carbon dioxide. Oxidative phosphorylation happens in the inner mitochondrial membrane and uses the reduced coenzymes to make the bulk of the ATP and to reduce oxygen to water.

The important idea is that respiration is staged: each stage does a specific job and the stages are connected. Glycolysis starts the breakdown of glucose. The link reaction converts pyruvate and removes carbon dioxide. The Krebs cycle oxidises the acetyl group and harvests hydrogen. Oxidative phosphorylation harvests the energy from the hydrogen and passes it to ATP. A good answer says that respiration is staged, gives the four stages in order, and says where each occurs. It does not say that respiration is a single reaction that turns glucose into ATP in one step, because that is not what happens and it loses marks.

A good answer also says that oxygen is the final electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation and that this is why the process is aerobic: without oxygen the chain stops and ATP production from oxidative phosphorylation stops. The link between oxygen and ATP is one of the reasons aerobic respiration yields more ATP than anaerobic alternatives, because the full oxidation is completed and the hydrogen carriers can be re-oxidised at the end of the chain. If you can say that, you have the aerobic idea in a form that scores marks.

3. Glycolysis: the investment and payoff phases and the net yield

Glycolysis is the first stage of respiration and it happens in the cytoplasm. It phosphorylates glucose, splits the phosphorylated intermediate, and then oxidises triose phosphate, producing pyruvate, a small net yield of ATP and reduced NAD. The investment phase uses ATP to phosphorylate glucose and its intermediates; the payoff phase produces the ATP and reduced NAD that make glycolysis worth doing.

The classic net yield for the overall equation taught in this specification is often stated as producing a small amount of ATP per glucose, with the rest coming later from the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. The important point is not to memorise only the number but to understand that glycolysis produces pyruvate, ATP and reduced NAD, and that the ATP comes from substrate-level phosphorylation, while the reduced NAD is a carrier of hydrogen that will feed into oxidative phosphorylation if oxygen is available. A good answer says that glycolysis phosphorylates glucose, splits it, oxidises triose phosphate, produces pyruvate and a small amount of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and produces reduced NAD. It does not say that glycolysis makes the most ATP, because it does not; that comes later.

The intermediate phosphorylation is the reason glycolysis is not just a simple split. Glucose has to be primed with phosphate so that it can be split and so that the triose phosphate can be oxidised. The ATP investment at the start pays off later, which is why the net yield is what it is. If you can say that, you have the logic of glycolysis rather than just a list of steps.

4. The link reaction and the Krebs cycle: decarboxylation and hydrogen harvesting

The link reaction converts pyruvate into acetyl coenzyme A, releasing carbon dioxide and reducing NAD. The Krebs cycle then oxidises the acetyl group, releasing more carbon dioxide, producing ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and generating reduced NAD and reduced FAD. The carbon dioxide released in these stages is the CO2 that the cell, and the organism, must dispose of, and the hydrogen carried by the reduced coenzymes is what feeds oxidative phosphorylation.

The link reaction is the bridge between glycolysis and the Krebs cycle. Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion, is oxidised and decarboxylated to form the acetyl group, which is attached to coenzyme A. The Krebs cycle then uses the acetyl group to regenerate oxaloacetate and to produce the reduced coenzymes and substrate-level phosphorylation that are the point of the cycle. A good answer says that the link reaction converts pyruvate to acetyl coenzyme A with release of CO2 and reduced NAD, and that the Krebs cycle oxidises the acetyl group with release of CO2, production of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and production of reduced NAD and reduced FAD. It does not say that the Krebs cycle happens in the cytosol, because it happens in the mitochondrial matrix. It also does not say that the Krebs cycle is the stage that uses oxygen, because oxygen is used in oxidative phosphorylation, not in the cycle itself.

The main conceptual point of the Krebs cycle is that it is a cycle that oxidises a two-carbon acetyl group and harvests hydrogen, releasing carbon dioxide along the way. The ATP made by substrate-level phosphorylation in the cycle is small compared with the ATP from oxidative phosphorylation, but the cycle’s real job is to supply the reduced coenzymes. If you can say that, you have the role of the Krebs cycle rather than just a sequence of intermediates.

5. Oxidative phosphorylation and the role of the inner membrane and oxygen

Oxidative phosphorylation is the stage that makes the most ATP and the stage where oxygen is used. It happens on the inner mitochondrial membrane, where the reduced coenzymes deliver hydrogen and the energy from the electrons is used to pump protons, creating a proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis as protons flow back through ATP synthase. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor at the end of the chain, and water is formed.

The key point is that ATP is made by chemiosmosis, not by a single enzyme directly handing a phosphate to ADP. Energy from the electron transport chain is used to pump protons from the matrix to the intermembrane space, and the resulting proton gradient is what drives ATP synthesis when protons flow back through ATP synthase. Oxygen accepts the electrons at the end of the chain and combines with protons to form water, so without oxygen the chain stops and the gradient cannot be maintained. A good answer says that oxidative phosphorylation happens on the inner mitochondrial membrane, that the energy from the electrons pumps protons, that the proton gradient drives ATP synthesis through ATP synthase, and that oxygen is the final electron acceptor forming water. It does not say that ATP is made directly by the electron transport chain itself; it is made by ATP synthase using the proton gradient.

The distinction between the electron transport chain and ATP synthase is important because it is one of the places where a lack of precision loses marks. The chain creates the gradient; ATP synthase uses it. If you keep that distinction clear, you can explain why a poison that blocks the chain, or a lack of oxygen, stops ATP production. The model is also the reason that the inner membrane is folded into cristae: it increases the surface area for the proteins of the chain and for ATP synthase. If you can say that, you have connected the structure to the function.

6. ATP as the energy currency and why respiration is staged

ATP is the immediate energy currency that respiration supplies to the cell. The energy for most cellular processes does not come directly from glucose or food; it comes from the hydrolysis of ATP. Respiration exists so that the energy in food can be used to regenerate ATP, and then the ATP can be used for endergonic processes, active transport, movement and biosynthesis. The role of ATP is to act as a small, reusable and immediately available packet of energy that can be used where and when it is needed.

The reason respiration is staged rather than a single big burn is that staged release is more controllable and more efficient in the biological sense. The energy is not released all at once as heat, but in a way that the cell can use to phosphorylate ADP; the carrier molecules handle the hydrogen and the energy between stages; and the stages can be regulated according to the cell’s needs. A good answer says that respiration is staged so that the energy is released in manageable amounts that the cell can use to make ATP, and that ATP is the energy currency used by the cell. It does not say that the stages are only for historical reasons or that the cell could simply burn glucose in one step for the same practical result, because the control and capture are the point.

The link between ATP and work is that ATP hydrolysis is endergonic to reverse but exergonic in the cell’s direction, so it provides energy for processes that would not otherwise occur. The cell uses ATP to drive active transport, to drive movement including muscle contraction, and to drive biosynthesis, and respiration is what keeps the ATP supply up. If you can say that, you have the currency idea in a form that scores marks.

7. Contraction as sliding filaments, not shortening of the filaments themselves

Muscle contraction works by the sliding filament model, not by the filaments shortening. The actin and myosin filaments slide past one another, so the sarcomere shortens even though the filaments themselves do not get shorter. The thick filaments are myosin, the thin filaments are actin, and the contraction happens when myosin heads bind to actin, pivot, release and re-bind further along, pulling the thin filament past the thick one.

The important point is that contraction is sliding, and that the length of the filaments does not change. A good answer says that during contraction the filaments slide past each other so the sarcomere shortens, that the filaments themselves do not shorten, and that myosin heads bind to actin and pivot to pull the thin filament past the thick one. It does not say that the filaments shorten; it says that they slide. That is one of the most common mistakes in this topic, because it is easy to think that contraction means the filaments get shorter when it actually means they get closer together and the overlap increases.

The energy for the sliding is provided by ATP. ATP is used both to power the power stroke and to detach the myosin head so the cycle can repeat. The calcium ions that are released into the sarcoplasm when the muscle is stimulated allow the myosin head to bind to actin in the first place. The full story is therefore ATP plus calcium plus the filament arrangement, but the most important exam point is the sliding filament idea itself. If you can say that, you have the contraction idea in a form that scores marks.

8. The role of ATP and calcium in the contraction cycle

The contraction cycle uses ATP and calcium. Calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum when the muscle is stimulated, and the calcium allows the myosin head to bind to actin by exposing the binding sites. ATP then is used to break the myosin-actin link and re-cock the myosin head, and another ATP is hydrolysed to position the head for the next stroke. When calcium is removed and the binding sites are covered again, the muscle relaxes.

A good answer says that calcium exposes the actin binding sites so myosin can bind, that ATP is used to break the cross-bridge and re-cock the head, and that the cycle is powered by ATP hydrolysis. It also says that relaxation happens when calcium is removed and the binding sites are covered. It does not say that relaxation uses no ATP, because it does not; the detachment and repositioning of myosin need ATP, and that is one reason rigor mortis happens, because ATP is no longer available and the myosin stays bound. If you can say that, you have the energy story of contraction in a form that scores marks.

The calcium role is essential, not optional. Without calcium, the myosin heads cannot bind to actin and the muscle cannot contract, even if ATP is present. ATP alone is not enough; you need calcium to start the cycle and ATP to keep it going. If you can keep that distinction clear, you can answer the question correctly and avoid the common mistake of saying that ATP alone is what starts contraction.

9. ATP supply during exercise and the limits of aerobic capacity

During exercise the demand for ATP rises, and the rate of respiration must rise to match it. Aerobic respiration can supply ATP for sustained moderate exercise, but when the rate of demand exceeds the rate at which oxygen can be supplied, the muscle shifts toward anaerobic pathways and the balance of products changes. The point is that exercise is a test of the energy supply system and of the system that supports it, including breathing and circulation.

Aerobic respiration is efficient and sustainable, but it depends on oxygen delivery. If oxygen delivery cannot keep up, the cell relies more on pathways that do not need as much oxygen, and this changes the products. A good answer says that aerobic respiration supplies ATP efficiently but needs oxygen, that during strenuous exercise the demand may outstrip oxygen supply, and that this forces a shift in the balance of ATP production. It does not say that the muscle simply switches off aerobic respiration and does nothing else; it says that the balance shifts. The energy story is continuous, not a simple on-off switch.

The practical point is that sustained exercise depends on the ability to deliver oxygen and remove waste, which is why breathing and heart rate rise. The biology here ties respiration, muscle and the internal environment together, because the muscle cannot work unless the supply system keeps up and the internal conditions stay tolerable. If you can see that, you can answer the questions that link the parts, which are often where the higher marks are.

10. The response to exercise: heart rate, breathing rate and breathing volume

During exercise, heart rate, breathing rate and the volume of air breathed per breath all increase. The heart pumps faster and harder to deliver more oxygenated blood to the muscles and to remove more carbon dioxide and heat. Breathing increases in frequency and depth to bring in more oxygen and to remove more carbon dioxide. The point is that the body responds to the higher demand on several fronts at once.

The increase in breathing is not just faster breathing; it is also deeper breathing, so the volume of air exchanged per minute rises more than the rate alone would suggest. The increase in heart rate rises the rate of blood delivery, and a stronger heartbeat can also increase the stroke volume, so the cardiac output rises. A good answer says that during exercise breathing rate and depth increase, that heart rate increases, and that these changes raise the supply of oxygen and the removal of carbon dioxide and heat. It does not say that only breathing rate changes, because depth matters too. It does not say that the heart only beats faster, because the strength of the beat can change as well.

A common mistake is to describe the response to exercise only in terms of breathing, or only in terms of heart rate, when the question asks for both. A good answer gives both and links them, because they are part of the same supply system. The internal environment is what both systems are serving: without the increased supply, the muscles cannot work and the internal conditions would drift out of limits. If you can say that, you have the response in a form that scores marks.

11. Thermoregulation, vasodilation and vasoconstriction, and the control of heat loss

Thermoregulation is the control of body temperature, which is part of homeostasis. The body controls heat loss and heat production to keep temperature within limits. When the body needs to lose heat, blood vessels near the skin surface dilate, allowing more blood flow near the surface so heat is lost to the environment; this is vasodilation. When the body needs to conserve heat, those vessels constrict, reducing blood flow near the surface and reducing heat loss; this is vasoconstriction.

A good answer says that vasodilation increases blood flow near the skin surface and increases heat loss, and that vasoconstriction reduces blood flow near the surface and reduces heat loss. It does not say that vasodilation happens only when it is hot and vasoconstriction only when it is cold, as absolute rules, though that is the typical pattern, because the system is about control, not just a fixed setting. The deeper point is that the skin blood flow is one of the ways the body moves heat around and loses it, and that the control is part of homeostasis.

Other responses to overheating may include sweating, which cools by evaporation, and behavioural changes. Responses to cold include shivering and reducing heat loss by vasoconstriction. The important idea is that the body has both heat-loss and heat-production responses, and that homeothermy is maintained by balancing them. A good answer says that the body controls temperature by adjusting heat loss and heat production, names vasodilation and vasoconstriction as examples of changing heat loss, and mentions that the responses are part of homeostasis. If you can say that, you have the thermoregulation idea in a form that scores marks.

12. The concept of the internal environment and why homeostasis matters

The internal environment is the fluid environment around the cells, and homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite changes outside and inside. The idea is important because cells can only work properly within a limited range of conditions, so the internal environment has to be kept within those limits: water balance, temperature, pH and the concentrations of substances have to be controlled, and respiration and exercise put demands on all of them.

Homeostasis is not a single process but a collection of control systems. Negative feedback is the main control principle, in which a change from the set point is detected and the system acts to bring it back. A good answer says that homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment, that cells can only function within narrow limits, and that negative feedback is the main control mechanism. It does not say that the internal environment never changes, because it does change; it says that it is kept within limits. That is the difference between a mark-scoring answer and one that treats homeostasis as meaning no change at all.

The link to respiration and muscles is that exercise stresses the internal environment: it produces heat, carbon dioxide and water, changes pH in the tissues and the blood, and demands more fuel and oxygen. Homeostasis has to cope with all of that, and that is why the topic brings together respiration, muscles and internal environment control. If you can say that, you have the unifying idea that makes the topic more than three separate lists.

13. Negative feedback and the way control systems work

Negative feedback is the main control principle in homeostasis. A change away from the set point is detected by a receptor, the information is passed to a control centre, and effectors act to reduce the change and bring the variable back toward the set point. The effect opposes the change, which is why it is called negative feedback. This is the principle behind temperature control, blood glucose control and the control of many other variables.

A good answer describes the components of a negative feedback system: receptor, coordination or control centre and effector, and says that the response reduces the original change. It does not describe positive feedback as the main homeostatic mechanism, because positive feedback amplifies the change and is used in a small number of cases such as childbirth, not as the general principle. The general principle is negative feedback, and the exam questions on this topic usually test that principle. If you can say that, you have the control idea in a form that scores marks.

The point of negative feedback is that it reduces the error from the set point. It does not have to eliminate the change entirely; real systems have a normal range. A good answer therefore does not say that homeostasis keeps every variable exactly constant at all times; it says that it keeps the variable within a normal range by opposing deviations. If you can say that, you have the principle and its limitations both correct.

14. Water and solute balance, and why the internal environment has to manage them

The internal environment has to manage water and solute balance because cells depend on the water potential of their surroundings. If the internal environment is too concentrated, water leaves cells by osmosis; if it is too dilute, water enters cells. Either can disrupt cell function. The control of water and solute balance is therefore part of homeostasis, and it connects to respiration and muscles because the body gains and loses water through breathing, sweating and urine, and because the balance matters for the tissues that are doing the work.

A good answer says that water and solute balance are part of homeostasis, that cells depend on the water potential of the internal environment, and that changes in water potential can move water by osmosis and affect cell function. It does not say that water balance is only about drinking, because the body also loses water in breathing, sweating and urine, and gains it in food and drink. The point is that the balance is dynamic and has to be controlled. If you can say that, you have the water-balance idea in a form that scores marks.

The link to respiration is that breathing loses water vapour, so respiration and breathing are part of the water balance as well as part of the gas exchange. The link to exercise is that sweating loses both water and heat, so the same response that cools can also disturb water balance. If you can see those links, you can answer questions that cross the parts, which are common at this level.

15. The role of the kidneys in the internal environment, briefly and at the right level

The kidneys are central to the internal environment because they control the composition of the urine and so the balance of water, ions and waste products in the blood. They remove waste from the blood and adjust the water and solute content of the body. In this topic the kidneys matter because they are one of the systems that keeps the internal environment within limits, and because the products of respiration have to be dealt with by the body as a whole.

A good answer describes the kidneys as organs that remove waste from the blood and help control water and solute balance, and links them to homeostasis and to the disposal of waste from respiration. It does not overreach by describing every nephron detail if the question does not ask for it; the key point is the role in the internal environment. The kidneys are part of the disposal and balance system that allows respiration and exercise to happen without wrecking the internal conditions. If you can say that, you have the right level.

The important idea is that the body is an integrated system: respiration makes ATP and produces waste, muscles use ATP and produce heat and waste, and the internal environment systems, including the kidneys, breathing and thermoregulation, keep the whole thing within limits. If you can see the integration, you can answer the questions that ask for the links, which are often the best-marked ones.

16. CPIR and the iodide concentration problem; the direction of control

The basics of thermoregulation include the idea that blood vessel diameter in the skin changes to control heat loss, and that the control is part of homeostasis. The anatomy point that is often tested is which vessels are involved and how they control the flow near the surface. In the skin, arteriole vasodilation and vasoconstriction change the flow to superficial vessels, and the presence of a rich superficial vessel bed lets the skin lose more heat when it is hot and conserve more when it is cold.

A good answer says that vasodilation near the skin surface increases heat loss and vasoconstriction near the skin surface reduces it, and that this is part of the way the body controls temperature. It does not say that the skin is the only place where this happens, or that the control is the only thermoregulatory response, because sweating, shivering and behaviour also matter. The point is to include the skin response correctly as part of the system, not to pretend it is the whole system. If you can say that, you have the idea in a form that scores marks.

The direction of control matters: more flow near the surface when hot, less when cold. A common mistake is to invert the relationship, so the answer says vasodilation happens in the cold, which is wrong. If you keep the direction straight, you can avoid that mistake. The reason the direction matters is that the surface vessels are the main route for losing heat to the environment, so opening them loses heat and closing them conserves it. If you can say that, you have both the direction and the reason.

17. Heat gain, heat loss, and the difference between conserving and producing heat

The body has two broad ways of dealing with cold: conserve the heat it has and make more heat. Vasoconstriction conserves heat by reducing loss from the skin surface. Shivering produces heat by making muscles contract repeatedly, which costs ATP and releases heat. Behavioural changes such as curling up, putting on clothing or moving to a warmer place also help. A good answer says that the body can conserve heat by vasoconstriction and produce heat by shivering and by other means, and that both are part of thermoregulation and homeostasis.

The distinction between conserving and producing heat is useful, because it helps explain why the responses are not all the same kind of thing. Vasoconstriction reduces loss; shivering increases production. A good answer makes that distinction, because it shows that the body has more than one tool for the job and that the tools work differently. If you can say that, you have a better answer than one that just lists “shivering, vasoconstriction” without saying what each does.

The energy angle is important too, because shivering uses ATP and therefore links back to respiration. Shivering keeps you warm by burning fuel, so it is not free; it increases the demand for ATP and therefore for oxygen and fuel. That is the kind of connection that examiners like, because it ties the topic together. If you can say that shivering increases respiratory demand, you have the link between thermoregulation and respiration.

18. The internal environment under exercise stress: what is pushed and what copes

Exercise pushes several variables at once, which is why the topic groups respiration, muscles and the internal environment. Muscles use ATP faster, so respiration must deliver more ATP, which raises the demand for oxygen and fuel and increases the production of carbon dioxide and heat. The heart and lungs respond to meet the oxygen demand and to remove the carbon dioxide. Thermoregulation responds to the heat. Water and solute balance are affected by sweating and by the increased rate of exchange. The overall point is that exercise is a stress test for homeostasis.

A good answer says that exercise raises ATP demand, that respiration and the supply systems respond, that more carbon dioxide and heat are produced, and that the internal environment systems, including breathing, circulation and thermoregulation, have to cope with the change. It does not just list the responses; it says that the internal environment has to keep working despite the stress. That is the unifying idea, and it is why the topic is taught as a unit rather than as three unrelated parts. If you can say that, you have the big picture in a form that scores marks.

A common mistake is to describe the responses as if they were isolated, with no mention of what they are responding to. A good answer links the response to the demand: the heart rate rises because the muscles need more oxygen; the breathing rises because the body needs to supply oxygen and remove carbon dioxide; the cooling responses rise because exercise generates heat. If you can make those links, you are answering at the higher level. The detail is only as good as the reasoning behind it.

19. How to read a respiration question and what examiners want

When a question asks about respiration, the examiner usually wants the pathway and the logic behind it, not just the final number. Say what the stages are, where they are, what they produce and why the process is staged and aerobic. If the question asks about the role of oxygen, say that oxygen is the final electron acceptor and that this is what allows oxidative phosphorylation to continue. If the question asks about ATP yield, say that most ATP comes from oxidative phosphorylation and that glycolysis and the Krebs cycle contribute smaller amounts by substrate-level phosphorylation. If you can do that, you can read the question the way the specification intends.

For muscles, the examiner usually wants the sliding filament idea, the role of ATP and calcium, and the reason the filaments do not shorten. If the question asks about contraction, say that the filaments slide past each other so the sarcomere shortens, that myosin heads bind to actin and pivot, that ATP powers the cycle and is needed for detachment, and that calcium exposes the binding sites. If you can do that, you can answer the muscle questions correctly and avoid the common mistake of saying that the filaments shorten.

For the internal environment, the examiner usually wants homeostasis, negative feedback, the key variables that are controlled, and the way the body responds to exercise or to temperature change. If the question asks about the response to exercise, include both heart rate and breathing rate and volume, and explain what each is doing. If the question asks about thermoregulation, include vasodilation and vasoconstriction and the direction of control. If you can do that, you can answer the internal environment questions at the right level.

20. How the parts connect: respiration powers muscles, muscles stress the internal environment, the internal environment has to cope

The topic is really about a chain: respiration makes ATP, muscles use ATP to do work, and the work changes the internal environment so the control systems have to respond. Respiration supplies ATP from glucose; the ATP is used for muscle contraction and for other cell work; muscle work produces heat and carbon dioxide and stresses the water and solute balance; the body responds by increasing supply and by controlling the internal conditions. The chain is why the topic is grouped together: the parts belong to the same system, even though they are listed under different headings.

A good answer can trace the chain: glucose to respiration to ATP to muscle contraction, muscle contraction to heat and CO2 production, heat to thermoregulation and CO2 to breathing and circulation. It can say that the internal environment system has to keep the body within limits while the muscles demand more and the metabolism produces more waste. It does not treat respiration, muscles and internal environment as three unrelated topics; it treats them as parts of one metabolic and homeostatic picture. That is what the topic is for, and it is what the better questions are testing. If you can see the chain, you can answer the questions that span the parts, which are often where the higher marks are.

21. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use this note by working through each section and checking that you can describe the stages of aerobic respiration and where they occur; explain the reason respiration is staged and aerobic; describe glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle; describe oxidative phosphorylation and the role of the inner membrane and oxygen; explain the role of ATP as the energy currency; describe the sliding filament model of contraction and say that the filaments do not shorten; describe the role of ATP and calcium in the contraction cycle; explain ATP supply during exercise and the limits of aerobic capacity; describe the response to exercise in breathing rate, breathing depth and heart rate; describe thermoregulation including vasodilation, vasoconstriction, shivering and other heat-loss and heat-production responses; explain homeostasis and negative feedback; and explain water and solute balance and the role of the kidneys in the internal environment. After this topic, revise the related systems, because the associations matter and the best questions ask for the links.

The note is long because the topic is broad and the specification asks for the biology behind the everyday events of exercise, temperature control and energy supply. A revision note has to cover the respiration pathway, the contraction mechanism, the exercise responses and the homeostasis principles in enough detail to be useful, and it has to link them, because the exam questions do. Study it section by section, check yourself against the specification statements, and practise the kinds of answer that explain rather than list. Then move on to the next topic and the related practicals, because the practicals are the way the specification ties the ideas to hands-on work.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying that respiration is one reaction that turns glucose straight into ATP, instead of a sequence of stages.
  • Saying the filaments shorten during contraction, instead of sliding past each other.
  • Saying that ATP alone starts contraction, instead of calcium exposing the binding sites first.
  • Saying the Krebs cycle happens in the cytoplasm, or that it is where oxygen is used.
  • Saying ATP is made directly by the electron transport chain, instead of by ATP synthase using the proton gradient.
  • Forgetting that oxygen is the final electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation.
  • Saying that breathing rate alone is the response to exercise, forgetting breathing depth and heart rate.
  • Inverting vasodilation and vasoconstriction, so vasodilation is linked to cold and vasoconstriction to heat.
  • Treating homeostasis as meaning the internal environment never changes, instead of staying within limits by negative feedback.
  • Forgetting that sweating and breathing both affect water balance, not just drinking and urine.
