title: Probability and Statistics I
content:
Probability and Statistics I

Permutations and Combinations

  • Permutations (order matters): ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!
  • Combinations (order irrelevant): ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!)

Example: choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people: C(8,3) = 56. Arranging 3 of 8 books on a shelf: P(8,3) = 336.

Probability Rules

  • P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
  • Independent events: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)
  • Complement: P(A′) = 1 − P(A)

Conditional Probability

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Tree diagrams multiply along branches and add across outcomes.

Example: P(two reds without replacement from 5 red + 3 blue) = (5/8)(4/7) = 5/14.

Discrete Random Variables

E(X) = Σ x P(X = x); Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².

Example: die: E(X) = 3.5; E(X²) = 91/6, so Var(X) ≈ 2.92.

Exam tips: decide permutation vs combination by testing whether swapping two items changes the outcome; always verify tree-branch probabilities sum to 1.

title: Complex Numbers — Study Notes
content:
Complex Numbers

Basics

i² = −1. A complex number z = a + bi has real part a and imaginary part b. Two numbers are equal iff both parts match.

Arithmetic: add/subtract parts; multiply with brackets and replace i² with −1.

Example: (2 + 3i)(1 − i) = 2 − 2i + 3i − 3i² = 5 + i.

Conjugates

z̄ = a − bi. zz̄ = a² + b² (real). Dividing: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate.

Example: 1/(3 − i) × (3 + i)/(3 + i) = (3 + i)/10.

Argand Diagram

Plot z as the point (a, b). |z| = √(a² + b²) is the modulus (distance from origin); arg z = tan⁻¹(b/a) is the argument (angle). Multiply two numbers: moduli multiply, arguments add.

Modulus–Argument Form

z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), r = |z|, θ = arg z. Useful for powers and roots.

de Moivre and Roots

[r(cos θ + i sin θ)]ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).

Example: (1 + i)⁸: |1 + i| = √2, arg = π/4, so z⁸ = (√2)⁸ cis 2π = 16.

An nth root gives n evenly spaced solutions, 2π/n apart on a circle of radius r^(1/n).

Exam tips: always give arguments in the required interval; when solving equations, remember complex roots come in conjugate pairs for real polynomials.

title: Edexcel IAL AS Biology: Molecules, Transport and Health Revision Notes
content:
Quick revision: Molecules, Transport and Health

Biology — AS. Edexcel IAL Biology WBI11, Topic 1. Living things are built from a small set of biological molecules. Their structure decides how they are used, how substances move in and out of cells, and how diet affects health.

Key areas to revise

  • Carbohydrates
  • Lipids and proteins
  • Enzymes
  • Transport
  • Health

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Core Biological Molecules & Water

Water is an important solvent for transport due to its dipole nature, forming hydrogen bonds. Carbohydrates consist of monosaccharides, disaccharides, and polysaccharides, including glycogen and starch (amylose and amylopectin), relating their structures to energy roles. Monosaccharides such as glucose, fructose, and galactose join via condensation reactions forming glycosidic bonds to create disaccharides like maltose, sucrose, and lactose, and polysaccharides, which split via hydrolysis. Core Practical 1 uses semi-quantitative Benedict's reagent for reducing sugars and iodine solution for starch with colour standards. Triglycerides form via condensation between glycerol and three fatty acids creating ester bonds, differing from saturated lipids lacking double bonds and unsaturated lipids containing carbon-carbon double bonds. Amino acids possess a basic structure with an amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen, and an R group, linking via condensation into peptide bonds forming polypeptides. Primary structure determines secondary structure (alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets via hydrogen bonding) and three-dimensional tertiary/quaternary structure, categorised into globular proteins (like haemoglobin) and fibrous proteins (like collagen) stabilised by hydrogen, ionic, and disulfide bonds. Core Practical uses biuret reagent and colour standards to estimate protein concentration.

Enzymes & Gas Exchange

Enzymes act as biological catalysts inside cells (intracellular) or outside (extracellular), reducing activation energy. Their three-dimensional active site provides high specificity for substrates, explained by the lock and key and induced fit models. Core Practical 4 investigates the effect of temperature, pH, enzyme concentration, and substrate concentration on initial reaction rates. Gas exchange surfaces require a large surface area to volume ratio, short diffusion distance (thinness), and a steep concentration gradient. Fick's Law calculates the rate of diffusion as proportional to (surface area × concentration difference) / thickness. Mammalian lungs adapt via millions of alveoli, a rich capillary network, and thin squamous epithelium for rapid gas exchange.

Transport & The Cardiovascular System

Mass transport in a mammalian heart and circulation overcomes the limitations of diffusion in meeting organism requirements. Blood vessels have distinct structures: arteries possess thick walls with elastic tissue and smooth muscle to withstand high pressure; veins have wider lumens, valves, and thinner walls; capillaries consist of a single layer of endothelial cells for rapid exchange. The cardiac cycle comprises atrial systole, ventricular systole, and cardiac diastole, operating via valves and pressure gradients driven by the mammalian heart and major blood vessels (aorta, vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein), excluding myogenic stimulation details at IAS. Recommended additional practical involves dissection of a mammalian heart. Haemoglobin transports oxygen and carbon dioxide, showing an oxygen dissociation curve with cooperative binding, the Bohr effect where high carbon dioxide partial pressure shifts the curve right, and fetal haemoglobin exhibiting higher oxygen affinity than adult haemoglobin.

Cardiovascular Disease (CVD), Health & Risk Factors

Atherosclerosis begins with endothelial dysfunction, leading to an inflammatory response, white blood cell accumulation, plaque (atheroma) formation, and raised blood pressure. The blood clotting process involves thromboplastin release, converting prothrombin into thrombin, which then converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads, creating a mesh that traps blood cells and can trigger CVD. Risk factors for CVD include genetics, diet, age, gender, high blood pressure, smoking, and physical inactivity. Dietary antioxidants reduce CVD risk. Core Practical 2 investigates vitamin C content in food and drink. Illness and mortality data analysis requires distinguishing between correlation and causation, recognising conflicting evidence, and evaluating study designs for sample selection and sample size validity and reliability. People often misperceive health risks, underestimating or overestimating lifestyle risks like diet. Blood cholesterol levels, high-density lipoproteins (HDLs), and low-density lipoproteins (LDLs) provide causal evidence linking high LDL and total cholesterol to CVD. Public health measures utilise body mass index (BMI) and waist-to-hip ratio as obesity indicators alongside diet, exercise, and smoking cessation to reduce coronary heart disease risk. CVD medical treatments carry both benefits and risks, including antihypertensives, statins, anticoagulants, and platelet inhibitors.

Worked example

Calculate the rate of diffusion using Fick's Law if the surface area is 200 mm squared, the concentration difference is 50 arbitrary units, and the membrane thickness is 0.05 mm. Step 1: Multiply surface area by concentration difference (200 × 50 = 10000). Step 2: Divide by thickness (10000 ÷ 0.05 = 200000). Answer: 200000 arbitrary units per second.

Key points to remember

Students often confuse condensation with hydrolysis; remember condensation releases water and forms bonds (glycosidic, ester, peptide), whilst hydrolysis breaks bonds using water. When discussing Fick's Law, always state that rate is directly proportional to surface area and concentration gradient, and inversely proportional to thickness.

In data analysis questions regarding health risks, never state correlation proves causation unless a clear mechanism is explained and confounding variables are controlled. Ensure you can differentiate between the protective role of HDLs carrying cholesterol to the liver and the harmful accumulation of LDLs forming plaques.

How to use this: read the full notes for any weak areas and complete the topic quiz.

title: Exam technique: Sine and Cosine Rules
content:
### What earns the marks
For the sine rule, the matched pairs written (b / sin 65 = 7 / sin 40) earn the method mark. For the cosine rule, the full substitution with cos evaluated earns the mark: write a squared = 25 + 64 - 2 x 5 x 8 x 0.5. For the largest angle, identifying the longest side first earns credit. For area, half a b sin C quoted earns the mark on its own.
### Traps
Error: sides paired with wrong angles in the sine rule. Correction: each side faces its angle. Error: 49 given as side a. Correction: root the cosine-rule result. Error: calculator-only acute angle for an obtuse ambiguous case. Correction: subtract from 180 by hand. Error: half a b without sine for a non-right triangle. Correction: area needs the sine factor unless the angle is 90 degrees.
### Worked example
Two sides are 7 cm and 9 cm, with an included angle of 40 degrees. The cosine rule gives x^2 = 7^2 + 9^2 - 2 x 7 x 9 x cos 40 = 130 - 126 x 0.766 = 33.5, so x is about 5.79 cm. Use the cosine rule when you have two sides and the angle between them.
### Check yourself
A right-angled triangle has legs 6 and 8. Compute the area as one half of 6 x 8 x sin 90 degrees, and the hypotenuse with the cosine rule. The area is 24, and the hypotenuse is sqrt(36 + 64) = 10, because cos 90 degrees is zero.

title: Electricity & Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity & Circuits

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): simple circuits, current, p.d., resistance, series/parallel, electrical safety, practical electricity.

1. Circuit symbols & current

Conventional current: + → − (electron flow opposite). I = Q/t. Ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel.

2. Current, p.d., e.m.f.

  • Current: rate of charge flow; same everywhere in series.
  • p.d.: energy per coulomb across a component; e.m.f.: electrical energy per coulomb given by the source.

3. Resistance

  • R = V/I. Ohmic conductor: V ∝ I at constant temperature.
  • Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + …; same current; p.d. shares in proportion to R.
  • Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂; same p.d.; current splits (inverse-R share).
  • Resistance ∝ length, ∝ 1/area (wires).

4. Components

Fixed/variable resistors, LDR (light ↑ R ↓), thermistor (T ↑ R ↓), diode/LED (one-way), relay, filament lamp (R grows as T rises — V–I curve flattens).

5. Power and energy

P = VI = I²R = V²/R; E = VIt. Fuse rating just above normal current; earth wire, double insulation, circuit breakers (trip quickly, resettable).

Example: 230 V, 2 A heater: P = 460 W; correct fuse 3 A or 5 A.

6. Digital electronics basics (syllabus 4.5 context)

Analogue vs digital; logic gates drive outputs from inputs (see CS link); sensors feed comparator-style circuits.

Exam tips: series: current same; parallel: p.d. same — say which before calculating; always compute total resistance first in mixed circuits.

title: Networking & Communication — Study Notes
content:
Networking & Communication

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): transmission modes, serial/parallel, packet switching, protocols, LAN/WAN, hardware, security layers.

1. Transmission basics

  • Serial: one bit at a time — reliable over distance, cheaper cable.
  • Parallel: several bits at once — faster over short runs; skew/crosstalk limit distance.
  • Simplex / half-duplex / full-duplex direction; bandwidth (bits/s) vs bit rate.

2. Packets

Header (sender/receiver addresses, sequence number) + payload + trailer (checksum). Packet switching: routes vary, packets reassembled at destination; checksum failure → re-request. Benefits: robustness, shared lines; delays/reassembly overhead.

3. Protocols

TCP/IP stack layers (application, transport, network, link). HTTP/HTTPS (TLS encryption), FTP (with login + commands), email: SMTP send, POP3/IMAP retrieve. Bluetooth/Wi-Fi for WPAN/WLAN.

4. Network types & hardware

LAN (site) vs WAN (internet). Router (joins networks, IP), switch (MAC frames within LAN), gateway (protocol translation), NIC, WAP. MAC address (burned-in, layer 2) vs IP address (assigned, layer 3).

5. Security in transmission

Encryption scrambles plaintext → ciphertext (key needed); HTTPS = HTTP over TLS; firewall packet filtering by port/IP; authentication (user+pass, 2FA); access levels.

Exam tips: explain why skew limits parallel over distance; compare MAC vs IP in a table; protocol questions want "rules for communication", not acronyms alone.

Packet switching and protocols

In packet switching, a message is divided into packets. Each packet carries a header with its source and destination addresses and a sequence number, so it can travel by any available route. The packets are reassembled in the correct order at the destination. Packet switching makes efficient use of the network, because no dedicated connection is held open for the whole transmission.

A protocol is an agreed set of rules that devices follow to communicate. TCP/IP is the set of protocols used on the internet. TCP splits data into packets and checks that they arrive, while IP handles addressing and routing between networks.

Exam tip: explain a protocol as a set of rules, and give one example of what it governs, such as addressing or error checking.

title: Permutations and Combinations — Study Notes
content:
Permutations and Combinations

The Multiplication Principle

If a task is done in successive stages with m, n, ... choices at each stage, the total is the product of the choices. This underpins every counting problem: a menu with 4 starters and 6 mains gives 24 meals.

Permutations — Order Matters

The number of ways of arranging r objects from n distinct objects is

  • ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!

The number of arrangements of n distinct objects is n!. Five books on a shelf: 5! = 120 ways.

Combinations — Order Irrelevant

The number of ways of choosing r objects from n is

  • ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!)

Choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people: ⁸C₃ = 56. Choosing is not arranging — a committee has no internal order, so we divide by r!.

Restricted Permutations

  • No two specified people adjacent: arrange everyone else, then slot the restricted people into gaps. For n people with 2 who must be separated: arrange the other n − 2 (ways), then place 2 people in distinct gaps between them.
  • Specified people together: bundle them as one item, arrange the bundle, then multiply by the internal arrangements of the bundle.
  • Words with repeated letters: divide by the factorials of each repeat count. ARRANGE has 7 letters with A appearing twice and R twice, so 7!/(2!·2!) = 1260.

Combinations with Constraints

  • At least / at most: split into cases and add. A team of 5 from 6 boys and 5 girls with at least 3 girls is ⁵C₃⁶C₂ + ⁵C₄⁶C₁ + ⁵C₅⁶C₀.
  • "Must include" pairs: choose the required items first, then choose freely from the remainder.

Exam tips: state whether a scenario is a permutation or combination before computing anything. Most lost marks come from counting an arrangement where order does not actually matter. Check every answer against a small case you can enumerate by hand.

Exam method: arrangements and selections

The number of arrangements of r objects from n distinct objects is nPr = n!/(n − r)!. The number of ways to select r objects from n, where order does not matter, is nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!). Ask first whether order matters, because that decides which formula to use.

Arrangements with restrictions are solved by treating a block as one object or by placing the restricted items first. For example, if two people must sit together, treat them as one unit and multiply by 2 for their internal order.

Use the identity nCr = nC(n − r) to check answers, and remember that nC0 = nCn = 1. Pascal's identity nCr = (n−1)C(r−1) + (n−1)Cr links the two formulae.

When a question has several groups with separate conditions, count each part on its own and multiply the results, provided the parts are independent.

Exam cue: Write the formula with the numbers substituted before simplifying, since method marks are given for the correct expression.

title: Exam technique: Integration
content:
### What earns the marks
For indefinite integrals, each term raised correctly plus the constant earns full marks. For definite integrals, the antiderivative quoted earns one mark and the correct upper-minus-lower evaluation earns the next. For area and curve-finding, the limits or the given point used earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: constant of integration omitted. Correction: +c always for indefinite. Error: limits subtracted backwards. Correction: upper minus lower. Error: power rule inverted on roots. Correction: root x is x to the half, integral goes up.
### Worked example
Find the integral of 6x² − 4x⁻³. Raise each power by one and divide by the new power: 6x² becomes 2x³, and −4x⁻³ becomes 2x⁻² because (−4)/(−2) = 2. Add the constant: 2x³ + 2x⁻² + c. Check by differentiating: 6x² + (−4)x⁻³, which matches the original.
### Check yourself
Evaluate the definite integral of 2x + 1 from 1 to 3. The antiderivative is x² + x, giving (9 + 3) − (1 + 1) = 10. Write both the antiderivative and the subtraction on the paper, because the method mark depends on them.

title: Communication and Networking — Study Notes
content:
`# Communication and Networking

Transmission

  • Serial: one bit at a time — cheaper, reliable over distance
  • Parallel: multiple bits simultaneously — fast but suffers skew and crosstalk over long runs
  • Direction: simplex (one way), half-duplex (alternating), full-duplex (both ways)

Packets and Protocols

Data splits into packets with header (addresses, sequence) and trailer (checksum). A protocol is an agreed rule set — without one, devices cannot interpret signals.

  • TCP/IP stack: application → transport → network → link
  • HTTP/HTTPS: web transfer; HTTPS encrypts with TLS
  • FTP: file transfer; SMTP/POP3/IMAP: email

Network Types

  • LAN: small site, privately owned; WAN: large geographic scale (the internet)
  • Topologies: bus, star, mesh (star is most common — central switch)

Hardware

Routers join networks by IP; switches forward frames by MAC within a LAN; gateways translate protocols.

Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer

Client-server: central services, easy administration, single point of failure. P2P: every node shares files directly — cheap, hard to manage (torrents, blockchain).

Exam tips: explain packet switching with header/trailer details; justify protocol choice per application (email vs streaming).

Network topologies and hardware

In a star topology every device connects to a central switch. If one cable or device fails, the others keep working, but if the central switch fails the whole network stops. In a bus topology all devices share one cable, which is cheap but means a break in the cable disables the network.

A switch connects devices within a local area network (LAN) and sends each frame only to the device it is addressed to, using MAC addresses. A router connects separate networks together and forwards packets using IP addresses. A wireless access point lets wireless devices join a wired LAN.

Exam tip: when comparing topologies, state what happens when one device fails and when the central device fails. Those two cases are the usual differentiators.

title: Circular Motion and SHM — Study Notes
content:
Circular Motion and SHM

Uniform circular motion

A particle moving in a circle of radius r at constant speed has a constantly changing velocity, because its direction changes. Angular speed ω is the rate of change of angle in radians per second: ω = 2π/T = 2πf. The linear speed is v = ωr.

Centripetal acceleration and force

The acceleration is directed towards the centre: a = v²/r = ω²r. The resultant force providing it is F = mv²/r = mω²r, also towards the centre. This force does no work, because it is always perpendicular to the velocity, so the kinetic energy stays constant.

Example: a particle on a 0.40 m radius with T = 2.0 s has ω = π rad s⁻¹, v = 1.26 m s⁻¹ and a = π² × 0.40 ≈ 3.9 m s⁻².

Simple harmonic motion as projected circular motion

The displacement of a point moving on a circle, projected onto a diameter, is x = x₀ sin ωt (or cos ωt). Its acceleration is a = −ω²x, always opposite to the displacement, so the defining condition for SHM is that acceleration is proportional to and opposite to displacement.

Solutions: x = x₀ sin ωt starts at the centre; x = x₀ cos ωt starts at an extreme. Time period T = 2π/ω.

Velocity and acceleration:

  • v = ±ω√(x₀² − x²); v_max = ωx₀ at the centre
  • a_max = ω²x₀ at the extremes; a = 0 at the centre

Example: a pendulum with x₀ = 0.02 m and f = 0.5 Hz has a_max = (2π × 0.5)² × 0.02 ≈ 0.20 m s⁻².

Energy in SHM

The total energy is E = ½mω²x₀², constant. It is exchanged between kinetic energy (maximum at the centre) and potential energy (maximum at the extremes). Kinetic energy is at a maximum when displacement is zero, not when acceleration is largest.

Damping and resonance

Damping removes energy from the oscillator. Light damping gives slow decay of amplitude; critical damping returns the system to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating; heavy damping is slower still. A system driven at its natural frequency resonates, giving maximum amplitude (playground swings, microwave ovens, bridges that must avoid the wind frequency).

Exam tips: quote a = −ω²x as the defining condition in SHM questions. Time-period questions often need only T = 2π/ω. State which energy is at a maximum and where.

Worked example: a mass on a string

A 0.50 kg mass on a string of length 0.80 m moves in a horizontal circle at 4.0 m/s. The tension supplies the centripetal force, so T = mv²/r = 0.50 × 4.0² / 0.80 = 10 N. If the same mass is swung in a vertical circle, the tension is least at the top. The minimum speed at the top occurs when the tension falls to zero, giving v = √(gr). Here that is √(9.8 × 0.80) ≈ 2.8 m/s. Below this speed the string goes slack and the mass no longer follows the circle.

Exam method: SHM equations

Use x = A sin(ωt) or x = A cos(ωt), depending on the point at which timing starts. The maximum speed is v₀ = Aω and the maximum acceleration is a₀ = Aω². Use ω = 2π/T, and convert any frequency in hertz by multiplying by 2π before you substitute, because ω is in radians per second. For a simple pendulum at small angles, the period is T = 2π√(L/g) and does not depend on the amplitude.

title: Electricity: D.C. Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity: D.C. circuits

Current and charge

  • Current I = charge Q ÷ time t, so Q = It. Unit: ampere (A), where 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹.
  • Electron drift velocity is very small, but the electric field propagates through the circuit almost at the speed of light.

Potential difference and power

  • Potential difference V = energy transferred ÷ charge. Unit: volt (V), where 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.
  • Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Unit: watt (W).

Resistance and resistivity

R = V/I (Ohm's law for an ohmic conductor, at constant temperature). For a wire of length L and cross-sectional area A, R = ρL/A, where ρ is the resistivity in Ω m. Resistance rises with length and falls with area.

Practical circuits

An ammeter is connected in series with the component it measures. A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance; an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.

Kirchhoff's laws

  • First law: at a junction, the total current entering equals the total current leaving (conservation of charge).
  • Second law: around any closed loop, the sum of the emfs equals the sum of the potential differences (conservation of energy).

Potential dividers

For two resistors R1 and R2 in series across a supply V, the potential difference across R2 is V × R2/(R1 + R2).

Worked example: a 100 Ω and a 300 Ω resistor are in series across 12 V. The current is 12/400 = 0.030 A, and the voltage across the 300 Ω resistor is 0.030 × 300 = 9.0 V.

Exam tips: draw the meter in the correct place, in series or in parallel. Apply Kirchhoff's first law to currents and the second law to loops, with consistent signs. Check that units are converted (e.g. mm² to m²) before using ρL/A.

Resistivity and temperature

For a metallic conductor at constant temperature, resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. Resistivity, ρ = RA/L, is a property of the material. As temperature rises, the ions in a metal vibrate more and impede the flow of electrons, so resistivity increases. A thermistor behaves differently: its resistance falls as temperature rises, because more charge carriers are released.

Exam tip: when asked to explain a resistance change, relate it to charge carriers and collisions, not just to the formula.

Worked example: resistors in series and in parallel

Two resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω in series have a combined resistance of 10 Ω, and the same current flows through each. In parallel, the same two resistors have a combined resistance found from 1/R = 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12, so R = 2.4 Ω. The combined resistance in parallel is always less than the smallest individual resistance, and adding a branch to a parallel circuit always reduces the total resistance.

Worked example: EMF and internal resistance

A cell with EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω supplies a current of 2 A. The terminal potential difference is V = E − Ir = 1.5 − (2 × 0.5) = 0.5 V. Writing V = E − Ir before substituting shows that the energy lost inside the cell is the difference between the EMF and the terminal voltage. A cell with a larger current supplied has a smaller terminal voltage.

The potential divider

Two resistors in series across a supply give an output voltage across one of them that depends on the ratio of the resistances. For a supply of 12 V with resistors of 2 kΩ and 4 kΩ in series, the voltage across the 4 kΩ resistor is 12 × 4 ÷ 6 = 8 V. A thermistor or light-dependent resistor in place of one of the resistors makes this arrangement a sensor, because the output voltage changes with temperature or light level.

title: Integration — Study Notes
content:
Integration

Indefinite Integrals

Reverse the power rule and add a constant: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + c (n ≠ −1).

Examples: ∫ x³ dx = x⁴/4 + c; ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c; ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c; ∫ e^x dx = e^x + c.

Definite Integrals

∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = [F(x)]ₐᵇ = F(b) − F(a). Constants of integration cancel.

Example: ∫₀¹ 6x² dx = [2x³]₀¹ = 2.

Areas Under Curves

Area between a curve and the x-axis = ∫ₐᵇ y dx, where y ≥ 0. If the curve dips below the axis, split the integral at the roots and add the absolute values.

Example: area between y = x² − 4 and the x-axis: roots ±2, and the area is |∫₋₂² (x² − 4) dx| = 32/3.

Trapezium Rule

A ≈ h/2 [y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ], h = (b − a)/n. More strips → better estimate; always an over-estimate for convex curves.

Exam tips: never forget +c on indefinite integrals; for areas with negative regions, sketch first and split.

title: Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression
content:
Quick revision: Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression

Biology — AS. Edexcel IAL Biology WBI11, Topic 2. DNA holds the code for proteins. Gene expression copies that code into mRNA and then builds the protein. Cell membranes control what enters and leaves the cell.

Key areas to revise

  • Cell membranes
  • DNA structure and replication
  • Protein synthesis
  • Mutations

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked example

Calculate the percentage change in mass of plant tissue in an osmosis experiment where initial mass is 2.50 g and final mass is 2.85 g. Step 1: Change in mass = Final − Initial = 2.85 − 2.50 = 0.35 g. Step 2: Percentage change = (Change ÷ Initial) × 100 = (0.35 ÷ 2.50) × 100 = 14.0%. Answer: +14.0%.

Key points to remember

For 2.2 (i) and (ii), the fluid mosaic model describes phospholipids, cholesterol, glycoproteins and glycolipids floating in a flexible bilayer; scientific models are interpretations of data like freeze-fracture electron microscopy. For 2.3 Core Practical 3, increasing temperature above 40 °C denatures membrane proteins and melts the phospholipid bilayer, increasing permeability, while alcohol dissolves lipids, leaking betalain pigment from beetroot. For 2.4, osmosis is the net movement of free water molecules through a partially permeable membrane down a water potential gradient from high to low water potential. For 2.5 (i) and (ii), passive transport (diffusion and facilitated diffusion) requires no ATP, active transport uses ATP via carrier proteins to move substances against a gradient, and bulk transport uses endocytosis and exocytosis. For 2.9 (i) and (ii), mononucleotides consist of pentose sugar (ribose or deoxyribose), phosphate group and a nitrogenous base (A, T, C, G, U), joined by phosphodiester bonds formed in condensation reactions, with complementary base pairing (A-T with 2 hydrogen bonds, C-G with 3 hydrogen bonds) forming the DNA double helix. For 2.10 (i) and (ii), semi-conservative DNA replication relies on DNA polymerase adding free nucleotides to the template strand, and Meselson and Stahl proved this using 14N and 15N nitrogen isotopes in E. coli DNA centrifugation. For 2.11 and 2.12, the genetic code is a triplet code (3 bases per amino acid), non-overlapping, and degenerate (multiple codons code for the same amino acid), where a gene is a sequence of bases coding for a polypeptide. For 2.13 (i) and (ii), transcription uses RNA polymerase to copy the antisense DNA strand into mRNA in the nucleus, and translation uses ribosomes, tRNA with specific anticodons, start codons and stop codons to assemble amino acids. For 2.14 (i) and (ii), mutations include base substitution, insertion and deletion, which can cause genetic disorders or cancer, though many are silent. For 2.15 (i), (ii) and (iii), key genetics terms include gene, allele, genotype, phenotype, recessive, dominant, codominance, homozygote and heterozygote, alongside monotypical pedigrees and X-linked recessive conditions like red-green colour blindness. For 2.16, the CFTR gene mutation in cystic fibrosis produces thick, sticky mucus impairing the gaseous exchange, digestive and reproductive systems. For 2.17 (i) and (ii) and 2.18, genetic screening includes carrier identification, PGD, amniocentesis and chorionic villus sampling, carrying social, moral and religious ethical implications regarding abortion and designer babies.

How to use this: read these concise summaries alongside your core practical notes, ensure definitions for water potential and transcription are precise, and apply your knowledge to pedigree and genetics problem questions.

title: System Software and Security — Study Notes
content:
`# System Software and Security

Operating System Roles

  • Manage memory (paging/segmentation, virtual memory to disk)
  • Schedule processes (round robin, priorities)
  • Handle I/O via device drivers and spooling
  • Provide the UI, file systems, and security (users, permissions)

Translators

  • Assembler: assembly → machine code (1:1)
  • Compiler: whole source → machine code, reports all errors, produces standalone executables
  • Interpreter: line-by-line execution, stops at first error, needs the interpreter present

Bytecode + VM (e.g. Java) combines both: compile once, run anywhere the VM exists.

Linkers and Loaders

Static linking copies library code into the executable; dynamic linking binds at runtime (smaller files, shared libraries). The loader places the program in memory, relocating addresses.

IDEs

Editors with syntax highlighting, autocompletion, debugger (breakpoints, stepping, variable watch), and integrated compilation.

Malware and Defences

Viruses, worms, trojans, spyware, phishing. Defences: antivirus (signature + heuristic scanning), firewalls (packet filtering by port/IP), sandboxing, user education, patches.

Exam tips: compare compiler vs interpreter with concrete error-handling differences; explain firewall rules using ports and addresses.

Malware types and prevention

A virus attaches itself to a file or program and needs a host to spread. A worm spreads across a network without a host file. A trojan looks like useful software but carries a hidden harmful payload. Phishing uses fake emails or websites to trick a user into revealing login details or other personal data.

A firewall monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and blocks traffic that does not meet its rules. Anti-malware software scans for and removes known threats. Regular software updates close security weaknesses, and regular backups allow data to be restored after an attack.

Exam tip: match each threat to how it spreads, and each prevention method to the threat it stops. Do not confuse a virus with a worm.

Worked example: tracing a program through the toolchain

A programmer writes the source code for a calculator in a high-level language. A compiler translates the whole program into machine code before it runs, and reports syntax errors as a list. A linker then joins this object code with the library routines it calls, producing one executable file. A loader copies that executable into main memory and starts it. If the same program were run by an interpreter, each statement would be translated and executed in turn, so an error in line 40 would only appear when the program reached line 40.

Comparing translators

  • Compiler: translates everything first, produces a fast executable and a separate file for the output, and is harder to debug while running.
  • Interpreter: translates line by line, starts quickly and eases debugging, but runs more slowly because it translates again each time.
  • Assembler: converts assembly language, which uses mnemonics such as ADD and MOV, into machine code, with a one-to-one correspondence between each instruction and its binary form.

Why the operating system loads the program

The loader is part of the operating system's work of managing memory. It reserves space, places the instructions and data in that space and sets the starting address. Without this step the processor would not know where the program begins or which memory it may use.

Exam point: name the translator for each stage in the question, and state one advantage and one disadvantage of the translator the question describes.

title: Algebra — Inequalities — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Inequalities

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): solving linear inequalities, integer solution sets, shading regions on graphs (linear programming context).

1. Solving

Like equations, but reverse the sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative: −2x ≥ 6 ⇒ x ≤ −3.

Example: 3x − 5 < 2x + 1 ⇒ x < 6.

2. Integer solutions

−1 ≤ x < 4 ⇒ x ∈ {−1, 0, 1, 2, 3}. Closed endpoint for ≤/≥, open for </>.

3. Double inequalities

Handle both sides: −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7 → −4 < 2x ≤ 6 → −2 < x ≤ 3.

4. Shading regions

  • Draw the boundary line: dashed for </>, solid for ≤/≥.
  • Test a point (usually (0,0)) to pick the wanted side; shade the unwanted side or label the wanted region.
  • Feasible region satisfies all constraints simultaneously.

Example: y ≤ 2x + 1: solid line, test (0,0): 0 ≤ 1 ✓ → region containing origin.

Exam tips: never divide by an unknown sign — move x terms first; list integer solutions inside curly brackets; state which region you shade.

Solving linear inequalities

Inequalities are solved like equations, with one crucial exception: multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. Answers are written as a single inequality such as x > 3, or as a set such as -2 < x ≤ 5 when two bounds are given.

Representing inequalities on a number line

An open circle marks a strict bound (< or >) that is not included; a filled circle marks an inclusive bound (≤ or ≥). Shade the region that satisfies the statement.

Regions on a coordinate grid

Draw each boundary line as a solid line for ≤ or ≥ and a dashed line for < or >. Test a point such as (0, 0) if it is not on the line; shade the side that makes the inequality true. Where several regions are required, the wanted region is the overlap of all the shaded areas. Integer points inside a region are counted when a question asks for them.

title: Exam technique: Information Representation
content:
### What earns the marks
For two complement, inversion plus one stated earns the method mark before the value. For floating point, mantissa plus exponent roles stated earn one mark each. For normalisation, the leading-bit rule quoted earns the precision mark.
### Traps
Error: sign bit ignored in range. Correction: an n-bit signed range tops at 2^(n-1) - 1. Error: larger exponent read as more precision. Correction: exponent sets range, mantissa sets precision. Error: normalised form guessed. Correction: mantissa starts with 0.1 or 1.0 pattern per the scheme.
### Worked example
Write -45 in 8-bit two's complement. First write 45 in binary: 00101101. Invert every bit to get 11010010, then add 1 to get 11010011. Check: the sign bit has weight -128, so the value is -128 + 64 + 16 + 2 + 1 = -45, which matches.
### Check yourself
State the range of an 8-bit two's complement integer, and say which bit sets the sign. The range is -128 to +127, and the leftmost bit is the sign bit with weight -128.

### Worked example
Write -45 in 8-bit two's complement. First write 45 in binary: 00101101. Invert every bit to get 11010010, then add 1 to get 11010011. Check: the sign bit has weight -128, so the value is -128 + 64 + 16 + 2 + 1 = -45, which matches.

title: Exam technique: Arithmetic and Place Value
content:
### What earns the marks
For HCF and LCM, the prime factorisation of each number earns the method mark; state highest powers for LCM and lowest for HCF. For bounds, half-the-precision stated (0.05 for 1 d.p.) earns the method mark before the bound. For estimation, the rounded line (50 x 20 / 10) must be shown: a bare calculator value scores nothing. For time and money, each conversion step shown earns its mark.
### Traps
Error: 16:80 as a time. Correction: 60 minutes carry. Error: largest rounded value confused with the upper bound (6.34 vs 6.35). Correction: the bound is the first value that rounds away. Error: HCF powers used for LCM. Correction: LCM takes the highest of each prime.
### Worked example
In 4 706 325 the digit 7 is in the hundred-thousands place, so its value is 700 000. For order of operations, 3 + 4 × (10 − 6)² is worked out as 3 + 4 × 4² = 3 + 4 × 16 = 3 + 64 = 67. Brackets and powers come before multiplication, and addition comes last.
### Check yourself
State the value of the digit 6 in 4 706 325, then calculate 20 − 2 × (3 + 4)². The 6 is worth 6000. The second is 20 − 2 × 49 = 20 − 98 = −78, which shows why the brackets must be done first.

title: Forces & Motion — Study Notes
content:
Forces & Motion

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): motion (speed, acceleration, graphs); mass & weight; density link; force basics (F = ma, resultant); momentum (Extended); turning effects; equilibrium.

1. Kinematics

  • Speed = distance/time; average speed = (u + v)/2 for uniform acceleration.
  • Acceleration a = (v − u)/t.
  • SUVAT (uniform a): v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as.

2. Motion graphs

  • Distance–time: gradient = speed.
  • Speed–time: gradient = acceleration; area = distance. Negative gradient = deceleration.
  • Free fall 1: g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (use 10) — v = gt from rest.

3. Mass, weight, density

W = mg (g ≈ 10 N/kg). Weight acts at the centre of mass; mass is invariant. Density ρ = m/V.

4. Newton's laws and resultant force

  • Resultant: colinear addition/subtraction; perpendicular by Pythagoras.
  • F = ma. Terminal velocity: drag grows with speed until it balances weight.
  • Third law pairs: equal magnitude, opposite direction, different bodies.

5. Momentum (Extended)

p = mv; impulse Ft = Δ(mv); conservation: Σpbefore = Σpafter (explosions, collisions).

Example: 2 kg at 3 m/s hits 1 kg at rest, combined 1 m/s: 6 = 3v ⇒ v = 2 m/s.

6. Moments and equilibrium

  • Moment = F × perpendicular distance from pivot.
  • Principle of moments: Σclockwise = Σanticlockwise.
  • Equilibrium: resultant force = 0 and resultant moment = 0.

Example: 100 N at 0.3 m balances F at 0.5 m: F = 60 N.

title: Transition Metals and their Chemistry - A2 Chemistry
content:
Transition Metals and their Chemistry - A2 Level

This topic belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Level (IAL) Chemistry specification, Unit 5 (WCH15), and covers the electronic configurations, variable oxidation states, complex ion formation, ligand exchange, colour changes, standard electrode potentials of vanadium and chromium systems, catalysis, and practical preparations associated with d-block transition elements of Period 4 from scandium to zinc.

Definition and Electronic Configurations of Transition Metals

Transition metals are defined as d-block elements that form one or more stable ions with incompletely-filled d-orbitals. Scandium and zinc are in the d-block but are not true transition metals because Sc3+ has an empty d-orbital (3d0) and Zn2+ has a completely filled d-orbital (3d10). To deduce electronic configurations of Period 4 atoms and ions from Sc to Zn, remember that the 4s orbital fills before 3d, but when positive ions are formed, electrons are always removed from the 4s orbital before the 3d orbitals.

  • Transition metals are d-block elements forming stable ions with incompletely-filled d-orbitals (17.1).
  • Electronic configuration rules: fill 4s then 3d, empty 4s before 3d when forming ions (17.2).
  • Example atom Ti (atomic number 22): 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d2 (17.2).
  • Example ion Fe2+ (atomic number 26): 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d6, with the two 4s electrons removed (17.2).
  • Example ion Cu+ (atomic number 29): 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10 (17.2).
  • Variable oxidation numbers occur because the 4s and 3d sub-shells have very similar energies, allowing different numbers of electrons to be lost or involved in bonding with minimal energy penalty (17.3).

Complex Ions, Ligands, and Coordination Numbers

A complex ion consists of a central metal ion surrounded by species called ligands. A ligand is a species containing at least one lone pair of electrons that forms a dative covalent (coordinate) bond to the central metal ion. The coordination number is the total number of coordinate bonds formed to the central metal ion. The nature and size of ligands determine the spatial arrangement and geometry of the resulting complex ion.

  • Ligand definition: a species with a lone pair that forms a dative covalent bond to a metal ion (17.4, 17.5).
  • Complex ion definition: a central metal ion surrounded by ligands (17.6).
  • Coordination number: the number of coordinate bonds to the central metal ion (17.10).
  • Monodentate ligands donate one pair of electrons; H2O, OH− and NH3 act as monodentate ligands (17.12).
  • Six-fold coordination complexes have an octahedral shape, such as [M(H2O)6]n+, [M(OH)6]n−, and [M(NH3)6]n+ (17.13).
  • Tetrahedral complexes form with relatively large ligands such as Cl−, for example [CuCl4]2− and [CoCl4]2−, due to steric hindrance preventing six chloride ions from packing around the small metal centre (17.14).
  • Square planar complexes are also formed by transition metal ions; cis-platin, [Pt(NH3)2Cl2], is a square planar complex used in cancer treatment supplied as a single active cis isomer rather than a mixture with the inactive trans form (17.15).
  • Bidentate ligands have two donor atoms donating two lone pairs, such as ethane-1,2-diamine (NH2CH2CH2NH2). Hexadentate ligands have six donor atoms, such as EDTA4− (17.16).
  • Haemoglobin is an iron(II) complex containing a polydentate porphyrin ring ligand; ligand exchange occurs when an oxygen molecule bound to haemoglobin in the lungs is replaced by a carbon monoxide molecule in the body tissues (17.17).

Colour and d-Orbital Splitting

Aqueous solutions of transition metal ions are usually coloured because the presence of surrounding ligands causes the five degenerate d-orbitals to split into two different energy levels. When white light passes through the solution, electrons absorb specific frequencies of visible light to jump from the lower d-orbitals to the higher d-orbitals. The colour observed is due to the remaining unabsorbed wavelengths transmitted or reflected. A lack of colour in some aqueous ions or complex ions, such as Sc3+ (3d0) or Zn2+ (3d10), occurs because their d-orbitals are either completely empty or completely full, so d-d electronic transitions are impossible.

  • Aqueous solutions of transition metal ions are usually coloured (17.7).
  • Colour arises from the splitting of the energy levels of d-orbitals by the electrostatic field of surrounding ligands (17.8).
  • Lack of colour in ions like Sc3+ (3d0) and Zn2+ (3d10) is due to empty or full d-orbitals preventing d-d electron transitions (17.9).
  • Colour changes in transition metal ions arise from changes in oxidation number, changes in ligand, or changes in the coordination number of the complex (17.11).

Vanadium and Chromium Redox Chemistry

Vanadium exhibits four stable oxidation states in aqueous solution, each with a characteristic colour: +5 (yellow, VO2+), +4 (blue, VO2+), +3 (green, V3+), and +2 (violet, V2+). These oxidation states can be interconverted via redox reactions using zinc metal in acidic conditions as a reducing agent, driven by standard electrode potential (Eo) values. Similarly, chromium chemistry involves the interconversion of Cr3+ and dichromate(VI) ions, Cr2O7 2−. Dichromate(VI) ions can be reduced using zinc in acid and produced by oxidising Cr3+ with hydrogen peroxide in alkaline conditions followed by acidification. In aqueous solution, dichromate(VI) ions exist in a pH-dependent equilibrium with chromate(VI) ions.

  • Vanadium oxidation states and colours: +5 is yellow (VO2+), +4 is blue (VO2+), +3 is green (V3+), and +2 is violet (V2+) (17.18).
  • Redox interconversion of vanadium oxidation states is achieved using zinc in acidic solution, evaluated through relevant Eo values where Zn/Zn2+ is sufficiently negative to reduce V5+ down to V2+ (17.19).
  • Dchromate(VI) ions (Cr2O7 2−) can be reduced to Cr3+ and further to Cr2+ using zinc in acidic conditions (17.20i).
  • Dichromate(VI) ions can be produced by the oxidation of Cr3+ ions using hydrogen peroxide in alkaline conditions, followed by subsequent acidification (17.20ii).
  • Dichromate(VI) ion equilibrium with chromate(VI): Cr2O7 2− + H2O <-> 2CrO4 2− + 2H+ (17.21). Adding acid shifts this equilibrium left towards orange dichromate; adding alkali shifts it right towards yellow chromate.

Reactions of Aqueous Transition Metal Ions with Hydroxide and Ammonia

Aqueous metal ions react with sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia to produce precipitates, which may show amphoteric behaviour or dissolve in excess reagent due to ligand exchange. You must know the exact observations and write balanced ionic equations for Cr3+(aq), Mn2+(aq), Fe2+(aq), Fe3+(aq), Co2+(aq), Ni2+(aq), Cu2+(aq), and Zn2+(aq).

  • Cr3+(aq) + 3OH−(aq) -> Cr(OH)3(H2O)3(s) (grey-green precipitate). Excess OH− gives [Cr(OH)6]3− (dark green solution) demonstrating amphoteric behaviour (17.22, 17.23).
  • Cr3+(aq) with NH3(aq): grey-green precipitate of Cr(OH)3(H2O)3, insoluble in excess ammonia (17.22).
  • Mn2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Mn(OH)2(s) (off-white precipitate, turns brown on standing in air due to oxidation). Insoluble in excess OH− and excess NH3 (17.22).
  • Fe2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Fe(OH)2(s) (green precipitate, turns brown on surface in air). Insoluble in excess OH− and excess NH3 (17.22).
  • Fe3+(aq) + 3OH−(aq) -> Fe(OH)3(s) (rusty-brown precipitate). Insoluble in excess OH− and excess NH3 (17.22).
  • Co2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Co(OH)2(s) (blue precipitate, turns pink on standing). Insoluble in excess OH−. With excess NH3, forms [Co(NH3)6]2+ (pale yellow solution turning brown) via ligand exchange (17.22, 17.23, 17.24).
  • Ni2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Ni(OH)2(s) (green precipitate). Insoluble in excess OH−. With excess NH3, dissolves to form [Ni(NH3)6]2+ (blue solution) (17.22, 17.23).
  • Cu2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Cu(OH)2(s) (pale blue precipitate). Insoluble in excess OH−. With excess NH3, dissolves to form [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ (deep blue solution) (17.22, 17.23, 17.24).
  • Zn2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Zn(OH)2(s) (white precipitate). Dissolves in excess OH− to form [Zn(OH)4]2− (colourless solution) demonstrating amphoteric behaviour (17.22, 17.23).
  • Zn2+(aq) with excess NH3(aq): white precipitate dissolves to form [Zn(NH3)4]2+ (colourless solution) (17.22, 17.23).
  • Deprotonation reactions involve aqueous metal ions losing protons from coordinated water molecules to form neutral hydroxide precipitates (17.23).

Specific Ligand Exchange Reactions and Entropy

Ligand exchange occurs when one ligand in a complex is replaced by another, accompanied by a distinct colour change and often a change in coordination number. The thermodynamic stability of complex ions is significantly enhanced when monodentate ligands are replaced by bidentate or hexadentate ligands, known as the chelate effect. This can be understood in terms of the positive increase in entropy (Ssystem) because there are more free moles of product species than reactant species in solution.

  • Formation of [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ (deep blue) from [Cu(H2O)6]2+ (pale blue) proceeds via an intermediate Cu(OH)2(H2O)4 precipitate upon adding ammonia, which then redissolves in excess ammonia (17.24i).
  • Formation of [CuCl4]2− (yellow-green) from [Cu(H2O)6]2+ (blue) occurs upon adding concentrated hydrochloric acid, resulting in a change in coordination number from 6 to 4 and a shape change from octahedral to tetrahedral (17.24ii).
  • Formation of [CoCl4]2− (blue) from [Co(H2O)6]2+ (pink) occurs on adding concentrated hydrochloric acid, changing coordination number from 6 to 4 and shape from octahedral to tetrahedral (17.24iii).
  • Substitution of monodentate ligands by bidentate or hexadentate ligands leads to a more stable complex ion due to a positive increase in system entropy (Ssystem), as the number of independent particles in solution increases (17.25).

Catalysis by Transition Metals

Transition metals and their compounds are exceptionally effective catalysts, operating as either heterogeneous catalysts (in a different phase from reactants, with reactions occurring on the catalyst surface) or homogeneous catalysts (in the same phase as reactants, proceeding via intermediate species). V2O5 acts as a heterogeneous catalyst in the Contact process for manufacturing sulfur trioxide. Catalytic converters in vehicles use solid platinum/rhodium heterogeneous catalysts to remove carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide emissions via adsorption, bond weakening, reaction, and desorption. Homogeneous catalysis is exemplified by Fe2+ catalysing the reaction between iodide and peroxydisulfate ions, and Mn2+ autocatalysing the reaction between manganate(VII) and ethanedioate ions.

  • Heterogeneous catalyst: in a different phase from reactants; reaction occurs at the active sites on the surface of the catalyst (17.26, 17.27).
  • V2O5 acts as a heterogeneous catalyst in the Contact process by being reduced from V(V) to V(IV) by SO2, then reoxidised back to V(V) by O2: SO2 + V2O5 -> SO3 + V2O4, followed by V2O4 + 0.5O2 -> V2O5 (17.28).
  • Catalytic converter mechanism: 1. Adsorption of CO and NO molecules onto the metal surface, weakening covalent bonds. 2. Chemical reaction between adsorbed species to form CO2 and N2. 3. Desorption of product molecules from the surface (17.29).
  • Homogeneous catalyst: in the same phase as reactants, proceeding through distinct intermediate species (17.30).
  • Role of Fe2+ in catalysing reaction between I− and S2O8 2−: Fe2+ reduces S2O8 2− to SO4 2− forming Fe3+ intermediate (S2O8 2− + 2Fe2+ -> 2SO4 2− + 2Fe3+), then Fe3+ oxidises I− back to I2 regenerating Fe2+ (2Fe3+ + 2I− -> 2Fe2+ + I2) (17.31).
  • Role of Mn2+ in autocatalysing reaction between MnO4 − and C2O4 2−: reaction starts very slowly, but the Mn2+ product acts as a catalyst, speeding up the reaction as its concentration increases (autocatalysis) (17.32).
  • Core Practical 14: The preparation of a transition metal complex, such as potassium tris(oxalato)ferrate(III) trihydrate, involving ligand substitution, precipitation, recrystallisation, and percentage yield calculation (17.33).

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Removing electrons from 3d orbitals before 4s orbitals when writing ion configurations. Correction: Always fill 4s before 3d, but remove electrons from the 4s orbital first when forming positive ions.
  • Mistake: Stating that Sc3+ or Zn2+ solutions are coloured. Correction: They are colourless because they do not have incompletely-filled d-orbitals to permit d-d electron transitions.
  • Mistake: Confusing coordination number with the number of ligands. Correction: Coordination number is the total number of coordinate bonds, which equals the number of monodentate ligands, but is double the number of bidentate ligands.
  • Mistake: Omitting phase or charge when writing complex ion formulas. Correction: Always enclose the complex in square brackets with the overall charge outside, e.g., [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that cis-platin must be supplied as a single isomer. Correction: Cis-platin is supplied specifically as the cis isomer because only this form binds to DNA to inhibit cancer cell replication.

Exam-style questions

  1. Deduce the ground state electronic configuration of a cobalt(II) atom (atomic number 27) and a cobalt(III) ion. (2 marks)

    Answer: Co atom is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d7 (1 mark). Co3+ ion is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d6, with electrons removed from 4s first (1 mark).

  2. Explain why aqueous copper(II) sulfate is blue, whereas aqueous scandium(III) chloride is colourless. (3 marks)

    Answer: Cu2+ has an incompletely-filled 3d9 configuration; d-orbitals split in the ligand field, allowing d-d electron transitions which absorb specific frequencies of visible light (2 marks). Sc3+ has a 3d0 configuration with no d-electrons, so no d-d transitions are possible, making it colourless (1 mark).

  3. Describe what you would observe when excess aqueous ammonia is added dropwise to an aqueous solution containing copper(II) ions. Write ionic equations for the reactions that occur. (4 marks)

    Answer: Observations: pale blue solution forms a pale blue precipitate of Cu(OH)2, which then dissolves in excess ammonia to form a deep blue solution (2 marks). Equations: Cu2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Cu(OH)2(s) followed by Cu(OH)2(s) + 4NH3(aq) + 2H2O(l) -> [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) (2 marks).

  4. Explain why the substitution of six monodentate water ligands by three bidentate ethane-1,2-diamine ligands in a complex ion is thermodynamically favoured by entropy. (2 marks)

    Answer: There is an increase in the total number of independent particles/molecules in solution from 4 reactants to 7 products (1 mark), leading to a positive entropy change (Ssystem > 0) making the complex more stable (1 mark).

  5. Outline how V2O5 acts as a heterogeneous catalyst in the Contact process, including chemical equations. (3 marks)

    Answer: V2O5 is in a different phase (solid) from the gaseous reactants (1 mark). It oxidises SO2 to SO3, being reduced itself: SO2 + V2O5 -> SO3 + V2O4 (1 mark). The V2O4 is then reoxidised by oxygen back to V2O5: V2O4 + 0.5O2 -> V2O5 (1 mark).

Use these revision notes alongside active recall of colour changes, precipitation reactions, and equation writing. Practise balancing redox equations for vanadium and chromium, and ensure you can explain the chelate effect using entropy arguments before moving on to past paper practice.

title: Exam technique: Differentiation
content:
### What earns the marks
For differentiation, every term handled earns credit: show each power lowered. For stationary points, setting dy/dx = 0 earns one mark and the second-derivative (or sign) test earns the next. For always-increasing proofs, the discriminant shown negative with positive leading coefficient earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: constants surviving differentiation. Correction: constants vanish. Error: tangent gradient used for normals. Correction: negative reciprocal first. Error: claiming increase without the discriminant. Correction: no roots plus positive shape proves it.

title: Earth & Space — Study Notes
content:
Earth & Space

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): Earth & Solar System; stars & the Universe (Extended).

1. Earth, Moon, Sun

Earth rotates 24 h (day/night), orbits 365¼ d (year + leap). Moon orbits Earth ~27.3 d; phases from viewing angle; lunar/solar eclipses when aligned. Seasons from axial tilt (23.5°), not distance.

2. Solar system

Planets (Mercury → Neptune), dwarf planets (Pluto), moons, asteroids, comets (eccentric orbits, tails away from Sun), natural satellites. Gravity keeps orbits; orbital speed & radius relate to the central mass.

3. Orbital motion

Orbital speed v = 2πr/T. T grows with r (Kepler trend). Comets speed up near the Sun (ellipse, Sun at focus).

4. Stars (Extended)

Star formation: nebula → protostar (gravity, KE→thermal) → main sequence (hydrogen fusion: H→He, radiation pressure balances gravity) → red giant → white dwarf (Sun-mass) or supergiant → supernova → neutron star/black hole (massive stars). Elements heavier than iron form in supernovae.

5. Universe (Extended)

The Sun is one star in the Milky Way; the Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies. Redshift: receding galaxies show stretched wavelengths → the Universe is expanding → Big Bang model; CMB is the afterglow. Hubble: farther ⇒ faster recession.

6. Scales

light-year = distance light travels in a year (9.5 × 10¹⁵ m); astronomical unit = Earth–Sun distance (1.5 × 10¹¹ m).

title: Programming Paradigms and Low-Level — Study Notes
content:
Programming Paradigms and Low-Level

Paradigms

  • Procedural: programs as sequences of instructions in procedures — good for straightforward algorithms.
  • Object-oriented: classes encapsulate state (attributes) and behaviour (methods); supports encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.
  • Declarative: state what is required, not how (SQL queries, logic programming).
  • Low-level: assembly maps closely to machine code; used where hardware control or timing precision is needed.

Assembly Essentials

The opcode names the operation (LDM load, STR store, ADD, CMP compare, JMP branch, IN/OUT for I/O). The operand names the data. The assembler translates mnemonics to machine code one-to-one; two-pass assemblers resolve forward references via the symbol table.

Addressing Modes

  • Immediate: operand is the constant itself, ADD #5.
  • Direct: operand is the memory address of the data.
  • Indirect: operand is the address OF the address; one extra memory read.
  • Indexed: effective address = base + index register; ideal for arrays.
  • Relative: address given as an offset from the program counter; enables position-independent code.

Fetch-Execute

Fetch: PC gives address, instruction loads into the CIR, PC increments. Decode: control unit interprets the opcode. Execute: the operation runs, possibly updating registers or memory. Interrupts are checked at cycle boundaries.

Exam tips: trace short assembly programs register by register; compute effective addresses for each addressing mode; state one advantage of OOP for large systems.

Programming paradigms

An imperative paradigm describes how to do a task as a sequence of statements that change state. An object-oriented paradigm groups data and the methods that act on it into classes. A declarative paradigm states the result wanted and leaves the method to the system, as in SQL.

Exception handling

An exception is a run-time error such as a missing file or a division by zero. A try block runs the risky code, and a catch (or except) block handles the exception so the program can recover rather than crash.

Exam tip: name the paradigm and give one feature that shows it, such as classes for object-oriented programming.

title: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — Study Notes
content:
Magnetism & Electromagnetism

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): magnets & fields; magnetic effect of a current; force on a current-carrying conductor; motor effect; electromagnetic induction (Extended); transformers (Extended).

1. Magnets and fields

Iron/steel/cobalt/nickel; like poles repel. Field lines exit N, enter S; compass plotting; plotting compass aligns with field. Induced magnetism: iron (temporary) vs steel (permanent).

2. Electromagnets

Solenoid field like a bar magnet; strength ↑ with current, turns, iron core. Uses: relays, scrapyard crane, electric bell, speaker. Hard/soft magnetic materials choose permanent vs core use.

3. Force on a current-carrying conductor

F = BIL, direction by Fleming's left hand (fIeld, current, force). Reversing current or field reverses force. D.C. motor: coil, commutator reverses current each half-turn for continuous rotation; speed/torque ↑ with current, field strength, turns/area.

4. Electromagnetic induction (Extended)

Induced e.m.f. when a conductor cuts field lines or flux changes. Fleming's right hand (generator). Factors: speed, field strength, turns. A.C. generator: slip rings; dynamo effect; Lenz's law opposes change (direction of induced current).

5. Transformers (Extended)

Vp/Vs = Np/Ns; Pin ≈ Pout (100% assumed): IpVp = IsVs. Step-up raises V, lowers I → lower I²R transmission losses; a.c. required (changing flux).

title: The Normal Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Normal Distribution

The Model

A continuous distribution with the familiar bell shape, symmetric about the mean, described by two parameters: X ~ N(μ, σ²). The curve is fully determined by μ (centre) and σ (width). Total probability is 1, and because X is continuous, P(X = a) = 0 for any single point — inequalities do not need strictness.

Standardising

Convert any normal variable to the standard normal Z ~ N(0, 1) with

  • Z = (X − μ)/σ

Then read probabilities from the normal table. For X ~ N(50, 4²): P(X > 56) = P(Z > 1.5) = 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668.

Backwards Problems

Given a probability, find μ or σ. Convert the target percentile to a z-value from the table, then solve (x − μ)/σ = z.

Example: P(X < 30) = 0.15 with unknown σ. From tables z = −1.036, so (30 − μ)/σ = −1.036 — one equation per unknown; use a second condition if both are missing.

Symmetry Shortcuts

P(X > μ) = 0.5. P(X < a) for a above the mean uses the complement. Tables usually give Φ(z) for z ≥ 0 only; use Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z).

Normal Approximation to the Binomial

For large n with p near ½, X ~ B(n, p) ≈ N(np, np(1 − p)). The condition usually quoted at this level is np > 5 and n(1 − p) > 5. Apply a continuity correction: to approximate P(X ≥ 12) for a binomial, compute P(Y > 11.5) for the normal Y.

Example: B(100, 0.5) ≈ N(50, 25). P(X ≥ 55) ≈ P(Y > 54.5) = P(Z > 0.9) = 0.1841.

Exam tips: always sketch and shade — the picture prevents complement errors. State the standardisation step explicitly; marks sit in the working. Check whether a question says "mean and standard deviation" (σ) or "variance" (σ²) before standardising.

Exam method: standardising and symmetry

For X ~ N(μ, σ²) the standard score is z = (x − μ)/σ, and Z ~ N(0, 1). Note that the second parameter is the variance, so take the square root to get σ before standardising. Many errors come from using 25 instead of 5 when the variance is 25.

Probabilities are found from the standard normal table or calculator using Φ(z) = P(Z ≤ z). Because the curve is symmetric about 0, Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z), and P(Z > z) = 1 − Φ(z).

For a probability between two values, P(a < X < b) = Φ(z_b) − Φ(z_a). Standardise each limit separately and subtract.

To find a value from a probability, read the z-value from the table with the required area, and then rearrange z = (x − μ)/σ to find x.

Exam cue: Sketch the curve and shade the area asked for, then match it to the table value, since the sketch catches sign errors.

### Worked example A parity bit makes the total number of 1s even (even parity) or odd. For the 7-bit pattern 1011001 there are four 1s, so the even-parity bit is 0. If the receiver counts an odd number of 1s, it knows an error occurred. Packet switching divides data into packets that can take different routes, and each packet is checked before reassembly. ### Check yourself Find the even-parity bit for 1100111. It has five 1s, so the parity bit is 1. Explain why parity detects a single flipped bit but cannot always correct it.
