title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Every question in this topic gives you some information about points and lines and asks you to turn it into an equation or a length. Decide which kind of information you have, then use the matching method below.

Which method to use

  • Two points given: find the distance, midpoint or gradient between them, or the perpendicular bisector.
  • A point and a direction given: build the line from the point and a gradient.
  • Two lines given: find where they meet, or check whether they are parallel or perpendicular.
  • A circle given: read off its centre and radius, or test a point against it.

Distance, midpoint and the perpendicular bisector

For A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂): AB = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²), the midpoint is ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2) and the gradient is (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through the midpoint and has the negative reciprocal of the gradient of AB.

Worked case: P(−2, 6) and Q(4, −2). PQ = √(36 + 64) = 10. The midpoint is (1, 2). The gradient of PQ is −8/6 = −4/3, so the bisector has gradient 3/4. Then y − 2 = 3/4(x − 1), which gives 3x − 4y + 5 = 0.

A line from a point and a direction

A straight line is fixed by one point on it and its gradient. Parallel lines share a gradient. Perpendicular lines have gradients whose product is −1. Once you have both, substitute into y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) and rearrange into the form the question asks for.

Parallel case: the line through (−3, 1) parallel to 5x − 2y + 4 = 0. Rearranging gives y = 5/2 x + 2, so m = 5/2. Then y − 1 = 5/2(x + 3), which rearranges to 5x − 2y + 17 = 0.

Perpendicular case: the line through (6, −1) perpendicular to 2x + 7y = 3. The given gradient is −2/7, so the required gradient is 7/2. Then y + 1 = 7/2(x − 6), which gives 7x − 2y − 44 = 0.

Where two lines meet

A common point satisfies both equations, so solve them simultaneously. If the gradients differ, the lines meet exactly once. If the gradients are equal, the lines are parallel: substitution then gives a false statement (no meeting point) or an identity (the same line).

Example: 3x + y = 7 and x − 2y = −4. The second equation gives x = 2y − 4. Substituting gives 7y − 12 = 7, so y = 19/7 and x = 10/7. The lines meet at (10/7, 19/7).

Where a line meets a circle

Substitute the line into the circle's equation. The result is a quadratic, and its discriminant tells you whether there are two intersection points, one (a tangent), or none. Solve the quadratic only when you need the coordinates.

Example: y = x + 1 and x² + y² = 13. Substituting gives 2x² + 2x − 12 = 0, so x² + x − 6 = 0 and (x + 3)(x − 2) = 0. The points are (−3, −2) and (2, 3).

Circles

The centre–radius form is (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r², with centre (a, b). For the general form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0, complete the square in x and in y: the centre is (−g, −f) and r² = g² + f² − c. To test a point, substitute it into the left-hand side of the centre–radius form and compare with r². A smaller value means inside the circle, equal means on it, and larger means outside.

Example: x² + y² − 8x + 2y − 8 = 0 becomes (x − 4)² + (y + 1)² = 25, so the centre is (4, −1) and the radius is 5. The point (1, 2) gives 9 + 9 = 18, which is less than 25, so it lies inside.

Tangents and normals

A tangent touches the circle at one point and is perpendicular to the radius at that point. A normal is the line through the point and the centre. Find the gradient of the radius, then take the negative reciprocal for the tangent.

Example: the point (8, 2) lies on the circle above, since 4² + 3² = 25. The radius has gradient 3/4, so the tangent has gradient −4/3 and equation 4x + 3y − 38 = 0. The normal has gradient 3/4 and equation 3x − 4y − 16 = 0, which passes through the centre (4, −1).

Exam technique

  • Draw a rough diagram first. It shows whether a point should lie inside or outside a circle before any algebra is done.
  • With a "show that" instruction, finish with the exact expression that was asked for.
  • To check a tangent, confirm that the distance from the centre to the line equals the radius.
  • Keep fractions exact until the final line; rounding early is the most common cause of a lost mark.

title: Electricity & Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity & Circuits

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): simple circuits, current, p.d., resistance, series/parallel, electrical safety, practical electricity.

1. Circuit symbols & current

Conventional current: + → − (electron flow opposite). I = Q/t. Ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel.

2. Current, p.d., e.m.f.

  • Current: rate of charge flow; same everywhere in series.
  • p.d.: energy per coulomb across a component; e.m.f.: electrical energy per coulomb given by the source.

3. Resistance

  • R = V/I. Ohmic conductor: V ∝ I at constant temperature.
  • Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + …; same current; p.d. shares in proportion to R.
  • Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂; same p.d.; current splits (inverse-R share).
  • Resistance ∝ length, ∝ 1/area (wires).

4. Components

Fixed/variable resistors, LDR (light ↑ R ↓), thermistor (T ↑ R ↓), diode/LED (one-way), relay, filament lamp (R grows as T rises — V–I curve flattens).

5. Power and energy

P = VI = I²R = V²/R; E = VIt. Fuse rating just above normal current; earth wire, double insulation, circuit breakers (trip quickly, resettable).

Example: 230 V, 2 A heater: P = 460 W; correct fuse 3 A or 5 A.

6. Digital electronics basics (syllabus 4.5 context)

Analogue vs digital; logic gates drive outputs from inputs (see CS link); sensors feed comparator-style circuits.

Exam tips: series: current same; parallel: p.d. same — say which before calculating; always compute total resistance first in mixed circuits.

title: Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment Revision Notes
content:
Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment A2 Level Biology

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI15, Topic 7. Respiration releases energy as ATP for muscle contraction. Homeostasis keeps the internal environment stable, and the kidney is central to this. The topic links biochemistry to physiology.

Aerobic Respiration Mechanics and Steps

Aerobic respiration is the overall reaction of splitting the respiratory substrate to release carbon dioxide as a waste product and reuniting hydrogen with atmospheric oxygen with the release of large amounts of energy. Respiration is a stepped process, with each step controlled and catalysed by a specific intracellular enzyme, though names of specific enzymes are not required. Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm, where glucose is phosphorylated using ATP and split into two pyruvate molecules, yielding a net gain of ATP produced by substrate-level phosphorylation, reduced coenzyme (reduced NAD), and pyruvate. The link reaction takes place in the mitochondrial matrix, converting pyruvate to acetyl coenzyme A via decarboxylation and dehydrogenation, producing carbon dioxide and reduced NAD. The Krebs cycle takes place in the matrix, involving a series of oxidation-reduction reactions that completely oxidise glucose derivatives, releasing carbon dioxide by decarboxylation, producing ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, and generating reduced NAD and reduced FAD by dehydrogenation. Oxidative phosphorylation takes place on the inner mitochondrial membrane, associated with the electron transport chain in mitochondria, where electrons passed along carriers release energy to pump protons into the intermembrane space, establishing a proton gradient for chemiosmosis where protons flow back through ATP synthase to synthesise ATP, with oxygen acting as the final electron acceptor.

  • Overall reaction: C6H12O6 + 6O2 yields 6CO2 + 6H2O + large amount of ATP.
  • Glycolysis: cytoplasm, phosphorylation of hexoses, substrate-level phosphorylation, production of pyruvate, reduced NAD, and ATP.
  • Link reaction and Krebs cycle: mitochondrial matrix, complete oxidation, decarboxylation producing CO2, substrate-level phosphorylation producing ATP, dehydrogenation producing reduced NAD and reduced FAD.
  • Oxidative phosphorylation: inner mitochondrial membrane, electron transport chain, chemiosmosis, ATP synthase.

Anaerobic Respiration and Lactate Metabolism

In the absence of oxygen, anaerobic respiration relies solely on glycolysis. In mammalian cells, pyruvate accepts hydrogen from reduced NAD to form lactate, catalysed by lactate dehydrogenase, which regenerates oxidised NAD so that glycolysis can continue to produce a small net amount of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation. After a period of anaerobic respiration in animals, the accumulated lactate is removed by being transported in the blood to the liver, where a proportion is oxidised back to pyruvate and then converted into glucose or glycogen, or respired aerobically, requiring an extra volume of oxygen known as the oxygen debt.

  • Role of glycolysis: phosphorylation of hexoses, production of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, reduced coenzyme, pyruvate and lactate.
  • Fate of lactate: transported to the liver, oxidised to pyruvate, converted to glucose or glycogen, or respired.

Worked Example: Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide produced if an organism consumes 20 cm³ of oxygen and has an RQ of 0.85.

  • Step 1: State the formula for respiratory quotient: RQ = volume of CO2 produced ÷ volume of O2 consumed.
  • Step 2: Rearrange the formula to solve for volume of CO2: volume of CO2 = RQ × volume of O2 consumed.
  • Step 3: Substitute the given values: volume of CO2 = 0.85 × 20 cm³.
  • Step 4: Calculate the final answer: volume of CO2 = 17 cm³.

Respiratory Quotient and Core Practical Measurements

The respiratory quotient (RQ) is defined as the ratio of the volume of carbon dioxide produced to the volume of oxygen consumed over a given period. Core Practical 15 involves using an artificial hydrogen carrier, such as methylene blue or DCPIP as a redox indicator, to investigate respiration in yeast by timing how long it takes for the indicator to change colour as it accepts hydrogen ions released during respiratory pathways. Core Practical 16 involves using a simple respirometer to determine the rate of respiration and RQ of a suitable material, such as germinating seeds or small invertebrates, by measuring the movement of a coloured drop in a capillary tube with and without carbon dioxide absorbents like soda lime.

  • RQ formula: RQ = volume of CO2 produced ÷ volume of O2 consumed.
  • Carbohydrate RQ is approximately 1.0, lipid RQ is approximately 0.7, protein RQ is approximately 0.9.
  • Core Practical 15: artificial hydrogen carrier redox indicator, yeast respiration rate.
  • Core Practical 16: simple respirometer, germinating seeds or small invertebrates, soda lime to absorb CO2.

Skeletal Muscles and Contraction Mechanism

Skeletal muscles, tendons, the skeleton, and ligaments interact to enable movement, operating via antagonistic muscle pairs where one muscle contracts (agonist) to pull a bone while the opposing muscle relaxes, consisting of extensors that straighten a limb and flexors that bend it. Mammalian skeletal muscle fibres are multinucleate cells containing myofibrils made of repeating units called sarcomeres, delineated by Z lines. Structurally and physiologically, slow twitch muscle fibres are adapted for endurance with high myoglobin content, numerous mitochondria, and a dense capillary network relying on aerobic respiration, whereas fast twitch muscle fibres are adapted for short, intense bursts of speed with fewer mitochondria, less myoglobin, a rich supply of glycogen, and reliance on anaerobic glycolysis. The process of contraction of skeletal muscle is explained by the sliding filament theory, where calcium ions (Ca2+) released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum bind to troponin, causing tropomyosin to shift and expose binding sites on actin. Myosin heads bind to these sites to form cross-bridges, hydrolysing ATP via ATPase to execute the power stroke, pulling actin filaments towards the centre of the sarcomere and shortening it without changing the lengths of the myofilaments themselves, with fresh ATP binding to myosin to break the cross-bridge.

  • Interactions: antagonistic muscle pairs, extensors, flexors, tendons attach muscle to bone, ligaments attach bone to bone.
  • Muscle fibre structure: sarcolemma, sarcoplasmic reticulum, transverse tubules, myofibrils, sarcomeres with actin and myosin.
  • Slow vs fast twitch: myoglobin, mitochondria, capillary density, respiration type, speed of contraction, fatigue resistance.
  • Sliding filament theory: actin, myosin, troponin, tropomyosin, calcium ions, ATP, ATPase.

Cardiac Muscle, ECGs, and Control of Circulation

Cardiac muscle is myogenic, meaning it initiates its own contraction without external nervous stimulation. The normal electrical activity of the heart coordinates the heartbeat: the sinoatrial node (SAN) acts as the pacemaker sending waves of electrical excitation across the atria, the atrioventricular node (AVN) delays the impulse before passing it down the bundle of His, and Purkyne fibres conduct the excitation rapidly up through the walls of the ventricles from the apex, causing coordinated ventricular contraction. Electrocardiograms (ECGs) record the electrical activity of the heart, showing P waves (atrial depolarisation), QRS complexes (ventricular depolarisation), and T waves (ventricular repolarisation), which aid in the diagnosis of abnormal heart rhythms such as tachycardia, bradycardia, or fibrillation. Cardiac output is calculated as heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. Variations in ventilation and cardiac output enable rapid delivery of oxygen to tissues and the removal of carbon dioxide from them, controlled by the cardiovascular control centre and the ventilation centre located in the medulla oblongata, which respond to changes in blood pH, carbon dioxide concentration, and blood pressure detected by chemoreceptors and baroreceptors.

  • Myogenic nature: intrinsic rhythmicity of cardiac muscle cells.
  • Conduction pathway: SAN to atria, AVN with delay, bundle of His, Purkyne fibres to ventricles.
  • ECG interpretation: P wave, QRS complex, T wave, diagnosing arrhythmias.
  • Cardiac output formula: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.
  • Medulla oblongata: cardiovascular control centre and ventilation centre regulating heart rate and breathing rate.

Fight or Flight Response and Spirometer Traces

The role of adrenaline in the fight or flight response includes binding to specific receptors on target cells, activating second messenger systems that prepare the body for intense physical activity by increasing heart rate, dilating bronchioles, and redirecting blood flow away from non-essential organs towards skeletal muscles. Core Practical 17 involves investigating the effects of exercise on tidal volume, breathing rate, respiratory minute ventilation, and oxygen consumption using data from spirometer traces, allowing precise calculation of lung volumes and metabolic rates.

  • Adrenaline: hormone secreted by adrenal glands, binds to surface receptors, triggers intracellular cascade via cyclic AMP.
  • Spirometer parameters: tidal volume, breathing rate, respiratory minute ventilation (tidal volume × breathing rate), oxygen consumption.

Worked Example: Calculate the respiratory minute ventilation for a person with a tidal volume of 0.5 dm³ and a breathing rate of 14 breaths per minute.

  • Step 1: State the formula: respiratory minute ventilation = tidal volume × breathing rate.
  • Step 2: Substitute the values: respiratory minute ventilation = 0.5 dm³ × 14 breaths per minute.
  • Step 3: Calculate the product: respiratory minute ventilation = 7.0 dm³ min−1.

Homeostasis, Negative Feedback, and Thermoregulation

Negative feedback is a control mechanism where a change in a variable from its set point triggers a response that opposes the change, bringing the system back within narrow limits to maintain dynamic equilibrium, whereas positive feedback amplifies the initial change away from the set point. Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment despite external fluctuations. During exercise, dynamic equilibrium is maintained, and the hypothalamus acts as the body's thermoregulation centre, monitoring core blood temperature via internal thermoreceptors and coordinating effector responses such as vasodilation, vasoconstriction, sweating, shivering, and behavioural changes to maintain optimal body temperature.

  • Negative feedback: sensor, coordinator, effector, corrective response reducing deviation from set point.
  • Positive feedback: deviation amplified, e.g., action potentials in neurones or oxytocin during birth.
  • Homeostasis: dynamic equilibrium, stability of internal environment.
  • Hypothalamus: thermoregulation control centre.

Kidney Structure and Osmoregulation

The gross and microscopic structure of the mammalian kidney includes the outer cortex, inner medulla, pelvis, ureter, and functional units called nephrons consisting of the Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule, and collecting duct. Urea is produced in the liver from excess amino acids via deamination (details of the ornithine cycle are not required), and it is removed from the bloodstream along with water, ions, and glucose by ultrafiltration in the Bowman's capsule under high hydrostatic pressure created by the difference in diameter between the afferent and efferent arterioles. In the proximal tubule, essential solutes such as glucose, amino acids, and mineral ions are selectively reabsorbed into the blood capillaries by active transport and cotransport mechanisms. The loop of Henle acts as a countercurrent multiplier to establish a steep sodium ion concentration gradient in the medulla, which maximises the reabsorption of water from the collecting duct. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus monitor blood water potential; when blood water potential drops, the posterior pituitary gland releases antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which travels to the kidneys and increases the permeability of the collecting duct cells to water via aquaporins, bringing about negative feedback control of mammalian plasma concentration and blood volume.

  • Gross structure: cortex, medulla, pelvis, ureter, renal artery, renal vein.
  • Urea production: deamination of excess amino acids in the liver.
  • Ultrafiltration: high hydrostatic pressure in glomerulus, basement membrane acting as a filter.
  • Proximal tubule reabsorption: active transport, cotransport, microvilli.
  • Loop of Henle: countercurrent multiplier, descending limb permeable to water, ascending limb impermeable to water and actively pumping sodium ions.
  • Osmoregulation loop: osmoreceptors in hypothalamus, posterior pituitary gland, ADH release, collecting duct permeability, negative feedback.

Exam tip: when you describe the link between ADH and water reabsorption, follow the steps in order: osmoreceptors detect water potential, posterior pituitary releases ADH, collecting duct walls become more permeable, water is reabsorbed into blood by osmosis.

Gene Control via Transcription Factors

Genes can be switched on and off by DNA transcription factors, which are proteins that bind to specific base sequences on DNA either promoting or blocking RNA polymerase binding. Peptide hormones act extracellularly by binding to cell surface membrane receptors and activating second messenger systems that trigger intracellular cascades involving transcription factors. In contrast, steroid hormones, being lipid-soluble, pass directly through the phospholipid bilayer of the cell membrane, bind to intracellular receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus, and the hormone-receptor complex acts directly as a transcription factor to switch specific genes on or off.

  • Transcription factors: proteins regulating transcription by binding to promoter regions.
  • Peptide hormones: hydrophilic, bind to surface receptors, use second messengers.
  • Steroid hormones: hydrophobic, cross cell membrane, bind to intracellular receptors, act directly on DNA.

Typical mistakes

  • Confusing substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle with oxidative phosphorylation at the electron transport chain. Correction: remember substrate-level phosphorylation involves direct transfer of a phosphate group to ADP from a reactive intermediate, whereas oxidative phosphorylation uses a proton gradient driven by electron transport.
  • Stating that the filaments shorten during muscle contraction in the sliding filament theory. Correction: actin and myosin filaments remain the same length; the sarcomere shortens because the filaments slide past each other, increasing the overlap.
  • Forgetting the exact sequence of osmoregulation. Correction: always start with blood water potential dropping, detected by osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus, leading to ADH release from the posterior pituitary, increasing collecting duct permeability.
  • Confusing the mechanism of peptide and steroid hormones. Correction: peptide hormones bind to extracellular surface receptors because they cannot cross the membrane, whereas steroid hormones cross membranes to bind intracellular receptors.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain how chemiosmosis leads to the synthesis of ATP during oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria. (Answer: electrons move along the electron transport chain releasing energy; this energy pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space creating a proton gradient; protons flow down their electrochemical gradient back into the matrix through ATP synthase channels, driving the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP.)
  2. Describe the role of calcium ions in the contraction of skeletal muscle. (Answer: calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the sarcoplasm; they bind to troponin molecules; this causes tropomyosin to change shape and move away from the binding sites on actin, allowing myosin heads to form cross-bridges.)
  3. Explain how the loop of Henle acts as a countercurrent multiplier to enable the production of concentrated urine. (Answer: sodium and chloride ions are actively pumped out of the ascending limb into the medulla; this lowers the water potential of the tissue fluid in the medulla; water moves out of the descending limb by osmosis; the hairpin countercurrent arrangement multiplies the concentration gradient down to the tip of the loop, facilitating maximum water reabsorption in the collecting duct.)
  4. Explain how negative feedback maintains blood glucose or plasma concentration within narrow limits. (Answer: a deviation from the set point is detected by sensory receptors; this sends a signal to a coordination centre; effectors are stimulated to bring about a corrective response that opposes the original change, returning the variable back to the set point.)
  5. Compare the action of peptide and steroid hormones in controlling gene transcription. (Answer: peptide hormones are water-soluble and bind to cell surface receptors, activating second messenger cascades that indirectly affect transcription factors; steroid hormones are lipid-soluble, diffuse through the cell membrane, bind to intracellular receptors, and the complex acts directly as a transcription factor to initiate or inhibit transcription of target genes.)

Use these notes alongside past paper practice questions to test your application of biochemical pathways and physiological feedback loops. Next, revise Topic 8: Genetics, Populations, Evolution and Ecosystems.

title: Exam technique: Ethics, Security & Impact
content:
### What earns the marks
To earn full marks on this topic, students need to precisely name the threat and provide the matched defence. For example, when asked to explain a security threat, students should state the threat, such as pharming, and then describe the defence, such as keeping DNS servers and hosts files secure and checking HTTPS certificates. Command words like explain, describe, and justify are commonly used in this topic's questions. Students should also be able to apply ethical principles to scenarios, as outlined in the ACM/IEEE-CS/BCS codes, and show how they affect stakeholders and consequences.
### Traps
A common mistake is confusing phishing and pharming. Another error is not providing a matched defence for a given threat. Students should also avoid giving opinions instead of principle-based answers in ethics questions.
### Memory hooks
To remember the types of malware, students can use the mnemonic VIRUS: V for virus, I for intercept, R for ransomware, U for unsecured, and S for spyware. Another hook is to associate each type of threat with its corresponding defence. For example, malware is defended against with anti-malware software. Students can also use a diagram to illustrate the blockchain concept and its components.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 10-15% of the paper, and students should budget around 10-12 minutes to answer the questions. Students should allocate their time according to the marks available for each question and make sure to read the questions carefully to avoid common traps.

title: Exam technique: Integration
content:
### What earns the marks
For indefinite integrals, each term raised correctly plus the constant earns full marks. For definite integrals, the antiderivative quoted earns one mark and the correct upper-minus-lower evaluation earns the next. For area and curve-finding, the limits or the given point used earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: constant of integration omitted. Correction: +c always for indefinite. Error: limits subtracted backwards. Correction: upper minus lower. Error: power rule inverted on roots. Correction: root x is x to the half, integral goes up.
### Worked example
Find the integral of 6x² − 4x⁻³. Raise each power by one and divide by the new power: 6x² becomes 2x³, and −4x⁻³ becomes 2x⁻² because (−4)/(−2) = 2. Add the constant: 2x³ + 2x⁻² + c. Check by differentiating: 6x² + (−4)x⁻³, which matches the original.
### Check yourself
Evaluate the definite integral of 2x + 1 from 1 to 3. The antiderivative is x² + x, giving (9 + 3) − (1 + 1) = 10. Write both the antiderivative and the subtraction on the paper, because the method mark depends on them.

### Worked example
Find the integral of 6x² − 4x⁻³. Raise each power by one and divide by the new power: 6x² becomes 2x³, and −4x⁻³ becomes 2x⁻² because (−4)/(−2) = 2. Add the constant: 2x³ + 2x⁻² + c. Check by differentiating: 6x² + (−4)x⁻³, which matches the original.

title: Algebra — Graphs — Study Notes
content:
Graphs

Key features of a curve

Find the y-intercept by setting x = 0, the x-intercepts by setting y = 0, and any turning point by completing the square or differentiating. A quadratic y = a(x − p)(x − q) crosses the x-axis at p and q.

Example: y = x² − 4x + 3 = (x − 1)(x − 3). The x-intercepts are 1 and 3, the y-intercept is 3, and completing the square gives the turning point (2, −1).

Transformations

  • y = f(x) + a translates the graph by a units up (down if a is negative).
  • y = f(x + a) translates the graph by a units to the left.
  • y = af(x) stretches the graph vertically by scale factor a, parallel to the y-axis.
  • y = f(ax) stretches the graph horizontally by scale factor 1/a, parallel to the x-axis.

Intersections of graphs

The points where two graphs meet are found by equating their equations. The resulting equation is solved for x, and the y-values are found by substituting back into either equation.

Exam technique

  • Label every intercept and turning point with its coordinates.
  • Check the sign of the leading coefficient to decide whether a quadratic has a minimum or a maximum.

title: Exam technique: Complex Numbers
content:
### What earns the marks
For modulus and argument, root(x squared + y squared) and tan inverse (y/x) each earn a mark with the quadrant checked. For quadratics, the negative discriminant shown earns the method mark and the a+bi pair earns the second. For loci, the geometric name (circle, line, half-line) earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: modulus squared reported as modulus. Correction: root last. Error: stopping at no real roots. Correction: continue into complex pair. Error: i squared treated as 1 in products. Correction: it equals -1.

title:
Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI12 Unit 1, Topic 2 Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression. It covers membrane structure and properties, osmosis and the different kinds of membrane transport, the structure of proteins and how they are built from amino acids, the structure of DNA and RNA and how DNA replicates, the genetic code and how genes work, transcription and translation, mutations and their effects, patterns of inheritance including sex linkage, cystic fibrosis as an example of a gene mutation in humans, and genetic screening and its ethical and social issues. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Cell membranes and the fluid mosaic model

The cell surface membrane (plasma membrane) is a phospholipid bilayer; each phospholipid has a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails, and the heads face out and in while the tails face each other, making a barrier to charged and water-soluble substances. The fluid mosaic model is the accepted interpretation: the membrane is fluid — the phospholipids and proteins can move laterally in the layer — and mosaic because it contains a variety of proteins embedded in or attached to the bilayer, including channel proteins and carrier proteins for transport, receptor proteins for signalling, and proteins for cell recognition. The model is an interpretation of data — it was built from evidence such as electron micrographs and the ability of membranes to fuse and to self-seal — and it explains the structure and properties of cell membranes and how they control what enters and leaves the cell. Cholesterol in the membrane reduces fluidity at high temperatures and prevents the membrane from becoming too rigid at low temperatures.

2. Core Practical 3 — investigating membrane properties

Investigate membrane properties including the effect of alcohol and of temperature on membrane permeability. A typical method uses beetroot cylinders, which contain the red pigment betalain in their vacuoles; as the membrane is damaged, pigment leaks out and the colour of the surrounding solution deepens. Cut cylinders to the same length, wash off surface pigment in distilled water, then place them in water at a range of temperatures or in different concentrations of alcohol for a fixed time, remove the tissue and measure the concentration of pigment in the solution with a colorimeter. As temperature rises or alcohol concentration rises, the membrane proteins denature and the lipid bilayer is disrupted, so permeability increases and more pigment leaks out; a control at room temperature or in distilled water shows the baseline. Record the colorimeter reading for each tube, plot a graph of permeability against temperature or against alcohol concentration, and explain the trend in terms of the effect on membrane proteins and lipids.

3. Osmosis and how water moves across membranes

Osmosis is the net movement of free water molecules through a partially permeable membrane, down a water potential gradient — from higher water potential to lower water potential. Water potential is the tendency of water to move; adding a solute lowers it, so a concentrated solution has a more negative water potential than a dilute one, and pure water has the highest (zero) water potential. If a cell is placed in a solution of higher water potential than its contents, water enters by osmosis and the cell swells; if it is an animal cell it may burst (haemolysis); if it is a plant cell the cell wall prevents bursting and the cell becomes turgid, which supports the plant. In a solution of lower water potential, water leaves and the cell shrinks — animal cells crenate and plant cells become plasmolysed, with the membrane pulling away from the wall. A recommended additional practical is to investigate tissue water potentials using plant tissue (for example potato or onion epidermis) and graded concentrations of a solute: place tissue in solutions of different molarity, note the change in length or mass, and find the concentration at which there is no change — that concentration has the same water potential as the tissue.

4. Passive transport, active transport, endocytosis and exocytosis

Passive transport needs no energy input because substances move down their concentration gradient. Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration; small, non-polar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse directly through the phospholipid bilayer, while ions and large polar molecules cannot. Facilitated diffusion is the movement of specific particles down their concentration gradient through channel proteins or carrier proteins — channel proteins form water-filled pores for ions, and carrier proteins change shape to carry molecules across. Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient (from low to high concentration) and needs energy directly from ATP; carrier proteins use ATP to pump substances across, as in the sodium–potassium pump. Endocytosis is the bulk movement of material into the cell inside a vesicle formed from the plasma membrane; phagocytosis takes in solid material and pinocytosis takes in fluid. Exocytosis is the reverse — material is moved out of the cell in a vesicle that fuses with the plasma membrane, as in the secretion of proteins and neurotransmitters. Carrier and channel proteins are involved in facilitated diffusion and active transport; the key difference is that active transport needs ATP and moves substances against their gradient.

5. Protein structure: from amino acid to three-dimensional shape

Amino acids are the monomers of proteins; the basic structure of an amino acid is an amino group, a carboxyl group and a variable R group all attached to a central carbon, with a hydrogen on the remaining bond. There are around 20 amino acids found in proteins, differing only in their R group, and the sequence of amino acids in a protein is its primary structure. Amino acids join by condensation reactions to form peptide bonds, making dipeptides and then polypeptides; a polypeptide chain is a protein's primary structure and it determines everything about the protein. The secondary structure is the local folding of the chain into alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between the peptide bonds. The tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of the whole polypeptide, held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions; it gives the protein its specific shape and therefore its function. Globular proteins are roughly spherical and usually soluble and active — haemoglobin is the classic example, with four polypeptide chains and a haem group each carrying one oxygen molecule, and it shows quaternary structure (several polypeptides together) plus the importance of the three-dimensional shape for its oxygen-carrying function. Fibrous proteins are long, insoluble and structural — collagen is the example, made of three polypeptide chains wound into a rope-like triple helix, giving strength for tendons, ligaments and skin. The shape of a protein determines its function, so a change to the primary structure can alter the folding and disable the protein.

6. DNA structure and replication

A DNA molecule is made of two nucleotide strands twisted into a double helix. Each nucleotide is made of a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group and a base — either adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) or thymine (T). The two strands run antiparallel and are linked by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases — A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds) and C pairs with G (three hydrogen bonds). RNA is similar but has ribose instead of deoxyribose, uracil instead of thymine, and is usually single-stranded. The two strands are complementary, so knowing one strand tells you the other, and the two strands separate at replication. DNA replication is semi-conservative: the double helix unzips, each strand acts as a template, and free nucleotides pair with their complementary bases; DNA polymerase joins the nucleotides into a new strand. The result is two identical DNA molecules, each with one old strand and one new strand. Meselson and Stahl's experiment supported this: they grew bacteria in a medium with a heavy isotope of nitrogen (15N), then moved them to a 14N medium and examined the DNA by centrifugation; the first generation was a single hybrid band (not one heavy and one light, which would be conservative replication), and later generations showed a mixture of hybrid and light bands — exactly what semi-conservative replication predicts and ruling out the conservative and dispersive alternatives.

7. The genetic code and how it works

The genetic code is the set of rules translating the base sequence of mRNA into the amino acid sequence of a protein. It is a triplet code — three bases (a base triplet on DNA, a codon on mRNA) code for one amino acid; it is non-overlapping — each base is read once in order; and it is degenerate — more than one codon can code for the same amino acid, which is why many mutations change a base but not the amino acid. Part of the code is a stop codon that signals the end of translation; there is no amino acid for it. A gene is a sequence of bases on a DNA molecule that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. In transcription, the gene is copied into a complementary mRNA molecule by the enzyme RNA polymerase, using the DNA template (antisense) strand; the mRNA is complementary to the template strand and the same as the coding (sense) strand except with uracil in place of thymine. mRNA leaves the nucleus and attaches to ribosomes in the cytoplasm; transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules carry amino acids to the ribosome, each with a three-base anticodon that pairs with the mRNA codon, so the ribosome joins the amino acids into a polypeptide chain in the order of the codons until a stop codon is reached.

8. Mutations: the changes and their effects

A mutation is a change in the DNA base sequence. A substitution replaces one base with another — it may do nothing, change one amino acid, or, rarely, create a stop codon that shortens the protein. An insertion adds one or more bases and a deletion removes one or more; because the code is read in triplets, an insertion or deletion not in a multiple of three causes a frameshift, changing every amino acid after the mutation and usually destroying the protein's function. Mutations are the only source of new alleles, and most have no observable effect — they may be in non-coding DNA, or a degenerate codon and amino acid may stay the same, or the changed protein still folds and works. Some mutations give rise to cancer (if they affect control of the cell cycle) or to genetic disorders. Ionising radiation such as X-rays and ultraviolet light, and some chemicals such as those in tobacco smoke, can increase the rate of mutation by damaging DNA.

9. Patterns of inheritance: monohybrid crosses, pedigree diagrams and sex linkage

A gene can have different alleles; the genotype is the alleles an organism has, the phenotype is the observable feature. Dominant alleles show in the phenotype even when heterozygous; recessive alleles only show when homozygous. A monohybrid cross is the inheritance of one gene with two alleles; the typical ratios are a 3:1 phenotype ratio in the F2 of a monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes, but only if the alleles are completely dominant and the gene is autosomal. Sex linkage is the inheritance of a gene on the X chromosome — because males have only one X, a recessive allele on it shows in their phenotype even though they are effectively hemizygous; red-green colour blindness and haemophilia are human X-linked conditions that are more common in males. Pedigree diagrams record which family members show a trait and are used to work out whether a trait is dominant or recessive and whether it is autosomal or sex-linked. Codominance is when both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote, as in the ABO blood group system where IA and IB are codominant and i is recessive, giving the four blood groups A, B, AB and O.

10. Cystic fibrosis: a mutation that affects three systems

Cystic fibrosis is caused by a mutation in a gene that codes for a chloride ion channel protein; in the most common form a deletion of three bases removes a single amino acid from the protein, so the channel does not work properly. As a result, chloride ions and water cannot move properly across cell membranes, and the mucus and other secretions become abnormally thick. In the gaseous exchange system the thick mucus blocks the airways and makes it hard to breathe and to clear infections; in the digestive system the pancreatic duct is blocked so digestive enzymes from the pancreas cannot reach the gut, so food is not digested and absorbed properly, and the person may be malnourished; in the reproductive system the vas deferens is often absent or blocked in males, causing infertility. Treatments include physiotherapy and antibiotics for the lungs, and enzyme supplements with meals for digestion, and newer treatments aim to correct the underlying defect.

11. Genetic screening: what it can do and the issues it raises

Genetic screening can identify carriers of recessive alleles (people who have one normal allele and one faulty allele and are unaffected but could pass the allele on), and prenatal testing can check a fetus: amniocentesis takes a sample of amniotic fluid at around 15–17 weeks, and chorionic villus sampling takes a sample of placental tissue at 8–12 weeks. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis is used with IVF to test embryos before implantation and select unaffected ones. Each raises ethical and social questions — the safety and reliability of the test, the risks of miscarriage with invasive prenatal testing, the right to know or not to know, who decides which conditions to test for, the possible choice to terminate a pregnancy, anxiety and guilt, and the risk that screening could be used to select non-medical traits. Students should be able to identify and discuss these from religious, moral and social viewpoints and to evaluate the implications of prenatal genetic screening.

12. How to use this note and what to revise next

content:
Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI12 Unit 1, Topic 2 Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression. It covers membrane structure and properties, osmosis and the different kinds of membrane transport, the structure of proteins and how they are built from amino acids, the structure of DNA and RNA and how DNA replicates, the genetic code and how genes work, transcription and translation, mutations and their effects, patterns of inheritance including sex linkage, cystic fibrosis as an example of a gene mutation in humans, and genetic screening and its ethical and social issues. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Cell membranes and the fluid mosaic model

The cell surface membrane (plasma membrane) is a phospholipid bilayer; each phospholipid has a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails, and the heads face out and in while the tails face each other, making a barrier to charged and water-soluble substances. The fluid mosaic model is the accepted interpretation: the membrane is fluid — the phospholipids and proteins can move laterally in the layer — and mosaic because it contains a variety of proteins embedded in or attached to the bilayer, including channel proteins and carrier proteins for transport, receptor proteins for signalling, and proteins for cell recognition. The model is an interpretation of data — it was built from evidence such as electron micrographs and the ability of membranes to fuse and to self-seal — and it explains the structure and properties of cell membranes and how they control what enters and leaves the cell. Cholesterol in the membrane reduces fluidity at high temperatures and prevents the membrane from becoming too rigid at low temperatures.

2. Core Practical 3 — investigating membrane properties

Investigate membrane properties including the effect of alcohol and of temperature on membrane permeability. A typical method uses beetroot cylinders, which contain the red pigment betalain in their vacuoles; as the membrane is damaged, pigment leaks out and the colour of the surrounding solution deepens. Cut cylinders to the same length, wash off surface pigment in distilled water, then place them in water at a range of temperatures or in different concentrations of alcohol for a fixed time, remove the tissue and measure the concentration of pigment in the solution with a colorimeter. As temperature rises or alcohol concentration rises, the membrane proteins denature and the lipid bilayer is disrupted, so permeability increases and more pigment leaks out; a control at room temperature or in distilled water shows the baseline. Record the colorimeter reading for each tube, plot a graph of permeability against temperature or against alcohol concentration, and explain the trend in terms of the effect on membrane proteins and lipids.

3. Osmosis and how water moves across membranes

Osmosis is the net movement of free water molecules through a partially permeable membrane, down a water potential gradient — from higher water potential to lower water potential. Water potential is the tendency of water to move; adding a solute lowers it, so a concentrated solution has a more negative water potential than a dilute one, and pure water has the highest (zero) water potential. If a cell is placed in a solution of higher water potential than its contents, water enters by osmosis and the cell swells; if it is an animal cell it may burst (haemolysis); if it is a plant cell the cell wall prevents bursting and the cell becomes turgid, which supports the plant. In a solution of lower water potential, water leaves and the cell shrinks — animal cells crenate and plant cells become plasmolysed, with the membrane pulling away from the wall. A recommended additional practical is to investigate tissue water potentials using plant tissue (for example potato or onion epidermis) and graded concentrations of a solute: place tissue in solutions of different molarity, note the change in length or mass, and find the concentration at which there is no change — that concentration has the same water potential as the tissue.

4. Passive transport, active transport, endocytosis and exocytosis

Passive transport needs no energy input because substances move down their concentration gradient. Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration; small, non-polar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse directly through the phospholipid bilayer, while ions and large polar molecules cannot. Facilitated diffusion is the movement of specific particles down their concentration gradient through channel proteins or carrier proteins — channel proteins form water-filled pores for ions, and carrier proteins change shape to carry molecules across. Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient (from low to high concentration) and needs energy directly from ATP; carrier proteins use ATP to pump substances across, as in the sodium–potassium pump. Endocytosis is the bulk movement of material into the cell inside a vesicle formed from the plasma membrane; phagocytosis takes in solid material and pinocytosis takes in fluid. Exocytosis is the reverse — material is moved out of the cell in a vesicle that fuses with the plasma membrane, as in the secretion of proteins and neurotransmitters. Carrier and channel proteins are involved in facilitated diffusion and active transport; the key difference is that active transport needs ATP and moves substances against their gradient.

5. Protein structure: from amino acid to three-dimensional shape

Amino acids are the monomers of proteins; the basic structure of an amino acid is an amino group, a carboxyl group and a variable R group all attached to a central carbon, with a hydrogen on the remaining bond. There are around 20 amino acids found in proteins, differing only in their R group, and the sequence of amino acids in a protein is its primary structure. Amino acids join by condensation reactions to form peptide bonds, making dipeptides and then polypeptides; a polypeptide chain is a protein''s primary structure and it determines everything about the protein. The secondary structure is the local folding of the chain into alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between the peptide bonds. The tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of the whole polypeptide, held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions; it gives the protein its specific shape and therefore its function. Globular proteins are roughly spherical and usually soluble and active — haemoglobin is the classic example, with four polypeptide chains and a haem group each carrying one oxygen molecule, and it shows quaternary structure (several polypeptides together) plus the importance of the three-dimensional shape for its oxygen-carrying function. Fibrous proteins are long, insoluble and structural — collagen is the example, made of three polypeptide chains wound into a rope-like triple helix, giving strength for tendons, ligaments and skin. The shape of a protein determines its function, so a change to the primary structure can alter the folding and disable the protein.

6. DNA structure and replication

A DNA molecule is made of two nucleotide strands twisted into a double helix. Each nucleotide is made of a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group and a base — either adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) or thymine (T). The two strands run antiparallel and are linked by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases — A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds) and C pairs with G (three hydrogen bonds). RNA is similar but has ribose instead of deoxyribose, uracil instead of thymine, and is usually single-stranded. The two strands are complementary, so knowing one strand tells you the other, and the two strands separate at replication. DNA replication is semi-conservative: the double helix unzips, each strand acts as a template, and free nucleotides pair with their complementary bases; DNA polymerase joins the nucleotides into a new strand. The result is two identical DNA molecules, each with one old strand and one new strand. Meselson and Stahl''s experiment supported this: they grew bacteria in a medium with a heavy isotope of nitrogen (15N), then moved them to a 14N medium and examined the DNA by centrifugation; the first generation was a single hybrid band (not one heavy and one light, which would be conservative replication), and later generations showed a mixture of hybrid and light bands — exactly what semi-conservative replication predicts and ruling out the conservative and dispersive alternatives.

7. The genetic code and how it works

The genetic code is the set of rules translating the base sequence of mRNA into the amino acid sequence of a protein. It is a triplet code — three bases (a base triplet on DNA, a codon on mRNA) code for one amino acid; it is non-overlapping — each base is read once in order; and it is degenerate — more than one codon can code for the same amino acid, which is why many mutations change a base but not the amino acid. Part of the code is a stop codon that signals the end of translation; there is no amino acid for it. A gene is a sequence of bases on a DNA molecule that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. In transcription, the gene is copied into a complementary mRNA molecule by the enzyme RNA polymerase, using the DNA template (antisense) strand; the mRNA is complementary to the template strand and the same as the coding (sense) strand except with uracil in place of thymine. mRNA leaves the nucleus and attaches to ribosomes in the cytoplasm; transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules carry amino acids to the ribosome, each with a three-base anticodon that pairs with the mRNA codon, so the ribosome joins the amino acids into a polypeptide chain in the order of the codons until a stop codon is reached.

8. Mutations: the changes and their effects

A mutation is a change in the DNA base sequence. A substitution replaces one base with another — it may do nothing, change one amino acid, or, rarely, create a stop codon that shortens the protein. An insertion adds one or more bases and a deletion removes one or more; because the code is read in triplets, an insertion or deletion not in a multiple of three causes a frameshift, changing every amino acid after the mutation and usually destroying the protein''s function. Mutations are the only source of new alleles, and most have no observable effect — they may be in non-coding DNA, or a degenerate codon and amino acid may stay the same, or the changed protein still folds and works. Some mutations give rise to cancer (if they affect control of the cell cycle) or to genetic disorders. Ionising radiation such as X-rays and ultraviolet light, and some chemicals such as those in tobacco smoke, can increase the rate of mutation by damaging DNA.

9. Patterns of inheritance: monohybrid crosses, pedigree diagrams and sex linkage

A gene can have different alleles; the genotype is the alleles an organism has, the phenotype is the observable feature. Dominant alleles show in the phenotype even when heterozygous; recessive alleles only show when homozygous. A monohybrid cross is the inheritance of one gene with two alleles; the typical ratios are a 3:1 phenotype ratio in the F2 of a monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes, but only if the alleles are completely dominant and the gene is autosomal. Sex linkage is the inheritance of a gene on the X chromosome — because males have only one X, a recessive allele on it shows in their phenotype even though they are effectively hemizygous; red-green colour blindness and haemophilia are human X-linked conditions that are more common in males. Pedigree diagrams record which family members show a trait and are used to work out whether a trait is dominant or recessive and whether it is autosomal or sex-linked. Codominance is when both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote, as in the ABO blood group system where IA and IB are codominant and i is recessive, giving the four blood groups A, B, AB and O.

10. Cystic fibrosis: a mutation that affects three systems

Cystic fibrosis is caused by a mutation in a gene that codes for a chloride ion channel protein; in the most common form a deletion of three bases removes a single amino acid from the protein, so the channel does not work properly. As a result, chloride ions and water cannot move properly across cell membranes, and the mucus and other secretions become abnormally thick. In the gaseous exchange system the thick mucus blocks the airways and makes it hard to breathe and to clear infections; in the digestive system the pancreatic duct is blocked so digestive enzymes from the pancreas cannot reach the gut, so food is not digested and absorbed properly, and the person may be malnourished; in the reproductive system the vas deferens is often absent or blocked in males, causing infertility. Treatments include physiotherapy and antibiotics for the lungs, and enzyme supplements with meals for digestion, and newer treatments aim to correct the underlying defect.

11. Genetic screening: what it can do and the issues it raises

Genetic screening can identify carriers of recessive alleles (people who have one normal allele and one faulty allele and are unaffected but could pass the allele on), and prenatal testing can check a fetus: amniocentesis takes a sample of amniotic fluid at around 15–17 weeks, and chorionic villus sampling takes a sample of placental tissue at 8–12 weeks. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis is used with IVF to test embryos before implantation and select unaffected ones. Each raises ethical and social questions — the safety and reliability of the test, the risks of miscarriage with invasive prenatal testing, the right to know or not to know, who decides which conditions to test for, the possible choice to terminate a pregnancy, anxiety and guilt, and the risk that screening could be used to select non-medical traits. Students should be able to identify and discuss these from religious, moral and social viewpoints and to evaluate the implications of prenatal genetic screening.

12. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working through each section and checking that you can draw a cell membrane from the fluid mosaic model and label the phospholipid bilayer, the proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins; state the difference between diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport, and give an example of each; outline the steps of DNA extraction (a simple practical with strawberries or onions is useful to remember); and carry out a genetic cross with a Punnett square and interpret the ratios. Revise by drawing protein structure from amino acid to tertiary, then drawing the DNA double helix and explaining semi-conservative replication and the Meselson–Stahl evidence. After this topic, revise Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development, because the same DNA and protein-synthesis processes control cell differentiation and the cell cycle.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Osmosis, applied to a potato cylinder placed in a sugar solution: water moves from the higher water potential to the lower one, down a gradient, through a partially permeable membrane. A cylinder that loses mass has been placed in a solution of lower water potential than its cells. Give the direction of water movement and the reason in the same sentence.
  • Monohybrid cross, applied to two heterozygotes (Aa × Aa): the offspring are 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, so the phenotypic ratio is 3 : 1. Write the parental genotypes, the gametes and the Punnett square, then state the ratio. A ratio alone earns less than the full working.
  • Sex linkage, applied to X-linked haemophilia: a carrier mother (XᴴXʰ) and a normal father (XᴴY) have a 50% chance of a son with haemophilia, but a daughter cannot be affected unless her father is affected. Use the X and Y chromosomes explicitly in the genotypes.
  • Mutation effects: a substitution may have no effect because the genetic code is degenerate, while a frameshift changes every codon after the mutation. Name the type of mutation and state whether the change alters the amino acid sequence.

title: Exam technique: Angles and Polygons
content:
### What earns the marks
For angle-chasing, justify earns marks for each reason stated alongside the value: angles on a straight line, vertically opposite, alternate, corresponding, and the circle theorems by name. For cyclic quadrilaterals, quote earns the theorem (opposite angles sum to 180) before the equation. For polygons, the formula (n - 2) x 180 stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: using adjacent instead of opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral. Correction: mark the diagram first. Error: answering each interior angle when the sum is asked. Correction: only divide at the very end. Error: treating any triangle in a circle as right-angled. Correction: the right angle needs the diameter as hypotenuse.
### Worked example
The sum of the interior angles of an n-sided polygon is (n − 2) × 180°. For a regular octagon (n = 8), each interior angle is 6 × 180 ÷ 8 = 135°, so each exterior angle is 45°. The exterior angles of any polygon add up to 360°, which gives a quick check: 8 × 45 = 360.
### Check yourself
Find the interior angle of a regular hexagon. Use (6 − 2) × 180 ÷ 6 = 120°. Explain why the exterior angle is 60° and why this matches 360 ÷ 6.

title: Integration II — Study Notes
content:
Integration II

Standard Integrals

  • ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c
  • ∫ cos x dx = sin x + c
  • ∫ e^x dx = e^x + c
  • ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c
  • ∫ sec²x dx = tan x + c

With linear arguments: ∫ e^(3x) dx = e^(3x)/3 + c; ∫ cos 2x dx = sin 2x/2 + c.

Substitution

Reverse of the chain rule. For ∫ 2x e^(x²) dx, let u = x²: du = 2x dx, so the integral is ∫ e^u du = e^(x²) + c.

Integration by Parts

∫ u (dv/dx) dx = uv − ∫ v (du/dx) dx. Choose u to be the part that simplifies when differentiated (LIATE: logs, inverse trig, algebraic, trig, exponential).

Example: ∫ x e^x dx = x e^x − ∫ e^x dx = x e^x − e^x + c.

Partial Fractions

Break rational functions into pieces like ∫ 1/(x+1) dx = ln|x + 1| + c.

Example: ∫ 4x/(x² − 1) dx = ∫ [2/(x − 1) + 2/(x + 1)] dx = 2 ln|x − 1| + 2 ln|x + 1| + c.

Exam tips: definite integrals: substitute limits into the transformed variable directly; for by-parts integrals like ∫ ln x dx, take u = ln x, dv/dx = 1.

Exam method: exponential and reciprocal integrals

The integral of e^(kx) is (1/k) e^(kx) + c, and the integral of e^x is e^x + c. The integral of 1/(ax + b) is (1/a) ln|ax + b| + c. Dividing by the coefficient of x is the step most often missed, so check it by differentiating your answer.

For a definite integral, evaluate the antiderivative at the upper limit, subtract its value at the lower limit, and write the bracket with its limits, such as [e^(2x)/2] from 0 to 1.

When the integrand is a product, integration by parts gives ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. Choose u to be the part that becomes simpler when differentiated, such as x in x eˣ.

Substitution changes the limits as well as the variable. Either change the limits to the new variable or substitute back before using the original limits; do not mix the two.

Exam cue: Give the answer as an exact value, such as (e² − 1)/2, unless the question asks for a decimal.

title: Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving — Study Notes
content:
Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving

Thinking Ahead, Abstractly, Systematically

  • Abstraction: keep essential features, drop detail — a metro map ignores street geometry.
  • Decomposition: split the problem into sub-problems solved independently.
  • Thinking ahead: pre-plan inputs, outputs and reusable components; pre-calculate tables where possible.

Recursion

A recursive routine calls itself with a smaller input and a base case that stops the recursion. Elegant for trees and divide-and-conquer, but each call consumes stack space — deep recursion can overflow. Any recursion can be rewritten with a loop and explicit stack.

Searching and Sorting

  • Linear search: O(n), works unsorted.
  • Binary search: O(log n), needs sorted data.
  • Bubble sort: O(n²) average; simple; detects a sorted pass.
  • Insertion sort: O(n²) average; fast on nearly-sorted data.
  • Merge sort: O(n log n) always; needs extra memory.

Testing

White-box tests trace internal paths; black-box tests check specification behaviour. Choose normal, boundary and erroneous data. Dry runs use trace tables recording variables line by line; a trace of recursion should log each call and its return.

Exam tips: write the base case before the recursive call in pseudocode; give the Big-O with a one-line justification; construct a trace table for a small loop or recursive call.

Recursion

A recursive routine calls itself on a smaller version of the problem. It needs a base case that stops the calls and a recursive case that moves towards the base case. Without a base case the routine never terminates and the call stack overflows.

Example: factorial(n) = 1 if n = 0, otherwise n × factorial(n − 1).

Recursion and iteration can solve the same problems. Recursion is often clearer for tree-shaped problems; iteration uses less memory because it does not build up stack frames.

title: Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7 — Study Notes
content:
Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 8. Redox reactions involve electron transfer. The same ideas explain the reactions of metals with water and acids, and the displacement reactions of the halogens.

Oxidation states

  • Oxidation state is the charge an atom would have if all bonds were ionic. Elements are 0, simple ions equal their charge, and the sum of oxidation states equals the overall charge.
  • Oxidation is an increase in oxidation state (loss of electrons); reduction is a decrease (gain of electrons).
  • The oxidising agent is reduced; the reducing agent is oxidised.

Redox equations

  • Half-equations balance atoms, then charge, with electrons added to show the transfer. Combine them so that electrons cancel.
  • Example: MnO4⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H2O, and acidified manganate(VII) decolourises when it is reduced.

Group 1 and Group 2

  • Reactivity increases down Group 1 because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily.
  • Group 2 metals form M²⁺ ions. Reactivity with water increases down the group: magnesium reacts slowly with cold water, while calcium reacts steadily.
  • The solubility of Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates changes down the group: magnesium sulfate is soluble, barium sulfate is not.

Group 7

  • Halogens are non-metals that form X2 molecules. Oxidising power decreases down the group: chlorine displaces bromide and iodide ions, bromine displaces iodide ions.
  • Halide ions are reducing agents, and reducing power increases down the group. Concentrated sulfuric acid is reduced by HI to hydrogen sulfide, because iodide ions are strong reducing agents.

Tests for halide ions

  • Silver nitrate solution forms precipitates: chloride gives white, bromide cream, iodide yellow. Dilute ammonia distinguishes the first two.

Exam tip: when balancing a redox equation in acid, add H⁺ and H2O before counting electrons, and always check that charge and atoms balance on both sides.

### Worked example An abstract data type defines the data and operations without fixing the implementation. A stack is last-in-first-out: push adds an item to the top and pop removes the top item. If you push 3, then 7, then pop twice, the first pop returns 7 and the second returns 3. A queue is first-in-first-out, so enqueue and dequeue return 3 then 7 in the same sequence. ### Check yourself Trace a queue after enqueue(A), enqueue(B), dequeue(). title: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation — Study Notes
content:
Measures of Variation

Range and Quartiles

The range is max − min — quick but destroyed by a single outlier. Quartiles split ordered data into quarters: Q₁ at position (n + 1)/4, Q₃ at 3(n + 1)/4 (raw data). The interquartile range, IQR = Q₃ − Q₁, is the spread of the middle 50% and resists outliers. Outliers are commonly flagged as values beyond Q₁ − 1.5·IQR or Q₃ + 1.5·IQR.

Variance and Standard Deviation

For raw data:

  • variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/n (the definitional form)
  • equivalently s² = Σx²/n − x̄² (the computational form)
  • standard deviation s = √(variance)

The standard deviation shares the units of the data; the variance does not. For frequency tables use Σf(x − x̄)²/Σf, or Σfx²/Σf − x̄².

Grouped Data

Use class midpoints as x. The result is an estimate — grouping discards within-class detail.

Combining and Scaling Datasets

Multiplying every value by b multiplies s by |b| and the variance by b². Adding a constant changes nothing in the spread. Two merged datasets: compute combined Σx and Σx² from each part, then apply the computational formula.

Example: data 1, 3, 4, 5, 7: mean 4, Σx² = 100, so variance = 100/5 − 16 = 4 and s = 2.

Exam tips: state units for s. When comparing consistency, the dataset with the smaller standard deviation (relative to its mean) is the more consistent. Always give the comparison sentence, not just the two numbers.

title: Probability Distributions — Study Notes
content:
Discrete Random Variables

Probability Distributions

A discrete random variable X takes values xᵢ with probabilities pᵢ where each pᵢ ≥ 0 and Σpᵢ = 1. A probability distribution can be given as a table, a formula, or a function. Any missing probability is found by subtraction.

Example: X = number of heads in 2 fair tosses: P(0) = 1/4, P(1) = 1/2, P(2) = 1/4.

Expectation

The mean of X is

  • E(X) = Σxᵢpᵢ

It is a weighted average — the long-run average value over many repetitions. E(X) need not equal any value X can actually take.

Variance

  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))²

where E(X²) = Σxᵢ²pᵢ — square the values before multiplying by probabilities. The standard deviation is √Var(X).

Linear Transforms

For constants a and b:

  • E(aX + b) = a·E(X) + b and Var(aX + b) = a²·Var(X)

Adding a constant shifts but does not spread; multiplying scales the spread by |a|.

Independent Variables

If X and Y are independent: E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y) and Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y). The addition rule for expectation always holds; the variance addition needs independence. The same applies to differences: Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) — the subtraction does not cancel spread.

Exam tips: first verify Σp = 1 in any given table. Write E(X²) and (E(X))² separately; merging them is the most common exam error. In games of chance, set the expected profit to zero to find a fair entry fee.

Exam method: discrete distributions

A discrete probability distribution gives P(X = x) for each value x. Each probability lies between 0 and 1, and the probabilities sum to 1. Use the sum to find an unknown constant before calculating any other probability.

The expected value is E(X) = Σ x P(X = x), and E(X²) = Σ x² P(X = x). The variance is Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]². Set out the values, probabilities and products in a table to keep the working clear.

For a function of X, such as Y = 2X + 3, the expected value is E(Y) = 2E(X) + 3. The variance changes as Var(2X + 3) = 4 Var(X), because adding a constant does not change the spread.

When a question asks for P(X ≤ x) or P(X ≥ x), add the probabilities for the values in the range.

Exam cue: Check that the probabilities sum to 1 before reporting any expected value, because a missing or wrong probability makes the rest of the answer wrong.

title: Waves — Study Notes
content:
Waves

Progressive waves

  • A progressive wave transfers energy without transferring matter. Its speed is v = fλ, where f is the frequency and λ the wavelength. Period T = 1/f.
  • Phase difference: two points separated by one wavelength are in phase. Points separated by half a wavelength are in antiphase.

Transverse and longitudinal waves

  • Transverse: the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. light, waves on a string).
  • Longitudinal: the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. sound in air, compressions and rarefactions).

Doppler effect for sound

When a source moves towards an observer, the observed frequency is higher and the wavelength is shorter. When it moves away, the observed frequency is lower and the wavelength is longer. The speed of sound in the medium does not change.

Electromagnetic spectrum

All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum. In order of increasing wavelength: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves, radio waves. Frequency increases in the reverse order.

Polarisation

Only transverse waves can be polarised. Polarisation restricts the oscillations to a single plane. Longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised.

Worked example: a wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 6.0 m. Its speed is v = fλ = 50 × 6.0 = 300 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: learn the spectrum order in terms of wavelength, not frequency. For the Doppler effect, state which way the source moves relative to the observer. Only transverse waves can show polarisation.

Polarisation and the Doppler effect

Only transverse waves can be polarised, because their oscillations can be restricted to one plane. A polariser passes only the component of the oscillation along its transmission axis. Light from a sky or a reflection is partly polarised, which is why polarising filters reduce glare. The Doppler effect for a moving source gives an observed frequency f' = f v/(v ± vs), where the upper sign applies when the source moves away from the observer and the lower sign when it approaches.

Exam tip: longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised, so say so explicitly if a question asks about it.

Worked example: wave speed from frequency and wavelength

A sound wave has frequency 680 Hz and wavelength 0.50 m. Using v = fλ, the speed is 680 × 0.50 = 340 m/s, close to the speed of sound in air. For an electromagnetic wave in a vacuum the same relation applies, with v = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Take the wavelength from a displacement–distance graph and the period from a displacement–time graph, then use f = 1/T before substituting.

Exam method: reading wave graphs

On a displacement–distance graph, the wavelength is the distance between two adjacent points in phase, such as two successive crests, not the distance between a crest and a trough. On a displacement–time graph, the period is the time for one complete oscillation at a fixed point. Mark the values on the axes carefully, because many lost marks come from reading half a wavelength or half a period.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Temperature and scales

Thermodynamic temperature is measured in kelvin. The kelvin and Celsius scales have the same size of degree, with T/K = θ/°C + 273. Absolute zero (0 K) is the lowest possible temperature, at which the particles of an ideal gas have minimum kinetic energy.

Example: 25 °C = 298 K.

Specific heat capacity and latent heat

Specific heat capacity c is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K: Q = mcΔθ. Latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg without a change in temperature: Q = mL. Melting and boiling absorb energy without a temperature rise, because the energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds, not into kinetic energy.

Example: warming 2.0 kg of water (c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) by 10 K needs 84 kJ. Melting 0.20 kg of ice (L = 334 kJ kg⁻¹) needs 67 kJ.

The mole and Avogadro constant

One mole contains N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ particles. The number of particles is N = nN_A, where n is the amount in moles. Molar mass is the mass of one mole, in kg mol⁻¹ in SI units.

Equation of state for an ideal gas

pV = nRT, where R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and T must be absolute. Equivalently pV = NkT, with k = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

Example: 0.10 mol at 300 K in 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ has p = nRT/V ≈ 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa.

Kinetic theory

The pressure of an ideal gas comes from molecules colliding with the container walls. The mean kinetic energy of a molecule is ⟨Ek⟩ = 3kT/2, so it depends only on the absolute temperature. At 300 K it is about 6.2 × 10⁻²¹ J.

Internal energy and the first law

The internal energy of an ideal gas is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its molecules. For an ideal gas there are no intermolecular forces, so internal energy depends only on temperature. The first law of thermodynamics is ΔU = Q + W, where Q is heat added to the system and W is work done on the system. Heat lost by a system is therefore negative.

Example: a gas has 500 J of work done on it and loses 200 J of heat. ΔU = −200 + 500 = +300 J.

Exam tips: convert to kelvin before using pV = nRT or the kinetic-energy formula. Check the sign convention for W in the question. Use latent heat only when the temperature is constant.

Worked example: pressure of a fixed amount of gas

A sample of 0.50 mol of ideal gas is at 300 K in a container of volume 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Using pV = nRT with R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, the pressure is p = (0.50 × 8.31 × 300) ÷ (2.0 × 10⁻³) ≈ 6.2 × 10⁵ Pa. If the same gas is heated to 600 K in a rigid container, the pressure doubles, because for a fixed amount of gas at constant volume p is proportional to T in kelvin. Converting temperatures to kelvin before multiplying is the step examiners check first.

Exam method: units and conversions

Convert cm³ to m³ by dividing by 1 000 000, and convert °C to K by adding 273 (or 273.15). Mass in grams must be turned into kilograms for kinetic energy calculations, and into moles using the molar mass. A quick unit check helps: pressure in pascals multiplied by volume in cubic metres gives joules, the unit of energy.

title: Integration — Study Notes
content:
Integration

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Integration reverses differentiation, so each method here is a differentiation rule read backwards. Two things cost most marks: the constant of integration, and the way limits are applied to a definite integral.

Indefinite integrals

∫axⁿ dx = a x^(n+1)/(n + 1) + c, for n ≠ −1. Add one to the power, divide by the new power, and always write +c. Multiply out brackets and rewrite roots as powers before you integrate.

Example: ∫(6x² − 4√x) dx = 2x³ − (8/3)x^(3/2) + c.

Example: ∫(x − 2)(x + 4) dx = ∫(x² + 2x − 8) dx = x³/3 + x² − 8x + c.

Finding a specific curve

The integral gives a family of curves, all differing by the constant c. A point the curve passes through fixes c. Integrate dy/dx, then substitute the coordinates of the point to find c.

Example: dy/dx = 3x² − 2x + 1, and the curve passes through (−1, 4). Integrating gives y = x³ − x² + x + c. Substituting x = −1 and y = 4 gives c = 7, so y = x³ − x² + x + 7.

Definite integrals

Evaluate the antiderivative at the upper limit and subtract its value at the lower limit. No +c is needed, because it cancels. A negative result is normal when the region lies below the x-axis.

Example: ∫ from −1 to 2 of (3x² − 4) dx = [x³ − 4x] from −1 to 2 = (8 − 8) − (−1 + 4) = −3.

Area under a curve

Find where the curve crosses the x-axis, then integrate between those points. Any part below the axis gives a negative integral, so take its sign off before adding the areas together.

Example: y = 4x − x² crosses the x-axis at 0 and 4, and lies above it between them. The area is ∫ from 0 to 4 of (4x − x²) dx = [2x² − x³/3] from 0 to 4 = 32/3 square units.

Area between two curves

Find the intersection points, then integrate the upper curve minus the lower curve between them. To check which curve is on top, test a value between the two points.

Example: y = x² and y = x + 2 meet where x² = x + 2, so x = −1 and x = 2. The area is ∫ from −1 to 2 of (x + 2 − x²) dx = 9/2 square units.

Trapezium rule

With strips of width h and ordinates y₀, y₁, …, yₙ, the estimate is (h/2)[y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ]. For a curve that bends upwards, the estimate is an overestimate.

Example: ∫ from 0 to 2 of (x² + 1) dx with two strips (h = 1). The ordinates are 1, 2 and 5, so the estimate is (1/2)(1 + 4 + 5) = 5. The exact value is 14/3, so the estimate is larger, as expected for a curve bending upwards.

Common errors

  • Integrating a product term by term without expanding the brackets first.
