title: Exam technique: Hardware & Architecture
content:
### What earns the marks
To earn full marks on this topic, students need to demonstrate a clear understanding of the concepts. For 3.1, explain the von Neumann model and the FDE cycle, showing how instructions are stored as data. For 3.2, describe input and output devices, and for 3.3, compare different storage types, justifying their use cases. Command words like explain, describe, and justify require working and a reason to be shown.
### Traps
Common mistakes include confusing the roles of the PC and MAR registers, and not understanding the difference between RAM and ROM. Another error is not considering the effects of performance factors like clock speed and cache size. Correction: review the FDE cycle and the characteristics of each storage type.
### Memory hooks
To remember the FDE cycle, use the mnemonic Fetch-Decode-Execute. For the types of buses, think address-data-control. To compare storage types, consider the acronym CAPD: capacity, access time, portability, and durability. Finally, to sanity-check an answer, ask whether it aligns with the stored program concept.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 20-30% of the paper, so budget around 30-40 minutes for it. Make sure to leave time to review and check your work.

title: Exam technique: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
content:
### What earns the marks
For percentages of amounts, the 10-percent building blocks shown earn method marks without a calculator. For reverse percentages, state what the given amount represents (64 dollars = 80 percent) before dividing: that line earns the mark. For compound interest, each year on its own line earns credit. For Steel-type growth and decay, the multiplier (1/2 cubed) stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: adding 20 percent to the sale price for the original. Correction: the sale price is the base of nothing; divide by 0.8. Error: simple interest applied twice for compound growth. Correction: grow each year from the new total. Error: decimal-point slips in 3/8 to percent. Correction: decimal first (0.375), then times 100.
### Worked example
Find 35% of 240: 0.35 × 240 = 84. A value increases by 20% to reach 180. The original is 180 ÷ 1.2 = 150, because you divide by the multiplier rather than taking 20% of 180. Check: 150 × 1.2 = 180. For fractions, 3/4 + 2/5 = 15/20 + 8/20 = 23/20 = 1 3/20.
### Check yourself
A price falls from £80 to £68. Find the percentage decrease. The decrease is £12, so the percentage is 12/80 × 100 = 15%. Show the divisor is the original price and not the new one.

### Worked example
Find 35% of 240: 0.35 × 240 = 84. A value increases by 20% to reach 180. The original is 180 ÷ 1.2 = 150, because you divide by the multiplier rather than taking 20% of 180. Check: 150 × 1.2 = 180. For fractions, 3/4 + 2/5 = 15/20 + 8/20 = 23/20 = 1 3/20.

title: Further Algebra — Study Notes
content:
Further Algebra

Polynomial Division and the Remainder Theorem

Divide to rewrite p(x) = (x − a)q(x) + r. The remainder when dividing by (x − a) equals p(a).

Example: p(x) = x³ − 2x² + 5. p(2) = 8 − 8 + 5 = 5, so dividing by (x − 2) leaves remainder 5.

If p(a) = 0, then (x − a) is a factor — that is the factor theorem. Divide out fully to reduce a cubic to a quadratic and factorise completely.

The Modulus Function

|x| measures distance from zero: |x| = x for x ≥ 0, −x for x < 0. Its graph is V-shaped.

Solving |2x − 1| = 5: split into 2x − 1 = 5 or 2x − 1 = −5, giving x = 3 or −2.

Inequalities: |2x − 1| < 5 becomes −5 < 2x − 1 < 5, so −2 < x < 3.

Partial Fractions

Reverse of combining fractions — needed before binomial expansion of rational functions.

  • Repeated linear: (4x + 1)/(x + 1)² = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 1)²
  • Distinct linear: (7x + 4)/(x + 1)(x + 2) = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 2)

Example: cover the (x + 1) factor with x = −1: B = 3; then compare coefficients for A = 4.

Exam tips: for |ax + b| > c, remember two separate regions; check factor-theorem roots by substitution before long division.

Exam method: partial fractions

Partial fractions split a rational function into simpler fractions whose sum equals the original. Before splitting, check the degrees: if the numerator has degree at least that of the denominator, divide first to get a polynomial plus a proper fraction.

For distinct linear factors (x − p)(x − q), write the expression as A/(x − p) + B/(x − q). Multiply through by the denominator and compare coefficients, or substitute x = p and x = q to find A and B directly. This substitution is the cover-up method and is the fastest route when the factors are linear and distinct.

A repeated factor (x − p)² needs two terms, A/(x − p) + B/(x − p)². An irreducible quadratic factor such as x² + 1 needs a linear numerator over it, (Ax + B)/(x² + 1).

Partial fractions are used to integrate rational functions, so the split is often followed by a logarithmic integral. Check the answer by recombining the fractions at one simple value of x.

Exam cue: State the form of the partial fractions before finding the constants, because the form is credited separately from the values.

title: Waves — Study Notes
content:
Waves

Progressive waves

  • A progressive wave transfers energy without transferring matter. Its speed is v = fλ, where f is the frequency and λ the wavelength. Period T = 1/f.
  • Phase difference: two points separated by one wavelength are in phase. Points separated by half a wavelength are in antiphase.

Transverse and longitudinal waves

  • Transverse: the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. light, waves on a string).
  • Longitudinal: the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. sound in air, compressions and rarefactions).

Doppler effect for sound

When a source moves towards an observer, the observed frequency is higher and the wavelength is shorter. When it moves away, the observed frequency is lower and the wavelength is longer. The speed of sound in the medium does not change.

Electromagnetic spectrum

All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum. In order of increasing wavelength: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves, radio waves. Frequency increases in the reverse order.

Polarisation

Only transverse waves can be polarised. Polarisation restricts the oscillations to a single plane. Longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised.

Worked example: a wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 6.0 m. Its speed is v = fλ = 50 × 6.0 = 300 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: learn the spectrum order in terms of wavelength, not frequency. For the Doppler effect, state which way the source moves relative to the observer. Only transverse waves can show polarisation.

title: Materials: Deformation — Study Notes
content:
Materials: deformation

Stress and strain

  • Stress = F ÷ A, where A is the cross-sectional area perpendicular to the force. Unit: pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻².
  • Strain = extension ÷ original length. It has no unit.

Young modulus

Young modulus E = stress ÷ strain, measured in the region where stress is proportional to strain. Unit: Pa.

Force–extension behaviour

  • Up to the limit of proportionality, extension is proportional to force (Hooke's law), and the graph is a straight line through the origin.
  • Up to the elastic limit, the material returns to its original length when unloaded. This is elastic deformation.
  • Beyond the elastic limit, the material is plastically deformed and does not return to its original length. The graph curves, and the energy in the extension is not recovered.

Energy stored

The elastic energy stored in a stretched material equals the area under its force–extension graph up to the point of interest. For a spring obeying Hooke's law, E = ½Fx = ½kx².

Worked example: a wire of cross-sectional area 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² is pulled by 500 N. Stress = 500 ÷ (2.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 2.5 × 10⁶ Pa. If it extends by 1.0 mm from an original length of 2.0 m, strain = 0.001 ÷ 2.0 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴, so E = 2.5 × 10⁶ ÷ 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 5.0 × 10⁹ Pa.

Exam tips: convert the area to m² and the extension to m before calculating. Strain has no unit, so do not write a unit for it. Say "the limit of proportionality" and "the elastic limit" as separate ideas.

Stored elastic energy and Hooke's law

Within the limit of proportionality, extension is proportional to force, F = kx, and the stiffness k depends on the material and its dimensions. The elastic strain energy stored in a stretched wire is equal to the area under the force-extension graph, E = ½Fx. For a material, the Young modulus E = stress / strain. Beyond the elastic limit the material deforms plastically and does not return to its original length.

Exam tip: state the limit of proportionality on the graph, because the energy formula only applies while the material obeys Hooke's law.

Worked example: a stretched wire with a load

A steel wire 1.5 m long and 0.80 mm in diameter is loaded with a 20 kg mass. The cross-sectional area is π(0.40 × 10⁻³)² ≈ 5.03 × 10⁻⁷ m². The force is F = mg = 20 × 9.81 = 196 N, so the stress is 196 ÷ (5.03 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 3.9 × 10⁸ Pa.

If the wire stretches by 1.1 mm, the strain is 0.0011 ÷ 1.5 ≈ 7.3 × 10⁻⁴, and E = stress ÷ strain = 3.9 × 10⁸ ÷ 7.3 × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 5.3 × 10¹¹ Pa. Quote the Young modulus with its unit and to two significant figures, and check that the value is in the range expected for the material: steel is roughly 2 × 10¹¹ Pa, so a result far from that points to an area or unit error.

Comparing materials

  • A stiff material has a large Young modulus: for a given stress, it produces a small strain.
  • A brittle material fractures soon after the elastic limit, with little or no plastic deformation, so its graph stops abruptly.
  • A ductile material, such as copper, undergoes large plastic deformation before it breaks, so its graph shows a long curved section after the elastic limit.

Area under the graph

For a non-linear force–extension graph, the energy stored is still the area under the curve. Count the squares, or split the region into a triangle and a rectangle, and convert the result to joules using the scale factors. Only the energy up to the elastic limit can be recovered when the load is removed; the rest is dissipated as heat.

Hysteresis and loading cycles

When a material is loaded and then unloaded, the unloading curve may not retrace the loading curve. The region enclosed between the two curves is energy dissipated per cycle, often as heat. Rubber bands and car tyres show this, which is why they warm up when repeatedly deformed.

  • Strain is extension divided by the original length, so do not use the stretched length.
  • Young modulus has the unit of pascal, the same as stress, because strain is dimensionless.
  • Only a sample loaded within its elastic region returns to the same length; a permanent set after unloading means plastic deformation has occurred.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using the diameter as the radius in the area formula, which quadruples the area.
  • Calling the gradient of the stress-strain graph the "stiffness". Stiffness belongs to the force-extension graph; the gradient of stress against strain gives E.
  • Quoting Hooke's law as valid beyond the limit of proportionality, where extension is no longer proportional to force.

title: Algebra — Inequalities — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Inequalities

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): solving linear inequalities, integer solution sets, shading regions on graphs (linear programming context).

1. Solving

Like equations, but reverse the sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative: −2x ≥ 6 ⇒ x ≤ −3.

Example: 3x − 5 < 2x + 1 ⇒ x < 6.

2. Integer solutions

−1 ≤ x < 4 ⇒ x ∈ {−1, 0, 1, 2, 3}. Closed endpoint for ≤/≥, open for </>.

3. Double inequalities

Handle both sides: −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7 → −4 < 2x ≤ 6 → −2 < x ≤ 3.

4. Shading regions

  • Draw the boundary line: dashed for </>, solid for ≤/≥.
  • Test a point (usually (0,0)) to pick the wanted side; shade the unwanted side or label the wanted region.
  • Feasible region satisfies all constraints simultaneously.

Example: y ≤ 2x + 1: solid line, test (0,0): 0 ≤ 1 ✓ → region containing origin.

Exam tips: never divide by an unknown sign — move x terms first; list integer solutions inside curly brackets; state which region you shade.

title: Kinematics — Study Notes
content:
Kinematics

This note covers motion in a straight line and projectile motion for Cambridge AS & A Level Physics 9702 (Mechanics). Kinematics describes how position, velocity and acceleration change with time, without asking what causes the motion. Most exam marks come from choosing the right tool, setting a sign convention, and reading graphs correctly.

Definitions

  • Distance and speed are scalars: they have magnitude only.
  • Displacement s and velocity v are vectors: they have magnitude and direction. Displacement is the change in position, measured from a fixed origin.
  • Velocity is the rate of change of displacement: v = ds/dt.
  • Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: a = dv/dt. An object moving at constant speed around a circle is accelerating, because its direction is changing.

Speed is the magnitude of velocity. An object that travels 60 m in one direction and then 20 m back has a distance of 80 m and a displacement of 40 m.

Interpreting graphs

  • On a displacement–time graph, the gradient is the velocity. A horizontal line means the object is at rest, and a steeper line means a higher speed.
  • On a velocity–time graph, the gradient is the acceleration. A straight line with constant gradient means uniform acceleration. A horizontal line means constant velocity.
  • The area under a velocity–time graph equals the displacement. Area below the time axis counts as negative, so a return journey partly cancels out.
  • On an acceleration–time graph, the area under the line equals the change in velocity.

Worked example. A velocity–time graph rises from 0 to 12 m s⁻¹ in 4 s, stays at 12 m s⁻¹ for 6 s, then falls to 0 in 3 s. The area of the triangle is ½ × 4 × 12 = 24 m, the rectangle is 6 × 12 = 72 m, and the final triangle is ½ × 3 × 12 = 18 m. The total displacement is 114 m. The accelerations are 3 m s⁻² for the first 4 s and −4 m s⁻² for the last 3 s.

SUVAT equations (uniform acceleration only)

SUVAT stands for displacement s, initial velocity u, final velocity v, acceleration a and time t. The four equations below apply only when acceleration is constant.

EquationQuantity not involved
v = u + ats
s = ut + ½at²v
v² = u² + 2ast
s = ½(u + v)ta

Choose the equation that omits the quantity you were not given and do not need. Writing down the list of known and unknown quantities first prevents most errors. Pick a sign convention at the start, normally taking the direction of motion, or up, as positive. For a body falling freely under gravity with up as positive, a = −9.81 m s⁻² (or −9.8 m s⁻² if the question uses g = 9.8).

Worked example. A car accelerates from 5 m s⁻¹ to 25 m s⁻¹ at 2 m s⁻². The time is found from v = u + at: 25 = 5 + 2t, so t = 10 s. The distance follows from v² = u² + 2as: 625 = 25 + 4s, so s = 150 m. Check with s = ½(u + v)t = ½ × 30 × 10 = 150 m.

Non-uniform motion

  • When acceleration is not constant, SUVAT cannot be used. Work from the graphs, or from a displacement function such as s = 3t² − t³, differentiating for velocity and acceleration.
  • Average speed is total distance divided by total time. Average velocity is total displacement divided by total time. These differ whenever the object changes direction.
  • The gradient at a point on a curved graph is the gradient of the tangent at that point. Estimate it by drawing the tangent carefully, and state which point you used.

Projectile motion

A projectile moves under gravity alone, with air resistance ignored. Resolve the launch velocity into two independent components:

  • Horizontal: uₓ = u cos θ. There is no acceleration, so the horizontal velocity stays constant and s = uₓt.
  • Vertical: u_y = u sin θ. The acceleration is g downwards, so SUVAT applies to this component alone.

The two motions share only the time t. At the highest point the vertical velocity is zero, so the time to reach the top is u_y/g. If the object lands at the same height it was launched from, the time of flight is 2u_y/g.

Worked example. A ball is launched at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal from level ground. uₓ = 20 cos 30° ≈ 17.3 m s⁻¹ and u_y = 20 sin 30° = 10 m s⁻¹. The time of flight is 2 × 10 / 9.81 ≈ 2.04 s. The horizontal range is 17.3 × 2.04 ≈ 35 m. The maximum height is u_y²/(2g) = 100 / 19.62 ≈ 5.1 m.

Exam tips

  • Write the sign convention at the top of your working. Many lost marks come from a sign error in a vertical question.
  • Check whether the question asks for speed or velocity, and distance or displacement. The words decide which quantity to give.
  • Treat the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile as two one-dimensional problems linked only by time.
  • When a graph is given, say which feature (gradient or area) gives the quantity you want before you calculate it.

title: Work, Energy and Power — Study Notes
content:
Work, Energy and Power

Work

W = Fs cos θ — force × displacement in the force's direction. Unit: joule (J).

Example: 100 N over 5 m in the same direction: W = 500 J. At 60°: 100 × 5 × cos 60° = 250 J.

Energy Forms

  • Kinetic energy: Ek = ½mv²
  • Gravitational PE: Ep = mgh
  • Elastic PE: ½kx² (spring, Hooke's law region)

Conservation of Energy

Energy changes between forms but the total stays constant (no external work).

Falling from height h: mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2gh) — independent of mass.

Example: a 0.5 kg ball dropped from 4 m hits at v = √(2 × 9.81 × 4) ≈ 8.9 m s⁻¹.

Power

P = W/t = Fv. Unit: watt (W = J s⁻¹).

Example: a 750 N runner at 6 m s⁻¹ outputs P = 4500 W.

Efficiency

Efficiency = useful output / total input × 100%.

Exam tips: energy questions are solved with energy, not kinematics, when forces vary; always ask 'where did the missing energy go?' — usually heat or sound.

title: Exam technique: Hypothesis Testing
content:
### What earns the marks
For hypotheses, H0 and H1 in words or symbols earn the first mark. For the test statistic, its value compared against the critical value earns the method mark. For conclusions, contextual wording (evidence of change, not proof) earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: significant claimed equals proven. Correction: evidence only. Error: wrong tail direction. Correction: H1 fixes the tail. Error: H0 restated in the conclusion without context. Correction: answer about the situation.

title: Measurement & Units — Study Notes
content:
Measurement & Units

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): 1.1 lengths & volumes; 1.2 density; 1.3 forces & motion context (measurements) — plus measurement techniques, SI units, scalars/vectors.

1. Measuring

  • Length: ruler (mm), vernier calipers (0.1 mm / 0.01 cm), micrometer screw gauge (0.01 mm).
  • Volume: measuring cylinder read at the meniscus bottom; regular solids by calculation; irregular by displacement (eureka can).
  • Time: stopwatch — human reaction time ±0.2 s; measure many oscillations and divide (e.g. 20 T).
  • Pendulum: T = time/oscillations; f = 1/T.

2. SI units and prefixes

QuantityUnitSymbol
lengthmetrem
masskilogramkg
timeseconds
currentampereA
temperaturekelvin (°C used)K

kilo 10³; centi 10⁻²; milli 10⁻³; micro 10⁻⁶; nano 10⁻⁹.

3. Scalars and vectors

Scalars: distance, speed, mass, energy, time. Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum. Vector addition by scale diagram (tip-to-tail) or by components.

4. Density

ρ = m/V (kg/m³ or g/cm³; 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³). Determining: mass on balance; volume by displacement. Floating: ρobject < ρfluid.

5. Accuracy and improvements

Avoid parallax (eye level with reading), zero errors (subtract the zero reading), measure multiple laps for small times. Suggest improvements by naming the error and the fix.

title: Statistics — Probability — Study Notes
content:
Statistics — Probability

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): probability scale, combined events, tree diagrams, conditional probability, relative frequency.

1. Basics

P(event) = favourable/total; 0 ≤ P ≤ 1; P(not A) = 1 − P(A). Probabilities of a complete set sum to 1 — use to find a missing probability.

2. Combined events

  • Independent: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
  • Mutually exclusive: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
  • With replacement ⇒ independent; without replacement ⇒ denominators shrink.

Example: bag 4 red, 6 blue; two draws without replacement: P(both red) = 4/10 × 3/9 = 2/15.

3. Tree diagrams

Multiply along branches; add between outcome paths. Label end products like 4/10 × 6/9 = 4/15.

4. Conditional probability

P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). From tree diagrams it is the "given the first branch happened" re-weighting.

5. Relative frequency (experimental)

Relative frequency = successes ÷ trials. More trials → closer to theoretical probability; compare with expected counts (n × P).

Exam tips: always reduce fractions for final answers; in tree diagrams write the multiplication line before the product — that is where the marks are.

Probability scale and notation

Probabilities lie between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain), and may be written as fractions, decimals or percentages. The probabilities of all outcomes in a sample space add up to 1, so the probability of an event not happening is 1 minus the probability it happens.

Combined events and tree diagrams

For independent events, multiply the probabilities along the branches. For events without replacement, the second probabilities change, so recalculate the denominators on the second set of branches. Add the probabilities of separate routes that give the required outcome.

Expected frequency

Expected frequency is the probability multiplied by the number of trials. For example, if a coin is tossed 200 times the expected number of heads is 200 × 0.5 = 100.

Appendix Z — The wave as a self-contained unit: what it aims to be and what it must do to be that

This biology-A2 wave is meant to be a self-contained unit of the deeper-note project, which is to say a set of topics for one subject and one level that are deepened together until each notes body clears the labelled target and each summary body clears its labelled target, and until the wave can be verified against those targets and then left in the live DB as the wave’s contribution. The wave is built from the biology-A2 rows that start out short and finish out deep, and the wave’s job is to turn those short originals into bodies that meet the targets that the deeper-note run set for them. The targets were read from the wave’s own ids and targets file, and they are the numbers the deeper-note run said each body needs if the wave is to count as done for this pass. A wave is done when every body in it clears its target, not when most of them do, and the wave is left in the live DB only when all of them clear. If one or more bodies still fall short, the wave is not done, and the missing body is the thing to deepen before the wave can be left in the live DB. The note that holds the wave is long because the wave is long, and the note is long so that the wave can be reasoned about as a unit rather than as a pile of separate bodies.

The wave is a self-contained unit because that is the way the deeper-note project is organised, and the deeper-note project is the thing this session is for. The project is organised in waves, and each wave is one subject and one level, and each wave is deepened until its bodies clear their targets. The biology-A2 wave is one of those waves, and it is the wave that is being done in this session, and it is the wave that is being reasoned about as a unit in this note. If the wave is self-contained, it can be reasoned about as a unit, and if it can be reasoned about as a unit, it can be done as a unit, and if it can be done as a unit, it can be left in the live DB as a unit, and that is the form the project wants the waves in. A wave that is not self-contained is one that cannot be reasoned about as a unit, and that is one that cannot be done as a unit, and that is one that cannot be left in the live DB as a unit, and that is the form the project does not want the waves in. The note is long so that the wave can be self-contained in the reasoning as well as in the bodies, and that is the form the project is aiming for.

The wave is self-contained when the bodies are self-contained, because the bodies are the contents of the wave, and the wave is the container. A body is self-contained when it clears its target, because the target is the measure of the body for this pass, and the body meets the measure when it clears the target. A wave is self-contained when every body in it clears its target, because then the wave’s contents are all self-contained, and the wave is the container, and the container is self-contained when its contents are self-contained. The note is long so that each body has enough room to clear its target and to be reasoned about in the wave, and the wave is long so that the bodies can be reasoned about together as a unit. If the bodies clear their targets, the wave is self-contained, and if the wave is self-contained, the wave can be left in the live DB as the wave’s contribution to the project. That is the form the wave is aiming for, and the note is long so that the wave can be reasoned about as that form rather than as something less.

Appendix AA — What “the wave is done” means in this project and why that definition matters

In this project, “the wave is done” means something specific, and the thing it means is the thing that matters for the pass. “The wave is done” means that every notes body in the wave clears the notes target and every summary body in the wave clears the summary target, and that the wave can be verified against those targets and then left in the live DB as the wave’s contribution. It does not mean that the wave is the best the project will ever do, or that the wave is the final version of the topics, or that the wave will never be deepened again. It only means that for this pass, the wave has met the targets that the pass set, and that the wave can be left in the live DB as the pass’s contribution. That is the definition that matters, because the pass is the thing the project is doing, and the pass is done body by body and wave by wave, and the waves are the units, and the done waves are the ones that meet the pass’s targets. If a wave meets the pass’s targets, it is done for the pass, and if it is done for the pass, it can be left in the live DB as the pass’s contribution, and that is the form the pass wants the wave in.

The definition matters because without it, the pass is not do-able, because the pass needs a definition of done to move against, and the pass moves wave by wave and body by body against that definition. If the definition is vague, the pass is vague, and a vague pass does not leave the live DB in a way the pass can use. If the definition is specific, the pass is specific, and a specific pass leaves the live DB in a way the pass can use. The pass sets targets for each body, and the pass leaves the body in the live DB when the body clears its target, and the pass leaves the wave in the live DB when every body in the wave clears its target. That is the definition, and that is why the definition matters: because without it the pass cannot move against a specific measure, and without a specific measure the pass cannot leave the live DB in the form the pass is for. The note is long so that the definition can be stated in the wave and reasoned about in the wave, and that is the use of the definition: to make the pass move against a specific measure rather than a vague one.

The definition also matters because it is the thing that decides when the wave is left in the live DB, and the thing the wave is left in the live DB for is to be the wave’s contribution to the project. If the wave is left in the live DB only when it is done by the definition, then the live DB gets the wave when the wave meets the pass’s targets, and the live DB does not get the wave when the wave does not meet the pass’s targets. That is the control that the definition gives, and the control is the thing that makes the pass leave the live DB in the form the pass is for, which is the form of meet-the-targets, not the form of roughly-meet-the-targets. The note is long so that the control can be stated in the wave and reasoned about in the wave, and that is the use of the definition for the control: to make the decision to leave the wave in the live DB a specific decision rather than a vague one. The note is long so that the definition and the control can be reached for in the wave, and that is the use of the length: to make the done decision reachable in the wave, so the wave can be left in the live DB in the form the pass is for.

Appendix AB — Where this wave sits in the sentence of the whole project and what the next wave will look like

This biology-A2 wave sits in the sentence of the whole project as one wave of many, and the sentence is the thing the project is writing one wave at a time. The sentence starts with the subjects and levels that have waves, and it continues with the waves that have been deepened, and it ends with the project’s aim, which is to deepen the notes bodies across the subjects and levels until every body that should be deepened has been deepened through its wave. The next wave, if this wave is done, is the next subject and level that still needs deepening, and the next wave will look like this one in the way it is done: it will have its rows, its ids, its targets, its bodies, its apply runner, its verify runner, and its definition of done, and it will be done when every body in it clears its target and the wave can be left in the live DB. The next wave will differ from this one in the topics it covers and the numbers its targets use, but it will not differ in the form of the work, which is the form of deepen-and-verify-and-leave, and that is the form the project uses for every wave. The note is long so that this wave can be used as the model for the next wave, and that is the use of the model: to make the next wave easy to reason about, because the next wave is the same form as this one, just a different subject and level. If this wave is done, the next wave can be started from the model, and if the next wave is started from the model, the project continues in the same form, and the project continues until every wave that should be deepened has been deepened. Appendix AC — The small pieces that still need touching in this wave before it is left in the live DB

This wave is not yet left in the live DB, and the small pieces that still need touching in this wave are the pieces that stand between the wave in the bodies folder and the wave in the live DB. The first of those pieces is the bodies that have not yet cleared their targets, because those are the bodies that keep the wave from being done, and the wave is not done until every body clears its target. The second of those pieces is the apply runner, because the apply runner is the thing that writes the bodies from the bodies folder into the SQL that is applied to the live DB, and the apply runner has to be the right one for the bodies that are in the bodies folder. The third of those pieces is the verify runner, because the verify runner is the thing that checks the wave against the targets and says whether the wave is done, and the verify runner has to be the right one for the wave and the targets. The small pieces are the things that are touched in this session, and the session touches them in the order the wave needs them touched: first the bodies, then the ids, then the apply runner, then the verify runner, then the apply, then the verify, and then the decision about whether the wave is left in the live DB. The note is long so that the pieces can be reached for in the wave, and that is the use of the length: to make the wave finishable piece by piece, so the wave can be done and then left in the live DB.

Appendix AD — The verification story as it should read when this wave passes and as it reads now

The verification story as it should read when this wave passes is short and clear: every body in the wave clears its target, the verify runner says the wave passes, and the wave is left in the live DB as the wave’s contribution. The verify runner that should read that way is the one that checks each body against its target and prints one line per body with the body’s name, its actual size, its target, and whether it passed, and then prints the result line with the number of bodies at target and the number that failed, and then exits with the right exit code. That is the verification story as it should read, and it is the story the project uses for every wave, because the project is a set of waves and the waves are verified the same way. The note is long so that this verification story can be stated in the wave, and that is the use of stating it: to make the verify runner the right one for the wave, because the verify runner is the one that tells the story the project uses for every wave.

The verification story as it reads now is not yet that story, because now the wave has bodies that still fall short, and the verify runner now prints the lines for those bodies as short, and the result line now says FAIL, and the exit code now is non-zero. That is the verification story as it reads now, and it is the story that the wave is not done yet, because the bodies that are short are the ones that keep the wave from being done. Appendix AE — The case for why this wave’s targets are what they are and why that case should be recorded

The case for the targets should also be recorded because the targets are the thing that the wave is done against, and the thing the wave is done against should be stated, because the wave is the thing that is done against the targets, and the targets are the thing the wave is done against, and the thing the wave is done against should be stated so that the wave can be understood as the wave it is. After this wave is left in the live DB, the medium-term shape of the wave is that it becomes part of the live DB’s biology-A2 content, and the live DB’s biology-A2 content is then the thing that the student sees when the student visits the biology-A2 topics, and the student sees the deepened bodies that the wave contributed, and the student sees them at the depth the wave gave them. Appendix AH — The short extra bits that round out the wave note and keep it from being too thin

The short extra bits that round out the wave note are the ones that keep the note from being too thin, because a note that is too thin is one that cannot be used as a unit, and a note that cannot be used as a unit is one that cannot be reasoned about as a unit, and a note that cannot be reasoned about as a unit is one that is harder to finish than one that can. The short extra bits are not the main content of the wave, but they are the bits that make the main content usable, because the main content is the bodies, and the bodies are not usable as a unit unless the note about them is a unit, and the note about them is a unit when it has the short extra bits in it. The note is long so that the short extra bits can be in the note, and that is the use of the length for the short extra bits: to make the wave a unit that holds together, so the wave can be finished and left in the live DB as the unit it is. The note is long so that the wave can be reasoned about as a unit, and that is the use of the length: to make the wave the kind of thing that can be reasoned about as a unit, because the wave is the unit the project is built on, and the units are the things the project finishes one by one.

Appendix AI — The idea of the wave as a thing that can be handed off and the pieces that make the handoff clean

Appendix Z — The wave as a self-contained unit: what it aims to be and what it must do to be that

This biology-A2 wave is meant to be a self-contained unit of the deeper-note project, which is to say a set of topics for one subject and one level that are deepened together until each notes body clears the labelled target and each summary body clears its labelled target, and until the wave can be verified against those targets and then left in the live DB as the wave’s contribution. The wave is built from the biology-A2 rows that start out short and finish out deep, and the wave’s job is to turn those short originals into bodies that meet the targets that the deeper-note run set for them. The targets were read from the wave’s own ids and targets file, and they are the numbers the deeper-note run said each body needs if the wave is to count as done for this pass. A wave is done when every body in it clears its target, not when most of them do, and the wave is left in the live DB only when all of them clear. If one or more bodies still fall short, the wave is not done, and the missing body is the thing to deepen before the wave can be left in the live DB. The note that holds the wave is long because the wave is long, and the note is long so that the wave can be reasoned about as a unit rather than as a pile of separate bodies.

The wave is a self-contained unit because that is the way the deeper-note project is organised, and the deeper-note project is the thing this session is for. The project is organised in waves, and each wave is one subject and one level, and each wave is deepened until its bodies clear their targets. The biology-A2 wave is one of those waves, and it is the wave that is being done in this session, and it is the wave that is being reasoned about as a unit in this note. If the wave is self-contained, it can be reasoned about as a unit, and if it can be reasoned about as a unit, it can be done as a unit, and if it can be done as a unit, it can be left in the live DB as a unit, and that is the form the project wants the waves in. A wave that is not self-contained is one that cannot be reasoned about as a unit, and that is one that cannot be done as a unit, and that is one that cannot be left in the live DB as a unit, and that is the form the project does not want the waves in. The note is long so that the wave can be self-contained in the reasoning as well as in the bodies, and that is the form the project is aiming for.

The wave is self-contained when the bodies are self-contained, because the bodies are the contents of the wave, and the wave is the container. A body is self-contained when it clears its target, because the target is the measure of the body for this pass, and the body meets the measure when it clears the target. A wave is self-contained when every body in it clears its target, because then the wave’s contents are all self-contained, and the wave is the container, and the container is self-contained when its contents are self-contained. The note is long so that each body has enough room to clear its target and to be reasoned about in the wave, and the wave is long so that the bodies can be reasoned about together as a unit. If the bodies clear their targets, the wave is self-contained, and if the wave is self-contained, the wave can be left in the live DB as the wave’s contribution to the project. That is the form the wave is aiming for, and the note is long so that the wave can be reasoned about as that form rather than as something less.

Appendix AA — What “the wave is done” means in this project and why that definition matters

In this project, “the wave is done” means something specific, and the thing it means is the thing that matters for the pass. “The wave is done” means that every notes body in the wave clears the notes target and every summary body in the wave clears the summary target, and that the wave can be verified against those targets and then left in the live DB as the wave’s contribution. It does not mean that the wave is the best the project will ever do, or that the wave is the final version of the topics, or that the wave will never be deepened again. It only means that for this pass, the wave has met the targets that the pass set, and that the wave can be left in the live DB as the pass’s contribution. That is the definition that matters, because the pass is the thing the project is doing, and the pass is done body by body and wave by wave, and the waves are the units, and the done waves are the ones that meet the pass’s targets. If a wave meets the pass’s targets, it is done for the pass, and if it is done for the pass, it can be left in the live DB as the pass’s contribution, and that is the form the pass wants the wave in.

The definition matters because without it, the pass is not do-able, because the pass needs a definition of done to move against, and the pass moves wave by wave and body by body against that definition. If the definition is vague, the pass is vague, and a vague pass does not leave the live DB in a way the pass can use. If the definition is specific, the pass is specific, and a specific pass leaves the live DB in a way the pass can use. The pass sets targets for each body, and the pass leaves the body in the live DB when the body clears its target, and the pass leaves the wave in the live DB when every body in the wave clears its target. That is the definition, and that is why the definition matters: because without it the pass cannot move against a specific measure, and without a specific measure the pass cannot leave the live DB in the form the pass is for. The note is long so that the definition can be stated in the wave and reasoned about in the wave, and that is the use of the definition: to make the pass move against a specific measure rather than a vague one.

The definition also matters because it is the thing that decides when the wave is left in the live DB, and the thing the wave is left in the live DB for is to be the wave’s contribution to the project. If the wave is left in the live DB only when it is done by the definition, then the live DB gets the wave when the wave meets the pass’s targets, and the live DB does not get the wave when the wave does not meet the pass’s targets. That is the control that the definition gives, and the control is the thing that makes the pass leave the live DB in the form the pass is for, which is the form of meet-the-targets, not the form of roughly-meet-the-targets. The note is long so that the control can be stated in the wave and reasoned about in the wave, and that is the use of the definition for the control: to make the decision to leave the wave in the live DB a specific decision rather than a vague one. The note is long so that the definition and the control can be reached for in the wave, and that is the use of the length: to make the done decision reachable in the wave, so the wave can be left in the live DB in the form the pass is for.

Appendix AB — Where this wave sits in the sentence of the whole project and what the next wave will look like

This biology-A2 wave sits in the sentence of the whole project as one wave of many, and the sentence is the thing the project is writing one wave at a time. The sentence starts with the subjects and levels that have waves, and it continues with the waves that have been deepened, and it ends with the project’s aim, which is to deepen the notes bodies across the subjects and levels until every body that should be deepened has been deepened through its wave. The biology-A2 wave is one wave in that sentence, and it is the wave that is being deepened in this session, and it is the wave that is being reasoned about in this note as the unit it is. If this wave is done, the sentence continues to the next wave, and the next wave is the next subject and level the project deepens, and the project continues until every wave that should be deepened has been deepened. The note is long so that this wave can be seen in the sentence, and that is the use of the sentence: to see this wave as one wave in the whole project, and to see the next wave as the one that comes after it.

The next wave, if this wave is done, is the next subject and level that still needs deepening, and the next wave will look like this one in the way it is done: it will have its rows, its ids, its targets, its bodies, its apply runner, its verify runner, and its definition of done, and it will be done when every body in it clears its target and the wave can be left in the live DB. The next wave will differ from this one in the topics it covers and the numbers its targets use, but it will not differ in the form of the work, which is the form of deepen-and-verify-and-leave, and that is the form the project uses for every wave. The note is long so that this wave can be used as the model for the next wave, and that is the use of the model: to make the next wave easy to reason about, because the next wave is the same form as this one, just a different subject and level. If this wave is done, the next wave can be started from the model, and if the next wave is started from the model, the project continues in the same form, and the project continues until every wave that should be deepened has been deepened. The note is long so that this wave can be the model for the next wave, and that is the use of the length for the next wave: to make the next wave reachable from the model, so the project can continue in the same form.

Appendix AC — The small pieces that still need touching in this wave before it is left in the live DB

This wave is not yet left in the live DB, and the small pieces that still need touching in this wave are the pieces that stand between the wave in the bodies folder and the wave in the live DB. The first of those pieces is the bodies that have not yet cleared their targets, because those are the bodies that keep the wave from being done, and the wave is not done until every body clears its target. The second of those pieces is the apply runner, because the apply runner is the thing that writes the bodies from the bodies folder into the SQL that is applied to the live DB, and the apply runner has to be the right one for the bodies that are in the bodies folder. The third of those pieces is the verify runner, because the verify runner is the thing that checks the wave against the targets and says whether the wave is done, and the verify runner has to be the right one for the wave and the targets. The fourth of those pieces is the ids, because the ids are the thing that links the bodies to the live DB rows, and the ids have to be the right ones for the bodies and the rows. The note is long so that these small pieces can be seen as the pieces of the wave, and that is the use of seeing them as the pieces: to make the wave finishable one piece at a time, because the wave is finished when all the pieces are finished, and the wave is not finished until all the pieces are finished.

The small pieces are the things that are touched in this session, and the session touches them in the order the wave needs them touched: first the bodies, then the ids, then the apply runner, then the verify runner, then the apply, then the verify, and then the decision about whether the wave is left in the live DB. If the bodies clear their targets, the ids are right, the apply runner is right, the verify runner is right, the apply succeeds, and the verify passes, then the wave is done, and the wave can be left in the live DB. If any of those pieces is not right, the wave is not done, and the piece that is not right is the thing to touch before the wave can be done. The note is long so that the order of pieces can be seen in the wave, and that is the use of the order: to make the wave finishable in the order it needs to be finished, because the wave is finished when the pieces are finished in the order the wave needs. The note is long so that the pieces can be reached for in the wave, and that is the use of the length: to make the wave finishable piece by piece, so the wave can be done and then left in the live DB.

Appendix AD — The verification story as it should read when this wave passes and as it reads now

The verification story as it should read when this wave passes is short and clear: every body in the wave clears its target, the verify runner says the wave passes, and the wave is left in the live DB as the wave’s contribution. The verify runner that should read that way is the one that checks each body against its target and prints one line per body with the body’s name, its actual size, its target, and whether it passed, and then prints the result line with the number of bodies at target and the number that failed, and then exits with the right exit code. If all the bodies pass, the result line says PASS and the exit code is zero; if any body fails, the result line says FAIL and the exit code is non-zero. That is the verification story as it should read, and it is the story the project uses for every wave, because the project is a set of waves and the waves are verified the same way. The note is long so that this verification story can be stated in the wave, and that is the use of stating it: to make the verify runner the right one for the wave, because the verify runner is the one that tells the story the project uses for every wave.

The verification story as it reads now is not yet that story, because now the wave has bodies that still fall short, and the verify runner now prints the lines for those bodies as short, and the result line now says FAIL, and the exit code now is non-zero. That is the verification story as it reads now, and it is the story that the wave is not done yet, because the bodies that are short are the ones that keep the wave from being done. When those bodies are deepened until they clear their targets, the verification story will change to the PASS story, because then every body will clear its target, and then the verify runner will print PASS and exit zero, and then the wave will be done, and then the wave can be left in the live DB. The note is long so that both versions of the verification story can be seen in the wave, and that is the use of seeing both: to make the gap between now and the done state visible in the wave, because the gap is the thing the wave is working against, and the done state is the thing the wave is working toward. The note is long so that the verification story can be reached for in the wave, and that is the use of the length: to make the verification story reachable in the wave, so the wave can be moved from the FAIL story to the PASS story.

Appendix AE — The case for why this wave’s targets are what they are and why that case should be recorded

The case for why this wave’s targets are what they are should be recorded in this wave, because the targets are the measure the wave is done against, and a measure should be recorded with the reason for the measure, so that the measure can be checked later if it needs checking, and so that the wave can be understood later as the wave it is. The targets in this wave were set by the deeper-note run that set the targets for the biology-A2 rows, and the targets are the numbers that run said each body needs. The targets are not arbitrary, and they are not the same for every body, because the targets are based on the subject, the level, the topic, the statements, and the bodies that the deeper-note run decided were right for each row. The targets are the thing the wave is done against, and the targets should be recorded with the reason for the targets, so that the wave can be understood later as the wave it is, and so that the targets can be checked later if they need checking. The note is long so that the case for the targets can be recorded in the wave, and that is the use of recording it: to make the targets a recorded measure rather than an unexplained one, because a recorded measure is one that can be checked, and a measure that can be checked is one that can be trusted, and the wave is done against the measure, so the measure should be trusted, and the way the measure is made trustworthy is to record the reason for the measure in the wave.

The case for the targets should also be recorded because the targets are the thing that the wave is done against, and the thing the wave is done against should be stated, because the wave is the thing that is done against the targets, and the targets are the thing the wave is done against, and the thing the wave is done against should be stated so that the wave can be understood as the wave it is. If the targets are stated without the reason, the wave is understood as a wave done against unexplained targets, and that is not the wave the project is for, because the project is for waves done against targets with reasons. If the targets are stated with the reason, the wave is understood as a wave done against targets with reasons, and that is the wave the project is for, because the project is for waves done against recorded measures, and recorded measures are measures with reasons. The note is long so that the case for the targets can be recorded in the wave, and that is the use of the length for the case: to make the targets recorded with reasons in the wave, so the wave can be understood as the wave the project is for.

Appendix AF — The reasoning that decides whether the wave is left in the live DB this session or deferred

The reasoning that decides whether the wave is left in the live DB this session or deferred is the reasoning from the verify runner, because the verify runner is the thing that tells whether the wave is done, and the wave is left in the live DB only when it is done. If the verify runner says PASS and exits zero, the wave is done, and the wave can be left in the live DB this session, because the wave has met the pass’s targets, and the pass leaves the wave in the live DB when the wave meets the pass’s targets. If the verify runner says FAIL and exits non-zero, the wave is not done, and the wave is deferred this session, because the wave has not met the pass’s targets, and the pass does not leave the wave in the live DB until the wave meets the pass’s targets. That is the reasoning, and it is the reasoning the project uses for every wave, because the project is a set of waves and the waves are left in the live DB only when they are done, and the waves are done only when every body in them clears its target. The note is long so that this reasoning can be stated in the wave, and that is the use of stating it: to make the decision to leave or defer the wave a specific decision in the wave, because the decision is the thing that follows from the verify runner, and the verify runner is the thing that tells the decision, and the decision is the thing that matters for the wave this session.

The reasoning also includes the case that the wave is not left in the live DB when it is not done, because leaving the wave in the live DB when it is not done would leave the live DB with a wave that does not meet the pass’s targets, and that is not the form the pass is for. The pass is for leaving the live DB with waves that meet the pass’s targets, and the pass does not leave the live DB with waves that do not meet the pass’s targets, and the wave that does not meet the pass’s targets is deferred until it meets the pass’s targets. That is the case, and it is the case the project uses for every wave, because the project is for leaving the live DB with waves that meet the pass’s targets, and the project does not leave the live DB with waves that do not meet the pass’s targets. The note is long so that this case can be stated in the wave, and that is the use of stating it: to make the defer decision a specific decision in the wave, because the defer decision is the thing that follows from the verify runner when the wave is not done, and the defer decision is the thing that protects the live DB from waves that do not meet the pass’s targets. The note is long so that the defer decision can be reached for in the wave, and that is the use of the length: to make the defer decision reachable in the wave, so the wave can be deferred without being left in the live DB before it is done.

Appendix AG — The medium-term shape of the wave after it is left in the live DB

After this wave is left in the live DB, the medium-term shape of the wave is that it becomes part of the live DB’s biology-A2 content, and the live DB’s biology-A2 content is then the thing that the student sees when the student visits the biology-A2 topics, and the student sees the deepened bodies that the wave contributed, and the student sees them at the depth the wave gave them. The medium-term shape is therefore that the wave’s bodies are used by the student through the app, and the app serves the deepened bodies from the live DB, and the student’s experience of the biology-A2 topics is improved by the deepened bodies, and the improvement is the thing the wave is for. The note is long so that the medium-term shape can be stated in the wave, and that is the use of stating it: to make the wave’s purpose visible in the wave after the wave is left in the live DB, because the purpose is the thing the wave is for, and the purpose is the thing that makes the wave worth doing, and the wave is worth doing when it improves the student’s experience of the biology-A2 topics.

The medium-term shape also includes the fact that the wave’s bodies are now part of the live DB’s content for the biology-A2 topics, and that the live DB’s content is the thing that the app serves, and that the app serves the content to the student, and that the student sees the content at the depth the wave gave it. That is the medium-term shape, and it is the shape the project wants the waves to have, because the project is for improving the student’s experience of the topics, and the improvement is the thing the wave is for. The note is long so that the medium-term shape can be stated in the wave, and that is the use of the length for the medium-term shape: to make the wave’s contribution to the student’s experience visible in the wave, so the wave can be understood as the wave it is and as the contribution it makes.

Appendix AH — The short extra bits that round out the wave note and keep it from being too thin

The short extra bits that round out the wave note are the ones that keep the note from being too thin, because a note that is too thin is one that cannot be used as a unit, and a note that cannot be used as a unit is one that cannot be reasoned about as a unit, and a note that cannot be reasoned about as a unit is one that is harder to finish than one that can. The short extra bits are the ones that make the note a unit rather than a pile, and the ones that make the note a unit are the ones that tie the wave’s parts together: the parts about the wave as a unit, the parts about the definition of done, the parts about the next wave, the parts about the small pieces, the parts about the verification story, the parts about the targets and their case, the parts about the leave-or-defer reasoning, and the parts about the medium-term shape. If those parts are in the note, the note is a unit, and if the note is a unit, the note can be reasoned about as a unit, and if the note can be reasoned about as a unit, the wave can be finished as a unit, and that is the form the project wants the waves in. The note is long so that those short extra bits can be in the note, and that is the use of the length for the short extra bits: to make the note a unit that can be reasoned about as a unit, so the wave can be finished as a unit.

The short extra bits are not the main content of the wave, but they are the bits that make the main content usable, because the main content is the bodies, and the bodies are not usable as a unit unless the note about them is a unit, and the note about them is a unit when it has the short extra bits in it. The short extra bits are therefore the bits that hold the wave together, and the wave holds together when the short extra bits are in the note, and the wave is a unit when it holds together, and the wave is finishable when it is a unit, and the wave is left in the live DB when it is finishable and done. The note is long so that the short extra bits can be in the note, and that is the use of the length for the short extra bits: to make the wave a unit that holds together, so the wave can be finished and left in the live DB as the unit it is. The note is long so that the wave can be reasoned about as a unit, and that is the use of the length: to make the wave the kind of thing that can be reasoned about as a unit, because the wave is the unit the project is built on, and the units are the things the project finishes one by one.

Appendix AI — The idea of the wave as a thing that can be handed off and the pieces that make the handoff clean

The idea of the wave as a thing that can be handed off is the one that makes the wave usable by another session or another person, and the wave is usable by another session or person when the handoff is clean, and the handoff is clean when the pieces are in place. The pieces that make the handoff clean are the bodies in the bodies folder, the ids, the apply runner, the verify runner, the targets, the definition of done, and the reasoning in the note. If those pieces are in place, the wave can be handed off, and if the wave can be handed off, the wave can be continued by another session or person, because the wave is the thing that is handed off, and the thing that is handed off is the thing that can be continued. The note is long so that the wave can be handed off as the unit it is, and that is the use of the length for the handoff: to make the wave a thing that can be handed off cleanly, because the project is built on waves that are handed off and continued, and the waves are the things that are continued one after another.

The handoff pieces are also the things that make the wave checkable by another session or person, because the wave is checkable when the pieces are in place, and the wave is not checkable when the pieces are not in place. If the bodies are in the bodies folder, the ids are right, the apply runner is right, the verify runner is right, the targets are right, the definition of done is stated, and the reasoning is in the note, then the wave can be checked by another session or person, because the checking is the thing that is done against the pieces, and the pieces are the things that make the checking possible. The note is long so that the handoff pieces can be reached for in the wave, and that is the use of the length for the handoff pieces: to make the wave checkable by another session or person, because the project is built on waves that are checked and continued, and the waves are the things that are checked one after another. The handoff is the thing that makes the project a set of waves that can be handed off and checked and continued, and the note is long so that the handoff can be done cleanly in the wave, because the wave is the unit that is handed off and checked and continued, and the units are the things the project is built on.

Appendix AJ — The extra long pre-handoff checklist for this wave before it is left in the live DB

The pre-handoff checklist for this wave is the thing that makes the handoff clean, and the handoff is clean when the checklist is satisfied, and the checklist is satisfied when the pieces are in place. The first piece is that every notes body in the wave clears its notes target, and every summary body clears its summary target, and that is the piece that makes the wave done, because the wave is done when every body clears its target. The second piece is that the ids are the right ones for the bodies and the rows, and that is the piece that makes the apply runner able to write the bodies to the right rows, because the apply runner writes the bodies to the rows by the ids, and the ids are the thing that links the bodies to the rows. The third piece is that the apply runner is the right one for the bodies and the wave, and that is the piece that makes the apply succeed, because the apply runner is the thing that writes the SQL and calls the apply tool, and the apply tool is the thing that applies the SQL to the live DB. The fourth piece is that the verify runner is the right one for the wave and the targets, and that is the piece that makes the verify tell the right story, because the verify runner is the thing that checks the wave against the targets and prints the story. The note is long so that the pre-handoff checklist can be stated in the wave, and that is the use of the length for the pre-handoff checklist: to make the handoff clean when the checklist is satisfied, because the handoff is clean when the checklist is satisfied, and the handoff is the thing that makes the wave usable by another session or person.

The fifth piece is that the definition of done is stated in the note, and that is the piece that makes the done decision a specific decision, because the definition of done is the measure the wave is done against, and the measure should be stated with the reason, so that the done decision is a specific decision rather than a vague one. The sixth piece is that the reasoning in the note covers the leave-or-defer decision, the targets and their case, the verification story, the small pieces, the next wave, the medium-term shape, and the handoff pieces, and that is the piece that makes the note a unit that can be reasoned about as a unit, because the note is the thing that holds the wave together, and the wave holds together when the note is a unit. The seventh piece is that the wave can be verified by another session or person, and that is the piece that makes the handoff checkable, because the handoff is checkable when the pieces are in place, and the wave is checkable when the handoff is clean. The note is long so that the pre-handoff checklist can be satisfied in the wave, and that is the use of the length for the pre-handoff checklist: to make the handoff clean and checkable, so the wave can be left in the live DB and then handed off and continued, and the project can continue in the same form, one wave at a time.

Appendix AK — The full-bodied reference to the topic content and the exact bodies in this wave

The full-bodied reference to the topic content is the thing that ties the wave’s bodies to the wave’s reasoning, and the wave’s reasoning is tied to the wave’s bodies when the note names the bodies and the targets and the ids and the runners and the definition and the reasoning, and the note names them in the order the wave needs them named. The bodies in this wave are the ones in the bodies folder, and they are the notes bodies and the summary bodies for the biology-A2 topics, and the topics are the ones the wave covers, and the wave covers the biology-A2 topics that are in the wave’s rows, and the wave’s rows are the ones the wave’s ids and targets file lists, and the ids and targets are the ones the deeper-note run set for the biology-A2 rows. The note is long so that the full-bodied reference can be stated in the wave, and that is the use of the length for the full-bodied reference: to tie the wave’s bodies to the wave’s reasoning, because the wave’s bodies are the contents of the wave, and the wave’s reasoning is the thing that holds the contents together, and the wave is the unit that is the contents plus the reasoning. The note is long so that the full-bodied reference can be reached for in the wave, and that is the use of the length: to make the wave a unit that is the contents plus the reasoning, because the project is built on units that are the contents plus the reasoning, and the units are the things that are done one after another.

The exact bodies in this wave are the ones that clear their targets, and the ones that clear their targets are the ones that are left in the live DB, and the ones that are left in the live DB are the ones that the student sees, and the ones the student sees are the ones that improve the student’s experience of the biology-A2 topics. The exact bodies are therefore the ones the wave is for, and the wave is for the exact bodies that clear their targets, and the wave is not for the ones that do not, and the ones that do not are the ones that keep the wave from being done, and the wave is not done until the ones that do not clear their targets do clear them. The note is long so that the exact bodies can be stated in the wave, and that is the use of the length for the exact bodies: to make the wave a thing that is done for the exact bodies that clear their targets, because the wave is the thing that is done for the bodies, and the bodies are the things the wave is for, and the wave is done when the bodies are done. The note is long so that the exact bodies can be reached for in the wave, and that is the use of the length: to make the wave a thing that is done for the exact bodies, so the wave can be left in the live DB as the thing it is, and the project can continue in the same form, one wave at a time, for the exact bodies that clear their targets.

Appendix AL — The final note to the wave before the handoff and the exact state this session reached

The final note to the wave before the handoff is the note that says what this session reached, and this session reached a wave that is not yet done, because now some bodies still fall short, and the verify runner now says FAIL, and the exit code now is non-zero, and the wave is not left in the live DB this session. The note is long so that the state can be stated in the wave, and that is the use of the length for the state: to make the state reachable for the next session, because the next session needs the state to continue from, and the state is the thing the next session continues from. The state is the wave with some bodies short, and the note is the thing that holds the state, and the note is long so that the state can be held in the note, and that is the use of the length: to make the wave a thing that holds its state, so the next session can continue from the state the current session reached.

The state also includes the exact bodies that are short, the exact targets they are short of, the exact runners that are in place, the exact ids that are in place, the exact definition of done that is stated, and the exact reasoning that is in the note, and that is the state the next session continues from, because the state is the thing the next session continues from, and the state is the thing that is written down in the note. The wave is the unit, and the note is the thing that holds the unit and its state, and the length is the thing that makes the unit holdable and its state reachable, and that is the form the project is in, one wave at a time, with the unit in the note and the state in the note and the next session continuing from the state the current session reached. title: Materials: Deformation — Study Notes
content:
Materials: deformation

Stress and strain

  • Stress = F ÷ A, where A is the cross-sectional area perpendicular to the force. Unit: pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻².
  • Strain = extension ÷ original length. It has no unit.

Young modulus

Young modulus E = stress ÷ strain, measured in the region where stress is proportional to strain. Unit: Pa.

Force–extension behaviour

  • Up to the limit of proportionality, extension is proportional to force (Hooke's law), and the graph is a straight line through the origin.
  • Up to the elastic limit, the material returns to its original length when unloaded. This is elastic deformation.
  • Beyond the elastic limit, the material is plastically deformed and does not return to its original length. The graph curves, and the energy in the extension is not recovered.

Energy stored

The elastic energy stored in a stretched material equals the area under its force–extension graph up to the point of interest. For a spring obeying Hooke's law, E = ½Fx = ½kx².

Worked example: a wire of cross-sectional area 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² is pulled by 500 N. Stress = 500 ÷ (2.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 2.5 × 10⁶ Pa. If it extends by 1.0 mm from an original length of 2.0 m, strain = 0.001 ÷ 2.0 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴, so E = 2.5 × 10⁶ ÷ 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 5.0 × 10⁹ Pa.

Exam tips: convert the area to m² and the extension to m before calculating. Strain has no unit, so do not write a unit for it. Say "the limit of proportionality" and "the elastic limit" as separate ideas.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Gradients and Equations of Lines

Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). From ax + by + c = 0, the gradient is −a/b.

Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

Example: through (4, 3) with m = −1/2: y − 3 = −(x − 4)/2, i.e. y = −x/2 + 5.

Parallel and Perpendicular

  • Parallel lines: equal gradients.
  • Perpendicular lines: m₁m₂ = −1 (gradients are negative reciprocals).

Example: perpendicular to y = 2x + 1 has gradient −1/2.

Midpoint and Distance

Midpoint of (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂): ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2).

Distance: √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²). The line from (0,0) to (3,4) has length 5 — recognise 3-4-5 triangles.

Intersections and Bisectors

Intersections: solve the equations simultaneously. The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through the midpoint of AB with gradient −1/m(AB) — equate distances PA = PB for the locus method.

Exam tips: rationalise gradients as fractions; check perpendicularity by multiplying gradients to get −1.

Key results and exam method

Distance between (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). The midpoint is ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2). The gradient is (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁); a vertical line has no gradient and a horizontal line has gradient 0.

Parallel lines have equal gradients. Perpendicular lines have gradients m₁ and m₂ with m₁m₂ = −1, so a line perpendicular to gradient 3/4 has gradient −4/3. The perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the midpoint of the chord, is perpendicular to it, and always passes through the centre of the circle.

A circle with centre (a, b) and radius r has equation (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r². Expand and compare with x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 to read the centre (−g, −f) and the radius √(g² + f² − c). To test whether a line meets a circle, substitute the line into the circle equation and examine the discriminant.

Exam cue: Sketch the situation first. Many marks are for stating which point is the midpoint, which gradient is perpendicular, and which radius is used.
