Key Identities

  • sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
  • tan θ = sin θ / cos θ
  • sec²θ = 1 + tan²θ

Solving Equations

Use the symmetry of the graphs. For sin x = 1/2 in 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π: the acute answer is π/6, and the second solution is π − π/6 = 5π/6.

For cos x = 0.5 in 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°: x = 60° and 360° − 60° = 300°.

Always check the required interval and give every solution.

Graphs and Transformations

y = a sin(bx) + c has amplitude a, period 2π/b, and vertical shift c.

Example: y = 3 sin(2x) has amplitude 3 and period π.

Using Identities

If sin x = 0.6 with x acute, then cos x = √(1 − 0.36) = 0.8 (positive in the first quadrant).

Exam tips: write the general second solution using graph symmetry rather than memorising CAST blindly; square both sides only with care, as it can add false solutions.

title: Exam technique: Thermal Physics
content:
### What earns the marks
For conduction, free electrons named earn the explanation mark. For convection, rise of hot less-dense fluid earns the mark. For radiation, matt black as best emitter and absorber earns the mark; Q = mcT quoted earns the calculation marks.
### Traps
Error: convection claimed in solids. Correction: conduction only in solids. Error: shiny surfaces called best emitters. Correction: matt black emits and absorbs best. Error: evaporation cooling unexplained. Correction: fastest molecules escape.

title: Data Structures — Study Notes
content:
`# Data Structures

Arrays and Lists

Contiguous, indexed, O(1) access; fixed size. 2D arrays: element (i, j) — rows × columns.

Stack (LIFO)

push/pop/peek at one end. Uses: call stacks, undo, expression evaluation, DFS.

Example: evaluating 3 4 + : push 3, push 4, pop both, push 7.

Queue (FIFO)

enqueue at rear, dequeue at front. Uses: print queues, schedulers, BFS. A circular queue reuses vacated slots with head/tail pointers modulo capacity.

Linked List

Nodes with data + pointer. Insert/delete O(1) at a known node; search O(n). Traversal follows next pointers until null.

Hash Table

Hash function maps keys → index. Collisions resolved by chaining or open addressing. Average O(1) lookup, worst O(n).

Complexity

OperationArrayLinked ListHash
Access by indexO(1)O(n)—
SearchO(n)O(n)O(1) avg
Insert/deleteO(n)O(1)O(1) avg

Exam tips: trace pointers carefully in linked-list diagrams; for circular queues, show head/tail movement and overflow/underflow checks.

Two-dimensional arrays and records

A two-dimensional array stores values in rows and columns, and each element is found with two indexes, usually written A[row, column]. A table of marks for five students in three subjects is a 5 by 3 array. Indexes normally start at 0, so the last element of an array with 8 elements has index 7.

A record groups fields of different data types under one name. A student record might hold a name as a string, an age as an integer and a pass flag as a Boolean. An array of records lets a program store a whole list of students, each with several fields, in one structure.

Exam tip: an array holds one data type throughout, while a record can mix types. Say this when asked to compare them.

Worked example: a stack trace

Start with an empty stack. Push A, push B and push C, so the stack holds A, B, C with C on top. Pop returns C, and a second pop returns B. Push D, and the stack now holds A and D. A trace table with one row per operation is the method examiners expect in a trace question.

Choosing a structure

  • Use a queue for tasks processed in arrival order, such as a print queue.
  • Use a stack for reversing data, undo operations and backtracking, because the last item added is the first removed.
  • Use a hash table for fast lookup by key. A good hash gives average-case constant-time access, but collisions must be handled, usually by chaining or open addressing.

Linked list pointers

Each node holds a data item and a pointer to the next node. Inserting or deleting a node means changing pointers rather than moving elements, so the change is quick once the position is known. Finding a node by its position still means following pointers from the start of the list, which is a linear search.

Exam point: state the behaviour precisely. Describing a queue as first in, last out loses the mark; the correct description is first in, first out (FIFO).

title: Number — Indices and Standard Form — Study Notes
content:
Number — Indices and Standard Form

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): index laws, negative and fractional indices, standard form arithmetic, surds and rationalising denominators.

1. Index laws

  • aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ
  • a⁰ = 1; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ; a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a; a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ

Examples: 27^(2/3) = (³√27)² = 9; 5⁻² = 1/25; (2x³)² = 4x⁶.

2. Standard form

a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10.

  • 47 382 = 4.7382 × 10⁴; 0.0056 = 5.6 × 10⁻³
  • Multiplication: multiply a's, add powers. Division: divide a's, subtract powers.

Example: (3 × 10⁵) × (4 × 10⁻²) = 12 × 10³ = 1.2 × 10⁴.

3. Calculator use

Use the ×10ˣ key, not 10 ^; keep working in standard form and convert at the end. Give final answers in the form asked (often 3 s.f. standard form).

4. Solving index equations

Match bases: 2ˣ = 32 ⇒ 2ˣ = 2⁵ ⇒ x = 5. With different bases, rewrite (8 = 2³).

5. Surds

A surd is a root that cannot be written as a rational number: √2, √3, 3√5.

  • Rules: √a × √b = √(ab); √a ÷ √b = √(a/b); (√a)² = a.
  • Simplify by taking out the largest square factor: √50 = √25 × √2 = 5√2; √72 = 6√2; √(9/16) = 3/4.
  • Add and subtract like surds: √18 + √8 = 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2. Unlike surds cannot be combined: 2√3 + √5 stays as it is.
  • Rationalise the denominator so no root is left below the line: 6/√3 = 6√3/3 = 2√3; 1/(3 + √2) = (3 − √2) / ((3 + √2)(3 − √2)) = (3 − √2)/7 — multiply top and bottom by the conjugate.
  • Expanding: (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 3 = 1; difference of two squares clears the surd.

Example: write √12 + √75 in the form k√3 → 2√3 + 5√3 = 7√3.

Exam tips: check a is in [1, 10) before writing standard form; in "multiply out" questions apply the power to every factor including coefficients.

title: Astronomy and Cosmology — Study Notes
content:
Astronomy and Cosmology

Luminosity and Intensity

Luminosity L is total power radiated (W). Intensity at distance d: I = L/(4πd²) — the key to distances.

Standard candles (Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) have known L, so measuring I gives d.

Example: the Sun: I = 1370 W m⁻² at d = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m gives L ≈ 3.9 × 10²⁶ W.

Stellar radii (25.2)

A star radiates as a black body of surface temperature T, so L = 4πR²σT⁴. Rearranged, R = √(L / 4πσT⁴). Luminosity therefore depends on both radius and temperature.

Example: with L = 3.9 × 10²⁶ W and T = 5800 K, R = √(3.9 × 10²⁶ / (4π × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 5800⁴)) ≈ 7.0 × 10⁸ m.

Doubling the temperature at fixed radius multiplies L by 2⁴ = 16. A cool red giant can be far more luminous than the Sun because its radius is very large.

Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann

  • Wien: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K — hotter stars are bluer
  • Stefan: L = σAT⁴, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸

Hubble's Law

Galaxies recede with v = Hd, H₀ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Redshift z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c for small z.

Example: a galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at v = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 100 × 3.09 × 10²² ≈ 6800 km s⁻¹.

The Big Bang

Evidence: Hubble expansion, cosmic microwave background (2.7 K), hydrogen/helium abundance. Age estimate: t ≈ 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years. The fate question: critical density, Ω.

Exam tips: convert Mpc to metres (×3.09 × 10²²) before Hubble arithmetic; distinguish redshift of light from distance ladder methods.

Standard candles and the cosmic distance ladder

A standard candle is an object whose luminosity is known, such as a Type Ia supernova or a Cepheid variable star. Comparing its known luminosity with its observed brightness gives its distance, using the inverse-square law. Stellar radii can be found in the same way: the luminosity L = 4πR2σT4 links radius, surface temperature and output power.

Exam tip: state which assumption you are making, such as that the star radiates as a black body, before you calculate the radius.

title: Materials: Deformation — Study Notes
content:
Materials: deformation

Stress and strain

  • Stress = F ÷ A, where A is the cross-sectional area perpendicular to the force. Unit: pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻².
  • Strain = extension ÷ original length. It has no unit.

Young modulus

Young modulus E = stress ÷ strain, measured in the region where stress is proportional to strain. Unit: Pa.

Force–extension behaviour

  • Up to the limit of proportionality, extension is proportional to force (Hooke's law), and the graph is a straight line through the origin.
  • Up to the elastic limit, the material returns to its original length when unloaded. This is elastic deformation.
  • Beyond the elastic limit, the material is plastically deformed and does not return to its original length. The graph curves, and the energy in the extension is not recovered.

Energy stored

The elastic energy stored in a stretched material equals the area under its force–extension graph up to the point of interest. For a spring obeying Hooke's law, E = ½Fx = ½kx².

Worked example: a wire of cross-sectional area 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² is pulled by 500 N. Stress = 500 ÷ (2.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 2.5 × 10⁶ Pa. If it extends by 1.0 mm from an original length of 2.0 m, strain = 0.001 ÷ 2.0 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴, so E = 2.5 × 10⁶ ÷ 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 5.0 × 10⁹ Pa.

Exam tips: convert the area to m² and the extension to m before calculating. Strain has no unit, so do not write a unit for it. Say "the limit of proportionality" and "the elastic limit" as separate ideas.

Stored elastic energy and Hooke's law

Within the limit of proportionality, extension is proportional to force, F = kx, and the stiffness k depends on the material and its dimensions. The elastic strain energy stored in a stretched wire is equal to the area under the force-extension graph, E = ½Fx. For a material, the Young modulus E = stress / strain. Beyond the elastic limit the material deforms plastically and does not return to its original length.

Exam tip: state the limit of proportionality on the graph, because the energy formula only applies while the material obeys Hooke's law.

title: Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation Revision Notes
content:
Quick revision: Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation

Biology — AS. Edexcel IAL Biology WBI12, Topic 4. Plant tissues are arranged to transport water, move sugars and carry out photosynthesis. Biodiversity measures and conservation methods show how ecosystems are monitored and protected.

Key areas to revise

  • Plant tissues
  • Stomata and transpiration
  • Measuring biodiversity
  • Sampling
  • Conservation

Worked example

Calculate the index of diversity (D) for a habitat containing 5 species with individual counts of 10, 25, 5, 40 and 20. First find N, the total number of organisms: 10 + 25 + 5 + 40 + 20 = 100. Next, calculate n(n − 1) for each species: 10(9) = 90, 25(24) = 600, 5(4) = 20, 40(39) = 1560, 20(19) = 380. Sum these values to get the denominator: 90 + 600 + 20 + 1560 + 380 = 2650. Now calculate N(N − 1): 100 × 99 = 9900. Divide 9900 by 2650 to get D = 3.74.

Key points to remember

Plant cells possess a rigid cell wall made of cellulose microfibrils, chloroplasts for photosynthesis, amyloplasts for starch storage, a large permanent vacuole bounded by a tonoplast, plasmodesmata for cytoplasmic connection, pits, and a middle lamella acting as an adhesive layer. Animal cells lack cell walls, chloroplasts, amyloplasts, large vacuoles, tonoplasts, plasmodesmata, pits and middle lamellae.

Cellulose is a polymer of beta-glucose molecules joined by 1,4-glycosidic bonds, where alternate glucose monomers are inverted by 180 degrees. Hydrogen bonds form between adjacent chains, grouping together to form microfibrils, which bundle into macrofibrils with secondary thickening to give high tensile strength to xylem vessels and sclerenchyma fibres.

Xylem vessels provide structural support and transport water and mineral ions upwards. Sclerenchyma fibres provide mechanical support with thick lignified walls. Phloem sieve tubes transport organic solutes by translocation. Roots, stems and leaves show distinct tissue arrangements visible under light microscopes using stained transverse section sections.

Sustainable use of plant materials involves replacing oil-based plastics with plant-based starches and fibres. Plants require inorganic ions: nitrates for amino acids and proteins, calcium ions for calcium pectate in the middle lamella, and magnesium ions to form chlorophyll. Deficiencies in these ions cause characteristic symptoms in plant growth.

Bacterial growth requires an appropriate temperature, moisture, pH, oxygen availability, and nutrient supply. Plants produce antimicrobial substances tested using aseptic techniques. Drug testing protocols have evolved from William Withering's digitalis soup to modern clinical trials involving double-blind trials, placebos, and three distinct phases.

Biodiversity includes species richness and genetic diversity measured via the heterozygosity index (number of heterozygotes divided by total individuals). The index of diversity formula is D = N(N − 1) / sum of n(n − 1). The Hardy-Weinberg equation (p squared + 2pq + q squared = 1 and p + q = 1) tracks allele frequency changes driven by mutation, natural selection, and reproductive isolation leading to speciation. Conservation employs zoos and seed banks via scientific research, captive breeding, reintroduction, and education.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Organic Nitrogen Compounds: Amines, Amides, Amino Acids and Proteins Revision Notes
content:
Organic Nitrogen Compounds: Amines, Amides, Amino Acids and Proteins A2 Level Chemistry

These revision notes cover Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15 Topic 19, focusing on the structures, preparations, reactions, and physical properties of amines, amides, amino acids, and polymers including polyamides and addition polymers, alongside Core Practical 15.

Nomenclature and Formulae of Nitrogen Compounds

Students must be able to name and draw structural, displayed, and skeletal formulae for amides, primary amines, and amino acids according to IUPAC rules.

  • Primary aliphatic amines are named by adding the suffix -amine to the alkyl chain, such as butylamine (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂).
  • Aromatic amines feature an amino group directly attached to a benzene ring, such as phenylamine (C₆H₅NH₂).
  • Amides are named based on the corresponding carboxylic acid chain with the suffix -amide, such as ethanamide (CH₃CONH₂).
  • Amino acids contain both an amine group and a carboxylic acid group, typically on the same carbon, such as 2-aminopropanoic acid (CH₃CH(NH₂)COOH).
  • Structural formulae show every atom and bond clearly in displayed formulae, while skeletal formulae omit carbon and hydrogen labels from carbon chains for simplicity.

Reactions and Basicity of Amines

Amines act as bases due to the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom, which can accept a proton.

  • Primary aliphatic amines like butylamine are miscible with water due to hydrogen bonding between the nitrogen and hydrogen atoms of water and the amine.
  • Basicity varies: ammonia has a base dissociation constant dependent on its lone pair availability; primary aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia because alkyl groups push electron density onto the nitrogen via the positive inductive effect, increasing lone pair availability.
  • Primary aromatic amines like phenylamine are weaker bases than ammonia because the nitrogen lone pair delocalises into the delocalised pi-system of the benzene ring, decreasing its availability to accept protons.
  • Reaction with water: primary aliphatic amines dissolve to form alkaline solutions containing hydroxide ions, for example CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂ + H₂O gives CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₃⁺ + OH⁻.
  • Reaction with acids: amines react with mineral acids like hydrochloric acid to form soluble alkylammonium salts, such as CH₃NH₂ + HCl gives CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻.
  • Reaction with halogenoalkanes: primary amines react with halogenoalkanes via nucleophilic substitution to produce secondary and tertiary amines.
  • Reaction with acyl chlorides: primary amines react with ethanoyl chloride to form N-substituted amides, releasing misty fumes of hydrogen chloride.
  • Reaction with copper(II) ions: dropwise addition of aqueous copper(II) sulfate to an excess of an aliphatic amine like butylamine forms a pale blue precipitate that dissolves in excess amine to form a deep blue complex ion, [Cu(CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂)₄(H₂O)²]²⁺.

Preparation of Aliphatic and Aromatic Amines

Different synthetic routes are required to produce aliphatic versus aromatic amines.

  • Preparation of primary aliphatic amines from halogenoalkanes: heating a haloalkane with excess ethanolic ammonia in a sealed tube via nucleophilic substitution; excess ammonia is essential to prevent further substitution leading to secondary and tertiary amines.
  • Preparation of primary aliphatic amines from nitriles: reduction of a nitrile using lithium aluminium hydride in dry ether followed by dilute acid, or catalytic hydrogenation using hydrogen and a nickel catalyst.
  • Preparation of aromatic amines: reduction of an aromatic nitro-compound, such as nitrobenzene, using tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid heated under reflux, followed by the addition of sodium hydroxide to release the free phenylamine base.

Azo Dyes and Diazonium Salts

Aromatic amines undergo specific reactions involving nitrous acid to form useful colorants.

  • Reaction of aromatic amines with nitrous acid: phenylamine reacts with nitrous acid (formed in situ from sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid) at temperatures below 5°C to form a benzenediazonium ion (C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻).
  • Coupling reaction: the benzenediazonium ion undergoes an electrophilic substitution coupling reaction with alkaline phenol at low temperatures to form a brightly coloured azo dye, such as 4-hydroxyphenylazobenzene.

Preparation and Properties of Amides

Amides are carboxylic acid derivatives containing the carbonyl-nitrogen bond.

  • Preparation: amides are prepared from acyl chlorides by reacting them with ammonia or a primary amine at room temperature, for example ethanoyl chloride with ammonia gives ethanamide and hydrogen chloride.
  • Hydrolysis: amides undergo acid hydrolysis when heated with dilute hydrochloric acid to yield a carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt, or alkaline hydrolysis with sodium hydroxide to yield a carboxylate salt and ammonia gas.

Polymers: Polyamides and Addition Polymers

Polymerisation processes link small monomer units into large macromolecules.

  • Condensation polymerisation: involves the reaction of monomers with two functional groups, releasing a small molecule such as water or hydrogen chloride; polyamides like nylon-6,6 are formed from hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid.
  • Proteins are natural polyamides formed from amino acid monomers linked by peptide bonds.
  • Addition polymerisation: involves unsaturated monomers opening their double bonds without eliminating small molecules; examples include poly(propenamide) and poly(ethenol).
  • Structural formulae: students must be able to draw repeat units of nylon, proteins, poly(propenamide), and poly(ethenol) enclosed in square brackets with an extension bond outside the brackets.
  • Physical properties of polyamides: strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds form between the polar carbonyl and N-H groups of adjacent polymer chains, resulting in high tensile strength and high melting points.
  • Solubility of poly(ethenol): despite being an addition polymer, poly(ethenol) is soluble in water because its numerous pendant alcohol (-OH) groups form extensive hydrogen bonds with water molecules, making it ideal for soluble laundry bags and liquid-detergent capsules (liquitabs).

Amino Acids, Zwitterions, and Peptides

Amino acids exhibit amphoteric properties and form complex structural hierarchies in proteins.

  • Zwitterions: in the solid state and near neutral pH, amino acids exist as dipolar ions called zwitterions, ⁺H₃NCH(R)COO⁻, carrying no net overall charge due to internal proton transfer from the carboxylic acid group to the amine group.
  • Acidity and basicity: at the isoelectric point, the zwitterion has a net charge of zero. In strong acid solutions, the amino group accepts a proton to form a positive cation; in strong alkali solutions, the carboxylic acid group loses a proton to form a negative anion.
  • Optical activity: aqueous solutions of standard amino acids contain chiral carbon atoms (except glycine) and rotate plane-polarised monochromatic light because they are optically active.
  • Peptide bond formation: a peptide link (-CONH-) forms when the carboxylic acid group of one amino acid condenses with the amine group of another, eliminating a molecule of water via condensation polymerisation.
  • Protein structure: proteins possess primary structure (amino acid sequence), secondary structure (alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets held by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N-H groups), and tertiary structure (3D folding stabilized by ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds, and disulfide bridges). Complete hydrolysis of proteins with hot concentrated hydrochloric acid yields a mixture of constituent amino acids.

Core Practical 15: Analysis of Unknowns

Practical analysis involves systematic chemical tests to identify functional groups in organic and inorganic unknowns.

  • Testing for amines: use universal indicator to confirm an alkaline pH, or react with ethanoyl chloride to observe misty fumes of hydrogen chloride.
  • Testing for amino acids: use paper chromatography followed by locating agents like ninhydrin to reveal purple spots.
  • Testing for amides: warm with sodium hydroxide and test evolved ammonia gas with damp red litmus paper, which turns blue.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: stating that alkyl groups attract electron density in amines. Correction: alkyl groups push electron density onto the nitrogen atom via a positive inductive effect.
  • Mistake: drawing the zwitterion structure with a neutral carboxylic acid and amine group at neutral pH. Correction: draw the zwitterion with a protonated amine (⁺H₃N-) and deprotonated carboxylate (-COO⁻).
  • Mistake: omitting the repeat brackets or extension bonds when drawing polymer repeat units. Correction: always enclose repeat units in square brackets with bonds extending outside the brackets.
  • Mistake: confusing addition polymerisation with condensation polymerisation. Correction: addition polymerisation involves unsaturated monomers with no eliminated small molecules, whereas condensation polymerisation eliminates small molecules like water.

Exam-style questions

  2. Explain why phenylamine is a weaker base than butylamine. Answer: Phenylamine's nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, decreasing proton acceptance ability, whereas butylamine's alkyl group pushes electron density onto nitrogen via a positive inductive effect, increasing lone pair availability.
  5. Describe the reagents and conditions needed to prepare phenylamine from nitrobenzene. Answer: Heat nitrobenzene under reflux with tin (Sn) and concentrated hydrochloric acid, followed by addition of sodium hydroxide.
  8. Draw the structural repeat unit of nylon-6,6. Answer: [−NH−(CH₂)₆−NH−CO−(CH₂)₄−CO−].
  11. Explain why poly(ethenol) dissolves in water while poly(ethene) does not. Answer: Poly(ethenol) has pendant −OH groups that form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, whereas poly(ethene) is non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds.
  14. Write the ionic equation for the reaction of butylamine with hydrochloric acid. Answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂ + H⁺ gives CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₃⁺.

Use these notes alongside past paper practice questions to test your knowledge of reaction conditions and mechanisms. Revise aromatic chemistry and polymer chemistry next to consolidate your understanding of WCH15.

title: Measurement & Units — Study Notes
content:
Measurement & Units

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): 1.1 lengths & volumes; 1.2 density; 1.3 forces & motion context (measurements) — plus measurement techniques, SI units, scalars/vectors.

1. Measuring

  • Length: ruler (mm), vernier calipers (0.1 mm / 0.01 cm), micrometer screw gauge (0.01 mm).
  • Volume: measuring cylinder read at the meniscus bottom; regular solids by calculation; irregular by displacement (eureka can).
  • Time: stopwatch — human reaction time ±0.2 s; measure many oscillations and divide (e.g. 20 T).
  • Pendulum: T = time/oscillations; f = 1/T.

2. SI units and prefixes

QuantityUnitSymbol
lengthmetrem
masskilogramkg
timeseconds
currentampereA
temperaturekelvin (°C used)K

kilo 10³; centi 10⁻²; milli 10⁻³; micro 10⁻⁶; nano 10⁻⁹.

3. Scalars and vectors

Scalars: distance, speed, mass, energy, time. Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum. Vector addition by scale diagram (tip-to-tail) or by components.

4. Density

ρ = m/V (kg/m³ or g/cm³; 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³). Determining: mass on balance; volume by displacement. Floating: ρobject < ρfluid.

5. Accuracy and improvements

Avoid parallax (eye level with reading), zero errors (subtract the zero reading), measure multiple laps for small times. Suggest improvements by naming the error and the fix.

title: Web Technologies — Study Notes
content:
Web Technologies

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): HTML structure/tags, CSS styling, JS interactivity, the DOM, microprocessors/controllers in web context.

1. HTML

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head><title>Page</title></head>
<body>
  <h1>Heading</h1>
  <p>Paragraph with <strong>bold</strong> text</p>
  <img src="pic.jpg" alt="description">
  <a href="https://example.com">Link</a>
  <table><tr><td>cell</td></tr></table>
</body>
</html>

Head holds metadata/title; body holds visible content; hypertext links via <a href>.

2. CSS

p { color: red; font-size: 14px; }
.highlight { background-color: yellow; }
#header { text-align: center; }

Element, class (.) and id (#) selectors; inline vs external stylesheets; separation of content (HTML) from presentation (CSS).

3. JavaScript and the DOM

document.getElementById("demo").innerHTML = "Hello";
document.getElementsByClassName("item")[0].style.color = "blue";

DOM = the browser's object model of the page; JS reads/changes it for interactivity (validation, sliders, dynamic text). Events (click, submit) trigger functions.

4. How pages load

URL → DNS lookup → server request → HTML parsed → assets fetched → DOM built → render. Layers: structure (HTML) → presentation (CSS) → behaviour (JS).

Exam tips: write tags with correct closing pairs; explain DOM operations as "find element by id … then change property"; separate structure/presentation/behaviour in answers.

title: Continuous Random Variables — Study Notes
content:
Continuous Random Variables

Probability Density Functions

A continuous variable X is described by a density f(x) with f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫f(x)dx = 1 over all x. Probabilities are areas:

  • P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx

Single points have zero probability, so strict or loose inequalities make no difference: P(X < 2) = P(X ≤ 2).

Finding Unknown Constants

Piecewise densities carry an unknown k: impose that the total area is 1 (and continuity at joins where required). One equation, one unknown.

Example: f(x) = kx on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area: k·(2²/2) = 2k = 1, so k = ½.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = ∫x·f(x) dx
  • E(X²) = ∫x²·f(x) dx
  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))²

The mean is the balancing point of the area under the density. For symmetric densities the mean sits at the symmetry point — worth spotting before integrating.

The Median and Mode

The median m solves ∫₋∞ᵐ f(x) dx = 0.5 (left half of the area). The mode is the x maximising f(x). For uniform densities the median is the midpoint.

Uniform Distribution

If f(x) = 1/(b − a) on [a, b], every point is equally likely. Then E(X) = (a + b)/2 and Var(X) = (b − a)²/12 — memorise both; they are quick exam marks.

Exam tips: always verify ∫f = 1 before computing anything else. Sketch the density — area intuitions catch algebra slips. Median questions are integration-to-0.5 questions; set them up before calculating.

title: Robotics & AI — Study Notes
content:
Robotics & AI

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): AI characteristics, machine learning basics, robotics/simulation contexts, automated systems.

1. AI characteristics

Systems exhibiting: planning, learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, knowledge representation. Narrow (task-specific) vs general AI distinction for discussion answers.

2. Machine learning

Supervised (labelled data — spam filters), unsupervised (clusters — segmentation), reinforcement (rewards — game agents). Training/evaluation loop: train on a set, test on unseen data; overfitting = memorising rather than generalising.

3. Robotics

Components: sensors (input), processors (decision), actuators/motors (output), power. Examples: manufacturing arms, delivery drones, autonomous vehicles (LIDAR + vision). Benefits: precision, 24/7 operation, dangerous jobs; concerns: job displacement, safety, cost.

4. Automated systems & simulation

Sensors → processor → actuators loops (greenhouses, traffic lights, self-checkouts). Simulation models real systems cheaply and safely (flight training, weather, crash tests) — limitations: model quality, missing variables.

5. Ethics of AI

Bias from unrepresentative training data; opacity of decisions; accountability for errors; privacy of training data; effect on employment.

Exam tips: for "describe how AI could be used in X" — tie each AI characteristic to a concrete step in the scenario; for evaluations, give both sides then a justified conclusion.

title: Abstract Data Types — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Abstract Data Types

Computer Science — A2. An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Key areas to revise

  • What is an ADT?
  • Linked Lists
  • Stacks and Queues
  • Binary Search Trees
  • Hash Tables

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example An abstract data type defines the data and operations without fixing the implementation. A stack is last-in-first-out: push adds an item to the top and pop removes the top item. If you push 3, then 7, then pop twice, the first pop returns 7 and the second returns 3. A queue is first-in-first-out, so enqueue and dequeue return 3 then 7 in the same sequence. ### Check yourself Trace a queue after enqueue(A), enqueue(B), dequeue(). State which item is returned and what remains. The result is A, and the queue now holds B.

title: Exam technique: Pressure and Density
content:
### What earns the marks
For solids, p = F/A with substitution earns both marks. For liquids, proportionality with depth stated earns the explanation mark. For hydraulics, pressure equated across pistons earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: force and pressure interchanged. Correction: pressure divides by area. Error: depth effect inverted. Correction: deeper means greater pressure. Error: atmospheric pressure guessed at 10 Pa. Correction: about 100 kPa at sea level.
### Method marks
Pressure = force ÷ area, and the area must be in m² for the answer in pascals. Density = mass ÷ volume. For an irregular solid, find the volume from the displacement of water.
### Explain, do not just name
Pressure in a liquid increases with depth because the weight of the column above increases. Write p = hρg and name each symbol in the explanation.
### Traps
Using cm² without converting: 1 cm² = 10^-4 m². Forgetting that the pressure in a fluid at a given depth acts equally in all directions.

title: Exam technique: Congruence and Similarity
content:
### What earns the marks
For similarity lengths, calculate earns marks for the scale factor stated (larger over smaller, matched pairs) and then applied. For area and volume, the squared and cubed factors stated earn the method mark before any multiplication: write k squared or k cubed explicitly. For symmetry, count earns marks per correct count with the reasoning (vertices, rotation step 360 / n). For congruence, name earns the test (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) with the matching parts listed.
### Traps
Error: adding the length difference instead of scaling. Correction: similarity always multiplies. Error: using k instead of k squared for area or k cubed for volume. Correction: write the power first. Error: equal angles claimed as congruence. Correction: angles alone prove similarity; a matching side upgrades it.
### Worked example
Two triangles have sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm, and a second triangle has sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm. The second triangle is an enlargement with scale factor 2. Each length is multiplied by 2, so each area is multiplied by 2² = 4. If the lengths are scaled by 2.5, the areas are scaled by 6.25.
### Check yourself
Two triangles have all three angles equal. Are they similar, congruent, or neither? They are similar, because equal angles give equal shape but not necessarily equal size. They are congruent only if the side lengths also match, which you check using SSS, SAS, ASA or RHS.

title: Databases and Data Definition — Study Notes
content:
Databases and Data Definition

Relational Concepts

A table (relation) stores rows (tuples) and columns (attributes). The primary key uniquely identifies each row; a foreign key references a primary key in another table, creating the relationship. A composite key uses two or more columns together.

Normalisation

  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups.
  • 2NF: 1NF plus every non-key attribute depends on the whole key (kills partial dependency in composite keys).
  • 3NF: 2NF plus no transitive dependency — non-key attributes must not depend on other non-key attributes.

Normalisation reduces redundancy and prevents update, insert and delete anomalies.

DDL and DML

DDL defines structure: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP. DML manipulates data: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE, INSERT INTO, UPDATE, DELETE. Joins combine related tables: FROM Student s JOIN Enrolment e ON s.id = e.StudentID. Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG with GROUP BY and HAVING.

Transactions and Concurrency

A transaction is a unit of work obeying ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules preserved), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes). Record locking blocks conflicting simultaneous edits; a deadlock occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs.

Exam tips: normalise a small table through 1NF, 2NF, 3NF naming the dependency removed at each step; write a two-table SELECT with JOIN; state which ACID property a scenario breaks.

title: Electricity: D.C. Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity: D.C. Circuits

Current and Charge

I = Q/t — charge per second, in amperes. Conventional current flows + to − (electrons drift the other way).

I = nAvq links microscopic drift to macroscopic current (n = carrier density).

Voltage and Power

  • V = W/Q (joules per coulomb)
  • P = VI = I²R = V²/R

Resistance and Resistivity

R = V/I; R = ρL/A. Resistivity ρ is a material property (Ω m). Metals' resistance rises with temperature; thermistors' falls (NTC).

Example: a wire 2 m long, 0.5 mm² cross-section, ρ = 5 × 10⁻⁷: R = 2 Ω.

Series and Parallel

  • Series: same current, R_total = R₁ + R₂ + …
  • Parallel: same voltage, 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …

EMF and Internal Resistance

ε = I(R + r) — some voltage is 'lost' inside the battery. Terminal voltage V = ε − Ir drops as load current rises.

Potential Dividers

V_out = V_in × R₂/(R₁ + R₂). Used with LDRs/thermistors to make sensor circuits.

Exam tips: redraw messy networks with clean junctions; always account for internal resistance in 'maximum power' questions.

title: Organic Chemistry: Arenes (Edexcel IAL A2 Chemistry)
content:
Organic Chemistry: Arenes - Edexcel IAL A2 Chemistry

This topic belongs to Edexcel International A-Level Chemistry WCH15, Topic 18, and covers the structure, stability, and characteristic reactions of arenes, specifically benzene, alongside activating and directing effects including phenol.

Structure and Evidence for Benzene

Benzene is an arene with the molecular formula C6H6, possessing a planar ring structure supported by multiple lines of physical and chemical evidence.

  • Thermochemical evidence: The measured enthalpy of hydrogenation of benzene is approximately −208 kJ mol−1, which is significantly less exothermic than the theoretical value of −360 kJ mol−1 calculated for a hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene with three isolated double bonds. The difference of about 150 kJ mol−1 is the stabilisation energy, also known as the delocalisation energy, proving benzene is much more stable than the classical Kekule structure.
  • X-ray diffraction data: X-ray crystallography shows that all six carbon-carbon bond lengths in benzene are identical at 0.139 nm, a value intermediate between a typical carbon-carbon single bond (0.154 nm) and a carbon-carbon double bond (0.134 nm).
  • Infrared spectroscopy: IR data shows characteristic carbon-carbon aromatic ring stretching absorptions and aromatic carbon-hydrogen stretching bands.
  • Delocalised model: The delocalised model for the structure of benzene involves the sideways overlap of unhybridised p-orbitals on each of the six carbon atoms, forming a continuous ring of pi-bonds above and below the plane of the carbon ring. Students may represent the structure of benzene as a ring inside a hexagon or as alternating double and single bonds as appropriate in equations and mechanisms.

Resistance to Bromination and Comparison with Alkenes

Benzene displays very different chemical reactivity compared to alkenes due to the nature of its bonding.

  • Resistance to bromination: Benzene is resistant to bromination compared to alkenes because of the delocalisation of pi-bonds in benzene, which spreads the electron density over the whole ring, making it a stable region. In contrast, alkenes possess a localised electron density in their pi-bond situated between two carbon atoms, which polarises approaching electrophiles much more readily.
  • Reactivity consequence: Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition reactions readily at room temperature without a catalyst, whereas benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution reactions and requires a halogen carrier catalyst to polarise non-polar molecules like bromine.

Reactions of Benzene

Benzene undergoes a variety of chemical reactions under specific conditions.

  • Combustion: Benzene burns in oxygen in air with a smoky flame due to its high carbon-to-hydrogen ratio, indicating unburnt carbon particles.
  • Halogenation: Benzene reacts with bromine in the presence of a catalyst such as iron(III) bromide or aluminium bromide.
  • Nitration: Benzene reacts with a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acids heated to about 50 degrees Celsius.
  • Sulfonation: Benzene reacts with fuming sulfuric acid (sulfuric(VI) acid containing dissolved sulfur trioxide).
  • Friedel-Crafts reactions: Benzene reacts with halogenoalkanes (alkylation) and acyl chlorides (acylation) with anhydrous aluminium chloride as a catalyst.

Mechanisms of Electrophilic Substitution

Electrophilic substitution in benzene proceeds through the generation of an electrophile followed by attack and proton loss.

  • Generation of electrophiles: For nitration, concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid generate the nitronium ion electrophile: HNO3 + 2H2SO4 yields NO2+ + 2HSO4− + H3O+. For halogenation, bromine reacts with an aluminium halide catalyst to generate the Br+ or polarised Br-Br-AlCl3 electrophilic species. For Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation, the halogenoalkane or acyl chloride reacts with aluminium chloride, acting as a Lewis acid, to generate a carbocation or acylium ion electrophile: RCl + AlCl3 yields R+ + AlCl4−.
  • Substitution mechanism: The electron-rich pi system of the benzene ring acts as a nucleophile and donates a pair of electrons to the electrophile, forming an unstable arenium intermediate where the positive charge is delocalised over the remaining five carbon atoms of the ring. A base removes a hydrogen ion from the substituted carbon, restoring the stable delocalised pi system of the benzene ring and regenerating the catalyst.

Reactivity of Phenol

Phenol contains a hydroxyl group attached directly to an aromatic ring, significantly altering its reactivity compared to benzene.

  • Reaction with bromine water: Phenol reacts readily with bromine water at room temperature without any halogen carrier catalyst, instantly decolorising the orange bromine water and giving a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol, accompanied by steamy fumes of hydrogen bromide.
  • Reasons for relative ease: The lone pair of electrons on the oxygen atom of the −OH group in phenol overlaps with the pi system of the benzene ring. This partially delocalises the lone pair into the ring, significantly increasing the electron density of the ring compared to benzene. As a result, the benzene ring in phenol is strongly activated, polarizing incoming electrophiles like bromine much more effectively and attracting them faster than benzene can.

Side-Chain Oxidation and Directing Effects

Substituents on the benzene ring affect both the position of further substitution and the reactivity of side chains.

  • Directing effects: Alkyl groups, such as the methyl group in methylbenzene, and activating groups direct a second incoming substituent primarily to the 2- and 4- positions (ortho and para). A nitro group is a deactivating group and directs incoming electrophiles to the 3- (meta) position. Hydroxyl and amino groups are strongly activating.
  • Side-chain oxidation: Hot, acidified potassium manganate(VII) solution oxidises any alkyl side chain on a benzene ring directly to a carboxylic acid group, regardless of the length of the alkyl chain, provided there is at least one benzylic hydrogen atom. For example, methylbenzene is oxidised to benzoic acid.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Stating that benzene undergoes electrophilic addition because it has double bonds. Correction: Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution to preserve the stable delocalised pi electron system.
  • Mistake: Omitting the catalyst in Friedel-Crafts equations or halogenation. Correction: Always include anhydrous aluminium chloride or iron(III) bromide as catalysts.
  • Mistake: Drawing the positive charge inside the intermediate horseshoe incorrectly. Correction: Ensure the incomplete horseshoe representing the positive charge in the arenium intermediate extends over five carbon atoms and does not touch the carbon bonded to the incoming electrophile and leaving hydrogen.
  • Mistake: Confusing the conditions for phenol bromination with benzene bromination. Correction: Phenol reacts with aqueous bromine without a catalyst at room temperature, whereas benzene requires liquid bromine and a halogen carrier catalyst.

Exam-style questions

  1. Question: State the thermochemical evidence that supports the delocalised model of benzene over the Kekule structure of cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene. Answer: The measured enthalpy of hydrogenation of benzene is approximately −208 kJ mol−1, whereas the theoretical value for cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene is −360 kJ mol−1. The difference of about 150 kJ mol−1 is the delocalisation energy, proving benzene is thermodynamically more stable. (Earns credit by stating both values, their difference, and naming delocalisation energy).
  2. Question: Explain why benzene is resistant to bromination compared to cyclohexene. Answer: Benzene has a delocalised ring of pi-electrons which spreads electron density, whereas cyclohexene has a localised pi-bond between two carbons. The localised electron density in cyclohexene polarises bromine molecules much more readily than the stable delocalised ring of benzene. (Earns credit for contrasting delocalised and localised electron density).
  3. Question: Write the equation for the generation of the electrophile in the nitration of benzene using concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids. Answer: HNO3 + 2H2SO4 yields NO2+ + 2HSO4− + H3O+. (Earns credit for correct reactants, products, and stoichiometry).
  4. Question: Outline the mechanism for the alkylation of benzene with chloromethane in the presence of aluminium chloride. Include curly arrows and the intermediate. Answer: CH3Cl + AlCl3 yields CH3+ + AlCl4−. The benzene ring pi electrons attack the CH3+ electrophile to form the arenium intermediate with a positive charge spread over five carbons, followed by loss of H+ to form methylbenzene and regenerate AlCl3 alongside HCl. (Earns credit for electrophile generation, curly arrows from the ring, correct arenium intermediate structure, and loss of H+).
  5. Question: Explain why phenol reacts with bromine water much more readily than benzene does. Answer: The oxygen atom in the −OH group of phenol has a lone pair of electrons that overlaps with the pi system of the benzene ring. This increases the electron density of the ring, activating it and allowing it to polarise bromine molecules without a catalyst. (Earns credit for mentioning lone pair overlap, increased electron density, and ring activation).

Use these notes alongside active recall of mechanisms, reagent-condition pairs, and thermochemical definitions. Revise next the chemistry of carbonyl compounds, carboxylic acids, and esters to complete your organic chemistry mastery for WCH15.

title: Exam technique: Hardware & Architecture
content:
### What earns the marks
For the fetch-execute cycle, each stage in order earns stepwise credit. For CPU parts, control unit versus ALU roles stated earn one mark each. For sensors, the named sensor matched to its use earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: RAM and ROM roles swapped. Correction: RAM is working memory, ROM holds boot code. Error: control unit claimed to compute. Correction: the ALU computes, the CU coordinates. Error: stages given out of order. Correction: fetch, decode, execute, store.

title: Exam technique: Databases and Data Definition
content:
### What earns the marks
For DDL vs DML, purpose decides: structure changes are DDL, row changes are DML. For transactions, atomicity (all-or-nothing rollback) and durability (surviving crashes) each earn a mark when tied to the failure. For concurrency, the lost-update mechanism described earns the mark before locking is prescribed.
### Traps
Error: SELECT classed as DDL. Correction: queries read rows, so DML. Error: half-applied transfers accepted. Correction: atomicity rolls them back. Error: views claimed as backups. Correction: views are access windows, not copies.

title: Exam technique: Angles and Polygons
content:
### What earns the marks
For angle-chasing, justify earns marks for each reason stated alongside the value: angles on a straight line, vertically opposite, alternate, corresponding, and the circle theorems by name. For cyclic quadrilaterals, quote earns the theorem (opposite angles sum to 180) before the equation. For polygons, the formula (n - 2) x 180 stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: using adjacent instead of opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral. Correction: mark the diagram first. Error: answering each interior angle when the sum is asked. Correction: only divide at the very end. Error: treating any triangle in a circle as right-angled. Correction: the right angle needs the diameter as hypotenuse.

title: Exam technique: Arithmetic and Place Value
content:
### What earns the marks
For HCF and LCM, the prime factorisation of each number earns the method mark; state highest powers for LCM and lowest for HCF. For bounds, half-the-precision stated (0.05 for 1 d.p.) earns the method mark before the bound. For estimation, the rounded line (50 x 20 / 10) must be shown: a bare calculator value scores nothing. For time and money, each conversion step shown earns its mark.
### Traps
Error: 16:80 as a time. Correction: 60 minutes carry. Error: largest rounded value confused with the upper bound (6.34 vs 6.35). Correction: the bound is the first value that rounds away. Error: HCF powers used for LCM. Correction: LCM takes the highest of each prime.

title: Exam technique: Materials and Deformation
content:
### What earns the marks
For stress and strain, each definition quoted with units or unitless noted earns a mark. For Young modulus, stress over strain earns the method mark with a steel-scale answer. For graphs, area read as stored energy earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: strain given units. Correction: strain is a pure ratio. Error: force-extension gradient called energy. Correction: gradient is stiffness; area is energy. Error: plastic region called elastic. Correction: only the straight line obeys Hooke.

title: Exam technique: Bearings and Loci
content:
### What earns the marks
For bearings, measure earns marks for the angle taken clockwise from north with three figures in the final answer: add leading zeros (075, 008). For back bearings, the 180-degree adjustment stated earns the method mark. For scale drawings, the scale multiplication shown earns a mark independent of arithmetic. For loci, construct earns marks for the correct locus type (circle, bisector, parallel pair) drawn and labelled.
### Traps
Error: measuring anticlockwise or from the wrong datum. Correction: north line up, clockwise. Error: dropping leading zeros. Correction: three figures always. Error: one angle bisector instead of the pair for intersecting lines. Correction: two lines cross, so two bisectors. Error: dividing by the scale instead of multiplying. Correction: real distances exceed map distances.
### Worked example
A boat sails from A on a bearing of 065° and reaches B. Its back bearing from B to A is 065 + 180 = 245°. Draw the north line at both points, because the angles at the two north lines are alternate and the back bearing follows from that.
### Check yourself
Describe the locus of points exactly 3 cm from a fixed point P, and the locus of points equidistant from two points A and B. The first is a circle of radius 3 cm centred on P. The second is the perpendicular bisector of the line AB. State both in words and draw them with compasses and a ruler.

title: Electricity: D.C. Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity: D.C. circuits

Current and charge

  • Current I = charge Q ÷ time t, so Q = It. Unit: ampere (A), where 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹.
  • Electron drift velocity is very small, but the electric field propagates through the circuit almost at the speed of light.

Potential difference and power

  • Potential difference V = energy transferred ÷ charge. Unit: volt (V), where 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.
  • Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Unit: watt (W).

Resistance and resistivity

R = V/I (Ohm's law for an ohmic conductor, at constant temperature). For a wire of length L and cross-sectional area A, R = ρL/A, where ρ is the resistivity in Ω m. Resistance rises with length and falls with area.

Practical circuits

An ammeter is connected in series with the component it measures. A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance; an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.

Kirchhoff's laws

  • First law: at a junction, the total current entering equals the total current leaving (conservation of charge).
  • Second law: around any closed loop, the sum of the emfs equals the sum of the potential differences (conservation of energy).

Potential dividers

For two resistors R1 and R2 in series across a supply V, the potential difference across R2 is V × R2/(R1 + R2).

Worked example: a 100 Ω and a 300 Ω resistor are in series across 12 V. The current is 12/400 = 0.030 A, and the voltage across the 300 Ω resistor is 0.030 × 300 = 9.0 V.

Exam tips: draw the meter in the correct place, in series or in parallel. Apply Kirchhoff's first law to currents and the second law to loops, with consistent signs. Check that units are converted (e.g. mm² to m²) before using ρL/A.

Resistivity and temperature

For a metallic conductor at constant temperature, resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. Resistivity, ρ = RA/L, is a property of the material. As temperature rises, the ions in a metal vibrate more and impede the flow of electrons, so resistivity increases. A thermistor behaves differently: its resistance falls as temperature rises, because more charge carriers are released.

Exam tip: when asked to explain a resistance change, relate it to charge carriers and collisions, not just to the formula.

title: Algebra — Equations — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Equations

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): linear equations, simultaneous equations, quadratic formula, completing the square, forming equations from words.

1. Linear equations

3(x − 2) = x + 4 → 3x − 6 = x + 4 → 2x = 10 → x = 5. With fractions, multiply through by the LCD first.

2. Forming equations

Translate shapes/situations: "rectangle length 3 cm more than width, perimeter 34" → 2w + 2(w + 3) = 34 → w = 7.

3. Simultaneous equations

  • Elimination: 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2 → add → 3x = 9 → x = 3, y = 1.
  • Substitution for linear–quadratic: substitute y = 2x into x² + y² = 20 → 5x² = 20 → x = ±2.

4. Quadratics by formula

x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a.

Example: 2x² − 4x − 3 = 0 → x = (4 ± √(16 + 24))/4 = 2.58 or −0.58 (2 d.p.).

5. Completing the square

x² + bx + c = (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c. x² − 6x + 5 = (x − 3)² − 4 → minimum at (3, −4). Use for turning points and for solving when factorising fails.

Exam tips: substitute answers back to verify; in word problems define the unknown clearly ("let w = width in cm"); give quadratic solutions to the accuracy demanded.

Solving linear equations step by step

Collect the unknown on one side and the numbers on the other, undoing operations in the reverse order to BODMAS. Whatever you do to one side you must do to the other. When brackets are present, expand first, then collect like terms. Fractions are cleared by multiplying every term by the lowest common denominator.

Simultaneous equations

Two linear equations in x and y can be solved by elimination (make the coefficient of one unknown equal and opposite, then add or subtract) or by substitution (rearrange one equation for one unknown and put it into the other). Check the answer in both original equations. Examiners award method marks for a correct, clearly shown elimination even when arithmetic slips later.

Rearranging formulae

Treat the subject letter as the unknown and apply inverse operations. Where the subject appears twice, gather every term containing it, factorise, then divide. Square roots or squares are undone with a square and a root, applied to both sides.

title: Integration II — Study Notes
content:
Integration II

Standard Integrals

  • ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c
  • ∫ cos x dx = sin x + c
  • ∫ e^x dx = e^x + c
  • ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c
  • ∫ sec²x dx = tan x + c

With linear arguments: ∫ e^(3x) dx = e^(3x)/3 + c; ∫ cos 2x dx = sin 2x/2 + c.

Substitution

Reverse of the chain rule. For ∫ 2x e^(x²) dx, let u = x²: du = 2x dx, so the integral is ∫ e^u du = e^(x²) + c.

Integration by Parts

∫ u (dv/dx) dx = uv − ∫ v (du/dx) dx. Choose u to be the part that simplifies when differentiated (LIATE: logs, inverse trig, algebraic, trig, exponential).

Example: ∫ x e^x dx = x e^x − ∫ e^x dx = x e^x − e^x + c.

Partial Fractions

Break rational functions into pieces like ∫ 1/(x+1) dx = ln|x + 1| + c.

Example: ∫ 4x/(x² − 1) dx = ∫ [2/(x − 1) + 2/(x + 1)] dx = 2 ln|x − 1| + 2 ln|x + 1| + c.

Exam tips: definite integrals: substitute limits into the transformed variable directly; for by-parts integrals like ∫ ln x dx, take u = ln x, dv/dx = 1.

title: Exam technique: Nuclear Physics (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For energy, mass defect times c squared with units earns both marks. For decay, ln2 over half-life quoted earns the method mark; activity as lambda N earns the second. For radii, the cube-root rule applied to ratios earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: half-life used as the decay constant. Correction: divide ln2 by it. Error: fission named for the Sun. Correction: fusion powers stars. Error: radius scaled linearly with A. Correction: cube root of nucleon number.

title: Hardware & Architecture — Study Notes
content:
Hardware & Architecture

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): von Neumann model, FDE cycle, registers, buses, RAM/ROM, secondary storage, embedded systems.

1. Von Neumann model

CPU (ALU, control unit, registers) + memory + I/O on shared buses; instructions stored as data (stored program concept).

2. Registers

RegisterRole
PCaddress of next instruction
MARaddress being read/written
MDRdata/instruction in transit
ACCALU results accumulator

3. FDE cycle

Fetch: PC → MAR; memory → MDR → CIR; PC + 1. Decode: control unit interprets opcode. Execute: ALU/registers act. Interrupts can pause between cycles.

4. Buses and performance

Address bus (one-way, width ⇒ addressable memory), data bus (two-way, width ⇒ bits per transfer), control bus. Performance factors: clock speed, cache size, core count — explain the effect, not just the name.

5. RAM vs ROM

RAM: volatile, read/write, holds running programs + data. ROM: non-volatile, read-only, bootstrap/firmware. Embedded systems: dedicated microprocessors inside devices (washing machines, engines) — one function, low cost, hard to update.

6. Secondary storage

  • Magnetic (HDD): platters, read/write heads; high capacity, cheap per GB, moving parts (shock-sensitive).
  • Optical (CD/DVD/Blu-ray): laser pits/lands; cheap, portable, slow, small capacity.
  • Solid state (SSD/flash): NAND cells; fast, silent, robust, no moving parts, more expensive per GB, finite write cycles.

Choose by use case: video editing (SSD), archive (optical/magnetic), tablets (flash).

Exam tips: trace FDE with register values; compare storage on capacity, speed, cost, durability, portability; always tie a performance factor to its effect.
