content:
Quick revision: Algebra — Equations

Mathematics — OL. linear equations, simultaneous equations, quadratic formula, completing the square, forming equations from words.

  • 1. Linear equations
  • 2. Forming equations
  • 3. Simultaneous equations
  • 4. Quadratics by formula
  • 5. Completing the square

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

### Worked example Solve 3(x − 2) = 2x + 5. Expand to 3x − 6 = 2x + 5, then subtract 2x and add 6 to get x = 11. Check by substitution: 3(11 − 2) = 27 and 2(11) + 5 = 27. For rearranging, make t the subject of v = u + at by subtracting u and dividing by a, giving t = (v − u)/a. ### Check yourself Solve 5(y + 1) = 2y + 13 and verify your answer. Expand to 5y + 5 = 2y + 13, so 3y = 8 and y = 8/3. Check: 5(8/3 + 1) = 5 × 11/3 = 55/3, and 2 × 8/3 + 13 = 16/3 + 39/3 = 55/3.

title: Dynamics — Study Notes
content:
Dynamics

Momentum

  • Momentum p = mv. It is a vector, with unit kg m s⁻¹, and it has the same direction as the velocity.
  • Momentum and kinetic energy are different. Momentum is a vector and changes sign with direction. Kinetic energy is a scalar.

Newton's laws of motion

  • First law: a body stays at rest or keeps moving at constant velocity unless a resultant (net) force acts on it.
  • Second law: the resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = ma for constant mass. The acceleration is in the direction of the resultant force.
  • Third law: when body A exerts a force on body B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. The two forces are the same type and act on different bodies, so they never cancel.

Weight and mass

Mass is the amount of matter (scalar, kg). Weight is the gravitational force on it, W = mg (vector, N). Mass is the same everywhere; weight changes with the value of g.

Impulse

Impulse = FΔt = Δp = m(v − u). The area under a force–time graph equals the impulse. A longer contact time for the same change in momentum means a smaller average force, which is why airbags and crumple zones work.

Conservation of linear momentum

For a system with no resultant external force, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after. In an elastic collision momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved. In an inelastic collision only momentum is conserved. In a collision where the bodies stick together, the kinetic energy lost is greatest.

Worked example: a 0.5 kg trolley moving at 4 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 1.0 kg trolley and they stick together. Total momentum before = 0.5 × 4 = 2.0 kg m s⁻¹. Common velocity = 2.0 / 1.5 ≈ 1.3 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: choose a positive direction and keep signs consistent in every momentum term. State that the system is isolated before applying conservation. For a recoil question, the two momenta are equal and opposite.

title: Algebra — Sequences and Functions — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): nth term (linear & quadratic), special sequences, function notation, composites, inverses.

1. Linear sequences

nth term = a + (n − 1)d. 5, 8, 11, … → 3n + 2. Check n = 1, 2, 3.

2. Quadratic sequences

Second difference = 2a → an² + bn + c. 3, 8, 15, 24 … has second difference 2 → n² + bn + c; subtract n² → 2, 4, 6, 8 → 2n; so nth term = n² + 2n.

3. Special sequences

Even/odd, triangular (½n(n+1)), squares, cubes, Fibonacci-type (each term = sum of previous two), geometric (×r).

4. Function notation

f(x) = 2x − 5: f(3) = 1. Solve f(x) = 11 → x = 8.

5. Composite functions

fg(x) = f(g(x)) — g first. f(x) = 2x − 5, g(x) = x²: gf(2) = g(1) = 1; fg(3) = f(9) = 13.

6. Inverse functions

Swap x and y, rearrange. f(x) = 2x − 5 ⇒ f⁻¹(x) = (x + 5)/2. Domain of inverse = range of original. Verify: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x.

Exam tips: write the bracket order explicitly in composites; show the "swap and rearrange" line for inverses — answer-only scores little.

Finding the nth term of a linear sequence

For a sequence with a constant difference d, the nth term is dn + (a − d), where a is the first term. Check the rule by substituting n = 1, 2 and 3 before using it. Given a term value, set the nth term equal to it and solve for n to test whether it belongs to the sequence.

Functions as machines

A function takes an input and gives exactly one output. Composite functions are applied right to left: fg(x) means apply g first, then f. The inverse f⁻¹ reverses each step, found by writing y = f(x), swapping x and y, and rearranging for y.

Domain and range

The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of outputs produced. Restrictions usually come from division by zero or from taking square roots of negative numbers. State both when asked to describe a function fully.

Worked examples: sequences

Linear. The sequence 5, 9, 13, 17 has a common difference of 4. The nth term is 4n + 1, since the nth term of a linear sequence is dn + (first term − d). Check the 10th term: 4 × 10 + 1 = 41.

Quadratic. For 2, 6, 12, 20, the first differences are 4, 6, 8 and the second difference is 2. The coefficient of n² is half the second difference, so it is 1. Subtract n² from each term: 1, 2, 3, 4, which is linear with nth term n. So the nth term is n² + n. Check n = 3: 9 + 3 = 12 ✓.

Function notation with composites

Let f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x − 1. Then fg(x) means f(g(x)) = f(x − 1) = 2(x − 1) + 3 = 2x + 1. Note that gf(x) = g(2x + 3) = 2x + 2, which is different. Composition is not commutative, and questions often ask for both to test whether you apply the inner function first.

Inverse functions

To find f⁻¹(x) for f(x) = 2x + 3: write y = 2x + 3, swap to x = 2y + 3 and solve, giving y = (x − 3)/2. So f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2. Check by substituting: f(f⁻¹(x)) = 2(x − 3)/2 + 3 = x ✓. The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of f in the line y = x.

Domain and range

For f(x) = √(x − 2), the expression under the root must be non-negative, so the domain is x ≥ 2. The output of a square root is never negative, so the range is f(x) ≥ 0. For a rational function such as 1/(x − 4), the domain excludes x = 4, and the range excludes y = 0, since the value 0 is never reached.

Common errors

  • Taking the nth term of a quadratic sequence from the first term alone; the second difference must be used.
  • Reversing the order of composition: fg(x) and gf(x) are not the same.
  • Writing the domain as x > 2 when the question allows equality, or stating the range with an inequality in the wrong direction.
  • Forgetting to swap x and y before solving for the inverse.

title: Molecules, Transport and Health Revision Notes
content:
Molecules, Transport and Health AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International AS Level Biology specification, covering biological molecules, transport mechanisms, gas exchange, and cardiovascular health.

Water and Its Biological Importance

Water is essential for life due to its chemical properties. It acts as an important solvent in transport because of its dipole nature, where the oxygen atom has a partial negative charge and hydrogen atoms have partial positive charges. This allows polar molecules and ionic substances to dissolve and be transported easily in blood and plant sap.

  • Dipole nature: polar molecule with uneven charge distribution.
  • Solvent properties: allows chemical reactions and transport of dissolved ions and molecules.

Carbohydrates and Sugars

Carbohydrates exist as monosaccharides, disaccharides, and polysaccharides. Monosaccharides include glucose, fructose, and galactose. They join via condensation reactions, forming glycosidic bonds and releasing water molecules, creating disaccharides such as maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose), and lactose (glucose + galactose), and polysaccharides such as glycogen, amylose, and amylopectin. Glycosidic bonds can be split through hydrolysis reactions using water molecules. Amylose has a helical structure formed by 1,4-glycosidic bonds, while amylopectin is branched with 1,4 and 1,6-glycosidic bonds, making both suited for energy storage in plants. Glycogen is highly branched with many 1,4 and 1,6-glycosidic bonds for rapid hydrolysis to release glucose in animals.

  • Monosaccharides: single sugar units like glucose, fructose, galactose.
  • Disaccharides: two monosaccharides joined by a glycosidic bond via condensation.
  • Polysaccharides: long chains of monosaccharides acting as energy stores (starch, glycogen).
  • Hydrolysis: breaks glycosidic bonds using water.

Core Practical 1: Estimating Sugar and Starch Concentrations

Semi-quantitative methods use colour standards to estimate concentrations. For reducing sugars, add Benedict's reagent to the sample, heat in a water bath, and observe the colour change from blue to green, yellow, orange, or brick-red. Compare against standard known concentrations. For starch, add iodine dissolved in potassium iodide solution and observe the colour change from browny-orange to blue-black, comparing with standard concentrations.

  • Reducing sugars test: Benedict's reagent, heat, observe colour change from blue to brick-red.
  • Starch test: iodine solution, observe colour change from orange-brown to blue-black.
  • Colour standards: compare unknowns against solutions of known concentrations.

Lipids and Triglyceride Synthesis

Triglycerides are synthesised by condensation reactions between one glycerol molecule and three fatty acids, forming ester bonds. Saturated lipids contain only single carbon-carbon bonds in their hydrocarbon chains, whereas unsaturated lipids contain one or more carbon-carbon double bonds, causing kinks that prevent tight packing.

  • Triglyceride: 1 glycerol + 3 fatty acids linked by 3 ester bonds.
  • Saturated fatty acids: no carbon-carbon double bonds, solid at room temperature.
  • Unsaturated fatty acids: contain carbon-carbon double bonds, liquid at room temperature.

Proteins and Amino Acids

Proteins are polymers made of amino acid monomers. An amino acid consists of a central carbon atom bonded to an amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom, and a variable R group. Amino acids join by peptide bonds formed in condensation reactions to create polypeptides. The primary structure is the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. This determines the secondary structure (alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets held by hydrogen bonds), which further folds into the three-dimensional tertiary structure held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bridges, and hydrophobic interactions. Globular proteins, such as haemoglobin, are folded into spherical, soluble shapes with hydrophilic groups on the outside, and function in metabolic roles. Fibrous proteins, such as collagen, form long, strong, insoluble fibres made of triple helices with cross-linking, providing structural strength.

  • Amino acid structure: central carbon, amine group, carboxyl group, hydrogen, R group.
  • Peptide bond: formed between amine and carboxyl groups via condensation.
  • Primary structure: amino acid sequence.
  • Secondary structure: alpha-helix or beta-pleated sheet formed by hydrogen bonding.
  • Tertiary structure: 3D folding stabilised by hydrogen, ionic, disulfide, and hydrophobic interactions.
  • Globular vs Fibrous: globular is soluble and spherical (haemoglobin); fibrous is structural and insoluble (collagen).

Enzymes and Biological Catalysts

Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up metabolic reactions by lowering the activation energy without being used up. They are globular proteins with a specific active site whose three-dimensional shape is complementary to a specific substrate. Intracellular enzymes catalyse reactions inside cells, while extracellular enzymes are secreted to catalyse reactions outside cells. Enzyme action depends on temperature, pH, enzyme concentration, and substrate concentration.

  • Mechanism: substrate binds to active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex.
  • Activation energy: lowered by enzymes, increasing the rate of reaction.
  • Specificity: determined by the precise 3D shape of the active site.

Core Practical 4: Investigating Enzyme-Catalysed Reactions

To investigate the effect of temperature, pH, enzyme concentration, or substrate concentration on the initial rate of reaction, measure the formation of products or disappearance of substrate over time using continuous or initial rate sampling.

  • Independent variables: temperature, pH, enzyme concentration, substrate concentration.
  • Dependent variable: initial rate of reaction, calculated from the linear steepest part of a product against time graph.
  • Control variables: keep all non-tested variables constant.

Mass Transport and Circulation

Many animals have a heart and circulation because mass transport is necessary to overcome the limitations of diffusion in meeting the metabolic requirements of large, multicellular organisms with small surface area to volume ratios. Blood vessels have specific adaptations: arteries have thick walls with elastic tissue and smooth muscle to withstand high pressure from the heart; veins have thinner walls, wider lumens, and valves to prevent backflow of blood under low pressure; capillaries have walls that are one cell thick to provide a short diffusion distance for exchanging substances with tissues.

  • Diffusion limits: inadequate for deep body tissues in large organisms.
  • Arteries: thick muscular and elastic walls to withstand high pulse pressure.
  • Veins: thin walls, large lumen, valves to prevent backflow.
  • Capillaries: single endothelial cell layer for rapid exchange.

The Mammalian Heart and Cardiac Cycle

The mammalian heart pumps blood through a double circulatory system. The cardiac cycle consists of three stages: atrial systole, where the atria contract and push blood into the ventricles through open atrioventricular valves; ventricular systole, where the ventricles contract, increasing pressure and closing atrioventricular valves while forcing semilunar valves open to push blood into the aorta and pulmonary artery; and cardiac diastole, where all chambers relax, and blood passively fills the atria and ventricles. Major blood vessels include the vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein, and aorta. Dissection of a mammalian heart allows the identification of atria, ventricles, valves, and thick-walled muscular left ventricles compared to thin-walled right ventricles.

  • Atrial systole: atria contract, ventricles relax, atrioventricular valves open.
  • Ventricular systole: ventricles contract, atrioventricular valves close, semilunar valves open.
  • Cardiac diastole: heart chambers relax, blood flows into atria and ventricles.

Gas Exchange and Fick's Law

Gas exchange surfaces have a large surface area to volume ratio, a short diffusion distance due to being thin, and a steep concentration gradient maintained by ventilation and blood flow. The rate of diffusion depends on these properties and is calculated using Fick's Law of Diffusion: Rate is proportional to (surface area × concentration difference) ÷ thickness of membrane. The mammalian lung is adapted for rapid gaseous exchange through millions of alveoli providing a massive surface area, capillary walls that are one cell thick, and a constant supply of blood to maintain the concentration gradient.

  • Fick's Law: Rate proportional to Area × Concentration Difference ÷ Thickness.
  • Alveoli adaptations: thin squamous epithelium, extensive capillary network, moist lining.

Haemoglobin and Oxygen Transport

Haemoglobin is a globular protein with four polypeptide chains, each containing a haem group with an iron ion. It transports oxygen by forming oxyhaemoglobin. The oxygen dissociation curve shows the relationship between percentage saturation of haemoglobin and partial pressure of oxygen. The sigmoidal curve occurs because the binding of the first oxygen molecule alters the protein's tertiary structure, making it easier for subsequent oxygen molecules to bind (positive cooperativity). The Bohr effect describes how an increase in carbon dioxide partial pressure decreases haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, shifting the curve to the right and unloading more oxygen in respiring tissues. Fetal haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen than adult haemoglobin, shifting its dissociation curve to the left, allowing it to extract oxygen from maternal blood across the placenta.

  • Haemoglobin structure: 4 polypeptide subunits, each with an iron-containing haem group.
  • Oxygen dissociation curve: sigmoidal shape due to cooperative binding.
  • Bohr effect: high carbon dioxide concentration shifts curve right, increasing oxygen unloading.
  • Fetal haemoglobin: higher oxygen affinity, curve shifts left compared to adult.

Cardiovascular Disease (CVD) and Risk Factors

Cardiovascular disease often begins with endothelial dysfunction, where damage to the arterial lining leads to an inflammatory response. White blood cells accumulate, absorbing cholesterol to form fatty streaks, which develop into atheromas or plaques. Plaque formation narrows arteries and raises blood pressure. The blood clotting process is triggered when damage exposes tissue factor; thromboplastin is released, catalysing the conversion of prothrombin into the active enzyme thrombin. Thrombin then catalyses the soluble protein fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin fibres, which mesh with platelets to form a blood clot, potentially blocking coronary arteries and causing myocardial infarction.

  • Atherosclerosis sequence: endothelial damage, inflammatory response, plaque/atheroma formation, raised blood pressure.
  • Blood clotting cascade: thromboplastin released, prothrombin converted to thrombin, fibrinogen converted to fibrin.
  • Risk factors: genetics, high-fat/salt diet, age, gender, high blood pressure, smoking, physical inactivity.

Health Studies and Risk Evaluation

Epidemiological data on illness and mortality rates help determine health risks. It is vital to distinguish between correlation and causation and to recognise conflicting evidence. When evaluating the design of studies used to determine health risk factors, consider sample selection, sample size, and whether the data collected is both valid and reliable. People's perception of risks often differs from actual risks due to underestimating or overestimating lifestyle factors. Body mass index (BMI) is calculated as mass (kg) divided by height squared (m squared), and waist-to-hip ratio are obesity indicators used alongside diet, exercise, and smoking cessation to reduce coronary heart disease risk.

  • BMI formula: mass (kg) ÷ height squared (m squared).
  • Correlation vs causation: correlation does not prove one variable causes another.
  • Study design evaluation: check for representative sample size, control of variables, validity, and reliability.

Treatments for Cardiovascular Disease (CVD)

Treatments for cardiovascular disease carry both benefits and risks. Antihypertensives lower blood pressure but can cause dizziness and fatigue. Statins lower blood cholesterol by inhibiting liver enzymes but may cause muscle pain and liver damage. Anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors reduce blood clotting but increase the risk of uncontrolled bleeding from injuries.

  • Antihypertensives: reduce blood pressure; risk of dizziness and nausea.
  • Statins: lower blood cholesterol; risk of muscle damage and liver inflammation.
  • Anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors: reduce clotting risk; risk of haemorrhage.

Worked Examples

Calculating BMI: A person has a mass of 70 kg and a height of 1.75 m.

  • Square the height: 1.75 × 1.75 = 3.0625.
  • Divide mass by squared height: 70 ÷ 3.0625 = 22.86.
  • State the unit: 22.86 kg per m squared.

Typical mistakes

  • Confusing condensation and hydrolysis: condensation joins molecules and releases water; hydrolysis splits molecules using water.
  • Stating correlation is proof of causation: correlation only shows a relationship, not a causal mechanism.
  • Forgetting the units in Fick's Law or BMI calculations: always include correct units in answers.
  • Confusing adult and fetal haemoglobin curves: fetal curve is to the left of the adult curve, indicating higher oxygen affinity at lower partial pressures.

Exam-style questions

  1. Describe how the structure of an artery is related to its function. Answer: Arteries have thick walls containing collagen for strength, elastic tissue to stretch and recoil under high pressure, and smooth muscle to constrict and dilate the lumen.
  2. Explain why high levels of LDL cholesterol increase the risk of cardiovascular disease. Answer: LDLs transport cholesterol to tissues where they can deposit it in artery walls, leading to atheroma formation, narrowing of arteries, and increased blood pressure.
  3. Explain the significance of the Bohr effect in actively respiring tissues. Answer: Respiring tissues produce high levels of carbon dioxide, which lowers pH, causing haemoglobin to release more oxygen more readily.
  4. Explain how glycogen's structure relates to its function as an energy storage molecule in animals. Answer: Glycogen is branched, allowing rapid hydrolysis to release glucose monomers, and is insoluble so it does not affect water potential.
  5. State the role of thromboplastin in blood clotting. Answer: Thromboplastin is released from damaged tissue and catalyses the conversion of prothrombin into thrombin.

Use these notes alongside active recall and past paper practice questions. Revise enzymes, gas exchange, and transport mechanisms next.

title: Operating Systems — Study Notes
content:
Operating Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): OS roles, memory/process management, hardware–software layer, interrupts, buffers, utility software.

1. What an OS does

Manages memory, processes/files, I/O via drivers, security (users, permissions), and provides the UI (CLI/GUI) between user, applications and hardware.

2. Memory and process management

  • Paging/segmentation move programs in/out; virtual memory extends RAM to disk when RAM is full.
  • Multitasking: scheduler gives each process time slices; context switching saves/restores state.

3. Interrupts and buffers

Interrupts signal events (I/O complete, timer); CPU saves context, services via ISR, resumes. Buffers hold data in transit (printing) so slow devices don't block the CPU; spooling queues jobs.

4. Utility software

Disk formatter, defragmenter (reduces head movement on HDDs; unnecessary for SSD), backup scheduler, compression, antivirus, file compression.

5. UI and drivers

CLI: precise, scriptable, low overhead. GUI: icons/windows, discoverable, more resources. Device drivers translate OS calls to hardware specifics — each device needs its own.

Exam tips: "manage" verbs earn marks: manages memory, manages processes, manages peripherals; explain virtual memory by RAM-full scenario, not definition alone.

title: Sampling and Estimation — Study Notes
content:
Sampling and Estimation

Populations, Samples, Statistics

A parameter describes the population (μ, σ²); a statistic describes the sample (x̄, s²). A statistic is unbiased if its expectation equals the population parameter: E(x̄) = μ always holds for the sample mean.

Unbiased Variance

The estimator with divisor (n − 1) is the unbiased sample variance:

  • s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)

Why n − 1: deviations are measured from x̄ rather than μ, slightly underestimating spread; the smaller divisor corrects it. At A2, state which estimator you are using — the unbiased one is the default.

Distribution of the Sample Mean

For a sample of size n from a population with mean μ and variance σ²:

  • E(x̄) = μ and Var(x̄) = σ²/n

Averaging shrinks spread — bigger samples give steadier estimates.

Central Limit Theorem

Whatever the population shape, for large n (rule of thumb n ≥ 30) the sample mean is approximately normal: x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n). This is why the normal appears constantly in inference.

Example: population mean 50, s.d. 12, n = 36. Then x̄ ~ N(50, 4) and P(x̄ > 51) = P(Z > 0.5) = 0.3085.

Using x̄ to Estimate

Given sample data, estimate μ by x̄ and σ² by the unbiased s². When the population is normal, x̄ is exactly normal for any n — the CLT is only needed for non-normal populations.

Exam tips: distinguish σ²/σ (population) from s²/s (sample) in notation. Standard error means √(σ²/n) — smaller with larger n. Quote probabilities for x̄ with the variance divided by n; forgetting that division is the classic error.

Exam method: estimators and sample variance

The sample mean x̄ is an unbiased estimate of the population mean μ. The unbiased estimate of the population variance is s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1), which divides by n − 1 rather than n. Using n gives the population variance of the sample, which tends to underestimate the true value.

When the sum of squared deviations is given, divide it by n − 1 directly. When the raw data are given, it is quicker to compute s² = (Σx² − n x̄²)/(n − 1).

A random sample gives each member of the population an equal chance of selection. Bias means the estimator does not equal the parameter on average, so the sample must be random to make the estimate reliable.

The standard error of the sample mean is σ/√n. It decreases as the sample size grows, so larger samples give more precise estimates.

Exam cue: Name the estimator and state whether it is unbiased, because the question often asks for both the value and the reason.

Population and sample

A population is the complete set of items being studied, and a sample is the subset that is actually measured. A sample is used because measuring the whole population is too slow or too costly. A random sample gives every member an equal chance of selection, and a sample that is not random may be biased. A sample statistic, such as the sample mean, is used to estimate a population parameter, such as the population mean.

Worked example: an unbiased estimate of the population variance

A sample of size 5 has values 4, 6, 7, 8 and 10. The sample mean is 35 ÷ 5 = 7. The sum of squared deviations from the mean is 9 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 9 = 20. Dividing by n gives 4, but the unbiased estimate of the population variance divides by n − 1, which gives s² = 20 ÷ 4 = 5. The divisor n − 1 is used because the sample mean is itself estimated from the data, and it corrects the tendency of the divisor n to underestimate the population variance.

Confidence intervals for a mean

For a large sample from a population with known standard deviation σ, a 95% confidence interval for the population mean is the sample mean plus or minus 1.96 multiplied by σ divided by the square root of n. The quantity σ divided by the square root of n is the standard error. A wider interval means less precision, and increasing the sample size narrows the interval. Give the interval as two values and state the confidence level in the conclusion.

title: Web Technologies — Study Notes
content:
Web Technologies

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): HTML structure/tags, CSS styling, JS interactivity, the DOM, microprocessors/controllers in web context.

1. HTML

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head><title>Page</title></head>
<body>
  <h1>Heading</h1>
  <p>Paragraph with <strong>bold</strong> text</p>
  <img src="pic.jpg" alt="description">
  <a href="https://example.com">Link</a>
  <table><tr><td>cell</td></tr></table>
</body>
</html>

Head holds metadata/title; body holds visible content; hypertext links via <a href>.

2. CSS

p { color: red; font-size: 14px; }
.highlight { background-color: yellow; }
#header { text-align: center; }

Element, class (.) and id (#) selectors; inline vs external stylesheets; separation of content (HTML) from presentation (CSS).

3. JavaScript and the DOM

document.getElementById("demo").innerHTML = "Hello";
document.getElementsByClassName("item")[0].style.color = "blue";

DOM = the browser's object model of the page; JS reads/changes it for interactivity (validation, sliders, dynamic text). Events (click, submit) trigger functions.

4. How pages load

URL → DNS lookup → server request → HTML parsed → assets fetched → DOM built → render. Layers: structure (HTML) → presentation (CSS) → behaviour (JS).

Exam tips: write tags with correct closing pairs; explain DOM operations as "find element by id … then change property"; separate structure/presentation/behaviour in answers.

HTML, CSS and the client-server model

HTML defines the structure and content of a web page using tags, such as headings and paragraphs. CSS controls how that content looks, including colour, layout and font size. Keeping structure and style separate means one stylesheet can change the appearance of many pages.

In the client-server model, a client such as a browser sends a request, and a server returns the requested resources. When a web page is requested, the browser uses the domain name to look up the server's IP address through the Domain Name System (DNS), then sends the request over HTTP or HTTPS.

Exam tip: describe a web request as a sequence: DNS lookup, request, server response, rendering in the browser.

title: Exam technique: Waves (AS)
content:
### What earns the marks
For phase, one lambda equated to 360 degrees earns the mark. For refraction, n = c/v quoted earns the method mark. For TIR, both conditions stated earn one mark each with sin c = 1/n earning the calculation mark.

title: Databases and Data Definition — Study Notes
content:
Databases and Data Definition

Relational Concepts

A table (relation) stores rows (tuples) and columns (attributes). The primary key uniquely identifies each row; a foreign key references a primary key in another table, creating the relationship. A composite key uses two or more columns together.

Normalisation

  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups.
  • 2NF: 1NF plus every non-key attribute depends on the whole key (kills partial dependency in composite keys).
  • 3NF: 2NF plus no transitive dependency — non-key attributes must not depend on other non-key attributes.

Normalisation reduces redundancy and prevents update, insert and delete anomalies.

DDL and DML

DDL defines structure: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP. DML manipulates data: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE, INSERT INTO, UPDATE, DELETE. Joins combine related tables: FROM Student s JOIN Enrolment e ON s.id = e.StudentID. Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG with GROUP BY and HAVING.

Transactions and Concurrency

A transaction is a unit of work obeying ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules preserved), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes). Record locking blocks conflicting simultaneous edits; a deadlock occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs.

Exam tips: normalise a small table through 1NF, 2NF, 3NF naming the dependency removed at each step; write a two-table SELECT with JOIN; state which ACID property a scenario breaks.

DDL and DML

Data Definition Language (DDL) creates and changes the structure of a database: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE. Data Manipulation Language (DML) works with the data inside the structure: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.

Example: CREATE TABLE Student (ID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(30)); is DDL; INSERT INTO Student VALUES (1, 'Ana'); is DML.

Exam tip: classify each statement by whether it changes structure or changes data.

title: Astronomy and Cosmology — Study Notes
content:
Astronomy and Cosmology

Luminosity and Intensity

Luminosity L is total power radiated (W). Intensity at distance d: I = L/(4πd²) — the key to distances.

Standard candles (Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) have known L, so measuring I gives d.

Example: the Sun: I = 1370 W m⁻² at d = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m gives L ≈ 3.9 × 10²⁶ W.

Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann

  • Wien: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K — hotter stars are bluer
  • Stefan: L = σAT⁴, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸

Hubble's Law

Galaxies recede with v = Hd, H₀ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Redshift z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c for small z.

Example: a galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at v = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 100 × 3.09 × 10²² ≈ 6800 km s⁻¹.

The Big Bang

Evidence: Hubble expansion, cosmic microwave background (2.7 K), hydrogen/helium abundance. Age estimate: t ≈ 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years. The fate question: critical density, Ω.

Exam tips: convert Mpc to metres (×3.09 × 10²²) before Hubble arithmetic; distinguish redshift of light from distance ladder methods.

### Worked example An abstract data type defines the data and operations without fixing the implementation. A stack is last-in-first-out: push adds an item to the top and pop removes the top item. If you push 3, then 7, then pop twice, the first pop returns 7 and the second returns 3. A queue is first-in-first-out, so enqueue and dequeue return 3 then 7 in the same sequence. ### Check yourself Trace a queue after enqueue(A), enqueue(B), dequeue(). title: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table Revision Notes Edexcel IAL AS Chemistry
content:
Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table AS Level Chemistry

These revision notes cover Topic 2 of the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary Chemistry specification. They detail subatomic particles, mass spectrometry, ionisation energies, quantum shells, orbitals, and periodic trends across periods 2 and 3.

Subatomic Particles and Isotopes

Atoms consist of a central nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in quantum shells. The atomic proton number is the number of protons in the nucleus, which defines the element. The mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons combined. You can determine the number of each subatomic particle in any neutral atom or ion by subtracting the atomic number from the mass number to find neutrons, while electrons equal protons in a neutral atom or are adjusted according to the ionic charge. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, resulting in different mass numbers. Isotopes share identical chemical properties because they have the same electron configuration, but they possess different physical properties such as density and mass.

  • Proton: relative mass 1, relative charge +1.
  • Neutron: relative mass 1, relative charge 0.
  • Electron: relative mass 1 / 1836, relative charge −1.
  • Atomic number equals the number of protons.
  • Mass number equals protons plus neutrons.
  • Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
  • Electrons = protons minus positive charge, or plus negative charge.

Mass Spectrometry and Relative Masses

A mass spectrometer determines the isotopic composition of elements and relative molecular masses of compounds. A vaporised sample is ionised by high-energy electrons to form positive ions, accelerated by an electric field, deflected by a magnetic field according to mass-to-charge ratio, and detected. Ions in a mass spectrometer may occasionally acquire a 2+ charge, producing a signal at half their actual mass-to-charge ratio. Mass spectra display percentage abundance or relative abundance on the vertical axis against mass-to-charge ratio on the horizontal axis. For diatomic molecules such as chlorine, you can predict mass spectra and relative peak heights given isotopic abundances by using probability combinations of isotopes like chlorine-35 and chlorine-37.

  • Relative atomic mass is the weighted mean mass of an atom of an element compared with one-twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
  • Relative molecular mass is the sum of relative atomic masses of all atoms in the molecular formula.
  • Formula for relative atomic mass = sum of (isotopic mass × relative abundance) ÷ total abundance.
  • Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 exist in a 3:1 ratio, producing molecular ion peaks at m/z 70, 72, and 74 with a 9:6:1 ratio.

Worked example: calculate the relative atomic mass of element X with isotopes 24X (78.9%), 25X (10.0%), and 26X (11.1%).

  • Step 1: Multiply each isotopic mass by its percentage abundance. (24 × 78.9) = 1893.6; (25 × 10.0) = 250.0; (26 × 11.1) = 288.6.
  • Step 2: Sum these values. 1893.6 + 250.0 + 288.6 = 2432.2.
  • Step 3: Divide by 100. 2432.2 ÷ 100 = 24.3 to 3 significant figures.

Ionisation Energies and Quantum Evidence

First ionisation energy is the energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions. Second and third ionisation energies remove subsequent moles of electrons from 1+ and 2+ gaseous ions respectively. All ionisation energies are endothermic because energy must be put in to overcome the electrostatic attraction between the outer electrons and the positive nucleus. Ionisation energies are influenced by the positive nuclear charge, electron shielding from inner shells, and the distance of the sub-shell from the nucleus. Successive ionisation energies provide decisive evidence for quantum shells and the group number because a large jump occurs when an electron is removed from a shell closer to the nucleus. The first ionisation energy trend across successive elements provides direct evidence for electron sub-shells.

  • First ionisation energy equation: X (g) yields X+ (g) + e−.
  • Second ionisation energy equation: X+ (g) yields X2+ (g) + e−.
  • Endothermic process: delta H is positive.
  • Nuclear charge increases across a period, increasing attraction.
  • Shielding increases down a group, decreasing attraction.

Orbitals, Sub-shells and Electronic Configurations

An orbital is a region within an atom that can hold up to two electrons with opposite spins. Orbitals in sub-shells each take a single electron before pairing up with two electrons of opposite spin. Orbitals come in different shapes: s-orbitals are spherical, and p-orbitals are dumbbell-shaped along x, y, and z axes. Sub-shells are designated s, p, d, and f. The first four quantum shells hold maximums of 2, 8, 18, and 32 electrons respectively, corresponding to 1, 4, 9, and 16 orbitals. You can predict electronic configurations from hydrogen to krypton inclusive and their ions using s, p, d notation and electron-in-boxes notation. Electronic configuration determines the chemical properties of an element because elements in the same group share outer shell configurations. The Periodic Table is divided into blocks corresponding to the sub-shell containing the highest energy electron.

  • s-block: groups 1 and 2, outer electrons in s-orbitals.
  • p-block: groups 13 to 18, outer electrons in p-orbitals.
  • d-block: transition metals, outer electrons in d-sub-shells.
  • Hunds rule: electrons fill singly before pairing in degenerate orbitals.
  • Transition metal ion formation: 4s electrons are lost before 3d electrons.

Worked example: write the electronic configuration of a titanium atom (atomic number 22) and a titanium 2+ ion.

  • Step 1: Follow the filling order up to 22 electrons. 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d2.
  • Step 2: When forming the 2+ ion, remove electrons from the highest principal quantum number first. Remove 2 electrons from the 4s sub-shell.
  • Step 3: Write the ionic configuration as 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d2.

Periodic Trends and Graphical Data

Data represented graphically, including logarithms of first ionisation energies for elements 1 to 36, demonstrate the periodic nature of properties. A periodic property is one that repeats in a regular pattern across periods. Across periods 2 and 3, melting and boiling temperatures depend on structure and bonding: giant metallic structures have high melting points, giant covalent structures have very high melting points due to strong covalent bonds, and simple molecular structures have low melting and boiling points due to weak intermolecular forces. First ionisation energies generally increase across periods due to increasing nuclear charge and constant shielding, with slight drops between group 2 and 13 due to sub-shell changes, and between group 15 and 16 due to spin-pairing repulsion. First ionisation energy decreases down a group due to increased atomic radius and shielding.

  • Period 2 and 3 trends: metallic bonding peaks at group 13, covalent macromolecular peaks at group 14, simple molecules drop sharply at group 15 or 16.
  • Group 2 to 13 drop: outer electron enters a higher-energy p-sub-shell, which is further shielded by the s-sub-shell.
  • Group 15 to 16 drop: pairing of electrons in a p-orbital causes mutual repulsion, making it easier to remove.
  • Logarithm graphs of ionisation energy clearly show the periodicity of quantum shells.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Stating that ionisation energy is exothermic because energy is released. Correction: Ionisation energy is always endothermic because energy is required to overcome the electrostatic attraction between electrons and protons.
  • Mistake: Removing 3d electrons before 4s electrons when ionising transition metal atoms. Correction: Always remove 4s electrons first because the 4s orbital is of higher energy once filling is complete and sits further out.
  • Mistake: Confusing mass number with relative atomic mass. Correction: Mass number is a whole number representing protons plus neutrons in a specific isotope, whereas relative atomic mass is a weighted mean of all naturally occurring isotopes.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that a chlorine mass spectrum has peaks for Cl2 molecules, not just chlorine atoms. Correction: Diatomic chlorine molecules produce molecular ion peaks at m/z 70, 72, and 74 based on combinations of Cl-35 and Cl-37.

Exam-style questions

  1. Define the term first ionisation energy. Answer: The energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions. (Earns 2 marks for stating moles of gas and 1+ ions).
  2. Explain why the first ionisation energy of oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen. Answer: Nitrogen has a half-filled 2p3 sub-shell configuration, whereas oxygen has a 2p4 configuration with paired electrons. The mutual repulsion of the paired electrons in oxygen makes the electron easier to remove. (Earns credit for mentioning electron pairing and repulsion).
  3. Calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium given isotopes: Mg-24 (78.99%), Mg-25 (10.00%), Mg-26 (11.01%). Answer: ((24 × 78.99) + (25 × 10.00) + (26 × 11.01)) ÷ 100 = 24.3 to 1 decimal place. (Earns credit for correct working and units).
  4. State and explain the trend in first ionisation energy down Group 2. Answer: First ionisation energy decreases down Group 2 because atoms have more quantum shells, increasing atomic radius and electron shielding, which outweighs the increased nuclear charge and reduces outer shell attraction. (Earns credit for naming shielding, distance, and attraction).
  5. Write the full electronic configuration for a chromium atom, atomic number 24, using s, p, d notation. Answer: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1 3d5. (Earns credit for the stable half-filled d-sub-shell exception).

Use these notes alongside active recall and past paper question practice. Focus next on mastering redox equations and stoichiometry in Topic 3.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Relative atomic mass, applied to chlorine with 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl: (35 × 75 + 37 × 25) ÷ 100 = 35.5. Multiply each mass by its abundance as a fraction, then divide by 100. Give the answer to one decimal place when the abundances are given to two significant figures.
  • Electron configuration traps: chromium is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and copper is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, because half-filled and full d sub-shells are unusually stable. Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶: the 4s electrons are removed first when a transition metal forms an ion, even though 4s fills first.
  • Ionisation energy dip, applied to Mg to Al: aluminium's outer electron is in a 3p sub-shell, which is higher in energy than 3s, so less energy removes it. The dip at O compared with N occurs because O has a paired 2p electron, and the repulsion between the paired electrons makes it easier to remove. Name the sub-shell or the repulsion in the answer.
  • Successive ionisation energies: a large jump between two values shows the electron has moved to a new, inner shell. For example, a jump between the second and third values for an element with two outer electrons identifies it as Group 2.

title: Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment
content:
Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment

Biology — A2. Edexcel IAL Biology WBI14, Topic 5. Energy enters most ecosystems as light, is fixed by photosynthesis and then passes along food chains. Nutrients cycle, and human activity can disrupt those cycles.

  • Photosynthesis and limiting factors
  • Energy transfer through trophic levels
  • Nutrient cycles
  • Human impact

Key areas to revise

  • Photosynthesis overall reaction (5.1): light energy splits water strong bonds, hydrogen combines with carbon dioxide to form glucose, releasing oxygen.
  • Photophosphorylation of ADP (5.2): requires energy; ATP hydrolysis provides immediate biological energy.
  • Light-dependent reactions (5.3): light excites chlorophyll electrons, generating ATP, reducing NADP via cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation, and producing oxygen through water photolysis.
  • Light-independent reactions (5.4): carbon dioxide reduction via Calvin cycle using GP, GALP, RuBP, and RUBISCO; products form simple sugars used in respiration and biological molecules (polysaccharides, amino acids, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids).
  • Chloroplast structure (5.5): thylakoids, grana, stroma, and membranes related to photosynthetic roles.
  • Spectra and chromatography (5.6, 5.7): absorption spectrum, action spectrum, pigment separation, and Rf value identification.
  • Core Practical 10 (5.8): investigating light intensity, wavelength, temperature, and carbon dioxide availability on aquatic plant photosynthesis rates.
  • Primary productivity (5.9): GPP, NPP, and plant respiration relationship where NPP = GPP − R.
  • Trophic transfer (5.10): calculating biomass and energy transfer efficiency between trophic levels as (energy transferred ÷ energy intake) × 100%.
  • Ecological terms (5.11): population, community, habitat, and ecosystem definitions.
  • Abiotic and biotic factors (5.12): controlling numbers and distribution of organisms.
  • Niche concept (5.13): accounts for organism distribution and abundance.
  • Core Practical 11 (5.14): quadrats, transects, distribution, abundance, and abiotic factor measurement.
  • Succession (5.15): stages from colonisation to climax community.
  • Climate change evidence (5.16): carbon dioxide levels, temperature records, pollen in peat bogs, dendrochronology, correlations, and causal relationships.
  • Anthropogenic causes (5.17): greenhouse gases and greenhouse effect.
  • Carbon cycle application (5.18): methods to reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide.
  • Extrapolation and models (5.19): predictions, climate models, and limitations.
  • Climate change effects (5.20): changing rainfall patterns, seasonal cycles, distribution, development, and lifecycles.
  • Enzyme activity and temperature (5.21): Q10 calculation and metabolic impact.
  • Core Practical 12 (5.22): temperature effects on organism development (seedling growth, brine shrimp hatch rates) with ethical considerations.
  • Evolution (5.23): gene mutation and natural selection changing allele frequencies.
  • Speciation (5.24): isolation reducing gene flow leading to allopatric or sympatric speciation.
  • Scientific conclusions (5.25): evaluating controversial issues like climate change actions based on sources.
  • Conservation (5.26): reforestation, sustainable resources, and biofuels managing human needs and conservation conflicts.

Worked example

Calculate the net primary productivity if gross primary productivity is 14000 kJ m⁻² year⁻² and plant respiration is 5500 kJ m⁻² year⁻². Using NPP = GPP − R, NPP = 14000 − 5500 = 8500 kJ m⁻² year⁻².

Key points to remember

Examiners frequently note that students confuse GPP and NPP; always subtract plant respiration (R) from gross primary productivity to find net primary productivity. When calculating ecological efficiencies, ensure units match across trophic levels and multiply by 100 to yield a percentage. Remember that allopatric speciation requires geographical isolation, whereas sympatric speciation occurs within the same habitat via behavioural, temporal, or anatomical isolation. When discussing climate change evidence, distinguish between correlation and causal relationships explicitly in your exam answers.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Temperature and scales

Thermodynamic temperature is measured in kelvin. The kelvin and Celsius scales have the same size of degree, with T/K = θ/°C + 273. Absolute zero (0 K) is the lowest possible temperature, at which the particles of an ideal gas have minimum kinetic energy.

Example: 25 °C = 298 K.

Specific heat capacity and latent heat

Specific heat capacity c is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K: Q = mcΔθ. Latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg without a change in temperature: Q = mL. Melting and boiling absorb energy without a temperature rise, because the energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds, not into kinetic energy.

Example: warming 2.0 kg of water (c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) by 10 K needs 84 kJ. Melting 0.20 kg of ice (L = 334 kJ kg⁻¹) needs 67 kJ.

The mole and Avogadro constant

One mole contains N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ particles. The number of particles is N = nN_A, where n is the amount in moles. Molar mass is the mass of one mole, in kg mol⁻¹ in SI units.

Equation of state for an ideal gas

pV = nRT, where R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and T must be absolute. Equivalently pV = NkT, with k = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

Example: 0.10 mol at 300 K in 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ has p = nRT/V ≈ 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa.

Kinetic theory

The pressure of an ideal gas comes from molecules colliding with the container walls. The mean kinetic energy of a molecule is ⟨Ek⟩ = 3kT/2, so it depends only on the absolute temperature. At 300 K it is about 6.2 × 10⁻²¹ J.

Internal energy and the first law

The internal energy of an ideal gas is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its molecules. For an ideal gas there are no intermolecular forces, so internal energy depends only on temperature. The first law of thermodynamics is ΔU = Q + W, where Q is heat added to the system and W is work done on the system. Heat lost by a system is therefore negative.

Example: a gas has 500 J of work done on it and loses 200 J of heat. ΔU = −200 + 500 = +300 J.

Exam tips: convert to kelvin before using pV = nRT or the kinetic-energy formula. Check the sign convention for W in the question. Use latent heat only when the temperature is constant.

Heat transfer and heat capacity

Energy transfer by conduction happens through a solid when particles vibrate and pass energy to their neighbours, with free electrons carrying energy in metals. Convection in fluids occurs because hotter, less dense fluid rises and is replaced by cooler, denser fluid. Black, matt surfaces are good absorbers and emitters of infrared radiation.

The energy needed to change the temperature of a substance is Q = mcΔT, where c is the specific heat capacity. Latent heat is the energy absorbed or released during a change of state with no change in temperature.

title:
Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI12 Unit 1, Topic 4 Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation. It covers plant cell ultrastructure and the functions of the organelles and cell wall components, starch and cellulose and how their structure fits their role, how cellulose microfibrils and secondary thickening give physical properties to xylem and sclerenchyma fibres, the similarities and differences between sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem and their structure, position and function, the light microscope practical on transverse sections, the uses of plant fibres and starch in sustainability, the importance of water and mineral ions to plants and the practical on mineral deficiency, the tensile strength practical, bacterial growth requirements, antimicrobial plant substances and the aseptic practical, the development of drug testing from Withering's digitalis to modern three-phased testing, classification and the species concept and the three-domain system, biodiversity and endemism and how they are measured, species richness and the heterozygosity index, the index of diversity and how it is compared between habitats, and the concept of niche and examples of adaptations — behavioural, anatomical and physiological. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Plant cell ultrastructure: what is in a plant cell and why

Plant cells share the common eukaryotic features with animal cells — a plasma membrane (cell surface membrane), cytoplasm and ribosomes — but add several structures that animal cells do not have. The cell wall is a rigid outer layer of cellulose microfibrils embedded in a gel-like matrix; it gives shape and support, prevents the cell from bursting when turgid, and limits uncontrolled expansion. Chloroplasts are double-membraned organelles containing chlorophyll and the enzymes for photosynthesis; inside, stacked membranes (thylakoids, often stacked into grana) carry out the light-dependent reactions, and the surrounding stroma contains the enzymes for the light-independent reactions. Amyloplasts are colourless plastids that store starch; they are found especially in storage organs such as potato tubers. Vacuoles are membrane-bound sacs; a large central vacuole in mature plant cells is filled with cell sap — a watery solution of sugars, salts, pigments and waste — surrounded by the tonoplast membrane, and it maintains turgor pressure and gives the cell its rigidity. Plasmodesmata are thread-like channels through the cell walls of adjacent plant cells, connecting the cytoplasm and allowing communication and transport between cells. Pits are thin regions in the cell wall where the wall is localy thinner or absent, allowing water and solutes to pass between cells; the middle lamella is the layer that cements together the cell walls of adjacent cells. Ribosomes are present (80S in the cytoplasm) and the nucleus, nucleolus, mitochondria and golgi apparatus are all present, as in animal cells, except that plant cells do not have centrioles (higher plants lack them, though they still divide).

2. Recognising plant organelles from electron micrographs

On an electron micrograph of a plant cell you should be able to recognise the plasma membrane, nucleus with nucleolus, chloroplasts with their stacked thylakoid membranes (grana), mitochondria, rough endoplasmic reticulum with ribosomes, golgi (dictyosomes in plants), a large central vacuole with the tonoplast, the cell wall (with middle lamella where two cells meet), and plasmodesmata. Chloroplasts are especially characteristic: the grana appear as stacks of disc-like membranes. Amyloplasts appear as colourless, starch-filled plastids without grana. A good exercise is to label each of these in an EM image and to explain the function of each. Compare the plant cell with an animal cell: plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts, a large central vacuole and plasmodesmata, and generally no centrioles, and their shape is more regular because of the wall.

3. Starch and cellulose: polysaccharides that do different jobs

Starch and cellulose are both polymers of glucose, but alpha-glucose for starch and beta-glucose for cellulose, and that difference determines their properties. Alpha-glucose has the hydroxyl groups on the same side of the ring (in the usual representation), so when polymerised with 1,4-glycosidic bonds the chain coils into a helix, forming amylose, and with 1,6-branches forming amylopectin — compact, helical and branched, so starch is an excellent storage material: compact to pack a lot of glucose into little space, and with no osmotic effect, because the large insoluble starch granules do not draw water into the cell by osmosis. Cellulose is made from beta-glucose, in which the hydroxyl on carbon 1 is on the opposite side, so when linked the chain is straight rather than coiled; the linear chains run parallel and form many hydrogen bonds between adjacent chains, making strong cellulose microfibrils. Cellulose microfibrils are the main structural component of the cell wall, giving strength and rigidity; the way they are arranged determines the properties of the cell and of the whole plant. The structure of starch suits it for storage in plant cells; the structure of cellulose suits it for strength and support — two polymers from the same monomer with very different roles because of the different glycosidic bonds and the different shape of the chain.

4. Cellulose microfibrils, secondary thickening and the properties of xylem and sclerenchyma

The physical properties of plant tissues depend on how the cellulose microfibrils are arranged. In a young, growing cell the microfibrils are laid down mainly at right angles to the direction of growth, so the cell can expand in length; when growth stops, the cell can become strengthened by secondary thickening — more cellulose and, in some cells, lignin deposited on the inside of the primary wall — which makes the wall rigid and waterproof. In sclerenchyma fibres, the cells die at maturity and are left with heavily thickened, lignified walls, often with the microfibrils arranged in spiral or ring patterns; the result is strong, flexible but tough fibres that give mechanical support and can be used by humans (for example in textiles and ropes). In xylem vessels, the wall is lignified and the cells are dead at maturity, forming long tubes with the end walls broken down or absent — the vessel elements are linked end to end to form a continuous tube for the transport of water and mineral ions, and the lignified thickening (in rings, spirals or nets) prevents collapse under the negative pressure of the transpiration stream. So the arrangement of cellulose microfibrils and the deposition of lignin determine what a plant part can do: support, flexibility, or transport of water under tension. The secondary thickening of xylem and the lignification of sclerenchyma are the adaptations that let land plants grow tall and stand upright and transport water from the roots to the leaves.

5. Sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem: structure, position and function

Sclerenchyma fibres and xylem vessels provide support and, for xylem, transport; phloem translocates organic solutes. Sclerenchyma fibres are long, narrow cells with thick lignified walls and a small lumen, dead at maturity; they occur in bundles and, because of their strength and flexibility, they give support to stems and leaves and can be used in textiles and ropes. Xylem vessels are long, continuous tubes formed from vessel elements with lignified walls and pits in the walls, dead at maturity with no contents, and their function is transport of water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves — and they also provide support. Phloem is a living tissue; sieve tube elements are the conducting cells, arranged end to end with perforated end walls (sieve plates) between them, reduced cytoplasm at the edges and no nucleus at maturity; each sieve tube element has a companion cell beside it, connected by plasmodesmata, which keeps the sieve element alive and supplies it with ATP, because the sieve element itself has lost its nucleus and most organelles. Phloem transports organic solutes (mainly sucrose, in solution in water) from sources (leaves, storage organs) to sinks (growing points, roots, developing fruits) by mass flow driven by the pressure gradient built up by the loading of sucrose into the sieve tubes. Compare: sclerenchyma fibres = support, dead, lignified; xylem vessels = support and water/mineral transport, dead, lignified, open tube; phloem = translocation of organic solutes, living sieve tubes with companion cells, perforated end walls, no lignin.

6. Core Practical 7 — transverse sections of roots, stems and leaves

Use a light microscope to make observations, draw and label plan diagrams of transverse sections of roots, stems and leaves, and to observe and label cells of plant tissues, identifying sclerenchyma fibres, phloem, sieve tubes and xylem vessels and their location. To make a transverse section, cut a very thin slice across a stem or root with a razor blade (a sharp blade and a steady hand or a sectioning technique), float the section onto water on a slide, lower a coverslip at an angle, stain if needed (for example with toluidine blue or iodine) to distinguish lignified xylem, sclerenchyma and phloem, and observe under the microscope at several magnifications. In a stem transverse section, note the positions of the epidermis, cortex, the vascular bundles (with xylem toward the inside and phloem toward the outside, and sclerenchyma fibres often outside the phloem in a bundle cap), and the pith in the centre; in roots the vascular tissue is central. Draw a plan diagram (an outline of the whole section showing the arrangement of tissues, not the cells) with the correct relative sizes and positions, label the tissues, give a title and magnification. Then observe and label the cells: look for the thick lignified walls of xylem and sclerenchyma, the sieve plates and companion cells of phloem, and the thin-walled cells of the cortex and pith.

7. Plant fibres and starch in sustainability

Plant fibres and starch can contribute to sustainability and to replacing oil-based plastics. Plant fibres (from sclerenchyma or from phloem fibres) are strong, renewable and biodegradable, and they can be used in textiles, paper, building materials and composites that replace oil-based plastics and synthetic fibres; water transport in plants today parallels the transport of sap and provides a model for how plants already do this. Starch can be used to make bioplastics — for example, starch can be processed into film-forming materials suitable for packaging, plates and disposable items — and because starch is a renewable, biodegradable material made from crops such as potatoes, maize or cassava, it can replace oil-based plastics in some uses. Using plant fibres and starch reduces reliance on oil, is renewable and can be more sustainable if the crops are grown responsibly; but there are trade-offs: land, water and energy for the crops, possible competition with food production, and the need to assess the whole life cycle. The use of plant products to replace oil-based plastics is a topic that connects plant structure (cellulose and starch), to sustainability, to human decisions informed by science.

8. Water and inorganic ions to plants, and mineral deficiency

Plants need water for photosynthesis (a reactant and the medium in which it happens), for transport (water is the solvent for minerals and for sucrose in the phloem), for support (turgor pressure keeps non-woody parts rigid), and for cooling (transpiration). Water enters the roots by osmosis from the soil and moves up the xylem. Inorganic ions are essential: nitrate ions (NO3-) are needed for making amino acids, proteins, DNA and chlorophyll — a deficiency causes stunted growth and yellowing of older leaves (chlorosis); calcium ions are needed for the middle lamella (pectin in the cell wall) and for cell membranes — a deficiency gives stunted growth and necrosis of the growing point and young leaves; magnesium ions are the central atom in chlorophyll — a deficiency causes chlorosis of the older leaves. A recommended additional practical is to investigate plant mineral deficiencies: grow plants in a solution with all minerals (complete) and in solutions missing one of nitrate, calcium or magnesium, observe and measure the effects on growth and leaf colour over weeks, and explain the results in terms of the roles of the missing ion.

9. Core Practical 8 — tensile strength of plant fibres

Determine the tensile strength of plant fibres — the force a fibre can take before it breaks. A typical method: take strands of a plant fibre (for example the fibres from celery stalks or nettle stems, or a piece of a plant stem with visible fibres), clamp one end, hang weights from the other, and add weights until the fibre breaks; record the mass (converted to a force, weight = mass × g) needed to break the fibre. Repeat for several fibres, present the results, and compare fibres from different plants or different parts of a plant. Safety: sharp blades and falling weights. The practical shows how the arrangement of cellulose and lignin gives the fibre its strength, and connects the cell-level structure to a macroscopic useful property.

10. Conditions for bacterial growth

Bacteria need certain conditions to grow: a supply of nutrients (carbon, nitrogen, minerals and, for some, specific organic factors), water, a suitable temperature (most pathogenic bacteria around 37 °C, though many grow across a range), oxygen (some need it — aerobic bacteria — some do not — anaerobic bacteria — and some can manage with or without), a suitable pH, and, for many, time to multiply. In the laboratory these conditions can be met and controlled: cultures are grown in nutrient broth or on agar plates, at a set temperature (often 25 °C for environmental organisms and 37 °C for those that grow at body temperature), with or without oxygen, and in sterile conditions so that only the desired organism grows. Aseptic technique is essential to avoid contaminating the culture or releasing harmful bacteria into the environment — sterilise equipment (by flame or autoclave), work near a flame to create an upward air current, work quickly and cover the plates, and dispose of cultures by sterilising before disposal.

11. Antimicrobial plant substances and the aseptic practical

Substances derived from plants can have antimicrobial and other therapeutic properties. Some plant extracts inhibit the growth of bacteria or fungi — for example, garlic has been traditionally used and does have some antibacterial effects; other plants yield useful compounds (aspirin from willow bark, morphine from poppies, and many modern drugs are derived from plants). A recommended additional practical is to investigate the antimicrobial properties of plants, including aseptic techniques for the safe handling of bacteria: prepare agar plates, use sterile swabs or paper discs impregnated with different plant extracts, incubate and measure the zones of inhibition around the discs — the diameter of the clear zone where bacteria did not grow — and compare the effectiveness of different extracts or the same extract at different concentrations. Use aseptic technique: sterilise the discs and loops, work near a flame, spread the bacteria in a controlled way, seal the plates with tape (but do not seal all the way so they do not become anaerobic), and incubate at a safe temperature. Measure the zones of inhibition and record them, including in a table, and draw a conclusion about which extract is most effective and about concentration.

12. Drug testing: from Withering's digitalis soup to modern trials

The development of drug testing has moved from historic, uncontrolled methods to contemporary, rigorous protocols. William Withering's digitalis soup in the 18th century was an early use of a plant-derived medicine — foxglove (Digitalis) — for dropsy (oedema), tested by trial and observation on patients, but with no controls, no placebo, no blinding and no large sample, so the evidence was weak and mixed with other treatments. Placebos are used to control for the placebo effect (improvement from the belief of being treated). The modern protocol — double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-centre, large trials — is far more reliable than Withering's soup, and it protects patients and produces trustworthy evidence. Students should be able to describe this progression and evaluate the designs.

13. Classification: organising life, the species concept and the three domains

Classification is a means of organising the variety of life based on relationships between organisms, using differences and similarities in phenotypes (observable features) and in genotypes (the DNA and the proteins the DNA codes for). It is built around the species concept — a species is a group of organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring — and a hierarchy of groups above it: genus, family, order, class, phylum and kingdom, with organisms grouped because they share common ancestry. The classification has changed as new data — especially molecular evidence from DNA and protein sequences — have come in, leading to critical evaluation of existing groupings and new taxonomic groupings. The three-domain system, based on molecular evidence, divides life into the Archaea, the Bacteria and the Eukarya (which includes all eukaryotes, plants, animals, fungi and protists); the Archaea are distinct from the Bacteria and include organisms that often live in extreme environments, and the evidence from ribosomal RNA sequences and other molecular data led to this reclassification, replacing the older five-kingdom system. The process of critical evaluation of new data by the scientific community — comparing, testing and debating — is what leads to new groupings and to science being self-correcting.

14. Biodiversity, endemism and threats from human activity

Biodiversity is the variety of life — the variety within a habitat, within a species or across the whole planet; it can refer to species richness (the number of different species in a habitat) or to genetic diversity within a species. Endemism is the state of a species being found only in one particular place (an endemic species, such as a plant found only on a particular island). Over time the variety of life has become extensive through evolution, but it is now being threatened by human activity — habitat destruction (deforestation, drainage, conversion to agriculture), over-exploitation (hunting, fishing, logging), pollution, the introduction of invasive species, and climate change, all of which can reduce biodiversity and cause extinctions. Biodiversity matters because it provides ecosystem services, genetic resources for medicines and crops, and is itself valuable; its loss affects ecosystems, food security and human health. Understanding the causes of the loss is important so that conservation measures can be designed to address them.

15. Measuring biodiversity: species richness, genetic diversity and heterozygosity

Biodiversity can be measured in different ways. Species richness — the number of different species in a given area — is one simple measure of biodiversity within a habitat; a habitat with more species is generally more diverse, though this ignores the abundance of each species (a habitat dominated by one common species and several rare ones may have the same species richness as one where all are equally common). Genetic diversity within a species can be measured by the heterozygosity index (also called heterozygosity): the proportion of individuals in a population that are heterozygous at a locus. It is calculated as the number of heterozygotes divided by the number of individuals in the population (for a single locus); a higher heterozygosity means more genetic diversity within that population. This matters because genetic diversity helps a population adapt to changes, resist disease and avoid the problems of inbreeding; loss of genetic diversity raises the risk of extinction.

16. Comparing habitats with the index of diversity

Biodiversity can be compared between different habitats using the formula for the index of diversity, D: D = (N(N−1)) / (Σ n(n−1)), where N is the total number of organisms of all species in the habitat, and n is the number of organisms of a particular species. Calculation: for each species, work out n(n−1); sum these to get Σ n(n−1); then divide N(N−1) by that sum to give D, the index of diversity. Worked example: in a habitat with species counts 10, 15, 5, 2 (N = 32): Σ n(n−1) = (10×9)+(15×14)+(5×4)+(2×1) = 90+210+20+2 = 322; N(N−1) = 32×31 = 992; D = 992 / 322 ≈ 3.08. A larger D means a more diverse habitat, because it reflects both the number of species and how evenly the individuals are distributed among them. To compare habitats, calculate D for each and compare the values, stating which is more diverse and what that suggests. The formula must be applied correctly: calculate n(n−1) for each species, sum them, and divide N(N−1) by the sum.

17. Niche and adaptations: behavioural, anatomical and physiological

A niche is the role of an organism in a habitat — the conditions in which it lives and the resources it uses, and how it interacts with other organisms; it is more than just the physical place (the habitat) where it lives, and no two species can occupy exactly the same niche for long because of competition. Adaptations are features that help an organism survive and reproduce in its niche, and they can be behavioural, anatomical or physiological. Behavioural adaptations are things the organism does — for example migration to avoid harsh conditions, hunting in packs, basking to warm up, or the specific foraging behaviour of a bird. Anatomical (structural) adaptations are physical features of the body — for example the shape of a bird's beak for its food, the camouflage colours of a prey animal, the thick fur of an arctic mammal, or the long beak of a nectar-feeding bird. Physiological adaptations are internal functions — for example a camel's ability to tolerate dehydration and to conserve water, the production of venom by a snake, the production of antifreeze proteins in some polar fish, or the specialised nitrogen excretion of desert animals. The concept of niche and the types of adaptation help explain how different organisms fit into their environments and how competition and adaptation shape communities.

18. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes section by section, checking that you can identify plant cell ultrastructure and organelles in an electron micrograph and state their functions, explain how starch and cellulose differ in structure and role, describe the secondary thickening and the properties of xylem vessels and sclerenchyma fibres, compare sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem in structure, position and function, carry out the transverse section and tensile strength practicals and explain the variables and safety, describe the conditions for bacterial growth and the aseptic practical, describe the development of drug testing from Withering's digitalis to modern three-phased trials and evaluate the designs, define classification and the species concept, describe the three-domain system and the molecular evidence for it, define biodiversity and endemism and the threats from human activity, carry out the species richness and heterozygosity and index of diversity calculations, and define niche and give behavioural, anatomical and physiological adaptations. After this topic, revise Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development (plant and animal cells, division) and Topic 5 Energy flow, ecosystems and the environment, because classification and biodiversity sit within ecology.

1. Plant cell ultrastructure: what is in a plant cell and why

Plant cells share the common eukaryotic features with animal cells — a plasma membrane (cell surface membrane), cytoplasm and ribosomes — but add several structures that animal cells do not have. The cell wall is a rigid outer layer of cellulose microfibrils embedded in a gel-like matrix; it gives shape and support, prevents the cell from bursting when turgid, and limits uncontrolled expansion. Chloroplasts are double-membraned organelles containing chlorophyll and the enzymes for photosynthesis; inside, stacked membranes (thylakoids, often stacked into grana) carry out the light-dependent reactions, and the surrounding stroma contains the enzymes for the light-independent reactions. Amyloplasts are colourless plastids that store starch; they are found especially in storage organs such as potato tubers. Vacuoles are membrane-bound sacs; a large central vacuole in mature plant cells is filled with cell sap — a watery solution of sugars, salts, pigments and waste — surrounded by the tonoplast membrane, and it maintains turgor pressure and gives the cell its rigidity. Plasmodesmata are thread-like channels through the cell walls of adjacent plant cells, connecting the cytoplasm and allowing communication and transport between cells. Pits are thin regions in the cell wall where the wall is localy thinner or absent, allowing water and solutes to pass between cells; the middle lamella is the layer that cements together the cell walls of adjacent cells. Ribosomes are present (80S in the cytoplasm) and the nucleus, nucleolus, mitochondria and golgi apparatus are all present, as in animal cells, except that plant cells do not have centrioles (higher plants lack them, though they still divide).

2. Recognising plant organelles from electron micrographs

Chloroplasts are especially characteristic: the grana appear as stacks of disc-like membranes. Amyloplasts appear as colourless, starch-filled plastids without grana. A good exercise is to label each of these in an EM image and to explain the function of each.
