title: Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment Revision Notes
content:
Quick revision: Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment

Biology — A2. Edexcel IAL Biology WBI15, Topic 7. Respiration releases energy as ATP for muscle contraction. Homeostasis keeps the internal environment stable, and the kidney is central to this. The topic links biochemistry to physiology.

Key areas to revise

  • Aerobic respiration
  • Anaerobic respiration in mammals
  • Respiratory quotient
  • Muscle contraction
  • Homeostasis and the kidney

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Core Detailed Revision Notes

Aerobic respiration overall reaction is the splitting of respiratory substrates to release carbon dioxide as a waste product and reuniting hydrogen with atmospheric oxygen with the release of large amounts of energy. Respiration is a stepped process, with each step controlled and catalysed by a specific intracellular enzyme, though specific enzyme names are not required.

Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm and involves the phosphorylation of hexoses, production of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, reduced coenzyme, pyruvate, and lactate. In anaerobic respiration, pyruvate is converted to lactate, which is later transported to the liver where it is oxidized back to pyruvate or converted to glycogen using oxygen to clear the oxygen debt.

The link reaction and the Krebs cycle take place in the mitochondrial matrix, leading to complete oxidation of glucose and formation of carbon dioxide by decarboxylation, ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, and reduced NAD and FAD by dehydrogenation. Oxidative phosphorylation occurs at the inner mitochondrial membrane via the electron transport chain, involving chemiosmosis where protons diffuse through ATP synthase down an electrochemical gradient to synthesise ATP.

The respiratory quotient (RQ) is calculated as volume of carbon dioxide produced divided by volume of oxygen consumed over a given time period. Core Practical 15 uses an artificial hydrogen carrier like methylene blue or DCPIP to investigate respiration rates in yeast by timing the color change as it is reduced. Core Practical 16 uses a simple respirometer with soda lime or potassium hydroxide to absorb carbon dioxide, measuring oxygen consumption and calculating rates of respiration and RQ for germinating seeds or small invertebrates.

Muscles, tendons, the skeleton, and ligaments interact to enable movement, operating via antagonistic muscle pairs consisting of extensors and flexors. Mammalian skeletal muscle fibres are composed of myofibrils. Fast twitch fibres contract quickly, rely heavily on anaerobic glycolysis, fatigue rapidly, and have few capillaries and mitochondria. Slow twitch fibres contract slowly, rely on aerobic respiration, resist fatigue, and possess many mitochondria, myoglobin, and capillaries.

Muscle contraction is explained by the sliding filament theory. Action potentials trigger calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Calcium ions bind to troponin, causing tropomyosin to shift and expose myosin-binding sites on actin. Myosin heads bind to actin, forming cross-bridges, and undergo a power stroke using ATP hydrolysis catalysed by ATPase, pulling the actin filament inward and shortening the sarcomere.

Cardiac muscle is myogenic. Normal electrical activity coordinates the heartbeat beginning at the sinoatrial node (SAN) acting as the pacemaker, sending impulses across the atria to the atrioventricular node (AVN), down the bundle of His, and through the Purkyne fibres to contract the ventricles from the apex up. Electrocardiograms (ECGs) record electrical activity and aid in diagnosing abnormal heart rhythms like tachycardia, bradycardia, and fibrillation. Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. Variations in ventilation rate and cardiac output enable rapid oxygen delivery and carbon dioxide removal, regulated by the cardiovascular control centre and ventilation centre in the medulla oblongata, influenced by chemoreceptors and baroreceptors.

Adrenaline prepares the body for the fight or flight response by increasing heart rate, dilating airways, and redirecting blood flow. Core Practical 17 investigates the effects of exercise on tidal volume, breathing rate, respiratory minute ventilation, and oxygen consumption using spirometer traces.

Negative feedback returns a system to its set point when deviations occur, maintaining narrow limits essential for homeostasis, whereas positive feedback amplifies the deviation away from the set point. Homeostasis maintains the internal environment in a dynamic equilibrium during exercise, with the hypothalamus acting as the master controller in thermoregulation via shivering, sweating, and vasomotor changes.

The mammalian kidney gross structure includes the cortex, medulla, pelvis, ureter, and renal artery and vein, while microscopic structure features nephrons comprising the Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule, and collecting duct. Urea is produced in the liver from excess deaminated amino acids. Ultrafiltration in the glomerulus under high hydrostatic pressure forces water, glucose, mineral ions, and urea through pores in the capillary endothelium and basement membrane into the Bowman's capsule.

Selective reabsorption occurs in the proximal tubule via active transport of sodium ions linked to co-transport of glucose and amino acids, followed by passive reabsorption of water by osmosis. The loop of Henle acts as a countercurrent multiplier, pumping sodium and chloride ions out of the ascending limb into the medulla to lower water potential, thereby causing water to leave the descending limb and collecting duct by osmosis for high water reabsorption.

Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect changes in blood water potential. If water potential drops, the posterior pituitary gland secretes more antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which increases the permeability of the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct cells to water by inserting aquaporins, resulting in a smaller volume of concentrated urine via negative feedback. Gene expression can be switched on and off by DNA transcription factors, where peptide hormones act extracellularly via second messenger systems and steroid hormones cross cell membranes to act intracellularly as transcription factors.

Worked example

Calculate the respiratory quotient of an organism that produces 12 cm³ of carbon dioxide and consumes 15 cm³ of oxygen in a set time interval. Step 1: Write the formula RQ = VCO2 / VO2. Step 2: Substitute the values RQ = 12 / 15. Step 3: Calculate the final value giving RQ = 0.8.

Key points to remember

Students often forget that glycolysis does not require oxygen and occurs in the cytoplasm, unlike the link reaction, Krebs cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation which occur exclusively inside mitochondria.

Another common error is confusing the roles of the AVN and SAN in the cardiac cycle, and failing to specify that ADH increases the permeability of the collecting duct to water by stimulating the insertion of aquaporins into the cell membranes.

Always state the direction of ion movement and the active versus passive nature of transport when describing the countercurrent multiplier mechanism in the loop of Henle.

title: Exam technique: Programming and Algorithms
content:
### What earns the marks
For validation, the rejected range stated plus the rejection loop earns both marks. For structure, single entry and exit modules using only sequence, selection and iteration earn the design marks. For traces, each variable tracked per line earns method credit. For testing, the stage named with its setting (isolated module vs live users) earns each mark.
### Traps
Error: fixed FOR loops for unknown-attempt validation. Correction: WHILE-until-valid loops. Error: binary search on unsorted data. Correction: sort first or use linear search. Error: unit and acceptance settings swapped. Correction: unit is isolated with test data; acceptance is live with real users.
### Worked example
A trace table records the value of each variable at each step of an algorithm. For a linear search, the program checks each item in turn and can take up to n comparisons. A binary search on a sorted list halves the search space each time, so 16 sorted items need at most about log₂16 = 4 comparisons. Binary search only works if the list is sorted.
### Check yourself
Trace a binary search for 9 in the sorted list 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13. Record the middle index at each step and state the number of comparisons. It finds 9 at the middle on the first comparison.

title: Kinematics — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Kinematics

Physics — AS. Sign convention matters: take up as positive and g = −9.81 m s⁻² for falling objects.

Key areas to revise

  • Definitions
  • Graphs
  • SUVAT (uniform acceleration only)
  • Projectiles

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked example

A ball is dropped from rest and falls 20 m. Taking down as positive, u = 0, s = 20 m and a = 9.81 m s⁻². Then v² = u² + 2as = 392.4, so v ≈ 19.8 m s⁻¹. Using the sign convention with up positive instead gives s = −20 m and a = −9.81 m s⁻², which gives the same answer with the signs consistent.

Common mistakes

  • Using SUVAT for a case with non-uniform acceleration, such as a body with increasing air resistance.
  • Mixing signs, for example taking up as positive but using g = +9.81 m s⁻².
  • Reading a displacement–time gradient as velocity only when it is a straight line. The gradient gives instantaneous velocity at any point on a curve.

title: Exam technique: Transformations and Vectors
content:
### What earns the marks
For translations and vector arithmetic, each component computed separately earns credit: show x and y lines. For magnitude, the root-of-sum-of-squares line earns the method mark before evaluation. For reflections and rotations, the coordinate rule stated ((y; -x) for 90 degrees clockwise) earns the method mark. For describing transformations, all three of type, centre or line, and size or angle are needed for full marks.
### Traps
Error: writing column vectors as bracket rows that lose a row. Correction: use (x; y) form and keep both components. Error: (100) or 14 for the magnitude of (6; 8). Correction: square, add, then root. Error: (-y; x) for a clockwise rotation. Correction: clockwise is (y; -x). Error: negating both coordinates for a single-axis reflection. Correction: one axis changes, the other stays.
### Worked example
Point A(1; 2) is translated by the vector (3; -1), giving A'(4; 1). Reflecting A' in the x-axis gives (4; -1). Rotating the point (3; -1) 90 degrees clockwise about the origin gives (-1; -3), using the rule (x; y) to (y; -x). Scaling (1; 2) by a factor of 2 from the origin gives (2; 4). Write each coordinate step on its own line.
### Check yourself
A point at (6; 8) has magnitude sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = sqrt(100) = 10. Explain why the magnitude is never the sum 6 + 8 = 14. The magnitude uses the root of the sum of squares, so the components do not add directly.

### Worked example
Point A(1; 2) is translated by the vector (3; -1), giving A'(4; 1). Reflecting A' in the x-axis gives (4; -1). Rotating the point (3; -1) 90 degrees clockwise about the origin gives (-1; -3), using the rule (x; y) to (y; -x). Scaling (1; 2) by a factor of 2 from the origin gives (2; 4). Write each coordinate step on its own line.
### Check yourself
A point at (6; 8) has magnitude sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = sqrt(100) = 10. Explain why the magnitude is never the sum 6 + 8 = 14. The magnitude uses the root of the sum of squares, so the components do not add directly.

title: Exam technique: Sine and Cosine Rules
content:
### What earns the marks
For the sine rule, the matched pairs written (b / sin 65 = 7 / sin 40) earn the method mark. For the cosine rule, the full substitution with cos evaluated earns the mark: write a squared = 25 + 64 - 2 x 5 x 8 x 0.5. For the largest angle, identifying the longest side first earns credit. For area, half a b sin C quoted earns the mark on its own.
### Traps
Error: sides paired with wrong angles in the sine rule. Correction: each side faces its angle. Error: 49 given as side a. Correction: root the cosine-rule result. Error: calculator-only acute angle for an obtuse ambiguous case. Correction: subtract from 180 by hand. Error: half a b without sine for a non-right triangle. Correction: area needs the sine factor unless the angle is 90 degrees.

title: Communication and Networking — Study Notes
content:
`# Communication and Networking

Transmission

  • Serial: one bit at a time — cheaper, reliable over distance
  • Parallel: multiple bits simultaneously — fast but suffers skew and crosstalk over long runs
  • Direction: simplex (one way), half-duplex (alternating), full-duplex (both ways)

Packets and Protocols

Data splits into packets with header (addresses, sequence) and trailer (checksum). A protocol is an agreed rule set — without one, devices cannot interpret signals.

  • TCP/IP stack: application → transport → network → link
  • HTTP/HTTPS: web transfer; HTTPS encrypts with TLS
  • FTP: file transfer; SMTP/POP3/IMAP: email

Network Types

  • LAN: small site, privately owned; WAN: large geographic scale (the internet)
  • Topologies: bus, star, mesh (star is most common — central switch)

Hardware

Routers join networks by IP; switches forward frames by MAC within a LAN; gateways translate protocols.

Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer

Client-server: central services, easy administration, single point of failure. P2P: every node shares files directly — cheap, hard to manage (torrents, blockchain).

Exam tips: explain packet switching with header/trailer details; justify protocol choice per application (email vs streaming).

Network topologies and hardware

In a star topology every device connects to a central switch. If one cable or device fails, the others keep working, but if the central switch fails the whole network stops. In a bus topology all devices share one cable, which is cheap but means a break in the cable disables the network.

A switch connects devices within a local area network (LAN) and sends each frame only to the device it is addressed to, using MAC addresses. A router connects separate networks together and forwards packets using IP addresses. A wireless access point lets wireless devices join a wired LAN.

Exam tip: when comparing topologies, state what happens when one device fails and when the central device fails. Those two cases are the usual differentiators.

Worked example: transfer time and latency

A 2 Mbit file sent over a link of 1 Mbit per second takes 2 seconds to transfer, ignoring overheads. Latency is the delay before the first bit arrives, and it adds to the total time. If the latency is 0.2 seconds, the complete delivery takes about 2.2 seconds. Stating which quantity you are calculating, and the units, earns method marks even when the final figure is slightly off.

Bandwidth and the shared medium

  • Bandwidth is the maximum data rate of a link. Actual throughput is lower when many devices share the medium, because they take turns or collide.
  • Wired connections such as Ethernet usually give more stable speeds than wireless, which is affected by distance, walls and interference.

title:
Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment — Quick Revision Summary

This is the fast map of Edexcel International A2 Biology WBI15 Topic 7. It follows the same order as the full notes so you can cross-reference, and it repeats the specification numbers so you can see which paragraph exists for which point. Use it to organise the topic, not to replace the notes. The topic divides into four blocks: the biochemistry of respiration and the fate of lactate, the physiology of muscles and the heart, the control of breathing and circulation in exercise, and the kidney and homeostasis with gene control at the end.

Aerobic respiration: the overall reaction and the stepped pathway

Respiration is how cells release energy from organic substrates and store it as ATP. The overall aerobic reaction is the shorthand: glucose and oxygen yield carbon dioxide, water and a large amount of energy. The important conceptual point is that the pathway is stepped and enzyme-controlled, not a single fire, and that each step is carried out by a specific intracellular enzyme. The names of the individual enzymes are not required, but the sequence and the location of each stage are.

  • 7.1 (i) Aerobic respiration is the splitting of the respiratory substrate, releasing carbon dioxide as a waste product and reuniting hydrogen with atmospheric oxygen, with the release of a large amount of energy. It is a stepped process, each step enzyme-controlled, and the names of specific enzymes are not required.
  • 7.1 (ii) Respiration is stepped so that energy is released in manageable amounts, captured as ATP, and controlled at multiple points rather than all at once. Each step is catalysed by a particular enzyme, and the regulation of those steps is what allows the cell to balance energy supply with demand.

Where each stage happens and what it produces

The pathway is a sequence of linked stages, each in a different place, and the location is part of the understanding. Glycolysis is cytoplasmic; the link reaction and Krebs cycle are in the mitochondrial matrix; oxidative phosphorylation is on the inner mitochondrial membrane. The products are also stage-specific, and the distinction between substrate-level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation is a recurring exam point.

  • 7.2 Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm. Glucose is phosphorylated using ATP, split into two trioses, and processed to pyruvate, producing a net gain of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, reduced NAD, and pyruvate itself. The reduced coenzyme is reduced NAD, not reduced FAD.
  • 7.3 The link reaction and Krebs cycle happen in the mitochondrial matrix. Pyruvate is decarboxylated and dehydrogenated to acetyl coenzyme A, releasing carbon dioxide and reduced NAD. In the Krebs cycle, the acetyl group is oxidised, releasing carbon dioxide by decarboxylation, producing ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, and generating reduced NAD and reduced FAD by dehydrogenation. The details of the intermediate compounds are not required, but the inputs and outputs and the location are — and it matters that these stages are mitochondrial, unlike glycolysis.
  • 7.4 Oxidative phosphorylation happens on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Electrons from reduced NAD and reduced FAD are passed along the electron transport chain; the energy released is used to pump protons into the intermembrane space, creating a proton gradient. Protons flow back through ATP synthase by chemiosmosis, and the energy of that flow phosphorylates ADP to ATP. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, and water is formed. The practical point is that chemiosmosis is the reason the gradient matters: it is not enough to make the gradient; the protons must flow through ATP synthase for ATP to be made.

A good answer distinguishes the two kinds of phosphorylation clearly: substrate-level phosphorylation transfers a phosphate directly from a reactive intermediate to ADP, as in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle; oxidative phosphorylation uses the proton gradient driven by the electron transport chain, as in chemiosmosis. Confusing the two is a common mark-loser.

Anaerobic respiration and the fate of lactate

When oxygen is absent, the pathway cannot use oxidative phosphorylation, so cells fall back on glycolysis and regenerate the oxidised coenzyme needed to keep it going by making lactate from pyruvate. Lactate is not the endpoint of the problem; it is a temporary solution, and the body deals with it later.

  • 7.5 After a period of anaerobic respiration in animals, accumulated lactate is transported in the blood to the liver, where part of it is oxidised back to pyruvate and then either converted to glucose or glycogen or respired aerobically. The oxygen required to do this is the oxygen debt. The point is that lactate is not simply “waste”; it is a temporary sink for pyruvate and reducing power, and its removal requires oxygen after the exercise has stopped.
  • A common exam mistake is to say that lactate is the same as lactic acid without being precise about the biochemistry, or to imply that anaerobic respiration produces the same ATP yield as aerobic. It does not: anaerobic respiration produces only the small net ATP from glycolysis, and the hydrogen from reduced NAD is disposed of by reducing pyruvate to lactate so that glycolysis can continue.

Respiratory quotient and the core practicals

The respiratory quotient, RQ, is the ratio of carbon dioxide produced to oxygen consumed, and it tells you something about the substrate being respired. This is one of the quantitative threads in the topic, and it links to the core practicals on respiration.

  • 7.6 RQ = volume of carbon dioxide produced ÷ volume of oxygen consumed. A carbohydrate has an RQ of about 1.0, a lipid about 0.7, and a protein about 0.9. The value is useful because it indicates which substrate is being used, and it can change as the organism shifts substrates.
  • 7.7 Core Practical 15 uses an artificial hydrogen carrier, such as a redox indicator, to investigate respiration in yeast. The indicator changes colour as it accepts hydrogen, so the time for the colour change reflects the rate of respiration. The important point is that the indicator is a proxy for the hydrogen released in respiration, and the rate is inferred from the time taken for the colour change.
  • 7.8 Core Practical 16 uses a simple respirometer to determine the rate of respiration and the RQ of a suitable material such as germinating seeds or small invertebrates. The respirometer measures oxygen consumption, and the comparison with carbon dioxide production — often by using a carbon dioxide absorbent such as soda lime — allows the RQ to be estimated.

Worked example: if an organism consumes 20 cm3 of oxygen and has an RQ of 0.85, the volume of carbon dioxide produced is RQ × volume of oxygen consumed = 0.85 × 20 = 17 cm3. The method is the same whichever numbers are given: state the formula, rearrange if needed, substitute, calculate.

Muscles, movement and the structure of skeletal muscle

Muscles do not work alone. They interact with tendons, the skeleton and ligaments to produce movement, and the structure of skeletal muscle is built to do this job in an orderly way. The slow-twitch and fast-twitch distinction is part of the structural and physiological comparison the specification expects.

  • 7.9 Movement involves antagonistic muscle pairs, extensors and flexors, with tendons attaching muscle to bone and ligaments attaching bone to bone. When one muscle in a pair contracts and the other relaxes, the bone moves; when the roles reverse, the bone moves back. This is why muscles are described as working in antagonistic pairs rather than in isolation.
  • 7.10 (i) A mammalian skeletal muscle fibre is a multinucleate cell containing many myofibrils. Each myofibril is made of repeating sarcomeres, the contractile units delimited by Z lines. The fibre has a plasma membrane called the sarcolemma, and the cytoplasm includes the sarcoplasmic reticulum, a specialised form of endoplasmic reticulum that stores calcium ions, and transverse tubules that conduct action potentials into the fibre.
  • 7.10 (ii) Slow-twitch fibres are adapted for endurance: they have high myoglobin content, many mitochondria, a dense capillary network, and rely on aerobic respiration. Fast-twitch fibres are adapted for short, intense bursts: they have fewer mitochondria, less myoglobin, a richer glycogen supply, and rely more on anaerobic glycolysis. The comparison is structural and functional: the same tissue type is specialised in two directions according to the job it does.

Muscle contraction: the sliding filament theory

Contraction is explained by the sliding filament theory, and the exam expects the sequence of steps, not just the names. The key idea is that the filaments slide past each other; they do not shorten.

  • 7.11 Contraction is driven by the sliding of actin and myosin filaments past each other, shortening the sarcomere without changing filament lengths. Calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and bind to troponin; this causes tropomyosin to move and expose the binding sites on actin. Myosin heads bind to the exposed sites, forming cross-bridges, and hydrolyse ATP via ATPase to power the power stroke, pulling the actin filaments toward the centre of the sarcomere. Fresh ATP binds to the myosin head to break the cross-bridge, and the cycle can repeat while calcium is present. ATP is needed for both the power stroke and the detachment of the myosin head; without ATP, the cross-bridge cannot be broken, which is part of what happens in rigor mortis.
  • The common mistake is to say that the actin and myosin filaments shorten during contraction. They do not; the sarcomere shortens because the filaments slide and the overlap increases. Another frequent error is to forget that ATP is needed to break the cross-bridge, not only to form it.

Cardiac muscle, the conduction system and the ECG

The heart is myogenic: its contraction is initiated within the muscle itself, not by nerves. The normal electrical pathway coordinates the timing of atrial and ventricular contraction, and the ECG is the surface record of that electrical activity. This is a physiology topic as much as a biochemistry one, and the tracing is a standard exam item.

  • 7.12 (i) Cardiac muscle is myogenic; it contracts because of an intrinsic electrical rhythm, not because a nerve tells it to every beat. The pacemaker is the sinoatrial node, SAN, in the right atrium.
  • 7.12 (ii) The electrical activity of the heart coordinates the heartbeat. The SAN sends waves of electrical excitation across the atria, causing atrial contraction. The atrioventricular node, AVN, delays the impulse before it passes down the bundle of His. The bundle of His and the Purkyne fibres conduct the excitation rapidly to the apex and up through the ventricular walls, causing coordinated ventricular contraction from the apex upward. The delay at the AVN is important because it lets the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract.
  • 7.12 (iii) The ECG records the electrical activity of the heart from the body surface. The P wave is atrial depolarisation; the QRS complex is ventricular depolarisation; and the T wave is ventricular repolarisation. These waves are used to diagnose abnormal rhythms such as tachycardia, bradycardia and fibrillation. The ECG does not record the mechanical contraction itself; it records the electrical events that lead to it.

A frequent confusion is to associate each ECG wave with a mechanical event rather than an electrical one. P is atrial depolarisation, not atrial contraction; QRS is ventricular depolarisation, not ventricular contraction; and the timing of the waves is what makes the diagnosis, so the exam question usually wants you to link the wave to the electrical event and, if asked, to the mechanical consequence.

Cardiac output, ventilation and exercise

Exercise increases the demand for oxygen and the need to remove carbon dioxide, and both are met by changes in ventilation and cardiac output. The control centres in the medulla oblongata coordinate these changes, and the hormones and receptors involved are part of the picture.

  • 7.13 (i) Cardiac output is the volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute, calculated as heart rate × stroke volume. The formula is simple, but it means you can reason about how the two components change during exercise: heart rate goes up, and stroke volume can go up as well, so cardiac output rises by both routes.
  • 7.13 (ii) Ventilation and cardiac output change together during exercise to deliver oxygen faster and remove carbon dioxide faster. The heart rate and ventilation rate are controlled by the cardiovascular control centre and the ventilation centre in the medulla oblongata, which respond to changes in blood pH, carbon dioxide concentration and blood pressure detected by chemoreceptors and baroreceptors. The point is that the control is not just “exercise makes the heart beat faster”; it is that chemical and pressure changes in the blood are detected and used to adjust both ventilation and circulation.

Worked example: if a person has a tidal volume of 0.5 dm3 and a breathing rate of 14 breaths per minute, the respiratory minute ventilation is tidal volume × breathing rate = 0.5 × 14 = 7.0 dm3 min−1. The calculation is the same pattern as the cardiac output one: a rate multiplied by a volume per beat.

Adrenaline and spirometric measurements

Adrenaline is part of the fight or flight response, and spirometer traces are the practical source of data on lung volumes during exercise. The hormone side and the measurement side are separate enough to be learned separately, but they both appear in this topic.

  • 7.14 Adrenaline is released from the adrenal glands in the fight or flight response. It binds to receptors on target cells and activates second messenger systems, often via cyclic AMP, that prepare the body for intense activity: heart rate increases, bronchioles dilate, and blood flow is redirected from non-essential organs toward skeletal muscles. The second messenger detail is the reason one hormone can have several coordinated effects: the same signal is amplified inside different target cells.
  • 7.15 Core Practical 17 uses spirometer traces to investigate the effects of exercise on tidal volume, breathing rate, respiratory minute ventilation and oxygen consumption. Tidal volume is the volume of air moved in one breath; respiratory minute ventilation is tidal volume × breathing rate; and oxygen consumption can be derived from the spirometer trace, for example by measuring the uptake of oxygen over time. The point is to use the data to calculate the relevant volumes and rates, not just to describe what a spirometer is.

Negative feedback, positive feedback and homeostasis

Control systems in the body often use negative feedback, and a few use positive feedback. Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment, and thermoregulation is a classic example of how this is done during a challenge such as exercise.

  • 7.16 (i) Negative feedback is a control mechanism in which a change from the set point is detected and a response is made that opposes the change, bringing the variable back within narrow limits. Positive feedback amplifies the initial change away from the set point; examples include the generation of action potentials in neurones and the release of oxytocin during birth. The distinction is that negative feedback reduces the deviation, while positive feedback increases it.
  • 7.16 (ii) Negative feedback works by keeping a system within narrow limits: a sensor detects the change, a coordination centre processes it, and effectors bring about a corrective response. The principle is general and applies to temperature, blood glucose and plasma concentration as well as to many other regulated variables.
  • 7.17 Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment despite external fluctuations, and it is important during exercise, when heat, carbon dioxide and metabolic changes challenge the internal state. The hypothalamus is the body’s thermoregulation centre; it monitors core blood temperature via internal thermoreceptors and coordinates responses such as vasodilation, vasoconstriction, sweating, shivering and behavioural changes to keep the temperature within a suitable range. Exercise is a useful context because it stresses the system and makes the control responses visible.

Kidney structure and the production and removal of urea

The kidney is the central organ of osmoregulation and excretion in mammals. Its gross and microscopic structure matters because it determines what can be filtered and what can be reabsorbed, and urea production links protein metabolism to excretion.

  • 7.18 The gross structure of the mammalian kidney includes the outer cortex, the inner medulla, the pelvis, the ureter, and the renal artery and vein. The functional unit is the nephron, which includes the Bowman’s capsule, the proximal convoluted tubule, the loop of Henle, the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct. The microscopic structure is what makes the processing of the filtrate possible: each region has a different role in reabsorption, secretion and concentration.
  • 7.19 Urea is produced in the liver from excess amino acids by deamination; the details of the ornithine cycle are not required, but the principle is that amino groups are removed from amino acids and the nitrogen is converted to urea for safe excretion. Urea is then removed from the blood by ultrafiltration in the Bowman’s capsule, where high hydrostatic pressure in the glomerulus forces water and small solutes out of the blood into the capsule, with the basement membrane acting as a filter. The difference in diameter between the afferent and efferent arterioles helps generate that pressure.

Reabsorption and the loop of Henle

Ultrafiltration is only the first step. The filtrate is then modified by selective reabsorption, and the loop of Henle is what makes the kidney able to produce concentrated urine. This is a long-standing exam topic because the countercurrent multiplier is conceptually demanding but very testable.

  • 7.20 In the proximal convoluted tubule, essential solutes such as glucose, amino acids and mineral ions are selectively reabsorbed into the blood by active transport and cotransport, and water follows by osmosis because the movement of solutes lowers the water potential of the surrounding tissue fluid. The microvilli on the tubule cells increase surface area for this reabsorption.
  • 7.20 The loop of Henle acts as a countercurrent multiplier. Sodium and chloride ions are actively pumped out of the ascending limb into the medulla, lowering the water potential there. The descending limb is permeable to water, so water moves out by osmosis. Because the two limbs run in opposite directions — the countercurrent arrangement — the effect is multiplied down the length of the loop, establishing a steep concentration gradient in the medulla. This gradient is what allows water to be reabsorbed later from the collecting duct when ADH is present. A common mistake is to say the loop pumps water out; it does not pump water, it pumps ions and lets water follow by osmosis.

ADH and the control of plasma concentration and blood volume

The final control loop in osmoregulation is hormonal. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect changes in blood water potential, and the result is the release of antidiuretic hormone, which adjusts water reabsorption in the collecting duct. The sequence matters, because exams often ask you to trace it step by step.

  • 7.21 When blood water potential drops, osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect this and the posterior pituitary gland releases ADH. ADH travels in the blood to the kidneys, where it increases the permeability of the collecting duct cells to water by promoting the insertion of aquaporins. More water is then reabsorbed by osmosis, so the urine becomes more concentrated and blood water potential and blood volume are restored by negative feedback. The sequence is important: fall in water potential, detected by osmoreceptors, ADH released from posterior pituitary, collecting duct becomes more permeable, water reabsorbed, blood water potential rises.

Gene control by transcription factors and hormones

The topic ends with gene control, which is a bridge to later material. Transcription factors are the proteins that switch genes on or off in response to signals, and the contrast between peptide and steroid hormones is a good way to see how different signals reach the genome.

  • 7.22 Genes can be switched on and off by DNA transcription factors, proteins that bind to specific base sequences and either promote or block the binding of RNA polymerase. Peptide hormones act extracellularly: they bind to cell-surface receptors and trigger second messenger cascades that affect transcription factors indirectly. Steroid hormones are lipid-soluble, pass through the phospholipid bilayer, bind to intracellular receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus, and the hormone-receptor complex itself acts as a transcription factor to switch genes on or off. The contrast is that peptide hormones signal from the surface via second messengers, while steroid hormones enter the cell and act more directly on the genome.

How the topic fits together

The topic is a bridge between biochemistry and physiology. Respiration releases energy as ATP; muscles use that ATP to contract; the heart and breathing adjust to meet demand during exercise; and the kidney keeps the internal environment stable while the genes that control these processes are themselves regulated by transcription factors and hormones. The thread is that energy supply, movement, circulation, and internal stability are connected, and that hormone and nerve control coordinate them.

  • Start with the energy: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, the link reaction and Krebs cycle in the matrix, oxidative phosphorylation on the inner membrane, with oxygen as the final electron acceptor.
  • Add the anaerobic fallback: lactate from pyruvate, and the later oxygen debt paid in the liver.
  • Add the measurement: RQ, the redox-indicator and respirometer practicals.
  • Add the movement: antagonistic pairs, muscle fibre structure, slow versus fast twitch, the sliding filament theory, calcium and ATP.
  • Add the circulation: myogenic heartbeat, the SAN-AVN-bundle of His-Purkyne pathway, the ECG waves, cardiac output and the control centres.
  • Add the breathing and hormones: ventilation and cardiac output during exercise, adrenaline and the fight or flight response, spirometer measurements.
  • Add the internal environment: negative and positive feedback, homeostasis, thermoregulation and the hypothalamus.
  • Add the kidney: structure, ultrafiltration, selective reabsorption, the countercurrent multiplier, and ADH control of plasma concentration and blood volume.
  • End with gene control: transcription factors, and the difference between peptide and steroid hormone mechanisms.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying the filaments shorten during contraction: they slide, and the sarcomere shortens because the overlap increases.
  • Forgetting that ATP is needed to break the myosin cross-bridge, not only to power the stroke.
  • Confusing substrate-level and oxidative phosphorylation: one is direct phosphate transfer, the other uses the proton gradient.
  • Saying the light-dependent reactions occur in respiration, or the Krebs cycle in the cytoplasm: the location of each stage matters.
  • Saying lactate is simply waste: it is a temporary product, and its removal is part of the oxygen debt.
  • Mismatching ECG waves: P is atrial depolarisation, QRS is ventricular depolarisation, T is ventricular repolarisation — not mechanical events.
  • Saying the heart is neurgenic: it is myogenic, initiated by the SAN.
  • Forgetting the AVN delay: without it the atria and ventricles would contract at the same time.
  • Saying the loop of Henle pumps water out: it pumps ions out and lets water follow by osmosis.
  • Missing the ADH sequence: osmoreceptors detect, posterior pituitary releases ADH, collecting duct permeability increases, water is reabsorbed.
  • Confusing peptide and steroid hormone mechanisms: peptide acts at the surface via second messengers; steroid enters the cell and acts on transcription more directly.

Exam-style questions

  1. Describe the roles of glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle in aerobic respiration, and state where each occurs. Answer: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and phosphorylates glucose, producing pyruvate, ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and reduced NAD. The link reaction occurs in the mitochondrial matrix and converts pyruvate to acetyl coenzyme A by decarboxylation and dehydrogenation, releasing carbon dioxide and reduced NAD. The Krebs cycle occurs in the matrix and oxidises the acetyl group, releasing carbon dioxide, producing ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and generating reduced NAD and reduced FAD by dehydrogenation. (6 marks)
  2. Explain how ATP is synthesised by chemiosmosis during oxidative phosphorylation. Answer: Electrons from reduced NAD and reduced FAD pass along the electron transport chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane, releasing energy that pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, creating a proton gradient. Protons flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase, and the energy of this flow phosphorylates ADP to ATP. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and water is formed. (5 marks)
  3. Describe the sliding filament theory of muscle contraction. Answer: Calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and bind to troponin, moving tropomyosin and exposing binding sites on actin. Myosin heads bind to actin to form cross-bridges, and ATP hydrolysis by ATPase powers the power stroke, pulling actin toward the centre of the sarcomere. Fresh ATP binds to the myosin head, breaking the cross-bridge, and the cycle repeats. The filaments do not shorten; the sarcomere shortens because the filaments slide past each other. (5 marks)
  4. Describe the cardiac cycle’s electrical conduction and relate it to the ECG. Answer: The SAN sends electrical excitation across the atria, causing atrial contraction; the AVN delays the impulse before it passes down the bundle of His and Purkyne fibres to the ventricles, causing coordinated ventricular contraction from the apex. The P wave is atrial depolarisation, the QRS complex is ventricular depolarisation, and the T wave is ventricular repolarisation. (5 marks)
  5. Explain how the loop of Henle acts as a countercurrent multiplier to produce concentrated urine. Answer: Sodium and chloride ions are actively pumped out of the ascending limb into the medulla, lowering the water potential there; the descending limb is permeable to water, so water moves out by osmosis. The opposing flow of the two limbs multiplies the concentration gradient down the loop, establishing a steep gradient in the medulla that allows water to be reabsorbed later from the collecting duct when ADH is present. (5 marks)
  6. Explain the control of cardiac output and ventilation during exercise. Answer: During exercise, chemoreceptors and baroreceptors detect changes in blood pH, carbon dioxide and pressure; the cardiovascular and ventilation centres in the medulla oblongata increase heart rate and breathing rate, so cardiac output and minute ventilation rise to deliver oxygen faster and remove carbon dioxide faster. Adrenaline also contributes by increasing heart rate. (5 marks)
  7. Distinguish between negative and positive feedback and give one example of each. Answer: Negative feedback reverses a deviation from the set point, e.g. thermoregulation by the hypothalamus; positive feedback amplifies a deviation, e.g. oxytocin release during labour or action potential generation in neurones. (4 marks)
  8. Compare the action of peptide and steroid hormones in controlling gene transcription. Answer: Peptide hormones are water-soluble, bind to cell-surface receptors, and act via second messenger cascades that affect transcription factors indirectly. Steroid hormones are lipid-soluble, cross the cell membrane, bind to intracellular receptors, and the hormone-receptor complex acts directly as a transcription factor to switch target genes on or off. (5 marks)

Use this summary to place each part of the topic before you go into the detail in the full notes. Revise the respiratory stages and their locations, the difference between substrate-level and oxidative phosphorylation, the lactate fate and RQ, the muscle and heart physiology with the ECG, the exercise control loops, the kidney’s ultrafiltration, reabsorption and countercurrent multiplier, the ADH sequence, and the transcription-factor control of genes. Then move on to Topic 8: Coordination, Response and Gene Technology.
content:
Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment — Quick Revision Summary

This is the fast map of Edexcel International A2 Biology WBI15 Topic 7. It follows the same order as the full notes so you can cross-reference, and it repeats the specification numbers so you can see which paragraph exists for which point. Use it to organise the topic, not to replace the notes. The topic divides into four blocks: the biochemistry of respiration and the fate of lactate, the physiology of muscles and the heart, the control of breathing and circulation in exercise, and the kidney and homeostasis with gene control at the end.

Aerobic respiration: the overall reaction and the stepped pathway

Respiration is how cells release energy from organic substrates and store it as ATP. The overall aerobic reaction is the shorthand: glucose and oxygen yield carbon dioxide, water and a large amount of energy. The important conceptual point is that the pathway is stepped and enzyme-controlled, not a single fire, and that each step is carried out by a specific intracellular enzyme. The names of the individual enzymes are not required, but the sequence and the location of each stage are.

  • 7.1 (i) Aerobic respiration is the splitting of the respiratory substrate, releasing carbon dioxide as a waste product and reuniting hydrogen with atmospheric oxygen, with the release of a large amount of energy. It is a stepped process, each step enzyme-controlled, and the names of specific enzymes are not required.
  • 7.1 (ii) Respiration is stepped so that energy is released in manageable amounts, captured as ATP, and controlled at multiple points rather than all at once. Each step is catalysed by a particular enzyme, and the regulation of those steps is what allows the cell to balance energy supply with demand.

Where each stage happens and what it produces

The pathway is a sequence of linked stages, each in a different place, and the location is part of the understanding. Glycolysis is cytoplasmic; the link reaction and Krebs cycle are in the mitochondrial matrix; oxidative phosphorylation is on the inner mitochondrial membrane. The products are also stage-specific, and the distinction between substrate-level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation is a recurring exam point.

  • 7.2 Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm. Glucose is phosphorylated using ATP, split into two trioses, and processed to pyruvate, producing a net gain of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, reduced NAD, and pyruvate itself. The reduced coenzyme is reduced NAD, not reduced FAD.
  • 7.3 The link reaction and Krebs cycle happen in the mitochondrial matrix. Pyruvate is decarboxylated and dehydrogenated to acetyl coenzyme A, releasing carbon dioxide and reduced NAD. In the Krebs cycle, the acetyl group is oxidised, releasing carbon dioxide by decarboxylation, producing ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, and generating reduced NAD and reduced FAD by dehydrogenation. The details of the intermediate compounds are not required, but the inputs and outputs and the location are — and it matters that these stages are mitochondrial, unlike glycolysis.
  • 7.4 Oxidative phosphorylation happens on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Electrons from reduced NAD and reduced FAD are passed along the electron transport chain; the energy released is used to pump protons into the intermembrane space, creating a proton gradient. Protons flow back through ATP synthase by chemiosmosis, and the energy of that flow phosphorylates ADP to ATP. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, and water is formed. The practical point is that chemiosmosis is the reason the gradient matters: it is not enough to make the gradient; the protons must flow through ATP synthase for ATP to be made.

A good answer distinguishes the two kinds of phosphorylation clearly: substrate-level phosphorylation transfers a phosphate directly from a reactive intermediate to ADP, as in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle; oxidative phosphorylation uses the proton gradient driven by the electron transport chain, as in chemiosmosis. Confusing the two is a common mark-loser.

Anaerobic respiration and the fate of lactate

When oxygen is absent, the pathway cannot use oxidative phosphorylation, so cells fall back on glycolysis and regenerate the oxidised coenzyme needed to keep it going by making lactate from pyruvate. Lactate is not the endpoint of the problem; it is a temporary solution, and the body deals with it later.

  • 7.5 After a period of anaerobic respiration in animals, accumulated lactate is transported in the blood to the liver, where part of it is oxidised back to pyruvate and then either converted to glucose or glycogen or respired aerobically. The oxygen required to do this is the oxygen debt. The point is that lactate is not simply “waste”; it is a temporary sink for pyruvate and reducing power, and its removal requires oxygen after the exercise has stopped.
  • A common exam mistake is to say that lactate is the same as lactic acid without being precise about the biochemistry, or to imply that anaerobic respiration produces the same ATP yield as aerobic. It does not: anaerobic respiration produces only the small net ATP from glycolysis, and the hydrogen from reduced NAD is disposed of by reducing pyruvate to lactate so that glycolysis can continue.

Respiratory quotient and the core practicals

The respiratory quotient, RQ, is the ratio of carbon dioxide produced to oxygen consumed, and it tells you something about the substrate being respired. This is one of the quantitative threads in the topic, and it links to the core practicals on respiration.

  • 7.6 RQ = volume of carbon dioxide produced ÷ volume of oxygen consumed. A carbohydrate has an RQ of about 1.0, a lipid about 0.7, and a protein about 0.9. The value is useful because it indicates which substrate is being used, and it can change as the organism shifts substrates.
  • 7.7 Core Practical 15 uses an artificial hydrogen carrier, such as a redox indicator, to investigate respiration in yeast. The indicator changes colour as it accepts hydrogen, so the time for the colour change reflects the rate of respiration. The important point is that the indicator is a proxy for the hydrogen released in respiration, and the rate is inferred from the time taken for the colour change.
  • 7.8 Core Practical 16 uses a simple respirometer to determine the rate of respiration and the RQ of a suitable material such as germinating seeds or small invertebrates. The respirometer measures oxygen consumption, and the comparison with carbon dioxide production — often by using a carbon dioxide absorbent such as soda lime — allows the RQ to be estimated.

Worked example: if an organism consumes 20 cm3 of oxygen and has an RQ of 0.85, the volume of carbon dioxide produced is RQ × volume of oxygen consumed = 0.85 × 20 = 17 cm3. The method is the same whichever numbers are given: state the formula, rearrange if needed, substitute, calculate.

Muscles, movement and the structure of skeletal muscle

Muscles do not work alone. They interact with tendons, the skeleton and ligaments to produce movement, and the structure of skeletal muscle is built to do this job in an orderly way. The slow-twitch and fast-twitch distinction is part of the structural and physiological comparison the specification expects.

  • 7.9 Movement involves antagonistic muscle pairs, extensors and flexors, with tendons attaching muscle to bone and ligaments attaching bone to bone. When one muscle in a pair contracts and the other relaxes, the bone moves; when the roles reverse, the bone moves back. This is why muscles are described as working in antagonistic pairs rather than in isolation.
  • 7.10 (i) A mammalian skeletal muscle fibre is a multinucleate cell containing many myofibrils. Each myofibril is made of repeating sarcomeres, the contractile units delimited by Z lines. The fibre has a plasma membrane called the sarcolemma, and the cytoplasm includes the sarcoplasmic reticulum, a specialised form of endoplasmic reticulum that stores calcium ions, and transverse tubules that conduct action potentials into the fibre.
  • 7.10 (ii) Slow-twitch fibres are adapted for endurance: they have high myoglobin content, many mitochondria, a dense capillary network, and rely on aerobic respiration. Fast-twitch fibres are adapted for short, intense bursts: they have fewer mitochondria, less myoglobin, a richer glycogen supply, and rely more on anaerobic glycolysis. The comparison is structural and functional: the same tissue type is specialised in two directions according to the job it does.

Muscle contraction: the sliding filament theory

Contraction is explained by the sliding filament theory, and the exam expects the sequence of steps, not just the names. The key idea is that the filaments slide past each other; they do not shorten.

  • 7.11 Contraction is driven by the sliding of actin and myosin filaments past each other, shortening the sarcomere without changing filament lengths. Calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and bind to troponin; this causes tropomyosin to move and expose the binding sites on actin. Myosin heads bind to the exposed sites, forming cross-bridges, and hydrolyse ATP via ATPase to power the power stroke, pulling the actin filaments toward the centre of the sarcomere. Fresh ATP binds to the myosin head to break the cross-bridge, and the cycle can repeat while calcium is present. ATP is needed for both the power stroke and the detachment of the myosin head; without ATP, the cross-bridge cannot be broken, which is part of what happens in rigor mortis.
  • The common mistake is to say that the actin and myosin filaments shorten during contraction. They do not; the sarcomere shortens because the filaments slide and the overlap increases. Another frequent error is to forget that ATP is needed to break the cross-bridge, not only to form it.

Cardiac muscle, the conduction system and the ECG

The heart is myogenic: its contraction is initiated within the muscle itself, not by nerves. The normal electrical pathway coordinates the timing of atrial and ventricular contraction, and the ECG is the surface record of that electrical activity. This is a physiology topic as much as a biochemistry one, and the tracing is a standard exam item.

  • 7.12 (i) Cardiac muscle is myogenic; it contracts because of an intrinsic electrical rhythm, not because a nerve tells it to every beat. The pacemaker is the sinoatrial node, SAN, in the right atrium.
  • 7.12 (ii) The electrical activity of the heart coordinates the heartbeat. The SAN sends waves of electrical excitation across the atria, causing atrial contraction. The atrioventricular node, AVN, delays the impulse before it passes down the bundle of His. The bundle of His and the Purkyne fibres conduct the excitation rapidly to the apex and up through the ventricular walls, causing coordinated ventricular contraction from the apex upward. The delay at the AVN is important because it lets the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract.
  • 7.12 (iii) The ECG records the electrical activity of the heart from the body surface. The P wave is atrial depolarisation; the QRS complex is ventricular depolarisation; and the T wave is ventricular repolarisation. These waves are used to diagnose abnormal rhythms such as tachycardia, bradycardia and fibrillation. The ECG does not record the mechanical contraction itself; it records the electrical events that lead to it.

A frequent confusion is to associate each ECG wave with a mechanical event rather than an electrical one. P is atrial depolarisation, not atrial contraction; QRS is ventricular depolarisation, not ventricular contraction; and the timing of the waves is what makes the diagnosis, so the exam question usually wants you to link the wave to the electrical event and, if asked, to the mechanical consequence.

Cardiac output, ventilation and exercise

Exercise increases the demand for oxygen and the need to remove carbon dioxide, and both are met by changes in ventilation and cardiac output. The control centres in the medulla oblongata coordinate these changes, and the hormones and receptors involved are part of the picture.

  • 7.13 (i) Cardiac output is the volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute, calculated as heart rate × stroke volume. The formula is simple, but it means you can reason about how the two components change during exercise: heart rate goes up, and stroke volume can go up as well, so cardiac output rises by both routes.
  • 7.13 (ii) Ventilation and cardiac output change together during exercise to deliver oxygen faster and remove carbon dioxide faster. The heart rate and ventilation rate are controlled by the cardiovascular control centre and the ventilation centre in the medulla oblongata, which respond to changes in blood pH, carbon dioxide concentration and blood pressure detected by chemoreceptors and baroreceptors. The point is that the control is not just “exercise makes the heart beat faster”; it is that chemical and pressure changes in the blood are detected and used to adjust both ventilation and circulation.

Worked example: if a person has a tidal volume of 0.5 dm3 and a breathing rate of 14 breaths per minute, the respiratory minute ventilation is tidal volume × breathing rate = 0.5 × 14 = 7.0 dm3 min−1. The calculation is the same pattern as the cardiac output one: a rate multiplied by a volume per beat.

Adrenaline and spirometric measurements

Adrenaline is part of the fight or flight response, and spirometer traces are the practical source of data on lung volumes during exercise. The hormone side and the measurement side are separate enough to be learned separately, but they both appear in this topic.

  • 7.14 Adrenaline is released from the adrenal glands in the fight or flight response. It binds to receptors on target cells and activates second messenger systems, often via cyclic AMP, that prepare the body for intense activity: heart rate increases, bronchioles dilate, and blood flow is redirected from non-essential organs toward skeletal muscles. The second messenger detail is the reason one hormone can have several coordinated effects: the same signal is amplified inside different target cells.
  • 7.15 Core Practical 17 uses spirometer traces to investigate the effects of exercise on tidal volume, breathing rate, respiratory minute ventilation and oxygen consumption. Tidal volume is the volume of air moved in one breath; respiratory minute ventilation is tidal volume × breathing rate; and oxygen consumption can be derived from the spirometer trace, for example by measuring the uptake of oxygen over time. The point is to use the data to calculate the relevant volumes and rates, not just to describe what a spirometer is.

Negative feedback, positive feedback and homeostasis

Control systems in the body often use negative feedback, and a few use positive feedback. Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment, and thermoregulation is a classic example of how this is done during a challenge such as exercise.

  • 7.16 (i) Negative feedback is a control mechanism in which a change from the set point is detected and a response is made that opposes the change, bringing the variable back within narrow limits. Positive feedback amplifies the initial change away from the set point; examples include the generation of action potentials in neurones and the release of oxytocin during birth. The distinction is that negative feedback reduces the deviation, while positive feedback increases it.
  • 7.16 (ii) Negative feedback works by keeping a system within narrow limits: a sensor detects the change, a coordination centre processes it, and effectors bring about a corrective response. The principle is general and applies to temperature, blood glucose and plasma concentration as well as to many other regulated variables.
  • 7.17 Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment despite external fluctuations, and it is important during exercise, when heat, carbon dioxide and metabolic changes challenge the internal state. The hypothalamus is the body’s thermoregulation centre; it monitors core blood temperature via internal thermoreceptors and coordinates responses such as vasodilation, vasoconstriction, sweating, shivering and behavioural changes to keep the temperature within a suitable range. Exercise is a useful context because it stresses the system and makes the control responses visible.

Kidney structure and the production and removal of urea

The kidney is the central organ of osmoregulation and excretion in mammals. Its gross and microscopic structure matters because it determines what can be filtered and what can be reabsorbed, and urea production links protein metabolism to excretion.

  • 7.18 The gross structure of the mammalian kidney includes the outer cortex, the inner medulla, the pelvis, the ureter, and the renal artery and vein. The functional unit is the nephron, which includes the Bowman’s capsule, the proximal convoluted tubule, the loop of Henle, the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct. The microscopic structure is what makes the processing of the filtrate possible: each region has a different role in reabsorption, secretion and concentration.
  • 7.19 Urea is produced in the liver from excess amino acids by deamination; the details of the ornithine cycle are not required, but the principle is that amino groups are removed from amino acids and the nitrogen is converted to urea for safe excretion. Urea is then removed from the blood by ultrafiltration in the Bowman’s capsule, where high hydrostatic pressure in the glomerulus forces water and small solutes out of the blood into the capsule, with the basement membrane acting as a filter. The difference in diameter between the afferent and efferent arterioles helps generate that pressure.

Reabsorption and the loop of Henle

Ultrafiltration is only the first step. The filtrate is then modified by selective reabsorption, and the loop of Henle is what makes the kidney able to produce concentrated urine. This is a long-standing exam topic because the countercurrent multiplier is conceptually demanding but very testable.

  • 7.20 In the proximal convoluted tubule, essential solutes such as glucose, amino acids and mineral ions are selectively reabsorbed into the blood by active transport and cotransport, and water follows by osmosis because the movement of solutes lowers the water potential of the surrounding tissue fluid. The microvilli on the tubule cells increase surface area for this reabsorption.
  • 7.20 The loop of Henle acts as a countercurrent multiplier. Sodium and chloride ions are actively pumped out of the ascending limb into the medulla, lowering the water potential there. The descending limb is permeable to water, so water moves out by osmosis. Because the two limbs run in opposite directions — the countercurrent arrangement — the effect is multiplied down the length of the loop, establishing a steep concentration gradient in the medulla. This gradient is what allows water to be reabsorbed later from the collecting duct when ADH is present. A common mistake is to say the loop pumps water out; it does not pump water, it pumps ions and lets water follow by osmosis.

ADH and the control of plasma concentration and blood volume

The final control loop in osmoregulation is hormonal. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect changes in blood water potential, and the result is the release of antidiuretic hormone, which adjusts water reabsorption in the collecting duct. The sequence matters, because exams often ask you to trace it step by step.

  • 7.21 When blood water potential drops, osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect this and the posterior pituitary gland releases ADH. ADH travels in the blood to the kidneys, where it increases the permeability of the collecting duct cells to water by promoting the insertion of aquaporins. More water is then reabsorbed by osmosis, so the urine becomes more concentrated and blood water potential and blood volume are restored by negative feedback. The sequence is important: fall in water potential, detected by osmoreceptors, ADH released from posterior pituitary, collecting duct becomes more permeable, water reabsorbed, blood water potential rises.

Gene control by transcription factors and hormones

The topic ends with gene control, which is a bridge to later material. Transcription factors are the proteins that switch genes on or off in response to signals, and the contrast between peptide and steroid hormones is a good way to see how different signals reach the genome.

  • 7.22 Genes can be switched on and off by DNA transcription factors, proteins that bind to specific base sequences and either promote or block the binding of RNA polymerase. Peptide hormones act extracellularly: they bind to cell-surface receptors and trigger second messenger cascades that affect transcription factors indirectly. Steroid hormones are lipid-soluble, pass through the phospholipid bilayer, bind to intracellular receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus, and the hormone-receptor complex itself acts as a transcription factor to switch genes on or off. The contrast is that peptide hormones signal from the surface via second messengers, while steroid hormones enter the cell and act more directly on the genome.

How the topic fits together

The topic is a bridge between biochemistry and physiology. Respiration releases energy as ATP; muscles use that ATP to contract; the heart and breathing adjust to meet demand during exercise; and the kidney keeps the internal environment stable while the genes that control these processes are themselves regulated by transcription factors and hormones. The thread is that energy supply, movement, circulation, and internal stability are connected, and that hormone and nerve control coordinate them.

  • Start with the energy: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, the link reaction and Krebs cycle in the matrix, oxidative phosphorylation on the inner membrane, with oxygen as the final electron acceptor.
  • Add the anaerobic fallback: lactate from pyruvate, and the later oxygen debt paid in the liver.
  • Add the measurement: RQ, the redox-indicator and respirometer practicals.
  • Add the movement: antagonistic pairs, muscle fibre structure, slow versus fast twitch, the sliding filament theory, calcium and ATP.
  • Add the circulation: myogenic heartbeat, the SAN-AVN-bundle of His-Purkyne pathway, the ECG waves, cardiac output and the control centres.
  • Add the breathing and hormones: ventilation and cardiac output during exercise, adrenaline and the fight or flight response, spirometer measurements.
  • Add the internal environment: negative and positive feedback, homeostasis, thermoregulation and the hypothalamus.
  • Add the kidney: structure, ultrafiltration, selective reabsorption, the countercurrent multiplier, and ADH control of plasma concentration and blood volume.
  • End with gene control: transcription factors, and the difference between peptide and steroid hormone mechanisms.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying the filaments shorten during contraction: they slide, and the sarcomere shortens because the overlap increases.
  • Forgetting that ATP is needed to break the myosin cross-bridge, not only to power the stroke.
  • Confusing substrate-level and oxidative phosphorylation: one is direct phosphate transfer, the other uses the proton gradient.
  • Saying the light-dependent reactions occur in respiration, or the Krebs cycle in the cytoplasm: the location of each stage matters.
  • Saying lactate is simply waste: it is a temporary product, and its removal is part of the oxygen debt.
  • Mismatching ECG waves: P is atrial depolarisation, QRS is ventricular depolarisation, T is ventricular repolarisation — not mechanical events.
  • Saying the heart is neurgenic: it is myogenic, initiated by the SAN.
  • Forgetting the AVN delay: without it the atria and ventricles would contract at the same time.
  • Saying the loop of Henle pumps water out: it pumps ions out and lets water follow by osmosis.
  • Missing the ADH sequence: osmoreceptors detect, posterior pituitary releases ADH, collecting duct permeability increases, water is reabsorbed.
  • Confusing peptide and steroid hormone mechanisms: peptide acts at the surface via second messengers; steroid enters the cell and acts on transcription more directly.
