content:
Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics

Edexcel IAL Biology 9BI0 A2, topic 6. Every statement 6.1 to 6.20 is covered below, with its code in the heading. The topic links three big ideas: how microorganisms are grown and measured, how the body defends itself and why pathogens keep finding ways around those defences, and how DNA techniques are used to identify organisms and people.

6.1: Culturing microorganisms with aseptic technique

  • Aseptic technique keeps a culture pure: only the wanted microorganism grows. Sterilise media and equipment first, usually in an autoclave at 121 °C under pressure for about 15 minutes.
  • Work close to a Bunsen flame, flame the inoculating loop until red-hot before and after use, keep Petri dish lids mostly closed, and never pipette by mouth.
  • Incubate cultures inverted at a safe temperature, usually 25 °C for school work, so condensation does not drip onto the agar.

6.2: Measuring the growth of microorganisms

  • Direct cell counts: use a haemocytometer (counting chamber) under a microscope, counting cells in a known volume to get the number per cm³.
  • Viable counts by dilution plating: make a serial dilution, spread known volumes on agar, incubate, and count colonies on plates with about 30 to 300 colonies. Each colony is assumed to grow from one viable cell, so the count shows living cells only.
  • Mass methods: measure the dry mass of cells collected by centrifuging or filtering a known volume of culture.
  • Optical methods (turbidity): a colorimeter or spectrophotometer measures how much light the cloudy culture absorbs. Absorbance rises with cell density, so a calibration curve converts it to cell numbers.

6.3: The bacterial growth curve and the growth rate constant

  • Lag phase: cells adapt to the medium and synthesise enzymes; there is little or no division.
  • Exponential (log) phase: cells divide at a constant rate, so the population doubles each generation. N = N₀ × 2ⁿ, where n is the number of doublings.
  • Stationary phase: births equal deaths, because nutrients run short and waste builds up.
  • Death phase: deaths exceed births and the population falls.
  • Growth rate constant: in exponential growth N = N₀eᵏᵗ. So k = (ln N₂ − ln N₁) ÷ (t₂ − t₁). Plotting ln N against time gives a straight line whose gradient is k.

6.4: Core practical 13: growth of microorganisms in liquid culture

  • Inoculate a sterile liquid medium, take samples at regular intervals, and measure turbidity or cell count each time.
  • Plot the results to show the four phases of the curve, then calculate the exponential growth rate constant from the straight-line part.
  • Safe and ethical use: use only non-pathogenic strains, keep the culture closed, disinfect the bench, and autoclave all used material before disposal.

6.5: Structure of bacteria and viruses

  • Bacteria are cells with a cell wall (peptidoglycan), cell membrane, cytoplasm with ribosomes, and a circular DNA loop, often with plasmids. They have no nucleus.
  • Viruses are not cells. They have a nucleic acid core, either DNA or RNA, surrounded by a protein capsid. Some also have a lipid envelope taken from the host.
  • Comparisons: Ebola virus has single-stranded RNA and an envelope. Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) has single-stranded RNA in a helical capsid, with no envelope. HIV has two RNA strands, reverse transcriptase and an envelope. Lambda phage, a virus of bacteria, has double-stranded DNA in a head with a tail and no envelope.
  • Lytic cycle: the virus takes over the host cell, makes new viruses, and the cell bursts (lyses) to release them.
  • Latency: the viral genome stays in the host cell without producing new viruses, and can become active later.

6.6: How Mycobacterium tuberculosis and HIV infect human cells

  • Tuberculosis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is inhaled into the alveoli. Macrophages engulf it, but the bacterium survives inside them and multiplies. The body forms granulomas (tubercles) around the infection, and the lung tissue is destroyed. Symptoms include a persistent cough, fever, night sweats and weight loss. If untreated it can be fatal.
  • HIV: the virus binds to CD4 receptors and a co-receptor on helper T cells. Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from its RNA, which is inserted into the host genome. New viruses bud from the cell. The helper T cell population falls, so the immune system fails and opportunistic infections and cancers take hold (AIDS).

6.7: Routes of entry and barriers

  • Routes: inhalation (airborne droplets), ingestion (contaminated food and water), contact through broken skin or wounds, sexual contact, and vectors such as mosquitoes.
  • Barriers: intact skin (keratin, dryness, and the skin flora that competes with pathogens), stomach acid (pH about 2, which kills many ingested microbes), and gut flora that competes for space and nutrients. Mucus and cilia in the airways trap and move pathogens out.

6.8: Non-specific responses to infection

  • Inflammation: damaged cells release chemicals such as histamine, which dilate blood vessels and make them leaky. The area becomes red, hot and swollen, and white blood cells are recruited to the site.
  • Lysozyme: an enzyme in tears, saliva and mucus that breaks the peptidoglycan of bacterial cell walls.
  • Interferon: proteins released by virus-infected cells that warn neighbouring cells, which then resist viral replication. Interferon is antiviral, not a direct killer of the virus.
  • Phagocytosis: neutrophils and macrophages engulf a pathogen into a phagosome. Lysosomes fuse with it and enzymes digest the contents.

6.9: Antigens, antibodies, plasma cells, macrophages and antigen-presenting cells

  • An antigen is a foreign molecule, usually a protein or glycoprotein on a pathogen's surface, that triggers an immune response.
  • An antibody is a Y-shaped glycoprotein whose binding sites are complementary to one specific antigen. Antibodies mark pathogens for destruction and neutralise toxins.
  • Plasma cells are B cells that have been activated and that secrete antibodies in large amounts.
  • Macrophages and antigen-presenting cells engulf the pathogen, break it down, and display its antigens on their surface (on MHC proteins). This shows helper T cells what to respond to.

6.10: B cells and T cells

  • B effector (plasma) cells secrete antibodies. B memory cells survive for years and give a faster, larger response on the next exposure to the same antigen.
  • T helper cells (CD4) recognise the antigen on an antigen-presenting cell and release cytokines that activate B cells and T killer cells.
  • T killer (cytotoxic, CD8) cells bind to infected or abnormal cells and kill them, for example by releasing perforin.
  • T memory cells persist after the infection and respond quickly if the same pathogen returns.

6.11: Types of immunity

  • Natural active: the person is infected and makes their own antibodies and memory cells.
  • Natural passive: antibodies pass from mother to baby across the placenta or in breast milk. Protection is immediate but short-lived, and no memory cells are formed.
  • Artificial active: vaccination with an antigen, a weakened or dead pathogen, or a toxoid. The person makes antibodies and memory cells without becoming ill.
  • Artificial passive: injected antibodies, such as antivenom or antitoxin. Protection is immediate and short-lived, and the person's own immune system does not learn.

6.12: The evolutionary race between pathogens and hosts

  • Pathogens evolve evasion mechanisms. Antigenic variation changes the surface antigens: influenza and HIV mutate rapidly, so antibodies no longer fit.
  • Other evasion: hiding inside host cells (tuberculosis in macrophages, HIV in T cells), entering latency, and suppressing the immune response.
  • The host responds with new antibodies and T cells, so pathogens and hosts keep evolving against each other. This is the evolutionary race.

6.13: Bacteriostatic and bactericidal antibiotics

  • Bacteriostatic antibiotics stop bacteria growing and dividing, for example by blocking protein synthesis. The immune system then clears the infection.
  • Bactericidal antibiotics kill bacteria, for example penicillin, which stops cell wall synthesis so the cell bursts.
  • Antibiotics do not act on viruses, which use the host cell's machinery.

6.14: Core practical 14: the effect of antibiotics on bacteria

  • Spread a lawn of bacteria on agar, place antibiotic discs on it, and include a control disc with no antibiotic.
  • Incubate, then measure the diameter of each clear zone of inhibition. A larger zone means the bacteria are more sensitive.
  • Use aseptic technique and non-pathogenic strains, and autoclave the plates before disposal.

6.15: Hospital-acquired infections and codes of practice

  • Contributory causes include overuse of broad-spectrum antibiotics, which selects for resistant strains such as MRSA, poor hand hygiene, indwelling catheters, surgical wounds, and immunocompromised patients.
  • Codes of practice respond to these causes: prescribe antibiotics only when needed and according to guidelines, enforce hand hygiene, isolate infected patients, and clean equipment and wards.

6.16: Decomposition and the carbon cycle

  • Bacteria and fungi are the main decomposers. They secrete extracellular enzymes that digest complex organic matter such as cellulose and proteins, then absorb the simpler products.
  • Respiration by decomposers releases carbon dioxide, which returns carbon to the atmosphere for producers. Ammonium released from proteins feeds the nitrogen cycle.

6.17: The polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

  • Each cycle has three steps: denaturation at about 95 °C separates the strands, annealing at about 50 to 65 °C lets primers bind, and extension at about 72 °C is when Taq polymerase builds the new strands.
  • Taq polymerase comes from the heat-tolerant bacterium Thermus aquaticus, so it survives the high temperatures. Around 30 cycles give an exponential increase in the number of copies.

6.18: Gel electrophoresis of DNA fragments

  • DNA carries a negative charge from its phosphate groups, so it moves towards the positive electrode (anode) through a gel.
  • Smaller fragments move faster and further, so fragments separate by length. A DNA ladder of known sizes is run alongside for comparison, and the bands are stained to make them visible.

6.19: DNA profiling for identification and relatedness

  • DNA profiling compares short tandem repeats (STRs) or variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs). These regions vary in length between individuals, so each person gives a distinctive band pattern.
  • Uses include identifying suspects, establishing paternity, and comparing the banding patterns of plants or animals to show how closely related they are.

6.20: Estimating the time of death from forensic evidence

  • Body temperature: the body cools towards the surroundings, so the rate of cooling gives an estimate of time since death.
  • Muscle contraction: rigor mortis sets in over hours, peaks, then fades over about a day or two.
  • Decomposition and succession: bacterial decomposition gives a predictable sequence of changes. Forensic entomology uses the stage of blowfly larvae and the succession of insect species to estimate how long the body has been exposed.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Growth rate, 6.3 applied: a culture grows from 2.0 × 10⁴ cells cm⁻³ at 2 hours to 1.6 × 10⁵ at 5 hours. N₂ ÷ N₁ = 8 = 2³, so three doublings in three hours. k = (ln 1.6 × 10⁵ − ln 2.0 × 10⁴) ÷ 3 = ln 8 ÷ 3 = 0.69 per hour. The doubling time is ln 2 ÷ k = 1.0 hour. Check the answer against the doubling count before you write it down.
  • Viable count, 6.2 applied: 150 colonies grow from 0.1 cm³ of a 10⁻⁵ dilution. That is 150 ÷ 0.1 = 1500 colonies per cm³ in the diluted sample, and multiplying by the dilution factor gives 1.5 × 10⁸ viable cells per cm³. A haemocytometer count would include dead cells, so the two methods can give different numbers from the same culture. Name which one you are using.
  • Log phase, 6.3 applied: plotting ln N against time gives a straight line only during exponential growth. A curve that bends is a sign that the lag, stationary or death phase has been included by mistake. Use only the straight section to find k.
  • Primary and secondary immune response, 6.10 and 6.12 applied: the first exposure has a lag of several days before antibodies peak at a lower level. A second exposure gives a faster, larger and longer-lasting response, because memory cells are already present. Use all three words, faster, larger and longer, to earn the full mark.
  • Antigen presentation, 6.9 applied: helper T cells (CD4) recognise antigen presented on MHC class II proteins, and killer T cells (CD8) recognise it on MHC class I, as on infected body cells. Naming the MHC class shows you understand which cell carries the antigen.
  • Antibiotic action, 6.13 applied: penicillin blocks the cross-linking of peptidoglycan in the cell wall, so a growing cell bursts. An antibiotic that targets a process human cells do not use, such as the bacterial ribosome, is more selective. Resistance arises by chance mutation and is selected for by the antibiotic, so the explanation must say the mutation was already present and survived.
  • PCR, 6.17 applied: after n cycles one DNA molecule has become 2ⁿ molecules. After 30 cycles that is 2³⁰, about 1.07 × 10⁹ copies. This is why a very small sample is enough, and why contamination with foreign DNA is a serious error.
  • Gel electrophoresis, 6.18 applied: the distance moved is roughly linear with the logarithm of the fragment length. Use a DNA ladder to plot log size against distance, then read the unknown band from that graph rather than from the ladder bands by eye.
  • Forensic estimates, 6.20 applied: a time-of-death answer is always a range. Temperature cooling assumes a stable environment, and a hot or wet site or a body wrapped in clothing changes the rate. Say which factor is most uncertain and why.

Exam tip: time-of-death questions are estimates. Name the method, say what it measures, and state the limitation, for example that temperature depends on the environment.

title: Superposition — Study Notes
content:
Superposition

Principle of superposition

When two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements. Constructive interference occurs where the waves are in phase; destructive interference occurs where they are in antiphase.

Stationary waves

  • A stationary wave forms when two progressive waves of the same frequency, amplitude and wavelength travel in opposite directions and superpose.
  • Nodes are points of zero amplitude; antinodes are points of maximum amplitude. Adjacent nodes (or antinodes) are separated by λ/2.
  • On a string fixed at both ends, the fundamental frequency is f = v/(2L), so the wavelength is λ = 2L.

Interference

For coherent sources (same frequency and a constant phase difference) with slit separation a and screen distance D, the fringe spacing is Δx = λD/a.

Diffraction

Diffraction is the spreading of a wave after it passes through a gap or round an edge. It is greatest when the gap width is comparable to the wavelength.

Diffraction grating

For a grating with slit spacing d, the angle θ of the nth-order maximum satisfies nλ = d sin θ. A grating with more lines per metre gives a smaller d and larger angles of diffraction.

Worked example: light of wavelength 600 nm passes through two slits 0.30 mm apart, with a screen 1.5 m away. Fringe spacing Δx = λD/a = (600 × 10⁻⁹ × 1.5) ÷ (3.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.0 mm.

Exam tips: convert nm and mm to metres before using Δx = λD/a. Check the order n when using a grating. Coherence is a requirement for interference, so state it.

title: Algebra — Inequalities — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Algebra — Inequalities

Mathematics — OL. solving linear inequalities, integer solution sets, shading regions on graphs (linear programming context).

  • 1. Solving
  • 2. Integer solutions
  • 3. Double inequalities
  • 4. Shading regions

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Worked example

Solve 2x − 3 < 7. Add 3 to both sides to get 2x < 10, then divide by 2 to get x < 5. If x is an integer and −2 ≤ x < 5, the integer solutions are −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. The bounds are inclusive on the left and exclusive on the right, so the endpoint −2 is included and 5 is not.

Common mistakes

  • Reversing the inequality sign when you multiply or divide by a negative number, for example in −3x > 6, which gives x < −2.
  • Using a solid line for a strict inequality. Use a dashed line for < or >, and a solid line for ≤ or ≥.
  • Shading the wrong side. Test a point such as (0, 0) and shade the region that makes the inequality true.

title: Statistics — Data Handling — Study Notes
content:
Statistics — Data Handling

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): averages from lists and tables, quartiles/IQR, charts, cumulative frequency, histograms.

1. Averages

  • Mean = Σfx/Σf from frequency tables. Median = middle value (ordered data). Mode = most frequent. Range = max − min.
  • Choose the best average: mode for shoe sizes, median when outliers distort the mean.

Example (table): goals 0,1,2,3 with f 5,8,4,3: mean = (0+8+8+9)/20 = 1.25.

2. Quartiles and IQR

Q₁ at n/4, Q₃ at 3n/4 (position); IQR = Q₃ − Q₁ — less affected by outliers than the range.

3. Charts

Bar charts, pie charts (angle = fraction × 360°), time series, pictograms. Compare data sets with like-for-like totals; comment on trends.

4. Cumulative frequency

Running totals vs upper class boundaries; the curve ends at (max, n). Median at n/2; Q₁/Q₃ at n/4 and 3n/4; box plot from the five-figure summary.

5. Histograms

Bar area ∝ frequency: FD = frequency ÷ class width. Recover frequencies as FD × width; unequal widths need FDs on the axis.

Exam tips: read cumulative-frequency answers with dashed construction lines; always compare spreads, not just averages, when asked to compare data.

Mean, median, mode and range

For ungrouped data, the mean is the sum of values divided by the number of values; the median is the middle value after ordering (the average of the two middle values if there is an even count); the mode is the most frequent value; the range is the largest minus the smallest value.

Frequency tables and grouped data

For a frequency table, the mean is the sum of (value × frequency) divided by the total frequency. For grouped data, use the midpoint of each class as the value and state that the answer is an estimate.

Charts and diagrams

Pie charts use angles: each sector angle is the category frequency divided by the total, multiplied by 360°. Bar charts have gaps between bars; histograms have no gaps, and for unequal class widths the height shown is frequency density.

title: Bonding and Structure — Study Notes
content:
Bonding and Structure

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 3. Every statement 3.1 to 3.22 is covered below, with its code in the heading so you can check your own gaps against the specification. The big idea: the type of bonding and the shape of a molecule explain almost every physical property a question can ask about, including melting point, conductivity, solubility and polarity.

3.1 to 3.2: Evidence for ions, and how they form

  • Evidence for ions: ionic compounds conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved, because the ions are then free to move. In electrolysis, a coloured ion such as manganate(VII), MnO₄⁻, migrates to the positive electrode (the anode), which is direct evidence that it carries a negative charge.
  • Electron density maps for ionic compounds show near-spherical regions of electron density around each ion, with a clear drop in density between them.
  • Formation by loss or gain of electrons: sodium loses one electron to form Na⁺ (2,8,1 becomes 2,8), while chlorine gains one to form Cl⁻ (2,8,7 becomes 2,8,8). A metal loses electrons to form a positive ion; a non-metal gains electrons to form a negative ion.

3.3: Dot-and-cross diagrams for ions

  • Show the outer electrons of each atom as dots or crosses. For a cation such as Mg²⁺, the outer shell is empty, so the symbol is written with square brackets and the charge: [Mg]²⁺.
  • For an anion such as O²⁻, the transferred electrons are added to the outer shell, which then holds eight electrons: [O]²⁻ with eight dots and crosses inside the brackets.
  • Always put the charge outside the brackets, and check that the total number of electrons transferred matches the charges.

3.4 to 3.5: Giant ionic lattices and the ionic bond

  • An ionic crystal is a giant lattice of alternating positive and negative ions, repeating in three dimensions. There are no discrete molecules, so the formula, such as NaCl, is only the simplest ratio of ions. In sodium chloride each Na⁺ is surrounded by six Cl⁻ ions and each Cl⁻ by six Na⁺ ions (6:6 coordination).
  • An ionic bond is the strong net electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. "Net" matters: the attraction between a cation and an anion is partly cancelled by repulsion between like ions, but the attraction wins at the equilibrium distance.

3.6: Effect of ionic radius and ionic charge on bond strength

  • The electrostatic attraction grows with the charge on the ions and falls as the ions get larger, because the centres of charge are further apart.
  • Compare MgO (melting point about 2850 °C) with NaCl (about 800 °C). Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double charges and are small, so their attraction is much stronger than that between the singly charged, larger Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.

3.7: Trends in ionic radius

  • Down a group, ionic radius increases, because each ion has an additional electron shell. Li⁺ is smaller than Na⁺, which is smaller than K⁺.
  • Across a set of isoelectronic ions, all the species have the same number of electrons (ten, in the series N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺). The nuclear charge rises from 7 to 13 across the series, so the outer electrons are pulled in more strongly and the radius falls. N³⁻ is the largest and Al³⁺ the smallest.

3.8 to 3.9: Polarisation of ions

  • Polarisation is the distortion of the electron cloud of an anion by a nearby cation. The cation pulls the anion's electron density towards itself, so the bonding stops being purely ionic and gains covalent character.
  • The polarising power of a cation is greatest when it is small and highly charged. Al³⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Na⁺.
  • The polarisability of an anion is greatest when it is large and highly charged, because its outer electrons are held loosely. I⁻ is more polarisable than Br⁻, which is more polarisable than Cl⁻, which is more polarisable than F⁻.
  • Example: aluminium chloride has a low melting point and sublimes, far below what a purely ionic lattice would need. The small, highly charged Al³⁺ polarises the chloride ions strongly, so the bonding is largely covalent.

3.10: Covalent bonding and the evidence for it

  • A covalent bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between two nuclei (both positive) and the shared pair of electrons between them.
  • Evidence: giant atomic structures such as diamond and silicon(IV) oxide have very high melting points, which only strong covalent bonds can explain. Electron density maps for simple molecules such as hydrogen show a build-up of electron density between the two nuclei.

3.11: Dot-and-cross diagrams for covalent substances

  • Multiple bonds: in carbon dioxide, O=C=O, each double bond is two shared pairs. In nitrogen, N≡N, there are three shared pairs.
  • Dative (coordinate) bonds: both electrons in the shared pair come from one atom, the donor, which has a lone pair. The arrow points from donor to acceptor. In the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, the nitrogen in NH₃ donates its lone pair to H⁺.
  • Aluminium chloride dimer, Al₂Cl₆: each aluminium has four chlorines. Two of the chlorines bridge the two aluminium atoms, and each bridging chlorine forms a dative bond from a chlorine lone pair into the empty orbital of the other aluminium.

3.12: Giant carbon structures: diamond, graphite and graphene

  • Diamond: each carbon forms four single covalent bonds in a tetrahedral giant lattice. It is very hard, has a very high melting point and does not conduct, because there are no free electrons. It is used in cutting and drilling tools.
  • Graphite: each carbon forms three bonds in flat hexagonal sheets. The fourth outer electron on each carbon is delocalised, so graphite conducts along the sheets. The sheets are held by weak forces and slide over each other, so graphite is soft and is used as a lubricant and as electrodes.
  • Graphene: a single sheet of graphite, one atom thick. It is very strong, conducts well and is light and flexible. Applications include electronics, sensors and composite materials.

3.13 to 3.14: Electronegativity and the bonding continuum

  • Electronegativity is the power of an atom to attract the bonding pair of electrons in a covalent bond. Fluorine is the most electronegative element (4.0 on the Pauling scale).
  • The bonding continuum: the bigger the electronegativity difference between two atoms, the more polar the bond. A very small difference gives a non-polar covalent bond, a moderate difference gives a polar covalent bond (as in HCl), and a very large difference gives essentially ionic bonding (as in NaCl). Ionic and covalent bonding are the two ends of this continuum, not separate categories.

3.15: Polar bonds and polar molecules

  • A polar bond has a permanent dipole. A molecule is polar only if its bond dipoles do not cancel, so polar bonds do not automatically make a polar molecule.
  • Carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄: the C–Cl bonds are polar, but the tetrahedral arrangement cancels them, so the molecule is non-polar.
  • Water, H₂O, is bent, so its dipoles add up and the molecule is polar. Carbon dioxide is linear, so its two C=O dipoles cancel and it is non-polar.

3.16 to 3.19: Electron-pair repulsion and molecular shapes

  • Electron-pair repulsion theory: bonding pairs and lone pairs around a central atom repel each other and arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible.
  • Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, so lone pairs compress bond angles. The order of repulsion is lone pair to lone pair, then lone pair to bonding pair, then bonding pair to bonding pair.
  • 3.17, bond length and bond angle: bond length is the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms. Bond angle is the angle between two bonds at the central atom. Triple bonds are shorter than double bonds, which are shorter than single bonds (C≡C shorter than C=C shorter than C–C).

3.18, the shapes and bond angles of the named species:

SpeciesElectron pairs on central atomShapeBond angle
BeCl₂2 bondingLinear180°
BCl₃3 bondingTrigonal planar120°
CH₄4 bondingTetrahedral109.5°
NH₃3 bonding, 1 loneTrigonal pyramidalabout 107°
NH₄⁺4 bondingTetrahedral109.5°
H₂O2 bonding, 2 loneBentabout 104.5°
CO₂2 bonding (double bonds)Linear180°
PCl₅ (gas)5 bondingTrigonal bipyramidal90° and 120°
SF₆6 bondingOctahedral90°
C₂H₄3 regions around each carbonPlanar around each carbonabout 120°

Applying the same rules to analogous species (3.19): SiH₄ is tetrahedral (109.5°), BF₃ is trigonal planar (120°), PH₃ is pyramidal (about 93°), H₂S is bent (about 92°), XeF₄ is square planar (90°, with two lone pairs), and ClF₃ is T-shaped. Count the electron pairs first, then decide how many are lone pairs.

3.20 to 3.22: Metallic bonding and the properties of metals

  • A metal is a giant lattice of positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, the outer electrons that are free to move through the whole structure.
  • 3.21, metallic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between the metal cations and the delocalised electrons. It is not a bond between two particular atoms.
  • Electrical conduction: the delocalised electrons carry charge through the metal when a voltage is applied.
  • High melting temperature: the attraction is strong and is non-directional, so a lot of energy is needed to overcome it. Magnesium melts at about 650 °C, far above sodium at about 98 °C, because Mg²⁺ carries a double charge and provides two delocalised electrons per atom.
  • Malleability: the layers of ions can slide over each other, and the delocalised electrons keep the ions attracted to each other as they move, so the metal does not shatter.

A* extension: worked reasoning for the hardest bonding questions

  • Bond angles, 3.18 applied: CH₄ is 109.5°, NH₃ about 107°, and H₂O about 104.5°. Each lone pair pushes the bonding pairs closer together, because lone pair to bonding pair repulsion is stronger than bonding pair to bonding pair. So the angle falls by roughly 2.5° per lone pair. An A* answer states the reason in these terms, not just the number.
  • Polarity, 3.15 applied: CH₃Cl is polar, because the C–Cl dipole is not cancelled by the C–H bonds, which point in roughly symmetrical directions but carry much smaller dipoles. CCl₄ is non-polar, because four identical C–Cl dipoles point to the corners of a tetrahedron and cancel exactly. Always say which dipoles cancel and why.
  • Electronegativity and bonding continuum, 3.14 applied: aluminium chloride has an electronegativity difference of about 1.5 between Al and Cl. That is not large enough to make it purely ionic, so it is a polar covalent bond, which is consistent with its low melting point and the polarisation argument in 3.8 to 3.9.
  • Lattice and bond strength, 3.6 applied: when asked to compare two ionic compounds, name both the charge and the radius, and say which one dominates. Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ beat Na⁺ and Cl⁻ on both counts, so MgO has the much higher melting point.
  • Mark-scheme phrasing for metallic bonding (3.21): "giant lattice of positive ions", "sea of delocalised electrons", "strong electrostatic attraction between the ions and the delocalised electrons". Each phrase earns its own mark, so use all three.
  • Graphite versus graphene, 3.12 applied: an electrode question expects you to name the delocalised electron, and a lubricant question expects you to name the weak forces between layers. Give both mechanisms when the question says "explain".

Common errors that lose marks

  • Saying covalent or metallic bonds are "between molecules" (they are within the structure; the forces between molecules are intermolecular forces).
  • Calling a polar bond a polar molecule. Always check the shape before you decide the molecule's polarity.
  • Saying ions "move" in solid ionic compounds. They vibrate in place; only molten or dissolved compounds conduct through ion movement.

title: Quadratics — Study Notes
content:
Quadratics

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Quadratic questions ask for a turning point, the roots, or a condition on a parameter. Most multi-part questions use all three, so decide the job of each part before you calculate.

Start from a question

The function is f(x) = 2x² − 8x + 11.

  1. Find the minimum value of f(x) and the value of x at which it occurs.
  2. Find the values of k for which f(x) = k has real roots.
  3. Find the value of m for which the line y = x + m is a tangent to y = f(x).

Part 1. Complete the square: f(x) = 2(x − 2)² + 3. The minimum value is 3, at x = 2.

Part 2. f(x) = k gives 2x² − 8x + (11 − k) = 0. The discriminant is 64 − 8(11 − k) = 8k − 24. Real roots need 8k − 24 ≥ 0, so k ≥ 3, which agrees with Part 1.

Part 3. Substituting y = x + m gives 2x² − 9x + (11 − m) = 0. A tangent needs equal roots, so 81 − 8(11 − m) = 0. That gives 8m − 7 = 0, so m = 7/8.

Turning points and the square

For ax² + bx + c, the turning point is at x = −b/2a. The sign of a decides the type: a > 0 gives a minimum and a < 0 gives a maximum. Example: for 2x² − 12x + 7, the turning point is at x = 3, and the value there is 18 − 36 + 7 = −11.

Solving

Try factorising first. If that fails, use x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/2a and simplify the surd. Example: 3x² + 5x − 4 = 0 has discriminant 25 + 48 = 73, so x = (−5 ± √73)/6.

The discriminant counts roots

D = b² − 4ac gives the number of real roots: D > 0 gives two distinct roots, D = 0 gives one repeated root, and D < 0 gives none. Example: 4x² + kx + 9 = 0 has equal roots when k² = 4 × 4 × 9 = 144, so k = ±12. With k = 12 the equation is (2x + 3)² = 0.

A parameter inside the discriminant

When D contains an unknown, form the inequality and solve it. Example: x² + (k − 1)x + 4 = 0 has real roots when (k − 1)² − 16 ≥ 0. So |k − 1| ≥ 4, which gives k ≤ −3 or k ≥ 5.

Sketch, then read the region

For a positive a, the curve is below the x-axis between its roots and above it outside them. Example: 2x² − x − 6 < 0 factorises as (2x + 3)(x − 2) < 0, so −3/2 < x < 2.

Example: 5 − 3x − 2x² ≥ 0. Multiplying by −1 gives 2x² + 3x − 5 ≤ 0, and the inequality reverses. (2x + 5)(x − 1) ≤ 0 gives −5/2 ≤ x ≤ 1.

A line and a curve

Set the two equations equal and rearrange into one quadratic. Example: y = x + 3 and y = 2x² − x meet where 2x² − 2x − 3 = 0. Here D = 28 > 0, so the line cuts the curve at two points.

Traps that cost marks

  • Multiplying an inequality by a negative number and forgetting to reverse it.
  • Using D = 0 for a "no real roots" condition, when it should be D < 0.
  • Giving a single value when the question allows a range of values.
  • Dropping the ± when taking the square root of both sides.

title: Coordination, Response and Gene Technology
content:
Quick revision: Coordination, Response and Gene Technology

Biology — A2. Edexcel IAL Biology WBI15, Topic 8. Nervous and hormonal systems coordinate the body, and plants respond to light and gravity using hormones. Gene technology uses enzymes to cut, join and copy DNA for medicine, research and agriculture.

  • 8.1 Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS, relay neurones connect sensory and motor neurones within the CNS, and motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors, all featuring Schwann cells wrapping around axons to form a myelin sheath that insulates the axon.
  • 8.2 The nervous system causes effectors such as muscles or glands to respond to a stimulus by generating action potentials that travel to neuromuscular junctions or gland endings.
  • 8.3 A spinal reflex arc consists of a receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone in the grey matter of the spinal cord, motor neurone, and effector, with white matter containing myelinated axons ascending and descending to the brain.
  • 8.4 Action potentials are conducted along an axon via depolarisation caused by voltage-gated sodium ion channels opening and sodium ions rushing in, followed by repolarisation caused by voltage-gated potassium ion channels opening and potassium ions rushing out.
  • 8.5 Myelination allows saltatory conduction where the action potential jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next, drastically increasing the speed of nerve impulse transmission.
  • 8.6 Synapses transmit impulses between neurones using neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine diffusing across the synaptic cleft, and the pupil dilates via radial muscles in dim light and contracts via circular muscles in bright light.
  • 8.7 Drugs affect nerve transmission such as nicotine mimicking acetylcholine, lidocaine blocking voltage-gated sodium channels, cobra venom blocking acetylcholine receptors, L-DOPA acting as a dopamine precursor to treat Parkinson's disease, and MDMA increasing neurotransmitter release.
  • 8.8 Rods in the retina detect light when photon absorption converts cis-retinal to trans-retinal, causing rhodopsin to break down into opsin and retinal, closing sodium cation channels, stopping sodium influx, and hyperpolarising the rod cell to initiate action potentials in optic neurones.
  • 8.9 Habituation is a decrease in response to a repeated stimulus that is harmless, preventing unnecessary energy expenditure.
  • 8.10 The mammalian nervous system consists of the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system (cranial and spinal nerves).
  • 8.11 Plant responses are controlled by phytochrome which changes form in red and far-red light affecting transcription, auxin (IAA) which causes cell elongation and affects transcription, and gibberellins which stimulate seed germination by promoting amylase transcription.
  • 8.12 Core Practical 18 investigates the production of amylase in germinating cereal grains by measuring starch breakdown under varying conditions.
  • 8.13 Coordination in animals is brought about through rapid, targeted nervous control and slower, chemical hormonal control travelling in the blood.
  • 8.14 The cerebral hemispheres control conscious thought and sensory processing, the hypothalamus regulates homeostasis, the pituitary gland secretes hormones, the cerebellum coordinates balance and voluntary movement, and the medulla oblongata controls involuntary functions like heart rate and breathing.
  • 8.15 Medical imaging techniques include MRI and CT for structural detail, fMRI for localized brain activity during tasks, and PET for metabolic activity using radioactive tracers.
  • 8.16 Imbalances in brain chemicals cause ill health, such as a shortage of dopamine in Parkinson's disease and low serotonin levels in depression, informing the design of new drugs.
  • 8.17 Therapeutic drugs and proteins can be produced using genetically modified organisms including transgenic plants, animals, and microorganisms like bacteria and yeast.
  • 8.18 Recombinant DNA is produced by using restriction endonucleases to cut DNA at specific palindromic recognition sites to yield sticky or blunt ends, and DNA ligase to join the sugar-phosphate backbones of the DNA insert and vector.
  • 8.19 Recombinant DNA can be inserted into host cells using vectors such as plasmids, bacteriophages, or through methods like electroporation, microinjection, and liposomes.
  • 8.20 Microarrays use fluorescently labelled cDNA to hybridise with fixed single-stranded DNA probes, identifying which genes are actively being transcribed in a cell.
  • 8.21 Bioinformatics is the collection, storage, and computational analysis of large biological datasets such as genomic sequences and amino acid databases using software tools.
  • 8.22 Genetically modified organisms carry risks such as gene transfer to wild relatives and ethical concerns, alongside benefits like increased crop yields, disease resistance, and mass production of essential medical proteins.

Worked example

Explain how lidocaine affects the transmission of a nerve impulse. Step 1: Identify that lidocaine is a local anaesthetic drug. Step 2: Relate its mechanism of action to axonal membranes. Lidocaine binds to and blocks voltage-gated sodium ion channels on the axon membrane. Step 3: State the consequence on the action potential. Sodium ions cannot enter the axon, preventing the membrane from depolarising, so the action potential cannot be generated or propagated along the neurone, blocking pain signals to the CNS.

Key points to remember

Students often confuse hyperpolarisation in rod cells with depolarisation in axons; remember that in the dark rod cells are depolarised and releasing neurotransmitter, but light hyperpolarises them and stops neurotransmitter release.

When describing recombinant DNA, always mention the specific roles of both restriction endonucleases for cutting DNA and DNA ligase for sealing phosphodiester bonds, as omitting either loses credit.

For plant growth factors, make sure to link auxin and gibberellin action directly to transcription and protein synthesis rather than just simple cell stretching.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Exam technique: Probability (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For conditional probability, the restricted sample space stated earns the method mark. For independence checks, P(A)P(B) compared with P(A and B) earns both marks. For Bayes-style updates, the tree fractions multiplied along branches earn stepwise credit.
### Traps
Error: mutually exclusive assumed independent. Correction: test, never assume. Error: given-condition ignored. Correction: shrink the denominator first. Error: branches added instead of multiplied. Correction: multiply along, add across.
### Worked example
Event A has P(A) = 0.5 and event B has P(B) = 0.4. Given that A and B are independent, P(A and B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20. If the question instead gives P(A and B) = 0.3, then the events are not independent, because 0.3 does not equal 0.20. The conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B) = 0.3 ÷ 0.4 = 0.75.
### Check yourself
Two events are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.2. Are they independent? No. P(A and B) = 0 but P(A)P(B) = 0.06, so the events are dependent. Mutually exclusive events are always dependent when both have non-zero probability.

### Worked example
Event A has P(A) = 0.5 and event B has P(B) = 0.4. Given that A and B are independent, P(A and B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20. If the question instead gives P(A and B) = 0.3, then the events are not independent, because 0.3 does not equal 0.20. The conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B) = 0.3 ÷ 0.4 = 0.75.

title: Exam technique: Sampling
content:
### What earns the marks
For method choice, random vs stratified vs systematic justified earns the mark. For stratified allocation, the proportion of each stratum applied earns the method mark. For bias discussion, the named source of bias with its effect earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: sample claimed unbiased with no method. Correction: name and justify the method. Error: equal numbers per stratum. Correction: allocate proportionally. Error: population confused with frame. Correction: frame is the list used.
### Worked example
A school has 600 students: 120 in Year 11 and 480 in Year 10. A stratified sample of 50 is needed with proportional allocation. Year 11 gets 120/600 x 50 = 10 students, and Year 10 gets 480/600 x 50 = 40 students. The two numbers add to 50, which confirms the allocation. Random selection then happens inside each group.
### Check yourself
A teacher samples 50 students from the first 50 names on the register. Name the sampling method and the main source of bias. This is a convenience sample, and the bias comes from the register order, which may not represent the whole school.

title: Differentiation II — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation II

Product and Quotient Rules

  • (uv)′ = u′v + uv′
  • (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²

Example: y = x² e^x gives dy/dx = 2x e^x + x² e^x = e^x(2x + x²).

Standard Derivatives

  • sin x → cos x; cos x → −sin x; tan x → sec²x
  • e^x → e^x; ln x → 1/x

Chain Rule Everywhere

d/dx [ln(3x)] = 3/(3x) = 1/x; d/dx [e^(2x)] = 2e^(2x); d/dx [sin²x] = 2 sin x cos x.

Implicit Differentiation

Differentiate both sides w.r.t. x, treating y as a function of x (terms in y pick up dy/dx).

Example: x² + y² = 25 → 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0 → dy/dx = −x/y.

Parametric Curves

For x = f(t), y = g(t): dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

Example: x = t², y = t³ gives dy/dx = 3t²/2t = 3t/2.

Exam tips: quote the rule you use; for tangent/normal on parametric curves, find t at the point first, and simplify implicit answers using the original equation.

Exam method: exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric rules

The derivative of eˣ is eˣ, and the derivative of e^(kx) is k e^(kx). The derivative of ln x is 1/x, and for ln(f(x)) the chain rule gives f′(x)/f(x). The derivative of sin x is cos x and of cos x is −sin x; for a function of kx, multiply by k.

When a product contains an exponential or trigonometric function, use the product rule d/dx(uv) = u dv/dx + v du/dx. Factorising the result, such as eˣ(1 + x), makes it easier to evaluate at a point.

Quotients use d/dx(u/v) = (v du/dx − u dv/dx)/v². Write tan x as sin x/cos x when the quotient rule is easier, and remember that d/dx(tan x) = sec² x.

Second derivatives follow by differentiating again. Use them to classify stationary points, or to check the concavity of a curve, when the question asks for it.

Exam cue: Show each rule as you apply it. Method marks are awarded for a correct product or chain step even if the final arithmetic is wrong.

title:
Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment — Edexcel International A2 Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International A2 Level Biology specification and covers the topics that connect the biochemistry of photosynthesis to the way energy moves through ecosystems, the way ecologists measure populations and communities, the evidence for and the causes of climate change, and the biological ideas that tie the whole topic together in metabolism and evolution. It is written to be complete enough to revise from and to check yourself against the specification, so each numbered section is built around one or more specification statements rather than around a loose theme. The note deliberately stays at exam depth: it explains the reasoning behind each idea, gives the typical worked examples and comparisons that examiners look for, and lists the common mistakes that lose marks in this topic.

1. The overall photosynthesis reaction and the role of light energy in splitting water

Photosynthesis is the process that captures light energy and stores it in chemical form by using that energy to split water, combine the hydrogen with carbon dioxide, and release oxygen. The overall equation is the shorthand, carbon dioxide and water, with light, yield glucose and oxygen, but the important point is what the light energy is actually doing: it is splitting the strong bonds in water molecules, releasing oxygen gas into the atmosphere and storing hydrogen in glucose by combining it with carbon dioxide. This is the entry point for energy into ecosystems and the source of the atmospheric oxygen that most organisms use.

The significance of the water-splitting step is that it is what makes photosynthesis more than just a rearrangement of carbon. The energy from light is used to break the bonds in water, and the hydrogen that results is what ends up in glucose, while the oxygen from water is what is released to the atmosphere. If you remember that, you can explain why the equation is written the way it is and why light is necessary: without light, water is not split, hydrogen is not made available, and glucose cannot be formed from carbon dioxide. The overall reaction is therefore not just a summary but a statement of where the energy comes in and where the oxygen comes from.

A good answer says that light energy splits the strong bonds in water, that the hydrogen is stored in glucose by combining with carbon dioxide, and that oxygen is released. It does not merely repeat the equation; it explains what the light is for. That is the difference between a mark-scoring answer and one that simply copies the equation without understanding it. The equation is the starting point, not the answer.

2. Photophosphorylation and the role of ATP as an immediate energy supply

The immediate energy currency in cells is ATP, and photosynthesis makes it by photophosphorylation, the use of light energy to phosphorylate ADP to ATP. ATP is then used as a fast, small packet of energy for endergonic processes, and its hydrolysis provides an immediate supply of energy that can be used where and when it is needed. The link between the light-dependent and light-independent reactions is therefore not a direct transfer of glucose but a transfer of ATP and reduced NADP, which are the energy and reducing power needed to fix carbon in the Calvin cycle.

Photophosphorylation happens in the light-dependent reactions on the thylakoid membranes. Light energy excites electrons in chlorophyll, and the energy from those electrons is used to make ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. The ATP is then available for the Calvin cycle and for other cellular processes, and its hydrolysis provides a quick source of energy for endergonic processes, which are processes that would not otherwise occur because they require an input of energy. The important conceptual point is that ATP is the link between the energy captured in the light and the work done by the cell, and that the light-dependent reactions exist largely to make the ATP and reduced NADP that the Calvin cycle needs.

A good answer says that photophosphorylation converts ADP and inorganic phosphate into ATP using light energy, that ATP hydrolysis provides an immediate supply of energy for biological processes, and that the ATP made in the light-dependent reactions is used in the Calvin cycle. It does not say that the light reactions make glucose; they make ATP and reduced NADP, and glucose comes later. That distinction is one of the most common mark-losers in this topic, so it is worth keeping it clear.

3. The light-dependent reactions: cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation and the role of photolysis

The light-dependent reactions take place on the thylakoid membranes and are where light energy is converted into chemical energy in the form of ATP and reduced NADP, with oxygen released from the splitting of water. Light excites electrons in chlorophyll, and those electrons are passed along an electron transport chain, releasing energy that is used to make ATP and to reduce NADP to reduced NADP. Water is split by photolysis, releasing oxygen, protons and replacement electrons, so that the chlorophyll can lose electrons to the electron transport chain without running out of them. The two forms of photophosphorylation are cyclic and non-cyclic, and they are not the same thing, which is why the comparison matters.

Non-cyclic photophosphorylation produces ATP, reduced NADP and oxygen. Electrons from photosystem II are passed along the electron transport chain to photosystem I, and the energy released is used to make ATP. The electrons are then re-excited in photosystem I and used to reduce NADP to reduced NADP. Water is split in photosystem II to replace the electrons lost, releasing oxygen in the process. The overall result is that light energy drives the making of ATP and reduced NADP and the release of oxygen from water. This is the photophosphorylation that is linked to the Calvin cycle, because both ATP and reduced NADP are needed for carbon fixation.

Cyclic photophosphorylation produces ATP only. Electrons from photosystem I are passed back to the electron transport chain and return to photosystem I, rather than being used to reduce NADP. The energy released is used to make ATP, but no reduced NADP is made and no oxygen is produced from water splitting in the same way as in non-cyclic photophosphorylation. Cyclic photophosphorylation therefore makes extra ATP when the Calvin cycle needs more ATP than reduced NADP, balancing the ATP and reduced NADP supply to match the needs of the Calvin cycle.

A good answer says that non-cyclic photophosphorylation makes ATP, reduced NADP and oxygen, and that cyclic photophosphorylation makes ATP only. It explains that water is split in photolysis to replace electrons in non-cyclic photophosphorylation, releasing oxygen. It does not say that cyclic photophosphorylation makes oxygen or reduced NADP, and it does not say that non-cyclic photophosphorylation makes only ATP. The distinction between the two forms is one of the things examiners look for, because it shows that the student understands that the light reactions can adjust their outputs to the needs of the Calvin cycle.

4. The light-independent reactions: the Calvin cycle, RuBP, GP, GALP and RuBisCO

The light-independent reactions, the Calvin cycle, take place in the stroma of the chloroplast and use the ATP and reduced NADP from the light-dependent reactions to fix carbon dioxide into organic molecules. The key enzyme is RuBisCO, which fixes carbon dioxide onto ribulose bisphosphate, RuBP, forming glycerate 3-phosphate, GP. GP is then reduced using ATP and reduced NADP to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, GALP. Some GALP leaves the cycle to make glucose and other products; some is used to regenerate RuBP so the cycle can continue.

The cycle is a cycle because RuBP is regenerated, so carbon dioxide can continue to be fixed. The ATP provides the energy for the reduction of GP to GALP, and the reduced NADP provides the reducing power, the hydrogen and electrons, for that reduction. The glucose and other products made from GALP are then used in respiration and in the synthesis of new biological molecules, including polysaccharides, amino acids, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. The point is that photosynthesis does not just make glucose; it makes the raw materials for the rest of the organism’s biochemistry.

A good answer says that the Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma, that RuBisCO fixes carbon dioxide onto RuBP, that GP is reduced to GALP using ATP and reduced NADP, that some GALP leaves the cycle to make glucose and other products and some regenerates RuBP, and that the products are used in respiration and in the synthesis of polysaccharides, amino acids, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. It does not say that the Calvin cycle does not need the light reactions; it needs ATP and reduced NADP from them, which is why the light-independent reactions are not independent of light in the long run. The name “light-independent” means they do not directly use light, not that they can continue indefinitely without the products of the light reactions.

5. Chloroplast structure and function: thylakoids, stroma, envelope and pigments

The chloroplast is built so that its structure matches its function. The thylakoids provide a large surface area for light absorption and for the pigment arrays and electron transport chain, and they are where the light-dependent reactions happen. The stroma contains the enzymes of the Calvin cycle, including RuBisCO, and is where the light-independent reactions happen. The double membrane envelope keeps the internal conditions separated from the cytoplasm and isolates the biochemical machinery of the chloroplast.

The structure is not just a set of facts to memorise; each part exists for a reason. The thylakoids are stacked and membrane-bound because that gives a large surface area for the pigments and the electron transport chain, and the stroma is the fluid around the thylakoids because that is where the enzymes of the Calvin cycle are. The envelope keeps the chloroplast as a compartment distinct from the rest of the cell, so the internal conditions can be maintained. A good answer says that the thylakoids are the site of the light-dependent reactions and that the stroma is the site of the Calvin cycle, and it links the structure to the function rather than just listing the parts.

The pigments are part of the chloroplast too, and they are the reason different wavelengths of light matter. Chlorophylls and carotenoids absorb light at different wavelengths, and the separation of pigments by chromatography is both a practical skill and a way to understand the absorption spectrum, which is the spectrum of wavelengths a pigment absorbs. The pigments are embedded in the thylakoid membranes, which is why the thylakoids are the site of the light reactions: that is where the pigments and the electron transport chain are. A good answer links the pigments to the thylakoids and the light reactions, and does not treat the pigments as separate from the structure of the chloroplast.

6. Absorption spectra, action spectra, and the separation and identification of pigments

The absorption spectrum shows how much light of each wavelength a pigment absorbs, and the action spectrum shows the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength. In an ideal case the two track each other, because the wavelengths that a pigment absorbs are the ones that drive photosynthesis, but the two are not the same concept: one is about the pigment, the other about the whole process. The absorption spectrum is about what the pigment takes in; the action spectrum is about what the plant does with the light.

Chloroplast pigments can be separated by paper or thin-layer chromatography, and the distance each pigment moves compared with the solvent front gives the Rf value, which helps identify the pigment. The Rf value is the distance moved by the pigment divided by the distance moved by the solvent front. Chlorophylls, carotenoids and xanthophylls all have characteristic Rf values, so the method can be used to identify which pigments are present in a leaf extract. A good answer says that chromatography separates the pigments, that the Rf value helps identify them, and that the Rf value is the distance moved by the pigment divided by the distance moved by the solvent front. A common mistake is to invert the ratio, so the Rf value ends up greater than one, which is impossible. If you remember that the pigment moves less far than the solvent front, you can avoid that mistake.

The distinction between absorption spectrum and action spectrum is important because it is a common exam comparison. The absorption spectrum is about the pigment’s absorption of light; the action spectrum is about the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength. They are related but not identical, because the rate of photosynthesis depends on more than just the absorption of a single pigment, and because the two are measuring different things. A good answer says that the absorption spectrum shows the wavelengths a pigment absorbs and the action spectrum shows the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength, and it does not say they are the same thing.

7. Core Practical 10: the factors affecting the rate of photosynthesis

Core Practical 10 is the practical that investigates the effects of light intensity, light wavelength, temperature and carbon dioxide availability on the rate of photosynthesis using a suitable aquatic plant, measuring oxygen bubbles or gas volume. The point of the practical is not only to run the experiment but to understand that photosynthesis is affected by more than one factor and that one of them will be limiting at any moment. The practical is the place where the limiting factor idea becomes visible.

A typical setup uses an aquatic plant such as Elodea or Cabomba in water, with light as the independent variable, and oxygen production as the proxy for the rate of photosynthesis. The plant is left to adjust before the measurement starts, and the light intensity is varied, for example by changing the distance of the lamp. The number of bubbles per minute or the volume of gas collected in a fixed time is the dependent variable. The temperature, carbon dioxide concentration and the plant itself are control variables, because if they change the result is no longer a fair test of the effect of light. The point is that the rate depends on light, but only up to the point where another factor becomes limiting, so the graph of rate against light intensity levels off as the plant becomes limited by something else, such as carbon dioxide or temperature.

A good answer describes the method clearly enough to be repeatable, names the control variables, and explains that the rate of photosynthesis depends on light but is also limited by temperature and carbon dioxide. It also notes that oxygen production is a proxy for photosynthesis, not a direct measure of carbon fixed, and that the rate is measured by counting bubbles or gas volume. If you can describe that, you have the practical in a form that scores marks. The limiting factor idea is the reason the experiment matters: it shows that a biological rate is controlled by more than one factor and that the factor in shortest supply is the one that limits the rate.

8. Gross primary productivity and net primary productivity

Gross primary productivity, GPP, is the total chemical energy fixed by photosynthesis in a given area and time. Net primary productivity, NPP, is the gross productivity minus the energy lost in plant respiration, R, so NPP is the energy actually available to the next trophic level because it is what remains after the plant has used some of the fixed energy itself. The relationship is NPP equals GPP minus R. The distinction between GPP and NPP is one of the most important ideas in this topic, because it explains why the energy available to consumers is less than the total energy fixed by the plants.

The calculation of NPP is a simple subtraction, but the understanding behind it is what matters. Respiration is the loss, and plants are not perfectly efficient converters of light energy into stored chemical energy either, because they use some of the fixed energy themselves. A forest can have a high GPP but much of that is respired away, so NPP is what matters for the consumers, not GPP. If a question asks for NPP and gives GPP and R, the answer is GPP minus R, with the units stated. If a question asks why NPP is the more important figure for consumers, the answer is that NPP is the energy left after the plant’s own respiration, and that is the energy that can pass to the next level.

A good answer says that GPP is the total energy fixed, that R is the energy lost in respiration, that NPP equals GPP minus R, and that NPP is the energy available to consumers. It does not say that GPP and NPP are the same thing, or that the plant uses no energy itself. The idea that the plant respires some of the fixed energy is the reason NPP is less than GPP, and that is the point the examiners are after. The units matter too, because energy per unit area and time is what is meant, so the answer should include them.

9. The efficiency of energy transfer between trophic levels

The efficiency of energy transfer between trophic levels is calculated as the energy or biomass transferred to the next level divided by the energy or biomass received at the previous level, multiplied by 100. The typical figure is well below 100 percent, often around 10 percent as a rough guide, because energy is lost in respiration, in egested material, in uneaten parts, and in the energy used by the level itself. This inefficiency is why food chains are short and why the biomass and energy at higher trophic levels are much smaller than at lower ones.

The calculation itself is simple, but the reason for the inefficiency is what makes it a biology topic rather than just arithmetic. Energy is lost because organisms use some of it in respiration, because not all of a consumed organism is eaten or digested, because some material is egested, and because each level uses energy for its own metabolism. The result is that only a fraction of the energy at one level becomes biomass at the next. A good answer says that the efficiency is the energy transferred divided by the energy received times 100, that the figure is typically low, and that the reasons are respiration, egestion, uneaten material and the energy used by the level itself. If you can say that, you have the efficiency idea in a form that scores marks.

Worked example: if a producer level contains 15000 kilojoules per square metre per year and the primary consumer level contains 1400 kilojoules per square metre per year, the transfer efficiency is 1400 divided by 15000 times 100, which is 9.33 percent. The number itself is not memorable; what matters is that the calculation shows how small the fraction is and why the higher levels get progressively smaller. If a question gives numbers, the answer is to state the formula, substitute, and calculate, with the units stated. If the numbers are in different units or at different times, the answer should note that and check they are comparable.

10. Ecology vocabulary: population, community, habitat, ecosystem and niche

Ecology is the study of how organisms interact with each other and with their environment, and the basic vocabulary here is the foundation for the rest of the topic. A population is a group of interbreeding individuals of the same species in a habitat. A community is all the populations of different species living and interacting in a habitat. A habitat is the place where an organism lives. An ecosystem is a self-sustaining system of living organisms interacting with their non-living surroundings. The ecosystem is larger than the community because it includes the abiotic part as well as the biotic part.

The niche concept explains distribution and abundance. A niche is the role of a species in its ecosystem, including the conditions it tolerates, the resources it uses and the interactions it has. Two species cannot indefinitely occupy exactly the same niche, because one will outcompete the other, competitive exclusion. This is one reason species partition resources and why communities can be diverse. The niche is not just what the species eats; it is the whole set of conditions and roles that define how the species fits into the ecosystem. If you can say that, you have the niche idea in a form that scores marks.

A good answer says that a population is a group of interbreeding individuals of the same species, a community is all the populations of different species in a habitat, a habitat is the place where an organism lives, an ecosystem is a self-sustaining system of living organisms and their non-living surroundings, and a niche is the role of a species including its conditions, resources and interactions. It also says that two species cannot occupy exactly the same niche indefinitely. If you can say that, you have the vocabulary and the competitive exclusion idea that examiners look for. The distinction between community and ecosystem is the one most often confused, so it is worth keeping clear that the ecosystem includes the abiotic part and the community does not.

11. Biotic and abiotic factors and what limits populations

The numbers and distribution of organisms are controlled by biotic factors such as competition, predation and disease, and by abiotic factors such as temperature, pH, light intensity and moisture. Which factor limits a population depends on the organism and the environment, so in one place it may be food, in another it may be temperature or water. The important idea is that populations are limited by a combination of living and non-living factors, and that the limiting factor can change with context.

Competition is a biotic factor in which organisms compete for limited resources such as food, space or mates. Predation is a biotic factor in which one organism eats another, with effects on both populations. Disease is a biotic factor that can reduce a population. The abiotic factors are the non-living conditions that affect the organism’s ability to survive and reproduce, such as temperature, pH, light and moisture. A good answer names both sets of factors and says that the limiting factor depends on the organism and the environment. It does not say that only one factor matters, or that the same factor limits every population. The context-dependence is the point: the factor that limits one population in one place may be different in another.

A frequent exam question is to ask what limits a particular population, and the answer is to consider both biotic and abiotic factors and to say which is most likely in the context given. The ability to reason about which factor matters in a particular situation is what the examiners are after, not just the list of possibilities. If you can say that, you can answer the question rather than just reciting factors.

12. Core Practical 11: fieldwork with quadrats and transects

Core Practical 11 is the fieldwork snapshot: use quadrats to sample abundance and transects, belt or line, to sample distribution, and record abiotic factors at the same time. The point is not just to count organisms but to relate their distribution to the environmental gradient being surveyed. Random sampling is used for abundance where the habitat is uniform, so that every part of the area has an equal chance of being sampled; systematic sampling along a transect is used where there is a gradient, such as trampling, exposure or moisture.

A quadrat is a square frame of known area used to sample the abundance of organisms in a habitat. The number of organisms inside the quadrat is counted, and the result can be expressed as a frequency or a population estimate depending on the sampling design. A line transect records the organisms touching a line, a belt transect records organisms within a belt, and both can be used to follow a change in distribution along a gradient. Abiotic factors are recorded at the same time so that the distribution can be related to the environment. A good answer says why a quadrat or a transect is chosen for a particular question, and relates the distribution to the abiotic factors measured.

The practical point is that sampling has to be done in a way that is fair and representative, and that the choice of method matches the question. If the habitat is uniform and you want abundance, random quadrats are appropriate. If there is a gradient and you want distribution, a transect is appropriate. If you can say that, you have the practical in a form that scores marks. The fieldwork is also the place where the ecological vocabulary becomes real, because the quadrat and transect are how the population, community and abiotic factors are actually measured.

13. Succession from pioneer species to climax community

Succession is the sequence of change from colonisation by pioneer species to a climax community. Pioneer species colonise bare or hostile substrate, change the abiotic conditions, for example by building soil or adding shade, and make the environment less hostile for later species. The community passes through seral stages of increasing complexity and biodiversity until a climax community forms, which is relatively stable and dominated by species adapted to the conditions at that stage.

Succession is not random; it is directional and partly predictable, because the early species modify the environment in ways that favour later ones. The climax community is not necessarily a permanent fixed end in every case, because if the environment changes the community can move again, but in a stable environment the climax community persists. A good answer says that pioneer species colonise bare substrate, change the abiotic conditions, and make the environment less hostile for later species, that the community passes through seral stages, and that a climax community eventually forms. It also says that the climax community is relatively stable and that succession is directional because the early species alter the conditions for the later ones.

The exam point is that succession is not just change over time; it is a sequence in which the species present reflect both the history of the site and the current conditions. The pioneer species are adapted to hostile conditions, and the later species are adapted to the conditions the pioneers helped create. The ability to say that is what the examiners are after, not just the names of the stages. The climax community is the endpoint in a stable environment, but the idea that succession is directional and partly predictable is the deeper point.

14. Evidence for climate change: CO2 records, temperature records, pollen in peat bogs, dendrochronology

Evidence for climate change comes from several independent sources. Atmospheric carbon dioxide records, such as the Mauna Loa curve, show a rising trend. Temperature records show a warming trend. Pollen preserved in peat bogs gives information about past vegetation and so past climate. Dendrochronology, tree-ring analysis, gives year-by-year information about growth conditions. The key skill is to recognise that correlation does not prove causation, and that each line of evidence has limitations and possible confounding factors.

A rising temperature and a rising carbon dioxide curve can be correlated without the student yet having explained the mechanism, and the mechanism is asked for separately. The evidence is that the trends exist and are correlated in time, but the cause is not proved by the correlation alone. To show causation, you need a plausible mechanism, such as the greenhouse effect, and evidence that linking the variables is not better explained by something else. A good answer says that the evidence includes the CO2 records, the temperature records, the pollen record and the tree-ring record, and that correlation does not prove causation by itself. If you can say that, you can answer the question without overclaiming.

A common mistake is to treat the correlation as proof of causation without mentioning the mechanism or the limitations. Another is to rely on a single line of evidence as if it were enough. The point is that the evidence is multiple and each line has limitations: tree rings reflect growth conditions, not just temperature, and pollen in peat bogs reflects past vegetation, which is influenced by climate but also by other factors. A good answer recognises that the evidence is convergent rather than a single proof, and that the mechanism is what turns correlation into causation. If you can say that, you are answering at the right level.

15. The greenhouse effect, greenhouse gases, and the enhanced greenhouse effect

The natural greenhouse effect is what makes Earth warm enough to live on. Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and water vapour absorb and re-radiate infrared radiation, keeping more energy in the atmosphere. The enhanced greenhouse effect is the additional warming from the extra greenhouse gases released by human activity. The important point is that the greenhouse effect itself is not a bad thing; it is necessary for life. What is happening now is that the enhanced greenhouse effect is raising the temperature above the natural level.

The mechanism is that the greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation emitted by the Earth’s surface and re-radiate some of it back, so that more energy is retained in the atmosphere than would otherwise be the case. Carbon dioxide is the most important long-lived greenhouse gas for the enhanced effect, methane is more potent per molecule but shorter-lived, nitrous oxide is also a greenhouse gas, and water vapour is the most abundant greenhouse gas but acts as a feedback rather than a primary forcing in this context. A good answer names the gases and describes the mechanism, not just says that humans cause warming. The mechanism is what makes the claim scientific rather than a slogan.

A common mistake is to say that the greenhouse effect is caused by trapping heat as if it were a blanket in the everyday sense, without explaining that it is about absorbing and re-radiating infrared radiation. Another is to forget that water vapour is the most abundant greenhouse gas and to treat carbon dioxide as the only one. If you name the gases and describe the mechanism, you can answer the question correctly. The enhanced greenhouse effect is the key term, because it distinguishes the natural effect from the human-caused increase, and that distinction matters for the quality of the answer.

16. Using the carbon cycle to reduce atmospheric CO2: reforestation, peatlands, fossil fuels and carbon capture

Knowledge of the carbon cycle is used to reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide. Methods include reforestation and afforestation, which increase the removal of CO2 by photosynthesis; protecting peatlands and other carbon-rich ecosystems; reducing fossil fuel combustion; and carbon capture and storage. Each method works by changing the size or direction of a carbon flux, and each has limitations. Trees take time to grow and can be lost again; peatlands can be damaged; and capture and storage is not yet universally practical or cheap.

The carbon cycle is the set of processes that move carbon between the atmosphere, living organisms, soils and the oceans. Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and fixes it in biomass; respiration and decomposition return it; and the burning of fossil fuels adds carbon dioxide that had been stored for geological time. The methods for reducing atmospheric CO2 all work by affecting one of these fluxes: growing more plants increases the removal, protecting peatlands keeps carbon in the soil, reducing fossil fuel combustion reduces the addition, and carbon capture and storage keeps some of the carbon from reaching the atmosphere. A good answer says that the methods are applications of the carbon cycle, and that each has limitations.

A good answer does not say that planting trees is a complete solution, because it is not: trees take time to grow, can be lost to fire or disease, and can compete with other land uses. It does not say that carbon capture and storage is available everywhere at low cost, because it is not yet. The point is to apply the carbon cycle idea to the mitigation methods and to recognise their limitations, not to pretend that any one method is a complete answer. If you can do that, you are answering at the right level.

17. Extrapolation and the limitations of climate models

Data can be extrapolated to make predictions, and models of future climate change are built from such extrapolations and from our understanding of the system. Models are useful precisely because they let us explore the consequences of different scenarios. They are not crystal balls; they are tools for working out what might happen under different assumptions, and their value is in that exploration, not in certainty.

The limitations of models include complex feedback loops that are hard to quantify, such as cloud cover and ice albedo, incomplete historical data, and the unpredictability of future human behaviour, including policy, technology and emissions. A good answer says that models are the best tool available, not that they are perfect, and explains the nature of the uncertainty. It does not say that models are unreliable in the sense of being useless, because they are not; it says that they have limitations and that the limitations matter for how the results should be interpreted.

The distinction between a model and a prediction is useful here. A model is a representation of the system; a prediction is what the model says might happen under a particular scenario. The uncertainty in the prediction comes from both the model and the scenario, and a good answer recognises both. If you can say that, you can answer the question without either dismissing models or treating them as certain. The examiners are after the balanced answer, not the extreme one.

18. The effects of climate change on plants, animals and development

The effects of climate change include changing rainfall patterns and changes in seasonal cycles, which affect the distribution of species, their development and life cycles. Temperature affects enzyme activity, so it can affect metabolism and development directly as well as shifting the ranges of species. Phenological changes, the timing of flowering, breeding, migration and other seasonal events, are evidence of these effects. The point is that climate change is not just a temperature story; it is a biology story because organisms are sensitive to the conditions.

A good answer says that the effects of climate change include changing rainfall patterns and seasonal cycles, that these affect species distribution, development and life cycles, and that temperature affects enzyme activity and can affect metabolism and development.
