title: Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance — Study Notes
content:
Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 1. The mole is the bridge between the mass you can weigh and the number of particles a reaction actually uses, so every quantitative question in the course depends on it.

Relative masses and the mole

  • Relative atomic mass (Ar) and relative molecular mass (Mr) are based on the carbon-12 scale.
  • One mole contains the Avogadro constant, 6.02 × 10²³ particles, and the molar mass in g mol⁻¹ equals Mr numerically.
  • Moles: n = m / M. Rearrange to find mass (m = n × M) or molar mass (M = m / n).

Empirical and molecular formulae

  • Convert percentage (or mass) composition to moles, divide by the smallest value and multiply until the ratios are whole numbers.
  • The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula: n = Mr / Mr(empirical formula).

Equations and reacting masses

  • Balance equations by conserving each element, then use the coefficients as mole ratios.
  • Limiting reagent: work out the moles each reactant could give, then take the smallest.
  • Percentage yield = actual yield / theoretical yield × 100.

Solutions and gases

  • Concentration c = n / V, with V in dm³ (cm³ ÷ 1000). Titration data follow the same route.
  • At room temperature and pressure one mole of gas occupies 24 dm³, so n = V / 24.

Exam tip: write the unit on every line of working, and check that your final answer has the same number of significant figures as the least precise data given.

title: Transformations and Vectors — Study Notes
content:
Transformations and Vectors

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): reflection, rotation, translation, enlargement (incl. negative SF); vector notation, resultant, magnitude, vector geometry.

1. Transformations — full descriptions

  • Reflection: mirror line (x = 0, y = x, y = −x…).
  • Rotation: centre, angle, direction (anticlockwise positive).
  • Translation: column vector.
  • Enlargement: centre + scale factor; negative SF inverts through the centre.

"Enlargement, SF 2, centre (0, 3)" — every word earns a mark.

2. Combined transformations

Apply right-to-left: "reflect in y = x, then rotate 90°" — rotate the reflected image.

3. Vectors

  • Column vector (x; y); magnitude = √(x² + y²).
  • Resultant by component addition; parallel vectors are scalar multiples.
  • Position vectors: AB = OB − OA.

Example: A(1, 2), B(4, 6): AB = (3; 4), |AB| = 5.

4. Vector geometry

Midpoint of AB = ½(a + b). Prove collinearity: show AB = k·BC (shared point). Prove parallelogram: AB = DC. Use route paths: AC = AB + BC.

Exam tips: tracing paper is allowed for transformations; in proofs, end with a conclusion sentence ("hence A, B, C are collinear").

Translations

A translation moves every point the same distance in the same direction, described by a column vector (x; y): x units across (positive to the right) and y units up (positive upwards). The shape and orientation do not change.

Reflections, rotations and enlargements

A reflection is described by its mirror line, such as x = 2 or y = x. A rotation needs its centre, angle and direction. An enlargement needs its centre and scale factor; a negative scale factor inverts the image. Check the image by measuring its distance from the centre.

Vectors and magnitude

Write a column vector as (x; y). Its magnitude is √(x² + y²). Adding vectors adds the corresponding components, and multiplying by a scalar multiplies each component. The vector from A to B is found as the position vector of B minus the position vector of A.

title: A2 Level Chemistry: Entropy and Energetics
content:
A2 Level Chemistry: Entropy and Energetics

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 12 covers the concept of entropy and energetics, including the relationship between enthalpy, entropy, and the feasibility of reactions. This topic explains that enthalpy alone does not decide whether a reaction happens, and that entropy measures how energy and matter are spread out. The Gibbs energy combines enthalpy and entropy to predict feasibility.

Entropy

Entropy S measures the disorder or the number of ways energy can be dispersed. Its standard unit is J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Entropy increases when a solid melts or dissolves, when a liquid evaporates, and when the number of gas molecules increases. Entropy decreases when gas molecules condense or when a crystal forms from solution.

  • Entropy increases with temperature.
  • Entropy increases as solid, liquid, gas.
  • Perfect crystals at zero kelvin have zero entropy.
  • Standard entropy values are given in data books.
  • The entropy change for a reaction is ΔS = Σ S(products) − Σ S(reactants).

Entropy Changes

Entropy changes occur during changes of state, dissolving of a solid ionic lattice, and reactions in which there is a change in the number of moles from reactants to products.

  • ΔS = +ve for endothermic processes.
  • ΔS = -ve for exothermic processes.
  • ΔS = +ve for increase in moles of gas.
  • ΔS = -ve for decrease in moles of gas.

Total Entropy Change

The total entropy change is ΔS total = ΔS system + ΔS surroundings. For the surroundings, ΔS surroundings = −ΔH / T.

  • ΔS total = ΔS system + ΔS surroundings.
  • ΔS surroundings = −ΔH / T.

Gibbs Free Energy

The Gibbs energy change is ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, where T is in kelvin. ΔH is in J mol⁻¹ and ΔS in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, so convert ΔH from kJ to J before calculating.

  • ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
  • A reaction is feasible when ΔG is negative.
  • When ΔG = 0 the system is at equilibrium.

Temperature and Feasibility

For a reaction with positive ΔH and positive ΔS, ΔG becomes negative above the temperature T = ΔH / ΔS. High temperature therefore makes the reaction feasible.

  • For a reaction with ΔH positive and ΔS positive, ΔG becomes negative above T = ΔH / ΔS.
  • For a reaction with ΔH positive and ΔS negative, ΔG is always positive, so the reaction is never feasible.

Worked Example

For CaCO3 → CaO + CO2, ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. The temperature at which ΔG = 0 is T = 178 000 / 161 = 1106 K, so the decomposition becomes feasible above about 1100 K.

Thermodynamic Stability and Kinetic Stability

Thermodynamic stability refers to the feasibility of a reaction, while kinetic stability refers to the rate of the reaction.

  • Thermodynamic stability: ΔG negative.
  • Kinetic stability: slow reaction rate.

Standard Enthalpy Change of Atomisation

The standard enthalpy change of atomisation is the energy required to break one mole of a substance into its constituent atoms.

  • ΔH atomisation = energy required to break one mole of a substance into its constituent atoms.

Electron Affinity

Electron affinity is the energy released when an electron is added to an atom.

  • Electron affinity = energy released when an electron is added to an atom.

Lattice Energy

Lattice energy is the energy released when one mole of an ionic solid is formed from its gaseous ions.

  • Lattice energy = energy released when one mole of an ionic solid is formed from its gaseous ions.

Born-Haber Cycle

A Born-Haber cycle is a diagram that shows the energy changes involved in the formation of an ionic solid from its constituent elements.

  • Born-Haber cycle: diagram showing energy changes involved in the formation of an ionic solid.

Covalent Bonding

Covalent bonding refers to the sharing of electrons between atoms.

  • Covalent bonding: sharing of electrons between atoms.

Polarisation of Anions

Polarisation of anions refers to the distortion of the electron cloud of an anion by a nearby cation.

  • Polarisation of anions: distortion of electron cloud of an anion by a nearby cation.

Enthalpy Change of Solution

Enthalpy change of solution is the energy change involved in the dissolution of a substance.

  • Enthalpy change of solution = energy change involved in the dissolution of a substance.

Enthalpy Change of Hydration

Enthalpy change of hydration is the energy change involved in the hydration of an ion.

  • Enthalpy change of hydration = energy change involved in the hydration of an ion.

Typical Mistakes

  • Forgetting to convert ΔH from kJ to J before calculating ΔG.
  • Not using the correct units for ΔS and ΔH.
  • Not considering the sign of ΔS and ΔH when determining the feasibility of a reaction.

Exam-Style Questions

  1. What is the entropy change for the reaction CaCO3 → CaO + CO2? Answer: ΔS = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
  2. What is the temperature at which the reaction CaCO3 → CaO + CO2 becomes feasible? Answer: T = 1106 K.
  3. What is the lattice energy of an ionic solid? Answer: Lattice energy = energy released when one mole of an ionic solid is formed from its gaseous ions.

To revise this topic, make sure to understand the concepts of entropy, Gibbs free energy, and thermodynamic stability. Practice calculating ΔG and determining the feasibility of reactions. Also, make sure to remember the typical mistakes and how to avoid them. After revising this topic, move on to the next topic, which covers the kinetics of chemical reactions.

Detailed Born-Haber Cycle Calculations

Constructing a Born-Haber cycle requires applying Hess's Law to equate the enthalpy change of formation of an ionic compound to the sum of its stepwise enthalpy changes: atomisation of the metal, first (and subsequent) ionisation energies of the metal, atomisation of the non-metal, electron affinities of the non-metal, and lattice energy. For magnesium chloride, MgCl2, the cycle starts with Mg(s) + Cl2(g) going to MgCl2(s). The steps are: enthalpy of atomisation of Mg, first and second ionisation energies of Mg, twice the enthalpy of atomisation of chlorine (or bond enthalpy of Cl2), twice the first electron affinity of chlorine, and lattice energy. Rearranging the energy level loop allows any single unknown enthalpy term to be calculated.

  • Write the thermochemical equation for formation at the bottom level.
  • Draw upward arrows for endothermic processes: atomisation, ionisation energies, and bond dissociation.
  • Draw downward arrows for exothermic processes: electron affinities and lattice energy.
  • Set the sum of energy changes along the direct route equal to the alternative pathway route.

Worked Example: Born-Haber Cycle for Sodium Chloride

Calculate the lattice energy of sodium chloride, NaCl, using the following standard enthalpy changes: enthalpy of formation of NaCl = −411 kJ mol⁻¹, enthalpy of atomisation of Na = +107 kJ mol⁻¹, first ionisation energy of Na = +496 kJ mol⁻¹, enthalpy of atomisation of Cl2 = +121 kJ mol⁻¹, and first electron affinity of Cl = −364 kJ mol⁻¹. The equation linking these is: ΔHf = ΔHat(Na) + IE1(Na) + 1/2 ΔHdiss(Cl2) + EA1(Cl) + Lattice Energy. Substituting the values: −411 = 107 + 496 + 121 + (−364) + Lattice Energy. Solving gives: −411 = 360 + Lattice Energy, so Lattice Energy = −411 − 360 = −771 kJ mol⁻¹.

Experimental Versus Theoretical Lattice Energies

Perfect ionic model assumes spherical point charges with 100 percent electrostatic attraction. When experimental lattice energies obtained from Born-Haber cycles are more exothermic than theoretical values calculated from electrostatic theory, it indicates that additional bonding character is present. This extra stability arises from partial covalent character caused by the polarisation of the anion.

  • Larger difference between experimental and theoretical values signifies greater covalent character.
  • Polarisation is promoted by small, highly charged cations (high charge density) and large, easily polarisable anions.
  • Fajans' rules help rationalize these trends across different halides and oxides.

Hydration Enthalpies and Enthalpy of Solution

Enthalpy change of solution is the enthalpy change when one mole of a solute dissolves in water to form an infinitely dilute solution. This is related to lattice energy and hydration enthalpies by the equation: ΔHsol = Lattice Energy + Σ ΔHhyd(ions). Because lattice energy is endothermic when viewed as breaking the lattice (positive value) and hydration is exothermic (negative value), the overall enthalpy of solution can be slightly positive, zero, or negative. For sparingly soluble salts, ΔHsol is strongly positive.

  • Hydration enthalpy is always exothermic (negative) due to ion-dipole attractions between the gaseous ions and water molecules.
  • Magnitude of hydration enthalpy increases with increasing ionic charge and decreasing ionic radius.
  • Magnitude of lattice energy also increases with high charge and small radius, meaning lattice energy and hydration enthalpy tend to counteract each other across periodic trends.

Solubility Trends in Group 1 and Group 2 Compounds

The solubility of ionic compounds depends on the balance between lattice energy and hydration enthalpies, alongside the entropy change of the system and surroundings. Down Group 2, both lattice energy and hydration enthalpies decrease in magnitude as the cation radius increases, but hydration enthalpy decreases faster for smaller anions (like sulfates) compared to larger anions (like hydroxides).

  • Group 2 sulfates become less soluble down the group because the hydration enthalpy drops faster than the lattice energy, making ΔHsol increasingly endothermic.
  • Group 2 hydroxides become more soluble down the group because lattice energy decreases more rapidly than hydration enthalpy, making ΔHsol less endothermic or more exothermic.
  • Overall feasibility of dissolving requires calculating ΔStotal using ΔHsol and the entropy change of the solution process.

Typical Mistakes in Energetics and Born-Haber Cycles

  • Omitting the stoichiometric multipliers when using bond enthalpies or atomisation energies for diatomic gases like chlorine or oxygen.
  • Confusing first and second electron affinities, where second electron affinities are endothermic due to repulsion with the incoming electron.
  • Forgetting that lattice energy in standard definitions is exothermic, but must be treated with the correct sign when substituting into energy cycle equations depending on the cycle direction used.

Exam-Style Questions and Worked Solutions

  1. Define the standard enthalpy change of atomisation. Answer: The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element in its standard state under standard conditions. Credit is earned by mentioning 'one mole of gaseous atoms' and 'element in its standard state'.
  2. Explain why the experimental lattice energy of silver iodide is significantly more exothermic than the theoretical value. Answer: Silver ions have a d-block configuration that polarises the large iodide ion effectively, introducing covalent character which releases extra energy. Credit is earned by linking cation polarisation of the anion to increased stability.
  3. Calculate the enthalpy of solution of potassium chloride given that its lattice energy is −701 kJ mol⁻¹ and the sum of the hydration enthalpies of its ions is −684 kJ mol⁻¹. Answer: ΔHsol = Lattice Energy + Σ ΔHhyd = 701 (if defined as formation) or using standard sign conventions, ΔHsol = −684 − (−701) = +17 kJ mol⁻¹ (or using the exact cycle definition, −701 + 684 = −17 kJ mol⁻¹ depending on data book sign convention for lattice energy release vs absorption). Step for credit: showing ΔHsol = Lattice Energy + Hydration Enthalpies with proper sign substitution.

title: Binomial Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Binomial Distribution

When Binomial Applies

X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

  • a fixed number n of identical trials,
  • each trial ends in success or failure,
  • constant success probability p,
  • trials are independent.

Check all four before using the model — "justifying a binomial model" is a real exam question.

The Formula

P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The ⁿCᵣ counts which r of the n trials were the successes.

Example: X ~ B(5, 0.3). P(X = 2) = ¹⁰C₂? No — ⁵C₂ × 0.3² × 0.7³ = 10 × 0.09 × 0.343 = 0.3087.

Cumulative Probabilities

P(X ≤ 2) = P(0) + P(1) + P(2). "At least" questions convert by the complement: P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(X ≤ 1). Keep one extra decimal place in intermediate steps to avoid rounding drift.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 − p)

For X ~ B(20, 0.4): E(X) = 8 and Var(X) = 4.8.

Modelling Decisions

If trials are dependent (drawing without replacement from a small population) binomial is not appropriate. If p changes between trials it is not binomial. When n is large and p small, the binomial is approximately Poisson — but at A2 you usually stay exact.

Exam tips: identify n and p in words before touching the calculator. For P(X ≥ k) always rewrite as 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1). Tables give cumulative values — use them rather than summing by hand.

Exam method: binomial probabilities

If X ~ B(n, p) then X counts successes in n independent trials, each with probability p. P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The mean is np and the variance is np(1 - p).

Check the conditions first: a fixed number of trials, two outcomes, a constant p and independent trials. If any condition fails, the binomial model does not apply.

Exam cue: Always state n and p before calculating, and say which condition you are checking. For P(X ≥ r) or P(X > r), use the complement 1 − P(X ≤ r − 1), read from the cumulative table or calculator, and state the final probability to three significant figures.

Worked example: a binomial probability

A biased coin lands on heads with probability 0.3. Let X be the number of heads in 10 throws, so X ~ B(10, 0.3). The probability of exactly 3 heads is P(X = 3) = C(10, 3) × 0.3³ × 0.7⁷ = 120 × 0.027 × 0.08235 = 0.2668 (to 4 decimal places). The coefficient 120 counts the arrangements of the 3 heads among 10 throws, and it is needed because the heads may fall in any of those positions.

At least one success

For P(X ≥ 1), use the complement: P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − P(X = 0) = 1 − 0.7¹⁰ = 1 − 0.02825 = 0.9718. Examiners look for this shortcut, and writing the full sum from X = 1 to X = 10 is both slower and more error-prone.

Checking the mean and variance

  • Mean: E(X) = np = 10 × 0.3 = 3.
  • Variance: Var(X) = np(1 − p) = 10 × 0.3 × 0.7 = 2.1, so the standard deviation is √2.1 = 1.45 (to 2 decimal places).

Use these values to judge whether a stated answer is sensible: a mean of 3 with a standard deviation of 1.45 means most results fall between 1 and 5.

Exam point: a binomial model needs a fixed number of trials, independence, and the same probability of success on each trial. If the items are drawn without replacement from a small group, the probability changes after each draw and the binomial model is not valid.

title: Exam technique: Operating Systems
content:
### What earns the marks
To earn full marks on this topic, students need to demonstrate their understanding of the operating system's roles and functions, as stated in 4.1. For example, when asked to explain how an OS manages memory, students should describe the process of paging and segmentation, and explain how virtual memory extends RAM to disk when RAM is full. The command words that appear in questions are explain, describe, and state. Explain earns the most marks, as it requires students to provide a detailed description of a concept, such as interrupts and buffers.
### Traps
One common mistake is to confuse the terms paging and segmentation. Paging refers to the process of dividing memory into fixed-size blocks, while segmentation refers to the process of dividing memory into variable-size blocks. Another mistake is to think that multitasking is the same as multithreading. Multitasking refers to the ability of an OS to run multiple processes simultaneously, while multithreading refers to the ability of a process to run multiple threads simultaneously.
### Memory hooks
A useful mnemonic to remember the functions of an OS is MANPS: Memory management, Application management, Network management, Process management, and Security. Another memory hook is to think of the OS as a manager that allocates resources, such as memory and I/O devices, to applications. A shortcut to understanding virtual memory is to think of it as a way to extend RAM to disk when RAM is full.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 10-15% of the total marks on the paper. Students should budget around 10-15 minutes to answer questions on this topic, depending on the length and complexity of the questions.

title: Exam technique: Abstract Data Types
content:
### What earns the marks
For ADT choice, the access pattern stated earns the mark: LIFO for stacks, FIFO for queues, keyed jumps for BSTs. For traversals, the visit order written (root-left-right for preorder) earns each mark. For linked structures, pointer relinking described earns the insertion mark without any shifting claim.
### Traps
Error: queues for undo. Correction: undo is LIFO, so stack. Error: inorder claimed as root-first. Correction: preorder is root-first. Error: arrays claimed best for mid-list churn. Correction: shifting costs every insert.
### Worked example
Trace a stack. Push A, push B, push C, then pop, then push D, then pop. After the three pushes the top is C, so the first pop returns C. Pushing D leaves the stack as A, B, D, so the second pop returns D and B is left on top. A stack is last in, first out, so the top item always leaves first.
### Check yourself
State which structure a printer queue uses and why, in one sentence that names the order of service. A print queue serves the first job submitted first, so it is first in, first out.

### Worked example
Trace a stack. Push A, push B, push C, then pop, then push D, then pop. After the three pushes the top is C, so the first pop returns C. Pushing D leaves the stack as A, B, D, so the second pop returns D and B is left on top. A stack is last in, first out, so the top item always leaves first.

title: Exam technique: Transformations and Vectors
content:
### What earns the marks
For translations and vector arithmetic, each component computed separately earns credit: show x and y lines. For magnitude, the root-of-sum-of-squares line earns the method mark before evaluation. For reflections and rotations, the coordinate rule stated ((y; -x) for 90 degrees clockwise) earns the method mark. For describing transformations, all three of type, centre or line, and size or angle are needed for full marks.
### Traps
Error: writing column vectors as bracket rows that lose a row. Correction: use (x; y) form and keep both components. Error: (100) or 14 for the magnitude of (6; 8). Correction: square, add, then root. Error: (-y; x) for a clockwise rotation. Correction: clockwise is (y; -x). Error: negating both coordinates for a single-axis reflection. Correction: one axis changes, the other stays.
### Worked example
Point A(1; 2) is translated by the vector (3; -1), giving A'(4; 1). Reflecting A' in the x-axis gives (4; -1). Rotating the point (3; -1) 90 degrees clockwise about the origin gives (-1; -3), using the rule (x; y) to (y; -x). Scaling (1; 2) by a factor of 2 from the origin gives (2; 4). Write each coordinate step on its own line.
### Check yourself
A point at (6; 8) has magnitude sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = sqrt(100) = 10. Explain why the magnitude is never the sum 6 + 8 = 14. The magnitude uses the root of the sum of squares, so the components do not add directly.

title: Kinematics — Study Notes
content:
Kinematics

Definitions

  • Displacement s: distance in a given direction (vector)
  • Velocity v: rate of change of displacement, v = ds/dt
  • Acceleration a: rate of change of velocity, a = dv/dt

Graphs

  • Gradient of a displacement–time graph = velocity
  • Gradient of a velocity–time graph = acceleration
  • Area under a velocity–time graph = displacement
  • Area under an acceleration–time graph = change in velocity

SUVAT (uniform acceleration only)

EquationMissing
v = u + ats
s = ut + ½at²v
v² = u² + 2ast
s = ½(u + v)ta

Sign convention matters: take up as positive and g = −9.81 m s⁻² for falling objects.

Projectiles

Resolve into independent components: horizontal at constant velocity (s = ut), vertical under gravity (SUVAT).

Example: a ball fired at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30°: uₓ = 20 cos 30° ≈ 17.3 m s⁻¹, u_y = 20 sin 30° = 10 m s⁻¹. Time of flight = 2u_y/g ≈ 2.04 s; range = uₓ × t ≈ 35 m.

Exam tips: state which direction is positive; projectile questions are two separate 1-D problems joined by time.

Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI12 Unit 1, Topic 4 Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation. It covers plant cell ultrastructure and the functions of the organelles and cell wall components, starch and cellulose and how their structure fits their role, how cellulose microfibrils and secondary thickening give physical properties to xylem and sclerenchyma fibres, the similarities and differences between sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem and their structure, position and function, the light microscope practical on transverse sections, the uses of plant fibres and starch in sustainability, the importance of water and mineral ions to plants and the practical on mineral deficiency, the tensile strength practical, bacterial growth requirements, antimicrobial plant substances and the aseptic practical, the development of drug testing from Withering's digitalis to modern three-phased testing, classification and the species concept and the three-domain system, biodiversity and endemism and how they are measured, species richness and the heterozygosity index, the index of diversity and how it is compared between habitats, and the concept of niche and examples of adaptations — behavioural, anatomical and physiological. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Plant cell ultrastructure: what is in a plant cell and why

Plant cells share the common eukaryotic features with animal cells — a plasma membrane (cell surface membrane), cytoplasm and ribosomes — but add several structures that animal cells do not have. The cell wall is a rigid outer layer of cellulose microfibrils embedded in a gel-like matrix; it gives shape and support, prevents the cell from bursting when turgid, and limits uncontrolled expansion. Chloroplasts are double-membraned organelles containing chlorophyll and the enzymes for photosynthesis; inside, stacked membranes (thylakoids, often stacked into grana) carry out the light-dependent reactions, and the surrounding stroma contains the enzymes for the light-independent reactions. Amyloplasts are colourless plastids that store starch; they are found especially in storage organs such as potato tubers. Vacuoles are membrane-bound sacs; a large central vacuole in mature plant cells is filled with cell sap — a watery solution of sugars, salts, pigments and waste — surrounded by the tonoplast membrane, and it maintains turgor pressure and gives the cell its rigidity. Plasmodesmata are thread-like channels through the cell walls of adjacent plant cells, connecting the cytoplasm and allowing communication and transport between cells. Pits are thin regions in the cell wall where the wall is localy thinner or absent, allowing water and solutes to pass between cells; the middle lamella is the layer that cements together the cell walls of adjacent cells. Ribosomes are present (80S in the cytoplasm) and the nucleus, nucleolus, mitochondria and golgi apparatus are all present, as in animal cells, except that plant cells do not have centrioles (higher plants lack them, though they still divide).

2. Recognising plant organelles from electron micrographs

On an electron micrograph of a plant cell you should be able to recognise the plasma membrane, nucleus with nucleolus, chloroplasts with their stacked thylakoid membranes (grana), mitochondria, rough endoplasmic reticulum with ribosomes, golgi (dictyosomes in plants), a large central vacuole with the tonoplast, the cell wall (with middle lamella where two cells meet), and plasmodesmata. Chloroplasts are especially characteristic: the grana appear as stacks of disc-like membranes. Amyloplasts appear as colourless, starch-filled plastids without grana. A good exercise is to label each of these in an EM image and to explain the function of each. Compare the plant cell with an animal cell: plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts, a large central vacuole and plasmodesmata, and generally no centrioles, and their shape is more regular because of the wall.

3. Starch and cellulose: polysaccharides that do different jobs

Starch and cellulose are both polymers of glucose, but alpha-glucose for starch and beta-glucose for cellulose, and that difference determines their properties. Alpha-glucose has the hydroxyl groups on the same side of the ring (in the usual representation), so when polymerised with 1,4-glycosidic bonds the chain coils into a helix, forming amylose, and with 1,6-branches forming amylopectin — compact, helical and branched, so starch is an excellent storage material: compact to pack a lot of glucose into little space, and with no osmotic effect, because the large insoluble starch granules do not draw water into the cell by osmosis. Cellulose is made from beta-glucose, in which the hydroxyl on carbon 1 is on the opposite side, so when linked the chain is straight rather than coiled; the linear chains run parallel and form many hydrogen bonds between adjacent chains, making strong cellulose microfibrils. Cellulose microfibrils are the main structural component of the cell wall, giving strength and rigidity; the way they are arranged determines the properties of the cell and of the whole plant. The structure of starch suits it for storage in plant cells; the structure of cellulose suits it for strength and support — two polymers from the same monomer with very different roles because of the different glycosidic bonds and the different shape of the chain.

4. Cellulose microfibrils, secondary thickening and the properties of xylem and sclerenchyma

The physical properties of plant tissues depend on how the cellulose microfibrils are arranged. In a young, growing cell the microfibrils are laid down mainly at right angles to the direction of growth, so the cell can expand in length; when growth stops, the cell can become strengthened by secondary thickening — more cellulose and, in some cells, lignin deposited on the inside of the primary wall — which makes the wall rigid and waterproof. In sclerenchyma fibres, the cells die at maturity and are left with heavily thickened, lignified walls, often with the microfibrils arranged in spiral or ring patterns; the result is strong, flexible but tough fibres that give mechanical support and can be used by humans (for example in textiles and ropes). In xylem vessels, the wall is lignified and the cells are dead at maturity, forming long tubes with the end walls broken down or absent — the vessel elements are linked end to end to form a continuous tube for the transport of water and mineral ions, and the lignified thickening (in rings, spirals or nets) prevents collapse under the negative pressure of the transpiration stream. So the arrangement of cellulose microfibrils and the deposition of lignin determine what a plant part can do: support, flexibility, or transport of water under tension. The secondary thickening of xylem and the lignification of sclerenchyma are the adaptations that let land plants grow tall and stand upright and transport water from the roots to the leaves.

5. Sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem: structure, position and function

Sclerenchyma fibres and xylem vessels provide support and, for xylem, transport; phloem translocates organic solutes. Sclerenchyma fibres are long, narrow cells with thick lignified walls and a small lumen, dead at maturity; they occur in bundles and, because of their strength and flexibility, they give support to stems and leaves and can be used in textiles and ropes. Xylem vessels are long, continuous tubes formed from vessel elements with lignified walls and pits in the walls, dead at maturity with no contents, and their function is transport of water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves — and they also provide support. Phloem is a living tissue; sieve tube elements are the conducting cells, arranged end to end with perforated end walls (sieve plates) between them, reduced cytoplasm at the edges and no nucleus at maturity; each sieve tube element has a companion cell beside it, connected by plasmodesmata, which keeps the sieve element alive and supplies it with ATP, because the sieve element itself has lost its nucleus and most organelles. Phloem transports organic solutes (mainly sucrose, in solution in water) from sources (leaves, storage organs) to sinks (growing points, roots, developing fruits) by mass flow driven by the pressure gradient built up by the loading of sucrose into the sieve tubes. Compare: sclerenchyma fibres = support, dead, lignified; xylem vessels = support and water/mineral transport, dead, lignified, open tube; phloem = translocation of organic solutes, living sieve tubes with companion cells, perforated end walls, no lignin.

6. Core Practical 7 — transverse sections of roots, stems and leaves

Use a light microscope to make observations, draw and label plan diagrams of transverse sections of roots, stems and leaves, and to observe and label cells of plant tissues, identifying sclerenchyma fibres, phloem, sieve tubes and xylem vessels and their location. To make a transverse section, cut a very thin slice across a stem or root with a razor blade (a sharp blade and a steady hand or a sectioning technique), float the section onto water on a slide, lower a coverslip at an angle, stain if needed (for example with toluidine blue or iodine) to distinguish lignified xylem, sclerenchyma and phloem, and observe under the microscope at several magnifications. In a stem transverse section, note the positions of the epidermis, cortex, the vascular bundles (with xylem toward the inside and phloem toward the outside, and sclerenchyma fibres often outside the phloem in a bundle cap), and the pith in the centre; in roots the vascular tissue is central. Draw a plan diagram (an outline of the whole section showing the arrangement of tissues, not the cells) with the correct relative sizes and positions, label the tissues, give a title and magnification. Then observe and label the cells: look for the thick lignified walls of xylem and sclerenchyma, the sieve plates and companion cells of phloem, and the thin-walled cells of the cortex and pith.

7. Plant fibres and starch in sustainability

Plant fibres and starch can contribute to sustainability and to replacing oil-based plastics. Plant fibres (from sclerenchyma or from phloem fibres) are strong, renewable and biodegradable, and they can be used in textiles, paper, building materials and composites that replace oil-based plastics and synthetic fibres; water transport in plants today parallels the transport of sap and provides a model for how plants already do this. Starch can be used to make bioplastics — for example, starch can be processed into film-forming materials suitable for packaging, plates and disposable items — and because starch is a renewable, biodegradable material made from crops such as potatoes, maize or cassava, it can replace oil-based plastics in some uses. Using plant fibres and starch reduces reliance on oil, is renewable and can be more sustainable if the crops are grown responsibly; but there are trade-offs: land, water and energy for the crops, possible competition with food production, and the need to assess the whole life cycle. The use of plant products to replace oil-based plastics is a topic that connects plant structure (cellulose and starch), to sustainability, to human decisions informed by science.

8. Water and inorganic ions to plants, and mineral deficiency

Plants need water for photosynthesis (a reactant and the medium in which it happens), for transport (water is the solvent for minerals and for sucrose in the phloem), for support (turgor pressure keeps non-woody parts rigid), and for cooling (transpiration). Water enters the roots by osmosis from the soil and moves up the xylem. Inorganic ions are essential: nitrate ions (NO3-) are needed for making amino acids, proteins, DNA and chlorophyll — a deficiency causes stunted growth and yellowing of older leaves (chlorosis); calcium ions are needed for the middle lamella (pectin in the cell wall) and for cell membranes — a deficiency gives stunted growth and necrosis of the growing point and young leaves; magnesium ions are the central atom in chlorophyll — a deficiency causes chlorosis of the older leaves. A recommended additional practical is to investigate plant mineral deficiencies: grow plants in a solution with all minerals (complete) and in solutions missing one of nitrate, calcium or magnesium, observe and measure the effects on growth and leaf colour over weeks, and explain the results in terms of the roles of the missing ion.

9. Core Practical 8 — tensile strength of plant fibres

Determine the tensile strength of plant fibres — the force a fibre can take before it breaks. A typical method: take strands of a plant fibre (for example the fibres from celery stalks or nettle stems, or a piece of a plant stem with visible fibres), clamp one end, hang weights from the other, and add weights until the fibre breaks; record the mass (converted to a force, weight = mass × g) needed to break the fibre. Repeat for several fibres, present the results, and compare fibres from different plants or different parts of a plant. Safety: sharp blades and falling weights. The practical shows how the arrangement of cellulose and lignin gives the fibre its strength, and connects the cell-level structure to a macroscopic useful property.

10. Conditions for bacterial growth

Bacteria need certain conditions to grow: a supply of nutrients (carbon, nitrogen, minerals and, for some, specific organic factors), water, a suitable temperature (most pathogenic bacteria around 37 °C, though many grow across a range), oxygen (some need it — aerobic bacteria — some do not — anaerobic bacteria — and some can manage with or without), a suitable pH, and, for many, time to multiply. In the laboratory these conditions can be met and controlled: cultures are grown in nutrient broth or on agar plates, at a set temperature (often 25 °C for environmental organisms and 37 °C for those that grow at body temperature), with or without oxygen, and in sterile conditions so that only the desired organism grows. Aseptic technique is essential to avoid contaminating the culture or releasing harmful bacteria into the environment — sterilise equipment (by flame or autoclave), work near a flame to create an upward air current, work quickly and cover the plates, and dispose of cultures by sterilising before disposal.

11. Antimicrobial plant substances and the aseptic practical

Substances derived from plants can have antimicrobial and other therapeutic properties. Some plant extracts inhibit the growth of bacteria or fungi — for example, garlic has been traditionally used and does have some antibacterial effects; other plants yield useful compounds (aspirin from willow bark, morphine from poppies, and many modern drugs are derived from plants). A recommended additional practical is to investigate the antimicrobial properties of plants, including aseptic techniques for the safe handling of bacteria: prepare agar plates, use sterile swabs or paper discs impregnated with different plant extracts, incubate and measure the zones of inhibition around the discs — the diameter of the clear zone where bacteria did not grow — and compare the effectiveness of different extracts or the same extract at different concentrations. Use aseptic technique: sterilise the discs and loops, work near a flame, spread the bacteria in a controlled way, seal the plates with tape (but do not seal all the way so they do not become anaerobic), and incubate at a safe temperature. Measure the zones of inhibition and record them, including in a table, and draw a conclusion about which extract is most effective and about concentration.

12. Drug testing: from Withering's digitalis soup to modern trials

The development of drug testing has moved from historic, uncontrolled methods to contemporary, rigorous protocols. William Withering's digitalis soup in the 18th century was an early use of a plant-derived medicine — foxglove (Digitalis) — for dropsy (oedema), tested by trial and observation on patients, but with no controls, no placebo, no blinding and no large sample, so the evidence was weak and mixed with other treatments. Modern drug testing uses a sequence of phases: pre-clinical testing in the lab and on animals; clinical trials in humans in three phases — Phase 1 tests safety in a small group, Phase 2 tests efficacy and side effects in a larger group of patients, and Phase 3 tests the drug against the current treatment or a placebo in a large group, in a double-blind trial (neither the patient nor the clinician knows which treatment is being used) so that expectations do not bias the result. Placebos are used to control for the placebo effect (improvement from the belief of being treated). The modern protocol — double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-centre, large trials — is far more reliable than Withering's soup, and it protects patients and produces trustworthy evidence. Students should be able to describe this progression and evaluate the designs.

13. Classification: organising life, the species concept and the three domains

Classification is a means of organising the variety of life based on relationships between organisms, using differences and similarities in phenotypes (observable features) and in genotypes (the DNA and the proteins the DNA codes for). It is built around the species concept — a species is a group of organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring — and a hierarchy of groups above it: genus, family, order, class, phylum and kingdom, with organisms grouped because they share common ancestry. The classification has changed as new data — especially molecular evidence from DNA and protein sequences — have come in, leading to critical evaluation of existing groupings and new taxonomic groupings. The three-domain system, based on molecular evidence, divides life into the Archaea, the Bacteria and the Eukarya (which includes all eukaryotes, plants, animals, fungi and protists); the Archaea are distinct from the Bacteria and include organisms that often live in extreme environments, and the evidence from ribosomal RNA sequences and other molecular data led to this reclassification, replacing the older five-kingdom system. The process of critical evaluation of new data by the scientific community — comparing, testing and debating — is what leads to new groupings and to science being self-correcting.

14. Biodiversity, endemism and threats from human activity

Biodiversity is the variety of life — the variety within a habitat, within a species or across the whole planet; it can refer to species richness (the number of different species in a habitat) or to genetic diversity within a species. Endemism is the state of a species being found only in one particular place (an endemic species, such as a plant found only on a particular island). Over time the variety of life has become extensive through evolution, but it is now being threatened by human activity — habitat destruction (deforestation, drainage, conversion to agriculture), over-exploitation (hunting, fishing, logging), pollution, the introduction of invasive species, and climate change, all of which can reduce biodiversity and cause extinctions. Biodiversity matters because it provides ecosystem services, genetic resources for medicines and crops, and is itself valuable; its loss affects ecosystems, food security and human health. Understanding the causes of the loss is important so that conservation measures can be designed to address them.

15. Measuring biodiversity: species richness, genetic diversity and heterozygosity

Biodiversity can be measured in different ways. Species richness — the number of different species in a given area — is one simple measure of biodiversity within a habitat; a habitat with more species is generally more diverse, though this ignores the abundance of each species (a habitat dominated by one common species and several rare ones may have the same species richness as one where all are equally common). Genetic diversity within a species can be measured by the heterozygosity index (also called heterozygosity): the proportion of individuals in a population that are heterozygous at a locus. It is calculated as the number of heterozygotes divided by the number of individuals in the population (for a single locus); a higher heterozygosity means more genetic diversity within that population. This matters because genetic diversity helps a population adapt to changes, resist disease and avoid the problems of inbreeding; loss of genetic diversity raises the risk of extinction.

16. Comparing habitats with the index of diversity

Biodiversity can be compared between different habitats using the formula for the index of diversity, D: D = (N(N−1)) / (Σ n(n−1)), where N is the total number of organisms of all species in the habitat, and n is the number of organisms of a particular species. Calculation: for each species, work out n(n−1); sum these to get Σ n(n−1); then divide N(N−1) by that sum to give D, the index of diversity. Worked example: in a habitat with species counts 10, 15, 5, 2 (N = 32): Σ n(n−1) = (10×9)+(15×14)+(5×4)+(2×1) = 90+210+20+2 = 322; N(N−1) = 32×31 = 992; D = 992 / 322 ≈ 3.08. A larger D means a more diverse habitat, because it reflects both the number of species and how evenly the individuals are distributed among them. To compare habitats, calculate D for each and compare the values, stating which is more diverse and what that suggests. The formula must be applied correctly: calculate n(n−1) for each species, sum them, and divide N(N−1) by the sum.

17. Niche and adaptations: behavioural, anatomical and physiological

A niche is the role of an organism in a habitat — the conditions in which it lives and the resources it uses, and how it interacts with other organisms; it is more than just the physical place (the habitat) where it lives, and no two species can occupy exactly the same niche for long because of competition. Adaptations are features that help an organism survive and reproduce in its niche, and they can be behavioural, anatomical or physiological. Behavioural adaptations are things the organism does — for example migration to avoid harsh conditions, hunting in packs, basking to warm up, or the specific foraging behaviour of a bird. Anatomical (structural) adaptations are physical features of the body — for example the shape of a bird's beak for its food, the camouflage colours of a prey animal, the thick fur of an arctic mammal, or the long beak of a nectar-feeding bird. Physiological adaptations are internal functions — for example a camel's ability to tolerate dehydration and to conserve water, the production of venom by a snake, the production of antifreeze proteins in some polar fish, or the specialised nitrogen excretion of desert animals. The concept of niche and the types of adaptation help explain how different organisms fit into their environments and how competition and adaptation shape communities.

18. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes section by section, checking that you can identify plant cell ultrastructure and organelles in an electron micrograph and state their functions, explain how starch and cellulose differ in structure and role, describe the secondary thickening and the properties of xylem vessels and sclerenchyma fibres, compare sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem in structure, position and function, carry out the transverse section and tensile strength practicals and explain the variables and safety, describe the conditions for bacterial growth and the aseptic practical, describe the development of drug testing from Withering's digitalis to modern three-phased trials and evaluate the designs, define classification and the species concept, describe the three-domain system and the molecular evidence for it, define biodiversity and endemism and the threats from human activity, carry out the species richness and heterozygosity and index of diversity calculations, and define niche and give behavioural, anatomical and physiological adaptations. After this topic, revise Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development (plant and animal cells, division) and Topic 5 Energy flow, ecosystems and the environment, because classification and biodiversity sit within ecology.

9. Core Practical 8 — tensile strength of plant fibres

Determine the tensile strength of plant fibres — the force a fibre can take before it breaks. A typical method: take strands of a plant fibre (for example the fibres from celery stalks or nettle stems, or a piece of a plant stem with visible fibres), clamp one end, hang weights from the other, and add weights until the fibre breaks; record the mass (converted to a force, weight = mass × g) needed to break the fibre. Repeat for several fibres, present the results, and compare fibres from different plants or different parts of a plant. Safety: sharp blades and falling weights. The practical shows how the arrangement of cellulose and lignin gives the fibre its strength, and connects the cell-level structure to a macroscopic useful property.

10. Conditions for bacterial growth

Bacteria need certain conditions to grow: a supply of nutrients (carbon, nitrogen, minerals and, for some, specific organic factors), water, a suitable temperature (most pathogenic bacteria around 37 °C, though many grow across a range), oxygen (some need it — aerobic bacteria — some do not — anaerobic bacteria — and some can manage with or without), a suitable pH, and, for many, time to multiply. In the laboratory these conditions can be met and controlled: cultures are grown in nutrient broth or on agar plates, at a set temperature (often 25 °C for environmental organisms and 37 °C for those that grow at body temperature), with or without oxygen, and in sterile conditions so that only the desired organism grows. Aseptic technique is essential to avoid contaminating the culture or releasing harmful bacteria into the environment — sterilise equipment (by flame or autoclave), work near a flame to create an upward air current, work quickly and cover the plates, and dispose of cultures by sterilising before disposal.

11. Antimicrobial plant substances and the aseptic practical

Substances derived from plants can have antimicrobial and other therapeutic properties. Some plant extracts inhibit the growth of bacteria or fungi — for example, garlic has been traditionally used and does have some antibacterial effects; other plants yield useful compounds (aspirin from willow bark, morphine from poppies, and many modern drugs are derived from plants). A recommended additional practical is to investigate the antimicrobial properties of plants, including aseptic techniques for the safe handling of bacteria: prepare agar plates, use sterile swabs or paper discs impregnated with different plant extracts, incubate and measure the zones of inhibition around the discs — the diameter of the clear zone where bacteria did not grow — and compare the effectiveness of different extracts or the same extract at different concentrations. Use aseptic technique: sterilise the discs and loops, work near a flame, spread the bacteria in a controlled way, seal the plates with tape (but do not seal all the way so they do not become anaerobic), and incubate at a safe temperature. Measure the zones of inhibition and record them, including in a table, and draw a conclusion about which extract is most effective and about concentration.

12. Drug testing: from Withering''s digitalis soup to modern trials

The development of drug testing has moved from historic, uncontrolled methods to contemporary, rigorous protocols. William Withering''s digitalis soup in the 18th century was an early use of a plant-derived medicine — foxglove (Digitalis) — for dropsy (oedema), tested by trial and observation on patients, but with no controls, no placebo, no blinding and no large sample, so the evidence was weak and mixed with other treatments. Modern drug testing uses a sequence of phases: pre-clinical testing in the lab and on animals; clinical trials in humans in three phases — Phase 1 tests safety in a small group, Phase 2 tests efficacy and side effects in a larger group of patients, and Phase 3 tests the drug against the current treatment or a placebo in a large group, in a double-blind trial (neither the patient nor the clinician knows which treatment is being used) so that expectations do not bias the result. Placebos are used to control for the placebo effect (improvement from the belief of being treated). The modern protocol — double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-centre, large trials — is far more reliable than Withering''s soup, and it protects patients and produces trustworthy evidence. Students should be able to describe this progression and evaluate the designs.

13. Classification: organising life, the species concept and the three domains

Classification is a means of organising the variety of life based on relationships between organisms, using differences and similarities in phenotypes (observable features) and in genotypes (the DNA and the proteins the DNA codes for). It is built around the species concept — a species is a group of organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring — and a hierarchy of groups above it: genus, family, order, class, phylum and kingdom, with organisms grouped because they share common ancestry. The classification has changed as new data — especially molecular evidence from DNA and protein sequences — have come in, leading to critical evaluation of existing groupings and new taxonomic groupings. The three-domain system, based on molecular evidence, divides life into the Archaea, the Bacteria and the Eukarya (which includes all eukaryotes, plants, animals, fungi and protists); the Archaea are distinct from the Bacteria and include organisms that often live in extreme environments, and the evidence from ribosomal RNA sequences and other molecular data led to this reclassification, replacing the older five-kingdom system. The process of critical evaluation of new data by the scientific community — comparing, testing and debating — is what leads to new groupings and to science being self-correcting.

14. Biodiversity, endemism and threats from human activity

Biodiversity is the variety of life — the variety within a habitat, within a species or across the whole planet; it can refer to species richness (the number of different species in a habitat) or to genetic diversity within a species. Endemism is the state of a species being found only in one particular place (an endemic species, such as a plant found only on a particular island). Over time the variety of life has become extensive through evolution, but it is now being threatened by human activity — habitat destruction (deforestation, drainage, conversion to agriculture), over-exploitation (hunting, fishing, logging), pollution, the introduction of invasive species, and climate change, all of which can reduce biodiversity and cause extinctions. Biodiversity matters because it provides ecosystem services, genetic resources for medicines and crops, and is itself valuable; its loss affects ecosystems, food security and human health. Understanding the causes of the loss is important so that conservation measures can be designed to address them.

15. Measuring biodiversity: species richness, genetic diversity and heterozygosity

Biodiversity can be measured in different ways. Species richness — the number of different species in a given area — is one simple measure of biodiversity within a habitat; a habitat with more species is generally more diverse, though this ignores the abundance of each species (a habitat dominated by one common species and several rare ones may have the same species richness as one where all are equally common). Genetic diversity within a species can be measured by the heterozygosity index (also called heterozygosity): the proportion of individuals in a population that are heterozygous at a locus. It is calculated as the number of heterozygotes divided by the number of individuals in the population (for a single locus); a higher heterozygosity means more genetic diversity within that population. This matters because genetic diversity helps a population adapt to changes, resist disease and avoid the problems of inbreeding; loss of genetic diversity raises the risk of extinction.

16. Comparing habitats with the index of diversity

Biodiversity can be compared between different habitats using the formula for the index of diversity, D: D = (N(N−1)) / (Σ n(n−1)), where N is the total number of organisms of all species in the habitat, and n is the number of organisms of a particular species. Calculation: for each species, work out n(n−1); sum these to get Σ n(n−1); then divide N(N−1) by that sum to give D, the index of diversity. Worked example: in a habitat with species counts 10, 15, 5, 2 (N = 32): Σ n(n−1) = (10×9)+(15×14)+(5×4)+(2×1) = 90+210+20+2 = 322; N(N−1) = 32×31 = 992; D = 992 / 322 ≈ 3.08. A larger D means a more diverse habitat, because it reflects both the number of species and how evenly the individuals are distributed among them. To compare habitats, calculate D for each and compare the values, stating which is more diverse and what that suggests. The formula must be applied correctly: calculate n(n−1) for each species, sum them, and divide N(N−1) by the sum.

17. Niche and adaptations: behavioural, anatomical and physiological

A niche is the role of an organism in a habitat — the conditions in which it lives and the resources it uses, and how it interacts with other organisms; it is more than just the physical place (the habitat) where it lives, and no two species can occupy exactly the same niche for long because of competition. Adaptations are features that help an organism survive and reproduce in its niche, and they can be behavioural, anatomical or physiological. Behavioural adaptations are things the organism does — for example migration to avoid harsh conditions, hunting in packs, basking to warm up, or the specific foraging behaviour of a bird. Anatomical (structural) adaptations are physical features of the body — for example the shape of a bird''s beak for its food, the camouflage colours of a prey animal, the thick fur of an arctic mammal, or the long beak of a nectar-feeding bird. Physiological adaptations are internal functions — for example a camel''s ability to tolerate dehydration and to conserve water, the production of venom by a snake, the production of antifreeze proteins in some polar fish, or the specialised nitrogen excretion of desert animals. The concept of niche and the types of adaptation help explain how different organisms fit into their environments and how competition and adaptation shape communities.

18. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes section by section, checking that you can identify plant cell ultrastructure and organelles in an electron micrograph and state their functions, explain how starch and cellulose differ in structure and role, describe the secondary thickening and the properties of xylem vessels and sclerenchyma fibres, compare sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem in structure, position and function, carry out the transverse section and tensile strength practicals and explain the variables and safety, describe the conditions for bacterial growth and the aseptic practical, describe the development of drug testing from Withering''s digitalis to modern three-phased trials and evaluate the designs, define classification and the species concept, describe the three-domain system and the molecular evidence for it, define biodiversity and endemism and the threats from human activity, carry out the species richness and heterozygosity and index of diversity calculations, and define niche and give behavioural, anatomical and physiological adaptations. After this topic, revise Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development (plant and animal cells, division) and Topic 5 Energy flow, ecosystems and the environment, because classification and biodiversity sit within ecology.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Simpson's index, applied to a quadrat with 10 daisies and 5 dandelions: N = 15, D = 1 − Σ(n ÷ N)² = 1 − [(10 ÷ 15)² + (5 ÷ 15)²] = 1 − (0.444 + 0.111) = 0.556. Use the index to compare two sites; a higher value means greater diversity.
  • Xylem and phloem: xylem transports water and minerals upwards and is made of dead, lignified cells with no end walls, so the water column is continuous. Phloem transports sucrose and amino acids in both directions and is made of living sieve tube elements with companion cells. Name the direction of transport and the living or dead state of the cells.
  • Cellulose versus starch: cellulose is made of β-glucose units linked alternately, which allows hydrogen bonding between chains, forming strong microfibrils. Starch is made of α-glucose, is coiled and is used for storage. The different glucose isomer explains the different shapes and functions.
  • Conservation: a protected area works only if the populations inside it are large enough to be viable. Name the factor, such as a wildlife corridor, that connects populations, because isolated populations lose genetic diversity over time.

title: Organic Synthesis — Study Notes
content:
Organic Synthesis

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 20. Organic synthesis plans a route from a starting material to a target molecule. You need to choose reagents and conditions, track functional groups and calculate the overall yield.

Planning a route

  • Retrosynthesis works backwards from the target: identify the functional group, then find a precursor that converts into it in one step.
  • Each step should be a known functional group interconversion with suitable reagents and conditions.
  • Carbon chain length can be increased with KCN, which turns a haloalkane into a nitrile. The nitrile can then be hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid or reduced to an amine.

Key interconversions

  • Primary alcohol to aldehyde: distillation with acidified dichromate(VI), so the aldehyde is removed before it oxidises further.
  • Primary alcohol to carboxylic acid: reflux with excess acidified dichromate(VI).
  • Aldehyde or ketone to alcohol: NaBH₄ (or LiAlH₄ for carboxylic acids and nitriles).
  • Alkene to haloalkane: addition of HBr. Alkene to alcohol: steam with an acid catalyst.
  • Nitrobenzene to phenylamine: reduction with Sn and concentrated HCl. Nitration of benzene is the first step of a route to phenylamine.

Yield calculations

  • Percentage yield = actual mass ÷ theoretical mass × 100.
  • Overall yield for a multi-step route is the product of the individual step yields. Two steps at 80% and 70% give 0.80 × 0.70 = 0.56, or 56% overall.
  • Atom economy measures the proportion of reactant atoms that end up in the desired product: (molar mass of desired product ÷ sum of molar masses of all products) × 100.

Exam tip: state the reagent, the condition (reflux, distillation, heat under pressure) and the product of each step. Marks are often given for the condition, not just the reagent.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Coordinate questions are multi-part: one part gives two points, the next gives a line, and the last asks for a proof or an area. Read the final part first, then pick the tools it needs.

Start from a question

The points A(−1, 4), B(5, 2) and C(3, −4) are given.

  1. Show that angle ABC is 90°.
  2. Find the area of triangle ABC.
  3. Find the equation of the line through A parallel to BC.

Part 1. The gradient of AB is (2 − 4)/(5 + 1) = −1/3. The gradient of BC is (−4 − 2)/(3 − 5) = 3. The product is −1, so AB is perpendicular to BC and the angle at B is 90°.

Part 2. AB² = 6² + 2² = 40 and BC² = 2² + 6² = 40, so AB = BC = √40. The right angle is at B, so the area is ½ × AB × BC = ½ × 40 = 20.

Part 3. Parallel lines share a gradient, so the line has gradient 3. Then y − 4 = 3(x + 1), which gives 3x − y + 7 = 0.

The tools

  • Distance: √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). When only a squared length is needed, leave out the root.
  • Midpoint: ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).
  • Gradient: (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Parallel lines have equal gradients. Perpendicular lines have gradients whose product is −1.
  • Equation of a line: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), using a known point and the gradient m. Rearrange into the form the question asks for.

Two lines: meeting, parallel or perpendicular

A meeting point satisfies both equations, so solve them together. Example: 2x − y = 1 and x + y = 5. Adding gives 3x = 6, so x = 2 and y = 3. Check: 4 − 3 = 1 and 2 + 3 = 5. The lines meet at (2, 3).

Perpendicular example: the line through (1, −3) perpendicular to 4x + y = 2. The given gradient is −4, so the required gradient is ¼. Then y + 3 = ¼(x − 1), which gives x − 4y − 13 = 0. Check at (1, −3): 1 + 12 − 13 = 0.

A circle and a line

Rewrite the circle x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 3 = 0 in centre–radius form by completing the square: (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 16. The centre is (3, −2) and the radius is 4.

Substitute the line y = x + 1 into the circle: x² + (x + 1)² − 6x + 4(x + 1) − 3 = 0 simplifies to 2x² + 2 = 0. Its discriminant is 0² − 4(2)(2) = −16 < 0, so there are no intersections and the line misses the circle.

Tangents and points against a circle

A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. The point (3, 2) lies on the circle, since 9 + 4 − 18 + 8 − 3 = 0. The radius from (3, −2) to (3, 2) is vertical, so the tangent is horizontal: y = 2.

To test a point (x, y), substitute into (x − a)² + (y − b)² and compare with r². A smaller value means inside the circle, equal means on it, and larger means outside. For (1, 2): (1 − 3)² + (2 + 2)² = 20 > 16, so the point lies outside.

Traps that cost marks

  • Using the given gradient for a perpendicular line instead of its negative reciprocal.
  • Squaring the points instead of the coordinate differences when finding a length.
  • Rounding √40 early. Keep it as 2√10 when the question asks for an exact value.
  • Leaving a line in gradient form when the question asks for the ax + by + c = 0 form.

title: Simulation, Sensors and Real Data — Study Notes
content:
Simulation, Sensors and Real Data

Simulation and Modelling

A simulation is a program that models a real system to test scenarios safely and cheaply: weather models, traffic flows, epidemic spread. Models use abstractions — chosen variables and equations — with a time step. Advantages: no real-world risk, repeatable, faster or slower than real time. Limitations: only as good as the model; rare events may be missed.

Sensors and Signals

Sensors measure physical quantities: temperature (thermistor), light (LDR), pressure, humidity, sound. Most output analogue signals varying continuously; computers need digital values, so an ADC (analogue-to-digital converter) samples the signal. Resolution depends on bits — an 8-bit ADC gives 256 levels. A DAC converts digital output back to analogue for actuators or speakers.

Monitoring vs Control

  • Monitoring: sensors feed data to the computer, which only records, displays or raises alarms — no action taken on the environment.
  • Control: the computer acts via actuators (motors, valves, heaters) based on sensor input — the classic feedback loop.

Real-Time Considerations

Control systems are often real-time: late output can be wrong output. Sampling rate must exceed twice the highest signal frequency (Nyquist) to avoid aliasing.

Exam tips: distinguish monitoring from control with a named example; describe the role of ADC and DAC in a greenhouse system; explain one limitation of a simulation.

Exam method: using simulation output with real data

Sensor readings are noisy, drift over time and can contain missing or impossible values. Before using them, check each reading against a sensible range, remove or flag outliers, and decide how to handle gaps, for example by ignoring them or interpolating between neighbouring readings. State which cleaning step you chose.

A simulation is only as reliable as its assumptions and its inputs. In an exam answer, state one assumption the model makes, explain how it could make the output differ from reality, and suggest a way to test the model against measured data.

Exam cue: When asked to evaluate a simulation, give a specific limitation tied to the scenario in the question rather than a general comment that simulations are approximate.

title: Statistics — Data Handling — Study Notes
content:
Statistics — Data Handling

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): averages from lists and tables, quartiles/IQR, charts, cumulative frequency, histograms.

1. Averages

  • Mean = Σfx/Σf from frequency tables. Median = middle value (ordered data). Mode = most frequent. Range = max − min.
  • Choose the best average: mode for shoe sizes, median when outliers distort the mean.

Example (table): goals 0,1,2,3 with f 5,8,4,3: mean = (0+8+8+9)/20 = 1.25.

2. Quartiles and IQR

Q₁ at n/4, Q₃ at 3n/4 (position); IQR = Q₃ − Q₁ — less affected by outliers than the range.

3. Charts

Bar charts, pie charts (angle = fraction × 360°), time series, pictograms. Compare data sets with like-for-like totals; comment on trends.

4. Cumulative frequency

Running totals vs upper class boundaries; the curve ends at (max, n). Median at n/2; Q₁/Q₃ at n/4 and 3n/4; box plot from the five-figure summary.

5. Histograms

Bar area ∝ frequency: FD = frequency ÷ class width. Recover frequencies as FD × width; unequal widths need FDs on the axis.

Exam tips: read cumulative-frequency answers with dashed construction lines; always compare spreads, not just averages, when asked to compare data.
