title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): nuclear model, radioactivity, decay types, half-life, safety, fission/fusion (Extended).

1. The nuclear model

Nucleus (protons +, neutrons 0) with orbiting electrons (−). Nuclide notation ᴬ_Z X. Isotopes: same Z, different A. Rutherford scattering established the nuclear model; proton number Z, nucleon number A.

2. Radiation types

TypeNatureRange (air)Stopped by
alpha αhelium nucleus (2p2n)few cmpaper
beta β⁻fast electron~20–30 cmfew mm aluminium
gamma γEM wavevery farthick lead/concrete

Deflection in fields: α/β opposite, γ none. Ionising: α > β > γ. Background radiation: radon, cosmic, rocks, medical, fallout.

3. Decay equations

  • α: A −4, Z −2 (e.g. ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + α).
  • β⁻: neutron → proton; A same, Z +1 (e.g. ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + β⁻).
  • γ: no change to A or Z.

Balance A and Z on both sides — that is the check.

4. Half-life

Time for half the unstable nuclei to decay (random process). Read from a decay curve or count halves: 80 → 40 → 20 over two half-lives.

Example: 800 Bq, half-life 2 h → 200 Bq after 4 h.

5. Safety and uses

Uses: medical tracers (β/γ), sterilisation, thickness gauge (β), dating (C-14), smoke alarms (α). Safety: distance, time, shielding, wear badges, store in lead. Handle with tongs; never point at people.

6. Fission and fusion (Extended)

Fission: heavy nucleus splits (U-235 + neutron), chain reaction controlled by moderators/control rods — power stations. Fusion: light nuclei join (stellar) — needs huge T/P; releases more energy per kg; no long-lived waste.

title: Exam technique: Information Representation
content:
### What earns the marks
For two complement, inversion plus one stated earns the method mark before the value. For floating point, mantissa plus exponent roles stated earn one mark each. For normalisation, the leading-bit rule quoted earns the precision mark.
### Traps
Error: sign bit ignored in range. Correction: an n-bit signed range tops at 2^(n-1) - 1. Error: larger exponent read as more precision. Correction: exponent sets range, mantissa sets precision. Error: normalised form guessed. Correction: mantissa starts with 0.1 or 1.0 pattern per the scheme.
### Worked example
Write -45 in 8-bit two's complement. First write 45 in binary: 00101101. Invert every bit to get 11010010, then add 1 to get 11010011. Check: the sign bit has weight -128, so the value is -128 + 64 + 16 + 2 + 1 = -45, which matches.
### Check yourself
State the range of an 8-bit two's complement integer, and say which bit sets the sign. The range is -128 to +127, and the leftmost bit is the sign bit with weight -128.

title: Abstract Data Types — Study Notes
content:
Abstract Data Types

What is an ADT?

An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Linked Lists

Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node; a start pointer marks the head and a null marks the end. Insertion rewires two pointers — no shifting — giving O(1) insertion at a known position, but access requires walking the list, O(n).

Stacks and Queues

A stack is LIFO (push and pop at the top); a queue is FIFO (enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front). Both can be arrays with index pointers or linked lists. Stack uses include call stacks and expression evaluation; queue uses include print buffers and breadth-first search.

Binary Search Trees

Each node has up to two children; left subtree keys are smaller, right subtree keys larger. Search, insert and (average-case) delete are O(log n). An in-order traversal outputs keys in ascending order. A degenerate (linear) tree from sorted input degrades to O(n).

Hash Tables

Covered in file organisation, but as an ADT a hash table pairs a hash function with bucket storage for O(1) average access.

Exam tips: be able to draw a tree after a sequence of insertions and write its three traversals; state the pointer changes for a linked-list insertion; compare ADT operations with Big-O.

Abstract data types in practice

An abstract data type is defined by the operations it supports and their behaviour, not by how it is stored. A stack is defined by push, pop and isEmpty; the programmer using it does not need to know whether it is built from an array or a linked list.

Separating the interface from the implementation lets the implementation change without breaking the code that uses it, and makes each part easier to test.

Exam tip: when asked to define an ADT, name the operations and say what each does, not how it is stored.

Worked example: building a binary search tree

Insert 8, 3, 10, 1 and 6 in that order. The first value, 8, becomes the root. Since 3 is less than 8, it goes to the left; 10 goes to the right. The value 1 is less than 8 and less than 3, so it sits to the left of 3. The value 6 is less than 8 and greater than 3, so it sits to the right of 3. An in-order traversal (left, node, right) then lists the values in sorted order: 1, 3, 6, 8, 10.

Complexity of the main operations

  • Search, insert and delete in a balanced tree take O(log n) time, because each comparison discards about half the remaining nodes.
  • If the values are inserted in sorted order, the tree becomes a chain and the same operations degrade to O(n).
  • Hash table lookup takes O(1) on average but gives no ordering, so a hash table cannot list the data in sorted order.

Choosing between the structures

A stack, a queue and a linked list each store a collection, but they differ in how items are added and removed. A stack is last in, first out. A queue is first in, first out. A linked list allows insertion and deletion at a known position without shifting other items. The exam question usually asks you to justify the choice, so state the access pattern the data needs.

title:
Appendix P — Using the note in a session: what to do first, what to do next, and what to leave for the end

A revision session on this topic works best if it has a clear order, because the topic is long enough that a session without an order can turn into a wandering through details that never adds up to an answer you can produce under time pressure. The first thing to do in a session is to take the durable ideas and say them out loud in your own words with a reason attached, because those are the ideas that hold the topic together and the ideas you most need under time pressure. Say the control idea with the reflex arc and the insulin-glucagon system as the anchors. Say the layered defence idea with the skin barrier and phagocytosis on one side and the antibody and memory cell response on the other. Say the timing idea with the primary and secondary response and vaccination. Say the matching idea with restriction enzymes, PCR and electrophoresis. If you can say those four durable ideas with their reasons and their anchors, you have the framework the session is built on, and the rest of the session is then filling in the detail under that framework rather than trying to hold the whole note in your head at once.

The second thing to do is to pick one comparison or one evaluation question and write the answer from the note under time pressure, then compare it with the model in the exam-style section and with the appendix that covers the same ground. Pick a comparison question such as nervous versus hormonal, primary versus secondary, or specific versus non-specific, or plant versus animal coordination. Pick an evaluation question such as vaccination, monoclonal antibodies, DNA profiling, gene therapy or GM organisms. Write the answer in the time you would have in the exam, and then check whether it has the sequence, the distinctions and the reasoning the model has. If it does, the session has done its job for that question. If it does not, the gap is the thing to practise before the next session, because the gap is the thing that will lose marks on the day. The reason for doing the comparison and evaluation questions in the session is that those are the questions where the marks are most often lost for want of precision, and the session is the place where precision can be built before the exam rather than rescued on the day.

The third thing to do is to use the appendices as the place where you go deeper when a topic needs it, and not as a separate first read. The appendices on practical microbiology, the immune process, forensic interpretation, cross-strand questions and the durable ideas are there because those are the places where the marks are most often lost for lack of depth or lack of connection, and they are the places to spend time when you practise those topics. If you read the main body for coverage and the appendices for depth, you get the best use of the note, because you get both the coverage and the reasoning. If you only read the main body, you may get the labels but not the reasoning. If you only read the appendices, you may get the depth but not the coverage. The session that reads both in the right order gets both, and that is the session that makes the note useful, because the note is long enough to cover the topic fully only if you use it fully.

The final thing to do in a session is to leave the last part of the session for the kind of question you are weakest at, because the last part of the session is the part that will determine what sticks. If you are weakest at evaluation, leave the evaluation question for last and make sure you can give a benefit and an issue for each technology without repeating the same issue in every case. If you are weakest at gene technology, leave the gene technology techniques for last and make sure you can say the principle and the purpose for each one without dropping the key step. If you are weakest at the immune response, leave the primary and secondary response and memory for last and make sure you can say why the secondary response is faster and stronger and what the memory cells do. If you leave the weakest part for last, you are practising the thing you most need to practise while it is still fresh from the session, and that is the practice that makes the difference on the day. The session is then not just a read-through of the note but a targeted practice session that builds the precision the exam is actually after.

Appendix Q — End-of-topic checklist and what “ready” should actually mean

The checklist for the end of the topic is not a list of every detail you can remember; it is a list of the things you should be able to do under time pressure, because that is what “ready” means for this topic. The first thing ready should mean is that you can describe the nervous and hormonal systems well enough to contrast them, with speed, range and duration and one concrete example of each. The second thing ready should mean is that you can describe a receptor well enough to pick one and give its structure, stimulus and transduction, whether it is a rod, a cone, a Pacinian corpuscle or another receptor the question gives you. The consolidation pass is then the last chance to close the gaps before the exam, and the last chance to make sure the answer you write under time pressure is the answer that earns the marks, not just the answer you can write with unlimited time. If the three timed answers are good, the exam is ready. If they are not, the gaps are the thing to close before the exam, and the note is there to close them.

The final part of the consolidation pass is to trust the durable ideas and the tying, and not to try to cram every detail at the last minute, because the last minute is too late for detail and too early for panic, and the right use of it is to reinforce the tying. If you have the durable ideas, the anchors and the distinctions, you can answer most of the topic, because those are the framework that the detail fits into. If you try to cram the detail at the last minute, you are likely to blur the distinctions you already have, and the distinctions are the marks. The consolidation pass is therefore about reinforcing the tying, not about adding more detail, and the note is there to reinforce the tying by giving you the durable ideas, the anchors and the distinctions in one place to reach for on the day. If you can reach for them under time pressure, the note has done its job, and the topic is ready for the exam in the form the exam is actually in.

title: Exam technique: Materials and Deformation
content:
### What earns the marks
For stress and strain, each definition quoted with units or unitless noted earns a mark. For Young modulus, stress over strain earns the method mark with a steel-scale answer. For graphs, area read as stored energy earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: strain given units. Correction: strain is a pure ratio. Error: force-extension gradient called energy. Correction: gradient is stiffness; area is energy. Error: plastic region called elastic. Correction: only the straight line obeys Hooke.
### Worked example
Under a rotation of 90° anticlockwise about the origin, the point (3, 1) maps to (−1, 3). Each point's x and y change places with one sign reversed. Under a reflection in the line y = x, the same point maps to (1, 3), so the coordinates swap. For a translation by vector (2; −3), the point (3, 1) maps to (5, −2).
### Check yourself
Describe the enlargement that maps a triangle with vertices (1, 1), (2, 1), (1, 3) onto one with vertices (2, 2), (4, 2), (2, 6). The scale factor is 2, and the centre must be stated: it is found by joining corresponding points, and the centre is the origin.

title: Forces and Equilibrium — Study Notes
content:
Forces and equilibrium

Moment of a force

  • The moment of a force about a point is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force: moment = F × d⊥. Unit: N m.
  • Only the perpendicular component of the force produces a turning effect. A force that passes through the pivot has zero moment.

Principle of moments

For a body in equilibrium the sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that point.

Couples

A couple is two equal and opposite parallel forces whose lines of action do not coincide. It produces a turning effect without a resultant force. The moment of a couple is F × d, where d is the perpendicular separation, and it is the same about every point.

Conditions for equilibrium

  • The resultant force in every direction is zero.
  • The resultant moment about any point is zero.

For three coplanar, non-parallel forces in equilibrium, the lines of action must meet at a single point.

Centre of gravity

The centre of gravity is the point through which the weight of a body appears to act. For a uniform symmetrical body it lies at the geometric centre.

Worked example: a uniform beam of weight 100 N rests horizontally on two supports at its ends. Each support carries half the weight, 50 N, because the beam is symmetrical and in equilibrium.

Exam tips: state the pivot you take moments about. Draw the perpendicular distance, not the slant distance. Show that the resultant force is zero in each direction before you use the principle of moments.

Conditions for equilibrium

A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force on it is zero and the resultant moment about any point is zero. For a body in equilibrium under three coplanar forces, the lines of action meet at a single point. The moment of a force about a pivot is Fd, where d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action. Taking moments about the pivot removes the unknown reaction force, which makes this a useful method in exam questions.

Exam tip: show the resolution of forces into horizontal and vertical components before you apply the equilibrium equations.

title: Abstract Data Types — Study Notes
content:
Abstract Data Types

What is an ADT?

An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Linked Lists

Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node; a start pointer marks the head and a null marks the end. Insertion rewires two pointers — no shifting — giving O(1) insertion at a known position, but access requires walking the list, O(n).

Stacks and Queues

A stack is LIFO (push and pop at the top); a queue is FIFO (enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front). Both can be arrays with index pointers or linked lists. Stack uses include call stacks and expression evaluation; queue uses include print buffers and breadth-first search.

Binary Search Trees

Each node has up to two children; left subtree keys are smaller, right subtree keys larger. Search, insert and (average-case) delete are O(log n). An in-order traversal outputs keys in ascending order. A degenerate (linear) tree from sorted input degrades to O(n).

Hash Tables

Covered in file organisation, but as an ADT a hash table pairs a hash function with bucket storage for O(1) average access.

Exam tips: be able to draw a tree after a sequence of insertions and write its three traversals; state the pointer changes for a linked-list insertion; compare ADT operations with Big-O.

Abstract data types in practice

An abstract data type is defined by the operations it supports and their behaviour, not by how it is stored. A stack is defined by push, pop and isEmpty; the programmer using it does not need to know whether it is built from an array or a linked list.

Separating the interface from the implementation lets the implementation change without breaking the code that uses it, and makes each part easier to test.

Exam tip: when asked to define an ADT, name the operations and say what each does, not how it is stored.

title: Exam technique: Programming and Algorithms
content:
### What earns the marks
For validation, the rejected range stated plus the rejection loop earns both marks. For structure, single entry and exit modules using only sequence, selection and iteration earn the design marks. For traces, each variable tracked per line earns method credit. For testing, the stage named with its setting (isolated module vs live users) earns each mark.

Error: fixed FOR loops for unknown-attempt validation. Correction: WHILE-until-valid loops. Error: binary search on unsorted data. Correction: sort first or use linear search. Error: unit and acceptance settings swapped. Correction: unit is isolated with test data; acceptance is live with real users.
### Worked example
A trace table records the value of each variable at each step of an algorithm. For a linear search, the program checks each item in turn and can take up to n comparisons. A binary search on a sorted list halves the search space each time, so 16 sorted items need at most about log₂16 = 4 comparisons. Binary search only works if the list is sorted.

title: Integration II — Study Notes
content:
Integration II

Standard Integrals

  • ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c
  • ∫ cos x dx = sin x + c
  • ∫ e^x dx = e^x + c
  • ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c
  • ∫ sec²x dx = tan x + c

With linear arguments: ∫ e^(3x) dx = e^(3x)/3 + c; ∫ cos 2x dx = sin 2x/2 + c.

Substitution

Reverse of the chain rule. For ∫ 2x e^(x²) dx, let u = x²: du = 2x dx, so the integral is ∫ e^u du = e^(x²) + c.

Integration by Parts

∫ u (dv/dx) dx = uv − ∫ v (du/dx) dx. Choose u to be the part that simplifies when differentiated (LIATE: logs, inverse trig, algebraic, trig, exponential).

Example: ∫ x e^x dx = x e^x − ∫ e^x dx = x e^x − e^x + c.

Partial Fractions

Break rational functions into pieces like ∫ 1/(x+1) dx = ln|x + 1| + c.

Example: ∫ 4x/(x² − 1) dx = ∫ [2/(x − 1) + 2/(x + 1)] dx = 2 ln|x − 1| + 2 ln|x + 1| + c.

Exam tips: definite integrals: substitute limits into the transformed variable directly; for by-parts integrals like ∫ ln x dx, take u = ln x, dv/dx = 1.

Exam method: exponential and reciprocal integrals

The integral of e^(kx) is (1/k) e^(kx) + c, and the integral of e^x is e^x + c. The integral of 1/(ax + b) is (1/a) ln|ax + b| + c. Dividing by the coefficient of x is the step most often missed, so check it by differentiating your answer.

For a definite integral, evaluate the antiderivative at the upper limit, subtract its value at the lower limit, and write the bracket with its limits, such as [e^(2x)/2] from 0 to 1.

When the integrand is a product, integration by parts gives ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. Choose u to be the part that becomes simpler when differentiated, such as x in x eˣ.

Substitution changes the limits as well as the variable. Either change the limits to the new variable or substitute back before using the original limits; do not mix the two.

Exam cue: Give the answer as an exact value, such as (e² − 1)/2, unless the question asks for a decimal.

Worked example: integration by parts

Find the integral of x e^x with respect to x. Let u = x and dv/dx = e^x, so du/dx = 1 and v = e^x. Then the integral equals x e^x minus the integral of e^x, which is x e^x − e^x + c = (x − 1) e^x + c. Differentiate the answer to check that it returns the integrand.

Definite integrals and area

For a region above the x-axis, the definite integral between the limits gives its area. If part of the curve lies below the axis, that part contributes a negative value to the integral, so the total area is the sum of the absolute values of each part. Sketch the curve first. Integrating across a point where the curve crosses the axis gives the signed net value, not the area.

Checking your answer

  • After integrating, differentiate the answer and confirm that it reproduces the original function.
  • Include the constant of integration on indefinite integrals, and never write it on a definite integral.
  • When a substitution changes the variable, change the limits too, or convert back to x before substituting the original limits.

The integration topic of the Cambridge AS and A Level Mathematics 9709 syllabus expects these methods to be applied to standard forms and to exam-style problems, with the method stated clearly at each step.

title: Exam technique: Integration
content:
### What earns the marks
For indefinite integrals, each term raised correctly plus the constant earns full marks. For definite integrals, the antiderivative quoted earns one mark and the correct upper-minus-lower evaluation earns the next. For area and curve-finding, the limits or the given point used earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: constant of integration omitted. Correction: +c always for indefinite. Error: limits subtracted backwards. Correction: upper minus lower. Error: power rule inverted on roots. Correction: root x is x to the half, integral goes up.

title: Chemical Equilibria — Study Notes
content:
Chemical Equilibria

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 13. In a closed system a reaction reaches a dynamic equilibrium, where the forward and reverse rates are equal. The equilibrium constant tells you the position of that equilibrium at a given temperature.

The equilibrium constant Kc

  • For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b). Only species in solution or gas phase appear in the expression.
  • Kc is constant for a given temperature. Changing concentration or pressure shifts the position but not the value of Kc.
  • The units of Kc depend on the stoichiometry. For N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, Kc has units of mol⁻² dm⁶.

Worked example

  • For H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI, at equilibrium [HI] = 1.60, [H2] = 0.20 and [I2] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³. Kc = 1.60² / (0.20 × 0.20) = 64.

Partial pressure and Kp

  • In gas equilibria, the partial pressure of a gas is its mole fraction multiplied by the total pressure.
  • Kp uses partial pressures instead of concentrations. For N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2, Kp = p(NO2)² / p(N2O4).

Effect of changes

  • Adding reactant or removing product shifts the position towards the products. Adding product shifts it towards the reactants.
  • Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules. Changing the volume has the same effect as changing pressure.
  • Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction. For an exothermic forward reaction, Kc decreases as temperature rises.
  • A catalyst changes the rate at which equilibrium is reached but not the position or Kc.

Exam tip: a change in temperature is the only change that alters Kc. Concentration, pressure and catalyst changes alter the position or rate, but not the constant.

title: Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria — Study Notes
content:
Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 9. Kinetics asks how fast a reaction goes, and equilibria asks how far it goes before the forward and backward reactions balance. Both depend on the same collision ideas.

Rates and collision theory

  • For a reaction to occur, particles must collide with enough energy (the activation energy, Ea) and in the correct orientation.
  • Increasing concentration or pressure increases the frequency of collisions. Increasing temperature raises the proportion of particles with energy above Ea, which has a larger effect than the increase in collision frequency.
  • A catalyst provides an alternative route with a lower Ea; it is not used up.

Measuring rates

  • Rates can be found from the gradient of a concentration–time graph at the start of the reaction (the initial rate).
  • Methods include measuring the volume of gas produced, the change in mass, or the time for a colour change to occur (1/time gives a relative rate).

Dynamic equilibrium

  • In a closed system, the forward and reverse rates become equal. Concentrations stop changing, but the reaction has not stopped.
  • Equilibrium constant Kc = [products]^n / [reactants]^m, with each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient. Kc is constant for a given temperature.

Le Chatelier's principle

  • If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the position shifts to oppose the change.
  • Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction. Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules. Adding a reactant shifts the position towards products.
  • A catalyst speeds up both directions equally, so it changes the rate of reaching equilibrium but not the equilibrium position or Kc.

Exam tip: say which direction is favoured and why, using the principle. Do not claim that a catalyst increases the yield.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Collision theory, applied to a rate change: raising the temperature increases the fraction of molecules with energy above the activation energy. The number of collisions barely changes, so the increase in rate comes from the larger fraction of successful collisions. Name the activation energy in the answer.
  • Le Chatelier and the Haber process, applied to N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ with ΔH negative: a low temperature favours the product, but the rate is slow, so a compromise temperature of about 450 °C is used with an iron catalyst. The catalyst changes the rate, not the yield.
  • Dynamic equilibrium: the forward and backward rates are equal, and the concentrations are constant. The equilibrium is dynamic, not static, so state both rates are equal and the reactions have not stopped.
  • Common mistake: saying that a catalyst shifts the equilibrium to increase yield. A catalyst lowers the activation energy for both directions, so it reaches equilibrium faster but does not change the yield.

title: Trigonometry — Study Notes
content:
Trigonometry

Exact Values

Anglesincostan
30°1/2√3/2√3/3
45°√2/2√2/21
60°√3/21/2√3

Key Identities

  • sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
  • tan θ = sin θ / cos θ
  • sec²θ = 1 + tan²θ

Solving Equations

Use the symmetry of the graphs. For sin x = 1/2 in 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π: the acute answer is π/6, and the second solution is π − π/6 = 5π/6.

For cos x = 0.5 in 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°: x = 60° and 360° − 60° = 300°.

Always check the required interval and give every solution.

Graphs and Transformations

y = a sin(bx) + c has amplitude a, period 2π/b, and vertical shift c.

Example: y = 3 sin(2x) has amplitude 3 and period π.

Using Identities

If sin x = 0.6 with x acute, then cos x = √(1 − 0.36) = 0.8 (positive in the first quadrant).

Exam tips: write the general second solution using graph symmetry rather than memorising CAST blindly; square both sides only with care, as it can add false solutions.

Exact values and exam method

Use CAST to find the quadrant signs: all positive in the first quadrant, sine in the second, tangent in the third, cosine in the fourth. Find the acute angle first, then the other solutions in the range the question specifies.

For sin x = k, the solutions in 0° to 360° are α and 180° − α, where α is the acute angle with sin α = |k|. For cos x = k they are α and 360° − α. Always check the range; an answer outside it earns no mark.

Write a sin x + b cos x as R sin(x + α) or R cos(x − α). Expanding gives R = √(a² + b²), and for the sine form tan α = b/a. The maximum value is R, which gives the turning points that exam questions often ask for.

Reciprocal functions: sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x, cot x = 1/tan x. Use sin²x + cos²x = 1 and 1 + tan²x = sec²x to simplify.

Exam cue: Show the working that gives the acute angle before stating the answers in the required range.

Worked example: exact values and a quadrant rule

Use the exact values sin 30° = ½, cos 45° = 1/√2 and tan 60° = √3. For an angle such as 150°, sin 150° = sin(180° − 30°) = sin 30° = ½, because sine is positive in the second quadrant. For 225°, tan 225° = tan 45° = 1, because tangent is positive in the third quadrant.

Draw a quick CAST diagram to decide the sign: all positive in the first quadrant, sine in the second, tangent in the third and cosine in the fourth.

Solving a trigonometric equation

Solve 2cos x = 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π. Then cos x = ½, so x = π/3 or x = 2π − π/3 = 5π/3. Always find the principal value first, then use the symmetry of the graph to find the other solutions in the range.

Solve 2sin²x − sin x − 1 = 0 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°. Factor as (2 sin x + 1)(sin x − 1) = 0. Then sin x = 1, giving x = 90°, or sin x = −½, giving x = 210° and 330°.

Proving an identity

Show that (sin x + cos x)² = 1 + sin 2x. Expand the left side: sin²x + 2 sin x cos x + cos²x. Use sin²x + cos²x = 1 to get 1 + 2 sin x cos x, and recall sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x, so the left side equals 1 + sin 2x.

Graphs and transformations

  • y = 3 sin 2x + 1 has amplitude 3, period 180° (or π radians), and the maximum value 4 occurs at x = 45°.
  • The range of y = 3 sin 2x + 1 is −2 ≤ y ≤ 4.
  • A horizontal stretch by factor ½ halves the period; a vertical shift of +1 moves the whole graph up by one unit.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Working in degrees when the question uses radians, or the reverse. Check the units in the question before you start.
  • Giving only the principal value and missing the other solutions in the range. Always check the quadrant signs.
  • Squaring both sides of an equation to remove a root, which can add extra solutions. Check each answer in the original equation.

title: Programming Concepts — Study Notes
content:
Programming Concepts

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): variables/constants, data types, selection/iteration, arrays, file handling, subroutines, scope, IDE tools.

1. Basics

Constants vs variables; types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE; casting between them. Declaration with meaningful names.

2. Selection and iteration

IF score >= 50 THEN
  grade ← "pass"
ELSE
  grade ← "fail"
ENDIF

CASE OF grade
  "A" : OUTPUT "excellent"
  OTHERWISE : OUTPUT "keep going"
ENDCASE

REPEAT
  INPUT pin
UNTIL pin = storedPin

FOR i ← 1 TO 10 STEP 2 ... NEXT i

WHILE: condition first (may not run); REPEAT: runs at least once.

3. Arrays

Fixed size, indexed (0- or 1-based per spec); 2D arrays: row, column. Bounds errors when index leaves range. Traversal with FOR loops.

4. Files

OPENFILE "data.txt" FOR READ
READFILE "data.txt", line
CLOSEFILE "data.txt"

OPENFILE "log.txt" FOR APPEND
WRITEFILE "log.txt", record

Modes: READ, WRITE (overwrites), APPEND (adds).

5. Subroutines

Procedure (no return) vs function (returns value). Parameters by value (copy) vs reference (original). Local scope inside; global shared — declare deliberately, avoid overuse.

6. IDE tools

Syntax highlighting, autocompletion, breakpoints, single stepping, variable watch — name the tool and its debugging benefit.

Exam tips: use the exam pseudocode style exactly; for 2D arrays, loop rows outer/columns inner; choose WHILE vs REPEAT by "must it run once?"

Selection and iteration in practice

Selection uses IF and CASE structures to choose between paths, and a branch runs only when its condition is true. Iteration repeats a block of code. A count-controlled loop, such as FOR, runs a known number of times. A condition-controlled loop, such as WHILE or REPEAT, runs until a condition changes. A WHILE loop may run zero times, but a REPEAT loop always runs at least once.

A well-written program uses meaningful identifiers, indents its code to show structure, and includes comments that explain why a piece of code exists. Subroutines split a large problem into smaller tasks that can be tested separately.

Exam tip: choose the loop type from whether the number of repetitions is known in advance.

title: Algebra — Inequalities — Study Notes
content:
Inequalities

Linear inequalities

Solve in the same way as an equation, with one rule: multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the inequality sign.

Example: 3(2x − 1) ≥ x + 4 gives 6x − 3 ≥ x + 4, so 5x ≥ 7 and x ≥ 7/5.

Quadratic inequalities

Solve the related quadratic equation first, then sketch the parabola to see where it lies above or below the axis. Do not divide by an expression in x unless its sign is known.

Example: x² − 2x − 8 < 0 factorises to (x − 4)(x + 2) < 0. The parabola is below the x-axis between its roots, so −2 < x < 4.

Example: x² > 9 has roots ±3, and the parabola is above the axis outside them, so x < −3 or x > 3.

Regions on a graph

A strict inequality such as y > 2x + 1 is drawn with a dashed boundary line, and a non-strict one with a solid line. Test a point not on the line to decide which side to shade.

Exam technique

  • Write the answer as an inequality or as an interval, as the question requires.
  • Test one value inside the solution set to confirm the answer.

title: Alkenes — Study Notes
content:
Alkenes

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 5. Alkenes contain a carbon–carbon double bond, which makes them far more reactive than alkanes. Their addition reactions are a central part of organic synthesis.

Structure and bonding

  • A C=C double bond consists of one sigma bond and one pi bond. The pi bond is an electron cloud above and below the plane of the atoms, and it is the reactive part.
  • The carbons of a C=C bond are planar, with bond angles of about 120°.

Addition reactions

  • Hydrogen adds across the double bond in the presence of a nickel catalyst to form an alkane.
  • Halogens (for example bromine water) add across the double bond: a colour change from orange to colourless is the test for an alkene.
  • Steam adds across the double bond in the presence of phosphoric acid to form an alcohol.
  • Hydrogen halides add to give halogenoalkanes; with unsymmetrical alkenes the Markovnikov rule predicts the major product.

Polymerisation

  • Addition polymers form when many alkene monomers join together. Poly(ethene) and poly(chloroethene) are examples.
  • The repeat unit is drawn with the double bond opened and the bonds extended through brackets.

Isomerism

  • Restricted rotation about the C=C bond allows E/Z isomers when each carbon carries two different groups.

Exam tip: when drawing a polymer, show the repeat unit with the bonds extending outwards, and do not leave a dangling double bond.

title: Proof — Study Notes
content:
Proof by induction and other formal arguments

A2 proof extends the AS toolkit with mathematical induction — the standard method for statements indexed by the positive integers (series formulae, divisibility, inequalities).

The structure of induction

1. Base case: verify the statement directly for n = 1 (or the stated starting value).

2. Inductive step: assume the statement true for n = k (the inductive hypothesis). Prove it true for n = k + 1, using that assumption.

3. Conclusion: by induction the statement is true for all positive integers n >= starting value.

Divisibility inductions

To prove "expression is divisible by m": the base case must divide exactly, and the inductive step writes P(k + 1) = P(k) + m x (something), so divisibility passes from k to k + 1.

Series inductions

To prove a sum formula: write S_{k+1} = S_k + a_{k+1}, substitute the assumed formula for S_k, and simplify to the claimed form with n replaced by k + 1.

When induction is NOT appropriate

  • Statements about all real numbers (use direct proof or contradiction).
  • Finite case lists (use exhaustion).
  • Disproving a universal claim (use a counter-example).

Contradiction and contrapositive

  • To prove "if P then Q" by contradiction: assume P and not Q, and derive nonsense.
  • Contrapositive: prove "if not Q then not P", which is logically equivalent and often cleaner — e.g. "if n^2 is even then n is even" is proved by "if n is odd then n^2 is odd".

title: Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): substitution, collecting like terms, expanding brackets, factorising (common factor, quadratics, difference of two squares), algebraic fractions.

1. Substitution

a = 3, b = −2: 2a² − b = 2(9) + 2 = 20. Always bracket substituted negatives.

2. Collecting like terms

5x + 3y − 2x + y = 3x + 4y. Terms need identical letter parts (x² and x are not like terms).

3. Expanding

  • Single: 3(2x − 5) = 6x − 15.
  • Double: (x + 3)(x − 4) = x² − x − 12 (grid or FOIL).
  • Cubic products: (x+2)³ = x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8.

4. Factorising

  • Common factor: 6x²y − 9xy² = 3xy(2x − 3y).
  • Quadratics: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) (two numbers ×6, sum −5).
  • Harder: 6x² + 7x + 2 = (3x + 2)(2x + 1) — split the middle term.
  • Difference of two squares: 9x² − 25 = (3x − 5)(3x + 5).

5. Algebraic fractions

Factorise top and bottom fully, then cancel: (x² − 9)/(x + 3) = (x − 3). To add, use a common denominator: 1/(x+1) + 2/(x−1) = (3x + 1)/((x+1)(x−1)).

Exam tips: always factorise out the highest common factor including the number; check expansion by substituting x = 1 into both forms.

Expanding brackets

Each term outside a bracket multiplies every term inside it. For a double bracket, multiply each term in the first by each term in the second, then collect like terms. Expanding (x + 3)(x − 5) gives x² − 2x − 15. Keep track of signs carefully, since most lost marks come from negative terms.

Factorising

Take out the highest common factor first, then look for a pair of brackets. For a quadratic x² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. For the difference of two squares, a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b). Check by expanding your answer.

Algebraic fractions

Simplify by factorising the numerator and denominator and cancelling common factors. Add or subtract fractions by writing them over a common denominator. Never cancel terms that are added, only factors that multiply.

title: Algorithms & Programming — Study Notes
content:
Algorithms & Programming

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): pseudocode, flowcharts, standard algorithms (linear/bubble), trace tables, validation & verification.

1. Pseudocode

OUTPUT "Enter n"
INPUT n
IF n MOD 2 = 0 THEN
  OUTPUT "even"
ELSE
  OUTPUT "odd"
ENDIF

FOR i ← 1 TO 10
  total ← total + i
NEXT i

WHILE total < 100
  total ← total + n
ENDWHILE

FUNCTION square(x : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
  RETURN x * x
ENDFUNCTION

Assignment ←, comparison =, MOD/DIV for remainders/quotients.

2. Flowchart symbols

Terminator (oval), process (rectangle), decision (diamond), input/output (parallelogram), flow lines with arrows.

3. Standard algorithms

  • Linear search: check each item until found/end — works unsorted.
  • Bubble sort: repeated adjacent swaps; largest bubbles to the end each pass; n−1 passes max; early exit when no swaps.
  • Counting/totaling patterns; max/min with a running best value.

4. Trace tables

One column per variable; log every assignment in order; watch loop counters and reassignments.

x ← 1; total ← 0
WHILE x <= 4
  total ← total + x * 2
  x ← x + 1
ENDWHILE  // total = 20

5. Validation vs verification

  • Validation: automatic checks on data — range (exam mark 0–100), length (password ≥ 8), type, format (postcode pattern), presence (field not empty), check digit (barcode).
  • Verification: data matches the source — double entry, visual/proof reading.

6. Testing

Normal (typical), abnormal (rejects invalid), boundary (extremes just inside/outside). Test data tables list input → expected output.

Exam tips: write pseudocode with ENDIF/NEXT/ENDWHILE terminators; in trace tables record the condition result too; boundary choices need "just above/below/at" values.

Algorithm design in practice

A good algorithm is correct, efficient and easy to follow. Designers begin by breaking the problem into smaller parts, a method called decomposition. Each part is then written as a step, and the steps are tested with sample data, including data at the limits of the input range.

Pseudocode is a way of writing an algorithm in plain structured English before it is coded in a specific language. It makes the logic clear, so it can be checked and changed without worrying about syntax. Flowcharts show the same logic with symbols for input, process, decision and output.

Exam tip: trace the algorithm step by step with a table of values to show that it produces the expected output.

title: Exam technique: Thermal Physics (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For gases, pV = nRT quoted earns the method mark with kelvin used. For theory, KE proportional to T stated earns the explanation mark. For heating, mcT and mL chosen by phase versus temperature change earn one mark each; first-law signs tracked earn the final mark.
### Traps
Error: Celsius used in gas laws. Correction: convert to kelvin. Error: latent heat applied to temperature change. Correction: latent is isothermal; mcT is for change. Error: work signs flipped in delta U. Correction: work done by the gas subtracts.

title: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table Revision Notes Edexcel IAL AS Chemistry
content:
Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table AS Level Chemistry

These revision notes cover Topic 2 of the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary Chemistry specification. They detail subatomic particles, mass spectrometry, ionisation energies, quantum shells, orbitals, and periodic trends across periods 2 and 3.

Subatomic Particles and Isotopes

Atoms consist of a central nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in quantum shells. The atomic proton number is the number of protons in the nucleus, which defines the element. The mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons combined. You can determine the number of each subatomic particle in any neutral atom or ion by subtracting the atomic number from the mass number to find neutrons, while electrons equal protons in a neutral atom or are adjusted according to the ionic charge. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, resulting in different mass numbers. Isotopes share identical chemical properties because they have the same electron configuration, but they possess different physical properties such as density and mass.

  • Proton: relative mass 1, relative charge +1.
  • Neutron: relative mass 1, relative charge 0.
  • Electron: relative mass 1 / 1836, relative charge −1.
  • Atomic number equals the number of protons.
  • Mass number equals protons plus neutrons.
  • Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
  • Electrons = protons minus positive charge, or plus negative charge.

Mass Spectrometry and Relative Masses

A mass spectrometer determines the isotopic composition of elements and relative molecular masses of compounds. A vaporised sample is ionised by high-energy electrons to form positive ions, accelerated by an electric field, deflected by a magnetic field according to mass-to-charge ratio, and detected. Ions in a mass spectrometer may occasionally acquire a 2+ charge, producing a signal at half their actual mass-to-charge ratio. Mass spectra display percentage abundance or relative abundance on the vertical axis against mass-to-charge ratio on the horizontal axis. For diatomic molecules such as chlorine, you can predict mass spectra and relative peak heights given isotopic abundances by using probability combinations of isotopes like chlorine-35 and chlorine-37.

  • Relative atomic mass is the weighted mean mass of an atom of an element compared with one-twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
  • Relative molecular mass is the sum of relative atomic masses of all atoms in the molecular formula.
  • Formula for relative atomic mass = sum of (isotopic mass × relative abundance) ÷ total abundance.
  • Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 exist in a 3:1 ratio, producing molecular ion peaks at m/z 70, 72, and 74 with a 9:6:1 ratio.

Worked example: calculate the relative atomic mass of element X with isotopes 24X (78.9%), 25X (10.0%), and 26X (11.1%).

  • Step 1: Multiply each isotopic mass by its percentage abundance. (24 × 78.9) = 1893.6; (25 × 10.0) = 250.0; (26 × 11.1) = 288.6.
  • Step 2: Sum these values. 1893.6 + 250.0 + 288.6 = 2432.2.
  • Step 3: Divide by 100. 2432.2 ÷ 100 = 24.3 to 3 significant figures.

Ionisation Energies and Quantum Evidence

First ionisation energy is the energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions. Second and third ionisation energies remove subsequent moles of electrons from 1+ and 2+ gaseous ions respectively. All ionisation energies are endothermic because energy must be put in to overcome the electrostatic attraction between the outer electrons and the positive nucleus. Ionisation energies are influenced by the positive nuclear charge, electron shielding from inner shells, and the distance of the sub-shell from the nucleus. Successive ionisation energies provide decisive evidence for quantum shells and the group number because a large jump occurs when an electron is removed from a shell closer to the nucleus. The first ionisation energy trend across successive elements provides direct evidence for electron sub-shells.

  • First ionisation energy equation: X (g) yields X+ (g) + e−.
  • Second ionisation energy equation: X+ (g) yields X2+ (g) + e−.
  • Endothermic process: delta H is positive.
  • Nuclear charge increases across a period, increasing attraction.
  • Shielding increases down a group, decreasing attraction.

Orbitals, Sub-shells and Electronic Configurations

An orbital is a region within an atom that can hold up to two electrons with opposite spins. Orbitals in sub-shells each take a single electron before pairing up with two electrons of opposite spin. Orbitals come in different shapes: s-orbitals are spherical, and p-orbitals are dumbbell-shaped along x, y, and z axes. Sub-shells are designated s, p, d, and f. The first four quantum shells hold maximums of 2, 8, 18, and 32 electrons respectively, corresponding to 1, 4, 9, and 16 orbitals. You can predict electronic configurations from hydrogen to krypton inclusive and their ions using s, p, d notation and electron-in-boxes notation. Electronic configuration determines the chemical properties of an element because elements in the same group share outer shell configurations. The Periodic Table is divided into blocks corresponding to the sub-shell containing the highest energy electron.

  • s-block: groups 1 and 2, outer electrons in s-orbitals.
  • p-block: groups 13 to 18, outer electrons in p-orbitals.
  • d-block: transition metals, outer electrons in d-sub-shells.
  • Hunds rule: electrons fill singly before pairing in degenerate orbitals.
  • Transition metal ion formation: 4s electrons are lost before 3d electrons.

Worked example: write the electronic configuration of a titanium atom (atomic number 22) and a titanium 2+ ion.

  • Step 1: Follow the filling order up to 22 electrons. 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d2.
  • Step 2: When forming the 2+ ion, remove electrons from the highest principal quantum number first. Remove 2 electrons from the 4s sub-shell.
  • Step 3: Write the ionic configuration as 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d2.

Periodic Trends and Graphical Data

Data represented graphically, including logarithms of first ionisation energies for elements 1 to 36, demonstrate the periodic nature of properties. A periodic property is one that repeats in a regular pattern across periods. Across periods 2 and 3, melting and boiling temperatures depend on structure and bonding: giant metallic structures have high melting points, giant covalent structures have very high melting points due to strong covalent bonds, and simple molecular structures have low melting and boiling points due to weak intermolecular forces. First ionisation energies generally increase across periods due to increasing nuclear charge and constant shielding, with slight drops between group 2 and 13 due to sub-shell changes, and between group 15 and 16 due to spin-pairing repulsion. First ionisation energy decreases down a group due to increased atomic radius and shielding.

  • Period 2 and 3 trends: metallic bonding peaks at group 13, covalent macromolecular peaks at group 14, simple molecules drop sharply at group 15 or 16.
  • Group 2 to 13 drop: outer electron enters a higher-energy p-sub-shell, which is further shielded by the s-sub-shell.
  • Group 15 to 16 drop: pairing of electrons in a p-orbital causes mutual repulsion, making it easier to remove.
  • Logarithm graphs of ionisation energy clearly show the periodicity of quantum shells.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Stating that ionisation energy is exothermic because energy is released. Correction: Ionisation energy is always endothermic because energy is required to overcome the electrostatic attraction between electrons and protons.
  • Mistake: Removing 3d electrons before 4s electrons when ionising transition metal atoms. Correction: Always remove 4s electrons first because the 4s orbital is of higher energy once filling is complete and sits further out.
  • Mistake: Confusing mass number with relative atomic mass. Correction: Mass number is a whole number representing protons plus neutrons in a specific isotope, whereas relative atomic mass is a weighted mean of all naturally occurring isotopes.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that a chlorine mass spectrum has peaks for Cl2 molecules, not just chlorine atoms. Correction: Diatomic chlorine molecules produce molecular ion peaks at m/z 70, 72, and 74 based on combinations of Cl-35 and Cl-37.

Exam-style questions

  1. Define the term first ionisation energy. Answer: The energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions. (Earns 2 marks for stating moles of gas and 1+ ions).
  2. Explain why the first ionisation energy of oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen. Answer: Nitrogen has a half-filled 2p3 sub-shell configuration, whereas oxygen has a 2p4 configuration with paired electrons. The mutual repulsion of the paired electrons in oxygen makes the electron easier to remove. (Earns credit for mentioning electron pairing and repulsion).
  3. Calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium given isotopes: Mg-24 (78.99%), Mg-25 (10.00%), Mg-26 (11.01%). Answer: ((24 × 78.99) + (25 × 10.00) + (26 × 11.01)) ÷ 100 = 24.3 to 1 decimal place. (Earns credit for correct working and units).
  4. State and explain the trend in first ionisation energy down Group 2. Answer: First ionisation energy decreases down Group 2 because atoms have more quantum shells, increasing atomic radius and electron shielding, which outweighs the increased nuclear charge and reduces outer shell attraction. (Earns credit for naming shielding, distance, and attraction).
  5. Write the full electronic configuration for a chromium atom, atomic number 24, using s, p, d notation. Answer: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1 3d5. (Earns credit for the stable half-filled d-sub-shell exception).

Use these notes alongside active recall and past paper question practice. Focus next on mastering redox equations and stoichiometry in Topic 3.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): nuclear model, radioactivity, decay types, half-life, safety, fission/fusion (Extended).

1. The nuclear model

Nucleus (protons +, neutrons 0) with orbiting electrons (−). Nuclide notation ᴬ_Z X. Isotopes: same Z, different A. Rutherford scattering established the nuclear model; proton number Z, nucleon number A.

2. Radiation types

TypeNatureRange (air)Stopped by
alpha αhelium nucleus (2p2n)few cmpaper
beta β⁻fast electron~20–30 cmfew mm aluminium
gamma γEM wavevery farthick lead/concrete

Deflection in fields: α/β opposite, γ none. Ionising: α > β > γ. Background radiation: radon, cosmic, rocks, medical, fallout.

3. Decay equations

  • α: A −4, Z −2 (e.g. ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + α).
  • β⁻: neutron → proton; A same, Z +1 (e.g. ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + β⁻).
  • γ: no change to A or Z.

Balance A and Z on both sides — that is the check.

4. Half-life

Time for half the unstable nuclei to decay (random process). Read from a decay curve or count halves: 80 → 40 → 20 over two half-lives.

Example: 800 Bq, half-life 2 h → 200 Bq after 4 h.

5. Safety and uses

Uses: medical tracers (β/γ), sterilisation, thickness gauge (β), dating (C-14), smoke alarms (α). Safety: distance, time, shielding, wear badges, store in lead. Handle with tongs; never point at people.

6. Fission and fusion (Extended)

Fission: heavy nucleus splits (U-235 + neutron), chain reaction controlled by moderators/control rods — power stations. Fusion: light nuclei join (stellar) — needs huge T/P; releases more energy per kg; no long-lived waste.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Distance and midpoint

For A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂): length AB = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). Midpoint M = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).

Gradients

Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), where x₂ ≠ x₁. A horizontal line has m = 0; a vertical line has no gradient.

Parallel lines have equal gradients. Perpendicular lines (neither vertical nor horizontal) satisfy m₁ × m₂ = −1.

Equations of a straight line

  • Gradient–intercept form: y = mx + c, where c is the y-intercept.
  • Point–gradient form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
  • General form: ax + by + c = 0, with gradient −a/b.

Example: Find the line through P(2, −1) perpendicular to y = 3x − 4. The perpendicular gradient is −1/3, so y + 1 = −1/3 (x − 2). Multiply by 3: 3y + 3 = −x + 2, giving x + 3y + 1 = 0.

Intersection of two lines

Solve the two equations simultaneously, by substitution or elimination. Lines with equal gradients and no common point are parallel.

Example: y = 2x + 1 and x + y = 7. Substituting gives x + 2x + 1 = 7, so 3x = 6, x = 2 and y = 5. The lines meet at (2, 5).

Circles

A circle with centre (a, b) and radius r has equation (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r².

The expanded form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (−g, −f) and radius √(g² + f² − c). Complete the square in x and y to convert between the forms.

Example: x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 3 = 0 has g = −3, f = 2, c = −3. Centre (3, −2), radius √(9 + 4 + 3) = 4.

Tangents

A tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. Find the radius gradient from the centre to the point, then take the negative reciprocal for the tangent.

Exam technique

  • Sketch the figure first, and check whether the question asks about a line, a circle or both.
  • Keep exact values (fractions and surds) until the final step unless decimals are requested.
  • Check that a line passes through a given point by substituting its coordinates.

title: Redox Equilibria Revision Notes A2 Chemistry
content:
Redox Equilibria A2 Level Chemistry

This revision note covers Edexcel International A Level Chemistry Topic 16, exploring redox equilibria, standard electrode potentials, electrochemical cells, thermodynamics of redox reactions, cell diagrams, advanced redox titrations, uncertainty analysis, and fuel cells.

Oxidation and Reduction in s-, p- and d-Block Elements

Redox processes involve electron transfer and shifts in oxidation numbers, applying seamlessly across s-, p-, and d-block elements.

  • Oxidation is defined as loss of electrons and an increase in oxidation state. Reduction is gain of electrons and a decrease in oxidation state.
  • The reducing agent is oxidised by losing electrons, whereas the oxidising agent is reduced by gaining electrons.
  • These rules apply whether dealing with simple s-block metal ions, p-block non-metals, or complex d-block transition metal ions showing multiple stable oxidation states.

Standard Electrode Potentials and the Standard Hydrogen Electrode

Standard electrode potentials provide a quantitative measure of a species' tendency to be reduced.

  • Standard electrode potentials, E-zero, are measured strictly at 298 K temperature, 100 kPa pressure of gases, and 1.00 mol dm-3 concentration of ions.
  • The standard hydrogen electrode serves as the universal reference electrode with an E-zero value defined as exactly 0.00 V.
  • A reference electrode is necessary because absolute electrode potentials cannot be measured in isolation; only potential differences can be determined.
  • The standard hydrogen electrode uses platinum foil coated in platinum black, immersed in 1.00 mol dm-3 hydrogen ions, with hydrogen gas bubbled at 100 kPa and 298 K.

Measuring Electrode Potentials and Electrochemical Cells

Different half-cell assemblies are required depending on the physical states of the species involved.

  • For metals or non-metals in contact with their aqueous ions, a metal rod is dipped into a 1.00 mol dm-3 solution of its ions, or an inert platinum electrode is used for non-metals like chlorine gas bubbling over chloride ions.
  • For systems involving ions of the same element with different oxidation numbers, an inert platinum electrode is immersed in a solution containing both species at 1.00 mol dm-3 concentration.
  • CORE PRACTICAL 12 involves investigating electrochemical cells by measuring cell potentials for various metal-metal ion combinations and redox systems.

Cell Diagrams and Standard Cell EMF Calculations

Electrochemical cells can be represented concisely using conventional notation and evaluated mathematically.

  • Cell diagrams use a single vertical line to represent a phase boundary and a double vertical line to represent a salt bridge.
  • Oxidised forms are written closer to the salt bridge in conventional half-cell representations, with the more negative half-cell conventionally written on the left.
  • Calculate standard cell emf, E-zero-cell, using the formula: E-zero-cell = E-zero(reduction) - E-zero(oxidation).

Thermodynamic Feasibility, Entropy, and Equilibrium Constants

Standard electrode potentials connect directly to thermodynamic feasibility, entropy changes, and equilibrium constants.

  • Standard electrode potentials are also known as standard reduction potentials and are listed in an electrochemical series.
  • A positive E-zero-cell value indicates that the forward reaction is thermodynamically feasible under standard conditions.
  • E-zero-cell is directly proportional to the total entropy change, delta-S-total, and to ln K for a reaction, meaning larger positive E-zero values correspond to larger equilibrium constants and greater spontaneity.
  • Standard electrode potentials can predict the thermodynamic feasibility of disproportionation reactions, where a species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced.

Limitations of Standard Electrode Potentials

Thermodynamic predictions do not always match real-world outcomes due to kinetic and condition factors.

  • Predictions made using standard electrode potentials have limitations due to the kinetic stability of systems; a reaction may be thermodynamically feasible with a positive E-zero-cell, but have an activation energy so high that the reaction rate is negligibly slow.
  • Departures from standard conditions, such as non-standard concentrations or temperatures, alter actual electrode potentials according to the Nernst equation, potentially reversing feasibility.

Redox Titrations and Uncertainty Analysis

Volumetric analysis using redox titrations allows accurate determination of concentrations in structured and unstructured problems.

  • CORE PRACTICALS 13a and 13b involve carrying out redox titrations with iron(II) ions and potassium manganate(VII), and with sodium thiosulfate and iodine.
  • Manganate(VII) titrations are self-indicating, turning from purple to colourless at the end point when excess MnO4- ions react to form colourless Mn2+ ions.
  • Iodine-thiosulfate titrations use starch indicator, which forms a deep blue-black complex with iodine and turns colourless at the end point when all iodine is consumed.
  • Discussing the uncertainty of measurements requires evaluating percentage errors of apparatus like burettes and volumetric flasks, and their implications for the validity of final results.

Fuel Cells

Fuel cells convert chemical energy directly into electrical energy through redox reactions.

  • Fuel cells use the energy released on the reaction of a fuel with oxygen to generate a voltage, utilising hydrogen-rich fuels like hydrogen and methanol.
  • In an acidic electrolyte hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, hydrogen is oxidised at the anode: H2 yields 2H+ + 2e-, and oxygen is reduced at the cathode: O2 + 4H+ + 4e- yields 2H2O.
  • In an alkaline electrolyte hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, hydrogen reacts at the anode: H2 + 2OH- yields 2H2H2O + 2e-, and oxygen reacts at the cathode: O2 + 2H2O + 4e- yields 4OH-.

Typical Mistakes

  • Mistake: Confusing the left and right sides of a cell diagram. Correction: Remember reduction always occurs at the right-hand electrode and oxidation at the left-hand electrode in conventional notation.
  • Mistake: Omitting the inert platinum electrode in half-cell descriptions containing only aqueous ions. Correction: Always include platinum in phase boundaries if no other solid conductor is present.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that E-zero-cell values are independent of the stoichiometry multipliers used to balance half-equations. Correction: Never multiply E-zero values by balancing coefficients when calculating E-zero-cell.
  • Mistake: Assuming a reaction with a positive E-zero-cell will occur rapidly at room temperature. Correction: Always consider kinetic stability; a positive E-zero only proves thermodynamic feasibility, not reaction rate.

Exam-Style Questions

  1. Question: State the standard conditions required for measuring standard electrode potentials. Answer: 298 K temperature, 100 kPa pressure of gases, and 1.00 mol dm-3 concentration of ions.
  2. Question: Write the conventional cell diagram for a cell formed by Zn(s) / Zn2+(aq) and Cu2+(aq) / Cu(s). Answer: Zn(s) | Zn2+(aq, 1.00 mol dm-3) || Cu2+(aq, 1.00 mol dm-3) | Cu(s).
  3. Question: Calculate the E-zero-cell for zinc and copper given E-zero(Zn2+/Zn) = −0.76 V and E-zero(Cu2+/Cu) = +0.34 V. Answer: E-zero-cell = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V.
  4. Question: State the colour change at the end point in a titration of potassium manganate(VII) with iron(II) ions. Answer: From colourless or very pale pink to permanent pale pink.
  5. Question: Write the anode half-equation for an alkaline hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell. Answer: H2 + 2OH- yields 2H2O + 2e-.

Use these notes alongside active practice of past paper calculation questions, ensuring all standard conditions and half-equation balancing steps are memorised. Revise transition metal chemistry next.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Cell EMF, applied to a zinc and copper cell: E(cell) = E(cathode, reduction) − E(anode, oxidation) = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V. Zinc is the anode because it has the more negative potential, and it is oxidised. Always identify the anode and cathode before you subtract.
  • Feasibility: ΔG = −nFE, so a positive E(cell) gives a negative ΔG and a feasible reaction. Under non-standard conditions, E changes with concentration, so a reaction can be feasible even when E(cell) under standard conditions is small.
  • Redox titration, applied to Fe²⁺ with acidified MnO₄⁻: 5Fe²⁺ + MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ → 5Fe³⁺ + Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O. The ratio is 5 : 1. The permanganate is its own indicator, so the end point is the first permanent pale pink colour.
  • Limitations of E° values: they apply only under standard conditions and say nothing about the rate. A reaction can be thermodynamically feasible but kinetically slow, so a metal can appear reactive from its potential yet react slowly in practice.

### Worked example Use i² = −1. The sum (2 + 3i) + (1 − 4i) = 3 − i. The product (2 + 3i)(1 − i) = 2 − 2i + 3i − 3i² = 2 + i + 3 = 5 + i. The modulus of 3 + 4i is √(9 + 16) = 5. The conjugate of 2 + 3i is 2 − 3i, and z multiplied by its conjugate gives |z|² = 13. ### Check yourself Find (1 + 2i)(3 − i). The answer is 5 + 5i. title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Coordinate questions fall into four types: a shape test, a line from two facts, a meeting point, and a circle. Identify the type from the wording before you touch a formula, because each type has its own first step.

Match the wording to the method

  • "Show that the shape is a rhombus, square or parallelogram": find side lengths and gradients, then compare them. Lengths decide equal sides; gradients decide right angles and parallel sides.
  • "Find the line through … parallel or perpendicular to …": take the gradient from the given line, change it if needed, then build the line from one point.
  • "Find where the line meets the curve or the other line": substitute one equation into the other, then solve the single equation that results.
  • "Find the circle … tangent at …": find the centre and radius first. Tangents are always perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.

Shape test: lengths first, then gradients

Take P(0, 1), Q(4, 4), R(8, 1) and S(4, −2). Side PQ has change (4, 3), so its length is √(16 + 9) = 5. QR has change (4, −3), length 5. RS has change (−4, −3), length 5, and SP has change (−4, 3), length 5. All four sides are equal.

Equal sides alone do not prove a rhombus when the shape could fold. Check one diagonal: PR has gradient (1 − 1)/(8 − 0) = 0, so it is horizontal. QS is vertical, since Q and S both have x = 4. The diagonals are perpendicular, so PQRS is a rhombus. The midpoints of both diagonals are (4, 1), which confirms the two diagonals bisect each other.

A line from two facts

Find the line through (3, −1) perpendicular to 2x − 5y + 1 = 0. Rearranging gives y = (2/5)x + 1/5, so the given gradient is 2/5. The perpendicular gradient is −5/2. Then y + 1 = −(5/2)(x − 3), which becomes 5x + 2y − 13 = 0.

Check the point: 5(3) + 2(−1) − 13 = 0. Always substitute the point you started from, because it catches sign errors in the gradient step.

Where two lines meet

For 3x + y = 7 and x − 2y = −4, rearrange the first to y = 7 − 3x and substitute into the second: x − 2(7 − 3x) = −4, so 7x = 10 and x = 10/7. Then y = 7 − 30/7 = 19/7. Check in the second equation: 10/7 − 38/7 = −4. The point is (10/7, 19/7).

Two lines with the same gradient and different intercepts never meet, so the substitution leaves a false statement such as 0 = 5. Report that as "no intersection", not as an error in your algebra.

Circles

A circle with centre (2, −3) through (5, 1) has r² = (5 − 2)² + (1 + 3)² = 25. Its equation is (x − 2)² + (y + 3)² = 25, which expands to x² + y² − 4x + 6y − 12 = 0.

The tangent at (5, 1) is perpendicular to the radius. The radius has gradient 4/3, so the tangent has gradient −3/4. Then y − 1 = −(3/4)(x − 5), which gives 3x + 4y − 19 = 0.

To find where the line y = 2x − 1 meets this circle, substitute: (x − 2)² + (2x + 2)² = 25. Expanding gives 5x² + 4x − 17 = 0. The discriminant is 16 + 340 = 356, which is positive, so the line cuts the circle at two points.

Converting between forms

Gradient form y = mx + c is easiest for comparing gradients. Form ax + by + c = 0 is what many final answers need. Going from the centre-radius form to the expanded form means multiplying out both brackets, then collecting the x, y and constant terms.

Traps that cost marks

  • Taking the gradient of the given line as its y-coefficient, rather than −(a/b) in ax + by + c = 0.
  • Forgetting to negate the gradient when the question asks for a perpendicular line.
  • Using the radius value r instead of r² in the circle equation.
  • Leaving a meeting point as one coordinate, when the question asks for both.

title: Differentiation — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Differentiation finds how fast y changes with x. Most questions ask for one of three things: a gradient at a point, a tangent or normal, or the nature of a stationary point.

Start from a question

The curve C has equation y = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x − 1.

  1. Find dy/dx.
  2. Find the coordinates of the stationary points and state their nature.
  3. Find the equation of the normal to C at x = 3.

Part 1. dy/dx = 6x² − 18x + 12 = 6(x − 1)(x − 2).

Part 2. dy/dx = 0 at x = 1 and x = 2. When x = 1, y = 4, and when x = 2, y = 3. Next, d²y/dx² = 12x − 18. At (1, 4) this is −6, so the point is a maximum. At (2, 3) it is 6, so the point is a minimum.

Part 3. At x = 3, dy/dx = 6(2)(1) = 12, so the normal has gradient −1/12. Also y = 54 − 81 + 36 − 1 = 8, so the point is (3, 8). The normal is y − 8 = −(x − 3)/12, which gives x + 12y − 99 = 0.

The power rule

If y = axⁿ, then dy/dx = naxⁿ⁻¹, for any rational n. A constant differentiates to zero. Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers first: 4√x − 6/x² = 4x^(1/2) − 6x⁻², so dy/dx = 2/√x + 12/x³.

Expand before you differentiate

Differentiation works term by term, so multiply out any brackets first. Example: y = (x + 2)(x − 5) = x² − 3x − 10, so dy/dx = 2x − 3.

A zero gradient is not always a turning point

Use the second derivative when it is non-zero at the point. If it is zero, test the sign of dy/dx on each side. Example: y = x⁴ − 4x³ gives dy/dx = 4x²(x − 3). At x = 0 the gradient is negative on both sides, so the curve keeps falling and (0, 0) is not a maximum or minimum. At x = 3 the gradient changes from negative to positive, so (3, −27) is a minimum.

Tangents and normals

Substitute x into the original equation to find y, and into dy/dx to find the gradient. The tangent uses that gradient, and the normal uses its negative reciprocal. Write both as y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) and simplify.

Traps that cost marks

  • Differentiating a product factor by factor instead of expanding it first.
  • Giving the normal the same gradient as the tangent, rather than the negative reciprocal.
  • Giving only the x-value of a stationary point, rather than its coordinates (x, y).
  • Calling a point a maximum or minimum from dy/dx = 0 alone, without checking the nature.

title: Exam technique: Mensuration
content:
### What earns the marks
For circles, sectors and arcs, the fraction of 360 stated earns the method mark: write 60/360 before multiplying. For cylinders, cones and spheres, the formula quoted earns a mark on its own, so write Volume = (1/3) pi r squared h even when confident. For compound shapes, split earns marks: compute each part separately, then add or subtract with a clear statement.
### Traps
Error: 2 pi r used for area. Correction: circumference versus area check first. Error: omitting 1/3 for cones and pyramids. Correction: quote the formula every time. Error: using diameter as radius in a semicircle cut-out. Correction: halve the diameter before any pi work. Error: forgetting the square root in a Pythagoras step. Correction: label squared lines as squared.
### Worked example
A cylinder has radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. Its volume is πr²h = π × 9 × 10 = 90π ≈ 282.7 cm³. A sector of angle 60° in a circle of radius 6 cm has arc length (60/360) × 2π × 6 = 2π cm.
### Check yourself
A trapezium has parallel sides 5 cm and 9 cm and a perpendicular height of 4 cm. Find its area. Use ½(a + b)h = ½ × (5 + 9) × 4 = 28 cm². State the units and show the substitution before the final value.

### Worked example
A rectangle is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide. Its perimeter is 2(8 + 5) = 26 cm and its area is 40 cm². A triangular prism with triangular cross-section area 12 cm² and length 7 cm has volume 12 × 7 = 84 cm³.

title: Exam technique: Sequences and Series
content:
### What earns the marks
For AP terms, a + (n-1)d with the brackets evaluated earns the mark; sums use n/2(2a + (n-1)d) quoted. For GP work, the ratio found by division earns one mark and the formula applied earns the next. For sum to infinity, the |r| < 1 check stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: n used instead of (n-1) in terms. Correction: first term needs zero gaps. Error: infinity sums with |r| >= 1. Correction: check convergence first. Error: differentiating S_n for the nth term. Correction: subtract S_{n-1}.
### Worked example
An arithmetic progression has a = 5 and d = 3. The 20th term is a + 19d = 5 + 57 = 62. The sum of the first 20 terms is S₂₀ = (20/2)(2a + 19d) = 10 × 67 = 670. A geometric progression with terms 2, 6, 18 has r = 3, so S₅ = 2(3⁵ − 1)/(3 − 1) = 242. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, so for r = 1/2 with a = 8 the sum is 8 / (1 − 1/2) = 16.
### Check yourself
State the nth term of a sequence from its sum. Find Sₙ, then subtract Sₙ₋₁. Do not differentiate Sₙ, because the sum is a discrete function.

title: Bonding and Structure — Study Notes
content:
Bonding and Structure

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 3. Bonding explains the physical properties of a substance: melting point, conductivity and solubility all follow from the type of bond and the way particles are packed.

Ionic bonding

  • Ionic bonds are the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice.
  • They have high melting points, are brittle and conduct only when molten or dissolved, because the ions are free to move.

Covalent bonding

  • A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two atoms. Simple molecular substances have low melting points because only weak intermolecular forces are overcome.
  • Giant covalent structures such as diamond and silicon(IV) oxide need many strong bonds broken to melt, so they have very high melting points.
  • Graphite conducts because each carbon uses three electrons in bonding, leaving one delocalised electron per atom.

Electronegativity and polarity

  • Electronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract the bonding pair. The difference between two atoms gives a polar bond.
  • A molecule is polar only if its bond dipoles do not cancel. Shape decides this: CO2 is linear and non-polar, while H2O is bent and polar.

Shapes of molecules

  • Electron pairs repel each other, so they arrange themselves as far apart as possible. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs.
  • Common shapes: linear (180°), trigonal planar (120°), tetrahedral (109.5°), and bent or pyramidal forms when lone pairs are present.

Metallic bonding

  • Metals consist of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, which explains conductivity, malleability and high melting points.

Exam tip: a question asking why a substance conducts must name the mobile particle — ions, delocalised electrons — not just "electrons".

title: Exam technique: Further Algebra
content:
### What earns the marks
For modulus equations, both branches solved earn a mark each. For inequalities, the two-sided split earns the method mark with the and/or structure correct. For equal-roots problems, discriminant zero stated earns the first mark and -b/2a earns the second.
### Traps
