title: Exam technique: Representation via Numerical Measures
content:
### What earns the marks
For skewness direction, mean vs median comparison stated earns the mark. For box plots, all five values labelled earn one mark and the skew comment earns the second. For outlier checks, the fence calculation shown earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: skew direction flipped. Correction: tail side names the skew. Error: quartiles mislabeled on plots. Correction: order min, Q1, median, Q3, max. Error: max value called an outlier by eye. Correction: test against the fence.
### Worked example
Data: 2, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 20. The mean is 49 / 7 = 7 and the median is 5, so the mean is larger and the skew is positive. The lower half {2, 4, 5} has median 4 (Q1). The upper half {6, 7, 20} has median 7 (Q3). IQR = 3, so the upper fence is 7 + 1.5 × 3 = 11.5, and 20 is an outlier.
### Check yourself
A box plot has its median closer to the lower quartile than to the upper quartile. Which way is the data skewed, and what words should the answer use? The data is positively skewed, because the longer right-hand part of the box shows the upper values are more spread out.

title: Electric Fields and Capacitance — Study Notes
content:
Electric Fields and Capacitance

Coulomb's Law

F = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r²). Field strength E = F/q (N C⁻¹); for a point charge E = q/(4πε₀r²).

Uniform Fields

Between parallel plates: E = V/d, constant.

Example: 2 kV across 5 mm: E = 400 kV m⁻¹. An electron feels F = eE ≈ 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ N toward the positive plate.

Potential

V = W/q, scalar; E = −dV/dr. Potential energy of q at V is qV.

Capacitance

C = Q/V (farads). Energy stored: W = ½QV = ½CV².

Combinations: parallel adds (C = C₁ + C₂); series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ (opposite to resistors).

Example: 10 μF and 20 μF in series: 1/C = 1/10 + 1/20 → C ≈ 6.7 μF.

Charging and Discharging

Exponential: V = V₀ e^(−t/RC). Time constant RC: after one RC, V falls to 37%. Half-life t½ = 0.69 RC.

Exam tips: field points from high to low potential; in discharge problems identify which quantity (V, Q or I) decays — all share the same exponential factor.

title: Exam technique: Transformations and Vectors
content:
### What earns the marks
For translations and vector arithmetic, each component computed separately earns credit: show x and y lines. For magnitude, the root-of-sum-of-squares line earns the method mark before evaluation. For reflections and rotations, the coordinate rule stated ((y; -x) for 90 degrees clockwise) earns the method mark. For describing transformations, all three of type, centre or line, and size or angle are needed for full marks.
### Traps
Error: writing column vectors as bracket rows that lose a row. Correction: use (x; y) form and keep both components. Error: (100) or 14 for the magnitude of (6; 8). Correction: square, add, then root. Error: (-y; x) for a clockwise rotation. Correction: clockwise is (y; -x). Error: negating both coordinates for a single-axis reflection. Correction: one axis changes, the other stays.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Nearly every question here is the same three-step job: translate the geometry into equations, solve them, then read the answer back against the diagram.

Core results

  • Distance between (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²).
  • The midpoint is ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).
  • Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Parallel lines share a gradient; perpendicular lines satisfy m₁m₂ = −1.

Finding the equation of a line

With a point and a gradient, use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁). With two points, find the gradient first. Give the answer in the form the question requests: y = mx + c, or ax + by + c = 0 with integer coefficients when it asks for that form.

Example: find the line through (−2, 5) perpendicular to 3x − 4y = 1. The given line has gradient 3/4, so the required gradient is −4/3. Then y − 5 = −4/3(x + 2), which rearranges to 4x + 3y − 7 = 0.

Intersections of a line and a curve

Points of intersection satisfy both equations at once, so substitute one into the other. The resulting quadratic has two roots, one repeated root, or no real roots, and the discriminant tells you which. Parallel lines give no intersection, and a repeated root means the line touches the curve.

Example: y = 2x − 1 and x² + y² = 10. Substituting gives 5x² − 4x − 9 = 0, so (5x − 9)(x + 1) = 0. The points are (9/5, 13/5) and (−1, −3).

Circles

A circle with centre (a, b) and radius r has equation (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r². Expanding gives the general form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0, where the centre is (−g, −f) and the radius is √(g² + f² − c). To test a point, substitute its coordinates: a value below r² means inside, equal means on the circle, above means outside.

Example: x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0 has centre (3, −2) and radius √(9 + 4 + 12) = 5.

Tangents and normals

A tangent touches the circle at one point and is perpendicular to the radius through that point. Find the gradient of the radius from the centre, take the negative reciprocal for the tangent, then use the point–gradient form. The normal is the radius itself, so it passes through the centre.

Example: the tangent to (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25 at (7, 1). The radius has gradient 3/4, so the tangent has gradient −4/3, and its equation is 4x + 3y − 31 = 0.

Exam technique

  • Draw a rough diagram first; it shows whether a point should be inside or outside a circle before any algebra is done.
  • With a "show that" instruction, finish with the exact expression that was asked for.
  • To check a tangent, confirm that the distance from the centre to the line equals the radius.

title: Waves & Sound — Study Notes
content:
Waves & Sound

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): general wave properties; reflection/refraction/diffraction; sound.

1. Wave basics

v = fλ. Transverse (oscillation ⊥ travel — light, water, S-waves) vs longitudinal (parallel — sound, P-waves). Amplitude, wavelength, frequency f = 1/T; wavefront diagrams.

2. Ripple tank behaviours

  • Reflection: angle in = angle out; speed/frequency unchanged, direction changes.
  • Refraction: speed change at boundary bends wavefronts (shallow water slows ripples).
  • Diffraction: spreading through gaps ≈ λ wide; around edges.

3. Electromagnetic spectrum (order)

Radio → micro → IR → visible (red 700 nm – violet 400 nm) → UV → X → gamma. All travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum; transverse; uses and dangers (IR heating; UV skin; X/gamma ionising).

4. Sound

  • Longitudinal; needs a medium (bell in vacuum demo). Speed ~340 m/s air, faster in liquids/solids.
  • Range 20 Hz–20 kHz; ultrasound > 20 kHz (sonar, prenatal scans, cleaning).
  • Pitch ↔ frequency; loudness ↔ amplitude.

5. Echo problems

Distance = (v × t)/2 (there and back).

Example: echo after 0.6 s, v = 340 → cliff 102 m away.

Exam tips: in diagrams always label wavelength as crest-to-crest; for refraction, state "changes speed" first, then direction; quote EM uses with the hazard.

title: Logic Gates & Boolean Logic — Study Notes
content:
Logic Gates & Boolean Logic

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): six gates, truth tables, building/describing circuits, problem-to-logic mapping.

1. The six gates

ABANDORNANDNORXOR
0000110
0101101
1001101
1111000

NOT inverts. NAND = AND + invert; NOR = OR + invert; XOR = 1 when inputs differ.

2. Truth tables

2 inputs → 4 rows; 3 inputs → 8 rows. Work gate by gate, adding intermediate columns for sub-circuit outputs.

3. Problem → logic

Define inputs/outputs first. Alarm rings (X=1) if sensor P triggered AND (door D OR window W): X = P AND (D OR W). Then draw the circuit: OR first, then AND.

4. Describing circuits

Write the expression from a diagram gate by gate; annotate output of each gate (X, Y) before combining.

Exam tips: check your truth table row count before writing; in problem questions, state "input P = 1 means sensor triggered" — definitions earn marks.

title: Acid-base Equilibria — Study Notes
content:
Acid-base Equilibria

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 14. Acids and bases are defined by proton transfer. The strength of an acid is given by its dissociation constant, and pH calculations, buffers and titrations all follow from it.

Strong and weak acids

  • A strong acid dissociates completely in water, so [H⁺] equals the acid concentration. For 0.010 mol dm⁻³ HCl, [H⁺] = 0.010 and pH = 2.00.
  • A weak acid dissociates only partly. For HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻, Ka = [H⁺][A⁻] / [HA].
  • pKa = −log10 Ka. A smaller pKa means a stronger acid.

pH calculations

  • pH = −log10[H⁺]. For a base, find pOH = −log10[OH⁻] and use pH = 14.00 − pOH at 298 K.
  • Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶ at 298 K.
  • For a 0.050 mol dm⁻³ NaOH solution, [OH⁻] = 0.050, pOH = 1.30 and pH = 12.70.

Buffers

  • A buffer contains a weak acid and its conjugate base (for example ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate). It resists large pH changes.
  • The pH of a buffer is given by pH = pKa + log([A⁻] / [HA]). When [A⁻] = [HA], pH = pKa.
  • Adding a small amount of strong acid is absorbed by the conjugate base, so the pH changes only slightly.

Titrations and indicators

  • Strong acid with strong base: the equivalence point is pH 7.
  • Weak acid with strong base: the equivalence point is above pH 7, so phenolphthalein (pH 8.3 to 10) is suitable.
  • Strong acid with weak base: the equivalence point is below pH 7, so methyl orange (pH 3.1 to 4.4) is suitable.
  • Choose an indicator whose colour change lies within the steep vertical section of the titration curve.

Exam tip: when pH is asked for a weak acid, calculate [H⁺] from Ka and the concentration before taking the logarithm.

title: Exam technique: Probability (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For conditional probability, the restricted sample space stated earns the method mark. For independence checks, P(A)P(B) compared with P(A and B) earns both marks. For Bayes-style updates, the tree fractions multiplied along branches earn stepwise credit.
### Traps
Error: mutually exclusive assumed independent. Correction: test, never assume. Error: given-condition ignored. Correction: shrink the denominator first. Error: branches added instead of multiplied. Correction: multiply along, add across.
### Worked example
Event A has P(A) = 0.5 and event B has P(B) = 0.4. Given that A and B are independent, P(A and B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20. If the question instead gives P(A and B) = 0.3, then the events are not independent, because 0.3 does not equal 0.20. The conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B) = 0.3 ÷ 0.4 = 0.75.
### Check yourself
Two events are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.2. Are they independent? No. P(A and B) = 0 but P(A)P(B) = 0.06, so the events are dependent. Mutually exclusive events are always dependent when both have non-zero probability.

title: Waves — Study Notes
content:
Waves

Basics

A wave transfers energy without net transfer of matter.

  • Transverse: oscillation ⊥ propagation (EM waves, water surface)
  • Longitudinal: oscillation ∥ propagation (sound)

The Wave Equation

v = fλ. Frequency f is set by the source; speed v by the medium.

Example: sound at 340 m s⁻¹, f = 512 Hz: λ = 340/512 ≈ 0.66 m.

Intensity

I = P/A. Intensity ∝ amplitude² — doubling the amplitude quadruples the intensity.

Doppler Effect

Observed frequency changes with relative motion: f′ = f(v ± v_o)/(v ∓ v_s). Approaching sources sound higher.

Example: an ambulance passing you: high pitch approaching, low pitch receding.

EM Spectrum

Radio → micro → IR → visible (400–700 nm) → UV → X-ray → gamma. All travel at c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in vacuum.

Polarization

Only transverse waves can be polarised — proof that light is transverse. Malus' law: I = I₀ cos²θ between polariser axes.

Exam tips: distinguish wave speed (set by medium) from frequency (set by source); in Doppler problems, signs depend on approach or recession.

title: Vectors — Study Notes
content:
Vectors

Components and Arithmetic

A vector a = 3i + 4j has magnitude |a| = √(3² + 4²) = 5. Parallel vectors are scalar multiples; unit vector = a/|a|.

Position and Direction

The line through point A with direction d: r = a + t d. Two lines are parallel if their directions are multiples.

Example: r = (1, 2) + t(3, −1).

Scalar (Dot) Product

a · b = |a||b| cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂.

Perpendicular ⇔ a · b = 0. Parallel ⇔ cross-multiplied components are equal (in 2D: a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ = 0).

Example: (2, 3) · (−6, 4) = −12 + 12 = 0, so they are perpendicular.

Angle Between Vectors

cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|).

Example: between (1, 0) and (1, 1): cos θ = 1/(1 × √2), θ = 45°.

Lines and Points

Foot of perpendicular from P to a line, intersection of two lines, and shortest distances all come from dot products and parameter t.

Exam tips: write column vectors cleanly; check answers by substituting the found t back into both position vectors; keep exact surd magnitudes rather than decimals.

Exam method: components, magnitude and scalar product

A vector in two dimensions is written as a column (x; y), and in three dimensions as (x; y; z) or in unit vector form xi + yj + zk. The magnitude is |a| = √(x² + y² + z²), which is Pythagoras applied in each direction.

The scalar product a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ is a number, not a vector. It also equals |a||b| cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors. Two vectors are perpendicular exactly when their scalar product is zero.

Use the scalar product to find the angle between two vectors: cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|). Give the angle in degrees or radians as the question asks.

A unit vector has magnitude 1. Divide a vector by its magnitude to find the unit vector in the same direction.

Exam cue: Write each component with its sign before adding, because a sign slip in the scalar product changes the answer without changing the method.

title: Statistics (S1) — Study Notes
content:
Statistics 1: data, sampling and correlation

S1 is about collecting, summarising and relating data. You must choose sensible models, compute summary statistics quickly, code data, spot outliers and fit a regression line.

Sampling

  • Random sample: every member of the population has equal chance of selection.
  • Systematic: every kth member. Stratified: split population into strata, sample each in proportion.
  • Bias must be avoided: random numbers, representative strata, no convenience sampling.

Averages

  • Mean: x-bar = (sum of x) / n. Sensitive to outliers.
  • Median: the middle value; for n values ordered, position (n + 1)/2. Robust to outliers.
  • Mode: the most frequent value.

Measuring spread

  • Range = largest - smallest.
  • Quartiles: Q1 is the median of the lower half, Q3 the median of the upper half; IQR = Q3 - Q1.
  • Variance = (sum of x^2)/n - (x-bar)^2, and SD = sqrt(variance).
  • The variance uses squared units; the SD returns to the original units.

Coding

For x = a + by: mean of x = a + b x-bar, SD of x = |b| SD of y. Coding never changes the correlation coefficient.

Outliers and box plots

An outlier lies below Q1 - 1.5 x IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 x IQR. Box plots show min, Q1, median, Q3, max (whiskers to the furthest non-outlier).

Correlation and regression

  • The product moment correlation coefficient r measures linear strength: -1 <= r <= 1.
  • r close to +1: strong positive linear; close to -1: strong negative; close to 0: no linear correlation. Correlation is not causation.
  • Regression line of y on x: y = a + bx with b = Sxy / Sxx and a = y-bar - b x-bar. Use it to interpolate, never extrapolate.

title: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism — Study Notes
content:
Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism

Magnetic flux density

A magnetic field is a region where a magnetic force acts on a magnet, a current-carrying conductor or a moving charge. Its strength is the magnetic flux density B, measured in tesla (T). Field lines run from north to south outside a magnet and never cross.

Force on a current-carrying conductor

A conductor of length L carrying current I at right angles to a field B feels F = BIL. In general F = BIL sin θ, where θ is the angle between the conductor and the field. The force is zero when the conductor is parallel to the field.

Fleming's left-hand rule: First finger = Field (from north to south), seCond finger = Current (conventional, positive to negative), thuMb = Motion (the force). Hold the hand so the three fingers are mutually perpendicular. Check the current direction: it is conventional current, from + to −, not electron flow.

Example: a 0.25 m wire carrying 3.0 A at right angles to a 0.40 T field feels F = 0.40 × 3.0 × 0.25 = 0.30 N.

Force on a moving charge

A charge Q moving with speed v at right angles to B feels F = BQv. The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so the speed does not change, only the direction. In a uniform field the charge follows a circular path of radius r = mv/BQ. The period T = 2πm/BQ does not depend on the speed.

Velocity selector: crossed electric and magnetic fields give undeflected motion when qE = qvB, so v = E/B.

Magnetic field due to a current

A long straight wire gives B = μ₀I/(2πd), with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹. Inside a long solenoid of n turns per metre, B = μ₀nI. The field is uniform inside the solenoid and weak outside it.

Electromagnetic induction

Magnetic flux is Φ = BA cos θ, measured in weber (Wb). Faraday's law states that the induced e.m.f. equals the rate of change of flux linkage: ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt. Lenz's law gives the direction: the induced e.m.f. opposes the change that produces it. This is the energy conservation principle, which is why the minus sign appears.

Example: a 200-turn coil whose flux changes by 2.0 mWb in 0.10 s has a mean e.m.f. of 4.0 V.

Alternating currents

For a sinusoidal current, the root-mean-square value is I_rms = I₀/√2, and similarly V_rms = V₀/√2. The mean power is P = I_rms²R = V_rms²/R, and it is the rms value that equals the d.c. value for the same heating effect.

Rectification and smoothing

A diode passes current in one direction only. A half-wave rectifier gives pulses for half of each cycle. A full-wave bridge rectifier uses all of the input, so its output frequency is twice the input frequency. A smoothing capacitor across the output charges at each peak and discharges between peaks, reducing the ripple.

Exam tips: use the rms value for power calculations, not the peak. For Lenz's law, always state the opposing effect in words. Show the angle when the field is not perpendicular to the wire.

title: Ethics and AI — Study Notes
content:
`# Ethics and AI

Professional Bodies

ACM/IEEE-CS and BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, avoid harm, respect privacy. Violations cost trust and employment.

Ethical Scenarios

  • Collecting more personal data than needed (privacy)
  • Releasing software with known bugs that risks safety (competence/honesty)
  • Automated decisions without human review (accountability)

Laws: data protection (GDPR-style), computer misuse (unauthorised access is a crime regardless of intent).

AI Characteristics

Systems exhibiting: planning, learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, knowledge representation.

Machine Learning

  • Supervised: learns from labelled data (spam detection)
  • Unsupervised: finds structure in unlabelled data (clustering)
  • Reinforcement: learns by reward signals (game agents)

Training/evaluation loop: fit on training data, test on unseen data to avoid overfitting. Neural networks adjust weights via backpropagation.

Ethics of AI

Bias in training data → unfair outputs; opaque decisions → accountability gaps; job displacement; autonomous weapons.

Exam tips: structure ethics answers as: identify the principle → apply to the scenario → give consequences for stakeholders.

Ownership, licensing and AI bias

Copyright gives the creator legal protection over how their software and other original work is copied, distributed and changed. Copying software without permission is a breach of copyright and can be illegal. Open source software is released under licences that allow others to use, study and modify it, often on the condition that changes are shared in the same way.

An AI system learns from its training data. If that data over-represents some groups or reflects past prejudice, the system's outputs can be biased, and it may treat people unfairly without anyone intending it. Developers can reduce this by checking the training data and testing the system on a wide range of cases.

Exam tip: link each ethical point to a consequence for a real user, such as a person losing a job or a loan being refused unfairly.

Worked example: a bias scenario

A facial recognition system is trained mostly on photographs of one group of people. When it is tested on a different group it misidentifies people far more often. The cause is sampling bias: the training data did not represent the people the system would be used on. The fix is to collect a training set that reflects the full user population, to test the system on each group separately, and to report the error rate for each group rather than one overall figure.

Bias can also come from the people who label the data. If labellers apply their own assumptions, those assumptions are learned by the model. Name the source of bias in your answer, because marks are given for identifying where the bias enters, not just for saying that it exists.

Ownership and licensing questions

  • Software written by an employee in the course of their job is normally owned by the employer, while software written by a freelancer is usually owned by the freelancer unless a contract says otherwise.
  • An open-source licence sets the conditions for using, changing and sharing code. Using open-source code in a commercial product still requires following its licence terms.

title: Further Trigonometry — Study Notes
content:
Further Trigonometry

Compound Angles

  • sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
  • cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B

Example: sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 + √2)/4.

Double Angles

  • sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A
  • cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A

Example: express 4 sin x cos x in one term: 2 sin 2x.

The R-Form

a sin x + b cos x = R sin(x + α) with R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b/a.

Example: 3 sin x + 4 cos x = 5 sin(x + 0.927). This instantly gives the maximum 5 and minimum −5.

Reciprocal Functions

sec θ = 1/cos θ, cosec θ = 1/sin θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ. Key identity: 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

Exam tips: choose the cos 2A form that eliminates the unwanted function; when solving with R-form, divide by R before using inverse trig, and translate intervals carefully.

Exam method: reciprocal functions and identities

The reciprocal functions are sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x and cot x = 1/tan x. Rewrite them in terms of sine and cosine when a question mixes functions, because this usually shows which identity to use.

The Pythagorean identities are sin² x + cos² x = 1, 1 + tan² x = sec² x and 1 + cot² x = cosec² x. Divide the first identity by cos² x or sin² x to obtain the second or third.

To solve an equation such as sec x = 2, first rewrite it as cos x = 1/2, then find the acute angle and the other solutions in the required range. For cos x = k the solutions in 0 to 2π are α and 2π − α, where α is the acute angle.

To prove an identity, work on the more complicated side only, and keep rewriting until it matches the other side.

Exam cue: Give each solution in the range asked for, using exact values such as π/3 when the angle is standard.

Exam method: R-form

To write a sinθ + b cosθ as R sin(θ + α), expand R sin(θ + α) = R sinθ cosα + R cosθ sinα and compare coefficients. This gives R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b / a, with α in the quadrant where cos α and sin α have the signs of a and b.

Exam cue: Find the maximum and minimum from R, then solve for θ over the stated interval. Give α in the correct quadrant before writing the final angles.

title: Exam technique: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
content:
### What earns the marks
For percentages of amounts, the 10-percent building blocks shown earn method marks without a calculator. For reverse percentages, state what the given amount represents (64 dollars = 80 percent) before dividing: that line earns the mark. For compound interest, each year on its own line earns credit. For Steel-type growth and decay, the multiplier (1/2 cubed) stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: adding 20 percent to the sale price for the original. Correction: the sale price is the base of nothing; divide by 0.8. Error: simple interest applied twice for compound growth. Correction: grow each year from the new total. Error: decimal-point slips in 3/8 to percent. Correction: decimal first (0.375), then times 100.
### Worked example
Find 35% of 240: 0.35 × 240 = 84. A value increases by 20% to reach 180. The original is 180 ÷ 1.2 = 150, because you divide by the multiplier rather than taking 20% of 180. Check: 150 × 1.2 = 180. For fractions, 3/4 + 2/5 = 15/20 + 8/20 = 23/20 = 1 3/20.
### Check yourself
A price falls from £80 to £68. Find the percentage decrease. The decrease is £12, so the percentage is 12/80 × 100 = 15%. Show the divisor is the original price and not the new one.

title: Exam technique: Database Systems
content:
### What earns the marks
For full marks on Database Systems questions, the examiner needs to see explanations of relational concepts, correct SQL syntax, and descriptions of DBMS features. The command words calculate, show that, explain, describe, justify, and state are used. For example, to justify why a relational database is used, cite reduced redundancy and flexible queries, relating to statement 9. Working and reasons must be shown for explain and justify questions.
### Traps
Common mistakes include not aliasing joined tables, incorrect use of SQL keywords, and not considering data integrity. Corrections include using aliases like s, l, f, writing SQL keywords in uppercase, and considering validation rules and access rights.
### Memory hooks
To remember the benefits of a relational database, use the mnemonic REDUCE: Reduced redundancy, Easy queries, Data integrity, Unique identifiers, Concurrent access, and Efficient storage. Another hook is to always write SQL keywords in uppercase and alias joined tables. A sanity check for SQL queries is to ensure the correct use of SELECT, FROM, WHERE, and JOIN.
### Timing
Database Systems questions typically account for 9 marks and should be budgeted around 15-20 minutes. This allows time to read the question, plan the answer, and write a clear and concise response.

title: Exam technique: Measures of Variation
content:
### What earns the marks
For standard deviation, mean first then the squared-deviation sum earns each mark. For coded data, the y-bar and s_y transformation earns the method mark. For comparisons, mean and spread commented together earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: variance reported as sd. Correction: root last. Error: comparing means only. Correction: comment on spread too. Error: coding applied once then forgotten. Correction: transform consistently.
### Worked example
Five values are 2, 4, 4, 6 and 9. The mean is 25 / 5 = 5. The squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 1 and 16, which sum to 28. The variance is 28 / 5 = 5.6, and the standard deviation is the square root, about 2.37. Show the squared deviations line on the paper, since the method mark depends on it.
### Check yourself
If each value in the list is increased by 10, state what happens to the mean and to the standard deviation. The mean rises by 10, while the standard deviation is unchanged, because adding a constant does not change the spread.

title: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — Study Notes
content:
Magnetism & Electromagnetism

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): magnets & fields; magnetic effect of a current; force on a current-carrying conductor; motor effect; electromagnetic induction (Extended); transformers (Extended).

1. Magnets and fields

Iron/steel/cobalt/nickel; like poles repel. Field lines exit N, enter S; compass plotting; plotting compass aligns with field. Induced magnetism: iron (temporary) vs steel (permanent).

2. Electromagnets

Solenoid field like a bar magnet; strength ↑ with current, turns, iron core. Uses: relays, scrapyard crane, electric bell, speaker. Hard/soft magnetic materials choose permanent vs core use.

3. Force on a current-carrying conductor

F = BIL, direction by Fleming's left hand (fIeld, current, force). Reversing current or field reverses force. D.C. motor: coil, commutator reverses current each half-turn for continuous rotation; speed/torque ↑ with current, field strength, turns/area.

4. Electromagnetic induction (Extended)

Induced e.m.f. when a conductor cuts field lines or flux changes. Fleming's right hand (generator). Factors: speed, field strength, turns. A.C. generator: slip rings; dynamo effect; Lenz's law opposes change (direction of induced current).

5. Transformers (Extended)

Vp/Vs = Np/Ns; Pin ≈ Pout (100% assumed): IpVp = IsVs. Step-up raises V, lowers I → lower I²R transmission losses; a.c. required (changing flux).

Magnetic fields and electromagnets

Like magnetic poles repel and unlike poles attract. Outside a bar magnet, field lines run from the north pole to the south pole. A solenoid is a coil of wire; its field is strengthened by increasing the current, increasing the number of turns, or placing a soft iron core inside it. An electromagnet can be switched on and off by the current, unlike a permanent magnet.

A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force, which is the basis of the motor effect used in electric motors.

Exam tip: when asked how to make an electromagnet stronger, give two changes, such as more turns and a larger current.

title: Superposition — Study Notes
content:
Superposition

Principle of superposition

When two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements. Constructive interference occurs where the waves are in phase; destructive interference occurs where they are in antiphase.

Stationary waves

  • A stationary wave forms when two progressive waves of the same frequency, amplitude and wavelength travel in opposite directions and superpose.
  • Nodes are points of zero amplitude; antinodes are points of maximum amplitude. Adjacent nodes (or antinodes) are separated by λ/2.
  • On a string fixed at both ends, the fundamental frequency is f = v/(2L), so the wavelength is λ = 2L.

Interference

For coherent sources (same frequency and a constant phase difference) with slit separation a and screen distance D, the fringe spacing is Δx = λD/a.

Diffraction

Diffraction is the spreading of a wave after it passes through a gap or round an edge. It is greatest when the gap width is comparable to the wavelength.

Diffraction grating

For a grating with slit spacing d, the angle θ of the nth-order maximum satisfies nλ = d sin θ. A grating with more lines per metre gives a smaller d and larger angles of diffraction.

Worked example: light of wavelength 600 nm passes through two slits 0.30 mm apart, with a screen 1.5 m away. Fringe spacing Δx = λD/a = (600 × 10⁻⁹ × 1.5) ÷ (3.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.0 mm.

Exam tips: convert nm and mm to metres before using Δx = λD/a. Check the order n when using a grating. Coherence is a requirement for interference, so state it.

The diffraction grating equation

A diffraction grating has many closely spaced slits. Light of wavelength λ leaves the grating at angle θ to form bright maxima when d sin θ = nλ, where d is the slit spacing and n is the order of the maximum. Each order is sharper and more widely separated than a double slit, because the many slits reinforce the bright positions. The number of orders visible is limited by the condition that sin θ cannot exceed 1.

Exam tip: convert the slit spacing to metres before using the grating equation, and note that the central maximum is n = 0.

title: Exam technique: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism
content:
### What earns the marks
For wires, BIL with right-angle condition earns both marks. For selectors, E/B equating the forces earns the method mark. For induction, Lenz opposition stated earns the explanation mark; power conserved in transformers earns the calculation marks.

Error: parallel motion assumed to feel force. Correction: only the perpendicular component counts. Error: induced current aiding the change. Correction: it opposes the change. Error: particle path guessed straight. Correction: perpendicular entry gives circular arcs.

title: Exam technique: Nuclear Physics
content:
### What earns the marks
For radiations, alpha-beta-gamma ordered by penetration earns one mark with absorbers earns the second. For half-life, each halving step shown earns stepwise credit. For deflection, mass difference used to explain earns the explanation mark.
### Traps
Error: paper claimed to stop beta. Correction: paper stops alpha only. Error: half-life mass subtracted linearly. Correction: halve each period. Error: closer source assumed lower rate. Correction: closer means higher count rate.

title: Exam technique: Programming Concepts
content:
### What earns the marks
To earn full marks on this topic, students need to demonstrate a clear understanding of programming concepts, including variables, data types, selection, iteration, arrays, file handling, and subroutines, as outlined in statements 4.2, 8.1, 8.2, and 8.3. Command words such as calculate, show that, explain, describe, justify, and state are used to assess this understanding. For example, a question may ask students to explain the difference between a WHILE loop and a REPEAT loop, or to describe how to declare and use a 2D array. Working and reasons must be shown to support answers.
### Traps
Common mistakes include using the wrong loop type, such as using a WHILE loop when a REPEAT loop is needed, or vice versa. Another error is failing to declare variables before use, or using the wrong data type. Additionally, students may forget to close files after use, or use the wrong file mode.
### Memory hooks
To remember the different data types, students can use the mnemonic INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE. To recall the difference between a procedure and a function, students can think of a procedure as a recipe that performs a task, while a function is a recipe that returns a value. When working with 2D arrays, students can use the pattern of looping over rows first, then columns.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 20-30% of the paper, and students should budget around 30-40 minutes to answer questions on programming concepts. Students should aim to spend around 10-15 minutes on each question, depending on the mark value and complexity.

title: Algebra — Equations — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Equations

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): linear equations, simultaneous equations, quadratic formula, completing the square, forming equations from words.

1. Linear equations

3(x − 2) = x + 4 → 3x − 6 = x + 4 → 2x = 10 → x = 5. With fractions, multiply through by the LCD first.

2. Forming equations

Translate shapes/situations: "rectangle length 3 cm more than width, perimeter 34" → 2w + 2(w + 3) = 34 → w = 7.

3. Simultaneous equations

  • Elimination: 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2 → add → 3x = 9 → x = 3, y = 1.
  • Substitution for linear–quadratic: substitute y = 2x into x² + y² = 20 → 5x² = 20 → x = ±2.

4. Quadratics by formula

x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a.

Example: 2x² − 4x − 3 = 0 → x = (4 ± √(16 + 24))/4 = 2.58 or −0.58 (2 d.p.).

5. Completing the square

x² + bx + c = (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c. x² − 6x + 5 = (x − 3)² − 4 → minimum at (3, −4). Use for turning points and for solving when factorising fails.

Exam tips: substitute answers back to verify; in word problems define the unknown clearly ("let w = width in cm"); give quadratic solutions to the accuracy demanded.

title: Exam technique: Poisson Distribution
content:
### What earns the marks
For lambda scaling, the rate times the interval stated earns the first mark. For probabilities, e^-lambda lambda^x / x! with values earns the method mark. For approximations, the condition named (n large, p small, lambda = np) earns credit.
### Traps
Error: unscaled lambda over a new interval. Correction: scale first. Error: binomial coefficients inside Poisson work. Correction: Poisson formula only. Error: mean and variance treated as different. Correction: both equal lambda.
### Worked example
Calls arrive at a rate of 3 per minute, so over 2 minutes λ = 6. The probability of exactly 2 calls is P(X = 2) = e⁻⁶ × 6² / 2! = 18e⁻⁶ ≈ 0.0446. The mean and the variance both equal λ, so the mean number in 2 minutes is 6.
### Check yourself
Explain why the rate must be scaled before you use the formula. The rate is given per minute, but the interval is 2 minutes, so λ must be the rate multiplied by the interval, giving 6 and not 3.

### Worked example
Calls arrive at a rate of 3 per minute, so over 2 minutes λ = 6. The probability of exactly 2 calls is P(X = 2) = e⁻⁶ × 6² / 2! = 18e⁻⁶ ≈ 0.0446. The mean and the variance both equal λ, so the mean number in 2 minutes is 6.

title: Data Structures — Study Notes
content:
`# Data Structures

Arrays and Lists

Contiguous, indexed, O(1) access; fixed size. 2D arrays: element (i, j) — rows × columns.

Stack (LIFO)

push/pop/peek at one end. Uses: call stacks, undo, expression evaluation, DFS.

Example: evaluating 3 4 + : push 3, push 4, pop both, push 7.

Queue (FIFO)

enqueue at rear, dequeue at front. Uses: print queues, schedulers, BFS. A circular queue reuses vacated slots with head/tail pointers modulo capacity.

Linked List

Nodes with data + pointer. Insert/delete O(1) at a known node; search O(n). Traversal follows next pointers until null.

Hash Table

Hash function maps keys → index. Collisions resolved by chaining or open addressing. Average O(1) lookup, worst O(n).

title:
Appendix Q — A full worked example of how the topic’s reasoning comes together in one long answer

A long answer on this topic is best understood by working through a single example from end to end, because that shows how the reasoning, the sequence and the distinctions are meant to come together. Suppose the question asks you to describe how the body responds when a skin infection is beginning to develop, and to explain how the response shows both non-specific and specific defence, and then to relate that to vaccination and to the idea of memory. A good answer starts with the first line: the skin has been breached, the immediate non-specific responses include the local inflammation and the arrival of phagocytes, and phagocytosis is non-specific because it acts against a broad range of pathogens. A good answer then moves to the specific response: the antigens from the pathogen are recognised, B cells produce antibodies specific to those antigens, T cells help and control and some T cells are important in dealing with infected cells, and memory cells are formed. A good answer then explains why this matters: the primary response is slower because the specific lymphocytes have to be activated and expanded, but the secondary response is faster and stronger because the memory cells are already present. And a good answer then relates it to vaccination: vaccination exposes the immune system to the antigen without the disease, so the memory is formed without the person having to suffer the infection first. If you can write that whole sequence from memory, you have the topic as a connected whole, and you have the kind of answer the long questions are after.

If you write that kind of answer with the right distinctions, you hit the marks that the question is really after. You hit the non-specific versus specific distinction, because you have said that the first line is non-specific and the specific response is specific. You hit the process distinction, because you have said that the primary response is slower and the secondary is faster because of memory. You hit the vaccination link, because you have said that vaccination primes the same memory system without the disease. You hit the cell distinction, because you have said that B cells make antibodies and T cells help and control and deal with infected cells. If you can write that whole sequence with those points in it, you are not just labelling; you are reasoning, and the reasoning is what the long-answer marks are about. If you write a shorter answer that only says “the body fights the infection with white blood cells and memory,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning.

The same kind of integrated answer is what the evaluation and ethics questions want, just with a different content. Suppose the question asks you to evaluate the use of vaccines in controlling an infectious disease, and to consider both benefits and issues. A good answer says that vaccines protect individuals by priming the immune system without disease, and that at high coverage they also protect the population through herd immunity by reducing the spread. A good answer then says that the issues include coverage, exemptions, side effects and public acceptance, and that the balance depends on the disease, the vaccine and the context. A good answer does not say only that vaccines are good or only that they are problematic; it says that the benefit is protection of the individual and, at coverage, the population, and that the issues are real but specific to the case. If you can write that, you have the evaluation. If you write only a slogan one way or the other, you have the label but not the evaluation, and the mark is in the evaluation.

The same kind of integrated answer is what the gene technology questions want when they ask you to relate the technique to the purpose and then to the application and the limits. Suppose the question asks you about PCR and how it is used in a forensic or diagnostic context. A good answer says that PCR amplifies a specific DNA sequence in vitro through repeated cycles, and that the primers define the target and the heat-stable polymerase survives the repeated heating. A good answer then says that this is useful because it lets a small sample be amplified enough to study or use, and that in a forensic or diagnostic context the result is interpreted in context with attention to sample quality and contamination. A good answer does not say only that PCR makes DNA, because that is the label but not the reasoning. It says that PCR amplifies a specific sequence, that is why it is useful, and that the result is interpreted with care. If you can write that, you have the gene technology answer that the question is after, and you have it at the level where the marks are actually given.

The final point about the integrated answer is that it should not be too long, because the exam rewards precision and sequence, not length for its own sake. The example answers above are long enough to earn the marks and not so long that they run out of time or lose focus. If you can write answers of that shape, with the right sequence and the right distinctions and the right level of detail, you are doing the topic as the exam expects it, and you are using the note the way it was meant to be used: as a source of reasoning, not as a script to recite. The length of the note is there to give you enough material to draw from, but the answers you write on the day have to be shaped for the exam, and that shaping is the skill the note is trying to build. If you can write shaped answers from the note, the note has done its job.

Appendix R — The most durable ideas in the topic, and how to hold onto them

The most durable ideas in this topic are the ones you should hold onto first, because they are the ones that carry the most marks and the ones that show up in the most different questions. The first is that the topic is really about control at several levels: detection, coordination, response and regulation, with nervous and hormonal systems as the main animal control systems, homeostasis as the regulation of the internal environment, and gene technology as the manipulation of the DNA that makes all of it possible. The second is that the body defends itself in layers: non-specific first line, then specific response with antibodies and memory, and that the two layers work together rather than one replacing the other. The third is that the immune system is a process with timing, so the primary and secondary responses are different mainly because of memory, and that is why vaccination works. The fourth is that gene technology is about matching techniques to purposes, and that the applications and the limits both matter. If you hold onto those four durable ideas, you can answer a large part of the topic even if you cannot recall every detail, because those four ideas are the framework that the details fit into.

The way to hold onto the durable ideas is to practise them as statements with reasons, not as bare labels. For the control idea, the reason is that different jobs need different speeds, ranges and durations, which is why we have nervous and hormonal systems and why we have immunity and homeostasis and gene technology as separate but related tools. For the layered defence idea, the reason is that the first line is broad and fast and the specific response is targeted and slower to start but stronger on later exposure, and that is why both exist. For the timing idea, the reason is that memory makes the secondary response faster and stronger, and that is why vaccination works. For the gene technology idea, the reason is that each technique is useful for a specific purpose, and that the purpose is what should explain the technique, not the other way around. If you can state those durable ideas with their reasons, you have a framework you can use in many different questions, and that is the use of the framework: to give you something to reach for when the question is not exactly the one you practised.

The worry with durable ideas is that they can sound so general that they become vague, so the way to keep them from becoming vague is to tie each one to one concrete example you can say precisely. For the control idea, tie it to the reflex arc and to the insulin-glucagon system, because those are two concrete cases of control where you can say the detail precisely. For the layered defence idea, tie it to the skin barrier and phagocytosis on one hand and to antibodies and memory cells on the other, because those are two concrete cases where you can say the detail precisely. For the timing idea, tie it to the primary and secondary response and to vaccination, because those are the concrete cases where the timing is most clearly at issue. For the gene technology idea, tie it to restriction enzymes, PCR and electrophoresis, because those are the concrete techniques where the purpose is clearest. If you tie each durable idea to one or two concrete cases you can say precisely, you keep the idea from becoming vague, because the concrete case anchors it. That is the way to hold onto the durable ideas without turning them into slogans, and it is the way to make them useful on the day.

Appendix S — The harder edge cases the specification can reach

The harder edge cases in this topic are the ones where the specification can ask a question that looks easy but is really testing a precise point, and the point is usually one of the distinctions that is easy to blur when writing fast. One edge case is the difference between the neuromuscular junction and a neurone-to-neurone synapse, because the question can ask you to say what is similar and what is different, and the similar part is the calcium entry and neurotransmitter release, while the different part is that the postsynaptic cell is a muscle fibre and the result is contraction. If you blur that, you lose the marks that depend on seeing both the similarity and the difference. Another edge case is the difference between the structure of a rod and the structure of a cone, because the question can ask you to say how they differ and why, and the difference is that rods are more sensitive and work in dim light without colour, while cones detect colour and work best in brighter light. If you blur that, you lose the marks that depend on the distinction.

Another edge case is the difference between the way a restriction enzyme works and the way a gene probe works, because the question can ask you to say how each contributes to gene technology, and the restriction enzyme cuts at a specific sequence so pieces can be joined, while the gene probe detects a specific sequence by hybridisation. If you blur that, you lose the marks that depend on seeing that one is about cutting and joining and the other is about detecting. Another edge case is the difference between somatic and germ-line gene therapy, because the question can ask you to say why the two are treated differently ethically, and the reason is that somatic treatment affects only the treated individual while germ-line treatment would be inherited and would affect future generations. If you blur that, you lose the marks that depend on the ethical distinction, which is often the whole point of the question.

Another edge case is the difference between herd immunity and individual immunity, because the question can ask you to say why high coverage matters, and the reason is that herd immunity is about reducing transmission through the population, not about making every individual immune. If you blur that, you lose the marks that depend on the population logic, which is often the whole point of the herd immunity question. Another edge case is the difference between the primary and secondary immune response in timing and strength, because the question can ask you to explain why the secondary response is faster and stronger, and the reason is the memory cells from the first exposure. If you blur that, you lose the marks that depend on the memory logic, which is often the whole point of the primary/secondary question.

The way to handle the edge cases is to be precise about the distinction the question is testing, and to say the distinction in a way that makes it clear you are seeing both sides. For the neuromuscular junction versus the synapse, say that the sequence is the same but the postsynaptic cell and the outcome are different. For the rod versus the cone, say that both are photoreceptors but they differ in sensitivity, colour and light level. For the restriction enzyme versus the probe, say that one is for cutting and joining and the other is for detecting. For the somatic versus the germ-line therapy, say that one affects the individual and the other is heritable. For the herd immunity versus the individual immunity, say that one is about coverage and transmission and the other is about the individual. For the primary versus the secondary response, say that one is slower and one is faster and stronger because of memory. If you can say those distinctions precisely, you can answer the edge cases, and the edge cases are the ones that separate a good answer from a very good one.

Appendix T — Final guide to using the note on the day, in time order

On the day, the guide to using this note is to use it in time order, from the first idea you reach for to the last. The first thing to reach for is the durable ideas, because those are the ones that give you the framework and keep you from losing the thread. If the question is about coordination, reach for the control idea: detection, coordination, response, with nervous and hormonal systems as the main animal systems, and with homeostasis as the regulation of the internal environment. If the question is about defence, reach for the layered defence idea: non-specific first line, then specific response with antibodies and memory, and the two working together. If the question is about memory, reach for the timing idea: primary is slower, secondary is faster and stronger because of memory, and vaccination works by priming the same memory system. If the question is about gene technology, reach for the matching idea: each technique has a purpose, and the purpose explains the technique. If you can reach for the right durable idea first, you are already in the right place for the answer, and the rest of the answer is then the detail that fits under that idea.

The second thing to reach for is the concrete example that anchors the durable idea, because that is what keeps the answer precise rather than vague. For the control idea, anchor it to the reflex arc or the insulin-glucagon system, whichever the question is about. For the layered defence idea, anchor it to the skin barrier and phagocytosis or to the antibody and memory cell response, whichever the question is about. For the timing idea, anchor it to the primary and secondary response and to vaccination. For the gene technology idea, anchor it to the technique the question is about. If you can anchor the durable idea to a concrete example you can say precisely, you keep the answer precise, and precision is what the marks are about. If you only have the durable idea without the anchor, the answer tends to become vague, and vagueness is what loses marks on the day, even when the idea is right.

The third thing to reach for is the distinction the question is really testing, because that is the mark the question is after. For a coordination question, the distinction may be nervous versus hormonal, or receptor versus effector, or synapse versus neuromuscular junction. For a defence question, the distinction may be non-specific versus specific, or B versus T, or primary versus secondary. For a gene technology question, the distinction may be the purpose of the technique, or somatic versus germ-line, or herd immunity versus individual immunity. If you can reach for the right distinction and say it precisely, you hit the mark the question is after. If you only give the general idea without the distinction, you often leave the mark on the table, because the mark is in the distinction, not in the general idea. The note is written to give you the distinctions as well as the ideas, and that is the use of the length: to make the distinctions available when the question is testing them.

The final thing on the day is to watch the time and the length, because the exam rewards a precise answer of the right length more than a long imprecise one. If you have reached for the durable idea, anchored it to a concrete example, and said the distinction precisely, you have the answer the question wants, and you should stop there and move on, rather than padding it out. If you pad it out, you usually lose precision, and precision is what the mark is after. If you stop at the precise answer, you have the mark, and you have time for the next question. That is the guide to using the note on the day: reach for the durable idea, anchor it, say the distinction, stop at precision, and move on. If you can do that, the note has given you what it was meant to give you: the reasoning that lets you answer the topic under time pressure, which is the only form the exam is in.

For the control idea, the reason is that different jobs need different speeds, ranges and durations, which is why we have nervous and hormonal systems and why we have immunity and homeostasis and gene technology as separate but related tools. For the layered defence idea, the reason is that the first line is broad and fast and the specific response is targeted and slower to start but stronger on later exposure, and that is why both exist. For the timing idea, the reason is that memory makes the secondary response faster and stronger, and that is why vaccination works. For the gene technology idea, the reason is that each technique is useful for a specific purpose, and that the purpose is what should explain the technique, not the other way around. If you can state those durable ideas with their reasons, you have a framework you can use in many different questions, and that is the use of the framework: to give you something to reach for when the question is not exactly the one you practised.

The worry with durable ideas is that they can sound so general that they become vague, so the way to keep them from becoming vague is to tie each one to one concrete example you can say precisely. For the control idea, tie it to the reflex arc and to the insulin-glucagon system, because those are two concrete cases of control where you can say the detail precisely. For the layered defence idea, tie it to the skin barrier and phagocytosis on one hand and to antibodies and memory cells on the other, because those are two concrete cases where you can say the detail precisely. For the timing idea, tie it to the primary and secondary response and to vaccination, because those are the concrete cases where the timing is most clearly at issue. For the gene technology idea, tie it to restriction enzymes, PCR and electrophoresis, because those are the concrete techniques where the purpose is clearest. If you tie each durable idea to one or two concrete cases you can say precisely, you keep the idea from becoming vague, because the concrete case anchors it. That is the way to hold onto the durable ideas without turning them into slogans, and it is the way to make them useful on the day.

Appendix S — The harder edge cases the specification can reach

The harder edge cases in this topic are the ones where the specification can ask a question that looks easy but is really testing a precise point, and the point is usually one of the distinctions that is easy to blur when writing fast. One edge case is the difference between the neuromuscular junction and a neurone-to-neurone synapse, because the question can ask you to say what is similar and what is different, and the similar part is the calcium entry and neurotransmitter release, while the different part is that the postsynaptic cell is a muscle fibre and the result is contraction. If you blur that, you lose the marks that depend on seeing both the similarity and the difference. Another edge case is the difference between the structure of a rod and the structure of a cone, because the question can ask you to say how they differ and why, and the difference is that rods are more sensitive and work in dim light without colour, while cones detect colour and work best in brighter light. If you blur that, you lose the marks that depend on the distinction.

Another edge case is the difference between the way a restriction enzyme works and the way a gene probe works, because the question can ask you to say how each contributes to gene technology, and the restriction enzyme cuts at a specific sequence so pieces can be joined, while the gene probe detects a specific sequence by hybridisation. If you blur that, you lose the marks that depend on seeing that one is about cutting and joining and the other is about detecting. Another edge case is the difference between somatic and germ-line gene therapy, because the question can ask you to say why the two are treated differently ethically, and the reason is that somatic treatment affects only the treated individual while germ-line treatment would be inherited and would affect future generations. If you blur that, you lose the marks that depend on the ethical distinction, which is often the whole point of the question.

Another edge case is the difference between herd immunity and individual immunity, because the question can ask you to say why high coverage matters, and the reason is that herd immunity is about reducing transmission through the population, not about making every individual immune. If you blur that, you lose the marks that depend on the population logic, which is often the whole point of the herd immunity question. Another edge case is the difference between the primary and secondary immune response in timing and strength, because the question can ask you to explain why the secondary response is faster and stronger, and the reason is the memory cells from the first exposure. If you blur that, you lose the marks that depend on the memory logic, which is often the whole point of the primary/secondary question.

The way to handle the edge cases is to be precise about the distinction the question is testing, and to say the distinction in a way that makes it clear you are seeing both sides. For the neuromuscular junction versus the synapse, say that the sequence is the same but the postsynaptic cell and the outcome are different. For the rod versus the cone, say that both are photoreceptors but they differ in sensitivity, colour and light level. For the restriction enzyme versus the probe, say that one is for cutting and joining and the other is for detecting. For the somatic versus the germ-line therapy, say that one affects the individual and the other is heritable. For the herd immunity versus the individual immunity, say that one is about coverage and transmission and the other is about the individual. For the primary versus the secondary response, say that one is slower and one is faster and stronger because of memory. If you can say those distinctions precisely, you can answer the edge cases, and the edge cases are the ones that separate a good answer from a very good one.

Appendix T — Final guide to using the note on the day, in time order

On the day, the guide to using this note is to use it in time order, from the first idea you reach for to the last. The first thing to reach for is the durable ideas, because those are the ones that give you the framework and keep you from losing the thread. If the question is about coordination, reach for the control idea: detection, coordination, response, with nervous and hormonal systems as the main animal systems, and with homeostasis as the regulation of the internal environment. If the question is about defence, reach for the layered defence idea: non-specific first line, then specific response with antibodies and memory, and the two working together. If the question is about memory, reach for the timing idea: primary is slower, secondary is faster and stronger because of memory, and vaccination works by priming the same memory system. If the question is about gene technology, reach for the matching idea: each technique has a purpose, and the purpose explains the technique. If you can reach for the right durable idea first, you are already in the right place for the answer, and the rest of the answer is then the detail that fits under that idea.

The second thing to reach for is the concrete example that anchors the durable idea, because that is what keeps the answer precise rather than vague. For the control idea, anchor it to the reflex arc or the insulin-glucagon system, whichever the question is about. For the layered defence idea, anchor it to the skin barrier and phagocytosis or to the antibody and memory cell response, whichever the question is about. For the timing idea, anchor it to the primary and secondary response and to vaccination. For the gene technology idea, anchor it to the technique the question is about. If you can anchor the durable idea to a concrete example you can say precisely, you keep the answer precise, and precision is what the marks are about. If you only have the durable idea without the anchor, the answer tends to become vague, and vagueness is what loses marks on the day, even when the idea is right.

The third thing to reach for is the distinction the question is really testing, because that is the mark the question is after. For a coordination question, the distinction may be nervous versus hormonal, or receptor versus effector, or synapse versus neuromuscular junction. For a defence question, the distinction may be non-specific versus specific, or B versus T, or primary versus secondary. For a gene technology question, the distinction may be the purpose of the technique, or somatic versus germ-line, or herd immunity versus individual immunity. If you can reach for the right distinction and say it precisely, you hit the mark the question is after. If you only give the general idea without the distinction, you often leave the mark on the table, because the mark is in the distinction, not in the general idea. The note is written to give you the distinctions as well as the ideas, and that is the use of the length: to make the distinctions available when the question is testing them.

The final thing on the day is to watch the time and the length, because the exam rewards a precise answer of the right length more than a long imprecise one. If you have reached for the durable idea, anchored it to a concrete example, and said the distinction precisely, you have the answer the question wants, and you should stop there and move on, rather than padding it out. If you pad it out, you usually lose precision, and precision is what the mark is after. If you stop at the precise answer, you have the mark, and you have time for the next question. That is the guide to using the note on the day: reach for the durable idea, anchor it, say the distinction, stop at precision, and move on. If you can do that, the note has given you what it was meant to give you: the reasoning that lets you answer the topic under time pressure, which is the only form the exam is in.

title: Quadratics — Study Notes
content:
Quadratics

A quadratic has the form ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0. Master three tools: completing the square, the discriminant, and inequalities.

Completing the Square

Rewrite x² + bx + c as (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c.

Example: x² + 6x + 5 = (x + 3)² − 9 + 5 = (x + 3)² − 4, so the vertex is at (−3, −4).

For a > 1, factor out a first: 2x² + 12x + 19 = 2(x² + 6x) + 19 = 2(x + 3)² − 18 + 19 = 2(x + 3)² + 1.

Vertex form a(x − h)² + k gives the minimum/maximum value k at x = h — this is how you find a maximum area or minimum cost.

The Discriminant

Δ = b² − 4ac decides how the curve meets the x-axis:

ΔRootsGraph
Δ > 0two distinct real rootscrosses x-axis twice
Δ = 0repeated roottouches (tangent)
Δ < 0no real rootsnever meets x-axis

Example: kx² + 4x + 1 = 0 has equal roots when 16 − 4k = 0, so k = 4.

Quadratic Inequalities

Solve by sketching. For x² − 5x + 4 < 0, factorise: (x − 1)(x − 4) < 0, and the curve is below the axis between the roots, so 1 < x < 4.

Tip: flip the inequality when dividing by a negative number, and always sketch to check which interval you need.

Curve and Line Intersections

Set the equations equal; the resulting quadratic's discriminant tells you if the line is a secant (Δ > 0), tangent (Δ = 0) or misses (Δ < 0).

Exam tips: complete the square before reading off turning points; state the discriminant condition explicitly before solving for an unknown coefficient.

Discriminant and inequalities: exam method

For ax² + bx + c = 0 the discriminant is b² − 4ac. Positive gives two distinct real roots, zero gives one repeated root, and negative gives no real roots. Use this without solving the equation when the question asks about the nature of the roots.

To find the values of k for which a quadratic has no real roots, require b² − 4ac < 0 and solve the resulting inequality in k.

To solve a quadratic inequality, find the roots, sketch the U-shaped (a > 0) or inverted-U (a < 0) curve, and read off the region above or below the axis. For x² − 5x + 6 < 0 the roots are 2 and 3, and the solution is 2 < x < 3.

Exam cue: Completing the square gives the turning point (p, q) and shows the minimum or maximum value directly.

Worked example: completing the square with a coefficient

Write 2x² + 8x + 3 in the form a(x + p)² + q. Factor the 2 from the first two terms: 2(x² + 4x) + 3. Complete the square inside the bracket: x² + 4x = (x + 2)² − 4. So the expression is 2((x + 2)² − 4) + 3 = 2(x + 2)² − 5.

The minimum value is −5, reached when x = −2, so the minimum point is (−2, −5). Always factor the leading coefficient out first, otherwise the constant term comes out wrong.

Discriminant and the range of a parameter

The equation x² + kx + 4 = 0 has no real roots when the discriminant is negative: k² − 16 < 0. Solve as a quadratic in k to get −4 < k < 4. Stating the range is the mark-earning step, so write the inequality in full.

If the discriminant equals zero, the line is a tangent to the curve; if it is positive the line cuts the curve at two points.

Tangent to a curve

Find where y = x² − 2x + 3 meets the line y = 2x + k. Substitute to get x² − 4x + (3 − k) = 0. For a tangent the discriminant is zero: 16 − 4(3 − k) = 0, so k = −1. The tangent is y = 2x − 1, touching the curve at x = 2, where y = 3 on both.

Solving a quadratic inequality with a sketch

Solve 2x² − 5x − 3 > 0. Factor as (2x + 1)(x − 3) and find the roots x = −½ and x = 3. The parabola has a positive leading coefficient, so it is above the axis outside the roots. The solution is x < −½ or x > 3. Note the word or: this is two separate intervals, not one.

  • Positive leading coefficient: the expression is positive outside the roots and negative between them.
  • Negative leading coefficient: the reverse is true.
  • If the quadratic has no real roots, the sign never changes, so test one value to decide whether the inequality holds for all x.

title: Mensuration — Bearings and Loci — Study Notes
content:
Mensuration — Bearings and Loci

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): compass bearings, scale drawings, constructions (perpendicular/angle bisectors), loci regions.

1. Bearings

  • Measured clockwise from north; three figures: 065°, 128°, 300°.
  • Back bearing = front bearing ± 180°.
  • Draw a north line at both points; north lines are parallel, giving Z-angles.

Example: B is on bearing 070° from A → A is on bearing 250° from B.

2. Scale drawings

1 cm : 500 m style scales; measure, convert, and quote distances/bearings from your drawing to the accuracy allowed.

3. Constructions

  • Perpendicular bisector of a segment: equal arcs from both ends, join the crossings.
  • Angle bisector: equal arcs from the vertex arms.
  • 60° and 90° constructions with compasses; leave all arcs visible.

4. Loci

Fixed distance from a point = circle; from a line = parallel lines with rounded ends; equidistant from two points = perpendicular bisector; from two lines = angle bisector.

Example: a goat tied by a 5 m rope to a corner of a 4 m × 6 m shed: the reachable region is ¾ circle radius 5 m + two ¼ circles radius 1 m where the rope wraps.

Exam tips: state "clockwise from north" in bearing definitions; shade/label locus regions clearly; use a ruler for construction lines too.

Three-figure bearings

A bearing is measured clockwise from north and written with three figures, so 045° is north-east and 250° is south-west. To find the back bearing, add or subtract 180°. Draw a north line at the starting point and measure the angle carefully with a protractor.

Scale drawings and distance

Use the scale given to convert a map distance to a real distance, and convert back when drawing. Scale 1:50 000 means 1 cm on the map represents 50 000 cm, or 0.5 km. Use Pythagoras or trigonometry to find distances where a direct measurement is not possible.

Loci

The locus of points at a fixed distance from a point is a circle. Points equidistant from two points lie on the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them. Points equidistant from two lines lie on an angle bisector. Shade a region by combining the loci and stating the condition clearly.

title: Database Systems — Study Notes
content:
Database Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): limitations of file-based systems; relational concepts; SQL (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT); DBMS features.

1. File-based problems

Data repetition (wasted space, inconsistency), fixed queries, no concurrent access control — solved by a DBMS with shared, structured tables.

2. Relational concepts

  • Table, record, field; primary key (unique); secondary key (indexed search field); foreign key links tables.
  • One-to-many relationships via foreign keys; no repeating groups (1NF mindset).

3. SQL

SELECT Title, Year FROM Films
WHERE Genre = 'Sci-Fi' AND Year > 2015
ORDER BY Year DESC;

SELECT Genre, COUNT(*) AS NumFilms, SUM(Rating) AS TotalRating
FROM Films
GROUP BY Genre;

SELECT s.Name, f.Title
FROM Students s INNER JOIN Loans l ON s.StudentID = l.StudentID
INNER JOIN Films f ON l.FilmID = f.FilmID;

WHERE filters rows; GROUP BY aggregates; JOIN combines on matching keys.

4. DBMS features

Data dictionary (schema, types, constraints), query processor, forms/reports, access rights (read/write per user), data integrity (validation rules), backup/recovery.

Exam tips: write SQL keywords uppercase; alias joined tables (s, l, f); when asked "why relational", cite reduced redundancy + flexible queries.
