title: Exam technique: Logic Gates & Boolean Logic
content:
### What earns the marks
For truth tables, every row completed correctly earns stepwise credit. For circuits, each gate output labelled earns one mark before the final column. For expressions, brackets showing the gate order earn the method mark.
### Traps
Error: NAND confused with AND plus NOT placed wrongly. Correction: NAND inverts the AND output. Error: half-filled tables guessed. Correction: list all input combinations. Error: XOR read as OR. Correction: XOR excludes both-1.

title: Logic Gates & Boolean Logic — Study Notes
content:
Logic Gates & Boolean Logic

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): six gates, truth tables, building/describing circuits, problem-to-logic mapping.

1. The six gates

ABANDORNANDNORXOR
0000110
0101101
1001101
1111000

NOT inverts. NAND = AND + invert; NOR = OR + invert; XOR = 1 when inputs differ.

2. Truth tables

2 inputs → 4 rows; 3 inputs → 8 rows. Work gate by gate, adding intermediate columns for sub-circuit outputs.

3. Logic expressions

A Boolean expression describes a circuit in logic: X = A AND NOT B, or X = (A OR B) AND C. Brackets fix the order — work out bracketed parts first, then AND, then OR.

  • Circuit → expression: label the output of every gate (P, Q, …), write one expression per gate in order, then combine them at the final gate.
  • Truth table → expression: mark the rows where the output is 1; for each such row write a term that is true only in that row (write NOT for an input that is 0, AND between the inputs); join the terms with OR. For XOR: X = (NOT A AND B) OR (A AND NOT B).
  • Expression → truth table: add an intermediate column for each sub-expression before the output column.
  • Rules used to simplify: A AND 1 = A; A AND 0 = 0; A OR 1 = 1; A OR 0 = A; A AND A = A; A AND NOT A = 0; A OR NOT A = 1; NOT(NOT A) = A; X OR (X AND Y) = X. (AS extension, 9618: De Morgan's laws — NOT(A AND B) = NOT A OR NOT B and NOT(A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B.)

Example: a light X is on only when switch A is on and switch B is off → X = A AND NOT B, so X = 1 in exactly one row of its truth table (A = 1, B = 0).

4. Problem → logic

Define inputs/outputs first. Alarm rings (X=1) if sensor P triggered AND (door D OR window W): X = P AND (D OR W). Then draw the circuit: OR first, then AND.

5. Describing circuits

Write the expression from a diagram gate by gate; annotate output of each gate (X, Y) before combining.

Exam tips: check your truth table row count before writing; in problem questions, state "input P = 1 means sensor triggered" — definitions earn marks.

title: Exam technique: Magnetism and Electromagnetism
content:
### What earns the marks
For electromagnets, turns plus current plus soft iron core earns each mark. For transformers, the turns ratio equation quoted earns the method mark. For induction, rate of change of flux linked to emf size earns the explanation mark.
### Traps
Error: steel chosen for electromagnet cores. Correction: soft iron; steel suits permanent magnets. Error: Fleming hands swapped. Correction: left for motor, right for generator. Error: step-up confused with step-down. Correction: more secondary turns means step-up.
### Worked example
A transformer has 2000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. The primary is supplied at 240 V. The turns ratio gives Vs = Vp × Ns / Np = 240 × 100 / 2000 = 12 V. More secondary turns than primary turns means a step-up transformer, so the output voltage rises.
### Check yourself
An ideal transformer has 12 V at its secondary and a current of 4.0 A there. Find the primary current when the primary is at 240 V. Power in equals power out, so Ip = (12 × 4.0) / 240 = 0.20 A.

### Worked example
A transformer has 2000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. The primary is supplied at 240 V. The turns ratio gives Vs = Vp × Ns / Np = 240 × 100 / 2000 = 12 V. More secondary turns than primary turns means a step-up transformer, so the output voltage rises.

title: Sequences and Series — Study Notes
content:
Sequences and Series

Arithmetic Progressions (AP)

Terms increase by a common difference d.

  • nth term: uₙ = a + (n − 1)d
  • Sum: Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]

Example: AP 5, 8, 11: the 20th term is 5 + 19 × 3 = 62.

Geometric Progressions (GP)

Terms multiply by a common ratio r.

  • nth term: uₙ = arⁿ⁻¹
  • Sum: Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r)
  • Sum to infinity (|r| < 1 only): S∞ = a/(1 − r)

Example: a = 8, r = 1/2 gives S∞ = 8/(1/2) = 16.

Binomial Expansion

(1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n − 1)/2! x² + n(n − 1)(n − 2)/3! x³ + …, valid for |x| < 1.

For positive integer n, coefficients come from Pascal's triangle: (1 + 2x)⁴ = 1 + 8x + 24x² + 32x³ + 16x⁴.

Exam tips: identify a, d or r first; for "sum to infinity" questions check |r| < 1 explicitly, and for binomial expansions give terms up to the power asked (usually x² or x³).

Formulae and exam method

Arithmetic progression: the nth term is Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d, where a is the first term and d the common difference. The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d], or Sₙ = n/2 (a + l) when the last term l is known.

Geometric progression: Tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹, and Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r).

To find the number of terms, substitute the known sum or term and solve for n. When n sits in an exponent, take logarithms. Check that n is a positive integer.

Sigma notation: Σ from r = 1 to n of (ar + b) is evaluated with the standard sums, but write out the first few terms when the pattern is unclear.

Exam cue: Identify whether the question is AP or GP before choosing a formula, and state the value of r when using the sum to infinity.

Exam method: arithmetic and geometric sums

For an arithmetic sequence with first term a and common difference d, the nth term is a + (n − 1)d and the sum of the first n terms is S_n = n/2 (2a + (n − 1)d). For a geometric sequence with ratio r, the nth term is ar^(n − 1) and S_n = a(1 − r^n)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1.

The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1, say so explicitly rather than applying the formula.

Exam cue: Identify whether the sequence is arithmetic or geometric from the common difference or ratio before choosing a formula. Check the number of terms n carefully when you set up the equation.

Worked example: arithmetic progression

The sequence 3, 7, 11, … has first term a = 3 and common difference d = 4. The 20th term is a + 19d = 3 + 76 = 79. The sum of the first 20 terms is Sₙ = n/2 (2a + (n − 1)d) = 10 × (6 + 76) = 820.

Check with the average method: the first and last terms average (3 + 79)/2 = 41, and 41 × 20 = 820.

Worked example: geometric progression

The sequence 5, 10, 20, … has r = 2. The 8th term is 5 × 2⁷ = 640. The sum of the first six terms is 5(2⁶ − 1)/(2 − 1) = 315. Adding them directly gives 5 + 10 + 20 + 40 + 80 + 160 = 315, which confirms the formula.

Sum to infinity

A geometric series has a sum to infinity only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r). For 81, 27, 9, … the ratio is 1/3, so S∞ = 81/(2/3) = 121.5. If |r| ≥ 1 the terms do not shrink and the sum does not converge, so say so rather than quoting a formula.

Binomial expansion

For (1 + 2x)⁵, the first terms are 1 + 5(2x) + 10(2x)² + … The coefficient of x² is C(5, 2) × 2² = 10 × 4 = 40. The expansion is valid for |2x| < 1, so the range of x must be stated when the question asks for it.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using n instead of n − 1 in the n-th term formula, which shifts every term.
  • Confusing the nth term with the sum of the first n terms, a very common error on exam questions that ask for both.
  • Dividing a/(1 − r) when the series starts at a term other than the first, so check the index on the first term before using the formula.
  • Forgetting that the binomial expansion of (a + b)ⁿ has a coefficient C(n, r) on each term, and that the powers of a and b add to n.

title: Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7 — Study Notes
content:
Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7

Edexcel IAL Chemistry 9CH0 AS, topic 8. Every statement 8.1 to 8.28 is covered below, with its code in the heading. Three ideas run through the whole topic: oxidation numbers track electron transfer, the Group 1 and 2 trends follow from atomic size and nuclear charge, and the Group 7 trends are the same ideas applied to halogens.

8.1 to 8.4: Oxidation numbers

  • Rules: an element is 0; a monatomic ion equals its charge; the sum of oxidation numbers equals the overall charge. Oxygen is usually −2 (but −1 in peroxides such as H₂O₂), hydrogen is usually +1 (but −1 in metal hydrides such as NaH), fluorine is always −1, Group 1 is +1 and Group 2 is +2.
  • 8.2: in MnO₄⁻, manganese must be +7, because four oxygens contribute −8 and the ion has a charge of −1.
  • 8.3: write the oxidation number as a Roman numeral in the name: manganese(VII), iron(III), copper(II).
  • 8.4: work backwards from oxidation numbers to a formula. Iron(III) sulfate is Fe₂(SO₄)₃, because Fe³⁺ must balance SO₄²⁻ in a 2:3 ratio.

8.5 to 8.9: Oxidation, reduction and disproportionation

  • 8.5: oxidation is loss of electrons, and it appears as an increase in oxidation number. Reduction is gain of electrons, a decrease in oxidation number. In 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl, sodium is oxidised (0 to +1) and chlorine is reduced (0 to −1). The same idea covers reactions of s-block metals and p-block non-metals.
  • 8.6: an oxidising agent gains electrons and is itself reduced. A reducing agent loses electrons and is itself oxidised.
  • 8.7: disproportionation is when one element in a single species is both oxidised and reduced at the same time. Chlorine in water is the standard example: Cl₂ → Cl⁻ (0 to −1) and HClO (0 to +1).
  • 8.8: oxidation numbers classify reactions. A reaction is redox if any oxidation number changes, and it is a disproportionation if the same element goes both up and down.
  • 8.9: metals form positive ions by losing electrons, so their oxidation number increases. Non-metals form negative ions by gaining electrons, so their oxidation number decreases.

8.10: Half-equations and full ionic equations

  • Write the oxidation and the reduction separately, balance atoms, then balance charge with electrons. For magnesium with chlorine: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ and Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻.
  • Add the half-equations so the electrons cancel, then cancel any spectator ions to give the full ionic equation.

8.11 to 8.13: Group 1 and Group 2 trends and reactions

  • 8.11: ionisation energy falls down Groups 1 and 2. The outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner shells, so less energy is needed to remove it.
  • 8.12: reactivity rises down Group 1 (Li to K) and Group 2 (Mg to Ba), for the same reason: the outer electron is removed more easily.
  • 8.13: Group 1 metals burn in oxygen and react vigorously with chlorine and water. Group 2 metals react with oxygen and chlorine to form oxides and chlorides. Magnesium reacts slowly with cold water and readily with steam, while calcium reacts steadily with cold water to form Ca(OH)₂ and hydrogen.

8.14: Reactions of oxides and hydroxides

  • Group 1 oxides dissolve in water to give alkaline hydroxides. Group 2 oxides react less vigorously, and CaO gives a limewater-type solution, Ca(OH)₂.
  • Oxides react with dilute acid to form a salt and water, for example MgO + 2H⁺ → Mg²⁺ + H₂O.
  • Hydroxides neutralise dilute acids: Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O.

8.15: Solubility trends of Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates

  • Hydroxides: solubility increases down the group. Magnesium hydroxide is almost insoluble, calcium hydroxide is slightly soluble, barium hydroxide is quite soluble.
  • Sulfates: solubility decreases down the group. Magnesium sulfate is soluble, barium sulfate is insoluble, which is why acidified barium chloride gives a white precipitate in the sulfate test.

8.16: Thermal stability of nitrates and carbonates

  • Stability increases down each group. A larger cation has a lower charge density, so it polarises the carbonate or nitrate ion less, and the anion breaks down less easily.
  • Carbonates: MCO₃ → MO + CO₂. Group 2 nitrates: 2M(NO₃)₂ → 2MO + 4NO₂ + O₂. Group 1 nitrates (other than lithium) give the nitrite and oxygen: 2NaNO₃ → 2NaNO₂ + O₂.
  • Lithium is the exception: its nitrate decomposes like a Group 2 nitrate, because the small Li⁺ ion polarises the nitrate strongly.

8.17: Flame colours

  • Heat excites outer electrons to higher energy levels. When they fall back, they emit light of a specific wavelength. Lithium is crimson, sodium is yellow-orange, potassium is lilac, calcium is brick red, strontium is red and barium is green.

8.18: Experiments on thermal decomposition

  • Heat a small sample of nitrate or carbonate in a test tube and test the gas. Brown NO₂ shows a nitrate; a glowing splint relit by O₂ shows oxygen. A carbonate gives CO₂, which turns limewater milky.
  • Compare the temperatures needed for decomposition down a group to show the trend in 8.16.

8.19: Identifying ions

  • Carbonate (CO₃²⁻) or hydrogencarbonate (HCO₃⁻): add dilute acid. CO₂ is released and turns limewater milky. Ionic equation: CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂.
  • Sulfate (SO₄²⁻): add acidified barium chloride. A white precipitate of BaSO₄ forms: Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄. The acid stops carbonate and sulfite interfering.
  • Ammonium (NH₄⁺): add sodium hydroxide and warm. Ammonia is released, turns damp red litmus blue, and gives white fumes with HCl.

8.20 to 8.23: Concentrations, titrations and uncertainty

  • 8.20: concentration in mol dm⁻³ = moles ÷ volume in dm³. To convert to g dm⁻³, multiply by the molar mass.
  • Indicators: methyl orange changes from red to yellow at about pH 3–4, suited to strong acid against weak base. Phenolphthalein changes from colourless to pink at about pH 8–10, suited to weak acid against strong base.
  • 8.21 (core practical 3): titrate hydrochloric acid against a standard alkali, record the titre and use the balanced equation to find the acid's concentration.
  • 8.22: reduce uncertainty by rinsing the pipette and burette, reading the meniscus at eye level, and repeating until two titres agree within 0.10 cm³. A burette reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³, so a titre has ±0.10 cm³. Calculate the percentage uncertainty as uncertainty ÷ reading × 100.
  • 8.23 (core practical 4): weigh a solid acid such as hydrated ethanedioic acid accurately, dissolve it, make it up to 250 cm³ in a volumetric flask, and use it as a standard solution to find the concentration of sodium hydroxide.

8.24: Trends in Group 7

  • Melting and boiling points rise down the group, because the molecules are larger and have stronger London forces. Fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid, iodine is a solid.
  • Electronegativity falls down the group, because the bonding pair sits further from the nucleus and is shielded more.
  • Reactivity (oxidising power) falls down the group, because the atoms are larger and gain an electron less readily.

8.25: Displacement reactions and colours

  • A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂, and Cl₂ or Br₂ + 2I⁻ → I₂ + halide.
  • Colours: in water, chlorine is pale green-yellow, bromine is orange and iodine is brown. In a non-polar organic solvent such as cyclohexane, bromine stays orange and iodine turns violet.

8.26: Reactions of the halogens, including disproportionation

  • (i) Halogens oxidise Group 1 and 2 metals to halides, for example 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.
  • (ii) Chlorine with water is a disproportionation: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO. The HClO is the basis of chlorine water treatment.
  • (iii) Chlorine with cold, dilute NaOH gives bleach: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O.
  • (iv) With hot concentrated alkali, chlorine disproportionates to chlorate: 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O.
  • (v) Bromine behaves in the same way with cold alkali. Use the oxidation number of each chlorine to check each product.

8.27: Reactions of halides and hydrogen halides

  • (i) Solid halides with concentrated H₂SO₄ show the reducing trend. NaCl gives HCl only. NaBr is oxidised further to Br₂ and SO₂. NaI is oxidised to I₂ and H₂S. The reducing ability is HI > HBr > HCl.
  • (ii) Silver nitrate with the halide ions in nitric acid: AgCl is white, AgBr is cream, AgI is yellow. AgCl dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia, AgBr only in concentrated ammonia, and AgI does not dissolve.
  • (iii) Hydrogen halides with ammonia give ammonium halides (NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl). With water they give acids.

8.28: Predicting fluorine and astatine

  • Fluorine is the most electronegative element and the strongest oxidising agent in the group. It reacts violently with water, displacing oxygen from it.
  • Astatine is at the bottom of the group, so by the trends it should be a dark, solid, less reactive halogen than iodine, with a lower electronegativity. It is radioactive, so its chemistry is hard to study directly, and predictions come from the trends.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using the wrong oxidation number for oxygen in a peroxide or hydrogen in a metal hydride.
  • Confusing reducing ability with reactivity for the halogens: reactivity falls down Group 7, but the reducing ability of the halide ions rises.
  • Writing the test for sulfate without acid. Without acid, carbonate would also give a white precipitate.

title: Abstract Data Types — Study Notes
content:
Abstract Data Types

What is an ADT?

An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Linked Lists

Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node; a start pointer marks the head and a null marks the end. Insertion rewires two pointers — no shifting — giving O(1) insertion at a known position, but access requires walking the list, O(n).

Stacks and Queues

A stack is LIFO (push and pop at the top); a queue is FIFO (enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front). Both can be arrays with index pointers or linked lists. Stack uses include call stacks and expression evaluation; queue uses include print buffers and breadth-first search.

Binary Search Trees

Each node has up to two children; left subtree keys are smaller, right subtree keys larger. Search, insert and (average-case) delete are O(log n). An in-order traversal outputs keys in ascending order. A degenerate (linear) tree from sorted input degrades to O(n).

Hash Tables

Covered in file organisation, but as an ADT a hash table pairs a hash function with bucket storage for O(1) average access.

Exam tips: be able to draw a tree after a sequence of insertions and write its three traversals; state the pointer changes for a linked-list insertion; compare ADT operations with Big-O.

title: Number — Ratio, Rate and Proportion — Study Notes
content:
Number — Ratio, Rate and Proportion

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): ratio notation, sharing, direct & inverse proportion (including squares/cubes), unit rates.

1. Simplifying and sharing ratios

  • Scale both parts by the same factor: 250 g : 0.4 kg = 250 : 400 = 5 : 8.
  • Share $200 in 3 : 5 → 8 parts → $75 : $125.
  • Part–whole: 3 : 5 ⇒ 3/8 of the total. Given one share, find others by scaling.

Example: A : B = 3 : 4 and B : C = 2 : 5 ⇒ A : B : C = 3 : 4 : 10 (make B equal: ×2).

2. Direct proportion

y = kx. Best method: find the unit value, then multiply.

Example: 5 pens cost $3.25 → 1 pen $0.65 → 8 pens $5.20.

Squared/cubed proportion: y ∝ x². y = 54 when x = 3 ⇒ k = 6 ⇒ y = 6x²; at x = 5, y = 150.

3. Inverse proportion

y = k/x (product constant). 4 workers 6 days ⇒ 24 worker-days ⇒ 8 workers take 3 days. Square-law: y ∝ 1/x².

4. Rates

Unit rates (per item, per litre), exchange rates (draw the arrow to the target currency), best buys (price per unit, careful with multi-packs). Speed/density/pressure are compound-measure rates (Mensuration).

Exam tips: write the proportional equation with k before substituting; check proportion type — "more workers, fewer days" = inverse.

Writing and simplifying ratios

A ratio a : b is simplified by dividing both parts by their highest common factor. Ratios with decimals or fractions are multiplied up to whole numbers first. A ratio shared between a total uses the total number of parts as the divisor.

Direct and inverse proportion

In direct proportion, y = kx, so doubling x doubles y. In inverse proportion, y = k ÷ x, so doubling x halves y. Find k from a known pair of values, then use it to answer the question.

Speed, density and rates

Rate questions are solved by identifying the two quantities and the unit of the answer. Speed = distance ÷ time; average speed for a journey is the total distance divided by the total time, not the mean of the speeds. Exchange rates and recipe scaling use the same unitary method: find the value of one unit first.

title: Database Systems — Study Notes
content:
Database Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): limitations of file-based systems; relational concepts; SQL (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT); DBMS features.

1. File-based problems

Data repetition (wasted space, inconsistency), fixed queries, no concurrent access control — solved by a DBMS with shared, structured tables.

2. Relational concepts

  • Table, record, field; primary key (unique); secondary key (indexed search field); foreign key links tables.
  • One-to-many relationships via foreign keys; no repeating groups (1NF mindset).

3. SQL

SELECT Title, Year FROM Films
WHERE Genre = 'Sci-Fi' AND Year > 2015
ORDER BY Year DESC;

SELECT Genre, COUNT(*) AS NumFilms, SUM(Rating) AS TotalRating
FROM Films
GROUP BY Genre;

SELECT s.Name, f.Title
FROM Students s INNER JOIN Loans l ON s.StudentID = l.StudentID
INNER JOIN Films f ON l.FilmID = f.FilmID;

WHERE filters rows; GROUP BY aggregates; JOIN combines on matching keys.

4. DBMS features

Data dictionary (schema, types, constraints), query processor, forms/reports, access rights (read/write per user), data integrity (validation rules), backup/recovery.

Exam tips: write SQL keywords uppercase; alias joined tables (s, l, f); when asked "why relational", cite reduced redundancy + flexible queries.

title: Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment - Edexcel International A2 Level Biology
content:
Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment - Edexcel International A2 Level Biology

This revision note belongs to Edexcel International A2 Level Biology WBI14 and covers energy transfers in ecosystems, photosynthesis mechanisms, ecological sampling, community succession, climate change evidence and causes, population genetics, and conservation management.

Photosynthesis and Biochemical Reactions

Photosynthesis is an energy-requiring pathway captured by the overall chemical equation 6CO2 + 6H2O yields C6H12O6 + 6O2, driven by light energy. Light energy splits the strong covalent bonds in water molecules (photolysis), releasing oxygen gas into the atmosphere while storing hydrogen atoms inside glucose by combining them with carbon dioxide. Energy currency within cells relies on photophosphorylation of ADP to synthesize ATP, which undergoes immediate hydrolysis to supply free energy for endergonic biological processes.

  • 5.1 Overall photosynthesis equation: light energy splits H2O, combines hydrogen with CO2 to form glucose, and releases O2.
  • 5.2 Photophosphorylation converts ADP and inorganic phosphate into ATP using energy; ATP hydrolysis releases an immediate supply of energy.
  • 5.3 Light-dependent reactions occur on thylakoid membranes: photons excite electrons in chlorophyll, generating ATP and reduced NADP via cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation, alongside oxygen via photolysis.
  • 5.4 (i) Light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle) occur in the stroma, fixing CO2 onto ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP) via RuBisCO to form glycerate 3-phosphate (GP), which is reduced using ATP and reduced NADP into glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (GALP).
  • 5.4 (ii) GALP molecules yield simple sugars for respiration and synthesise new biological molecules including polysaccharides, amino acids, proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids.
  • 5.5 Chloroplast structure relates to function: thylakoids provide a large surface area for light absorption and pigment arrays; the stroma contains enzymes for the Calvin cycle; double membranes isolate biochemical pathways.
  • 5.6 Absorption spectrum shows absorbance of light wavelengths by a pigment; action spectrum shows the rate of photosynthesis at different light wavelengths.
  • 5.7 Chloroplast pigments are separated using paper or thin-layer chromatography and identified by calculating Rf values (distance moved by pigment divided by distance moved by solvent front).
  • 5.8 Core Practical 10: Investigate effects of light intensity, light wavelength, temperature, and CO2 availability on photosynthetic rate using an aquatic plant such as Elodea or Cabomba, measuring oxygen bubbles released or volume of gas displaced.

Energy Transfer in Ecosystems

Energy flow through trophic levels begins with primary producers capturing sunlight. Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the total chemical energy fixed by photosynthesis. Net primary productivity (NPP) accounts for respiratory losses (R) and dictates plant tissue available to herbivores.

  • 5.9 (i) The relationship is NPP = GPP − R.
  • 5.9 (ii) Calculation of NPP requires subtracting plant respiration from gross primary productivity.
  • 5.10 Efficiency of biomass and energy transfers between trophic levels is calculated using (Energy or biomass transferred to next trophic level ÷ Energy or biomass received at previous trophic level) × 100%.

Worked example calculation of transfer efficiency: If a producer trophic level contains 15000 kJ m−2 year−1 and primary consumers contain 1400 kJ m−2 year−1, the transfer efficiency is (1400 ÷ 15000) × 100 = 9.33%.

Ecology and Populations

Ecosystems comprise biotic communities and abiotic factors governing species distributions. An organism's ecological niche describes its functional role and interactions within its habitat.

  • 5.11 Population is a group of interbreeding individuals of the same species in a habitat; community is all populations of different species living in a habitat; habitat is the place where an organism lives; ecosystem is a self-sustaining system of living organisms interacting with non-living surroundings.
  • 5.12 Numbers and distributions of organisms are controlled by biotic factors (competition, predation, disease) and abiotic factors (temperature, pH, light intensity, moisture).
  • 5.13 Niche concept accounts for distribution and abundance: no two species can occupy the exact same niche indefinitely without competitive exclusion.
  • 5.14 Core Practical 11: Carry out ecological studies using quadrats for abundance and transects (belt or line) for distribution, recording concurrent abiotic factors using appropriate sensors and meters.
  • 5.15 Succession stages: pioneer species colonise bare substrate, altering abiotic conditions to become less hostile, leading to seral stages of increasing biodiversity until a stable climax community forms.

Climate Change and Environmental Evidence

Anthropogenic activities release greenhouse gases, driving rapid climate change. Multiple proxy records allow scientists to track historical climates and establish causal links.

  • 5.16 Evidence for climate change includes atmospheric CO2 gas records (Mauna Loa curve), temperature records, pollen preservation in peat bogs indicating past flora, and dendrochronology (tree ring width analysis), distinguishing between correlation and causation.
  • 5.17 Anthropogenic climate change is caused by greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, water vapour) absorbing and reradiating infrared radiation back to the Earth's surface (the enhanced greenhouse effect).
  • 5.18 Carbon cycle knowledge is applied to reduce atmospheric CO2 via reforestation, protecting peatlands, reducing fossil fuel combustion, and using carbon capture and storage.
  • 5.19 (i) Data extrapolation allows mathematical models to predict future climate scenarios.
  • 5.19 (ii) Climate models have limitations due to complex feedback loops, incomplete historical datasets, and unpredictable human policy shifts.
  • 5.20 Effects of climate change include shifting rainfall patterns and altered seasonal phenology, impacting animal and plant distribution, development rates, and life cycles.

Metabolic Rates and Evolution

Temperature profoundly influences metabolic rates and enzyme kinetics. Evolutionary mechanisms alter allele frequencies over generations.

  • 5.21 Temperature affects enzyme activity up to an optimum; beyond this, denaturation occurs. Q10 temperature coefficient calculates the rate increase when temperature rises by 10 °C, using formula Q10 = (Rate at (T + 10 °C) ÷ Rate at T).
  • 5.22 Core Practical 12: Investigate temperature effects on organism development (such as seedling growth rate or brine shrimp hatch rates), maintaining ethical use of organisms.
  • 5.23 Evolution is a change in allele frequency within a gene pool over time, driven by gene mutations creating new alleles and natural selection increasing advantageous allele frequencies.
  • 5.24 Geographic, temporal, behavioural, or anatomical isolation reduces gene flow between populations, culminating in allopatric speciation (physical barrier) or sympatric speciation (same habitat, reproductive barrier).
  • 5.25 Scientific conclusions on controversial issues like climate change action and anthropogenic attribution can be influenced by funding sources, political agendas, and underlying stakeholder motives.
  • 5.26 Reforestation and sustainable resources (such as biofuels derived from fast-growing plants) manage the conflict between human economic needs and biological conservation.

Typical mistakes

  • Confusing absorption spectrum and action spectrum: remember absorption measures light energy captured by specific pigments, whereas action spectrum measures overall photosynthetic rate across light wavelengths.
  • Failing to state units in productivity calculations: always specify units such as kJ m−2 year−1 or g m−2 year−1.
  • Stating temperature denaturation destroys primary protein structure: clarify that tertiary and quaternary structures are disrupted via hydrogen and ionic bond breakage, leaving peptide bonds intact.
  • Treating correlation as direct causation in climate proxy data: always mention confounding variables and correlative limits.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain how non-cyclic photophosphorylation generates ATP and reduced NADP. Answer: Light photons excite electrons in chlorophyll photosystem II; electrons pass down an electron transport chain releasing energy to pump protons and synthesise ATP via ATP synthase; electrons replace those lost from photosystem I where reduced NADP is formed. (3 marks)
  2. Calculate the net primary productivity of a forest where gross primary productivity is 45000 kJ m−2 year−1 and plant respiration is 18000 kJ m−2 year−1. Answer: NPP = GPP − R = 45000 − 18000 = 27000 kJ m−2 year−1. (2 marks)
  3. Describe how allopatric speciation can occur following geographical isolation. Answer: A physical barrier separates a population into two groups; no gene flow occurs between them; different mutations and selection pressures operate in each isolated environment; advantageous alleles accumulate independently until interbreeding can no longer produce fertile offspring. (4 marks)
  4. Explain the term Q10 and how to calculate it. Answer: Q10 is the measure of the rate of reaction when the temperature is increased by 10 °C. Calculated using Q10 = (Rate at (T + 10 °C) ÷ Rate at T). (2 marks)
  5. Discuss why climate models have limitations when predicting future global temperatures. Answer: Models rely on assumptions about future greenhouse gas emissions, human policy changes, and complex feedback loops such as cloud cover or permafrost melting that are difficult to quantify accurately. (3 marks)

Use these revision notes alongside active recall of core practical steps and quantitative calculations for energy efficiencies and Q10 values. Proceed next to topic summaries on human impacts on biogeochemical cycles and global biodiversity.

title: Data Types and File Organisation — Study Notes
content:
Data Types and File Organisation

User-Defined Types

A user-defined type is derived from existing types. An enumerated type lists named values in order: TYPE Months = (Jan, Feb, Mar ...). Internally each value is an integer index starting at 0. Pointer types store a memory address; the dereference operator returns the value at that address, which is how linked structures reference their nodes. Set types store unordered collections of distinct values from an ordinal base type, supporting union, intersection and difference.

Records

A record groups related fields of different types under one identifier, for example a Student record with name : STRING and mark : INTEGER. Arrays of records are the standard structure for storing a table of items in memory.

File Organisation

  • Serial: records in insertion order; searching checks every record. Simple but slow.
  • Sequential: records kept in key order; binary search possible, but insertion needs rewriting.
  • Random (direct): a hashing function converts the key into a storage address, giving near-instant access. A poor hash causes collisions — two keys hashing to the same address — resolved by chaining or overflow areas.

Hashing

A common method is division hashing: Address = Key MOD TableSize. A good hash distributes keys evenly; load factor above roughly 70 percent degrades performance.

Exam tips: state the internal integer representation of enumerated values; define a collision before describing its resolution; compare the three file organisations in terms of search and insert cost.

File organisation and access

Serial files store records in the order they are written and suit sequential processing. Sequential files store records in key order, so a search can stop early. Random (direct) access files calculate a record's address from its key, using a hashing function, so any record can be reached quickly.

Exam tip: state the trade-off: sequential access is simple but slow for searching; direct access is fast but needs a hashing function and can produce collisions.

Worked example: a record definition

A record groups fields of different data types under one name. A record called Book might have Title (string), Pages (integer), Price (real) and InStock (Boolean). Each field is then referred to by the record name and the field name, for example Book.Pages. Records let a program keep related data together and pass it to a procedure as one item.

Worked example: hashing with linear probing

A hash table has 5 slots numbered 0 to 4, and the hash function is h(k) = k mod 5. Insert the keys 12, 27 and 8 in that order. The key 12 gives 12 mod 5 = 2, so it is stored in slot 2. The key 27 also gives 2, which is already occupied, so the next slot 3 is used. The key 8 gives 3, which is occupied, so it moves on to slot 4. A collision happens whenever two keys hash to the same slot, and the probing method determines where the second key is placed.

Comparing file access methods

  • Serial files store records one after another in the order they arrive, so finding one record means reading from the start.
  • Sequential files store records in key order, so a search can stop once it passes the place where the record should be.
  • Random (direct) files use a hash function to calculate the address of a record directly, which gives the fastest access for a single record.

Exam point: when asked to choose a file organisation, state the access pattern the question describes, such as frequent single-record look-ups or regular batch reads in order, and justify the choice from that pattern.

title: Exam technique: Data Handling
content:
### What earns the marks
For averages, the total shown earns a mark before any division. For even-count medians, the two middle values identified earn the method mark. For grouped data, the modal class stated as an interval earns full credit; single numbers score nothing. For cumulative frequency, the position formula (n + 1) / 2 quoted earns the method mark before reading off.
### Traps
Error: total given as the mean. Correction: divide by the count last. Error: 3rd value picked as median of six values. Correction: average the 3rd and 4th. Error: 40th value read for the median of 80. Correction: position 40.5. Error: quartiles read for median and vice versa. Correction: 20th/60th are quartiles at n = 80.
### Worked example
Four values are 2, 3, 3, 5, 8, 9 (six values in total). The median is the average of the 3rd and 4th values: (3 + 5) / 2 = 4. For a mean of 9 from four values, the total must be 36: write the sum first, then divide by 4. Both steps earn their own marks.

### Worked example Use the chain rule for composite functions. For y = (x² + 1)³, dy/dx = 3(x² + 1)² × 2x = 6x(x² + 1)². At x = 1 this is 6 × 1 × 4 = 24. Check using the derivative of the outer function at the inner value: 3 × 2² × 2 = 24. The product rule gives d/dx(x sin x) = sin x + x cos x. ### Check yourself Differentiate y = (3x − 1)⁴. The answer is dy/dx = 12(3x − 1)³. Check at x = 1: 12 × 2³ = 96.

title: Web Technologies and Security — Study Notes
content:
Web Technologies and Security

The Three Layers

  • HTML gives structure and content: elements, attributes, forms for user input.
  • CSS gives presentation: selectors, properties, responsive layout.
  • JavaScript gives client-side behaviour: validation before submission, DOM updates without reload.

Server-side scripting (PHP) runs on the server: reads form fields ($_POST), queries the database, outputs HTML. The client never sees PHP source.

SQL Injection

An attack where crafted input changes the meaning of a query. If a login query concatenates the username directly, entering X OR 1=1 can match every row. Defences: parameterised queries (prepared statements) that separate code from data, validation, and least-privilege database accounts.

Encryption

  • Symmetric: one shared key (AES). Fast, but key distribution is the weak point.
  • Asymmetric: public/private key pair (RSA). Anyone encrypts with the public key; only the holder decrypts with the private key. Slower, so used to exchange a symmetric session key.
  • SSL/TLS combines both: certificates verify the server, asymmetric key exchange establishes a symmetric session key, then traffic is encrypted. HTTPS = HTTP over TLS on port 443.

Hashing vs Encryption

Hashing (e.g. SHA-256) is one-way: passwords should be stored hashed with a unique salt, never encrypted reversibly.

Exam tips: explain why parameterised queries stop injection; describe the TLS handshake in three steps; distinguish hashing from encryption with password storage as the example.

title: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism — Study Notes
content:
Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism

Force on a Current

F = BIL sin θ (Fleming's left hand: field-index, current-first-finger, force-thumb).

Example: 0.5 m wire carrying 3 A at 90° to a 0.2 T field: F = 0.3 N.

Force on a Moving Charge

F = BQv sin θ, always perpendicular to v → circular paths: r = mv/(BQ) (basis of cyclotrons and mass spectrometers).

Example: an electron (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) at 2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ in 0.5 mT: r ≈ 2.3 cm.

Fields from Currents

  • Long straight wire: B = μ₀I/(2πr), circling by the right-hand grip rule
  • Solenoid: B = μ₀nI inside

Electromagnetic Induction

Faraday: induced EMF = rate of flux cutting = N dΦ/dt. Lenz: induced effects oppose the change (negative sign).

Example: a coil of 100 turns, flux changing 2 mWb in 50 ms induces EMF = 100 × 0.002/0.05 = 4 V.

Flux Φ = BA (B ⊥ A). Generators rotate coils in fields; transformers link two coils by a shared changing flux with V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂.

Exam tips: use left hand for motors (force on current), right hand for generators (induced current); state Lenz's law in explain questions.

title: Databases and Data Definition — Study Notes
content:
Databases and Data Definition

Relational Concepts

A table (relation) stores rows (tuples) and columns (attributes). The primary key uniquely identifies each row; a foreign key references a primary key in another table, creating the relationship. A composite key uses two or more columns together.

Normalisation

  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups.
  • 2NF: 1NF plus every non-key attribute depends on the whole key (kills partial dependency in composite keys).
  • 3NF: 2NF plus no transitive dependency — non-key attributes must not depend on other non-key attributes.

Normalisation reduces redundancy and prevents update, insert and delete anomalies.

DDL and DML

DDL defines structure: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP. DML manipulates data: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE, INSERT INTO, UPDATE, DELETE. Joins combine related tables: FROM Student s JOIN Enrolment e ON s.id = e.StudentID. Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG with GROUP BY and HAVING.

Transactions and Concurrency

A transaction is a unit of work obeying ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules preserved), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes). Record locking blocks conflicting simultaneous edits; a deadlock occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs.

Exam tips: normalise a small table through 1NF, 2NF, 3NF naming the dependency removed at each step; write a two-table SELECT with JOIN; state which ACID property a scenario breaks.

DDL and DML

Data Definition Language (DDL) creates and changes the structure of a database: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE. Data Manipulation Language (DML) works with the data inside the structure: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.

Example: CREATE TABLE Student (ID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(30)); is DDL; INSERT INTO Student VALUES (1, 'Ana'); is DML.

Exam tip: classify each statement by whether it changes structure or changes data.

Worked example: a SELECT query

To list the names of students in Year 11 who study Physics, sorted by surname, a query joins two tables and filters the result: SELECT Name FROM Student INNER JOIN Enrolment ON Student.StudentID = Enrolment.StudentID WHERE Year = 11 AND Subject = 'Physics' ORDER BY Name. Read the question word by word and map each condition onto a clause.

Keys and integrity

  • A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a table and cannot be null.
  • A foreign key holds the primary key of another table, which links the two tables together.
  • A candidate key is any field, or combination of fields, that could serve as the primary key.

Entity-relationship modelling

A one-to-many relationship, such as one teacher and many classes, is shown by placing the primary key of the "one" side in the "many" table. A many-to-many relationship, such as students and courses, needs a third, linking table that holds a foreign key for each side. Without it the database would repeat data or store several values in one field, which breaks normalisation.

Exam point: CREATE TABLE statements declare the data types, the primary key and each foreign key. DROP and ALTER change the structure; INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT work with the records.

title: Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules — Study Notes
content:
Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): area formula, sine rule, cosine rule, multi-step bearing and 3-D problems (Extended).

1. Area of a triangle

A = ½ab sin C (C = included angle between sides a and b).

Example: a = 8, b = 5, C = 48° → A = ½ × 8 × 5 × sin 48° = 14.8.

2. Sine rule

a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use when a matching angle–side pair is known.

Example: A = 40°, a = 7, B = 65°: b = 7 sin 65°/sin 40° = 9.98.

Ambiguous case: two triangles possible when finding an angle — check the obtuse option (180° − θ).

3. Cosine rule

a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A. Use with two sides + included angle, or all three sides (then cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc)).

Example: b = 7, c = 5, A = 52°: a² = 74 − 70 cos 52° = 30.9 → a = 5.56.

4. Bearing problems

Draw both north lines, transfer angles via parallel lines, then pick sine/cosine rule.

Example: QP = 60 km bearing 070° from Q; QR = 45 km bearing 150°. ∠PQR = 80° → PR² = 60² + 45² − 2·60·45 cos 80° → PR = 68.4 km.

5. 3-D trigonometry

Identify the plane containing the required angle; use 3-D Pythagoras d² = x² + y² + z² for space diagonals; angle between a line and a plane uses the projection onto the plane.

Exam tips: state which rule you are using and why; sketch a separate 2-D triangle for 3-D questions; answers to 3 s.f. / bearings as three digits.

The sine rule

For any triangle with sides a, b, c opposite angles A, B, C: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use it when you know a pair of opposite side and angle (for example, two angles and a side, or a side and its opposite angle with another side). Find the missing angle using the angle sum of 180° first.

The cosine rule

a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A, and cos A = (b² + c² − a²) ÷ 2bc. Use it when you know two sides and the included angle, or all three sides. Careful with negative cosines: an obtuse angle gives a negative cos value.

Area of a triangle

Area = ½ab sin C, using two sides and the included angle. This avoids finding the perpendicular height.

title: Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment — Study Notes
content:
Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI14, Topic 5. Energy enters most ecosystems as light, is fixed by photosynthesis and then passes along food chains. Nutrients cycle, and human activity can disrupt those cycles.

Photosynthesis and limiting factors

  • The light-dependent reactions take place on the thylakoid membranes. Light energy splits water (photolysis), releases oxygen and makes ATP and reduced NADP.
  • The light-independent reactions (the Calvin cycle) take place in the stroma. CO₂ is fixed by the enzyme RuBisCO onto ribulose bisphosphate, and the product is reduced to make triose phosphate.
  • Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature are limiting factors. The factor that is in shortest supply limits the rate.

Energy transfer through trophic levels

  • Gross primary productivity is the total energy fixed by plants. Net primary productivity is the energy left after respiration.
  • Energy is lost between trophic levels: in respiration, as heat, in faeces and urine, and in parts of organisms that are not eaten. Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is usually passed on.
  • Energy pyramids are always the right way up, because energy is lost at each step.

Nutrient cycles

  • In the carbon cycle, photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the air and respiration, decomposition and combustion return it.
  • Nitrogen fixing bacteria in root nodules convert nitrogen gas into ammonium ions. Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate, and denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen gas to the air.

Human impact

  • Fertiliser run-off causes eutrophication. Algae grow rapidly, block light, and then die. Decomposers use up the oxygen, and fish and other animals die.
  • Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane absorb infrared radiation and raise the temperature of the Earth.
  • Pesticides and persistent chemicals become more concentrated at higher trophic levels, which is called biomagnification.

Exam tip: when you explain a limiting factor, name the factor, state which reaction it slows, and say why the rate falls.

title: Database Systems — Study Notes
content:
Database Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): limitations of file-based systems; relational concepts; SQL (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT); DBMS features.

1. File-based problems

Data repetition (wasted space, inconsistency), fixed queries, no concurrent access control — solved by a DBMS with shared, structured tables.

2. Relational concepts

  • Table, record, field; primary key (unique); secondary key (indexed search field); foreign key links tables.
  • One-to-many relationships via foreign keys; no repeating groups (1NF mindset).

3. SQL

SELECT Title, Year FROM Films
WHERE Genre = 'Sci-Fi' AND Year > 2015
ORDER BY Year DESC;

SELECT Genre, COUNT(*) AS NumFilms, SUM(Rating) AS TotalRating
FROM Films
GROUP BY Genre;

SELECT s.Name, f.Title
FROM Students s INNER JOIN Loans l ON s.StudentID = l.StudentID
INNER JOIN Films f ON l.FilmID = f.FilmID;

WHERE filters rows; GROUP BY aggregates; JOIN combines on matching keys.

4. DBMS features

Data dictionary (schema, types, constraints), query processor, forms/reports, access rights (read/write per user), data integrity (validation rules), backup/recovery.

Exam tips: write SQL keywords uppercase; alias joined tables (s, l, f); when asked "why relational", cite reduced redundancy + flexible queries.

Primary keys, foreign keys and relationships

A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a table, so no two records can share its value. A foreign key is a field in one table that holds the primary key of a related table, and it creates a relationship between the tables. Relationships can be one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many. A many-to-many relationship is usually split into two one-to-many relationships through a linking table.

Foreign keys stop a record being added that points to a row which does not exist, which keeps the data consistent. Storing each fact once in the correct table also reduces redundancy, so an update is made in one place only.

Exam tip: when designing a table, name the primary key and say which field links it to another table.

title: Statistics — Data Handling — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Statistics — Data Handling

Mathematics — OL. averages from lists and tables, quartiles/IQR, charts, cumulative frequency, histograms.

  • 1. Averages
  • 2. Quartiles and IQR
  • 3. Charts
  • 4. Cumulative frequency
  • 5. Histograms

Formulas to learn

  • Mean from a grouped table: sum of f x divided by sum of f, using the class midpoints.
  • Interquartile range: Q3 - Q1. The median is Q2.
  • Histogram height: frequency density = frequency / class width. Area of each bar is proportional to frequency.

Worked example

A cumulative frequency curve has its points plotted against the upper class boundary. Reading the curve at 25 percent of the total gives Q1, at 50 percent gives the median, and at 75 percent gives Q3. The IQR is Q3 minus Q1, and it is less affected by outliers than the range.

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

title: Hypothesis Testing — Study Notes
content:
Hypothesis Testing

The Framework

The null hypothesis H₀ is the default claim (no change, p = p₀). The alternative H₁ is what a suspicious observation suggests (p > p₀, p < p₀, or p ≠ p₀). The significance level α is the probability of rejecting a true H₀ — the false-alarm rate, usually 5% or 1%.

Test for a Binomial Proportion

With X ~ B(n, p₀) under H₀, compute the probability of results at least as extreme as the observed count in the direction of H₁.

Example: H₀: p = 0.3 against H₁: p > 0.3, observed 10 successes in n = 20. Compute P(X ≥ 10) under B(20, 0.3). If that tail probability is below α, reject H₀.

One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed

One-tailed tests take the whole α in one direction. Two-tailed tests split α across both tails: compare against α/2 on each side, or equivalently check whether the observation falls in the extreme 2.5% (for α = 5%). Choose the tails from the wording of H₁, not from the data.

Critical Regions

The critical region is the set of values of the test statistic that would lead to rejection. Its boundary is the critical value. For B(20, 0.3) at the 5% level with H₁: p > 0.3, find the smallest k with P(X ≥ k) < 0.05 — that k opens the critical region.

Conclusions in Context

Never just say "reject H₀". Conclude in the language of the problem: "there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the proportion has increased". State the significance level, the direction, and the real-world quantity.

Exam tips: define H₀ and H₁ with symbols AND words. Verify which tail the observation sits in before computing. If the observed value lies in the critical region, evidence supports H₁; otherwise there is insufficient evidence — never "prove H₀ true".

title: Networking & Communication — Study Notes
content:
Networking & Communication

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): transmission modes, serial/parallel, packet switching, protocols, LAN/WAN, hardware, security layers.

1. Transmission basics

  • Serial: one bit at a time — reliable over distance, cheaper cable.
  • Parallel: several bits at once — faster over short runs; skew/crosstalk limit distance.
  • Simplex / half-duplex / full-duplex direction; bandwidth (bits/s) vs bit rate.

2. Packets

Header (sender/receiver addresses, sequence number) + payload + trailer (checksum). Packet switching: routes vary, packets reassembled at destination; checksum failure → re-request. Benefits: robustness, shared lines; delays/reassembly overhead.

3. Protocols

TCP/IP stack layers (application, transport, network, link). HTTP/HTTPS (TLS encryption), FTP (with login + commands), email: SMTP send, POP3/IMAP retrieve. Bluetooth/Wi-Fi for WPAN/WLAN.

4. Network types & hardware

LAN (site) vs WAN (internet). Router (joins networks, IP), switch (MAC frames within LAN), gateway (protocol translation), NIC, WAP. MAC address (burned-in, layer 2) vs IP address (assigned, layer 3).

5. Security in transmission

Encryption scrambles plaintext → ciphertext (key needed); HTTPS = HTTP over TLS; firewall packet filtering by port/IP; authentication (user+pass, 2FA); access levels.

Exam tips: explain why skew limits parallel over distance; compare MAC vs IP in a table; protocol questions want "rules for communication", not acronyms alone.

title: Differentiation II — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation II

Product and Quotient Rules

  • (uv)′ = u′v + uv′
  • (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²

Example: y = x² e^x gives dy/dx = 2x e^x + x² e^x = e^x(2x + x²).

Standard Derivatives

  • sin x → cos x; cos x → −sin x; tan x → sec²x
  • e^x → e^x; ln x → 1/x

Chain Rule Everywhere

d/dx [ln(3x)] = 3/(3x) = 1/x; d/dx [e^(2x)] = 2e^(2x); d/dx [sin²x] = 2 sin x cos x.

Implicit Differentiation

Differentiate both sides w.r.t. x, treating y as a function of x (terms in y pick up dy/dx).

Example: x² + y² = 25 → 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0 → dy/dx = −x/y.

Parametric Curves

For x = f(t), y = g(t): dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

Example: x = t², y = t³ gives dy/dx = 3t²/2t = 3t/2.

Exam tips: quote the rule you use; for tangent/normal on parametric curves, find t at the point first, and simplify implicit answers using the original equation.

### What earns the marks

title: Databases — Study Notes
content:
`# Databases

Relational Basics

Tables (relations) of records with fields. Keys:

  • Primary key: unique identifier
  • Foreign key: references another table's PK — creates relationships
  • Candidate/secondary keys: other unique identifiers

Normalisation

  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups
  • 2NF: 1NF + no partial dependency on a composite key
  • 3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependencies (non-key → non-key)

Example: (StudentID, Course, CourseFee) has CourseFee depending on Course, not StudentID — move course data to its own table (3NF).

SQL

SELECT name, grade FROM students
  WHERE grade >= 'A' ORDER BY name;
INSERT INTO students VALUES (...);
UPDATE students SET grade = 'B' WHERE id = 5;
DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 5;

Joins combine tables: FROM students s JOIN enrolments e ON s.id = e.sid.

Transactions

ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules hold), Isolation (no interference), Durability (committed = permanent). Record locking prevents conflicting simultaneous edits.

Exam tips: justify each normal form step with the dependency removed; write SQL with correct WHERE clauses to avoid accidental full-table updates.

Primary keys, foreign keys and redundancy

A primary key is a field, or combination of fields, that uniquely identifies each record in a table. A foreign key is a field in one table that holds the primary key of a record in another table. Foreign keys link the tables together and let the database check referential integrity, so that an order cannot refer to a customer who does not exist.

Storing data in one place rather than repeating it in several tables reduces data redundancy. Less redundancy saves storage, and it reduces the chance that an update is made in one copy but not the others. Normalisation is the process of organising tables to remove this repetition.

Exam tip: when asked about a foreign key, say which table it sits in and which primary key it refers to.

title: Exam technique: Sine and Cosine Rules
content:
### What earns the marks
For the sine rule, the matched pairs written (b / sin 65 = 7 / sin 40) earn the method mark. For the cosine rule, the full substitution with cos evaluated earns the mark: write a squared = 25 + 64 - 2 x 5 x 8 x 0.5. For the largest angle, identifying the longest side first earns credit. For area, half a b sin C quoted earns the mark on its own.
### Traps
Error: sides paired with wrong angles in the sine rule. Correction: each side faces its angle. Error: 49 given as side a. Correction: root the cosine-rule result. Error: calculator-only acute angle for an obtuse ambiguous case. Correction: subtract from 180 by hand. Error: half a b without sine for a non-right triangle. Correction: area needs the sine factor unless the angle is 90 degrees.
### Worked example
Two sides are 7 cm and 9 cm, with an included angle of 40 degrees. The cosine rule gives x^2 = 7^2 + 9^2 - 2 x 7 x 9 x cos 40 = 130 - 126 x 0.766 = 33.5, so x is about 5.79 cm. Use the cosine rule when you have two sides and the angle between them.
### Check yourself
A right-angled triangle has legs 6 and 8. Compute the area as one half of 6 x 8 x sin 90 degrees, and the hypotenuse with the cosine rule. The area is 24, and the hypotenuse is sqrt(36 + 64) = 10, because cos 90 degrees is zero.

### Worked example
Two sides are 7 cm and 9 cm, with an included angle of 40 degrees. The cosine rule gives x^2 = 7^2 + 9^2 - 2 x 7 x 9 x cos 40 = 130 - 126 x 0.766 = 33.5, so x is about 5.79 cm. Use the cosine rule when you have two sides and the angle between them.

title: Earth & Space — Study Notes
content:
Earth & Space

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): Earth & Solar System; stars & the Universe (Extended).

1. Earth, Moon, Sun

Earth rotates 24 h (day/night), orbits 365¼ d (year + leap). Moon orbits Earth ~27.3 d; phases from viewing angle; lunar/solar eclipses when aligned. Seasons from axial tilt (23.5°), not distance.

2. Solar system

Planets (Mercury → Neptune), dwarf planets (Pluto), moons, asteroids, comets (eccentric orbits, tails away from Sun), natural satellites. Gravity keeps orbits; orbital speed & radius relate to the central mass.

3. Orbital motion

Orbital speed v = 2πr/T. T grows with r (Kepler trend). Comets speed up near the Sun (ellipse, Sun at focus).

4. Stars (Extended)

Star formation: nebula → protostar (gravity, KE→thermal) → main sequence (hydrogen fusion: H→He, radiation pressure balances gravity) → red giant → white dwarf (Sun-mass) or supergiant → supernova → neutron star/black hole (massive stars). Elements heavier than iron form in supernovae.

5. Universe (Extended)

The Sun is one star in the Milky Way; the Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies. Redshift: receding galaxies show stretched wavelengths → the Universe is expanding → Big Bang model; CMB is the afterglow. Hubble: farther ⇒ faster recession.

6. Scales

light-year = distance light travels in a year (9.5 × 10¹⁵ m); astronomical unit = Earth–Sun distance (1.5 × 10¹¹ m).

Orbits and the Solar System in more depth

The planets orbit the Sun because the Sun's gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps them on their paths. A moon is a natural satellite that orbits a planet, and an artificial satellite is launched by people. The Earth rotates once on its axis in one day, and it orbits the Sun once in one year. The phases of the Moon are caused by the changing proportion of its sunlit side that we see as it orbits the Earth.

Exam tip: state the object that provides the gravitational force when you describe why an orbit is stable.

title: Intermolecular Forces — Study Notes
content:
Intermolecular Forces

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 7. Intermolecular forces are the attractions between molecules, not the bonds inside them. They determine boiling points, solubility and how molecules pack together.

Types of intermolecular force

  • London (instantaneous dipole–induced dipole) forces exist in all molecules. They grow with the number of electrons, so larger molecules have higher boiling points.
  • Permanent dipole–dipole forces occur between polar molecules, where the partial positive and negative charges attract one another.
  • Hydrogen bonding is a strong dipole–dipole attraction. It occurs when H is bonded to N, O or F and attracts a lone pair on another N, O or F.

Effect on physical properties

  • Boiling point depends on the strength of intermolecular forces: more energy is needed to separate molecules that attract strongly.
  • Water boils at a much higher temperature than hydrogen sulfide because hydrogen bonding is much stronger than the dipole forces between H2S molecules.
  • Branched alkanes have lower boiling points than straight-chain isomers because they have a smaller surface area for London forces.

Solubility

  • Substances dissolve when the new attractions between solute and solvent replace the attractions within each.
  • Polar solvents such as water dissolve ionic and polar solutes; non-polar solvents dissolve non-polar solutes.
  • Ethanol is miscible with water because its –OH group forms hydrogen bonds with water.

Ideal and real gases

  • A real gas deviates from ideal behaviour at high pressure and low temperature, because molecules have volume and attract one another.

Exam tip: when comparing boiling points, name the type of intermolecular force, state whether it is stronger or weaker, and say how much energy is needed to overcome it. Do not say that "bonds break" when a liquid boils.

title: Chemical Equilibria A2 Level Chemistry Revision Notes
content:
Chemical Equilibria A2 Level Chemistry Revision Notes

This revision note belongs to Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 13 Chemical Equilibria, covering homogeneous and heterogeneous systems, equilibrium constants Kc and Kp, the factors affecting equilibrium composition and constant values, total entropy links, and reaction extent predictions.

Expressions for Kc in Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Systems

When a reversible reaction takes place in a closed system, it eventually reaches a dynamic equilibrium where the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction, and the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant. The equilibrium constant Kc allows you to deduce the position of equilibrium quantitatively.

  • Be able to deduce an expression for Kc, for homogeneous and heterogeneous systems, in terms of equilibrium concentrations.
  • For a general homogeneous system where all species are in the same phase, such as aA + bB reversible cC + dD, the expression is Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b), where square brackets denote equilibrium concentrations in mol dm⁻³.
  • For heterogeneous systems containing species in different phases, pure solids and pure liquids are omitted from the Kc expression because their concentrations remain essentially constant throughout the reaction. For example, for the decomposition of calcium carbonate, CaCO3(s) reversible CaO(s) + CO2(g), the expression is simply Kc = [CO2].

Expressions for Kp in Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Systems

For systems involving gases, it is often more convenient to use partial pressures rather than concentrations to define the equilibrium position.

  • Be able to deduce an expression for Kp for homogeneous and heterogeneous systems, in terms of equilibrium partial pressures in atm.
  • The mole fraction of a gas in a mixture is calculated as the number of moles of that individual gas divided by the total number of moles of all gases present in the mixture.
  • The partial pressure of an individual gas is its mole fraction multiplied by the total pressure of the gas system, measured in units of atmospheres or atm.
  • For a homogeneous gas phase reaction such as N2O4(g) reversible 2NO2(g), the partial pressure expression is Kp = p(NO2)² / p(N2O4).
  • For a heterogeneous gas-solid equilibrium such as C(s) + CO2(g) reversible 2CO(g), pure solid carbon is omitted from the expression, giving Kp = p(CO)² / p(CO2).

Calculating Equilibrium Constants from Experimental Data

Calculations involving Kc and Kp require systematic tracking of initial moles, change in moles, and equilibrium moles, converting them to concentrations or partial pressures.

  • Be able to calculate a value, with units where appropriate, for the equilibrium constants Kc and Kp for homogeneous and heterogeneous reactions, from experimental data.
  • For Kc calculations, divide equilibrium moles by the total volume in dm³ to find equilibrium concentrations, substitute into the Kc formula, and cancel out units or combine them using indices such as mol⁻² dm⁶.
  • For Kp calculations, find total moles at equilibrium, determine mole fractions for each gas, multiply by total pressure to find partial pressures in atm, substitute into Kp, and derive units like atm or atm².

Worked Example for Kc Calculation

For H2 + I2 reversible 2HI, suppose 1.00 mol of hydrogen and 1.00 mol of iodine are heated in a 2.00 dm³ flask. At equilibrium, 1.60 mol of hydrogen iodide has formed.

  • Step 1: Set up an ICE table. Initial moles: H2 = 1.00, I2 = 1.00, HI = 0.00.
  • Step 2: Equilibrium moles: HI = 1.60. Since stoichiometry shows 2 mol of HI form, 0.80 mol of H2 and 0.80 mol of I2 must have reacted.
  • Step 3: Calculate remaining equilibrium moles: H2 = 1.00 − 0.80 = 0.20 mol; I2 = 1.00 − 0.80 = 0.20 mol.
  • Step 4: Convert to concentrations by dividing by the volume of 2.00 dm³: [HI] = 1.60 ÷ 2.00 = 0.80 mol dm⁻³, [H2] = 0.20 ÷ 2.00 = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, [I2] = 0.20 ÷ 2.00 = 0.10 mol dm⁻³.
  • Step 5: Substitute into Kc expression: Kc = [HI]² / ([H2] × [I2]) = 0.80² / (0.10 × 0.10) = 0.64 / 0.01 = 64. The units cancel out entirely because the number of moles of reactants equals the number of moles of products.

Effects of Changes on Equilibrium Composition

Le Chatelier's principle helps predict how a system responds to external stresses, altering equilibrium composition without changing the constant itself unless temperature changes.

  • Understand how, if at all, a change in temperature, pressure or the presence of a catalyst affects the equilibrium composition in a homogeneous or heterogeneous system.
  • Adding reactant or removing product shifts the position towards the products. Adding product shifts it towards the reactants.
  • Increasing pressure or decreasing volume favours the side of the reaction with fewer gas molecules. Changing the volume has the same effect as changing pressure.
  • Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction. Lowering the temperature shifts it in the exothermic direction.
  • A catalyst changes the rate at which equilibrium is reached by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, but it has no effect on the equilibrium position or composition.

Independence of Equilibrium Constants from Concentration and Pressure

While altering conditions shifts the position of equilibrium, the underlying constant remains strictly invariant under specific conditions.

  • Understand that the value of the equilibrium constant is not affected by changes in concentration or pressure or by the addition of a catalyst.
  • A change in concentration or pressure shifts the equilibrium composition to counteract the change, but the ratio of products to reactants at the new equilibrium exactly equals the original Kc or Kp value.
  • A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse rates equally, leaving the equilibrium constant completely unchanged.

Effect of Temperature on Equilibrium Constants

Temperature is unique because it alters the actual value of the equilibrium constant Kc and Kp, reflecting a change in the position of equilibrium.

  • Know the effect of changing the temperature on the equilibrium constant Kc and Kp for both exothermic and endothermic reactions.
  • Understand that the effect of temperature on the position of equilibrium is explained using a change in the value of the equilibrium constant.
  • For an exothermic forward reaction, raising the temperature decreases the value of Kc and Kp, as the equilibrium shifts to the left. Lowering the temperature increases Kc and Kp.
  • For an endothermic forward reaction, raising the temperature increases the value of Kc and Kp, as the equilibrium shifts to the right. Lowering the temperature decreases Kc and Kp.

Entropy, Total Entropy, and Equilibrium Constants

Thermodynamics links the position of equilibrium to total entropy change and the magnitude of the equilibrium constant.

  • Understand the effect of a change in temperature on the value of Stotal and the magnitude of the equilibrium constant, since Stotal = R ln K.
  • The equation Stotal = R ln K bridges kinetics, equilibrium, and thermodynamics, where R is the universal gas constant and ln K is the natural logarithm of the equilibrium constant.
  • When temperature changes, it alters Stotal, which in turn directly alters the magnitude of K. A larger positive Stotal corresponds to a much larger equilibrium constant, meaning the reaction goes virtually to completion.

Predicting the Extent of Reaction

The numerical value of an equilibrium constant gives immediate insight into whether a reaction proceeds far towards products or stays mostly as reactants.

  • Be able to apply knowledge of the value of equilibrium constants to predict the extent to which a reaction takes place.
  • When an equilibrium constant value is very large, greater than 10 to the power of 10, the numerator is vastly larger than the denominator, indicating that the reaction goes essentially to completion with very few reactants remaining.
  • When an equilibrium constant value is very small, less than 10 to the power of minus 10, the denominator dominates, indicating that virtually no reaction takes place and the system remains almost entirely as reactants.
  • When an equilibrium constant is around 1, significant amounts of both reactants and products are present at equilibrium.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Including pure solids or pure liquids in Kc or Kp expressions. Correction: Omit pure solids and pure liquids because their active masses do not change.
  • Mistake: Forgetting to divide equilibrium moles by volume when calculating Kc. Correction: Always divide moles by the volume in dm³ to obtain concentration values before substituting into Kc.
  • Mistake: Believing that increasing pressure changes the value of Kc. Correction: Pressure changes the position of equilibrium and shifts concentrations, but Kc remains constant at a fixed temperature.
  • Mistake: Using mass in grams instead of mole fractions or partial pressures for Kp calculations. Correction: Always convert mass to moles, find mole fractions, and multiply by total pressure in atm.

Exam-style questions

  1. Write the expression for Kc for the heterogeneous reaction C(s) + H2O(g) reversible CO(g) + H2(g).

    Answer: Kc = [CO] [H2] / [H2O]. Solid carbon is omitted.

  2. State and explain the effect of increasing the temperature on the value of Kc for an endothermic forward reaction.

    Answer: Kc increases. Raising temperature favours the endothermic direction, increasing product concentrations and decreasing reactant concentrations, raising the numerator of Kc.

  3. Calculate the units of Kp for the equilibrium N2(g) + 3H2(g) reversible 2NH3(g) when pressure is measured in atm.

    Answer: Kp = p(NH3)² / (p(N2) × p(H2)³). Units are atm² / (atm × atm³) = atm⁻².

  4. Explain why a catalyst has no effect on the numerical value of Kc.

    Answer: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse rates equally by lowering the activation energy, leaving the equilibrium constant ratio unchanged.

  5. Explain what a Kc value of 10 to the power of 15 indicates about the extent of a reaction.

    Answer: The reaction goes almost entirely to completion, with the equilibrium position lying far to the right.

Use these revision notes to test your understanding of equilibrium expressions, unit derivations, and thermodynamic links via Stotal. Next, revise reaction kinetics and acid-base equilibria.

title: Exam technique: Coordinate Geometry
content:
### What earns the marks
For lines, the gradient computation shown earns the first mark and the substitution of one point earns the second. For perpendicular bisectors, the midpoint plus the negative-reciprocal gradient each earn a mark. For circles, completing the square to centre-radius form earns the method mark; the root taken last earns the final one.
### Traps
Error: segment equation given for the bisector. Correction: midpoint plus perpendicular gradient. Error: r squared reported as the radius. Correction: root last. Error: intersection x-values presented as points. Correction: substitute back for y.

title: Dynamics — Study Notes
content:
Dynamics

Momentum

  • Momentum p = mv. It is a vector, with unit kg m s⁻¹, and it has the same direction as the velocity.
  • Momentum and kinetic energy are different. Momentum is a vector and changes sign with direction. Kinetic energy is a scalar.

Newton's laws of motion

  • First law: a body stays at rest or keeps moving at constant velocity unless a resultant (net) force acts on it.
  • Second law: the resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = ma for constant mass. The acceleration is in the direction of the resultant force.
  • Third law: when body A exerts a force on body B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. The two forces are the same type and act on different bodies, so they never cancel.

Weight and mass

Mass is the amount of matter (scalar, kg). Weight is the gravitational force on it, W = mg (vector, N). Mass is the same everywhere; weight changes with the value of g.

Impulse

Impulse = FΔt = Δp = m(v − u). The area under a force–time graph equals the impulse. A longer contact time for the same change in momentum means a smaller average force, which is why airbags and crumple zones work.

Conservation of linear momentum

For a system with no resultant external force, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after. In an elastic collision momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved. In an inelastic collision only momentum is conserved. In a collision where the bodies stick together, the kinetic energy lost is greatest.

Worked example: a 0.5 kg trolley moving at 4 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 1.0 kg trolley and they stick together. Total momentum before = 0.5 × 4 = 2.0 kg m s⁻¹. Common velocity = 2.0 / 1.5 ≈ 1.3 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: choose a positive direction and keep signs consistent in every momentum term. State that the system is isolated before applying conservation. For a recoil question, the two momenta are equal and opposite.

Worked example: explosion and recoil

A 2.0 kg gun at rest fires a 0.020 kg bullet at 300 m s⁻¹. Before the shot, total momentum is zero. After it, the bullet has momentum 0.020 × 300 = 6.0 kg m s⁻¹ forwards, so the gun must recoil with momentum 6.0 kg m s⁻¹ backwards. Its recoil velocity is 6.0/2.0 = 3.0 m s⁻¹. The same reasoning holds for any explosion from rest: the fragments' momenta sum to zero.

Two-dimensional collisions

Momentum is a vector, so it is conserved separately in each perpendicular direction. In a collision where a 2.0 kg ball moving east at 4.0 m s⁻¹ strikes a stationary ball of equal mass at an angle, resolve the momentum of each ball along the original direction and perpendicular to it. Apply conservation in both directions, then combine the components to find the resultant speed or angle.

Kinetic energy in collisions

Kinetic energy is lost in any inelastic collision. For the trolley example above, the initial kinetic energy is ½ × 0.5 × 4² = 4.0 J, and the final kinetic energy is ½ × 1.5 × (1.33)² ≈ 1.33 J. About 2.7 J has been transferred to sound, heat and deformation. Calculate the energies to show that the collision is inelastic, rather than just saying it is.

Impulse and the force–time graph

If a force of 40 N acts for 0.25 s, the impulse is 10 N s. Where the force varies, find the area under the force–time graph: count the squares, or split the area into triangles and rectangles. A large area means a large change in momentum, even if the peak force is modest.

  • Use Δp = m(v − u) with the sign of each velocity included. A ball that bounces back has a negative final velocity relative to its initial motion.
  • For a bounce, the change in momentum is larger than for a ball that stops, because the ball reverses direction.
  • When a question asks for the average force on a ball, use the impulse and the contact time, and state the direction of the force.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Adding the speeds of two bodies moving in opposite directions instead of subtracting, because direction was not included.
  • Treating a non-isolated system as isolated, for example ignoring friction or a gravitational force that acts on the system from outside.
  • Confusing the impulse with the force, or failing to convert the time into seconds.
