title: Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes — Study Notes
content:
Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 4. Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. Alkanes are the simplest family, and their reactions introduce the radical substitution mechanism used throughout the course.

Naming and formulae

  • A homologous series has the same general formula, similar chemical properties and a gradual change in physical properties.
  • Alkanes have the general formula CnH2n+2. Names depend on the longest carbon chain: meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex-.
  • Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different connectivity, such as butane and methylpropane.

Fossil fuels and cracking

  • Alkanes are obtained from crude oil by fractional distillation; the fractions separate by boiling point, which rises with chain length.
  • Cracking breaks long chains into shorter, more useful alkanes and alkenes, using heat or a catalyst.

Radical substitution

  • Alkanes react with chlorine or bromine under UV light by free-radical substitution.
  • The three stages are initiation (Cl2 → 2Cl•), propagation (a radical reacts with an alkane, regenerating a radical) and termination (two radicals combine).
  • Propagation steps form the product; termination steps are rare, so they do not appear in the main yield.

Combustion

  • Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water; limited oxygen gives carbon monoxide or carbon (soot).

Exam tip: when writing a radical mechanism, use a single-headed arrow for each electron moved and always show the radical dot.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Radical substitution, applied to methane and chlorine under UV light: initiation Cl₂ → 2Cl• (homolytic fission, UV required); propagation CH₄ + Cl• → CH₃• + HCl, then CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•; termination when two radicals combine. Each step needs its own equation for the marks.
  • Why a mixture forms: radical substitution is not selective, so chloromethane, dichloromethane and so on all form. Excess methane favours monosubstitution, because a chlorine radical is more likely to meet a methane molecule than a chloromethane molecule.
  • Combustion: complete combustion gives CO₂ and H₂O. Incomplete combustion, with limited oxygen, gives CO, which is toxic because it binds haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen does. State the limited oxygen supply in the answer.
  • Naming: the longest carbon chain gives the parent, and the lowest possible number goes to the first branch. Name branches alphabetically with their numbers, and use di-, tri- for repeated branches, for example 2,2-dimethylpropane.

title:
Appendix K — Deep practical microbiology: how to think about the culturing and safety questions on the paper

The practical microbiology questions are the ones where candidates most often lose marks by writing a method without the reasoning, or by writing a safety list without the reasoning, or by writing a result description without saying what the result means. The reasoning that the question is really after is usually one of three kinds: why the technique is done that way, what the control is for, or what the observation means about the organism or the condition. If you can answer any of those three in a microbiology context, you can handle the practical question when it appears. If you only know the method and not the reasoning, you are vulnerable on exactly the marks that the practical question is usually built from. The reason for that is that the practical question is not usually a memory test for the method alone; it is a reasoning test about the method, the safety and the interpretation.

For culturing, the reasoning is usually about purity, safety and the reason for the particular setup. A good answer about a culturing method does not just say “spread the inoculum on agar” but says why the inoculum is diluted or isolated, why the plate is incubated in a particular way, why the lid is not fully opened, why the workspace is treated the way it is, and why the waste is disposed of the way it is. If you can say that, you have the reasoning. If you only say “the plate is incubated,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning. For safety, the reasoning is about what could go wrong and how the procedure prevents it, so a good safety answer is about sterilisation, containment and disposal as connected ideas, not just a list of rules. For interpretation, the reasoning is about what the growth or the lack of growth means, so a good interpretation answer is about the conditions that favour or prevent growth and about the limits of what can be concluded from the result.

The practical microbiology reasoning is also the reasoning that connects back to the theory, because the same ideas that matter in the lab, purity, safety, growth and interpretation, are the ideas that matter in the theory questions. If you can see that the practical and the theory are two views of the same ideas, you can answer the questions that span them, which are often the best-marked ones. If you only see the practical as a separate thing from the theory, you are likely to lose the marks on the questions that ask you to connect the two. The note has covered both, and the length is there so that you have the connection as well as the parts. If you use the note as a set of connected ideas rather than as a set of separate facts, you get the connection, and that is the use of the length.

Appendix L — The immune response as a process with timing, not just as a set of cells and molecules

The immune response is the topic where a candidate can get all the cells and molecules right and still lose marks by not saying the process in time order and by not saying why the timing matters. The process is that on first exposure, the specific lymphocytes have to be activated, expanded and differentiated over time, so the primary response is slow; on later exposure, the memory cells are already present and ready, so the secondary response is fast and strong. The point of the timing is that the immune system is not a single instantaneous event; it is a process with stages, and the stages matter for the comparison between primary and secondary responses and for the explanation of vaccination. If you can say that, you have the immune process in a form that scores marks. If you only say “the body makes antibodies,” you have the label but not the process, and the mark is in the process, because that is what the comparison and the vaccination questions are built from.

The memory idea is the one where the timing matters most, because the mark is often about the difference that memory makes, not just about the existence of memory. A good answer says that memory cells from the first exposure are responsible for the faster and stronger secondary response, and that this is the basis of vaccination, because vaccination produces the memory without the disease. It does not say that the immune system “remembers” in a vague sense without saying what the memory cells do, because the memory cell is the point, and the timing is the point. If you can say that the memory cells are the reason the secondary response is faster, you have the memory idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “the second time is quicker,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the reasoning is what the mark is after.

The specificity is the other idea where timing and process meet, because the specific response is specific and the non-specific responses are not, and that distinction matters for the comparison between the first line and the specific response. A good answer says that the first line is non-specific and the specific response is specific, and that the specific response includes antibodies and memory cells, while the first line includes barriers, inflammation and phagocytosis. It does not say that the specific response replaces the first line, because it does not; the two work together, and the mark is often about seeing that the system has both parts and that they have different roles. If you can say that, you have the immune comparison in a form that scores marks. If you only say “the body has specific immunity,” you have the label but not the comparison, and the mark is in the comparison, because that is what the question is usually built from.

Appendix M — Forensic biology as interpretation, and the things that can go wrong with it

Forensic biology is the topic where candidates most often lose marks by treating the evidence as a simple fact rather than as something with an interpretation and a set of things that can go wrong. The precise idea is that biological evidence such as DNA can be used to identify individuals and to link evidence to people or scenes, but the evidence is interpreted, and the interpretation depends on the quality of the sample, on whether it was contaminated, on the chain of custody, and on the context of the question. A good answer says that, and also says that a match or a mismatch is not a simple yes-no answer in the abstract but a result to be interpreted in context. If you can say that, you have the forensic biology idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “DNA can identify someone,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the reasoning is what the mark is after.

The things that can go wrong are the other part of the forensic reasoning that is worth saying explicitly, because they are the things that make the evidence meaningful or not. Contamination can make the evidence unreliable. Poor handling can lose or degrade the sample. A broken chain of custody can make the evidence hard to interpret in a legal context. A match in the wrong context can mean something different from a match in the right context. A good answer says that these are the things that matter, and that the value of the evidence depends on them. It does not say that forensic biology is always straightforward, because it is not, and it does not say that it is never reliable, because it can be. If you can say that the evidence has limits as well as value, you have the forensic reasoning in a form that scores marks. If you only have the label of “biological evidence,” you are missing the reasoning that the mark is after.

The identification idea is the one where the forensic topic connects back to the biology, because DNA profiling works because there is variation between individuals in certain DNA regions, and that is a biological fact about variation, not a forensic trick. A good answer says that the method depends on variation between individuals and on the ability to detect and compare those differences, and that the result is a pattern that can be matched or excluded. It does not say that DNA profiling is a magic identification without the variation, because the variation is the point. If you can say that, you have the DNA profiling idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “DNA fingerprinting identifies people,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the reasoning is what the mark is after when the question asks about the principle.

Appendix N — How to plan a revision session on this topic so the length of the note becomes an advantage

The length of this note is an advantage if you plan the revision session around it, and a disadvantage if you read it as one long block without a plan. The plan is to work through the note in the order the exam uses the topic: description first, then comparison, then evaluation. For description, work through the organisms, the culturing and safety, the growth curve, the first line of defence, the antigen-antibody idea, the B and T cells, the memory and secondary response, the vaccination and herd immunity, the monoclonal antibodies, the epidemiology, and the forensic biology and DNA profiling. For comparison, work through the bacteria and viruses, the primary and secondary responses, the specific and non-specific defences, the humoral and cell-mediated arms, and the population and individual views. For evaluation, work through vaccination, monoclonal antibodies, DNA profiling, gene therapy and GM organisms, with a benefit and an issue for each. If you revise in that order, you are revising the topic as the marks are organised, rather than as one undifferentiated block.

The second part of the plan is to use the appendices as the place where you go deeper when a topic needs it, rather than as a separate thing to read first. The appendices on practical microbiology, the immune process, and forensic interpretation are there because those are the places where the marks are most often lost for lack of depth, and they are the places to spend time when you practise. If you read the main body for the coverage and the appendices for the depth, you get the best use of the note, because you get both the coverage and the reasoning. If you only read the main body, you may get the labels but not the reasoning. If you only read the appendices, you may get the depth but not the coverage. The plan that reads both in the right order gets both, and that is the plan that makes the note useful.

The third part of the plan is to self-test from the note under time pressure, because the note can tell you the reasoning but only the self-test can tell you whether you can produce it under the condition the exam is in. Pick one description, one comparison and one evaluation question each session, cover the model answer, write from the note and time yourself, then compare. If your answer has the same sequence and the same distinctions, move on. If it does not, the gap is the practice target. If you do that regularly, you turn the note from a reference into a practice tool, and that is the use that makes the length worth having. If you only read the note, you have familiarity but not ability, and the exam tests ability. The plan is therefore to use the note as a reference for coverage and as a practice source for ability, and to use the self-test to check the ability under time pressure. That is the plan that makes the note’s length an advantage rather than a burden.

Appendix O — Extended worked answers for the cross-strand questions this topic sets

When the question crosses the strands, the answer has to move between them without losing the thread, and that is the skill the note is trying to build. For a question that asks you to relate the care needed in microbiology culturing to the care needed in forensic biology, the answer is that both depend on controlling contamination and on handling the material in a way that keeps the result meaningful, but for different reasons: in microbiology the point is to keep the culture pure and contained, while in forensics the point is to keep the evidence reliable and interpretable. A good answer says that both need careful handling and contamination control, and that the reason differs by context. If you can say that, you have the cross-strand answer. If you only write two separate lists, one for microbiology and one for forensics, you have lost the connection, and the connection is what the question is after.

For a question that asks you to relate the immune recognition of antigens to the forensic comparison of DNA patterns, the answer is that both are about telling things apart by recognising specific features, but in different forms: the immune system recognises antigens and produces specific antibodies and memory cells, while DNA profiling compares patterns of variation in DNA and uses the differences between individuals to identify or exclude. A good answer says that both are recognition-and-comparison ideas, but in different systems and for different purposes. If you can say that, you have the cross-strand answer. If you only describe immunity and forensics separately, you have lost the connection, and the connection is what the question is after.

For a question that asks you to relate the population side of the topic, epidemiology and herd immunity, to the individual side, the answers to that are in the same note but the reasoning has to be moved between them. A good answer says that the individual side is about what happens to one organism or one person, while the population side is about patterns and spread and control, and that the population side depends on the individual side but is not the same as it. For herd immunity, it says that the protection of the population depends on coverage, not on every individual being immune. For epidemiology, it says that the study is about patterns and causes and control, not just about one case. If you can say that, you have the cross-strand answer that moves between the individual and the population, and that is the kind of answer the higher marks are after. If you only stay at one level, you lose the marks on the question that asks you to move between them.

The final cross-strand answer to practise is the one that brings together the three strands in a single example, because that is the question that tests the most integrated understanding. Suppose the question is about a disease outbreak and asks you about the pathogen, the immune response and the forensic or epidemiological use of evidence. A good answer says that the pathogen is a microorganism that can cause disease, that the body responds with barriers, phagocytosis and the specific antibody and memory response, and that if the outbreak is being investigated, biological evidence such as DNA may be used to identify the source or the spread, and that the evidence has to be collected and interpreted with care. If you can say that in one connected answer, you have the topic as a connected whole, and you have the kind of answer the most demanding questions are after. If you only give one strand, you have lost the others, and the others are part of the mark. The note is long enough to give you all three strands and the connections, and that is the use of the length: to make the most demanding questions answerable.

Appendix P — How this note should be revised against the specification after the pass

This note has been lengthened in this pass to cover the specification statements at the level where long-answer marks are earned, but a longer note can still be long in the wrong way if it drifts from the specification, so the note should be revised against the specification after the pass. The way to revise against the specification is to take the specification and see whether each statement has a place in the note, and whether the place is the kind of answer the specification rewards. If a statement is covered only by a label, that is the gap to fill. If a statement is covered by a reasoning sequence, that is usually the right level. If the note has become long by adding things the specification does not ask for, that is the part to cut. The note should be long enough to answer the specification questions, and not longer than that, because a note is a tool for revision, and a tool is only good if it is used well.

The second thing to check after the pass is that the note does not contradict itself, because a longer note can develop small contradictions as it is extended. The common places for contradiction are the distinctions that matter most: bacteria versus viruses, specific versus non-specific, B cells versus T cells, primary versus secondary, herd immunity as coverage versus herd immunity as every individual, and DNA profiling as interpretation versus DNA profiling as absolute proof. Appendix K — Deep practical microbiology: how to think about the culturing and safety questions on the paper

The practical microbiology questions are the ones where candidates most often lose marks by writing a method without the reasoning, or by writing a safety list without the reasoning, or by writing a result description without saying what the result means. The reasoning that the question is really after is usually one of three kinds: why the technique is done that way, what the control is for, or what the observation means about the organism or the condition. If you can answer any of those three in a microbiology context, you can handle the practical question when it appears. If you only know the method and not the reasoning, you are vulnerable on exactly the marks that the practical question is usually built from. The reason for that is that the practical question is not usually a memory test for the method alone; it is a reasoning test about the method, the safety and the interpretation.

For culturing, the reasoning is usually about purity, safety and the reason for the particular setup. A good answer about a culturing method does not just say “spread the inoculum on agar” but says why the inoculum is diluted or isolated, why the plate is incubated in a particular way, why the lid is not fully opened, why the workspace is treated the way it is, and why the waste is disposed of the way it is. If you can say that, you have the reasoning. If you only say “the plate is incubated,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning. For safety, the reasoning is about what could go wrong and how the procedure prevents it, so a good safety answer is about sterilisation, containment and disposal as connected ideas, not just a list of rules. For interpretation, the reasoning is about what the growth or the lack of growth means, so a good interpretation answer is about the conditions that favour or prevent growth and about the limits of what can be concluded from the result.

The practical microbiology reasoning is also the reasoning that connects back to the theory, because the same ideas that matter in the lab, purity, safety, growth and interpretation, are the ideas that matter in the theory questions. If you can see that the practical and the theory are two views of the same ideas, you can answer the questions that span them, which are often the best-marked ones. If you only see the practical as a separate thing from the theory, you are likely to lose the marks on the questions that ask you to connect the two. The note has covered both, and the length is there so that you have the connection as well as the parts. If you use the note as a set of connected ideas rather than as a set of separate facts, you get the connection, and that is the use of the length.

Appendix L — The immune response as a process with timing, not just as a set of cells and molecules

The immune response is the topic where a candidate can get all the cells and molecules right and still lose marks by not saying the process in time order and by not saying why the timing matters. The process is that on first exposure, the specific lymphocytes have to be activated, expanded and differentiated over time, so the primary response is slow; on later exposure, the memory cells are already present and ready, so the secondary response is fast and strong. The point of the timing is that the immune system is not a single instantaneous event; it is a process with stages, and the stages matter for the comparison between primary and secondary responses and for the explanation of vaccination. If you can say that, you have the immune process in a form that scores marks. If you only say “the body makes antibodies,” you have the label but not the process, and the mark is in the process, because that is what the comparison and the vaccination questions are built from.

The memory idea is the one where the timing matters most, because the mark is often about the difference that memory makes, not just about the existence of memory. A good answer says that memory cells from the first exposure are responsible for the faster and stronger secondary response, and that this is the basis of vaccination, because vaccination produces the memory without the disease. It does not say that the immune system “remembers” in a vague sense without saying what the memory cells do, because the memory cell is the point, and the timing is the point. If you can say that the memory cells are the reason the secondary response is faster, you have the memory idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “the second time is quicker,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the reasoning is what the mark is after.

The specificity is the other idea where timing and process meet, because the specific response is specific and the non-specific responses are not, and that distinction matters for the comparison between the first line and the specific response. A good answer says that the first line is non-specific and the specific response is specific, and that the specific response includes antibodies and memory cells, while the first line includes barriers, inflammation and phagocytosis. It does not say that the specific response replaces the first line, because it does not; the two work together, and the mark is often about seeing that the system has both parts and that they have different roles. If you can say that, you have the immune comparison in a form that scores marks. If you only say “the body has specific immunity,” you have the label but not the comparison, and the mark is in the comparison, because that is what the question is usually built from.

Appendix M — Forensic biology as interpretation, and the things that can go wrong with it

Forensic biology is the topic where candidates most often lose marks by treating the evidence as a simple fact rather than as something with an interpretation and a set of things that can go wrong. The precise idea is that biological evidence such as DNA can be used to identify individuals and to link evidence to people or scenes, but the evidence is interpreted, and the interpretation depends on the quality of the sample, on whether it was contaminated, on the chain of custody, and on the context of the question. A good answer says that, and also says that a match or a mismatch is not a simple yes-no answer in the abstract but a result to be interpreted in context. If you can say that, you have the forensic biology idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “DNA can identify someone,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the reasoning is what the mark is after.

The things that can go wrong are the other part of the forensic reasoning that is worth saying explicitly, because they are the things that make the evidence meaningful or not. Contamination can make the evidence unreliable. Poor handling can lose or degrade the sample. A broken chain of custody can make the evidence hard to interpret in a legal context. A match in the wrong context can mean something different from a match in the right context. A good answer says that these are the things that matter, and that the value of the evidence depends on them. It does not say that forensic biology is always straightforward, because it is not, and it does not say that it is never reliable, because it can be. If you can say that the evidence has limits as well as value, you have the forensic reasoning in a form that scores marks. If you only have the label of “biological evidence,” you are missing the reasoning that the mark is after.

The identification idea is the one where the forensic topic connects back to the biology, because DNA profiling works because there is variation between individuals in certain DNA regions, and that is a biological fact about variation, not a forensic trick. A good answer says that the method depends on variation between individuals and on the ability to detect and compare those differences, and that the result is a pattern that can be matched or excluded. It does not say that DNA profiling is a magic identification without the variation, because the variation is the point. If you can say that, you have the DNA profiling idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “DNA fingerprinting identifies people,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the reasoning is what the mark is after when the question asks about the principle.

The length of this note is an advantage if you plan the revision session around it, and a disadvantage if you read it as one long block without a plan. The plan is to work through the note in the order the exam uses the topic: description first, then comparison, then evaluation. For description, work through the organisms, the culturing and safety, the growth curve, the first line of defence, the antigen-antibody idea, the B and T cells, the memory and secondary response, the vaccination and herd immunity, the monoclonal antibodies, the epidemiology, and the forensic biology and DNA profiling. For comparison, work through the bacteria and viruses, the primary and secondary responses, the specific and non-specific defences, the humoral and cell-mediated arms, and the population and individual views. For evaluation, work through vaccination, monoclonal antibodies, DNA profiling, gene therapy and GM organisms, with a benefit and an issue for each. If you revise in that order, you are revising the topic as the marks are organised, rather than as one undifferentiated block.

The second part of the plan is to use the appendices as the place where you go deeper when a topic needs it, rather than as a separate thing to read first. The appendices on practical microbiology, the immune process, and forensic interpretation are there because those are the places where the marks are most often lost for lack of depth, and they are the places to spend time when you practise. If you read the main body for the coverage and the appendices for the depth, you get the best use of the note, because you get both the coverage and the reasoning. The third part of the plan is to self-test from the note under time pressure, because the note can tell you the reasoning but only the self-test can tell you whether you can produce it under the condition the exam is in. The plan is therefore to use the note as a reference for coverage and as a practice source for ability, and to use the self-test to check the ability under time pressure. That is the plan that makes the note’s length an advantage rather than a burden.

Appendix O — Extended worked answers for the cross-strand questions this topic sets

When the question crosses the strands, the answer has to move between them without losing the thread, and that is the skill the note is trying to build. For a question that asks you to relate the care needed in microbiology culturing to the care needed in forensic biology, the answer is that both depend on controlling contamination and on handling the material in a way that keeps the result meaningful, but for different reasons: in microbiology the point is to keep the culture pure and contained, while in forensics the point is to keep the evidence reliable and interpretable. A good answer says that both need careful handling and contamination control, and that the reason differs by context. If you can say that, you have the cross-strand answer. If you only write two separate lists, one for microbiology and one for forensics, you have lost the connection, and the connection is what the question is after.

For a question that asks you to relate the immune recognition of antigens to the forensic comparison of DNA patterns, the answer is that both are about telling things apart by recognising specific features, but in different forms: the immune system recognises antigens and produces specific antibodies and memory cells, while DNA profiling compares patterns of variation in DNA and uses the differences between individuals to identify or exclude. A good answer says that both are recognition-and-comparison ideas, but in different systems and for different purposes. If you can say that, you have the cross-strand answer. If you only describe immunity and forensics separately, you have lost the connection, and the connection is what the question is after.

For a question that asks you to relate the population side of the topic, epidemiology and herd immunity, to the individual side, the answers to that are in the same note but the reasoning has to be moved between them. A good answer says that the individual side is about what happens to one organism or one person, while the population side is about patterns and spread and control, and that the population side depends on the individual side but is not the same as it. For herd immunity, it says that the protection of the population depends on coverage, not on every individual being immune. For epidemiology, it says that the study is about patterns and causes and control, not just about one case. If you can say that, you have the cross-strand answer that moves between the individual and the population, and that is the kind of answer the higher marks are after. If you only stay at one level, you lose the marks on the question that asks you to move between them.

The final cross-strand answer to practise is the one that brings together the three strands in a single example, because that is the question that tests the most integrated understanding. Suppose the question is about a disease outbreak and asks you about the pathogen, the immune response and the forensic or epidemiological use of evidence. A good answer says that the pathogen is a microorganism that can cause disease, that the body responds with barriers, phagocytosis and the specific antibody and memory response, and that if the outbreak is being investigated, biological evidence such as DNA may be used to identify the source or the spread, and that the evidence has to be collected and interpreted with care. If you can say that in one connected answer, you have the topic as a connected whole, and you have the kind of answer the most demanding questions are after. If you only give one strand, you have lost the others, and the others are part of the mark. The note is long enough to give you all three strands and the connections, and that is the use of the length: to make the most demanding questions answerable.

title: Exam technique: Angles and Polygons
content:
### What earns the marks
For angle-chasing, justify earns marks for each reason stated alongside the value: angles on a straight line, vertically opposite, alternate, corresponding, and the circle theorems by name. For cyclic quadrilaterals, quote earns the theorem (opposite angles sum to 180) before the equation. For polygons, the formula (n - 2) x 180 stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: using adjacent instead of opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral. Correction: mark the diagram first. Error: answering each interior angle when the sum is asked. Correction: only divide at the very end. Error: treating any triangle in a circle as right-angled. Correction: the right angle needs the diameter as hypotenuse.
### Worked example
The sum of the interior angles of an n-sided polygon is (n − 2) × 180°. For a regular octagon (n = 8), each interior angle is 6 × 180 ÷ 8 = 135°, so each exterior angle is 45°. The exterior angles of any polygon add up to 360°, which gives a quick check: 8 × 45 = 360.
### Check yourself
Find the interior angle of a regular hexagon. Use (6 − 2) × 180 ÷ 6 = 120°. Explain why the exterior angle is 60° and why this matches 360 ÷ 6.

title: Differentiation — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Differentiation answers one question: how fast is y changing with x at a given point? Most questions either ask for the gradient function or use it at a particular point.

The power rule

If y = axⁿ then dy/dx = naxⁿ⁻¹, for any rational n. A constant term differentiates to zero. Write roots and reciprocals as powers before you start: √x = x^(1/2) and 1/x² = x⁻².

Example: y = 4√x − 6/x². Rewriting gives y = 4x^(1/2) − 6x⁻², so dy/dx = 2x^(−1/2) + 12x⁻³ = 2/√x + 12/x³.

Expand before you differentiate

Differentiation works term by term, so multiply out any brackets first. Differentiating each factor separately does not give the derivative of the product.

Example: y = (x + 2)(x − 5) = x² − 3x − 10, so dy/dx = 2x − 3.

Tangents and normals

Substitute the x-value into the original curve to get y, and into dy/dx to get the gradient. The tangent uses that gradient; the normal uses the negative reciprocal. Write both in the form y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) and then simplify.

Example: y = x³ − 2x at x = −1. Then y = 1 and dy/dx = 3x² − 2 = 1. The tangent is y = x + 2. The normal has gradient −1 and is y = −x, which also passes through (−1, 1).

Stationary points and their nature

Stationary points are where dy/dx = 0. Solve that equation for x, then use the second derivative: d²y/dx² > 0 gives a minimum and d²y/dx² < 0 gives a maximum. If the second derivative is zero at the point, check the sign of dy/dx on either side of it instead.

Example: y = x³ − 6x² + 9x. Then dy/dx = 3(x − 1)(x − 3), so the stationary points are at x = 1 and x = 3. Since d²y/dx² = 6x − 12, the point at x = 1 is a maximum at (1, 4), and the point at x = 3 is a minimum at (3, 0).

Increasing and decreasing

The curve increases where dy/dx > 0 and decreases where dy/dx < 0. For the example above, dy/dx is positive for x < 1 and for x > 3, and negative between them.

Common errors

  • Differentiating a product factor by factor instead of expanding it first.
  • Forgetting to subtract one from the power, or differentiating a constant to anything other than zero.
  • Giving the tangent without its point, or using the tangent's gradient for the normal.
  • Giving only the x-value of a stationary point instead of its coordinates (x, y).

title: Algebra — Equations — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Equations

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): linear equations, simultaneous equations, quadratic formula, completing the square, forming equations from words.

1. Linear equations

3(x − 2) = x + 4 → 3x − 6 = x + 4 → 2x = 10 → x = 5. With fractions, multiply through by the LCD first.

2. Forming equations

Translate shapes/situations: "rectangle length 3 cm more than width, perimeter 34" → 2w + 2(w + 3) = 34 → w = 7.

3. Simultaneous equations

  • Elimination: 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2 → add → 3x = 9 → x = 3, y = 1.
  • Substitution for linear–quadratic: substitute y = 2x into x² + y² = 20 → 5x² = 20 → x = ±2.

4. Quadratics by formula

x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a.

Example: 2x² − 4x − 3 = 0 → x = (4 ± √(16 + 24))/4 = 2.58 or −0.58 (2 d.p.).

5. Completing the square

x² + bx + c = (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c. x² − 6x + 5 = (x − 3)² − 4 → minimum at (3, −4). Use for turning points and for solving when factorising fails.

Exam tips: substitute answers back to verify; in word problems define the unknown clearly ("let w = width in cm"); give quadratic solutions to the accuracy demanded.

Solving linear equations step by step

Collect the unknown on one side and the numbers on the other, undoing operations in the reverse order to BODMAS. Whatever you do to one side you must do to the other. When brackets are present, expand first, then collect like terms. Fractions are cleared by multiplying every term by the lowest common denominator.

Simultaneous equations

Two linear equations in x and y can be solved by elimination (make the coefficient of one unknown equal and opposite, then add or subtract) or by substitution (rearrange one equation for one unknown and put it into the other). Check the answer in both original equations. Examiners award method marks for a correct, clearly shown elimination even when arithmetic slips later.

Rearranging formulae

Treat the subject letter as the unknown and apply inverse operations. Where the subject appears twice, gather every term containing it, factorise, then divide. Square roots or squares are undone with a square and a root, applied to both sides.

Worked example: equations with fractions

Solve 3(x − 2)/4 = x + 1. Multiply both sides by 4 to clear the denominator: 3(x − 2) = 4(x + 1), so 3x − 6 = 4x + 4, which gives −10 = x. Check by substitution: left side 3(−12)/4 = −9 and right side −10 + 1 = −9. Both agree, so x = −10.

Examiners award the method mark for clearing the fraction correctly, so write the line where every term is multiplied by the denominator before you expand.

Unknowns on both sides

Solve 5x + 3 = 2x − 9. Subtract 2x from both sides to get 3x + 3 = −9, then subtract 3 to get 3x = −12, so x = −4. Keeping the unknowns on the side where the coefficient stays positive avoids negative-sign slips.

Quadratics and the discriminant

For ax² + bx + c = 0, the discriminant b² − 4ac decides how many real roots there are. If it is positive there are two distinct real roots, if it is zero there is one repeated root, and if it is negative there are no real roots.

Example: 2x² + 3x − 5 = 0 has discriminant 9 + 40 = 49. The formula gives x = (−3 ± 7)/4, so x = 1 or x = −2.5. Check x = 1: 2 + 3 − 5 = 0.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Dividing both sides of an equation by a variable, which can lose a solution (for example x² = 4x has solutions 0 and 4).
  • Applying the quadratic formula with the wrong sign on b, for example writing −3 when b = +3 in the formula.
  • Stopping at a rearranged formula without isolating the subject, or leaving a square root unsimplified when the question asks for an exact answer.

title: Exam technique: Simplifying and Expanding
content:
### What earns the marks
For expansion, calculate earns a mark for every correct pair of products shown before collecting terms. For factorisation, the HCF stated earns the first mark and the fully divided bracket earns the second: partial factorisation scores at most half. For algebraic fractions, factorise first earns the method mark even when cancellation follows.
### Traps
Error: (x + 5)(x - 2) = x squared + 10. Correction: four products, then collect. Error: 3(2x squared - 3x) called fully factorised. Correction: extract x as well. Error: cancelling terms instead of factors in a fraction. Correction: factorise numerator and denominator first.
### Worked example
Expand (2x − 3)(x + 4). The four products are 2x², 8x, −3x and −12. Collecting terms gives 2x² + 5x − 12. For factorisation, 6x² − 9x has HCF 3x, so 6x² − 9x = 3x(2x − 3). Check by expanding the answer back to the original expression.
### Check yourself
Factorise 4x² − 9 completely. It is a difference of two squares: (2x − 3)(2x + 3). Mark schemes often award the first mark for recognising the form, so state it before writing the brackets.

title: Redox Equilibria Revision Notes A2 Chemistry
content:
Redox Equilibria A2 Level Chemistry

This revision note covers Edexcel International A Level Chemistry Topic 16, exploring redox equilibria, standard electrode potentials, electrochemical cells, thermodynamics of redox reactions, cell diagrams, advanced redox titrations, uncertainty analysis, and fuel cells.

Oxidation and Reduction in s-, p- and d-Block Elements

Redox processes involve electron transfer and shifts in oxidation numbers, applying seamlessly across s-, p-, and d-block elements.

  • Oxidation is defined as loss of electrons and an increase in oxidation state. Reduction is gain of electrons and a decrease in oxidation state.
  • The reducing agent is oxidised by losing electrons, whereas the oxidising agent is reduced by gaining electrons.
  • These rules apply whether dealing with simple s-block metal ions, p-block non-metals, or complex d-block transition metal ions showing multiple stable oxidation states.

Standard Electrode Potentials and the Standard Hydrogen Electrode

Standard electrode potentials provide a quantitative measure of a species' tendency to be reduced.

  • Standard electrode potentials, E-zero, are measured strictly at 298 K temperature, 100 kPa pressure of gases, and 1.00 mol dm-3 concentration of ions.
  • The standard hydrogen electrode serves as the universal reference electrode with an E-zero value defined as exactly 0.00 V.
  • A reference electrode is necessary because absolute electrode potentials cannot be measured in isolation; only potential differences can be determined.
  • The standard hydrogen electrode uses platinum foil coated in platinum black, immersed in 1.00 mol dm-3 hydrogen ions, with hydrogen gas bubbled at 100 kPa and 298 K.

Measuring Electrode Potentials and Electrochemical Cells

Different half-cell assemblies are required depending on the physical states of the species involved.

  • For metals or non-metals in contact with their aqueous ions, a metal rod is dipped into a 1.00 mol dm-3 solution of its ions, or an inert platinum electrode is used for non-metals like chlorine gas bubbling over chloride ions.
  • For systems involving ions of the same element with different oxidation numbers, an inert platinum electrode is immersed in a solution containing both species at 1.00 mol dm-3 concentration.
  • CORE PRACTICAL 12 involves investigating electrochemical cells by measuring cell potentials for various metal-metal ion combinations and redox systems.

Cell Diagrams and Standard Cell EMF Calculations

Electrochemical cells can be represented concisely using conventional notation and evaluated mathematically.

  • Cell diagrams use a single vertical line to represent a phase boundary and a double vertical line to represent a salt bridge.
  • Oxidised forms are written closer to the salt bridge in conventional half-cell representations, with the more negative half-cell conventionally written on the left.
  • Calculate standard cell emf, E-zero-cell, using the formula: E-zero-cell = E-zero(reduction) - E-zero(oxidation).

Thermodynamic Feasibility, Entropy, and Equilibrium Constants

Standard electrode potentials connect directly to thermodynamic feasibility, entropy changes, and equilibrium constants.

  • Standard electrode potentials are also known as standard reduction potentials and are listed in an electrochemical series.
  • A positive E-zero-cell value indicates that the forward reaction is thermodynamically feasible under standard conditions.
  • E-zero-cell is directly proportional to the total entropy change, delta-S-total, and to ln K for a reaction, meaning larger positive E-zero values correspond to larger equilibrium constants and greater spontaneity.
  • Standard electrode potentials can predict the thermodynamic feasibility of disproportionation reactions, where a species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced.

Limitations of Standard Electrode Potentials

Thermodynamic predictions do not always match real-world outcomes due to kinetic and condition factors.

  • Predictions made using standard electrode potentials have limitations due to the kinetic stability of systems; a reaction may be thermodynamically feasible with a positive E-zero-cell, but have an activation energy so high that the reaction rate is negligibly slow.
  • Departures from standard conditions, such as non-standard concentrations or temperatures, alter actual electrode potentials according to the Nernst equation, potentially reversing feasibility.

Redox Titrations and Uncertainty Analysis

Volumetric analysis using redox titrations allows accurate determination of concentrations in structured and unstructured problems.

  • CORE PRACTICALS 13a and 13b involve carrying out redox titrations with iron(II) ions and potassium manganate(VII), and with sodium thiosulfate and iodine.
  • Manganate(VII) titrations are self-indicating, turning from purple to colourless at the end point when excess MnO4- ions react to form colourless Mn2+ ions.
  • Iodine-thiosulfate titrations use starch indicator, which forms a deep blue-black complex with iodine and turns colourless at the end point when all iodine is consumed.
  • Discussing the uncertainty of measurements requires evaluating percentage errors of apparatus like burettes and volumetric flasks, and their implications for the validity of final results.

Fuel Cells

Fuel cells convert chemical energy directly into electrical energy through redox reactions.

  • Fuel cells use the energy released on the reaction of a fuel with oxygen to generate a voltage, utilising hydrogen-rich fuels like hydrogen and methanol.
  • In an acidic electrolyte hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, hydrogen is oxidised at the anode: H2 yields 2H+ + 2e-, and oxygen is reduced at the cathode: O2 + 4H+ + 4e- yields 2H2O.
  • In an alkaline electrolyte hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, hydrogen reacts at the anode: H2 + 2OH- yields 2H2H2O + 2e-, and oxygen reacts at the cathode: O2 + 2H2O + 4e- yields 4OH-.

Typical Mistakes

  • Mistake: Confusing the left and right sides of a cell diagram. Correction: Remember reduction always occurs at the right-hand electrode and oxidation at the left-hand electrode in conventional notation.
  • Mistake: Omitting the inert platinum electrode in half-cell descriptions containing only aqueous ions. Correction: Always include platinum in phase boundaries if no other solid conductor is present.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that E-zero-cell values are independent of the stoichiometry multipliers used to balance half-equations. Correction: Never multiply E-zero values by balancing coefficients when calculating E-zero-cell.
  • Mistake: Assuming a reaction with a positive E-zero-cell will occur rapidly at room temperature. Correction: Always consider kinetic stability; a positive E-zero only proves thermodynamic feasibility, not reaction rate.

Exam-Style Questions

  1. Question: State the standard conditions required for measuring standard electrode potentials. Answer: 298 K temperature, 100 kPa pressure of gases, and 1.00 mol dm-3 concentration of ions.
  2. Question: Write the conventional cell diagram for a cell formed by Zn(s) / Zn2+(aq) and Cu2+(aq) / Cu(s). Answer: Zn(s) | Zn2+(aq, 1.00 mol dm-3) || Cu2+(aq, 1.00 mol dm-3) | Cu(s).
  3. Question: Calculate the E-zero-cell for zinc and copper given E-zero(Zn2+/Zn) = −0.76 V and E-zero(Cu2+/Cu) = +0.34 V. Answer: E-zero-cell = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V.
  4. Question: State the colour change at the end point in a titration of potassium manganate(VII) with iron(II) ions. Answer: From colourless or very pale pink to permanent pale pink.
  5. Question: Write the anode half-equation for an alkaline hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell. Answer: H2 + 2OH- yields 2H2O + 2e-.

Use these notes alongside active practice of past paper calculation questions, ensuring all standard conditions and half-equation balancing steps are memorised. Revise transition metal chemistry next.

title: Exponentials and Logarithms — Study Notes
content:
Exponentials and logarithms

The exponential function e^x and the natural logarithm ln x are inverse functions. They model growth and decay (populations, radioactive decay, cooling) and appear in almost every AS/A2 paper.

The functions

  • e is Euler's number, e = 2.71828... to 4 s.f.
  • y = e^x is always positive, passes through (0, 1), and grows rapidly for large x.
  • y = ln x is defined for x > 0, passes through (1, 0), and is the inverse of e^x: ln(e^x) = x and e^(ln x) = x.
  • The graph of ln x is the reflection of e^x in the line y = x.

Logarithm laws

  • ln(ab) = ln a + ln b
  • ln(a/b) = ln a - ln b
  • ln(a^n) = n ln a
  • The same laws hold for logs to any base; log base a of x = ln x / ln a.

Solving equations

  • To solve e^(kx + c) = d: take ln of both sides, kx + c = ln d, then rearrange.
  • To solve ln(ax + b) = c: exponentiate, ax + b = e^c.
  • To solve a^x = b where a is not e: take logs, x = ln b / ln a.

Modelling

  • Growth/decay: N = N0 e^(kt), k > 0 for growth, k < 0 for decay.
  • Half-life: the time for a quantity to halve, found from ln(0.5) = k t_half.
  • Compound interest and continuously compounded growth use the same form.

Key results

  • The derivative of e^x is e^x; the derivative of ln x is 1/x (know these for later calculus).
  • e^0 = 1, ln 1 = 0, ln e = 1.
  • The curve y = e^x has gradient 1 at x = 0.

title: Electricity: D.C. Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity: D.C. circuits

Current and charge

  • Current I = charge Q ÷ time t, so Q = It. Unit: ampere (A), where 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹.
  • Electron drift velocity is very small, but the electric field propagates through the circuit almost at the speed of light.

Potential difference and power

  • Potential difference V = energy transferred ÷ charge. Unit: volt (V), where 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.
  • Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Unit: watt (W).

Resistance and resistivity

R = V/I (Ohm's law for an ohmic conductor, at constant temperature). For a wire of length L and cross-sectional area A, R = ρL/A, where ρ is the resistivity in Ω m. Resistance rises with length and falls with area.

Practical circuits

An ammeter is connected in series with the component it measures. A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance; an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.

Kirchhoff's laws

  • First law: at a junction, the total current entering equals the total current leaving (conservation of charge).
  • Second law: around any closed loop, the sum of the emfs equals the sum of the potential differences (conservation of energy).

Potential dividers

For two resistors R1 and R2 in series across a supply V, the potential difference across R2 is V × R2/(R1 + R2).

Worked example: a 100 Ω and a 300 Ω resistor are in series across 12 V. The current is 12/400 = 0.030 A, and the voltage across the 300 Ω resistor is 0.030 × 300 = 9.0 V.

Exam tips: draw the meter in the correct place, in series or in parallel. Apply Kirchhoff's first law to currents and the second law to loops, with consistent signs. Check that units are converted (e.g. mm² to m²) before using ρL/A.

title: Exam technique: Sine and Cosine Rules
content:
### What earns the marks
For the sine rule, the matched pairs written (b / sin 65 = 7 / sin 40) earn the method mark. For the cosine rule, the full substitution with cos evaluated earns the mark: write a squared = 25 + 64 - 2 x 5 x 8 x 0.5. For the largest angle, identifying the longest side first earns credit. For area, half a b sin C quoted earns the mark on its own.
### Traps
Error: sides paired with wrong angles in the sine rule. Correction: each side faces its angle. Error: 49 given as side a. Correction: root the cosine-rule result. Error: calculator-only acute angle for an obtuse ambiguous case. Correction: subtract from 180 by hand. Error: half a b without sine for a non-right triangle. Correction: area needs the sine factor unless the angle is 90 degrees.
### Worked example
Two sides are 7 cm and 9 cm, with an included angle of 40 degrees. The cosine rule gives x^2 = 7^2 + 9^2 - 2 x 7 x 9 x cos 40 = 130 - 126 x 0.766 = 33.5, so x is about 5.79 cm. Use the cosine rule when you have two sides and the angle between them.
### Check yourself
A right-angled triangle has legs 6 and 8. Compute the area as one half of 6 x 8 x sin 90 degrees, and the hypotenuse with the cosine rule. The area is 24, and the hypotenuse is sqrt(36 + 64) = 10, because cos 90 degrees is zero.

title: Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics Revision Notes A2 Biology
content:
Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics A2 Level Biology

This topic belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Level Biology specification WBI14, covering the growth and control of microorganisms, the immune response against pathogens, infection mechanisms, forensic DNA profiling techniques, and the estimation of time of death in forensic science.

Culturing and Measuring Microorganisms

Microorganisms require precise aseptic techniques to prevent contamination by unwanted microbes and to protect laboratory personnel from potential pathogens. Equipment must be sterilized using an autoclave, inoculating loops passed through a blue Bunsen flame until red hot, and petri dish lids lifted minimally. Growth can be quantified through various direct and indirect methods.

  • 6.1 principles and techniques involved in culturing microorganisms: use sterile nutrient broth or agar plates, incubate at or below 30 °C in school laboratories to prevent growth of human pathogens, and seal petri dishes loosely with adhesive tape to allow oxygen entry and prevent anaerobic conditions that favour harmful pathogens.
  • 6.2 methods of measuring microbial growth: direct cell counts using a haemocytometer with trypan blue to stain dead cells; serial dilution plating to count viable colonies expressed as colony-forming units per cubic centimetre; dry mass measurement following centrifugation and drying; and optical methods using a colorimeter or spectrophotometer to measure turbidity by recording absorbance or percentage transmission.
  • 6.3 phases of a bacterial growth curve: lag phase where cells adjust to the new environment and synthesize necessary enzymes with little population increase; exponential or log phase where cells divide at a constant maximum rate; stationary phase where nutrient depletion and toxic waste accumulation balance the rate of cell division and death; and death phase where cell death exceeds division.
  • 6.3 exponential growth rate constant formula: k = (log10(Nt) − log10(N0)) / (0.301 × t), where Nt is the number of bacteria at time t, N0 is the initial number of bacteria, and t is time.
  • 6.4 Core Practical 13 investigating the rate of growth of microorganisms in a liquid culture: use a spectrophotometer to record absorbance of a yeast or bacterial broth over time at regular intervals, maintaining constant temperature using a water bath and sterile controls, ensuring ethical handling and safe disposal of cultures.

Structure of Pathogens and Infection Mechanisms

Pathogens include both cellular bacteria and non-cellular viruses, each displaying distinct structural features that dictate their interaction with host cells and susceptibility to treatments.

  • 6.5 (i) bacterial structure: single-celled prokaryotes possessing 70S ribosomes, peptidoglycan cell walls, circular DNA, plasmids, and sometimes a capsule or flagella.
  • 6.5 (i) viral structure: acellular entities comprising genetic material enclosed within a protein coat called a capsid, surrounded in some viruses by a membrane envelope derived from host cell membranes. Examples include Ebola virus (filovirus with single-stranded RNA and an envelope), tobacco mosaic virus (rod-shaped helical capsid containing single-stranded RNA without an envelope), human immunodeficiency virus (retrovirus with RNA, capsid, and envelope), and lambda phage (dsDNA virus infecting bacteria with an isometric head and a contractile tail).
  • 6.5 (ii) lytic and latency: lytic cycle involves viral genetic material taking over host machinery to produce new virions, causing host cell lysis and death; latency (lysogeny) involves viral DNA integrating into the host genome as a provirus or prophage, remaining dormant and replicating alongside host DNA without causing immediate symptoms.
  • 6.6 Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection: bacteria are inhaled into the lungs, where they are engulfed by macrophages but can inhibit phagosome-lysosome fusion, surviving and multiplying inside macrophages to form tubercles, causing chronic coughing, tissue destruction, and eventual systemic spread.
  • 6.6 HIV infection: glycoprotein gp120 on the viral envelope binds specifically to CD4 receptors on T helper cells, allowing viral fusion and entry. The viral RNA uses reverse transcriptase to synthesize double-stranded DNA, which integrates into the host genome via integrase, eventually destroying T helper cells and leading to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.

The Body's Defences and Immunity

The human body employs physical, chemical, and biological barriers alongside multi-tiered immune responses to prevent and combat infection.

  • 6.7 (i) major entry routes for pathogens: gas exchange system, digestive system, reproductive system, and breaks in the skin.
  • 6.7 (ii) protective barriers: keratinized skin forming a tough physical barrier; stomach acid (hydrochloric acid at low pH) denaturing proteins and killing ingested pathogens; gut and skin flora competing with pathogenic microorganisms for resources and space while producing antagonistic chemical substances.
  • 6.8 non-specific responses to infection: inflammation triggered by histamine release from mast cells, causing vasodilation and increased capillary permeability; lysozyme action in tears, saliva, and mucus hydrolyzing peptidoglycan in bacterial cell walls; interferon produced by virus-infected cells to inhibit viral replication in neighbouring cells; and phagocytosis where neutrophils and macrophages engulf and digest foreign particles.
  • 6.9 roles of antigens and antibodies: antigens are molecules that trigger an immune response; antibodies are Y-shaped glycoproteins produced by plasma cells that bind specifically to antigens, promoting agglutination, neutralisation, and opsonisation. Macrophages act as antigen-presenting cells by displaying digested pathogen antigens on their surface using MHC proteins.
  • 6.10 roles of B and T cells: B effector cells differentiate into plasma cells to secrete antibodies, while B memory cells remain long-term for secondary responses; T helper cells release cytokines to activate B cells and killer T cells; T killer (cytotoxic) cells destroy infected host cells by releasing perforin; T memory cells provide long-term immunological memory.
  • 6.11 types of immunity: natural active immunity acquired via infection and primary immune response; natural passive immunity acquired via antibodies crossing the placenta or through breast milk; artificial active immunity acquired via vaccination containing antigens; artificial passive immunity acquired via injection of exogenous antibodies such as antitoxins.
  • 6.12 evolutionary race and evasion mechanisms: pathogens and hosts engage in co-evolutionary arms races; pathogens evade immune responses through antigenic variation (changing surface antigens such as in influenza and HIV), latency (hiding within host cells), and suppression of the host immune system.

Antibiotics and Clinical Practice

Antimicrobial substances are crucial for treating bacterial infections, though misuse has led to widespread resistance and clinical challenges.

  • 6.13 bacteriostatic vs bactericidal antibiotics: bacteriostatic antibiotics inhibit the growth and reproduction of bacteria without killing them, allowing the host immune system to clear the infection; bactericidal antibiotics kill bacteria outright by disrupting vital processes such as cell wall synthesis.
  • 6.14 Core Practical 14 investigate the effect of different antibiotics on bacteria: inoculate an agar plate with a bacterial lawn, place antibiotic-impregnated paper discs on the surface, incubate at 25 °C to 30 °C, and measure the diameter of the clear inhibition zones to calculate area and compare antibiotic effectiveness.
  • 6.15 hospital-acquired infections and prescribing codes: nosocomial infections such as MRSA spread in clinical settings due to vulnerable patients and antibiotic overuse. Codes of practice include strict hand hygiene, thorough cleaning of wards, isolation of infected patients, restricting broad-spectrum antibiotic prescriptions, and completing full courses of prescribed antibiotics to prevent selection for resistant strains.
  • 6.16 microbial decomposition and carbon recycling: saprobiotic microorganisms (bacteria and fungi) secrete extracellular enzymes onto dead organic matter, absorbing soluble products and releasing carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere via respiration, thereby maintaining the global carbon cycle.

Forensic Science and DNA Profiling

Forensic investigations rely on molecular biology techniques and physical evidence to determine genetic relationships and estimate the time of death.

  • 6.17 polymerase chain reaction (PCR): a method used to amplify small quantities of DNA in vitro using cycles of denaturation (94 °C to 95 °C to break hydrogen bonds), annealing (55 °C to 65 °C to allow primers to bind), and extension (72 °C for thermostable Taq DNA polymerase to synthesize new DNA strands).
  • 6.18 gel electrophoresis: a technique that separates DNA fragments based on size by applying an electric current through an agarose gel. Smaller fragments move faster and further toward the positive electrode than larger fragments.
  • 6.19 DNA profiling: analyzes short tandem repeats (STRs) at specific loci. The resulting banding patterns or electropherograms are compared for forensic identification of suspects, paternity testing, and determining genetic relationships in plants and animals.
  • 6.20 determining time of death: examining decomposition stages (fresh, bloated, active decay, advanced decay, skeletal remains); succession of insect species colonising the body (forensic entomology measuring blowfly life cycle stages); cooling rate of body temperature (algor mortis); and degree of muscle contraction (rigor mortis).

Worked Example: Exponential Growth Rate Constant Calculation

Calculate the exponential growth rate constant for a bacterial culture that grows from an initial concentration of 1.0 × 10^3 cells per cm³ to 5.0 × 10^6 cells per cm³ over a period of 12 hours.

  • Step 1: Identify the values: N0 = 1.0 × 10^3, Nt = 5.0 × 10^6, and t = 12 hours.
  • Step 2: Take the log10 of both population values: log10(N0) = 3.0 and log10(Nt) = 6.70.
  • Step 3: Substitute values into the formula k = (log10(Nt) − log10(N0)) / (0.301 × t).
  • Step 4: Calculate the numerator: 6.70 − 3.0 = 3.70.
  • Step 5: Calculate the denominator: 0.301 × 12 = 3.612.
  • Step 6: Divide numerator by denominator: k = 3.70 / 3.612 = 1.024 hours⁻¹.

Typical mistakes

  • Confusing bacteriostatic and bactericidal antibiotics: assuming all antibiotics kill bacteria directly, when bacteriostatic drugs merely halt division while the immune system does the destruction.
  • Misunderstanding viral replication: stating that antibiotics kill viruses, forgetting that viruses lack cellular structures and metabolic pathways targeted by antibiotics.
  • Describing antibiotic resistance incorrectly: writing that individual bacteria mutate in response to antibiotics, rather than recognizing that pre-existing random mutations provide resistance and selection pressure increases the frequency of the resistance allele in the population.
  • Confusing PCR temperatures: stating that Taq polymerase is denatured at 95 °C, when in fact it is heat-stable and only human DNA polymerase would denature at this temperature.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection leads to a progressive decline in the immune system. Answer: HIV infects T helper cells by binding gp120 to CD4 receptors. The virus replicates and destroys these cells, reducing cytokine production, which prevents the activation of B cells and cytotoxic T cells, leading to immunodeficiency (AIDS).
  2. Describe how gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments during DNA profiling. Answer: DNA fragments are loaded into wells in an agarose gel and subjected to an electric current. Because DNA is negatively charged due to phosphate groups, fragments move toward the positive anode. Smaller fragments travel faster and further through the gel mesh than larger fragments.
  3. Explain how natural selection drives the evolution of antibiotic-resistant bacterial populations. Answer: Within a bacterial population, random mutation produces an allele for antibiotic resistance. When the antibiotic is applied, non-resistant bacteria are killed, creating a selection pressure. Resistant bacteria survive, reproduce, and pass on the resistance allele, increasing its frequency in future generations.
  4. State the role of reverse transcriptase in the life cycle of HIV. Answer: Reverse transcriptase is a viral enzyme that catalyzes the transcription of single-stranded viral RNA into double-stranded DNA inside the host cell cytoplasm prior to viral integration.
  5. Outline the stages of a standard bacterial growth curve in a closed liquid culture. Answer: Lag phase (slow growth as cells adjust and synthesize enzymes); exponential phase (rapid cell division at a maximum rate); stationary phase (cell death rate equals division rate due to nutrient depletion and toxin accumulation); death phase (cell death exceeds division as conditions become lethal).

Use these revision notes alongside past paper practice questions. Focus your next revision sessions on mastering core practical calculations, tracing immunological pathways step by step, and applying forensic succession timelines accurately.

title: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation — Study Notes
content:
Measures of Variation

Range and Quartiles

The range is max − min — quick but destroyed by a single outlier. Quartiles split ordered data into quarters: Q₁ at position (n + 1)/4, Q₃ at 3(n + 1)/4 (raw data). The interquartile range, IQR = Q₃ − Q₁, is the spread of the middle 50% and resists outliers. Outliers are commonly flagged as values beyond Q₁ − 1.5·IQR or Q₃ + 1.5·IQR.

Variance and Standard Deviation

For raw data:

  • variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/n (the definitional form)
  • equivalently s² = Σx²/n − x̄² (the computational form)
  • standard deviation s = √(variance)

The standard deviation shares the units of the data; the variance does not. For frequency tables use Σf(x − x̄)²/Σf, or Σfx²/Σf − x̄².

Grouped Data

Use class midpoints as x. The result is an estimate — grouping discards within-class detail.

Combining and Scaling Datasets

Multiplying every value by b multiplies s by |b| and the variance by b². Adding a constant changes nothing in the spread. Two merged datasets: compute combined Σx and Σx² from each part, then apply the computational formula.

Example: data 1, 3, 4, 5, 7: mean 4, Σx² = 100, so variance = 100/5 − 16 = 4 and s = 2.

Exam tips: state units for s. When comparing consistency, the dataset with the smaller standard deviation (relative to its mean) is the more consistent. Always give the comparison sentence, not just the two numbers.

Exam method: variance and standard deviation

The variance is the mean of the squared deviations, or equivalently Var(x) = Σx²/n − x̄². The standard deviation is its square root, and it is in the same units as the data. Using the second form is quicker when the mean is already known.

Adding a constant to every value shifts the mean by that constant but leaves the standard deviation unchanged. Multiplying every value by a constant k multiplies the standard deviation by |k| and the variance by k². Use these rules to avoid recalculating from scratch.

For grouped data, use the class midpoints and the frequencies. The variance is Σfx²/Σf − x̄², with x̄ = Σfx/Σf.

The standard deviation is a measure of spread. Compare two data sets by stating which has the larger spread and linking that to the context of the data.

Exam cue: Show the sum of the values and the sum of squares before dividing, because the method marks depend on those totals.

Worked example: standard deviation from raw data

For the data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 there are n = 8 values with mean 5. The sum of the squares is 4 + 16 + 16 + 16 + 25 + 25 + 49 + 81 = 232. The variance is Σx²/n − (x̄)² = 232/8 − 25 = 29 − 25 = 4, and the standard deviation is √4 = 2. Using the formula with the sum of squared deviations gives the same answer and is a useful check on your working.

Exam method: outliers using the interquartile range

The interquartile range is Q3 − Q1. Under the usual rule, a value is an outlier if it lies below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. Use the definition given in the question if one is stated, and show the two boundary values in your working. Writing a conclusion in context, such as "the value 40 is an outlier for these hours", gains the communication mark.

title: Quantum Physics — Study Notes
content:
Quantum Physics

Photons and photon energy

Electromagnetic radiation travels as photons, each with energy E = hf, where h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s is the Planck constant. Since c = fλ, the energy is also E = hc/λ. Shorter wavelength means higher energy.

Example: a photon of wavelength 500 nm has E = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.0 × 10⁸)/(5.0 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, or about 2.5 eV.

The photoelectric effect

When light shines on a metal surface, electrons are emitted only if the frequency of the light is at or above the threshold frequency f₀. Each photon transfers its whole energy to a single electron. Increasing the intensity increases the number of photons per second, so more electrons are emitted, but it does not increase the energy of each electron. The emission is instantaneous, with no time delay.

Wave theory cannot explain the threshold frequency or the lack of a time delay. The photon model explains both.

Einstein's photoelectric equation

hf = φ + E_k(max), where φ is the work function of the metal, the minimum energy needed to free an electron. The threshold frequency is f₀ = φ/h. The stopping potential V_s satisfies eV_s = E_k(max).

Example: a work function of 2.0 eV gives f₀ = (2.0 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)/(6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) ≈ 4.8 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

Wave-particle duality

Particles also have wave properties. The de Broglie wavelength of a particle with momentum p is λ = h/p. Electrons diffract through crystal lattices, showing wave behaviour, while photons show particle behaviour in the photoelectric effect. Both are needed to describe the same entities.

Energy levels and line spectra

Electrons in an atom occupy discrete energy levels. When an electron falls from a higher level E₁ to a lower level E₂, it emits a single photon with hf = E₁ − E₂. Absorption happens when a photon with exactly this energy is taken in. Because only specific energies are allowed, the spectrum is a set of sharp lines rather than a continuous band.

Example: a transition from −3.4 eV to −13.6 eV releases 10.2 eV, a wavelength of about 122 nm.

Exam tips: convert eV to joules (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) before using E = hf. Say which quantity the intensity changes and which it does not. Quote hf = φ + E_k(max) in photoelectric questions.

Worked example: threshold frequency and stopping voltage

Zinc has a work function of 4.3 eV. Converted to joules, that is 6.9 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so the threshold frequency is f₀ = φ/h = 6.9 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ ≈ 1.04 × 10¹⁵ Hz. Light of frequency 1.5 × 10¹⁵ Hz gives photons of energy 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 1.5 × 10¹⁵ ≈ 9.9 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, or about 6.2 eV. The maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons is 6.2 − 4.3 ≈ 1.9 eV, so the stopping voltage is about 1.9 V. Quote values with their units, and keep eV and joules consistent within each step.

Exam method: photon energy and wavelength

Combine E = hf with c = fλ to give E = hc/λ. Convert wavelengths to metres before you substitute into hc, because a wavelength given in nanometres must be multiplied by 10⁻⁹ first. A wrong power of ten is the most common way to lose the final mark, so estimate the answer before you calculate it precisely.
