title: Exam technique: Continuous Random Variables
content:
### What earns the marks
For pdf constants, total area equals 1 stated earns the method mark. For probabilities, the integral with correct limits earns each mark. For mean and variance, E(X) and E(X squared) - E(X) squared each earn credit stepwise.
### Traps
Error: point probabilities given positive values. Correction: points have zero area. Error: mean mistaken for median. Correction: solve the half-area equation for medians. Error: variance sign reversed. Correction: E(X squared) minus mean squared.
### Worked example
A pdf is f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area is 1, so the integral of kx from 0 to 2 gives 2k = 1 and k = 1/2. Then P(X > 1) is the integral of x/2 from 1 to 2, which is [x²/4] from 1 to 2 = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. The mean is the integral of x · x/2 from 0 to 2, which is 8/6 = 4/3.
### Check yourself
For the same pdf, state why P(X = 1) is zero before you calculate anything. A single point has zero width, so its area is zero.

### Worked example
A pdf is f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area is 1, so the integral of kx from 0 to 2 gives 2k = 1 and k = 1/2. Then P(X > 1) is the integral of x/2 from 1 to 2, which is [x²/4] from 1 to 2 = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. The mean is the integral of x · x/2 from 0 to 2, which is 8/6 = 4/3.

title: Exam technique: Sequences and Series
content:
### What earns the marks
For AP terms, a + (n-1)d with the brackets evaluated earns the mark; sums use n/2(2a + (n-1)d) quoted. For GP work, the ratio found by division earns one mark and the formula applied earns the next. For sum to infinity, the |r| < 1 check stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: n used instead of (n-1) in terms. Correction: first term needs zero gaps. Error: infinity sums with |r| >= 1. Correction: check convergence first. Error: differentiating S_n for the nth term. Correction: subtract S_{n-1}.
### Worked example
An arithmetic progression has a = 5 and d = 3. The 20th term is a + 19d = 5 + 57 = 62. The sum of the first 20 terms is S₂₀ = (20/2)(2a + 19d) = 10 × 67 = 670. A geometric progression with terms 2, 6, 18 has r = 3, so S₅ = 2(3⁵ − 1)/(3 − 1) = 242. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, so for r = 1/2 with a = 8 the sum is 8 / (1 − 1/2) = 16.
### Check yourself
State the nth term of a sequence from its sum. Find Sₙ, then subtract Sₙ₋₁. Do not differentiate Sₙ, because the sum is a discrete function.

### Worked example
An arithmetic progression has a = 5 and d = 3. The 20th term is a + 19d = 5 + 57 = 62. The sum of the first 20 terms is S₂₀ = (20/2)(2a + 19d) = 10 × 67 = 670. A geometric progression with terms 2, 6, 18 has r = 3, so S₅ = 2(3⁵ − 1)/(3 − 1) = 242. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, so for r = 1/2 with a = 8 the sum is 8 / (1 − 1/2) = 16.

title: Processor Fundamentals — Study Notes
content:
`# Processor Fundamentals

The FDE Cycle

  • Fetch: PC → MAR; read memory → MDR; instruction → CIR; PC increments
  • Decode: control unit interprets the opcode
  • Execute: ALU/registers act; results stored; PC may be overwritten (jumps)

Registers

RegisterRole
PCaddress of next instruction
MARaddress being accessed
MDRdata in transit
CIRcurrent instruction
ACCaccumulator results

Buses

  • Address bus: one-way, CPU → memory (width sets addressable space)
  • Data bus: two-way, carries instructions/data
  • Control bus: timing and command signals

Interrupts

Signals that pause the current program (I/O complete, timer, errors). The CPU saves context, runs the ISR, then resumes — enabling multitasking.

Assembly and Addressing

Immediate (#5), direct (address holds value), indirect (address points to address), indexed (base + offset — arrays), relative (PC + offset — jumps).

Example: LDD 100 loads from 100 (direct); LDI 100 loads from the address stored at 100 (indirect).

Exam tips: trace register contents step by step in trace tables; explain the stored program concept — instructions as data in memory.

The fetch-decode-execute cycle and registers

The program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction. During fetch, that address is copied to the memory address register (MAR), the instruction is read into the memory data register (MDR) and then into the current instruction register (CIR), and the PC is incremented. During decode the control unit works out what the instruction means, and during execute the ALU or another part of the CPU carries it out.

The accumulator is a register that holds the results of arithmetic and logic operations. Registers are very fast storage inside the CPU, and the CPU uses them so that it does not have to wait for main memory on every step.

Exam tip: learn the purpose of each register in one sentence. Examiners often ask which register holds the address, and which holds the instruction.

title: Exam technique: Dynamics
content:
### What earns the marks
For resultant force, subtract opposition before applying F = ma to earn both marks. For collisions, total momentum before equated to total after earns the method mark. For rebounds, the sign change included earns the second mark.
### Traps
Error: friction ignored in acceleration. Correction: use the resultant, not the push alone. Error: rebound treated as stopping. Correction: add the speeds with the sign flip. Error: kinetic energy claimed conserved generally. Correction: momentum always, kinetic only when elastic.
### Worked example
A car of mass 800 kg has a driving force of 2400 N and a resistance of 400 N. The resultant force is 2400 - 400 = 2000 N, so a = F/m = 2000 / 800 = 2.5 m/s^2. Subtract the opposing force before you divide by the mass.
### Check yourself
A 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg trolley, and they stick together. Total momentum before is 2 x 3 = 6 kg m/s, so the joint speed is 6 / 3 = 2 m/s. Show the momentum equation even when the speed looks obvious.

### Worked example
A car of mass 800 kg has a driving force of 2400 N and a resistance of 400 N. The resultant force is 2400 - 400 = 2000 N, so a = F/m = 2000 / 800 = 2.5 m/s^2. Subtract the opposing force before you divide by the mass.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Intermolecular Forces
content:
AS Level Chemistry: Intermolecular Forces

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 7 explains the forces that hold molecules to one another, as distinct from the covalent bonds inside them. These forces are far weaker than covalent bonds, yet they decide boiling temperature, volatility, solubility and the anomalous behaviour of water, and they are the reason a molecule with polar bonds is not necessarily a polar molecule. Examiners test the explanation rather than the label, so every answer should name the force, say what causes it, and relate it to the property asked about.

Three types of intermolecular force

All intermolecular forces are electrostatic: they arise from the attraction between regions of opposite charge. They differ in what creates those regions.

ForceOriginTypical strength
London forces (instantaneous dipole–induced dipole)Fluctuating electron density in one molecule induces a dipole in a neighbourVery weak, but increases with the number of electrons
Permanent dipole–permanent dipolePermanently polar bonds and an asymmetric shape leave one end of the molecule slightly positive and the other slightly negativeWeak, roughly 5–20 kJ mol⁻¹
Hydrogen bondingA hydrogen atom bonded to N, O or F is attracted to a lone pair on N, O or F in another moleculeStrongest of the three, up to about 40 kJ mol⁻¹

London forces

Electrons are in constant motion, so at any instant the electron distribution in a molecule may be uneven. That creates an instantaneous dipole, which in turn distorts the electron cloud of a neighbouring molecule and induces a dipole in it. The two dipoles then attract. The effect is present in every substance, including the noble gases and non-polar molecules such as methane, and it is the only intermolecular force in a non-polar substance.

The strength of London forces depends on how easily the electron cloud can be distorted, which is called polarisability. Two factors control it:

  • Number of electrons: more electrons means a larger, more polarisable cloud. Iodine (I₂) is a solid and chlorine (Cl₂) a gas at room temperature for this reason.
  • Surface area and shape: a long unbranched chain has more surface contact between neighbouring molecules than a compact branched isomer with the same formula, so it has stronger London forces.

London forces are also the reason why a noble gas such as argon can be liquefied at low temperature, even though its atoms have no permanent dipole and no bonds to break.

Permanent dipole–dipole interactions

A bond between atoms of different electronegativity is polar: the more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge, δ−, and the less electronegative atom carries δ+. If the molecule is not symmetrical, the individual bond dipoles do not cancel, and the molecule as a whole has a permanent dipole. Neighbouring molecules then line up with opposite ends together, and the attraction is a permanent dipole–permanent dipole interaction.

Hydrogen chloride, HCl, is polar and its molecules attract this way. Carbon dioxide has two polar C=O bonds, but the molecule is linear and symmetrical, so the dipoles cancel exactly and CO₂ has no permanent dipole; its molecules are held only by London forces. Tetrachloromethane, CCl₄, is also symmetrical and non-polar for the same reason, while trichloromethane, CHCl₃, is polar because the fourth substituent is hydrogen rather than chlorine and the symmetry is broken. Whether a molecule is polar therefore needs two checks: are the bonds polar, and is the shape symmetrical?

Hydrogen bonding

Hydrogen bonding is a particularly strong form of permanent dipole attraction. It occurs only when two conditions are satisfied:

  • A hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom, limited to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine.
  • A lone pair is available on an N, O or F atom in a neighbouring molecule, which the δ+ hydrogen can approach.

The result is a strong attraction between the δ+ hydrogen and the lone pair, often drawn as a dotted line: O–H···O. The bond is directional, which is why hydrogen bonding produces specific structures rather than a random arrangement.

Water, ammonia and hydrogen fluoride all hydrogen bond:

SubstanceHydrogen-bonding unitNumber of hydrogen bonds per molecule in the liquid
H₂OO–H···OTwo hydrogen atoms and two lone pairs allow an extensive network
NH₃N–H···NThree hydrogen atoms but only one lone pair, so fewer bonds than water
HFF–H···FOne hydrogen atom and three lone pairs; chains of HF molecules

Hydrogen bonding is not the same as a covalent bond to hydrogen. It is an intermolecular attraction, so it is broken when a substance melts or boils, while the O–H covalent bond stays intact. That distinction is worth stating explicitly in an answer.

The anomalous properties of water

Water's properties do not follow the pattern of similar molecules, and hydrogen bonding is the explanation.

High melting and boiling temperatures. Compared with hydrogen sulfide, H₂S, which has a similar formula, water boils about 160 °C higher. The molecules of H₂S are held only by London forces and weak dipole–dipole attractions, whereas each water molecule can hydrogen bond to several neighbours. Breaking those attractions needs far more energy, so the melting and boiling temperatures are unusually high, and water is a liquid at room temperature while H₂S is a gas.

Ice is less dense than liquid water. In ice, each water molecule hydrogen bonds to four neighbours in a regular tetrahedral arrangement, which holds the molecules further apart than in the liquid and leaves open hexagonal spaces. When ice melts, much of that open framework collapses and the molecules pack more closely, so liquid water is denser than ice. This is why ice floats, and why a lake freezes from the top, insulating the water beneath and allowing aquatic life to survive.

Hydrogen bonding also gives water a high surface tension, a high specific heat capacity and a high enthalpy of vaporisation, all of which follow from the energy needed to overcome the network of hydrogen bonds.

Predicting hydrogen bonding

To decide whether a molecule can hydrogen bond, look for an O–H, N–H or F–H group and for a lone pair on O, N or F. Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, can hydrogen bond because of its O–H group; ethanal, CH₃CHO, has a C=O bond with lone pairs but no hydrogen attached to an electronegative atom, so it cannot donate a hydrogen bond, although its oxygen can accept one. A molecule such as CH₃F has no H–F bond, so it does not hydrogen bond. Methanol and water mix in all proportions because both can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, whereas methane, with only C–H bonds, cannot.

Intermolecular forces and physical properties

Boiling temperature is a measure of the energy needed to separate molecules, so it reports the strength of the intermolecular forces, not the strength of the covalent bonds. Four trends are examined.

Boiling temperature of alkanes increases with chain length. Each additional CH₂ group adds electrons and surface area, so the London forces between the molecules become stronger and more energy is needed to separate them. Methane boils at −162 °C, ethane at −89 °C and decane at 174 °C.

Branching lowers the boiling temperature. Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane have the same molecular formula, but the branched molecule is more compact. Its molecules have less surface contact, so its London forces are weaker and it boils at 9.5 °C compared with 36 °C for pentane. The same reasoning explains why branched isomers have lower boiling temperatures throughout the alkanes.

Alcohols have higher boiling temperatures than alkanes of similar electron count. Ethanol (46 electrons) boils at 78 °C while propane (26 electrons) boils at −42 °C. The comparison is not quite like for like, but the key point is that ethanol molecules hydrogen bond through the O–H group, while propane molecules have only London forces. The hydrogen bonding more than compensates for the smaller number of electrons.

Boiling temperatures of the hydrogen halides are not a simple trend. HF is the highest because of hydrogen bonding. From HCl to HBr to HI, London forces grow as the number of electrons increases, so the boiling temperatures rise in that order: HCl −85 °C, HBr −67 °C, HI −35 °C. HF, at 20 °C, sits far above the smooth trend, and that outlier is the evidence for hydrogen bonding.

Choosing a solvent

Dissolving depends on the solute particles being separated and surrounded by solvent particles, so the solute–solvent attractions must be comparable to the forces they replace. In practice, like dissolves like.

  • Water dissolves ionic compounds because the polar water molecules attract the ions: the partially negative oxygen surrounds a cation and the partially positive hydrogens surround an anion. This is hydration, and it releases hydration enthalpy that helps to compensate for the lattice enthalpy that must be overcome.
  • Water dissolves simple alcohols such as methanol and ethanol, because the alcohol's O–H group can both donate a hydrogen bond to water and accept one from it. As the hydrocarbon chain grows, the non-polar part becomes a larger fraction of the molecule and solubility falls: ethanol mixes with water in all proportions, but hexan-1-ol is only slightly soluble.
  • Water is a poor solvent for halogenoalkanes and other polar organic molecules such as chloroethane. The molecule has a dipole, so it is attracted to water to some extent, but it has no O–H group and cannot hydrogen bond with water, and its hydrocarbon part cannot interact favourably with the water network. The solute–solvent attractions are too weak to overcome the hydrogen bonding between water molecules.
  • Non-aqueous solvents are used when the solute's intermolecular forces resemble the solvent's. Iodine, a non-polar molecule held by London forces, dissolves in hexane, which is also non-polar; bromine dissolves in cyclohexane for the same reason. Propanone is a useful intermediate case, dissolving both polar and many non-polar substances because it has a polar C=O group and a hydrocarbon part.

A good answer states the force between solvent molecules, the force between solute and solvent, and whether the second is strong enough to replace the first.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying a substance has hydrogen bonds when the hydrogen is bonded to carbon; only N–H, O–H and F–H count.
  • Describing hydrogen bonding as a covalent bond, or claiming that boiling water breaks O–H bonds.
  • Assuming that a molecule with polar bonds must be polar, without checking whether the shape cancels the dipoles.
  • Attributing the trend in alkane boiling temperatures to stronger covalent bonds rather than to stronger London forces.
  • Explaining branching by saying the molecule has fewer electrons; the number of electrons is the same, the surface contact is not.
  • Explaining the lower density of ice as an expansion on freezing without mentioning the open hydrogen-bonded lattice.
  • Describing London forces as "weak covalent forces" or as attractions between permanent dipoles.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why the boiling temperature of iodine is higher than that of chlorine. Answer: iodine has more electrons and a larger, more polarisable electron cloud, so the London forces between its molecules are stronger; more energy is needed to separate the molecules.
  2. Explain why 2-methylbutane has a lower boiling temperature than pentane. Answer: both have the molecular formula C5H12 and the same number of electrons. 2-methylbutane is more branched and more compact, so its molecules have less surface area in contact, the London forces between them are weaker, and less energy is needed to separate them.
  3. Explain, in terms of intermolecular forces, why ethanol is soluble in water but chloroethane is not. Answer: ethanol has an O–H group and can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds with water, so the solute–solvent attractions are strong enough to replace the hydrogen bonds between water molecules. Chloroethane is polar but has no O–H group, so it cannot hydrogen bond with water; its attractions to water are too weak to compensate for breaking the water–water hydrogen bonds.
  4. Explain why ice is less dense than liquid water. Answer: in ice each water molecule forms hydrogen bonds to four neighbours in a tetrahedral arrangement, producing an open lattice with spaces between the molecules. When ice melts the lattice collapses and the molecules pack more closely, so the liquid is denser.
  5. Identify the strongest intermolecular force in each of the following and justify your answer: (a) HCl, (b) CH₃OH, (c) CCl₄. Answer: (a) permanent dipole–permanent dipole, because the molecule is polar and has no O–H, N–H or F–H group; (b) hydrogen bonding, because of the O–H group; (c) London forces, because the molecule is symmetrical and the bond dipoles cancel, so it is non-polar.

When revising, practise the three-part answer: name the force, explain what causes it in these molecules, then link it to the property in the question. Move on to Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria next, where the same molecular picture explains why reactions need collisions with sufficient energy.

title: Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7 — Study Notes
content:
Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 8. Every statement 8.1 to 8.28 is covered below, with its code in the heading. Three ideas run through the whole topic: oxidation numbers track electron transfer, the Group 1 and 2 trends follow from atomic size and nuclear charge, and the Group 7 trends are the same ideas applied to halogens.

8.1 to 8.4: Oxidation numbers

  • Rules: an element is 0; a monatomic ion equals its charge; the sum of oxidation numbers equals the overall charge. Oxygen is usually −2 (but −1 in peroxides such as H₂O₂), hydrogen is usually +1 (but −1 in metal hydrides such as NaH), fluorine is always −1, Group 1 is +1 and Group 2 is +2.
  • 8.2: in MnO₄⁻, manganese must be +7, because four oxygens contribute −8 and the ion has a charge of −1.
  • 8.3: write the oxidation number as a Roman numeral in the name: manganese(VII), iron(III), copper(II).
  • 8.4: work backwards from oxidation numbers to a formula. Iron(III) sulfate is Fe₂(SO₄)₃, because Fe³⁺ must balance SO₄²⁻ in a 2:3 ratio.

8.5 to 8.9: Oxidation, reduction and disproportionation

  • 8.5: oxidation is loss of electrons, and it appears as an increase in oxidation number. Reduction is gain of electrons, a decrease in oxidation number. In 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl, sodium is oxidised (0 to +1) and chlorine is reduced (0 to −1). The same idea covers reactions of s-block metals and p-block non-metals.
  • 8.6: an oxidising agent gains electrons and is itself reduced. A reducing agent loses electrons and is itself oxidised.
  • 8.7: disproportionation is when one element in a single species is both oxidised and reduced at the same time. Chlorine in water is the standard example: Cl₂ → Cl⁻ (0 to −1) and HClO (0 to +1).
  • 8.8: oxidation numbers classify reactions. A reaction is redox if any oxidation number changes, and it is a disproportionation if the same element goes both up and down.
  • 8.9: metals form positive ions by losing electrons, so their oxidation number increases. Non-metals form negative ions by gaining electrons, so their oxidation number decreases.

8.10: Half-equations and full ionic equations

  • Write the oxidation and the reduction separately, balance atoms, then balance charge with electrons. For magnesium with chlorine: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ and Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻.
  • Add the half-equations so the electrons cancel, then cancel any spectator ions to give the full ionic equation.

8.11 to 8.13: Group 1 and Group 2 trends and reactions

  • 8.11: ionisation energy falls down Groups 1 and 2. The outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner shells, so less energy is needed to remove it.
  • 8.12: reactivity rises down Group 1 (Li to K) and Group 2 (Mg to Ba), for the same reason: the outer electron is removed more easily.
  • 8.13: Group 1 metals burn in oxygen and react vigorously with chlorine and water. Group 2 metals react with oxygen and chlorine to form oxides and chlorides. Magnesium reacts slowly with cold water and readily with steam, while calcium reacts steadily with cold water to form Ca(OH)₂ and hydrogen.

8.14: Reactions of oxides and hydroxides

  • Group 1 oxides dissolve in water to give alkaline hydroxides. Group 2 oxides react less vigorously, and CaO gives a limewater-type solution, Ca(OH)₂.
  • Oxides react with dilute acid to form a salt and water, for example MgO + 2H⁺ → Mg²⁺ + H₂O.
  • Hydroxides neutralise dilute acids: Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O.

8.15: Solubility trends of Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates

  • Hydroxides: solubility increases down the group. Magnesium hydroxide is almost insoluble, calcium hydroxide is slightly soluble, barium hydroxide is quite soluble.
  • Sulfates: solubility decreases down the group. Magnesium sulfate is soluble, barium sulfate is insoluble, which is why acidified barium chloride gives a white precipitate in the sulfate test.

8.16: Thermal stability of nitrates and carbonates

  • Stability increases down each group. A larger cation has a lower charge density, so it polarises the carbonate or nitrate ion less, and the anion breaks down less easily.
  • Carbonates: MCO₃ → MO + CO₂. Group 2 nitrates: 2M(NO₃)₂ → 2MO + 4NO₂ + O₂. Group 1 nitrates (other than lithium) give the nitrite and oxygen: 2NaNO₃ → 2NaNO₂ + O₂.
  • Lithium is the exception: its nitrate decomposes like a Group 2 nitrate, because the small Li⁺ ion polarises the nitrate strongly.

8.17: Flame colours

  • Heat excites outer electrons to higher energy levels. When they fall back, they emit light of a specific wavelength. Lithium is crimson, sodium is yellow-orange, potassium is lilac, calcium is brick red, strontium is red and barium is green.

8.18: Experiments on thermal decomposition

  • Heat a small sample of nitrate or carbonate in a test tube and test the gas. Brown NO₂ shows a nitrate; a glowing splint relit by O₂ shows oxygen. A carbonate gives CO₂, which turns limewater milky.
  • Compare the temperatures needed for decomposition down a group to show the trend in 8.16.

8.19: Identifying ions

  • Carbonate (CO₃²⁻) or hydrogencarbonate (HCO₃⁻): add dilute acid. CO₂ is released and turns limewater milky. Ionic equation: CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂.
  • Sulfate (SO₄²⁻): add acidified barium chloride. A white precipitate of BaSO₄ forms: Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄. The acid stops carbonate and sulfite interfering.
  • Ammonium (NH₄⁺): add sodium hydroxide and warm. Ammonia is released, turns damp red litmus blue, and gives white fumes with HCl.

8.20 to 8.23: Concentrations, titrations and uncertainty

  • 8.20: concentration in mol dm⁻³ = moles ÷ volume in dm³. To convert to g dm⁻³, multiply by the molar mass.
  • Indicators: methyl orange changes from red to yellow at about pH 3–4, suited to strong acid against weak base. Phenolphthalein changes from colourless to pink at about pH 8–10, suited to weak acid against strong base.
  • 8.21 (core practical 3): titrate hydrochloric acid against a standard alkali, record the titre and use the balanced equation to find the acid's concentration.
  • 8.22: reduce uncertainty by rinsing the pipette and burette, reading the meniscus at eye level, and repeating until two titres agree within 0.10 cm³. A burette reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³, so a titre has ±0.10 cm³. Calculate the percentage uncertainty as uncertainty ÷ reading × 100.
  • 8.23 (core practical 4): weigh a solid acid such as hydrated ethanedioic acid accurately, dissolve it, make it up to 250 cm³ in a volumetric flask, and use it as a standard solution to find the concentration of sodium hydroxide.

8.24: Trends in Group 7

  • Melting and boiling points rise down the group, because the molecules are larger and have stronger London forces. Fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid, iodine is a solid.
  • Electronegativity falls down the group, because the bonding pair sits further from the nucleus and is shielded more.
  • Reactivity (oxidising power) falls down the group, because the atoms are larger and gain an electron less readily.

8.25: Displacement reactions and colours

  • A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂, and Cl₂ or Br₂ + 2I⁻ → I₂ + halide.
  • Colours: in water, chlorine is pale green-yellow, bromine is orange and iodine is brown. In a non-polar organic solvent such as cyclohexane, bromine stays orange and iodine turns violet.

8.26: Reactions of the halogens, including disproportionation

  • (i) Halogens oxidise Group 1 and 2 metals to halides, for example 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.
  • (ii) Chlorine with water is a disproportionation: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO. The HClO is the basis of chlorine water treatment.
  • (iii) Chlorine with cold, dilute NaOH gives bleach: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O.
  • (iv) With hot concentrated alkali, chlorine disproportionates to chlorate: 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O.
  • (v) Bromine behaves in the same way with cold alkali. Use the oxidation number of each chlorine to check each product.

8.27: Reactions of halides and hydrogen halides

  • (i) Solid halides with concentrated H₂SO₄ show the reducing trend. NaCl gives HCl only. NaBr is oxidised further to Br₂ and SO₂. NaI is oxidised to I₂ and H₂S. The reducing ability is HI > HBr > HCl.
  • (ii) Silver nitrate with the halide ions in nitric acid: AgCl is white, AgBr is cream, AgI is yellow. AgCl dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia, AgBr only in concentrated ammonia, and AgI does not dissolve.
  • (iii) Hydrogen halides with ammonia give ammonium halides (NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl). With water they give acids.

8.28: Predicting fluorine and astatine

  • Fluorine is the most electronegative element and the strongest oxidising agent in the group. It reacts violently with water, displacing oxygen from it.
  • Astatine is at the bottom of the group, so by the trends it should be a dark, solid, less reactive halogen than iodine, with a lower electronegativity. It is radioactive, so its chemistry is hard to study directly, and predictions come from the trends.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Half-equations in acid, 8.10 applied: dichromate(VI) reduced by iron(II). Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O, and Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ (multiply by 6). Adding gives Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6Fe²⁺ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O. Check atoms, then charge: both sides total +24.
  • Titration calculation, 8.20 and 8.22 applied: 25.0 cm³ of an iron(II) solution needs 18.0 cm³ of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ K₂Cr₂O₇. Moles of dichromate = 0.0200 × 0.0180 = 3.60 × 10⁻⁴ mol. Each dichromate needs six Fe²⁺, so Fe²⁺ = 2.16 × 10⁻³ mol. Concentration = 2.16 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0864 mol dm⁻³. An A* answer shows the ratio from the balanced equation before any arithmetic.
  • Disproportionation, 8.7 and 8.26 applied: chlorine with cold dilute NaOH gives Cl⁻ (0 to −1, reduction) and ClO⁻ (0 to +1, oxidation) in one reaction. Name both oxidation numbers when explaining why a reaction is disproportionation.
  • Group 2 hydroxide solubility, 8.15 applied: solubility rises down the group because hydration enthalpy falls more steeply than lattice enthalpy as the cation grows. Lattice enthalpy depends on the ion sizes and charges; hydration enthalpy depends on how strongly water molecules bind the cation. Both are needed for full marks.
  • Thermal stability, 8.16 applied: a small, highly charged cation such as Mg²⁺ polarises a carbonate ion strongly, which weakens its C–O bonds, so MgCO₃ decomposes at a lower temperature than BaCO₃. Use the word polarisation, not just "smaller ions decompose more easily".
  • Halogen displacement and redox direction, 8.25 and 8.27 applied: chlorine oxidises bromide and iodide, bromine oxidises iodide, but iodine oxidises neither. Read the direction from the reducing trend: iodide is the strongest reducing agent among the halides, which is why concentrated sulfuric acid reduces HI to H₂S.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using the wrong oxidation number for oxygen in a peroxide or hydrogen in a metal hydride.
  • Confusing reducing ability with reactivity for the halogens: reactivity falls down Group 7, but the reducing ability of the halide ions rises.
  • Writing the test for sulfate without acid. Without acid, carbonate would also give a white precipitate.

title: Mensuration — Bearings and Loci — Study Notes
content:
Mensuration — Bearings and Loci

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): compass bearings, scale drawings, constructions (perpendicular/angle bisectors), loci regions.

1. Bearings

  • Measured clockwise from north; three figures: 065°, 128°, 300°.
  • Back bearing = front bearing ± 180°.
  • Draw a north line at both points; north lines are parallel, giving Z-angles.

Example: B is on bearing 070° from A → A is on bearing 250° from B.

2. Scale drawings

1 cm : 500 m style scales; measure, convert, and quote distances/bearings from your drawing to the accuracy allowed.

3. Constructions

  • Perpendicular bisector of a segment: equal arcs from both ends, join the crossings.
  • Angle bisector: equal arcs from the vertex arms.
  • 60° and 90° constructions with compasses; leave all arcs visible.

4. Loci

Fixed distance from a point = circle; from a line = parallel lines with rounded ends; equidistant from two points = perpendicular bisector; from two lines = angle bisector.

Example: a goat tied by a 5 m rope to a corner of a 4 m × 6 m shed: the reachable region is ¾ circle radius 5 m + two ¼ circles radius 1 m where the rope wraps.

Exam tips: state "clockwise from north" in bearing definitions; shade/label locus regions clearly; use a ruler for construction lines too.

title: Hypothesis Testing — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Hypothesis Testing

Mathematics — A2. The null hypothesis H₀ is the default claim (no change, p = p₀). The alternative H₁ is what a suspicious observation suggests (p > p₀, p < p₀, or p ≠ p₀). The significance level α is the probability of rejecting a true H₀ — the false-alarm rate, usually 5% or 1%.

Key areas to revise

  • The Framework
  • Test for a Binomial Proportion
  • One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed
  • Critical Regions
  • Conclusions in Context

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A test of a claimed mean has a null hypothesis H₀ and an alternative H₁. Choose a significance level such as 5%, calculate the test statistic and its p-value, then reject H₀ if p < α. A two-tailed test looks for a change in either direction, so the 5% is split between the two tails. ### Check yourself Define a Type I error in words. It is rejecting H₀ when H₀ is actually true. Explain why lowering the significance level reduces the chance of a Type I error but increases the chance of a Type II error.

title: Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression - AS Level Biology
content:
Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression - AS Level Biology

These revision notes cover Edexcel International AS Level Biology WBI11 Topic 2, exploring how DNA holds genetic information, how gene expression translates that code into functional proteins, and how cell membranes regulate the internal environment of cells through specialized transport mechanisms.

Cell Membranes and Structure

Cell membranes act as barriers and exchange surfaces, understood scientifically through the fluid mosaic model. This model interprets experimental data regarding lipid and protein mobility to explain membrane properties. The phospholipid bilayer features hydrophilic phosphate heads facing outwards and hydrophobic fatty acid tails facing inwards. Cholesterol molecules fit between phospholipids, regulating membrane fluidity across varying temperatures. Glycoproteins and glycolipids project from the external surface, serving as cell recognition sites and receptors.

  • Fluid mosaic model: interpretation of data showing phospholipid and protein lateral movement.
  • Cholesterol: restricts excessive fluidity at high temperatures and prevents close packing at low temperatures.
  • Glycoproteins and glycolipids: carbohydrate chains attached to proteins or lipids for cell recognition and cell signaling.

Core Practical: Membrane Permeability

Core Practical 3 involves investigating membrane permeability by examining the effects of temperature and alcohol concentration on beetroot cell membranes. Betalain pigment leaks out when cell surface membranes and tonoplasts are damaged. Colorimetry quantifies the amount of pigment released by measuring absorbance.

  • Temperature effect: high temperatures increase kinetic energy, denature membrane proteins, and disrupt the phospholipid bilayer, increasing permeability.
  • Alcohol effect: organic solvents dissolve lipids in the membrane, creating gaps that allow pigment leakage.
  • Method: wash beetroot discs thoroughly to remove loose surface pigment, place in water baths at varying temperatures or alcohol concentrations for a set time, and use a colorimeter with a blue-green filter to measure absorbance.

Transport Across Membranes

Substances move across cell membranes via passive transport mechanisms such as simple diffusion and facilitated diffusion down concentration gradients without metabolic energy. Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient using carrier proteins and ATP as an immediate source of energy. Endocytosis and exocytosis transport bulk materials into and out of cells via vesicles. Channel proteins provide hydrophilic pores for charged ions, while carrier proteins change shape to transport specific molecules.

  • Simple diffusion: net movement of small, non-polar molecules down a concentration gradient.
  • Facilitated diffusion: passive movement of polar molecules or ions through specific channel or carrier proteins.
  • Active transport: movement against a concentration gradient requiring carrier proteins and ATP hydrolysis.
  • Endocytosis and exocytosis: bulk transport using vesicle formation and fusion, requiring ATP.

Osmosis and Water Potential

Osmosis is the net movement of free water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane down a water potential gradient. Water potential is measured in kilopascals (kPa), with pure water having a water potential of 0 kPa. Solute addition lowers water potential into negative values. Recommended additional practical work involves using plant tissue and graded solute concentrations to determine tissue water potentials.

  • Water potential formula concept: Ψ = Ψs + Ψp (solute potential plus pressure potential).
  • Plant tissue practical: immerse plant cylinders in sucrose solutions of varying concentrations, calculate percentage change in mass, and find the point of zero mass change where external water potential equals internal cell water potential.

DNA and RNA Structure

Mononucleotides are the building blocks of nucleic acids, consisting of a pentose sugar (deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA), a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base (adenine, thymine, cytosine, guanine, or uracil in RNA). Polynucleotides form via condensation reactions creating phosphodiester bonds between the sugar of one nucleotide and the phosphate of the next. DNA is a double helix composed of two antiparallel strands held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs: adenine pairs with thymine via two hydrogen bonds, and cytosine pairs with guanine via three hydrogen bonds.

  • Mononucleotide components: pentose sugar, phosphate group, nitrogenous base.
  • Bases in DNA: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C), guanine (G).
  • Bases in RNA: adenine (A), uracil (U), cytosine (C), guanine (G).
  • Bonding: phosphodiester bonds along the backbone; hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs.

DNA Replication and Meselson-Stahl Experiment

DNA replication is semi-conservative, ensuring genetic continuity. DNA helicase unwinds and unzips the double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds between bases. DNA polymerase catalyses the formation of phosphodiester bonds between free nucleotides, adding them to the 3' end of the growing strand. The Meselson-Stahl experiment provided data supporting semi-conservative replication and refuting conservative and dispersive models by growing bacteria in mediums containing heavy nitrogen (N15) and light nitrogen (N14).

  • Semi-conservative replication: each new DNA molecule contains one original strand and one newly synthesized strand.
  • DNA helicase: unwinds double helix and breaks hydrogen bonds.
  • DNA polymerase: aligns free mononucleotides and forms phosphodiester bonds.
  • Meselson-Stahl findings: after one generation in N14, DNA was a hybrid density (refuting conservative); after two generations, half hybrid and half light density (refuting dispersive).

Protein Synthesis and Genetic Code

A gene is a sequence of bases on a DNA molecule that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. The genetic code is a triplet code (three bases code for one amino acid), non-overlapping, and degenerate (multiple codons can code for the same amino acid). Protein synthesis involves transcription in the nucleus and translation on ribosomes. RNA polymerase binds to the promoter, and the DNA template (antisense) strand is transcribed into messenger RNA (mRNA). mRNA travels to ribosomes where transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules with specific anticodons bring amino acids. Start codons initiate translation, and stop codons terminate it.

  • Transcription: RNA polymerase synthesizes pre-mRNA complementary to the antisense DNA strand, which is processed into mature mRNA.
  • Translation: mRNA binds to a ribosome; tRNA anticodons bind to complementary mRNA codons. Peptide bonds form between adjacent amino acids.
  • Code properties: triplet, non-overlapping, degenerate, universal.

Mutations

Errors in DNA replication can cause gene mutations, classified as substitution, insertion, or deletion of bases. A substitution changes a single base, which may be silent, missense, or nonsense. Insertions and deletions cause a frameshift, altering every subsequent triplet codon. Many mutations have no observable effect due to the degenerate nature of the code or if they occur in non-coding regions. However, specific mutations give rise to genetic disorders or cancer.

  • Substitution: one base replaced by another, altering a single codon.
  • Insertion/deletion: addition or loss of bases causing a shift in the reading frame of all downstream codons.
  • Effects: silent (no amino acid change), missense (different amino acid), nonsense (premature stop codon).

Inheritance and Genetics Terminology

Genetics terminology underpins inheritance patterns. A gene is a sequence of DNA coding for a polypeptide; alleles are alternative forms of a gene. Genotype is the genetic makeup, while phenotype is the observable characteristic resulting from genotype and environment. Recessive alleles are expressed only in homozygotes, whereas dominant alleles are expressed in heterozygotes and homozygotes. Codominance occurs when both alleles contribute to the phenotype. Homozygotes possess two identical alleles; heterozygotes possess two different alleles. Monohybrid inheritance examines the transmission of a single gene, and genetic pedigree diagrams track phenotypes across generations. Sex linkage involves genes located on sex chromosomes, typically the X chromosome, such as the gene for red-green colour blindness.

  • Genotype and phenotype: genetic constitution versus expressed physical traits.
  • Homozygote vs heterozygote: matching versus contrasting allele pairs.
  • Codominance: both alleles equally expressed in the phenotype.
  • Sex-linked inheritance: X-linked recessive conditions show higher incidence in males who inherit a single affected X chromosome.

Cystic Fibrosis

Cystic fibrosis is caused by a gene mutation (often a deletion of three nucleotides coding for phenylalanine) affecting the CFTR protein, a chloride ion channel. This impairs water movement across epithelial tissues, producing thick, sticky mucus. In the gaseous exchange system, cilia cannot clear mucus effectively, leading to trapped bacteria and chronic lung infections. In the digestive system, pancreatic ducts become blocked by mucus, preventing digestive enzymes from reaching the small intestine and causing malabsorption. In the reproductive system, thickened cervical mucus or blocked sperm ducts can cause infertility.

  • CFTR protein defect: faulty chloride transport reduces water movement out of cells into mucus.
  • Gaseous exchange: accumulation of viscous mucus leads to frequent bacterial infections and damaged lung tissue.
  • Digestive system: blocked pancreatic ducts reduce enzyme secretion, impairing food digestion and nutrient uptake.

Genetic Screening and Ethics

Genetic screening identifies individuals carrying mutant alleles or affected fetuses. Methods include carrier testing for prospective parents, pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) during IVF, and prenatal testing via amniocentesis (taking amniotic fluid at 15 to 20 weeks) or chorionic villus sampling (sampling placental tissue at 11 to 14 weeks). Prenatal screening carries risks such as miscarriage. Ethical, moral, and social implications involve debates over the right to life, emotional stress of results, decisions regarding termination, and societal discrimination.

  • Amniocentesis and CVS: invasive prenatal tests to obtain fetal cells for karyotyping or DNA analysis, carrying a small risk of miscarriage.
  • Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD): screening embryos created via IVF before uterine implantation.
  • Ethical viewpoints: religious beliefs concerning the sanctity of life, moral arguments surrounding disability rights, and social impacts on healthcare resources and insurance access.

Typical mistakes

  • Confusing the sense (coding) and antisense (template) DNA strands: remember that RNA polymerase uses the antisense strand as the template to build complementary mRNA.
  • Stating that water moves down a concentration gradient in osmosis: always state that water moves down a water potential gradient from high to low water potential.
  • Forgetting to mention the exact role of ATP in active transport: state that ATP is hydrolyzed to provide energy for carrier protein conformational change.
  • Describing frameshift mutations for substitutions: substitution mutations alter only a single triplet, whereas insertions and deletions cause frameshifts.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why beetroot membrane permeability increases at temperatures above 60 °C. (Answer: High temperatures impart kinetic energy that disrupts the phospholipid bilayer and denatures membrane-bound transport proteins, allowing betalain pigment to leak out.)
  2. Describe the role of tRNA during translation. (Answer: tRNA molecules have a specific anticodon that binds to a complementary codon on mRNA and carry a specific amino acid to the ribosome to build the polypeptide chain.)
  3. Explain how a deletion mutation in the CFTR gene results in thick mucus in individuals with cystic fibrosis. (Answer: The deletion alters the amino acid sequence, leading to a non-functional CFTR chloride ion channel. Chloride ions cannot leave the cell, reducing water movement via osmosis and producing dehydrated, viscous mucus.)
  4. Compare amniocentesis and chorionic villus sampling as methods of prenatal screening. (Answer: Amniocentesis tests amniotic fluid cells and is performed later in pregnancy (15 to 20 weeks) with a slightly lower miscarriage risk, whereas chorionic villus sampling tests placental tissue earlier (11 to 14 weeks) but carries a slightly higher miscarriage risk.)

Use these notes alongside active recall of definitions, core practical method steps, and practice interpreting pedigree diagrams and genetic cross calculations. Review protein synthesis steps next.

title: Exam technique: Permutations and Combinations
content:
### What earns the marks
For counting, the permutation vs combination choice justified earns the method mark. For restricted arrangements, fixing the block first then permuting earns both marks. For probability of selections, the hypergeometric fraction built stepwise earns each mark.
### Traps
Error: P used where order is irrelevant. Correction: C for choose. Error: double counting symmetric selections. Correction: divide by the internal permutations. Error: identical items permuted fully. Correction: divide by repeats factorial.

title: Coordination, Response and Gene Technology
content:
Coordination, Response and Gene Technology - A2 Level Biology

This topic belongs to the Edexcel International AS/A Level Biology specification (WBI15) and covers how nervous and hormonal systems coordinate responses in animals, how plants respond to environmental cues via growth substances, the underlying cellular and molecular mechanisms of nerve transmission and brain function, and advanced gene technology techniques including recombinant DNA, microarrays, and bioinformatics.

Nervous Coordination, Neurones and Reflex Arcs

Animals detect and respond to internal and external stimuli using specialised cells and coordinated nervous pathways. A complete nervous response requires sensory receptors, neurones, synapses, and effectors.

  • 8.1 Sensory neurones transmit electrical impulses from receptors to the central nervous system. Relay neurones are located entirely within the central nervous system and connect sensory neurones to motor neurones. Motor neurones transmit impulses from the central nervous system to effectors such as muscles and glands. Schwann cells wrap around mammalian peripheral nerve axons, forming a fatty myelin sheath composed of multiple layers of cell membrane containing myelin. The gaps between adjacent Schwann cells are called nodes of Ranvier.
  • 8.2 The nervous system causes effectors to respond to a stimulus by generating action potentials along motor neurones that terminate at specialized junctions with effectors, prompting muscle contraction or glandular secretion.
  • 8.3 A spinal reflex arc consists of a receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone in the grey matter of the spinal cord, motor neurone, and effector. The spinal cord contains an inner region of grey matter, containing cell bodies and synapses, surrounded by white matter, containing myelinated axon tracts running up and down the spinal cord.
  • 8.4 At resting potential, the inside of an axon is at about −70 mV relative to the outside. The sodium-potassium pump actively transports 3 Na⁺ ions out of the axon for every 2 K⁺ ions pumped in, using ATP, maintaining electrochemical gradients. When a stimulus arrives, voltage-gated sodium channels open, causing Na⁺ to flood into the axon down an electrochemical gradient, leading to rapid depolarisation where the interior becomes positive (+40 mV). These sodium channels then close, and voltage-gated potassium channels open, allowing K⁺ ions to diffuse out of the axon, repolarising the membrane. An overshoot hyperpolarisation occurs before the sodium-potassium pump restores the resting potential.
  • 8.5 Myelination acts as an electrical insulator. In myelinated neurones, local circuits of current cannot flow through the thick myelin sheath; instead, depolarisation can only occur at the exposed nodes of Ranvier. This forces the nerve impulse to jump from one node of Ranvier to the next, a process called saltatory conduction, which significantly increases the speed of nerve impulse transmission compared to continuous conduction in unmyelinated axons.

Synapses, Brain Structure and Drug Action

Information transfer between neurones and across effectors occurs at specialised junctions called synapses, modulated by neurotransmitters, neurochemicals, and medical interventions.

  • 8.6 (i) At a cholinergic synapse, an arriving action potential causes voltage-gated calcium ion channels in the presynaptic membrane to open, causing Ca²⁺ to enter the presynaptic knob. This influx causes vesicles containing acetylcholine to fuse with the presynaptic membrane, releasing acetylcholine into the synaptic cleft by exocytosis. Acetylcholine diffuses across the cleft and binds to specific receptor proteins on the postsynaptic membrane, causing sodium ion channels to open, generating a postsynaptic action potential. Acetylcholinesterase then breaks down acetylcholine into choline and ethanoic acid to prevent continuous stimulation. (ii) Pupil dilation (mydriasis) occurs in dim light via contraction of the radial muscles of the iris under sympathetic control. Pupil constriction (miosis) occurs in bright light via contraction of the circular muscles of the iris under parasympathetic control.
  • 8.7 Drugs alter nerve impulse transmission. Nicotine mimics acetylcholine, binding to postsynaptic receptors and keeping sodium channels open, thus stimulating the nervous system. Lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing depolarisation and stopping the conduction of nerve impulses, acting as a local anaesthetic. Cobra venom alpha toxin binds irreversibly to acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane at neuromuscular junctions, preventing muscle contraction and causing paralysis. L-DOPA is a precursor to dopamine that crosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted into dopamine in the brain to treat Parkinson's disease symptoms. MDMA (ecstasy) increases the concentration of serotonin, dopamine, and noradrenaline in synaptic clefts by reversing the direction of transporter proteins that normally clear them.
  • 8.8 Mammalian retinal rod cells detect light intensity. In the dark, rhodopsin is inactive, cyclic GMP keeps sodium cation channels open, and Na⁺ continually enters the rod cell, causing a depolarised resting state around −40 mV that continuously releases neurotransmitters that inhibit bipolar neurones. Light hits rhodopsin, splitting it into retinal and opsin. Opsin activates a cascade that breaks down cyclic GMP, closing the sodium cation channels. Na⁺ can no longer enter, but K⁺ continues to leave, causing hyperpolarisation of the rod cell (down to −70 mV). Neurotransmitter release stops, removing the inhibition on bipolar neurones, which then generate an action potential in the optic neurones.
  • 8.9 Habituation is a learned decrease in response to a repeated stimulus that is determined to be harmless, caused by a reduction in calcium ion channels opening at presynaptic knobs over time, leading to less neurotransmitter release and a smaller postsynaptic response.
  • 8.10 The mammalian nervous system consists of the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system (cranial and spinal nerves).
  • 8.14 The human brain comprises specialized regions: the cerebral hemispheres control higher brain functions such as conscious thought, vision, hearing, speech and memory; the hypothalamus coordinates homeostatic responses, osmoregulation, and the autonomic nervous system; the pituitary gland secretes hormones regulating endocrine glands; the cerebellum coordinates balance, posture and fine voluntary muscle movement; and the medulla oblongata controls involuntary autonomic centres including heart rate and breathing rate.
  • 8.15 Medical imaging techniques diagnose brain conditions: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to produce high-resolution structural images of soft tissues; functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) measures changes in blood oxygenation and flow to map active brain areas in real time; positron emission tomography (PET) uses radioactive tracers (such as fluorodeoxyglucose) to visualise metabolic activity and chemical pathways in the brain; computed tomography (CT) uses X-rays fired from multiple angles to create cross-sectional structural images.
  • 8.16 Imbalances in brain chemicals cause ill health: a deficiency of dopamine-producing neurones in the substantia nigra leads to Parkinson's disease (treated with L-DOPA), while low serotonin levels in certain brain pathways contribute to clinical depression (treated with Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors, SSRIs). Pharmacists use this understanding to develop targeted new drugs.

Plant Coordination and Gene Technology

Plants coordinate growth responses via hormones such as auxins, gibberellins, and phytochromes. Modern biotechnology utilises enzymes, vectors, and screening tools to manipulate DNA for medicine and agriculture.

  • 8.11 Phytochromes are plant photoreceptors that exist in two interconvertible forms: Pr (absorbs red light at 660 nm) and Pfr (absorbs far-red light at 730 nm). Sunlight converts Pr to Pfr, triggering seed germination, flowering, and stem elongation by influencing transcription factors. Auxins, principally Indoleacetic Acid (IAA), are synthesized in shoot apices and transported basipetally. Auxin promotes cell elongation in shoots by loosening cell walls through proton pumping, activating expansins, whereas high concentrations inhibit root elongation. Gibberellins stimulate seed germination by diffusing to the aleurone layer of cereal grains, inducing transcription of the gene encoding amylase.
  • 8.12 Core Practical 18 involves investigating the production of amylase in germinating cereal grains (such as barley). Grains are cut, sterilized, and incubated on starch agar plates with varying concentrations of gibberellic acid. After incubation, the plates are flooded with iodine solution. A clear zone around the grains indicates starch hydrolysis, demonstrating that gibberellin triggers amylase enzyme production.
  • 8.13 Coordination in animals is achieved through nervous control (rapid, localized, electrical impulses via neurones) and hormonal control (slower, widespread, chemical signals transported in the blood via the endocrine system).
  • 8.17 Drugs and therapeutic proteins can be produced using genetically modified organisms: microorganisms (such as bacteria and yeasts) are cultured in large bioreactors to produce human insulin or antibodies; plants (such as transgenic rice or tobacco) can produce therapeutic proteins or vaccines (

    Gene Technology, Recombinant DNA and Bioinformatics

    Advanced molecular techniques allow scientists to isolate, modify, and amplify specific genes for industrial, agricultural, and medical applications.

    • 8.18 Recombinant DNA is produced by isolating the desired gene using restriction endonucleases (which cut DNA at specific palindromic recognition sequences, producing sticky or blunt ends) and joining it into a prepared plasmid vector using DNA ligase, which catalyses the formation of phosphodiester bonds between the sugar-phosphate backbones.
    • 8.19 Recombinant DNA is inserted into host cells using vectors such as plasmids, bacteriophages, or liposomes, or via direct methods such as electroporation, microinjection, or gene guns, allowing host cells (transformation) to express the foreign protein.
    • 8.20 DNA microarrays consist of a solid glass or silicon slide fixed with thousands of microscopic spots of single-stranded DNA probes corresponding to specific genes. Fluorescently labelled cDNA (derived from mRNA of test and control cells) is washed over the microarray; hybridisation reveals which genes are active or expressed by measuring fluorescence intensity at each spot.
    • 8.21 Bioinformatics involves the collection, storage, and computational analysis of biological data, such as genomic sequences and amino acid structures, using mathematical and statistical algorithms to identify gene functions, evolutionary relationships, and drug-binding sites.
    • 8.22 Genetically modified organisms offer significant benefits, including enhanced crop yields, nutritional fortification (such as Golden Rice), and low-cost pharmaceutical production, but carry risks such as horizontal gene transfer to wild relatives, the creation of invasive species, potential allergenicity, and ethical concerns regarding animal welfare and corporate monopolies.

    Examiner Guidance, Common Mistakes and Exam-Style Practice

    Candidates frequently lose marks in A2 Biology by confusing membrane mechanisms or omitting essential terminology in extended-response questions.

    • Common Mistake: Confusing the roles of sodium and potassium channels during an action potential, or stating that the sodium-potassium pump generates the action potential rather than maintaining the resting potential. Correction: Always state that voltage-gated sodium channels open first for depolarisation, voltage-gated potassium channels open second for repolarisation, and the sodium-potassium pump actively restores the resting electrochemical gradient using ATP.
    • Common Mistake: Describing plant phototropisms simply as 'auxin moving to the dark side' without explaining that IAA is actively transported laterally across the shoot tip, causing differential cell elongation down the shaded flank. Correction: Specify that lateral redistribution of IAA promotes proton pumping into cell walls, lowering pH to activate expansins that loosen cellulose microfibrils.
    • Exam-Style Question and Worked Answer: Explain how cobra venom alpha toxin prevents muscle contraction. Answer: Alpha toxin binds irreversibly to acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane at the neuromuscular junction (1 mark). This blocks acetylcholine from binding, preventing the opening of sodium ion channels and stopping the generation of a postsynaptic action potential (1 mark), meaning no depolarisation spreads across the sarcolemma to trigger calcium ion release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (1 mark).

title: Pressure & Density — Study Notes
content:
Pressure & Density

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): pressure & pressure differences in fluids, density review (Extended pressure-depth).

1. Pressure basics

p = F/A (Pa = N/m²). Increase F or decrease A to raise pressure; explain applications (snowshoes, knives, hydraulic press).

2. Liquids

  • Pressure increases with depth: p = ρgh (Extended).
  • Same level, same liquid ⇒ same pressure (hydrostatic paradox).
  • Hydraulic systems transmit pressure — force multiplier: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.

3. Atmospheric pressure

~10⁵ Pa at sea level; demonstrated by collapsing can, mercury barometer 760 mmHg; decreases with altitude.

4. Density revisited

ρ = m/V; floating condition; upthrust = weight of displaced fluid (qualitative).

5. Gas pressure (particle model)

Particles collide with walls → force per area. Volume ↓ at same T ⇒ pressure ↑ (more frequent collisions). Temperature ↑ ⇒ faster particles ⇒ more frequent, harder impacts.

Density in more depth

Density is mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V. Its SI unit is kg/m³, and 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. An object of a given density will float in a fluid only if the fluid has a higher density. To find the density of an irregular solid, measure its mass on a balance and its volume by displacement of water in a measuring cylinder.

Pressure and depth

Pressure is force per unit area, p = F/A, with unit the pascal (Pa = N/m²). In a liquid, the pressure increases with depth, p = hρg, and acts equally in all directions at a given depth. Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.

Exam tip: convert the area to m² before you calculate pressure, and use the density in kg/m³ in p = hρg.

title: Binomial Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Binomial Distribution

When Binomial Applies

X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

  • a fixed number n of identical trials,
  • each trial ends in success or failure,
  • constant success probability p,
  • trials are independent.

Check all four before using the model — "justifying a binomial model" is a real exam question.

The Formula

P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The ⁿCᵣ counts which r of the n trials were the successes.

Example: X ~ B(5, 0.3). P(X = 2) = ¹⁰C₂? No — ⁵C₂ × 0.3² × 0.7³ = 10 × 0.09 × 0.343 = 0.3087.

Cumulative Probabilities

P(X ≤ 2) = P(0) + P(1) + P(2). "At least" questions convert by the complement: P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(X ≤ 1). Keep one extra decimal place in intermediate steps to avoid rounding drift.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 − p)

For X ~ B(20, 0.4): E(X) = 8 and Var(X) = 4.8.

Modelling Decisions

If trials are dependent (drawing without replacement from a small population) binomial is not appropriate. If p changes between trials it is not binomial. When n is large and p small, the binomial is approximately Poisson — but at A2 you usually stay exact.

Exam tips: identify n and p in words before touching the calculator. For P(X ≥ k) always rewrite as 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1). Tables give cumulative values — use them rather than summing by hand.

Exam method: binomial probabilities

If X ~ B(n, p) then X counts successes in n independent trials, each with probability p. P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The mean is np and the variance is np(1 - p).

Check the conditions first: a fixed number of trials, two outcomes, a constant p and independent trials. If any condition fails, the binomial model does not apply.

title: Energetics — Study Notes
content:
Energetics

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 6. Energetics explains why reactions release or absorb heat, and it provides the enthalpy data that later decides whether a reaction is feasible.

Enthalpy change and types of reaction

  • The enthalpy change ΔH is the heat energy transferred at constant pressure. Exothermic reactions have a negative ΔH; endothermic reactions have a positive ΔH.
  • Standard conditions are 100 kPa and a stated temperature, usually 298 K, with substances in their standard states.
  • Important definitions include standard enthalpy of formation, combustion and neutralisation. Each is written for one mole of the stated substance.

Measuring enthalpy changes

  • In a calorimetry experiment, q = m × c × ΔT, where m is the mass of solution (usually assumed to be 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ for water-based solutions).
  • Convert heat to enthalpy change using moles: ΔH = −q / n. The sign is negative for an exothermic reaction.
  • Sources of error include heat loss to the surroundings and incomplete combustion; the answer is always lower than the data book value for combustion.

Hess's law

  • The total enthalpy change is independent of the route taken. Enthalpy cycles let you find an unknown ΔH from known values.
  • For formation values: ΔH = Σ ΔHf(products) − Σ ΔHf(reactants).

Bond enthalpies

  • Breaking bonds is endothermic; making bonds is exothermic. ΔH ≈ Σ bonds broken − Σ bonds formed.
  • Bond enthalpies are averages over many compounds, so values from bond enthalpy calculations differ from accurate formation data.

Entropy and free energy (introduced)

  • A reaction that increases disorder (more gas molecules, for example) has a positive entropy change, which favours spontaneous change.

Exam tip: a common mistake is to use the wrong sign for ΔH. Always check whether the process is releasing or taking in heat before writing the value.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Calorimetry, applied to burning a fuel: q = m c ΔT. Heating 100 g of water by 10.0 °C gives q = 100 × 4.18 × 10.0 = 4180 J. If 0.0100 mol of fuel was burnt, ΔH = −4180 J ÷ 0.0100 mol = −418 kJ mol⁻¹. The minus sign is required, because the reaction is exothermic.
  • Hess's law, applied to a cycle: ΔH = sum of ΔH(products) − sum of ΔH(reactants), with each enthalpy change taken in its direction in the cycle. Reversing a step changes the sign. Draw the cycle first, then write the equation, so the signs follow from the arrows.
  • Bond enthalpies: ΔH ≈ energy to break bonds − energy released when bonds form. For CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, use mean values for the bonds involved. The answer is an estimate, because the values are averages across different molecules.
  • Common losses of marks: forgetting that calorimetry gives the heat absorbed by the water, so the sign of ΔH is the opposite of q. Mixing up the units of kJ and J, and giving the answer per gram instead of per mole.

title: Further Trigonometry — Study Notes
content:
Further Trigonometry

Compound Angles

  • sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
  • cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B

Example: sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 + √2)/4.

Double Angles

  • sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A
  • cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A

Example: express 4 sin x cos x in one term: 2 sin 2x.

The R-Form

a sin x + b cos x = R sin(x + α) with R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b/a.

Example: 3 sin x + 4 cos x = 5 sin(x + 0.927). This instantly gives the maximum 5 and minimum −5.

Reciprocal Functions

sec θ = 1/cos θ, cosec θ = 1/sin θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ. Key identity: 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

Exam tips: choose the cos 2A form that eliminates the unwanted function; when solving with R-form, divide by R before using inverse trig, and translate intervals carefully.

Exam method: reciprocal functions and identities

The reciprocal functions are sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x and cot x = 1/tan x. Rewrite them in terms of sine and cosine when a question mixes functions, because this usually shows which identity to use.

The Pythagorean identities are sin² x + cos² x = 1, 1 + tan² x = sec² x and 1 + cot² x = cosec² x. Divide the first identity by cos² x or sin² x to obtain the second or third.

To solve an equation such as sec x = 2, first rewrite it as cos x = 1/2, then find the acute angle and the other solutions in the required range. For cos x = k the solutions in 0 to 2π are α and 2π − α, where α is the acute angle.

To prove an identity, work on the more complicated side only, and keep rewriting until it matches the other side.

Exam cue: Give each solution in the range asked for, using exact values such as π/3 when the angle is standard.

Exam method: R-form

To write a sinθ + b cosθ as R sin(θ + α), expand R sin(θ + α) = R sinθ cosα + R cosθ sinα and compare coefficients. This gives R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b / a, with α in the quadrant where cos α and sin α have the signs of a and b.

Exam cue: Find the maximum and minimum from R, then solve for θ over the stated interval. Give α in the correct quadrant before writing the final angles.

Worked example: solving sin 2x = cos x

Solve sin 2x = cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π. Using the double angle formula, 2 sin x cos x = cos x. Move everything to one side and factorise: cos x (2 sin x − 1) = 0. So cos x = 0, giving x = π/2 or 3π/2, or sin x = ½, giving x = π/6 or 5π/6. The four solutions are π/6, π/2, 5π/6 and 3π/2. Dividing both sides by cos x at the start would lose the two solutions where cos x = 0, and that is the most common way to drop marks on this type of question.

Exam method: choosing an identity

Before you start, look at which angles appear. If the question mixes x and 2x, rewrite the double angle first so that everything is in one angle. Always state the range of solutions in the form the question asks for, in radians or degrees, and check that each answer lies inside the range. Substituting each answer back into the original equation is a quick way to catch a sign error.

title: Exam technique: Magnetism and Electromagnetism
content:
### What earns the marks
For electromagnets, turns plus current plus soft iron core earns each mark. For transformers, the turns ratio equation quoted earns the method mark. For induction, rate of change of flux linked to emf size earns the explanation mark.
### Traps
Error: steel chosen for electromagnet cores. Correction: soft iron; steel suits permanent magnets. Error: Fleming hands swapped. Correction: left for motor, right for generator. Error: step-up confused with step-down. Correction: more secondary turns means step-up.
### Worked example
A transformer has 2000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. The primary is supplied at 240 V. The turns ratio gives Vs = Vp × Ns / Np = 240 × 100 / 2000 = 12 V. More secondary turns than primary turns means a step-up transformer, so the output voltage rises.
### Check yourself
An ideal transformer has 12 V at its secondary and a current of 4.0 A there. Find the primary current when the primary is at 240 V. Power in equals power out, so Ip = (12 × 4.0) / 240 = 0.20 A.

title: Molecules, Transport and Health — Study Notes
content:
Molecules, Transport and Health

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI11, Topic 1. Living things are built from a small set of biological molecules. Their structure decides how they are used, how substances move in and out of cells, and how diet affects health.

Carbohydrates

  • Monosaccharides such as glucose, fructose and galactose are the building blocks. Glucose is the main respiratory substrate.
  • Disaccharides form by a condensation reaction that releases water and creates a glycosidic bond. Maltose is glucose + glucose, sucrose is glucose + fructose, and lactose is glucose + galactose.
  • Starch (amylose and amylopectin) stores glucose in plants. Glycogen stores glucose in animals. Cellulose is a straight chain of beta-glucose with hydrogen bonds between chains, giving strength.

Lipids and proteins

  • A triglyceride is one glycerol with three fatty acids joined by ester bonds. Phospholipids have a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails.
  • Amino acids join by peptide bonds to form polypeptides. Tertiary structure is held by hydrogen, ionic, disulfide and hydrophobic interactions.

Enzymes

  • Enzymes have an active site with a shape complementary to the substrate. Rate rises with temperature until the enzyme denatures, and pH changes can alter the active site.

Transport

  • Diffusion moves substances down a concentration gradient without energy. Facilitated diffusion uses carrier or channel proteins. Active transport moves substances against a gradient and uses ATP.
  • Water moves by osmosis from a less negative water potential to a more negative water potential.
  • Large, multicellular organisms need exchange surfaces with a large surface area to volume ratio, such as alveoli and the villi of the small intestine.

Health

  • Body mass index (BMI) = mass (kg) ÷ height² (m²). Diet, exercise and cholesterol intake affect the risk of cardiovascular disease.

Exam tip: when you describe a transport process, state whether it needs energy, whether it uses a protein, and which way the gradient points.

title: Exam technique: Web Technologies
content:
### What earns the marks
For web roles, HTML for structure plus CSS for presentation plus JavaScript for behaviour earns each mark. For threats, phishing versus pharming versus smishing distinguished earns one mark each. For cookies, session versus persistent with a use earns both marks.
### Traps
