title: Exam technique: Transformations and Vectors
content:
### What earns the marks
For translations and vector arithmetic, each component computed separately earns credit: show x and y lines. For magnitude, the root-of-sum-of-squares line earns the method mark before evaluation. For reflections and rotations, the coordinate rule stated ((y; -x) for 90 degrees clockwise) earns the method mark. For describing transformations, all three of type, centre or line, and size or angle are needed for full marks.
### Traps
Error: writing column vectors as bracket rows that lose a row. Correction: use (x; y) form and keep both components. Error: (100) or 14 for the magnitude of (6; 8). Correction: square, add, then root. Error: (-y; x) for a clockwise rotation. Correction: clockwise is (y; -x). Error: negating both coordinates for a single-axis reflection. Correction: one axis changes, the other stays.
### Worked example
Point A(1; 2) is translated by the vector (3; -1), giving A'(4; 1). Reflecting A' in the x-axis gives (4; -1). Rotating the point (3; -1) 90 degrees clockwise about the origin gives (-1; -3), using the rule (x; y) to (y; -x). Scaling (1; 2) by a factor of 2 from the origin gives (2; 4). Write each coordinate step on its own line.
### Check yourself
A point at (6; 8) has magnitude sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = sqrt(100) = 10. Explain why the magnitude is never the sum 6 + 8 = 14. The magnitude uses the root of the sum of squares, so the components do not add directly.

### Worked example
Point A(1; 2) is translated by the vector (3; -1), giving A'(4; 1). Reflecting A' in the x-axis gives (4; -1). Rotating the point (3; -1) 90 degrees clockwise about the origin gives (-1; -3), using the rule (x; y) to (y; -x). Scaling (1; 2) by a factor of 2 from the origin gives (2; 4). Write each coordinate step on its own line.

title: Vectors — Study Notes
content:
Vectors

Components and Arithmetic

A vector a = 3i + 4j has magnitude |a| = √(3² + 4²) = 5. Parallel vectors are scalar multiples; unit vector = a/|a|.

Position and Direction

The line through point A with direction d: r = a + t d. Two lines are parallel if their directions are multiples.

Example: r = (1, 2) + t(3, −1).

Scalar (Dot) Product

a · b = |a||b| cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂.

Perpendicular ⇔ a · b = 0. Parallel ⇔ cross-multiplied components are equal (in 2D: a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ = 0).

Example: (2, 3) · (−6, 4) = −12 + 12 = 0, so they are perpendicular.

Angle Between Vectors

cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|).

Example: between (1, 0) and (1, 1): cos θ = 1/(1 × √2), θ = 45°.

Lines and Points

Foot of perpendicular from P to a line, intersection of two lines, and shortest distances all come from dot products and parameter t.

Exam tips: write column vectors cleanly; check answers by substituting the found t back into both position vectors; keep exact surd magnitudes rather than decimals.

Exam method: components, magnitude and scalar product

A vector in two dimensions is written as a column (x; y), and in three dimensions as (x; y; z) or in unit vector form xi + yj + zk. The magnitude is |a| = √(x² + y² + z²), which is Pythagoras applied in each direction.

The scalar product a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ is a number, not a vector. It also equals |a||b| cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors. Two vectors are perpendicular exactly when their scalar product is zero.

Use the scalar product to find the angle between two vectors: cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|). Give the angle in degrees or radians as the question asks.

A unit vector has magnitude 1. Divide a vector by its magnitude to find the unit vector in the same direction.

Exam cue: Write each component with its sign before adding, because a sign slip in the scalar product changes the answer without changing the method.

Worked example: angle between two vectors

Find the angle between a = (3; 4) and b = (5; −2). The scalar product is a·b = 15 − 8 = 7. The magnitudes are |a| = √(9 + 16) = 5 and |b| = √(25 + 4) = √29 ≈ 5.385. So cos θ = 7/(5 × 5.385) ≈ 0.260, giving θ ≈ 74.9°.

Perpendicular vectors

Two non-zero vectors are perpendicular exactly when their scalar product is zero. Use this to find an unknown component: if (2; k) is perpendicular to (4; −3), then 8 − 3k = 0, so k = 8/3.

Vector equation of a line

  • The line r = a + λd passes through the point with position vector a and has direction d; λ is the parameter.
  • To test whether a point lies on the line, find λ from one component and check that it satisfies the other components.
  • Two lines are parallel when their direction vectors are scalar multiples of each other. They are skew when they neither meet nor are parallel.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

The nucleus

The nucleus holds protons and neutrons, collectively nucleons. Nuclide notation ᴬZX gives Z protons and A nucleons, so N = A − Z neutrons. Isotopes share Z and differ in N. Nuclear densities are about 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, so nearly all the mass of an atom sits in a tiny volume.

Mass defect and binding energy (23.1)

The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its separate nucleons. This difference is the mass defect Δm. Energy equivalent to Δm, given by E = Δmc², is the binding energy: the energy released when the nucleus is assembled from separate nucleons, and the energy needed to separate it. In nuclear work, 1 u = 931 MeV.

Example: a mass defect of 0.0300 u corresponds to E = 0.0300 × 931 ≈ 27.9 MeV.

The binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56, the most tightly bound nucleus. Energy is released when the nucleons move toward this peak, by fission of heavy nuclei or by fusion of light ones.

Radioactive decay (23.2)

Decay is random and spontaneous. The effect of each type on the nucleus and its penetration are:

TypeWhat changesStopped by
alphaZ − 2, A − 4paper
beta-minusZ + 1, A unchangeda few mm of aluminium
gammano change to Z or Athick lead

The activity A = λN is the rate of decay, in becquerel (Bq). The decay constant λ and the half-life t½ are related by λ = ln 2 / t½. The number of nuclei left after time t is N = N₀e^(−λt).

Example: a sample with t½ = 10 days has 1/8 of its original activity after 30 days, since three half-lives have passed.

Example: with t½ = 5.0 h = 1.8 × 10⁴ s, λ = 0.693 / 1.8 × 10⁴ ≈ 3.9 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹.

Fission and fusion

Heavy nuclei split (fission) into lighter nuclei of greater binding energy per nucleon, which releases energy in reactors. Light nuclei merge (fusion), which releases energy in stars.

Exam tips: balance Z and A on both sides of every decay equation. Convert the half-life to seconds before finding λ. Use A = λN, not guesswork with halves, when the number of nuclei is needed.

Nuclear decay and half-life

Alpha particles are helium nuclei with two protons and two neutrons, and they are strongly ionising but have low penetration. Beta-minus emission happens when a neutron changes into a proton and an electron is emitted. Gamma radiation is electromagnetic, carries no charge and no mass, and has high penetration. Background radiation must be subtracted from measured count rates before a half-life is calculated.

title:
Appendix I — What has been added in this pass and where the extra depth lives

This revision note has been lengthened in this pass so that the specification statements are covered at the level where you can answer a long question without having to reconstruct the reasoning from a one-line memory each time. The extra depth lives in three places. First, the receptor, synapse and muscle topics now have a longer appendix that works through the reasoning as a sequence rather than as a list of terms, because that is where a lot of marks on this topic are lost when the answer becomes vague. Second, the homeostasis and insulin-glucagon section now has a longer appendix that treats homeostasis as a principle with examples rather than as a separate definition for every case, because that is the framing that makes the examples answerable without inventing a new answer each time. Third, the gene technology section now has a longer appendix that matches each technique to its purpose and then adds the applications and the limits, because that is the order that examiners usually reward: principle first, application second, evaluation third. If you read the note as a set of linked sections rather than as three unrelated topics, you get the cross-strand reasoning that the questions actually ask for, and the extra length is there to make that reasoning possible rather than to pad the note for its own sake.

The reason for making the note this long is that the specification for this topic is broad enough that a short note leaves real gaps on the higher-mark questions. A short note can cover the labels and a few examples, but it is hard to answer a question that asks you to explain why calcium matters at the synapse, or why the filaments do not shorten, or why insulin and glucagon work in opposition, or why herd immunity depends on coverage, or what a restriction enzyme does and why sticky ends matter, if you only remember a label for each one. The longer note gives you the reasoning for those answers so that under time pressure you can reach for the reasoning rather than for a vague memory. That is the practical reason for the length, and it is the reason the extra appendices exist. If you study the note as a set of reasons and not as a set of labels, you get the benefit it was lengthened to provide.

One thing this extra length should not be used for is trying to memorise the note word for word. The note is meant to be a reference for revision, not a script. The parts worth remembering are the sequences, the distinctions and the reasoning patterns: for example, the synaptic sequence with calcium, the sliding filament sequence with ATP and calcium, the hormonal opposition in the insulin-glucagon system, the comparison pattern for nervous and hormonal coordination, and the principle-first order for gene technology. If you can remember enough of those to reconstruct a precise answer under time pressure, you have the note’s job done. If you try to recall the note verbatim, you are likely to lose time and lose precision, and the marks are in the precision, not in the recall.

That is also the reason the common mistakes section is there at the end. The mistakes are not there to be a list of trivia; they are there because they are the places where a reasonable candidate loses marks by being almost right in a way that is still wrong. If you can read the list and recognise the ones you are tempted toward, you can avoid them on the day, and that is often worth more than adding one more detail to a correct answer. The same is true of the exam-style questions at the end of the main body: they are there to show what a mark-scoring answer looks like for the kinds of question the specification actually asks, not to be memorised as a fixed set of answers. If you read them as models of reasoning and then try to produce the same kind of reasoning for a new question, you are using them the way they are meant to be used.

The final practical point about this pass is that the note should be checked against the specification statements after it is written, because a longer note can still be long in the wrong way if it drifts from the specification. The way to check is to take the specification and see whether each statement has a place in the note, and whether the note’s treatment of each statement is the kind of answer the specification rewards. If a statement is covered only by a label, that is the gap to fill. If a statement is covered by a reasoning sequence, that is usually the right level. If the note has become long by adding things the specification does not ask for, that is the part to cut. The note should be long enough to answer the specification questions, and not longer than that, because a note is a tool for revision, and a tool is only good if it is used well.

Appendix J — Long-answer practice built around the comparison and evaluation questions this topic actually sets

If you want to practise the questions this topic actually sets, the best way is to build your practice around the comparison and evaluation questions, because those are the ones where a correct but non-comparative or non-evaluative answer loses marks. For the nervous and hormonal comparison, practise until you can state the difference in speed, range and duration and give one concrete example of each in the same answer, because that is the kind of question that tests whether you can apply the two systems rather than just label them. For the primary and secondary response comparison, practise until you can say why the secondary response is faster and stronger and what memory cells do, and until you can link that to vaccination without making vaccination sound as if it does something separate from the immune response. For the plant and animal coordination comparison, practise until you can state that plants use hormones and growth while animals use nerves and muscles, without lapsing into the vague “plants are different” answer that does not earn the comparison marks.

For the evaluation questions, practise until you can give a benefit and an issue for each of the main technologies in the topic: vaccination, monoclonal antibodies, DNA profiling, gene therapy, GM crops and GM microorganisms, without repeating the same issue for every one. The point is not to generate a generic “it has issues” line and move on; it is to show that you can see the case specifically. For vaccination, the issue is often about coverage and public acceptance and the fact that not everyone can be vaccinated, rather than a vague “some people don’t like it.” For GM crops, the issue is often about gene flow and resistance and ownership, rather than a vague “it changes nature.” For gene therapy, the issue is often about delivery and about the difference between somatic and germ-line therapy, rather than a vague “it is unnatural.” If you can give a specific benefit and a specific issue for each technology, you can answer the evaluation question when it appears, and you can do it for more than one technology, which is what a real exam question will ask.

For the description questions, practise until you can produce the sequence and the mechanism in the right order without dropping the key step. For the synapse, that means not dropping calcium. For the muscle, that means not saying the filaments shorten. For the immune system, that means not blurring B and T cells into “immune cells” without a functional distinction. For the gene technology, that means not saying “PCR is used” without saying what it amplifies and how. If you can produce the sequence and the mechanism in the right order under time pressure, you are practising the description question in the way it needs to be practised, which is to say, as a sequence you can produce rather than as a fact you can recognise. The difference matters, because the exam asks you to produce the answer, not just to recognise it when you see it.

The last practice point is to practise under time, because a precise answer produced with unlimited time is not the same as a precise answer produced under exam time. Under time, the temptation is to shorten the answer until it becomes vague, and that is where marks are lost. The practice is therefore to set a timer, pick a question, and produce the precise answer without padding it, and then to check whether the answer has the one or two distinctions that are actually being marked. If it does, you are doing the question at the right level. If it is long but vague, you are not, and the practice needs to be on precision, not on length. The note is long so that you have enough material to practise from, but the exam answer has to be precise, not long, and that is the distinction to keep in mind when you practise.

The extra depth lives in three places. First, the receptor, synapse and muscle topics now have a longer appendix that works through the reasoning as a sequence rather than as a list of terms, because that is where a lot of marks on this topic are lost when the answer becomes vague. Second, the homeostasis and insulin-glucagon section now has a longer appendix that treats homeostasis as a principle with examples rather than as a separate definition for every case, because that is the framing that makes the examples answerable without inventing a new answer each time. Third, the gene technology section now has a longer appendix that matches each technique to its purpose and then adds the applications and the limits, because that is the order that examiners usually reward: principle first, application second, evaluation third. If you read the note as a set of linked sections rather than as three unrelated topics, you get the cross-strand reasoning that the questions actually ask for, and the extra length is there to make that reasoning possible rather than to pad the note for its own sake.

The reason for making the note this long is that the specification for this topic is broad enough that a short note leaves real gaps on the higher-mark questions. A short note can cover the labels and a few examples, but it is hard to answer a question that asks you to explain why calcium matters at the synapse, or why the filaments do not shorten, or why insulin and glucagon work in opposition, or why herd immunity depends on coverage, or what a restriction enzyme does and why sticky ends matter, if you only remember a label for each one. The longer note gives you the reasoning for those answers so that under time pressure you can reach for the reasoning rather than for a vague memory. That is the practical reason for the length, and it is the reason the extra appendices exist. If you study the note as a set of reasons and not as a set of labels, you get the benefit it was lengthened to provide.

One thing this extra length should not be used for is trying to memorise the note word for word. The note is meant to be a reference for revision, not a script. The parts worth remembering are the sequences, the distinctions and the reasoning patterns: for example, the synaptic sequence with calcium, the sliding filament sequence with ATP and calcium, the hormonal opposition in the insulin-glucagon system, the comparison pattern for nervous and hormonal coordination, and the principle-first order for gene technology. If you can remember enough of those to reconstruct a precise answer under time pressure, you have the note’s job done. If you try to recall the note verbatim, you are likely to lose time and lose precision, and the marks are in the precision, not in the recall.

That is also the reason the common mistakes section is there at the end. The mistakes are not there to be a list of trivia; they are there because they are the places where a reasonable candidate loses marks by being almost right in a way that is still wrong. If you can read the list and recognise the ones you are tempted toward, you can avoid them on the day, and that is often worth more than adding one more detail to a correct answer. The same is true of the exam-style questions at the end of the main body: they are there to show what a mark-scoring answer looks like for the kinds of question the specification actually asks, not to be memorised as a fixed set of answers. If you read them as models of reasoning and then try to produce the same kind of reasoning for a new question, you are using them the way they are meant to be used.

The final practical point about this pass is that the note should be checked against the specification statements after it is written, because a longer note can still be long in the wrong way if it drifts from the specification. The way to check is to take the specification and see whether each statement has a place in the note, and whether the note’s treatment of each statement is the kind of answer the specification rewards. If a statement is covered only by a label, that is the gap to fill. If a statement is covered by a reasoning sequence, that is usually the right level. If the note has become long by adding things the specification does not ask for, that is the part to cut. The note should be long enough to answer the specification questions, and not longer than that, because a note is a tool for revision, and a tool is only good if it is used well.

Appendix J — Long-answer practice built around the comparison and evaluation questions this topic actually sets

If you want to practise the questions this topic actually sets, the best way is to build your practice around the comparison and evaluation questions, because those are the ones where a correct but non-comparative or non-evaluative answer loses marks. For the nervous and hormonal comparison, practise until you can state the difference in speed, range and duration and give one concrete example of each in the same answer, because that is the kind of question that tests whether you can apply the two systems rather than just label them. For the primary and secondary response comparison, practise until you can say why the secondary response is faster and stronger and what memory cells do, and until you can link that to vaccination without making vaccination sound as if it does something separate from the immune response. For the plant and animal coordination comparison, practise until you can state that plants use hormones and growth while animals use nerves and muscles, without lapsing into the vague “plants are different” answer that does not earn the comparison marks.

For the evaluation questions, practise until you can give a benefit and an issue for each of the main technologies in the topic: vaccination, monoclonal antibodies, DNA profiling, gene therapy, GM crops and GM microorganisms, without repeating the same issue for every one. The point is not to generate a generic “it has issues” line and move on; it is to show that you can see the case specifically. For vaccination, the issue is often about coverage and public acceptance and the fact that not everyone can be vaccinated, rather than a vague “some people don’t like it.” For GM crops, the issue is often about gene flow and resistance and ownership, rather than a vague “it changes nature.” For gene therapy, the issue is often about delivery and about the difference between somatic and germ-line therapy, rather than a vague “it is unnatural.” If you can give a specific benefit and a specific issue for each technology, you can answer the evaluation question when it appears, and you can do it for more than one technology, which is what a real exam question will ask.

For the description questions, practise until you can produce the sequence and the mechanism in the right order without dropping the key step. For the synapse, that means not dropping calcium. For the muscle, that means not saying the filaments shorten. For the immune system, that means not blurring B and T cells into “immune cells” without a functional distinction. For the gene technology, that means not saying “PCR is used” without saying what it amplifies and how. If you can produce the sequence and the mechanism in the right order under time pressure, you are practising the description question in the way it needs to be practised, which is to say, as a sequence you can produce rather than as a fact you can recognise. The difference matters, because the exam asks you to produce the answer, not just to recognise it when you see it.

The last practice point is to practise under time, because a precise answer produced with unlimited time is not the same as a precise answer produced under exam time. Under time, the temptation is to shorten the answer until it becomes vague, and that is where marks are lost. The practice is therefore to set a timer, pick a question, and produce the precise answer without padding it, and then to check whether the answer has the one or two distinctions that are actually being marked. If it does, you are doing the question at the right level. If it is long but vague, you are not, and the practice needs to be on precision, not on length. The note is long so that you have enough material to practise from, but the exam answer has to be precise, not long, and that is the distinction to keep in mind when you practise.

title: Exam technique: Forces and Motion
content:
### What earns the marks
For resultant force, F = ma with substitution earns both marks. For moments, clockwise set equal to anticlockwise earns the method mark. For terminal velocity, balanced forces stated earns the explanation mark.
### Traps
Error: zero velocity taken as zero acceleration at the top of flight. Correction: g acts throughout. Error: one-sided moments only. Correction: equate both sides of the pivot. Error: weight and mass interchanged. Correction: weight is a force in newtons.
### Method marks
For a resultant force, use F = ma with the net force on the object. Find acceleration from the gradient of a velocity-time graph, and distance from the area under it. Show the substitution line before the answer.
### Explain, do not just name
At terminal velocity drag equals weight, so the resultant force is zero and the velocity stays constant. Saying "air resistance" without linking it to a zero resultant force loses the explanation mark.

title: Ethics, Security & Impact — Study Notes
content:
Ethics, Security & Impact

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): ethics & professional codes, security threats, malware, online safety, environmental/employment impact.

1. Ethics and codes

ACM/IEEE-CS/BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, privacy. Applying: identify the principle → apply to scenario → stakeholders affected → consequences.

2. Threats

  • Malware: virus (attaches, replicates via host), worm (self-spreads), trojan (disguised), spyware, ransomware.
  • Social: phishing (fake emails/sites), pharming (DNS/hosts redirect), shoulder surfing, brute force.
  • Technical: interception (packet sniffing), SQL injection (malicious input into queries), DoS (flooding services).

3. Defences

Antivirus/antispyware (scan, quarantine), firewalls (port/IP filtering), 2FA + biometrics, strong passwords + managers, encryption (HTTPS, VPN), access levels, patches/updates, user training.

4. Online behaviour

Digital footprint, cyberbullying, fake news, privacy settings, verification of sources.

5. Wider impact

Employment: automation displaces roles but creates IT jobs. Environment: e-waste, energy use vs paperless efficiency. Monitoring: workplace tracking, CCTV — balance with privacy laws (GDPR-style).

Exam tips: name the threat precisely (pharming ≠ phishing), then the matched defence; ethics answers need principle + application, not opinion.

title: Organic Chemistry: Halogenoalkanes, Alcohols and Spectra — Study Notes
content:
Organic Chemistry: Halogenoalkanes, Alcohols and Spectra

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 10. Halogenoalkanes and alcohols are the first families where a functional group changes the reactivity of the molecule. Spectra are the tools that identify those groups in an unknown compound.

Halogenoalkanes

  • A halogenoalkane has a halogen atom bonded to a carbon atom. The C–X bond is polar because the halogen is more electronegative, so the carbon is slightly positive.
  • Reactivity rises down the group because the C–X bond gets weaker (C–I is weakest), so the iodoalkane reacts fastest.
  • Nucleophilic substitution with aqueous hydroxide ions gives an alcohol. The nucleophile donates a pair of electrons to the carbon atom.
  • Halogenoalkanes can be tested by warming with aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol: the precipitate forms at different rates, and iodoalkanes react fastest.

Alcohols

  • Alcohols contain the –OH group. Primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols depend on how many other carbons are attached to the carbon bearing the –OH.
  • Oxidation of primary alcohols with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) gives aldehydes, which can be oxidised further to carboxylic acids; excess oxidant and heat give the acid.
  • Secondary alcohols oxidise to ketones; tertiary alcohols are not oxidised under these conditions.
  • Dehydration with hot concentrated sulfuric acid or aluminium oxide forms an alkene.

Mass spectrometry

  • The molecular ion peak gives the relative molecular mass. Fragmentation patterns reveal structural features.
  • Peaks at m/z 15 and 29 can indicate CH3 and C2H5 fragments.

Infrared spectroscopy

  • Bonds absorb infrared radiation at characteristic wavenumbers. A broad absorption near 3200–3550 cm⁻¹ indicates an O–H group in an alcohol. A strong absorption near 1700 cm⁻¹ indicates a C=O group.
  • Use tables of characteristic absorptions with the spectrum, rather than memorised single values.

NMR (introduced)

  • The number of peaks in a proton NMR spectrum gives the number of environments of hydrogen atoms; the relative areas give the ratio of hydrogens.

Exam tip: when identifying an unknown, combine evidence: the molecular formula from mass spectrometry, the functional groups from infrared, and the environments from NMR.

title: Motion in a Circle and Gravity — Study Notes
content:
Motion in a circle and gravity

Circular motion

  • A body moving in a circle at constant speed has a centripetal acceleration of v²/r, directed towards the centre.
  • The centripetal force is F = mv²/r = mω²r, and it is provided by a real force such as tension, friction or gravity. It does no work on the body, because it is always perpendicular to the velocity.

Gravitational field

The gravitational field strength at a point is the force per unit mass placed at that point: g = F/m. Unit: N kg⁻¹. Field lines point towards the mass that creates the field.

Newton's law of gravitation

F = GMm/r², where r is measured from the centre of each point mass. Doubling the separation reduces the force to one quarter.

Gravitational field of a point mass

g = GM/r². Outside a uniform sphere, its field is the same as that of a point mass at its centre.

Gravitational potential

Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a small mass from infinity to that point. It is always negative, is zero at infinity, and becomes more negative closer to the mass: V = −GM/r. Gravitational potential energy of a mass m is Ep = mV.

Worked example: a 2.0 kg object moves in a circle of radius 0.50 m at 3.0 m s⁻¹. The centripetal force is F = mv²/r = (2.0 × 3.0²) ÷ 0.50 = 36 N.

Exam tips: use r as the distance from the centre, not the surface. State that gravitational potential is negative and rises to zero at infinity. Field strength and potential are different quantities: do not mix their units.

Gravitational potential and escape velocity

Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in moving a small mass from infinity to that point, so φ = -GM/r. Potential is negative because work must be done against gravity to remove a mass to infinity. The change in gravitational potential energy between two radii is GMm(1/r1 - 1/r2). A body escapes a planet when its kinetic energy equals the potential energy needed to reach infinity, which gives the escape speed v = √(2GM/r).

Exam tip: use the zero of potential at infinity, and keep the sign of the potential negative in every calculation.

Worked example: orbital speed and period

A satellite of mass m orbits a planet of mass M at radius r. Gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r). The orbital period follows from T = 2πr/v, which gives T² = (4π²/GM) r³. This is Kepler's third law in the form used at AS level.

Example: a satellite at radius 7.0 × 10⁶ m around a planet of mass 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg. The speed is v = √((6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6.0 × 10²⁴)/(7.0 × 10⁶)) = √(5.7 × 10⁷) ≈ 7.6 × 10³ m s⁻¹. The period is T = 2π × 7.0 × 10⁶ / 7.6 × 10³ ≈ 5.8 × 10³ s, about 97 minutes.

Geostationary orbit

A geostationary satellite has a period of exactly 24 hours and orbits in the equatorial plane. Its radius is fixed by the period, so every geostationary satellite has the same radius and speed, regardless of its mass. Its orbit must lie above the equator, which is why communication satellites sit over one point on the ground.

Why orbiting bodies are weightless

Astronauts in orbit are not outside the pull of gravity; gravity supplies their centripetal acceleration. The spacecraft and its occupants fall freely together, so there is no contact force, and the apparent weightlessness follows from that free fall.

Circular motion: banked roads and conical pendulums

On a banked road with no friction, the horizontal component of the normal reaction supplies the centripetal force: N sin θ = mv²/r, while the vertical component balances weight: N cos θ = mg. Dividing gives tan θ = v²/(rg). The design speed depends only on the angle, the radius and g, not on the mass of the vehicle.

  • For a conical pendulum, tension has a vertical component that balances weight and a horizontal component that supplies the centripetal force.
  • Always draw a free-body diagram and resolve forces into components along the radius and the vertical before writing equations.
  • The centripetal force is not an extra force on the diagram; name the real forces that supply it.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Including centripetal force as a separate force in the free-body diagram, which double-counts the force.
  • Using the planet's surface radius where the question gives the distance from the centre, or the reverse.
  • Stating that the satellite is stationary in orbit. It is moving at constant speed, so its velocity changes direction continuously and it is accelerating.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): kinetic particle model; thermal expansion; specific heat capacity; melting/boiling; conduction, convection, radiation.

1. Kinetic model

Solid: fixed positions, vibrate — fixed shape/volume. Liquid: move around, touching — fixed volume, flows. Gas: far apart, fast random motion — fills container. Brownian motion evidences random molecular motion.

2. Gas pressure and temperature

Pressure from wall collisions. Heating at fixed volume → faster particles → more frequent, harder collisions → higher pressure.

3. Thermal expansion

Heating → particles vibrate more → solids expand slightly (gases expand most). Applications: bimetallic strip (fire alarm/thermostat), gaps in bridges/rails; the liquid-in-glass thermometer.

4. Specific heat capacity

c = ΔE/(mΔθ). Heating: ΔE = mcΔθ.

Example: 2 kg water (c = 4200), 20→80 °C: ΔE = 2×4200×60 = 504 kJ.

High c of water → coolant; temperature rise measured with known heater power P in time t: c = Pt/(mΔθ).

5. State changes

Melting/boiling at fixed temperature despite heating (energy breaks bonds, not temperature). Condensation/ freezing release energy. Impurities raise melting point of mixtures/lower freezing; boiling needs nucleation.

6. Transfer: conduction, convection, radiation

  • Conduction: mainly metals (delocalised electrons + lattice vibration); non-metals poor; insulators trap air.
  • Convection: hot fluid expands, density falls, rises; denser cool fluid sinks — currents.
  • Radiation: infrared EM waves; no medium; matte black best absorber/emitter, shiny silver worst.

Applications: vacuum flask, house insulation, car radiators, solar heating panels.

title: Differentiation — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation

Basic Rules

  • d/dx (xⁿ) = n xⁿ⁻¹
  • d/dx (k) = 0, d/dx (kx) = k

Example: y = 5x² − 3x gives dy/dx = 10x − 3.

Chain Rule

dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx.

Example: y = (3x − 1)⁵: dy/dx = 5(3x − 1)⁴ × 3 = 15(3x − 1)⁴.

Tangents and Normals

The tangent gradient at a point is dy/dx there; the normal gradient is −1/(dy/dx).

Example: y = x² at (2, 4): tangent y = 4x − 4; normal has gradient −1/4.

Stationary Points

Set dy/dx = 0, then classify with the second derivative:

  • d²y/dx² > 0 → minimum
  • d²y/dx² < 0 → maximum
  • d²y/dx² = 0 → test either side

Example: y = x³ − 3x: dy/dx = 3x² − 3 = 0 at x = ±1; d²y/dx² = 6x, so a maximum at x = −1 and a minimum at x = 1.

Rates of Change

dy/dx is a rate: if V = 4/3 πr³, then dV/dr = 4πr² links volume change to radius change.

Exam tips: always restart gradients from the derivative at the exact point, and answer rate questions with units.

Rules and exam method

For y = axⁿ, dy/dx = naxⁿ⁻¹. Differentiate each term of a polynomial separately; a constant term differentiates to zero. Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers first: √x = x^(1/2) and 1/x² = x⁻².

Product rule: d/dx(uv) = u dv/dx + v du/dx. Quotient rule: d/dx(u/v) = (v du/dx − u dv/dx)/v². Chain rule: dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx. For (ax + b)ⁿ the result is na(ax + b)ⁿ⁻¹.

Stationary points occur where dy/dx = 0. Classify them by the sign of dy/dx either side of the point, or with d²y/dx²: positive gives a minimum, negative a maximum, and zero means use the sign change. The gradient at a point gives the tangent; the normal has the negative reciprocal gradient.

Exam cue: Give the tangent or normal as y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), or simplified to y = mx + c, as the question asks. Check it by substituting the point back into the line.

title: Exam technique: Indices and Standard Form
content:
### What earns the marks
For index laws, each law applied on its own line earns credit: subtract for division, multiply for powers of powers. For fractional powers, the root-first order (cube root, then square) stated earns the method mark. For standard form, the coefficient between 1 and 10 with the power justified by the point shift earns both marks. For surds, the split into square factor times prime remainder earns the method mark, and rationalising must finish simplified.
### Traps
Error: (x to the 5th / x squared) cubed answered x to the 6th. Correction: inner subtraction first, then multiply powers. Error: 27 x 2/3 for 27 to the 2/3. Correction: root, then power. Error: unsimplified 6 root 3 / 3 accepted as final. Correction: always cancel to 2 root 3. Error: non-standard-form coefficients (45 x 10 to the -5). Correction: one non-zero digit, then fix the power.

title: Sampling and Estimation — Study Notes
content:
Sampling and Estimation

Populations, Samples, Statistics

A parameter describes the population (μ, σ²); a statistic describes the sample (x̄, s²). A statistic is unbiased if its expectation equals the population parameter: E(x̄) = μ always holds for the sample mean.

Unbiased Variance

The estimator with divisor (n − 1) is the unbiased sample variance:

  • s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)

Why n − 1: deviations are measured from x̄ rather than μ, slightly underestimating spread; the smaller divisor corrects it. At A2, state which estimator you are using — the unbiased one is the default.

Distribution of the Sample Mean

For a sample of size n from a population with mean μ and variance σ²:

  • E(x̄) = μ and Var(x̄) = σ²/n

Averaging shrinks spread — bigger samples give steadier estimates.

Central Limit Theorem

Whatever the population shape, for large n (rule of thumb n ≥ 30) the sample mean is approximately normal: x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n). This is why the normal appears constantly in inference.

Example: population mean 50, s.d. 12, n = 36. Then x̄ ~ N(50, 4) and P(x̄ > 51) = P(Z > 0.5) = 0.3085.

Using x̄ to Estimate

Given sample data, estimate μ by x̄ and σ² by the unbiased s². When the population is normal, x̄ is exactly normal for any n — the CLT is only needed for non-normal populations.

Exam tips: distinguish σ²/σ (population) from s²/s (sample) in notation. Standard error means √(σ²/n) — smaller with larger n. Quote probabilities for x̄ with the variance divided by n; forgetting that division is the classic error.

title: Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes — Study Notes
content:
Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 4. Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. Alkanes are the simplest family, and their reactions introduce the radical substitution mechanism used throughout the course.

Naming and formulae

  • A homologous series has the same general formula, similar chemical properties and a gradual change in physical properties.
  • Alkanes have the general formula CnH2n+2. Names depend on the longest carbon chain: meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex-.
  • Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different connectivity, such as butane and methylpropane.

Fossil fuels and cracking

  • Alkanes are obtained from crude oil by fractional distillation; the fractions separate by boiling point, which rises with chain length.
  • Cracking breaks long chains into shorter, more useful alkanes and alkenes, using heat or a catalyst.

Radical substitution

  • Alkanes react with chlorine or bromine under UV light by free-radical substitution.
  • The three stages are initiation (Cl2 → 2Cl•), propagation (a radical reacts with an alkane, regenerating a radical) and termination (two radicals combine).
  • Propagation steps form the product; termination steps are rare, so they do not appear in the main yield.

Combustion

  • Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water; limited oxygen gives carbon monoxide or carbon (soot).

Exam tip: when writing a radical mechanism, use a single-headed arrow for each electron moved and always show the radical dot.

title: Integration — Study Notes
content:
Integration

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Integration reverses differentiation. Questions want a general antiderivative, a specific curve through a point, a definite integral, or an area. Most lost marks come from the constant of integration, the limits, and the sign of a region below the axis.

Start from a question

A curve passes through (1, 1) and has dy/dx = 3√x − 2/x² for x > 0.

  1. Find y in terms of x.
  2. Evaluate the integral of (3√x − 2/x²) from x = 1 to x = 4.
  3. Find the area between the curve y = x² − 4 and the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 3.

Part 1. Integrate term by term: 3x^(1/2) gives 2x^(3/2), and −2x⁻² gives 2x⁻¹. So y = 2x^(3/2) + 2/x + c. Substituting (1, 1) gives 2 + 2 + c = 1, so c = −3 and y = 2x^(3/2) + 2/x − 3.

Part 2. The antiderivative at 4 is 16 + ½ = 33/2. At 1 it is 4 = 8/2. The definite integral is 33/2 − 8/2 = 25/2. No +c is needed.

Part 3. The curve y = x² − 4 crosses the x-axis at x = 2. Between 0 and 2 it lies below the axis, so that part of the integral is negative. The area is |∫ from 0 to 2| + ∫ from 2 to 3. The first integral is [x³/3 − 4x] from 0 to 2 = −16/3, so its area is 16/3. The second is [x³/3 − 4x] from 2 to 3 = −3 − (−16/3) = 7/3. The total is 23/3. Taking the integral from 0 to 3 directly gives −3, which is the wrong answer for an area.

Indefinite integrals

∫axⁿ dx = a xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c, for n ≠ −1. Add one to the power, divide by the new power, and write +c. Multiply out brackets and rewrite roots as powers first. Example: ∫(x − 2)(x + 4) dx = ∫(x² + 2x − 8) dx = x³/3 + x² − 8x + c.

Area between two curves

Find where the curves meet, then integrate the upper curve minus the lower curve between those x-values. Example: y = 2x and y = x² meet at x = 0 and x = 2. Between them 2x ≥ x², so the area is ∫ from 0 to 2 of (2x − x²) dx = [x² − x³/3] from 0 to 2 = 4/3.

Trapezium rule

With strips of width h and ordinates y₀, y₁, …, yₙ, the estimate is (h/2)[y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ]. Example: ∫ from 0 to 2 of (x² + 1) dx with h = 1. The ordinates are 1, 2 and 5, so the estimate is ½(1 + 4 + 5) = 5. The exact value is 14/3. The curve bends upwards, so the estimate is too large.

Traps that cost marks

  • Integrating a product term by term without expanding the brackets first.
  • Writing +c in a definite integral, or forgetting it in an indefinite one.
  • Subtracting the limits in the wrong order.
  • Quoting a negative answer for an area that lies below the x-axis.

Worked example: a definite integral

Evaluate the integral of (2x + 1) from x = 1 to x = 3. The indefinite integral is x² + x, so the value is [x² + x] between 1 and 3, which is (9 + 3) − (1 + 1) = 12 − 2 = 10. The constant of integration cancels when the limits are substituted, so it is not written in a definite integral. Substitute the upper limit first and subtract the lower limit, and do not evaluate the two ends separately and then add them.

Worked example: integrating a linear bracket

The integral of (2x + 1)³ with respect to x is (2x + 1)⁴ ÷ 8 + c. You can check this by differentiating: the chain rule gives 4 × 2 × (2x + 1)³ ÷ 8, which equals (2x + 1)³. Dividing by the derivative of the inside, here 2, is the reverse of the chain rule and is the quick method to use in the exam.

title: Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules — Study Notes
content:
Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): area formula, sine rule, cosine rule, multi-step bearing and 3-D problems (Extended).

1. Area of a triangle

A = ½ab sin C (C = included angle between sides a and b).

Example: a = 8, b = 5, C = 48° → A = ½ × 8 × 5 × sin 48° = 14.8.

2. Sine rule

a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use when a matching angle–side pair is known.

Example: A = 40°, a = 7, B = 65°: b = 7 sin 65°/sin 40° = 9.98.

Ambiguous case: two triangles possible when finding an angle — check the obtuse option (180° − θ).

3. Cosine rule

a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A. Use with two sides + included angle, or all three sides (then cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc)).

Example: b = 7, c = 5, A = 52°: a² = 74 − 70 cos 52° = 30.9 → a = 5.56.

4. Bearing problems

Draw both north lines, transfer angles via parallel lines, then pick sine/cosine rule.

Example: QP = 60 km bearing 070° from Q; QR = 45 km bearing 150°. ∠PQR = 80° → PR² = 60² + 45² − 2·60·45 cos 80° → PR = 68.4 km.

5. 3-D trigonometry

Identify the plane containing the required angle; use 3-D Pythagoras d² = x² + y² + z² for space diagonals; angle between a line and a plane uses the projection onto the plane.

Exam tips: state which rule you are using and why; sketch a separate 2-D triangle for 3-D questions; answers to 3 s.f. / bearings as three digits.

The point of the comparison is not to copy the model answer word for word, but to see whether your answer has the same sequence, the same distinctions and the same reasoning. If it does, you are ready for that question. If it does not, the gap is the thing to practise.

For the nervous and hormonal comparison, the practice answer should say that nervous coordination uses electrical impulses along neurones and produces fast, specific responses, with a reflex or voluntary movement as the example; that hormonal coordination uses hormones in the blood acting on target cells with the right receptors, and produces responses that are often slower, longer-lasting and more widespread, with growth, metabolism or reproduction as the example; and that both are needed because different jobs need different speeds, ranges and durations. If your answer has those three points, it has the comparison. If it only says “nerves are fast and hormones are slow” without range, duration, specificity or an example, it has the label but not the comparison the mark is really after. The note’s appendix on the comparison is there to make that sequence explicit, so use it as the model for your own practice answer rather than as something to memorise.

For the primary and secondary response comparison, the practice answer should say that the primary response is slower because the specific lymphocytes have to be activated and expanded, and that the secondary response is faster and stronger because memory cells from the first exposure are already present. It should then link that to vaccination by saying that vaccination primes the immune system with the antigen without causing the disease, so that memory cells are produced and the body is ready for real exposure. If your answer has those points, it has the comparison and the link. If it only says “the second time is faster,” it has the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning, not the label. If it treats vaccination as a separate magic trick instead of a priming of the same memory system, it has lost the link that the question is really asking for.

For the plant and animal coordination comparison, the practice answer should say that animals coordinate with nerves and hormones and use muscles for rapid, specific movement, while plants coordinate with hormones and growth and have no nerves or muscles, so their responses are slower and often involve bending, with phototropism or gravitropism as the example and auxins as the hormone. If your answer has those points, it has the comparison. If it only says “plants do not have nerves,” it has the label but not the comparison, because the comparison is about the way the two systems work, not just about the absence of one part in plants. If it treats plant coordination as if it were plant nervous coordination by another name, it has lost the distinction that the mark is really after.

For the evaluation questions, the practice answer should give a benefit and an issue for each technology without repeating the same issue in every case. For vaccination, the benefit is protection of the individual and, at high coverage, the population through herd immunity, and the issue is around coverage, exemptions, side effects and public acceptance. For monoclonal antibodies, the benefit is specificity and scale in diagnosis, research and therapy, and the issue is around cost, access and the limits of any one antibody for every case. For DNA profiling, the benefit is identification and exclusion and the establishment of biological relationships, and the issue is around sample quality, contamination, chain of custody and the interpretation of the result in context. For gene therapy, the benefit is the possibility of correcting or compensating for a faulty gene, and the issue is around delivery, the difference between somatic and germ-line therapy, and the ethics of heritable change. For GM crops and GM microorganisms, the benefit is the specific aim such as a useful protein, pest resistance, herbicide tolerance or nutrition, and the issue is around gene flow, non-target effects, resistance, ownership, labelling and consumer choice. If your answer has a specific benefit and a specific issue for each technology, it has the evaluation. If it has only a generic “it has issues” line, it has the label but not the evaluation, and the mark is in the specificity, not the slogan.

If your answer has the same sequence and the same distinctions, it is ready. If it has the sequence but misses a distinction, that distinction is the thing to practise. If it has the distinction but not the sequence, the sequence is the thing to practise. The connections are worth saying explicitly, because that is what the cross-chunk questions test. Muscles and the internal environment connect through the fact that muscle work produces heat, carbon dioxide and water and stresses the balance, so the internal environment has to respond. If you can produce the three answers in the time, you are practising the right condition. If you can only produce them without time, you are practising a different condition, and that is the gap that the exam will expose. For each technique, cover the note and write the principle and the purpose in your own words: what it does and why it is done. For restriction enzymes, that is cutting at specific recognition sequences and, for some cuts, leaving sticky ends that match with another piece cut with the same enzyme so they can be ligated. For PCR, that is amplifying a specific sequence in vitro through repeated cycles, with the primers defining the target and the heat-stable polymerase surviving the repeated heating. For gel electrophoresis, that is separating fragments by size in an electric field, with DNA moving toward the positive electrode and smaller fragments moving faster. For probing, that is using a labelled complementary sequence to detect a specific fragment by hybridisation. If you can only recognise the technique when you see the label, you are not yet ready, and the self-test is the way to get ready.

The final self-test point is to use the typical mistakes section as a checklist rather than as a list to read once. Before you write each answer, run it against the mistakes that apply to that question, because that is the fastest way to catch the errors that lose marks most often. If you are writing a muscle answer, check that you did not say the filaments shorten. If you are writing a respiration answer, check that you did not say ATP is made directly by the chain. If you are writing a coordination answer, check that you did not say the nervous system is slow and diffuse. If you are writing a gene technology answer, check that you did not say restriction enzymes cut at random or that PCR copies the whole genome. If you can run the checklist against your answer before you finish, you catch the most common marks-losing errors, and that is often worth more than adding one more detail to a correct answer. The checklist is there to be used, not just to be read.

title: Exam technique: Probability (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For conditional probability, the restricted sample space stated earns the method mark. For independence checks, P(A)P(B) compared with P(A and B) earns both marks. For Bayes-style updates, the tree fractions multiplied along branches earn stepwise credit.
### Traps
Error: mutually exclusive assumed independent. Correction: test, never assume. Error: given-condition ignored. Correction: shrink the denominator first. Error: branches added instead of multiplied. Correction: multiply along, add across.

title: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table — Study Notes
content:
Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 2. The periodic table is not a list to memorise: its rows and columns follow directly from how electrons fill shells and sub-shells.

Atoms, isotopes and mass spectrometry

  • Protons and neutrons make up the nucleus; the mass number is protons plus neutrons, and the atomic number is the number of protons.
  • Isotopes have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons, so the same chemistry but a different mass.
  • Relative atomic mass is the weighted mean of isotopic masses. In a mass spectrum, abundance is read from the peak heights.

Electron configuration

  • Electrons fill orbitals in order of energy: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d and so on, each orbital holding at most two electrons with opposite spins.
  • Write configurations such as 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ for neon; for transition metals the 4s electrons are lost before the 3d electrons when forming ions.

Periodic trends

  • Ionisation energy increases across a period because nuclear charge rises with similar shielding, and falls down a group as the outer electrons sit further from the nucleus.
  • Atomic radius falls across a period and rises down a group.
  • Successive ionisation energies reveal the group of an element: a large jump appears after the outer-shell electrons are removed.

Electron arrangement and the table

  • Period number = highest principal quantum number in use; group number relates to the number of outer electrons.
  • Blocks: s-block (groups 1-2), p-block (groups 13-18), d-block (transition metals).

Exam tip: when explaining an ionisation energy trend, name the factor (nuclear charge, shielding, distance) and say which way it changes.

title: Sequences and Series — Study Notes
content:
Sequences and series

An arithmetic progression (AP) adds a constant difference d each term; a geometric progression (GP) multiplies by a constant ratio r. You must master both closed forms, their sums, and the conditions for an infinite sum.

Arithmetic progression

  • nth term: a_n = a + (n - 1)d.
  • Sum: S_n = n/2 [2a + (n - 1)d] = n/2 (first + last).
  • The difference between consecutive terms is constant: a_{n+1} - a_n = d.

Geometric progression

  • nth term: a_n = a r^(n - 1).
  • Sum: S_n = a(r^n - 1)/(r - 1) = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r).
  • Sum to infinity: S_inf = a/(1 - r), valid ONLY when |r| < 1.

Sigma notation

  • sum of r from 1 to n = n(n + 1)/2; sum of r^2 = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6; sum of r^3 = [n(n + 1)/2]^2.
  • sum of a constant c over n terms is cn.
  • Split sums: sum (3r + 1) = 3 sum r + sum 1.

Modelling

  • Arithmetic: hire charges, stacked rows, simple interest.
  • Geometric: depreciation, compound interest, population growth, drug decay.
  • For repeated percentage change, multiplier = (1 + percentage/100) per period.

Exam technique

  • Write the first few terms before committing to a formula.
  • Check the sum formula by substituting n = 1 and n = 2.
  • For 'sum exceeds X' questions solve the inequality and take the first integer.

title: Number — Arithmetic and Place Value — Study Notes
content:
Number — Arithmetic and Place Value

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): 1.1 integers & place value; 1.2 fractions/decimals/percentages context; 1.3 powers & roots; HCF/LCM.

1. Types of number

  • Integers: … −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 … Primes: exactly two factors; 2 is the only even prime; 1 is not prime.
  • HCF = product of common prime factors (lowest powers); LCM = all prime factors (highest powers).

Example: 60 = 2²×3×5 and 84 = 2²×3×7 ⇒ HCF = 2²×3 = 12; LCM = 2²×3×5×7 = 420.

2. Place value

In 47 382 the digit 7 has value 7000. Rounding to significant figures: keep n digits, round using the next digit (≥5 up).

Estimation: round inputs to 1 s.f. first — 39.2 × 5.98 ≈ 40 × 6 = 240.

3. Order of operations

BIDMAS. 3 + 4 × 2² = 3 + 16 = 19. Insert brackets yourself when translating words: "3 added to the product of 4 and 2²" = 3 + (4 × 2²).

4. Negative numbers and calculators

Bracket negatives when substituting. Know the ×10ˣ, x², √, ˣ√ and fraction keys; give answers to 3 s.f. unless told otherwise.

5. Bounds (Extended)

Measured to nearest u: UB = +u/2, LB = −u/2. Division p/q: max = UBp ÷ LBq.

Example: 45 cm (nearest cm) in 6 s (nearest s): max speed = 45.5 ÷ 5.5 = 8.27 m/s (3 s.f.).

Exam tips: show prime-factor trees for HCF/LCM; always state rounding units (3 s.f., 1 d.p.); bounds answers quote both limits.

title: Exam technique: Measures of Variation
content:
### What earns the marks
For standard deviation, mean first then the squared-deviation sum earns each mark. For coded data, the y-bar and s_y transformation earns the method mark. For comparisons, mean and spread commented together earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: variance reported as sd. Correction: root last. Error: comparing means only. Correction: comment on spread too. Error: coding applied once then forgotten. Correction: transform consistently.
### Worked example
Five values are 2, 4, 4, 6 and 9. The mean is 25 / 5 = 5. The squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 1 and 16, which sum to 28. The variance is 28 / 5 = 5.6, and the standard deviation is the square root, about 2.37. Show the squared deviations line on the paper, since the method mark depends on it.
### Check yourself
If each value in the list is increased by 10, state what happens to the mean and to the standard deviation. The mean rises by 10, while the standard deviation is unchanged, because adding a constant does not change the spread.

### Worked example
Five values are 2, 4, 4, 6 and 9. The mean is 25 / 5 = 5. The squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 1 and 16, which sum to 28. The variance is 28 / 5 = 5.6, and the standard deviation is the square root, about 2.37. Show the squared deviations line on the paper, since the method mark depends on it.

title: Motion in a Circle and Gravity — Study Notes
content:
Motion in a circle and gravity

Circular motion

  • A body moving in a circle at constant speed has a centripetal acceleration of v²/r, directed towards the centre.
  • The centripetal force is F = mv²/r = mω²r, and it is provided by a real force such as tension, friction or gravity. It does no work on the body, because it is always perpendicular to the velocity.

Gravitational field

The gravitational field strength at a point is the force per unit mass placed at that point: g = F/m. Unit: N kg⁻¹. Field lines point towards the mass that creates the field.

Newton's law of gravitation

F = GMm/r², where r is measured from the centre of each point mass. Doubling the separation reduces the force to one quarter.

Gravitational field of a point mass

g = GM/r². Outside a uniform sphere, its field is the same as that of a point mass at its centre.

Gravitational potential

Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a small mass from infinity to that point. It is always negative, is zero at infinity, and becomes more negative closer to the mass: V = −GM/r. Gravitational potential energy of a mass m is Ep = mV.

Worked example: a 2.0 kg object moves in a circle of radius 0.50 m at 3.0 m s⁻¹. The centripetal force is F = mv²/r = (2.0 × 3.0²) ÷ 0.50 = 36 N.

Exam tips: use r as the distance from the centre, not the surface. State that gravitational potential is negative and rises to zero at infinity. Field strength and potential are different quantities: do not mix their units.

Gravitational potential and escape velocity

Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in moving a small mass from infinity to that point, so φ = -GM/r. Potential is negative because work must be done against gravity to remove a mass to infinity. The change in gravitational potential energy between two radii is GMm(1/r1 - 1/r2). A body escapes a planet when its kinetic energy equals the potential energy needed to reach infinity, which gives the escape speed v = √(2GM/r).

Exam tip: use the zero of potential at infinity, and keep the sign of the potential negative in every calculation.

title: Abstract Data Types — Study Notes
content:
Abstract Data Types

What is an ADT?

An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Linked Lists

Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node; a start pointer marks the head and a null marks the end. Insertion rewires two pointers — no shifting — giving O(1) insertion at a known position, but access requires walking the list, O(n).

Stacks and Queues

A stack is LIFO (push and pop at the top); a queue is FIFO (enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front). Both can be arrays with index pointers or linked lists. Stack uses include call stacks and expression evaluation; queue uses include print buffers and breadth-first search.

Binary Search Trees

Each node has up to two children; left subtree keys are smaller, right subtree keys larger. Search, insert and (average-case) delete are O(log n). An in-order traversal outputs keys in ascending order. A degenerate (linear) tree from sorted input degrades to O(n).

Hash Tables

Covered in file organisation, but as an ADT a hash table pairs a hash function with bucket storage for O(1) average access.

Exam tips: be able to draw a tree after a sequence of insertions and write its three traversals; state the pointer changes for a linked-list insertion; compare ADT operations with Big-O.

title: Probability and Statistics II
content:
Probability and Statistics II

Normal Distribution

Continuous, bell-shaped, defined by mean μ and variance σ². Standardise: Z = (X − μ)/σ ~ N(0, 1).

Example: X ~ N(50, 4²). P(X > 56) = P(Z > 1.5) = 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668.

Backwards problems: given a probability, find μ or σ from the z-value: x = μ + zσ.

Binomial Distribution

Fixed n independent trials, success probability p: P(X = r) = C(n, r) pʳ (1−p)^(n−r). Mean np, variance np(1 − p).

Example: n = 5, p = 0.2: P(X = 2) = 10 × 0.04 × 0.8³ = 0.2048.

Normal Approximation to Binomial

Valid when np > 5 and n(1 − p) > 5. Apply a continuity correction: P(X ≤ 10) becomes P(Y < 10.5) under Y ~ N(np, np(1−p)).

Expectation and Variance Rules

E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b; Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X). For sums: E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y).

Exam tips: always sketch the normal curve and shade the region; state the distribution you are using; never forget the continuity correction when approximating a discrete variable.

title: Exam technique: Scatter Diagrams
content:
### What earns the marks
For correlation, direction (rising or falling) and strength (tight or spread) each earn a mark: comment on both. For lines of best fit, the mean point plotted first earns the method mark. For estimation questions, naming interpolation versus extrapolation earns a mark before any value, with the reliability comment credited separately.
### Traps
Error: claiming correlation proves causation. Correction: name the confounder (hot weather drives both). Error: trusting extrapolation like interpolation. Correction: outside the range is always less reliable. Error: forcing the line through the origin. Correction: anchor at (mean x, mean y). Error: calling curved association zero correlation. Correction: zero means no pattern at all.
### Worked example
A scatter diagram shows a positive correlation between hours revised and test score. The line of best fit passes through the mean point (x̄, ȳ). If x̄ = 5 and ȳ = 12 with gradient 2, the line is y = 2x + 2. Estimating y for x = 8 is interpolation if 8 lies within the data range, which makes it more reliable than extrapolating beyond the data.
### Check yourself
Explain why the line of best fit should pass through (x̄, ȳ). Check that 2 × 5 + 2 = 12, so the line does pass through the mean point. State whether a prediction at x = 20 would be interpolation or extrapolation, and say why it is less reliable.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate geometry of circles

At A2, coordinate geometry centres on the circle: its equation, tangents, normals and the interaction with straight lines.

Circle equations

  • Centre (a, b), radius r: (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2.
  • General form x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (-g, -f) and radius sqrt(g^2 + f^2 - c).
  • Always complete the square to find centre and radius.

Tangents and normals

  • The tangent at a point is perpendicular to the radius at that point: gradient of tangent = -1 / (gradient of radius).
  • The normal at a point passes through the centre (it is the radius line extended).
  • For the circle x^2 + y^2 = r^2, the tangent at (x1, y1) is x x1 + y y1 = r^2.

Line and circle

  • Substituting a line into the circle gives a quadratic: two roots = two intersections (secant), one repeated root = tangent, no real roots = no intersection.
  • Tangency condition: the perpendicular distance from the centre to the line equals the radius.
  • Distance from (x0, y0) to ax + by + c = 0 is |ax0 + by0 + c| / sqrt(a^2 + b^2).

Tangent from an external point

The length of a tangent from an external point P to a circle is sqrt(d^2 - r^2), where d is the distance from P to the centre.

title: Hypothesis Testing — Quick Revision Summary

Quick revision: Hypothesis Testing

Mathematics — A2. The null hypothesis H₀ is the default claim (no change, p = p₀). The alternative H₁ is what a suspicious observation suggests (p > p₀, p < p₀, or p ≠ p₀). The significance level α is the probability of rejecting a true H₀ — the false-alarm rate, usually 5% or 1%.

Key areas to revise

  • The Framework
  • Test for a Binomial Proportion
  • One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed
  • Critical Regions
  • Conclusions in Context

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A test of a claimed mean has a null hypothesis H₀ and an alternative H₁. Choose a significance level such as 5%, calculate the test statistic and its p-value, then reject H₀ if p < α. A two-tailed test looks for a change in either direction, so the 5% is split between the two tails. ### Check yourself Define a Type I error in words. It is rejecting H₀ when H₀ is actually true. Explain why lowering the significance level reduces the chance of a Type I error but increases the chance of a Type II error. ### Worked example A test of a claimed mean has a null hypothesis H₀ and an alternative H₁. Choose a significance level such as 5%, calculate the test statistic and its p-value, then reject H₀ if p < α. A two-tailed test looks for a change in either direction, so the 5% is split between the two tails.

title: Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria — Study Notes
content:
Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 9. Kinetics asks how fast a reaction goes, and equilibria asks how far it goes before the forward and backward reactions balance. Both depend on the same collision ideas.

Rates and collision theory

  • For a reaction to occur, particles must collide with enough energy (the activation energy, Ea) and in the correct orientation.
  • Increasing concentration or pressure increases the frequency of collisions. Increasing temperature raises the proportion of particles with energy above Ea, which has a larger effect than the increase in collision frequency.
  • A catalyst provides an alternative route with a lower Ea; it is not used up.

Measuring rates

  • Rates can be found from the gradient of a concentration–time graph at the start of the reaction (the initial rate).
  • Methods include measuring the volume of gas produced, the change in mass, or the time for a colour change to occur (1/time gives a relative rate).

Dynamic equilibrium

  • In a closed system, the forward and reverse rates become equal. Concentrations stop changing, but the reaction has not stopped.
  • Equilibrium constant Kc = [products]^n / [reactants]^m, with each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient. Kc is constant for a given temperature.

Le Chatelier's principle

  • If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the position shifts to oppose the change.
  • Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction. Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules. Adding a reactant shifts the position towards products.
  • A catalyst speeds up both directions equally, so it changes the rate of reaching equilibrium but not the equilibrium position or Kc.

Exam tip: say which direction is favoured and why, using the principle. Do not claim that a catalyst increases the yield.

title: Exam technique: Sampling
content:
### What earns the marks
For method choice, random vs stratified vs systematic justified earns the mark. For stratified allocation, the proportion of each stratum applied earns the method mark. For bias discussion, the named source of bias with its effect earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: sample claimed unbiased with no method. Correction: name and justify the method. Error: equal numbers per stratum. Correction: allocate proportionally. Error: population confused with frame. Correction: frame is the list used.

title: Poisson Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Poisson Distribution

The Model

X ~ Po(λ) counts events in a fixed interval of time or space when events occur independently, at a constant average rate λ, and never twice at the same instant. Classic settings: calls per hour at a helpdesk, typos per page, cars per minute at a quiet junction.

The Formula

P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ / r! for r = 0, 1, 2, ...

Example: X ~ Po(2). P(X = 0) = e⁻² ≈ 0.1353. P(X = 1) = 2e⁻² ≈ 0.2707.

Mean and Variance

The defining signature of the Poisson:

  • E(X) = λ and Var(X) = λ — the mean and variance are equal.

If a question gives a mean m, then λ = m; the variance is also m.

Scaling the Interval

If X ~ Po(λ) per hour, then 3 hours gives Y ~ Po(3λ). Rates must be adjusted to the same interval before computing anything. Halving an interval halves λ.

Adding Poissons

If X ~ Po(λ₁) and Y ~ Po(λ₂) are independent, then X + Y ~ Po(λ₁ + λ₂). Two independent queues merging into one server produce a Poisson with summed rate.

Exam tips: check independence and constant rate before modelling — if events cluster (rush hours), Poisson fails. Convert the interval first: a rate of 8 per 20 minutes becomes 24 per hour. In "at least" questions use the complement exactly as with the binomial.
